Summarizing leaves the discounted sum of temporal differences.
\[
\boxed{\,v(s_t)=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\,\Big|\,\mathcal F_t\Big]+v(s_t),\qquad d_k:=r(s_k,\pi(s_k))+\gamma v(s_{k+1})-v(s_k).\,}
\]
↓ Down: Section 6.2.1 · Section 6.2.2 · Section 6.2.3 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.2.1 ✍ Derivation one line at a time
Guide Question:

After writing as \(v_t=(1-\lambda)\sum_\ell\lambda^\ell v_t\), what is substituted into the \(\ell\)-th piece?
Divide the result into a reward part \(A\) and a value part \(B\).
Change the order of the double sum of \(A\) and write the properties of the geometric series.
Divide \(B\) into two sums, and shift the index of the second sum by one position. Why does \(v_t\) remain?
After combining , group \(\gamma^k\) and change the index to absolute.







NoteSolution





1. Multiply both sides by 1. \[
v_t=(1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\lambda^\ell v_t.
\] \(v_t\) is divided into pieces of weight \((1-\lambda)\lambda^\ell\). Substitute the \((\ell+1)\)-step equation into the \(\ell\)-th piece, and take the sum inside using the linearity of expectation. \[
v_t=(1-\lambda)\,\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\lambda^\ell\Big(\sum_{k=0}^\ell\gamma^kr_{t+k}+\gamma^{\ell+1}v_{t+\ell+1}\Big)\,\Big|\,\mathcal F_t\Big].
\]
2. Divide into two chunks. \[
A:=(1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\lambda^\ell\sum_{k=0}^\ell\gamma^kr_{t+k},\qquad
B:=\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty(\lambda^\ell-\lambda^{\ell+1})\gamma^{\ell+1}v_{t+\ell+1}.
\] \(B\) is simply \((1-\lambda)\) distributed internally.
3. \(A\): Changes the order of the sum. If range \(0\le k\le\ell<\infty\) is read \(k\) first, then \(k\ge0\), \(\ell\ge k\) → Section 6.2.2 \[
A=(1-\lambda)\sum_{k=0}^\infty\gamma^kr_{t+k}\sum_{\ell=k}^\infty\lambda^\ell=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\lambda^k\gamma^kr_{t+k}.
\]
4. \(B\): Divide by the two sums and shift the index. \[
B=\underbrace{\sum_{\ell\ge0}\lambda^\ell\gamma^{\ell+1}v_{t+\ell+1}}_{B_1}-\underbrace{\sum_{\ell\ge0}\lambda^{\ell+1}\gamma^{\ell+1}v_{t+\ell+1}}_{B_2}.
\] \(B_1\) is \(\ell\), but \(k\). If \(B_2\) is set to \(j=\ell+1\), it becomes \(j\ge1\). Add and subtract the \(j=0\) term (\(v_t\)) to make it start from 0. \[
B_2=\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda^k\gamma^kv_{t+k}-v_t.
\] Therefore \[
B=\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda^k\gamma^{k+1}v_{t+k+1}-\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda^k\gamma^kv_{t+k}+v_t.
\] The last \(v_t\) is what remains because one term, \(k=0\), is missing. \(v_t\) is fixed when \(\mathcal F_t\) is given, so it falls outside the expected value.
5. Combine and group. Since \(\lambda^k\) has the same sum, \[
v_t=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{k=0}^\infty\lambda^k\big(\gamma^kr_{t+k}+\gamma^{k+1}v_{t+k+1}-\gamma^kv_{t+k}\big)\,\Big|\,\mathcal F_t\Big]+v_t.
\] If you take out \(\gamma^k\), it becomes \(\lambda^k\gamma^k(r_{t+k}+\gamma v_{t+k+1}-v_{t+k})=(\lambda\gamma)^kd_{t+k}\). If you change it to the absolute point \(j=t+k\) (\(k=0\leftrightarrow j=t\)), it becomes the expression inside the box.









NoteBasis: Reasons why the agreement exchange is justified





If the reward is bounded and \(\gamma<1\), \(\lambda<1\), then all series converge absolutely. By the Fubini–Tonelli theorem, the order exchange of infinite sums and the exchange of sums and expectations are valid.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2


6.2.2 How to mechanically change the order of the agreement
First question to think of. Can you change \(\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sum_{k=0}^\ell\) to \(\sum_k\sum_\ell\) without drawing a picture?
Answer. Combine the range into a single inequality, then read again starting from the new outer variable.**

Combine the ranges. Combine the outer and inner ranges: \(0\le\ell<\infty\), \(0\le k\le\ell\). Now, the double sum simply means “add for all \((\ell,k)\) that satisfy this inequality.”
Organize: \(0\le k\le\ell<\infty\).
Scope of new outer variable: The scope of \(\ell\) remaining after clearing inner variable \(k\). \(0\le k<\infty\).
Range of new inner variable: Treating \(k\) as a constant, from the maximum of the lower bounds of \(\ell\) to the minimum of the upper bounds. Since \(\ell\ge k\), \(\ell\ge0\), and \(\ell<\infty\), \(\ell=k,\dots,\infty\).

\[
\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\sum_{k=0}^\ell f(\ell,k)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\sum_{\ell=k}^\infty f(\ell,k).
\]
Index shifts are also performed mechanically in the same way. If it is \(j=\ell+1\), \(\ell=j-1\) is placed into the old range \(\ell\ge0\) to obtain \(j\ge1\), and all \(\ell\) within the sum are changed to \(j-1\).






NotePractice and Verification





Practice. The range of \(\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=i}^nf(i,j)\) is \(1\le i\le j\le n\). If we set the outside to \(j\), it is \(1\le j\le n\), and the inside is \(1\le i\le j\). Therefore, \(\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^jf(i,j)\).
Verification. Cut up to \(\ell\le2\), arrange the pairs, and compare.

Before replacement: \((0,0),\ (1,0),(1,1),\ (2,0),(2,1),(2,2)\)
After changing: \(k=0\) to \((0,0),(1,0),(2,0)\), \(k=1\) to \((1,1),(2,1)\), \(k=2\) to \((2,2)\)

If there are six identical pairs, it is correct.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2


6.2.3 What does this expression mean?
Answer. Since \(v(s_t)\) is present on both sides, the expression inside the box is as follows.
\[
\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\,\Big|\,\mathcal F_t\Big]=0.
\]
If \(v=v^\pi\), this is a natural result because the conditional mean of each \(d_k\) is already zero (due to the 1-step equation and the iterative expectation law). Although it is a contrived form, the form \(v=(\text{기댓값})+v\), with \(v(s_t)\) left on the right side, fits exactly the form \(x=Hx\) of SA. Therefore, the multi-step Bellman equation also becomes a fixed-point problem.






TipSignificance





Replacing the expectation digit of this fixed-point problem with a single locus sample yields TD(λ) → Section 6.3. Writing the fixed-point mapping \(H\) as a vector gives the starting point for the convergence proof → Section 8.1.1



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2

title: Temporal Difference Learning
text:
6.3 TD(λ) algorithm
First question to think of. If Robbins–Monroe is applied to Section 6.2’s fixed-point problem, what is the update formula? Up to how much data is needed to perform that update?
Answer. Weight the old estimate \(1-\alpha_t\) and the single-sample version of the new estimate \(\alpha_t\).
\[
v(s_t)\leftarrow(1-\alpha_t)v(s_t)+\alpha_t\Big(\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k+v(s_t)\Big).
\]
If you group it as \(\alpha_t\), the \(v(s_t)\) at the beginning and end will be erased.
\[
\boxed{\,v(s_t)\leftarrow v(s_t)+\alpha_t\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\,}
\]
TD(λ) Algorithm

Fix policy \(\pi\in\Pi\).
Initialize to \(v\equiv0\).
transition data \(\{(s_t,a_t,s_{t+1},r_t)\}\) to \(v(s_t)\leftarrow v(s_t)+\alpha_t\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\), where \(d_k:=r_k+\gamma v(s_{k+1})-v(s_k)\).

This is also a policy evaluation method, and only one element is updated in each iteration. Since \(k=t,t+1,\dots\)’s \(d_k\) is required for the update, it is not completely online unless TD(0) is collected, so it can be updated after collecting some trajectory data.
↓ Down: Section 6.3.1 · Section 6.3.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.3.1 ✍ Two extremes: λ = 0 and λ = 1
Guide Question:

When \(\lambda=0\), what is the coefficient \((\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}\) for \(k=t\) and \(k>t\), respectively? What convention is required?
If \(\lambda=1\), \(t=0\), then what is \(\sum_k\gamma^kd_k\)? Assume \(\gamma^Kv(s_K)\to0\).







NoteSolution





1. If we use the convention \(0^0=1\), \(k=t\) is 1 and \(k>t\) is 0. Only \(d_t\) remains in the sum. \[
v(s_t)\leftarrow v(s_t)+\alpha d_t=v(s_t)+\alpha\big[r_t+\gamma v(s_{t+1})-v(s_t)\big].
\] TD(0)
2. It becomes a telephoto lens. \[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty\gamma^kd_k=\sum_k\gamma^kr_k+\sum_k\big(\gamma^{k+1}v(s_{k+1})-\gamma^kv(s_k)\big)=\sum_k\gamma^kr_k-v(s_0).
\] Therefore, the updates are \(v(s_0)\leftarrow v(s_0)+\alpha\big(c-v(s_0)\big)\) and \(c=\sum_k\gamma^kr_k\). This is the same form as the Monte Carlo iteration of Section 4.1. All intermediate values are eliminated, and only the actual reward remains.









TipSignificance





TD(λ) is a continuous family with TD(0) and MC as the endpoints. λ controls how much to bootstrap on the current estimate and how far to use the actual reward → Section 7.1



↑ Go Up: Section 6.3


6.3.2 What is the “0” of TD(0)?
Answer. This means that 0 is entered for the parameter λ of TD(λ). If λ = 0, all weights of Section 6.2 are concentrated in the 1-step equation (\(\ell=0\)).
“0” is not the number of steps being looked ahead. TD(0) is a 1-step method that observes one reward and writes the value of the state one step later. In n-step TD notation where the number of steps is specified directly, TD(0) corresponds to 1-step TD.
↑ Go Up: Section 6.3

title: Temporal Difference Learning
text:
7.1 Bias–variance trade-off
First question to consider. Given the target value of TD(0) \(r_t+\gamma v(s_{t+1})\) and the target value of MC \(\sum_k\gamma^kr_k\), where does the bias come from and where does the variance come from?
Answer.
\[
\textbf{큰 }\lambda\textbf{: 작은 bias, 큰 variance}\qquad\qquad
\textbf{작은 }\lambda\textbf{: 큰 bias, 작은 variance}
\]

A large λ is close to MC. MC uses only actual rewards, so it is unbiased. However, since it sums up both random rewards and transitions from long trajectories, it has large variance.
Small λ is close to TD(0). Since it approximates a single sample with the current estimate \(v(s_{t+1})\), the bias is large while \(v\) is inaccurate. Instead, the variance is small because there is only one step of random elements.







NoteRationale: Comparison of target values





The update of TD(λ) is to move \(v(s_t)\) toward the next target value. \[
v(s_t)+\sum_{k\ge t}(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k.
\]

\(\lambda=1\): \(\sum_k\gamma^{k-t}r_k\), that is, the actual discount accumulation reward. Random terms are accumulated for the length of the trajectory.
\(\lambda=0\): \(r_t+\gamma v(s_{t+1})\). There is only one random term, \(s_{t+1}\). Instead, the error of \(v\) is incorporated directly into the target value.




↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 · Section 7.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

7.1.1 ✍ Two-state example
In a Markov chain, two states 1 and 2 are adjacent, \(p_{12}>0\) and \(p_{21}=0\). Each locus visits state 1 exactly once.
Guide Question:

Is the cumulative reward \(c(1,m)\) from state 1 at the trajectory \(m\)Z an unbiased estimator of \(v^\pi(1)\)? For which TD(λ) does using this sample mean correspond?
Let’s assume that an accurate estimate of \(v^\pi(2)\) already exists. Can TD(1) use this information for learning \(v^\pi(1)\)?
Compare the target value of TD(0) and the target value of MC when a 1→2 transition occurs. Which one has smaller variance?







NoteSolution





1. Since it is visited only once, \(c(1,m)\) is by definition an independent sample of \(G(1)\)Z and \(\mathbb{E}[c(1,m)]=v^\pi(1)\) (ignoring truncation). Writing the sample mean corresponds to TD(1).
2. Cannot be used. The target value of TD(1) is only the sum of actual rewards, and does not include any state value estimates → Section 6.3.1
3. Let \(r_1\) be the reward for a 1→2 transition.

TD(0): \(r_1+\gamma v^\pi(2)\). Randomness is only \(r_1\) (0 if the reward is deterministic like the model in this note).
MC: \(r_1+\gamma G(2)\). Due to Markov properties, the future after state 2 is independent of \(r_1\), so \[
\operatorname{Var}\big(r_1+\gamma G(2)\big)=\operatorname{Var}(r_1)+\gamma^2\operatorname{Var}\big(G(2)\big).
\]

TD(0) eliminates variance of \(\gamma^2\operatorname{Var}(G(2))\). This is because the noise of the entire future starting from state 2 has been replaced by a single accurate estimate.









TipSignificance





TD(0) utilizes already learned value information very efficiently and also reduces noise in the reward samples. However, that efficiency is only when \(v(2)\) is accurate. If \(v(2)\) is incorrect, that error is transferred directly to \(v(1)\). This is the price of bias.



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1


7.1.2 λ scheduling
First question to consider. How does the quality of \(v\) differ between the early and late stages of learning? Accordingly, which error should be a greater concern?
Answer. Start with a large λ and reduce to 0.

Initial: Since the quality of \(v\) is poor, relying on \(v\) results in a large bias. Reduce the bias by using a large λ to apply more real rewards.
Review: Since TD(λ) converges, the quality of \(v\) improves as the process progresses. Now, relying on \(v\) also results in small bias. By utilizing existing value information with a small λ, we reduce variance and update quickly.







TipSignificance





It is the principle that “the more reliable information accumulates, the more it relies on its own estimate.” It is a design in the same direction as the ε schedule, which starts with a large search probability and reduces it.



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

title: Temporal Difference Learning
text:
8.1 Convergence Theorem
Answer.






ImportantTheorem (Convergence of TD(λ))



Each state is visited infinitely often and \[
\sum_{t=0}^\infty\alpha_t=+\infty,\qquad\sum_{t=0}^\infty\alpha_t^2<+\infty
\] If , then for a given policy \(\pi\in\Pi\), the \(v(s)\) generated by TD(λ) converges to \(v^\pi(s)\) with probability 1 at each \(s\in S\).


Since TD(λ) is a stochastic approximation, the convergence theorem of SA is applied directly. Two of the step size conditions are assumptions, and the remaining two can be proven.

is the multi-step Bellman operator \(H\), which is an abbreviation.
The noise satisfies the conditional mean 0 and conditional variance bounded conditions.







TipSignificance





It is sufficient to know this theorem at the level of the result and the idea of the proof. In practice, satisfying the “visiting every state infinitely often” and step size conditions is very tricky. Remember the fact that theoretical guarantees exist and the structure in which they stem from the two axes of SA (contraction + noise conditions).



↓ Down: Section 8.1.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

8.1.1 ✍ Proof Idea: Contraction of \(H\) and noise conditions
Guide Question:

If we write the fixed-point equation of Section 6.2 as a vector, what is \(v=Hv\) and \(H\)? Find the constant term.
Show that \(H\) is a contraction of \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\)Z and find the coefficients. What are the coefficients for λ = 0 and λ → 1?
Define noise \(w_t\) and verify that the conditional mean is 0. Why is the conditional variance bounded?







NoteSolution





1. If we write the \((\ell+1)\)-step equation as a vector, it is \(v=\sum_{k=0}^\ell(\gamma P^\pi)^kR^\pi+(\gamma P^\pi)^{\ell+1}v\). Averaging with the weight \((1-\lambda)\lambda^\ell\) \[
v^\pi=\underbrace{(1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\lambda^\ell\sum_{k=0}^\ell(\gamma P^\pi)^kR^\pi}_{\text{상수항}}+(1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\lambda^\ell(\gamma P^\pi)^{\ell+1}v^\pi=:Hv^\pi.
\] The constant term is rearranged into the same order exchange as \(A\) of Section 6.2.1. \[
(1-\lambda)\sum_{k\ge0}(\gamma P^\pi)^kR^\pi\sum_{\ell\ge k}\lambda^\ell=\sum_{k=0}^\infty(\lambda\gamma P^\pi)^kR^\pi.
\] is equal to \(R^\pi\) only when ||| λ = 0. Since the constant term cancels out in \(Hv-Hu\), it is independent of whether it is abbreviated. Even if the constant term is simply written as \(R^\pi\), it does not affect the idea of the proof.
2. Since \(P^\pi\) is a probability matrix, it is \(\|(P^\pi)^nx\|_\infty\le\|x\|_\infty\). Therefore \[
\|Hv-Hu\|_\infty\le(1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell=0}^\infty\lambda^\ell\gamma^{\ell+1}\|v-u\|_\infty=\frac{\gamma(1-\lambda)}{1-\lambda\gamma}\|v-u\|_\infty.
\] If \(\gamma<1\), then \(\gamma-\lambda\gamma<1-\lambda\gamma\), so the coefficient is less than 1.

λ = 0: coefficient \(\gamma\). \(H=T^\pi\).
λ → 1: coefficient → 0. \(H\) becomes the MC target value with almost no dependence on \(v\).

3. \[
w_t:=\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k-\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{k=t}^\infty(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\,\Big|\,\mathcal F_t\Big].
\] Since the conditional expectation of the observed signal \(\sum_k(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k+v(s_t)\) is \((Hv)(s_t)\), the signal is \((Hv)(s_t)+w_t\). By definition, it is \(\mathbb{E}[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\). If \(|r|\le R_{\max}\), then \(|d_k|\le R_{\max}+(1+\gamma)\|v\|_\infty\), so \[
\Big|\sum_k(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\Big|\le\frac{R_{\max}+2\|v\|_\infty}{1-\lambda\gamma}.
\] Therefore, the conditional variance is bounded in the form \(C_0+C_1\|v\|^2\).









TipSignificance





\(v^\pi\) satisfies all \((\ell+1)\)-step equations, so it is the fixed point of \(H\). Since \(H\) is the contraction, the fixed point is unique. The contraction coefficient \(\gamma(1-\lambda)/(1-\lambda\gamma)\) decreases as λ increases. In terms of deterministic iteration, a larger λ contracts faster, but at the cost of increased noise (variance). This is the trade-off of Section 7.1 viewed from the operator side.

section: 3.1 What is an MDP problem, and why is it difficult to solve directly?
text:
3.1 What is an MDP problem, and why is it difficult to solve directly?
Answer. The goal is \(\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\big]\). The optimization variable \(\pi\) is a function that goes from a state to an action (distribution). Therefore, it is not clear what the gradient of this objective function with respect to \(\pi\) is, and conventional numerical optimization cannot be applied directly. The solution is dynamic programming (DP). It breaks down a single difficult problem into several easier problems called state-specific action optimizations.






TipSignificance: Why optimize policies rather than action sequences?





Since transitions are probabilistic, the next state cannot be known in advance. A pre-optimized sequence of actions is no longer optimal if it reaches a state different from what was expected. The policy contains responses in advance for all reachable states.









TipSignificance: Why it cannot be solved with supervised learning





Reward \(r(s,a)\) measures only the immediate gain of the current state and action, and cannot measure future gain. Therefore, a label stating “the correct action in this state is this” does not exist.









TipSignificance: The fact that behavior has long-term effects, and that it involves sacrificing immediate rewards





The current action changes the trajectory of the states that will be traversed in the future. Therefore, even if the immediate reward is small, if the long-term gain is large, that action should be chosen. The Bellman equation is the exact mathematical expression of this statement. The optimal action is the action that maximizes “immediate reward + γ × optimal value of the next state.”



Sub-question.

What is \(v^\pi(s)\)? The expected value of the cumulative reward obtained when starting from state \(s\) and continuing to follow \(\pi\).
What is \(v^*(s)\)? It is the maximum expected cumulative reward that can be obtained with any policy starting from state \(s\), i.e., the best performance of that MDP.
Why is it said that “the MDP is solved if \(v^*\) is found”? This is because with only \(v^*\), the optimal policy can be immediately created using the state-specific argmax. → Section 6.5
What if we evaluate policy using Monte Carlo? It is an unbiased estimator, but the variance is large, and it must be repeated separately for each starting state. Therefore, we use DP that splits the value function into two parts → Section 10.2

↓ Down: Section 4.1 Finite horizon · Section 5.1 Infinite policy evaluation · [@secc0] Infinite optimality

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 4.1 Why does backward induction accurately produce \(v_t^*\) and \(\pi_t^*\)
text:
4.1 Why does backward induction accurately produce \(v_t^*\) and \(\pi_t^*\)
Answer. It is because the two facts combine.

\(v_t^*\) satisfies the Bellman recursive \(v_t^*(s)=\max_a\big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}^*(s')\big]\) (optimality principle), and the endpoint \(v_T^*=r_T\) is fixed. Therefore, it is uniquely determined in reverse order of \(t=T-1,\dots,0\).
The deterministic Markov policy created with the argmax of each step is optimal.

The algorithm is as follows. \[
v_T^*:=r_T;\quad t=T-1{:}-1{:}0:\ \ v_t^*(s):=\max_a[\cdots],\ \ \pi_t^*(s)\in\arg\max_a[\cdots]\ \ \forall s.
\]






TipSignificance






\(v_t^*\) and \(\pi_t^*\) are updated together in the same loop because they both only need the information for \(t+1\).
Hidden Complexity: At every time step, for every state, the action maximization must be solved. In large-scale problems, this is the bottleneck.
In finite MDPs, the optimality is not lost even when only the deterministic Markov policy is considered.




↓ Down: Section 4.2 End-to-end condition · Section 4.4 Optimality principle · Section 4.5 Optimality of argmax policy · Section 4.6 Multiplicity ↑ Up: Section 3.1

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
text:
4.2 What are \(v_T^\pi(s)\) and \(v_T^*(s)\)?
Answer. Both are \(r_T(s)\).






NoteProof





When substituting \(t=T\) into \(v_t^\pi(s):=\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\sum_{\tau=t}^{T-1}r_\tau(s_\tau,a_\tau)+r_T(s_T)\ \big|\ s_t=s\big]\), the sum \(\sum_{\tau=T}^{T-1}\) is empty. What remains is \(r_T(s_T)\), and since the condition is \(s_T=s\), it is \(v_T^\pi(s)=r_T(s)\).
Since the policy only includes \(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1}\), the value at time \(T\) does not depend on any policy. Therefore, it is \(v_T^*(s)=\max_\pi v_T^\pi(s)=r_T(s)\).









TipSignificance






Reason why the terminal term is \(r_T(s_T)\) instead of \(r_T(s_T,a_T)\): The trajectory of interest extends up to \(s_T\). The behavior at time \(T\) is out of interest because it only affects \(s_{T+1}\).
Two characteristics of a finite horizon emerge here: (1) the value function depends on time. (2) there is a terminal condition. This terminal condition is the starting point for reverse calculation. An infinite horizon lacks both.




↑ Go Up: Section 4.1, Section 4.3

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 4.3 Why does the policy evaluation recursion hold?
text:
4.3 Why does the policy evaluation recursion hold?
Proposition. For a stochastic Markov policy \(\pi=(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1})\), \(v_T^\pi=r_T\) and \[
v_t^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}^\pi(s')\Big].
\]
Answer. This is because the value function is split into “current reward + cumulative reward from the next time point”, and the tower rule and Markov properties are applied to the second term in turn.






NoteProof





If you set it to \(G_t:=\sum_{\tau=t}^{T-1}r_\tau(s_\tau,a_\tau)+r_T(s_T)\), it is \(G_t=r_t(s_t,a_t)+G_{t+1}\).

Linearity: \(v_t^\pi(s)=\mathbb{E}^\pi[r_t(s_t,a_t)\mid s_t=s]+\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s]\).
tower: \(\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s]=\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid h_{t+1}]\mid s_t=s\big]\), \(h_{t+1}=(s_0,a_0,\dots,s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})\).
Markov: \(\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid h_{t+1}]=v_{t+1}^\pi(s_{t+1})\).
Joint Distribution Expansion: When \(s_t=s\), the distribution of \((a_t,s_{t+1})\) is \(\pi_t(a\mid s)\,p(s'\mid s,a)\). The first term is \(\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\,r_t(s,a)\), and the second term is \(\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}^\pi(s')\).










TipSignificance






The calculation order is reverse, from \(T\) to \(0\). You must finish all states of a current point in time to move to the previous point in time.
If it is a deterministic policy, \(\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\) will converge at one point, becoming \(r_t(s,\pi_t(s))+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi_t(s))\,v_{t+1}^\pi(s')\).
In stochastic policies, the action distribution must be multiplied not only by the immediate reward but also by the next value term.




↓ Down: Section 4.3.1 ↑ Up: Section 4.4, Section 4.5, Section 4.6

4.3.1 Where are the tower rule and Markov properties used respectively
Answer.

Tower rule: If \(\mathcal{G}_1\subset\mathcal{G}_2\), then \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}_1]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}_2]\mid\mathcal{G}_1]\). Used only in the step of applying an additional layer of conditions.
Markov property: Makes the inner conditional expectation \(\mathbb{E}[G_{t+1}\mid h_{t+1}]\) a function of only \(s_{t+1}\)Z, i.e., \(v_{t+1}^\pi(s_{t+1})\), independent of the past. To achieve this, the transition must be Markov and the policy \(\pi_{t+1},\dots\) must also be Markov.







TipSignificance





In the answer, the two justifications are written on different lines. If the policy is history-dependent, the 3-step process is broken. In an infinite horizon, stationarity is additionally required here → Section 5.2



↑ Go Up: Section 4.3, Section 4.4, Section 5.2

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 4.4 Optimality Principle: Why \(v_t^*\) satisfies Bellman recursion
text:
4.4 Optimality Principle: Why \(v_t^*\) satisfies Bellman recursion
Proposition. \(v_t^*(s)=\max_a\big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}^*(s')\big]\), \(v_T^*=r_T\).
Answer. If we separate (≤) and (≥), they become an equality sign.

(≤): Press down on the value after the next point in time as the optimal value.
(≥): Fixing the current action at any value and setting the subsequent actions to optimal results in an acceptable policy.







NoteProof (≤)





\[
\begin{aligned}
v_t^*(s)&=\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t(s_t,a_t)+G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s\big]\\
&=\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t+\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid h_{t+1}]\mid s_t=s\big] &&\text{(tower)}\\
&=\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t+v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s\big] &&\text{(Markov)}\\
&\le\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t+v^*_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s\big] &&(v^\pi_{t+1}\le v^*_{t+1},\ \text{기댓값의 단조성})\\
&=\max_\pi\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big]\\
&=\max_a\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big] &&(\text{볼록결합} \le \max,\ \text{Dirac에서 등호})
\end{aligned}
\]









NoteProof (≥): Two arguments





Argument (a), random policy + Dirac distribution. From the policy evaluation recursion(Section 4.3) for any \(\pi\) \[v_t^*(s)\ge v_t^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p\,v_{t+1}^\pi(s')\Big].\] On the right side, \(\pi_{t+1},\dots,\pi_{T-1}\) is random, so it can be replaced with the tail of the optimal policy. Then, \(v_{t+1}^*\) is placed in the position of \(v_{t+1}^\pi\). Now, since \(\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\) is also random, applying a Dirac distribution with mass concentrated on each action yields an inequality for all \(a\), and the process concludes by taking \(\max_a\).
Argument (b), Allow Policy. A policy that takes action \(a\) at time \(t\) and follows the optimal policy from \(t+1\) is an allow policy. Its value is \(r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\), so this value cannot exceed \(v_t^*(s)\). Since this holds for all \(a\), we take \(\max_a\).
Both arguments use the existence of an optimal policy. If existence is not guaranteed, the same argument is made using an ε-optimal policy, but the ε error must be managed.









TipSignificance






Optimization for policies (functions \(T\)) has been changed to optimization for a single action in each \((t,s)\). The cost is that the maximization must be solved for every state.
The Bellman formula has four uses: optimal value calculation, verification of which policy is optimal, efficient computational procedures, and structural analysis of the optimal policy.




↓ Down: Section 4.3, Section 4.3.1 ↑ Up: Section 4.1

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 4.5 Why is the deterministic Markov policy built with argmax optimal?
text:
4.5 Why is the deterministic Markov policy built with argmax optimal?
Proposition. If \(\pi_t^*(s)\in\arg\max_a\big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p\,v_{t+1}^*(s')\big]\), then in all \(t\)Z, \(v_t^{\pi^*}=v_t^*\).
Answer. (≤) is derived directly from the definition. (≥) appears to be reverse induction starting from \(t=T\).






NoteProof





(≤): \(v^*\) by definition of \(v_t^{\pi^*}\le v_t^*\).
(≥) Induction.

Base: \(t=T\) to \(v_T^{\pi^*}=r_T=v_T^*\).
Inductive Step: Assume \(v_{t+1}^{\pi^*}\ge v_{t+1}^*\).

Since the transition probability has non-negative weights, \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi_t^*(s))\,v_{t+1}^{\pi^*}(s')\ge\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi_t^*(s))\,v_{t+1}^*(s')\).
By the definition of argmax, for all \(a\), \(r_t(s,\pi_t^*(s))+\sum p(\cdot\mid s,\pi_t^*(s))\,v_{t+1}^*\ge r_t(s,a)+\sum p(\cdot\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}^*\).
Combining 1 and 2, for all \(a\), \(r_t(s,\pi_t^*(s))+\sum p(\cdot\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^{\pi^*}_{t+1}\ge r_t(s,a)+\sum p(\cdot\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}\).
The left side is \(v_t^{\pi^*}(s)\) by policy evaluation recursion (Section 4.3). Taking \(\max_a\) on the right side, it becomes \(v_t^*(s)\) by the Optimality Principle (Section 4.4).











TipSignificance





In a finite MDP, a deterministic Markov policy alone is sufficient. However, the decision rule may vary from time to time. The finite horizon policy must answer \(\pi_t^*\) for each time step.



↓ Down: Section 4.3, Section 4.4, Section 6.3.3 ↑ Up: Section 4.1

section: 4.6 How to construct a stochastic optimal policy, and why can there be multiple optimal policies
text:
4.6 How to construct a stochastic optimal policy, and why can there be multiple optimal policies
Proposition. If \(\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow a\in A_t^*(s):=\arg\max_a[\cdots]\), then \(\bar\pi\) is optimal.
Answer. argmax If there are multiple elements in a set, the values inside the parentheses are all the same for those actions. Therefore, no matter how the probabilities are divided among them, the same value is obtained. There may be multiple optimal policies, but the optimal value \(v^*\) is unique by definition.






NoteProof





It appears to be reverse induction. It is \(v_T^{\bar\pi}=r_T=v_T^*\). Assuming \(v_{t+1}^{\bar\pi}=v_{t+1}^*\), by policy evaluation recursion \[v_t^{\bar\pi}(s)=\sum_a\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p\,v_{t+1}^*(s')\Big].\] For \(a\) in the support set, the parentheses are the same as \(v_t^*(s)\). Therefore, it is \(v_t^{\bar\pi}(s)=v_t^*(s)\sum_a\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)=v_t^*(s)\).

section: 4.7 Finite horizon Why γ is not required in the Bellman equation
text:
4.7 Finite horizon Why γ is not required in the Bellman equation
Answer. Since the reward can be time-dependent, defining it as \(r_t(s,a):=\gamma^tr(s,a)\) absorbs the discount into \(r_t\). Conversely, using \(\gamma\) in the Bellman equation without separately defining \(r_t\) is a source of confusion.

section: 4.8 What Changes When Extended to Continuous States and Actions
text:
4.8 What Changes When Extended to Continuous States and Actions
Answer. Given the system model \(s_{t+1}=f(s_t,a_t,w_t)\) and the distribution \(w\)Z, \(p_w\), the following holds. \[p(s'\mid s,a)=p_w(w)\,\mathbf{1}\{s'=f(s,a,w)\},\qquad v_t(s)=\sup_a\Big[r(s,a)+\int v_{t+1}(f(s,a,w))\,p_w(dw)\Big].\] The Bellman equation can be used without explicitly calculating the transition probability. However, three problems arise.

argmax may not exist. In this case, use the ε-optimal policy.
Maximizing continuous actions itself is difficult.
Since updates cannot be made across the entire state space, discretization is necessary. If there are \(N\) points per axis, it becomes \(d\) points in \(N^d\) dimensions, resulting in the curse of dimension.







TipSignificance





This limitation is the motivation for moving on to function approximation (weight learning) and deep RL. DP breaks down difficult problems into many easy problems, but the number of those easy problems increases exponentially.



↑ Go Up: Section 4.1

section: 4.9 How to derive transition probability in descriptive questions
text:
4.9 How to derive transition probability in descriptive questions
Answer. Write the dynamics \(s'=g(s,a,W)\) and divide the region where \(s'\) can be into cases. There are three cases: interior, boundary (saturating max/min), and impossible (probability 0). Finally, check if \((s,a)\) is \(\sum_{s'}p=1\).






NoteExample: Inventory Management \(s_{t+1}=\max{s_t+a_t-D_t,0}\), \(p_j=\Pr(D=j)\)





The default settings are \(S=\{0,\dots,M\}\) and \(A_s=\{0,\dots,M-s\}\). The upper limit of \(A_s\) is due to storage capacity.
Transition probabilities are divided into three cases.

\(s+a<s'\le M\): Since the next stock cannot be greater than the stock after ordering, \(p(s'\mid s,a)=0\).
\(0<s'\le s+a\): Since the demand must be exactly \(D=s+a-s'\), \(p(s'\mid s,a)=p_{s+a-s'}\).
\(s'=0\): Excess demand is lost and cannot be sold. Since we add up all cases where demand is greater than inventory, \(p(0\mid s,a)=\sum_{j\ge s+a}p_j\).










TipSignificance: A space that must be entered in the answer






\(S\), \(A\)(or \(A_s\)), \(p(s'\mid s,a)\) (including boundaries), \(r_t(s,a)\) or \(c_t(s,a)\).
Termination \(r_T\): If not specified, write “\(r_T\equiv0\)” with the basis.
Objective function: \(\min\mathbb{E}[\sum c]\Leftrightarrow\max\mathbb{E}[\sum(-c)]\).
The sequence of events within a period (decision → cost incurrence → stochastic change) is directly reflected in the cost formula and transfer formula.

5.1 How is \(v^\pi\) calculated?
Answer. There are two methods.

Inverse Matrix: \(v^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi\).
Fixed Point Repeat: \(v_{k+1}=T^\pi v_k\), \(v_k\to v^\pi\).

Both come from decomposition formula \(v^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi\).






TipSignificance





The inverse matrix of is \(O(n^3)\), and since it has a large memory capacity, it is suitable for small-scale problems. For large-scale problems, iteration is used. The justification for iteration comes from the contraction of \(T^\pi\) and Banach’s theorem.
Hidden complexity of iteration: All states must be updated in a single iteration. However, since the policy is fixed, there is no maximization of actions.

section: 5.2 Why does the infinite horizon decomposition formula hold, and why is there no time index?
text:
5.2 Why does the infinite horizon decomposition formula hold, and why is there no time index?
Proposition. \(v^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi(s')\big]\).
Answer. A tower like a finite horizon → Stationarity is added to the Markov argument. If \(r\), \(p\), and \(\pi\) are all time-invariant, then the process starting at \(t+1\) has the same distribution as the process starting at \(0\). Therefore, it becomes the function \(v^\pi\), where the value of the next state is the same.






NoteProof





\[
\begin{aligned}
v^\pi(s)&=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma\sum_{\tau\ge t+1}\gamma^{\tau-t-1}r(s_\tau,a_\tau)\ \Big|\ s_t=s\Big]\\
&=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau\ge t+1}\gamma^{\tau-t-1}r_\tau\ \Big|\ s_{t+1}\Big]\ \Big|\ s_t=s\Big]&&(\text{tower, Markov})\\
&=\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma\,v^\pi(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s\big]&&(\text{stationarity})\\
&=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi(s')\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]









TipSignificance





In the finite horizon, since the right side was \(t+1\) and the left side was \(t\), reverse calculation was possible. In the infinite horizon, there is the same function \(v^\pi\) on both sides. Therefore, reverse calculation is impossible, and this expression must be solved as an equation (or fixed-point problem).



↓ Down: Section 4.3.1 ↑ Up: Section 5.1

section: 5.3 What are the elements of the vector \(v^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi\)
text:
5.3 What are the elements of the vector \(v^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi\)
Answer.

\(R^\pi(i)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid i)\,r(i,a)\): Immediate reward expectation when following \(\pi\) from state \(i\).
\(P^\pi_{ij}=\sum_a\pi(a\mid i)\,p(j\mid i,a)\): Probability that the next state is \(j\) when following \(\pi\) from state \(i\).

If it is a deterministic policy, it is \(R^\pi(i)=r(i,\pi(i))\) and \(P^\pi_{ij}=p(j\mid i,\pi(i))\). It is \(n\) of the state-specific equations written in a single line.






TipSignificance: Standard flow of calculation problems






\(R^\pi\), \(P^\pi\) is created.
Solve \((I-\gamma P^\pi)v=R^\pi\).
Calculate \(Q^\pi(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi(s')\).
Verify with \(v^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\,Q^\pi(s,a)\).

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
text:
5.4 Why is \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) always reversible?
Answer. The eigenvalue of \(P^\pi\) is \(\gamma<1\), and its absolute value is 1 or less. Therefore, the eigenvalue of \(I-\gamma P^\pi\), \(1-\gamma\mu\), cannot be 0.






NoteProof





Step 1: \(|\mu|\le1\). Let \(P^\pi x=\mu x\) and \(x\ne0\), and select \(i\), which is \(|x_i|=\|x\|_\infty\). Then \[|\mu|\,|x_i|=\Big|\sum_jP^\pi_{ij}x_j\Big|\le\sum_jP^\pi_{ij}|x_j|\le\|x\|_\infty\sum_jP^\pi_{ij}=\|x\|_\infty\] is used. Non-negative and row 1 were used. Therefore, \(|\mu|\le1\).
Step 2: Reversibility. If \((I-\gamma P^\pi)x=0\), then \(P^\pi x=\gamma^{-1}x\). However, the eigenvalue \(\gamma^{-1}>1\) contradicts Step 1. Therefore, \(x=0\) and \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) are reversible.
Step 3: Series Representation. Since \(\|\gamma P^\pi\|_\infty=\gamma<1\), the Neumann series converges. \[(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}=\sum_{t\ge0}(\gamma P^\pi)^t.\]









TipSignificance






In \(v^\pi=\sum_t(\gamma P^\pi)^tR^\pi\), the \(t\) term is the “discounted value of the expected reward after \(t\) steps.” Therefore, it exactly matches the definition of the value function.
If \(\gamma=1\), then \(P^\pi\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}\), so \(I-P^\pi\) is a singular matrix.
Since each term is nasal, it is \((I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\ge0\) → Section 6.3.3

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
text:
5.5 Why is \(T^\pi\) a \(\gamma\)-abbreviation?
Proposition. \(\|T^\pi v-T^\pi w\|_\infty\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty\).
Answer. \(T^\pi v-T^\pi w=\gamma P^\pi(v-w)\), and since each row of \(P^\pi\) is a probability distribution, the weighted average cannot exceed the maximum value.






NoteProof





\[|(T^\pi v-T^\pi w)(s)|=\gamma\Big|\sum_{s'}P^\pi_{ss'}(v-w)(s')\Big|\le\gamma\sum_{s'}P^\pi_{ss'}\|v-w\|_\infty=\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty.\] It ends by taking the max for \(s\).









TipSignificance





Applying the Banach theorem (Section 6.2.3) yields two results: (1) \(v^\pi\) is the unique fixed point of \(T^\pi\). (2) Iterating \(T^\pi\) from any \(v_0\) converges to \(v^\pi\). This is the iterative algorithm for policy evaluation. Thanks to this uniqueness, we can say, “If it converges, it is \(v^\pi\).”

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 6.1 The Bellman equation \(v=Tv\) has a unique solution, and that solution is \(v^*\).
text:
6.1 The Bellman equation \(v=Tv\) has a unique solution, and that solution is \(v^*\).
\[(Tv)(s)=\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\Big].\]
Answer. It is divided into two arguments.

Unique: Since \(T\) is a \(\gamma\)-reduction, by (1) of the Banach fixed point theorem.
The solution is \(v^*\): By the comparison lemma “\(v\ge Tv\Rightarrow v\ge v^*\), \(v\le Tv\Rightarrow v\le v^*\)”. Since the solution \(v\) satisfies both inequalities simultaneously, it is \(v=v^*\).







TipSignificance






This is a theorem that forms the basis of optimal control and RL.
“It is unique” and “It is equal to \(v^*\)” are different claims, and their grounds are also different. They are not mixed in the answer.
uniqueness must exist so that we can say that the convergence point of VI is \(v^*\), and the limits of LP and SA also point to the same object.




↓ Down: Section 6.2 Uniqueness · Section 6.3 The solution is in the form of \(v^*\) · Section 6.4 \(T\) · Section 6.5 Optimal policy ↑ Up: Section 3.1

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
text:
6.2 Why is it unique?
Answer. This is because \(T\) is a \(\gamma\)-reduction with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\)Z (Section 6.2.1), and a reduction mapping has a unique fixed point by the first property of the Banach fixed point theorem (Section 6.2.3).
↓ Down: Section 6.2.1, Section 6.2.3 ↑ Up: Section 6.1

6.2.1 Why is \(T\) a \(\gamma\)-abbreviation?
Proposition. \(\|Tv-Tw\|_\infty\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty\).
Answer. If we apply the inequality (Section 6.2.2) that removes the maximum for each state, what remains is the difference in the weighted average of the transition probabilities. This difference does not exceed \(\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty\).






NoteProof





If you set it to \(q_v(s,a):=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\), it is \((Tv)(s)=\max_aq_v(s,a)\). \[
\begin{aligned}
|(Tv)(s)-(Tw)(s)|&\le\max_a|q_v(s,a)-q_w(s,a)| &&\text{(max 차이 부등식)}\\
&=\max_a\gamma\Big|\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)(v-w)(s')\Big|\\
&\le\gamma\max_a\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,|v(s')-w(s')|\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty.
\end{aligned}
\] It ends when you take the max for \(s\).









NoteAnother proof: Monotonicity + Constant shift





If \(\delta=\|v-w\|_\infty\), then it is \(w-\delta\mathbf{1}\le v\le w+\delta\mathbf{1}\). \(T\) is monotonic (Section 6.3.2) and since \(T(w+c\mathbf{1})=Tw+\gamma c\mathbf{1}\), \[Tw-\gamma\delta\mathbf{1}\le Tv\le Tw+\gamma\delta\mathbf{1}.\] Since the structure of max is not handled directly, it is transferred as is to the Q-operator.



↓ Down: Section 6.2.2 ↑ Up: Section 6.2, Section 11.2


6.2.2 max difference inequality holds
Proposition. \(\left|\max_ax_a-\max_ay_a\right|\le\max_a|x_a-y_a|\).






NoteProof





For all \(a\), it is \(x_a\le y_a+|x_a-y_a|\le\max_by_b+\max_b|x_b-y_b|\). Taking \(\max_a\) on the left side gives \(\max x-\max y\le\max|x-y|\). Swapping the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) yields the opposite direction.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2.1


6.2.3 What is the Banach Fixed Point Theorem?
Proposition. On a complete normed space (here, \((\mathbb{R}^n,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\)), if \(T\) is a \(\gamma\)-reduction, then the following two conditions hold.

\(T\) has a unique fixed point \(v^\star\): \(v^\star=Tv^\star\).
If we define \(v_0\) as \(v_{k+1}=Tv_k\), then it is \(v_k\to v^\star\).

Answer. If we show that the repeating sequence in (2) is a Cauchy sequence, the limit exists. Since that limit is a fixed point, the existence of the fixed point follows. Uniqueness is expressed in a single line of reduced inequality.
↓ Down: Section 6.2.4 Proof · Section 6.2.5 Significance ↑ Up: Section 6.2, Section 5.5, Section 7.2


6.2.4 How are each proposition of Banach’s theorem proven?






Noteconvergence, and the existence part of (1)





① Consecutive difference. \(\|v_{k+1}-v_k\|=\|Tv_k-Tv_{k-1}\|\le\gamma\|v_k-v_{k-1}\|\le\cdots\le\gamma^k\|v_1-v_0\|\).
② Cauchy. \(m>n\), with telescopic sum and triangle inequality \[\|v_m-v_n\|\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}\|v_{k+1}-v_k\|\le\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}\gamma^k\|v_1-v_0\|=\frac{\gamma^n}{1-\gamma}\|v_1-v_0\|\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0.\]
③ Existence of the limit. Since the space is complete, the Cauchy sequence has the limit \(v^\star\).
④ The limit is a fixed point. \[\|Tv^\star-v^\star\|\le\|Tv^\star-Tv_k\|+\|v_{k+1}-v^\star\|\le\gamma\|v^\star-v_k\|+\|v_{k+1}-v^\star\|\to0.\]









NoteUniqueness





If \(v^\star\) and \(\tilde v\) are both fixed points \[\|v^\star-\tilde v\|=\|Tv^\star-T\tilde v\|\le\gamma\|v^\star-\tilde v\|\] Since , it is \((1-\gamma)\|v^\star-\tilde v\|\le0\). Since \(1-\gamma>0\), it is \(v^\star=\tilde v\).









NoteConvergence rate





\(\|v_k-v^\star\|=\|Tv_{k-1}-Tv^\star\|\le\gamma\|v_{k-1}-v^\star\|\le\cdots\le\gamma^k\|v_0-v^\star\|\). It is geometric convergence.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2.3


6.2.5 What is the significance of Banach’s theorem?






TipSignificance






(1) Uniqueness: It guarantees that when a fixed point is reached through iteration, it is the target intended (\(v^\pi\) or \(v^*\)). If there were multiple fixed points, it would be impossible to know which point of convergence is the point of convergence. This is key not only theoretically but also practically.
(2) Iterative Convergence: If the model is known, a simple iterative algorithm called VI emerges. The model-free version of this is the SA-based algorithm (TD, Q-learning).
Velocity \(\gamma^k\|v_0-v^\star\|\): The number of iterations depends on how close the initialization is to the fixed point. Unlike a finite horizon, the number of iterations is not fixed at \(T\).
We apply the same theorem to ZZZPH0014559ZZZ for \(T^\pi\), \(T\), \(T_Q\), and the multilevel operator of TD(λ). The only thing that needs to be changed is “whether that operator is a contraction.”




↑ Go Up: Section 6.2.3

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
text:
6.3 Why is that unique year \(v^*\)
Answer. This is due to the Comparison Lemma (Section 6.3.1). If \(v=Tv\), then \(v\ge Tv\) and \(v\le Tv\) are satisfied simultaneously, so \(v\ge v^*\) and \(v\le v^*\) hold together. Therefore, it is \(v=v^*\).
↓ Down: Section 6.3.1 ↑ Up: Section 6.1

6.3.1 Comparison Lemma: \(v\ge Tv\Rightarrow v\ge v^*\), \(v\le Tv\Rightarrow v\le v^*\)
Answer.

(≥ side): If we fix an arbitrary policy \(\pi\) and repeatedly substitute \(v\ge Tv\ge T^\pi v\) into itself, we get \(v\ge v^\pi\). Since this holds for all \(\pi\), we get \(v\ge v^*\).
(≤ side): Applying a greedy policy to \(v\) results in \(v\le Tv=T^{\pi_v}v\). Repeating monotonically results in \(v\le v^{\pi_v}\le v^*\).







NoteProof (v ≥ Tv ⇒ v ≥ v*)





For any stationary \(\pi\), by the definition of \(T\), \(Tv\ge T^\pi v=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v\). Therefore \[v\ge R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v\ge R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi(R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v)\ge\cdots\ge\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(\gamma P^\pi)^tR^\pi+(\gamma P^\pi)^nv.\] The inequality holds even when multiplying by \(\gamma P^\pi\ge0\) at each step (Section 6.3.3). Since \(\|(\gamma P^\pi)^nv\|_\infty\le\gamma^n\|v\|_\infty\to0\), \(n\to\infty\), we have \(v\ge\sum_t(\gamma P^\pi)^tR^\pi=v^\pi\) (Section 5.4). Taking \(\max_\pi\) on both sides gives \(v\ge v^*\).
Refinement. For the abnormal Markov policy \((\pi_0,\pi_1,\dots)\), if \(Tv\ge T^{\pi_t}v\) is used at each step, \(v\ge T^{\pi_0}\cdots T^{\pi_{n-1}}v\to v^{(\pi_0,\pi_1,\dots)}\) is obtained through the same iteration.









NoteProof (v ≤ Tv ⇒ v ≤ v*)





If we set it to \(\pi_v(s)\in\arg\max_a[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum p\,v]\), then it is \(Tv=T^{\pi_v}v\)(Section 6.5.1). Then it is \(v\le T^{\pi_v}v\), and if we repeat with the monotonality of \(T^{\pi_v}\), \[v\le(T^{\pi_v})^nv\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}v^{\pi_v}\le v^*.\] The limit comes from the contraction (Section 5.5) of \(T^{\pi_v}\), and the final inequality comes from the definition of \(v^*\). (If this direction is proven using the “fixed point of \(T^nv\to\) \(T\),” it amounts to a circular argument, as it implies that the fixed point is already \(v^*\).)



↓ Down: Section 6.3.2, Section 6.3.3, Section 6.5.1 ↑ Up: Section 6.3, Section 8.2


6.3.2 Why is \(T\) a forged key?
Proposition. \(v\le w\Rightarrow Tv\le Tw\). \(T^\pi\) is also the same.






NoteProof





Since \(p\ge0\), for all \((s,a)\), it is \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\le\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,w(s')\). Therefore, it is \(q_v(s,a)\le q_w(s,a)\), and taking \(\max_a\) on both sides gives \((Tv)(s)\le(Tw)(s)\).



↑ Go Up: Section 6.3.1, Section 6.2.1, Section 7.3


6.3.3 Why do non-negative matrices preserve element-wise order?
Proposition. If \(B\ge0\) (elementally) and \(v\le w\), then \(Bv\le Bw\).






NoteProof





If \(d=w-v\ge0\), then it is \((Bd)(i)=\sum_jB_{ij}d_j\ge0\).









TipSignificance






\(\gamma P^\pi\), \((\gamma P^\pi)^n\), and \((I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\) are all nasal sounds, so the order is preserved.
On the other hand, \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) itself contains negative elements and does not preserve order. It should not be multiplied to both sides of the inequality.
The elemental order is partial order. \(v\not\le w\) does not mean \(v>w\).




↑ Go Up: Section 6.3.1, Section 4.5, Section 8.2

text:
6.4 What is the reason why \(T\) can be used as the action max instead of the policy max?
Proposition. \(\max_\pi\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\,q(s,a)=\max_aq(s,a)\).
Answer. Since the left side is a convex combination of \(q(s,\cdot)\), it cannot exceed \(\max_aq\). Equality holds in the Dirac distribution where mass is concentrated on the argmax behavior.






TipSignificance






Because of this max, \(T\) is nonlinear with respect to \(v\). \(T^\pi\) is affine.
Therefore, policy evaluation can be solved using the inverse matrix, but optimal value cannot. Iteration (VI), LP, and PI are used.

section: 6.5 Why is the greedy policy optimal for \(v^*\) and why is stationary sufficient?
text:
6.5 Why is the greedy policy optimal for \(v^*\) and why is stationary sufficient?
Proposition. If \(S\) and \(A\) are finite, then a deterministic stationary optimal policy exists. The following is an example. \[\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s')\Big]\]
Answer. Since \(T^{\pi^*}v^*=Tv^*=v^*\), \(v^*\) is the fixed point of \(T^{\pi^*}\). Since the unique fixed point of \(T^{\pi^*}\) is \(v^{\pi^*}\), it is \(v^{\pi^*}=v^*\).






NoteProof (Basis for each equality)






\(T^{\pi^*}v^*=Tv^*\): This is because \(\pi^*\) is greedy with respect to \(v^*\)(Section 6.5.1).
\(Tv^*=v^*\): \(v^*\) is a solution to the Bellman equation(Section 6.1).
\(v^*=v^{\pi^*}\): \(T^{\pi^*}\) is a contraction, so the fixed point is unique, and it is \(v^{\pi^*}\)(Section 5.5).










TipSignificance






This is the basis for considering only stationary policies in an infinite discount setup. It is optimal even if the same decision rule is used at every step. However, since the state changes, the action changes at every step.
With just \(v^*\), the optimal policy can be obtained immediately. This is the precise meaning of the statement, “If you find \(v^*\), the MDP is solved.”
Hidden Complexity: When extracting the policy, argmax must be solved for every state, and model \(p\) is needed for this → Section 8.7.1




↓ Down: Section 6.5.1, Section 5.5 ↑ Up: Section 6.1

6.5.1 Why does the greedy equation \(T^{\pi_v}v=Tv\) hold?
Answer. Since \(\pi_v(s)\) is the argmax of parentheses \(q_v(s,\cdot)\), it is \((T^{\pi_v}v)(s)=q_v(s,\pi_v(s))=\max_aq_v(s,a)=(Tv)(s)\).






TipSignificance and Pitfalls






This equation holds only when \(v\) is substituted. In general, it is \(T^{\pi_v}w\ne Tw\).
Conversely, for any \(\pi\), \(T^\pi v\le Tv\) always holds.
Both the monotonic enhancement and the proof of convergence of PI stand on this equation.




↑ Go Up: Section 6.5, Section 6.3.1, Section 7.3, Section 7.4

section: 7.1 Why do both VI and PI reach the optimal?
text:
7.1 Why do both VI and PI reach the optimal?
Answer.

VI: Since \(T\) is a contraction, by Banach’s theorem (2) it is \(v_k\to v^*\).
PI: Policy improvement monotonically increases the value. Since the value is bounded, a limit exists, and the policy value obtained at that limit is a solution to the Bellman equation.

↓ Down: Section 7.2 VI · Section 7.3 PI Monotonic Enhancement · Section 7.4 PI Convergence · Section 7.5 Compare · Section 7.6 RL Genealogy ↑ Up: Section 6.1

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 7.2 Why does VI: \(v_{k+1}=Tv_k\) converge, and what is the cost?
text:
7.2 Why does VI: \(v_{k+1}=Tv_k\) converge, and what is the cost?
Answer. By Banach’s theorem (2) and Section 6.1, it is \(v_k\to v^*\). The convergence rate is \(\|v_k-v^*\|\le\gamma^k\|v_0-v^*\|\).






TipSignificance






The policy evaluation iteration and template are the same. The only difference is that \(T\) is used instead of \(T^\pi\).
So in every iteration, action maximization is added in every state.
Difference from finite horizon: Since there is no terminal condition, neither the starting point nor the number of iterations is fixed. It runs until convergence, and the number of iterations depends on the initialization. Since the shape of the optimal value is not intuitive, it is usually initialized to 0 or a random vector.
After convergence, the policy is obtained as a greedy approach to \(v^*\)(Section 6.5). Even if the value has not yet converged, the greedy policy may have reached the optimal state first.




↓ Down: Section 6.2.3, Section 6.2.4 ↑ Up: Section 7.1

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
text:
7.3 PI: Why \(v^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}\)?
PI repeats two steps.

Policy Evaluation: \(v^{\pi_k}=T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\).
Policy Improvement: \(\pi_{k+1}(s)\in\arg\max_a\big[r+\gamma\sum p\,v^{\pi_k}\big]\).

Answer. If the operator of the new policy is applied once to the old value, it is greater than the old value. If this is repeated infinitely due to monotonicity, the limit is the new value.






NoteProof





Combine three facts.


Evaluation step: \(v^{\pi_k}=T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\).


Enhancement step: Since \(\pi_{k+1}\) is greedy for \(v^{\pi_k}\), \(T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}=Tv^{\pi_k}\) (Section 6.5.1).


Definition of \(T\): \(T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\le Tv^{\pi_k}\).


Therefore, it is \(v^{\pi_k}=T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\le Tv^{\pi_k}=T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}\).
By repeatedly applying the monotonicity of \(T^{\pi_{k+1}}\) to both sides, \(v^{\pi_k}\le(T^{\pi_{k+1}})^\ell v^{\pi_k}\) holds for all \(\ell\). By the contraction of \(T^{\pi_{k+1}}\) (Section 5.5), the right-hand side converges to \(v^{\pi_{k+1}}\) at \(\ell\to\infty\).









TipSignificance





“Improvement” is justified as the performance of the policy, that is, the element-wise increase of the value function. The key is the interpretation of step (b). \(v^{\pi_k}\) is placed on the right side of the Bellman equation as if it were the optimal value, and its argmax is taken out as the policy.



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

title: SCRL Midterm: Top-down Question Tree
section: 7.4 Why does PI converge to the optimal policy?
text:
7.4 Why does PI converge to the optimal policy?
Answer. It leads to five steps.

The value sequence is monotonically non-decreasing(Section 7.3).
Value is bounded(Section 7.4.1).
By the monotonic convergence theorem, the limit \(\bar v\) exists.
If we denote the greedy policy for \(\bar v\) as \(\bar\pi\), then \(v^{\bar\pi}=Tv^{\bar\pi}\) holds.
Therefore, it is \(v^{\bar\pi}=v^*\) by Section 6.1.







NoteProof





If you set it to \(\bar\pi(s)\in\arg\max_a[r+\gamma\sum p\,\bar v]\) \[v^{\bar\pi}=T^{\bar\pi}v^{\bar\pi}=T^{\bar\pi}\bar v=T\bar v=Tv^{\bar\pi}.\]

The first equal sign is the definition of policy evaluation.
The second and fourth equal signs are written as \(\bar v=v^{\bar\pi}\).
The third equality is a greedy equation.

Basis for \(\bar v=v^{\bar\pi}\). There are only \(m^n\) deterministic stationary policies. Therefore, PI reaches the point \(\pi_{k+1}=\pi_k\) within a finite number of moves, at which point it becomes \(\bar v=v^{\pi_k}\) and \(\bar\pi=\pi_k\). To achieve this, a tie-breaking rule is required: if the current action is at argmax, keep it. Otherwise, cycle between equally optimal policies.



↓ Down: Section 7.4.1, Section 6.5.1 ↑ Up: Section 7.1

7.4.1 Monotonic Convergence Theorem and Value Boundness
Answer.

Monotonic Convergence Theorem: A sequence of monotonically non-decreasing and bounded real vectors has a finite limit.
Boundness: Since \(S\) and \(A\) are finite, it is \(|r(s,a)|\le M\). Therefore \[|v^\pi(s)|\le\sum_t\gamma^tM=\frac{M}{1-\gamma}.\]







TipSignificance





All three assumptions of the infinite discount setup are used here: stationary \(r\) and \(p\), finite \(S\) and \(A\) (hence the reward being bounded), \(\gamma<1\). It is a neat setup where there is no concern about the accumulated reward diverging.

8.2 Proof






NoteProof





Take an arbitrary optimal solution \(v_{\rm opt}\).
(i) \(v_{\rm opt}\ge Tv_{\rm opt}\). If you repeatedly apply \(T\) with monotony \[v_{\rm opt}\ge Tv_{\rm opt}\ge T^2v_{\rm opt}\ge\cdots\to v^*\] Since , we have \(v_{\rm opt}\ge v^*\). The limit comes from Banach’s theorem. (You can also use the comparison lemma Section 6.3.1 directly.)
(ii) Since \(v^*=Tv^*\), \(v^*\) is feasible. Since \(v_{\rm opt}\) is the minimum solution, \(c^\top v^*\ge c^\top v_{\rm opt}\).
(iii) From (i) and \(c>0\), we get \(c^\top v_{\rm opt}\ge c^\top v^*\). When combined with (ii), we get \(c^\top(v_{\rm opt}-v^*)=0\). Since \(v_{\rm opt}-v^*\ge0\) and \(c>0\), we get \(v_{\rm opt}=v^*\).
The logic of (i) applies to all feasible \(v\). Therefore, the existence of an optimal solution is also guaranteed.

8.3 How is this problem an LP?
Answer. The constraint \(v(s)\ge\max_a[\cdots]\) is nonlinear due to the max. However, this is equivalent to “\(a\)Z for all \(v(s)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\)”. When written this way, both sides are affine for \(v\), so it becomes an LP.






TipSignificance






The number of variables remains \(n\), while the number of constraints increases from \(n\) to \(nm\).
LP is quickly solved by mature solvers such as interior-point and simplex.
In large-scale problems, the number of constraints is a burden.

8.4 What is the role of \(c\)
Answer. \(c_i\) is the weight assigned to the \(i\)-th element of the value. If \(c_i\) is increased, the search proceeds in the direction of further decreasing \(v_i\). If there is no prior knowledge of the optimal value, it is set to \(c=\mathbf{1}\).






TipSignificance (Refinement)





In an exact LP, as long as it is \(c>0\), the solution is always the same as \(v^*\)(Section 8.2). That is, \(c\) does not change the solution but only affects numerical efficiency. \(c\) changes the solution when \(v^*\) cannot be accurately represented as in an approximate LP, at which time \(c\) becomes the weight of the state-specific approximation error.

8.6 dual LP: How is it derived and why is it preferred?
Proposition. \[\max_{\lambda\ge0}\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad c(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,p(s'\mid s,a)-\sum_a\lambda(s',a)=0\ \ \forall s'.\]
Answer. If we organize the Lagrangian by the coefficients of \(v(s')\), we get \(\min_vL=-\infty\) when the coefficients are not 0. Therefore, “coefficients = 0” becomes a constraint of dual, and the remaining term \(\sum\lambda r\) becomes the objective function of dual.






NoteInduction





Lagrangian is as follows. \[L(v,\lambda)=\sum_sc(s)\,v(s)+\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')-v(s)\Big],\quad\lambda\ge0.\] To summarize \(v\) \[L=\sum_{s,a}\lambda r+\sum_{s'}v(s')\Big[c(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,p(s'\mid s,a)-\sum_a\lambda(s',a)\Big].\] If there is a non-zero bracket \(s'\), \(v(s')\) is moved to one side, becoming \(L\to-\infty\). Therefore, it is \(g(\lambda)=\min_vL=\sum\lambda r\), and the condition is the bracket \(=0\).









TipSignificance






dual is also an LP (linear with respect to λ).
There is no duality gap. Even when solving the dual, the exact optimal value is obtained.
The number of variables increases to \(nm\), but the number of constraints is reduced to \(n\). In LP, fewer constraints are usually computationally preferred.

text:
8.7 What is the Q-function, and which Bellman equation does it satisfy?
Answer. Two definitions and two relational expressions.

Definition: \(Q^*(s,a)=\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi[\sum\gamma^tr\mid s_0=s,a_0=a]\). This is the maximum expected value of the cumulative reward obtained after fixing the current action at \(a\).
Relation: \(v^*(s)=\max_aQ^*(s,a)\).
Bellman equation: \[Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s')=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a').\]
operator \(T_Q\) is monotonic and contracted, and is \(Q^*=T_QQ^*\).







TipSignificance: Its structure is different from the Bellman formula of v.






\(v\) Formula: max is outside the sum (choose the current action).
\(Q\) Formula: max is in the sum (choose the next action of the next state).

This difference creates a difference in the number of LP constraints → Section 8.7.2



↓ Down: Section 8.7.1, Section 8.7.2, Section 8.7.3, Section 11.2 ↑ Up: Section 8.1

8.7.1 Why does RL learn \(Q\) instead of \(v\)?
Answer. You just need to compare the formulas that extract the policy.

From \(v^*\): \(\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a[r+\gamma\sum p\,v^*]\). Models \(p\) and \(r\) are required.
From \(Q^*\): \(\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a)\). No model needed.

Even if we diligently train \(v^*\) in a model-free manner, a model is still needed when creating a policy. Therefore, we train \(Q\), which contains more information. The cost is that the training target has grown from \(n\) to \(nm\), requiring a larger sample size.
↑ Go Up: Section 8.7, Section 11.5


8.7.2 Why Q-LP is Inefficient
Answer. \(\min\sum c(s,a)\,Q(s,a)\) st The solution to \(Q\ge T_QQ\) is \(Q^*\). However, since the max is bound by \(a'\) inside the sum, to solve the max, we must apply the constraint \(Q(s,a)\ge r+\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,Q(s',a')\) to all \((s,a,a')\). The number of constraints increases to \(nm^2\).
↑ Go Up: Section 8.7


8.7.3 To what extent is Q-based PI model-free?
Answer.

Evaluation: Calculate \(Q^\pi\) using LP. Since there is no max in the constraint \(Q(s,a)\ge r+\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,Q(s',\pi(s'))\), \(nm\) is sufficient.
Enhancement: \(\pi(s)\in\arg\max_aQ(s,a)\). No model needed. The enhancement stage of the existing PI required a model for the bracket \(r+\gamma\sum p\,v^{\pi_k}\), because the entire bracket is \(Q^{\pi_k}(s,a)\).
Data-driven evaluation: Collect transition samples \((s,a,r,s')\) from each \((s,a)\), and approximate the expected value to the sample mean \(\frac1{|D|}\sum_{s'\in D}Q(s',\pi(s'))\). Then, the model becomes free up to the evaluation stage.

9.1 How to Solve Fixed-Point Equations Without a Model
Answer. Let’s assume that even if we cannot accurately calculate \(Hx\) from \(Hx=x\), we can observe the noisy value \(Hx_k+w_k\). Then write the following iteration. \[x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_k(Hx_k+w_k)\] If the step size and noise satisfy appropriate conditions, the influence of the noise disappears in the long term, resulting in \(x_k\to x^*\).






TipSignificance





This is the theoretical framework of value-based RL algorithms. Both TD and Q-learning have the same structure: “Bellman fixed-point equation + noisy right-hand side formed from a single sample”.

9.2 Why VI·PI cannot be used directly in RL settings
Answer. In the definition of VI’s \(T\), the transition probability \(p\) is included in both the evaluation (\(P^\pi\)) and enhancement (\(\sum p\,v\)) of PI. In RL, \(p\) (and sometimes \(r\) as well) is unknown, and there are only transition samples obtained through trial and error.






TipSignificance and Pitfalls






Stochastic transitions themselves are not the problem. VI accurately handles stochastic transitions as expected values. The problem is that there is no model to calculate those expected values.
Two limitations of DP: knowledge of the model, scalability (curse of dimensionality).
Reasons why RL is useful: Flexibility (no model required), Adaptability (does not rely on a fixed model), Scalability (aims for approximate solutions from the start).
Reasons why RL is difficult: Limited knowledge, exploration–exploitation, limited expressiveness.
Characteristics of RL: No leader, delayed feedback, data is not iid, actions change subsequent data, exploration–exploitation trade-off.

9.3 SA form: \(\alpha\) and what is the meaning of the step direction?
Answer. The form for each coordinate is as follows. \[x_{k+1}(i)=(1-\alpha_k(i))\,x_k(i)+\alpha_k(i)\big[(Hx_k)(i)+w_k(i)\big]\] \(\alpha\) is the learning rate or innovation rate, giving weights of \(1-\alpha\) to the old estimate and \(\alpha\) to the new estimate. Summarizing, since it is \(x_{k+1}(i)=x_k(i)+\alpha_k(i)\big[(Hx_k)(i)-x_k(i)+w_k(i)\big]\), the step direction is \((Hx_k)(i)-x_k(i)+w_k(i)\). Assumption: For each \(i\), there are infinitely many \(k\) which is \(\alpha_k(i)>0\).

9.4 Is Robbins–Monro a special case of SA?
Answer. View the Bellman equation as \(x=\mathbb{E}[f(x,\xi)]\). Using the mean of \(N\) samples at every step makes calculations and data inefficient. Instead, using only one sample is Robbins–Monroe. \[x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_kf(x_k,\hat\xi).\] If we map SA, it is as follows. \[Hx_k=\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)],\qquad w_k=f(x_k,\hat\xi)-\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)].\]






TipSignificance






The noise \(w_k\) has an average of 0. Therefore, the first condition of the noise condition (conditional average 0) is naturally satisfied.
TD(0), TD(λ), and Q-learning are all of this form. For each algorithm, you only need to specify “what is \(f\) and what is \(\hat\xi\)”.

9.5 Why are the step size conditions \(\sum\alpha=\infty\), \(\sum\alpha^2<\infty\) necessary?
Answer. Each condition blocks one failure mode.






NoteOption I: Constant step size → Convergence failed





Let ZZZPH0014794ZZZ \(w_k(i)\) be the variance of \(\sigma^2\) and be independent of \(x_k\). \[\mathrm{Var}(x_{k+1}(i))=\mathrm{Var}\big((1-\alpha)x_k(i)+\alpha(Hx_k)(i)\big)+\alpha^2\sigma^2\ \ge\ \alpha^2\sigma^2.\] The variance does not disappear. Therefore, even if it reaches the vicinity of \(x^*\), it moves randomly within that range. To eventually reduce the influence of noise, the step size must be reduced. \(\sum\alpha^2<\infty\) is what prevents this failure.









NoteOption II: Step size shrinking too fast → Escape failure





Let \(\sum\alpha_k\) be finite and the step direction be bounded. \[|x_k(i)-x_0(i)|\le\sum_{\tau<k}\alpha_\tau(i)\,\big|(Hx_\tau)(i)-x_\tau(i)+w_\tau(i)\big|\le\text{상수}.\] \(x_k\) cannot go beyond the fixed radius centered on \(x_0\). If \(x^*\) is outside of it, it cannot be reached. What prevents this failure is \(\sum\alpha=\infty\).

section: 9.6 What is the noise condition, and what does the convergence theorem mean?
text:
9.6 What is the noise condition, and what does the convergence theorem mean?
Answer. Let \(\mathcal{F}_k\) be the history up to step \(k\) (\(x_0,\dots,x_k\), \(w_0,\dots,w_{k-1}\), step size). There are two noise conditions.

Conditional average 0: \(\mathbb{E}[w_k(i)\mid\mathcal{F}_k]=0\).
Conditional variance limit: \(\mathbb{E}[w_k(i)^2\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\le C_0+C_1\|x_k\|^2\).

There are two convergence theorems.

Theorem 1 (Reduction): step size condition + noise condition + \(H\) reduction ⇒ probability 1 \(x_k\to x^*\).
Theorem 2 (Monotonic): Under three assumptions, if \(x_k\) is bounded with probability 1, then \(x_k\to x^*\) has probability 1. The three assumptions are as follows.

\(H\) is a monoton.
The fixed point is unique.
For all \(\eta>0\) \(Hx-\eta\mathbf{1}\le H(x-\eta\mathbf{1})\le H(x+\eta\mathbf{1})\le Hx+\eta\mathbf{1}\).








TipSignificance






For each algorithm, the order of verifying assumptions is more important than the proof of the theorem itself. The order is as follows: \(H\) specification → fixed point of the goal \(H\) → contraction of \(H\) → definition of \(w\) and conditional mean 0 → second moment limit → step size and visit condition. The convergence proofs of both TD(λ) and Q-learning follow this order.
Intuition: The noise must be conditionally unbiased and the variance appropriately bounded for the influence of the noise not to persist within the iterations.

10.2 Monte Carlo Policy Evaluation: What Are the Strengths and Limitations?
Answer. Generate \(M\) trajectories of length \(T\) that are negligible for \(\gamma^T\). Estimate \(v^\pi(x_0)\) using the sample mean of the cumulative reward \(c^\pi(x_0,m)=\sum_{t<T}\gamma^tr\big(s^{(m)}_t,\pi(s^{(m)}_t)\big)\) per trajectory. The incremental types are \(v(s)\leftarrow v(s)+\alpha_m\big(c(s,m)-v(s)\big)\) and \(\alpha_m=1/m\).






NoteWhy the incremental type is the same as the sample mean





\(v_m=v_{m-1}+\frac1m(c_m-v_{m-1})=\frac{(m-1)v_{m-1}+c_m}{m}\). Inductively, \(v_m=\frac1m\sum_{j\le m}c_j\).









TipSignificance






Advantage: It is an unbiased estimator.
Limit: Large variance. Since \(c\) can only be calculated after the trajectory ends, it is model-free but not online.

text:
10.3 How does TD(0) come out?
Answer. Replace the expected value of the policy evaluation equation \(v^\pi(s_t)=\mathbb{E}\big[r(s_t,\pi(s_t))+\gamma v^\pi(s_{t+1})\big]\) with the next observed state (Robbins–Monro). \[v(s_t)\leftarrow(1-\alpha_t)\,v(s_t)+\alpha_t\big(r_t+\gamma v(s_{t+1})\big)=v(s_t)+\alpha_t\underbrace{\big(r_t+\gamma v(s_{t+1})-v(s_t)\big)}_{d_t\ (\text{temporal difference})}.\]






TipSignificance






\(d_t\) is “new estimate − old estimate”. Since this is the difference between the estimate viewed at time \(t+1\) and the estimate at \(t\), it is called the temporal difference.
It is completely incremental. Since only one visited state is updated, a lookup table is required, and the entire learning process is slow.
Lightest. Only one transition sample \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\) is needed.
It is completely online. It updates whenever samples come in.
Notation Note: \(s_{t+1}\) in the expectation formula is a random variable, and \(s_{t+1}\) in the update formula is an observed sample.
In episode types with a termination state, set the subsequent term to 0: target value \(r_t+\gamma(1-\text{done})\,v(s_{t+1})\).

section: 10.4 How a multi-stage Bellman equation changes into TD form
text:
10.4 How a multi-stage Bellman equation changes into TD form
Proposition. If we set it as \(d_k=r_k+\gamma v(s_{k+1})-v(s_k)\) \[v(s_t)=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{k\ge t}(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k\ \Big|\ \mathcal{F}_t\Big]+v(s_t).\]
Answer. \((\ell+1)\)-step Bellman formula. Average the \(v(s_t)=\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}\gamma^kr_{t+k}+\gamma^{\ell+1}v(s_{t+\ell+1})\mid\mathcal{F}_t\big]\)s by the weight \((1-\lambda)\lambda^\ell\). Then rearrange the order of the sums.






NoteInduction





Below is \(r_{t+k}=r(s_{t+k},a_{t+k})\).
Step 1. Multiply \((1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell\ge0}\lambda^\ell=1\). \[v(s_t)=(1-\lambda)\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{\ell\ge0}\lambda^\ell\Big(\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}\gamma^kr_{t+k}+\gamma^{\ell+1}v(s_{t+\ell+1})\Big)\ \Big|\ \mathcal{F}_t\Big].\]
Step 2 (Reward term). If you change the order of the sums, the inner sum starts from \(\ell=k\). If you use \((1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell\ge k}\lambda^\ell=\lambda^k\) \[(1-\lambda)\sum_{\ell\ge0}\lambda^\ell\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}\gamma^kr_{t+k}=\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda^k\gamma^kr_{t+k}.\]
Step 3 (Value term). Split into \((1-\lambda)\lambda^\ell=\lambda^\ell-\lambda^{\ell+1}\). \[\sum_{\ell\ge0}(\lambda^\ell-\lambda^{\ell+1})\gamma^{\ell+1}v(s_{t+\ell+1})=\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda^k\gamma^{k+1}v(s_{t+k+1})-\sum_{k\ge1}\lambda^k\gamma^kv(s_{t+k}).\] If you change the sum after to \(k\ge0\), you must add the term \(v(s_t)\) again.
Step 4 (Merge). \[v(s_t)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k\ge0}(\lambda\gamma)^k\big(r_{t+k}+\gamma v(s_{t+k+1})-v(s_{t+k})\big)\ \Big|\ \mathcal{F}_t\Big]+v(s_t).\] If you move the exponent to \(k\to k-t\), it becomes a proposition.









TipSignificance





Although somewhat artificial, this is also a fixed-point equation. Therefore, SA can be applied.

text:
10.5 TD(λ) How is the update equation derived?
Answer. Apply Robbins–Monro to the right side of Section 10.4. \[v(s_t)\leftarrow(1-\alpha_t)\,v(s_t)+\alpha_t\Big(\sum_{k\ge t}(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k+v(s_t)\Big)\ \Longrightarrow\ v(s_t)\leftarrow v(s_t)+\alpha_t\sum_{k\ge t}(\lambda\gamma)^{k-t}d_k.\] In the process of grouping into \(\alpha\), the preceding and succeeding \(v(s_t)\) are canceled out.






TipSignificance






Still only updates one cell at a time.
Since the future TD error of \(k\ge t\) is needed, if it is \(\lambda>0\), update after collecting the trajectory to some extent. Only TD(0) is completely online.

10.6 What is TD(λ) for λ=0 and λ=1, respectively?
Answer.

\(\lambda=0\): \(0^0=1\) by convention \(v(s_t)\leftarrow v(s_t)+\alpha\,d_t\). TD(0)
\(\lambda=1\): \(t=0\) to \(v(s_0)\leftarrow v(s_0)+\alpha\sum_k\gamma^kd_k\). corresponds to Monte Carlo.







NoteReason why λ=1 is Monte Carlo (Telescopic sum)





\[\sum_{k\ge0}\gamma^kd_k=\sum_k\gamma^kr_k+\sum_k\big(\gamma^{k+1}v(s_{k+1})-\gamma^kv(s_k)\big)=\sum_k\gamma^kr_k-v(s_0)\quad(\gamma^Kv(s_K)\to0).\] Therefore, \(v(s_0)\leftarrow v(s_0)+\alpha\,(c-v(s_0))\) and \(c=\sum\gamma^kr_k\). This is equivalent to the Monte Carlo incremental expression (Section 10.2).

10.7 λ is chosen
Answer.

Large λ (MC side): Small bias and large variance.
Small λ(TD(0) side): Large bias and small variance.

Usually, we start with a large λ and reduce it to 0. Since TD(λ) converges, the quality of \(v\) improves as we progress, and then a small λ that reuses existing estimates becomes advantageous.






TipSignificance: Two states example





Let’s assume there are states 1 and 2, \(p_{12}>0\) and \(p_{21}=0\), and that each trajectory visits 1 exactly once.

The cumulative reward \(c(1,m)\) of TD(1) is the bias estimator of \(v^\pi(1)\).
However, let’s assume that there is already an accurate estimate of \(v^\pi(2)\). TD(1) cannot use this information for \(v^\pi(1)\) training. TD(0) uses this information efficiently while also reducing noise in the \(r_t\) sample.

The learning curve can be interpreted along the same axis. TD(1) has large variance because it uses the sample returns of the entire trajectory. TD(0) has small variance because it uses one step sample and the current estimate, but there is bias if the initial estimate is wrong.

text:
11.1 Q-learning is a model-free, off-policy algorithm that converges to \(Q^*\) under conditions.
Answer. This is the result of applying Robbins–Monro SA to \(Q^*=T_QQ^*\). The update formula is as follows. \[Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha_t\Big[r_t+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')-Q(s_t,a_t)\Big]\] The convergence condition for is the infinite visitation of all \((s,a)\) and the step size condition. Actions may be chosen using an arbitrary policy (off-policy).






TipSignificance: Summary






If you derive only the Bellman equation for Q, a fully online and model-free algorithm is immediately obtained using SA.
Since it is off-policy, samples can be reused (experience replay, basis of DQN).
Limit 1, exploration: not completely solved by ε-greedy. Simple but not efficient.
Limit 2, Scalability: Since updates are performed one step at a time, learning becomes very slow even with a slight increase in the number of state-behavior pairs. Function approximation is required.

11.2 Why is \(T_Q\) monotonous and contracted?
Proposition. \((T_QQ)(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) is monotonic and for \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\)Z, \(\gamma\)-contraction.
Answer. Since max is within the sum, write the max difference inequality for each state and average it using the transition probabilities.






NoteProof





Abbreviation. \[|(T_QQ)(s,a)-(T_QQ')(s,a)|\le\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big|\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-\max_{a'}Q'(s',a')\Big|\le\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,\max_{a'}|Q-Q'|(s',a')\le\gamma\|Q-Q'\|_\infty.\] It ends when you take the max for \((s,a)\).
Monotonic. If \(Q\le Q'\), then each \(s'\)Z becomes \(\max_{a'}Q\le\max_{a'}Q'\)Z and \(p\ge0\), so the weighted sum also preserves order.

11.3 How to transition from model-based Q-VI to Q-learning update expressions
Answer. If the model is known, the Q-VI is \(Q_{k+1}=T_QQ_k\), and in each iteration, update all \((s,a)\) and write \(p\). If the model is not known, replace \(T_Q\)’s \(\sum_{s'}p\max Q\) with the observed \(s_{t+1}\) (Robbins–Monro). \[Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow(1-\alpha)\,Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha\Big[r_t+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\Big].\]






TipSignificance






All that is needed is one transition sample \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\), so it is online.
It is completely incremental because it updates only one cell at a time.
All the ideas: \(1-\alpha\) on the old estimate, and \(\alpha\) on the single-sample estimate on the Bellman right-hand side.

11.4 What is the procedure for calculating Q-learning by hand?
Answer. For each transition, follow the next order.

Calculate the target value \(y=r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) using the current table. If not yet terminated, the max term is 0.
Update \(Q(s,a)\leftarrow Q(s,a)+\alpha\,(y-Q(s,a))\). Leave the other cells as they are.
Rewrite the entire table. The next transition uses this updated table.







TipSignificance and Pitfalls






Within the same transition, the target value is calculated using the table prior to the update.
When directly solving \(Q^*\) in a deterministic environment, solve the Bellman equations \(Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\) as a system. Solve by assuming that a certain action is optimal, and verify whether that assumption holds.

11.5 How is the policy obtained after training, and why is a model unnecessary?

11.6 Why is Q-learning off-policy?
Answer. The target value \(\max_{a'}\) determines the learning target (greedy policy). On the other hand, the actual action taken when creating the sample can be selected using a random policy. Since the policy to be learned and the policy for creating the action can be different, it is off-policy.






TipSignificance





It has high flexibility. Updates are valid even when reusing already collected samples (experience replay).

section: 11.7 How Should Actions Be Chosen: The Problem of Greed and Exploration
text:
11.7 How Should Actions Be Chosen: The Problem of Greed and Exploration
Answer. If Q is nearly optimal, the greedy policy is optimal. However, Q is inaccurate during the early stages of learning. If only greedy is used at this point, some \((s,a)\) states will not be visited at all. Even if all states are visited, some beneficial actions may never be attempted. This breaks the assumption of “infinite visits to every pair,” and convergence to the optimal Q is not guaranteed. Therefore, we search by sacrificing some of the immediate greedy gain.






TipSignificance: Search method






ε-greedy: Greedy behavior with probability \(1-\epsilon\), random behavior with probability \(\epsilon\). It is the most widely used because it is simple and easy to schedule. It is not used because it is efficient.
Segment Switching: Alternates between a search segment (random) and a greedy segment.
Boltzmann: \(\Pr(a\mid s)=\frac{\exp(Q(s,a)/T)}{\sum_{a'}\exp(Q(s,a')/T)}\), \(T>0\) are temperatures. If \(T\to0\), it is greedy; if \(T\to\infty\), it is uniform.
ε Schedule: Starts with a large ε and reduces it. Since there is no information at the beginning, it focuses on exploration to improve the quality of value.
The root of the exploration–exploitation trade-off is a lack of knowledge regarding system dynamics and compensation structures.




↓ Down: Section 11.7.1 ↑ Up: Section 11.1

11.7.1 What is the probability that each action is selected in ε-greedy?
Answer. When searching, if even sampling is performed from the entire set of actions, the probability when the greedy action is unique is as follows.

greedy behavior: \(1-\epsilon+\epsilon/|A|\) (A greedy behavior can be selected even during a search).
Remaining actions: \(\epsilon/|A|\).







TipTrap






The answer varies depending on whether the search is performed “among non-greedy actions” or “among the whole.” Check the problem definition first.
greedy If there is a tie in behavior, specify the tie handling rule (e.g., equality between tied behaviors) first.
