The central question of this topic is one: What must be learned to solve the optimality equation without a model, for each transition, and to which fixed-point equation is that learning applied the Robbins–Monroe algorithm? The algorithm is as simple as TD(0). It assigns weights \(1-\alpha\) to the old estimate and \(\alpha\) to the single-sample estimate on the right-hand side of the Bellman equation. The weight of understanding is placed in three places: (i) why \(Q^*\) rather than \(v^*\), (ii) why the action can be chosen with any policy (off-policy), and (iii) why search is still a problem. The convergence theorem is treated at the level of results and proof ideas.
Common notation:

discounted MDP \(\langle S,A,p,r,\gamma\rangle\), \(S\) and \(A\) are finite, \(\gamma\in(0,1)\).
\(Q^*\): Optimal Q-function. \(Q\): Estimator being trained (state-action lookup table).
Transition data \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\), \(r_t=r(s_t,a_t)\), \(s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)\).
\(T\): Bellman operator for Q-function. \(\mathcal F_t\): history up to time \(t\) (including action \(a_t\)).
\(\alpha_t(s,a)\): Step size of cell \((s,a)\). Cells not updated at time \(t\) are \(0\).
\(\|Q\|_\infty:=\max_{s,a}|Q(s,a)|\). The reward is the spirit world, \(|r|\le R_{\max}\).
\(\varepsilon\): ε-greedy search probability. \(\tau>0\): Boltzmann search temperature (written as \(\tau\) to distinguish it from the operator \(T\)).

title: Q-Learning
section: 3.1 Can the optimality equation be solved without a model?
text:
3.1 Can the optimality equation be solved without a model?
First question to consider. TD(0) was obtained by replacing the expected value of the policy evaluation equation \(v=T^\pi v\) with a single sample. What happens if we apply the same operation to the optimality equation \(v=Tv\)? And even if we obtain \(v^*\), what is required again when selecting a policy?
Answer. The problem to be solved
\[
\max_\pi\ \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\Big]
\]
and the optimization target is policy. What is desired is a model-free variant of VI·PI. \(v=Tv\) has two stumbling blocks.

max is outside the expected value. \(v(s)=\max_a\big[r(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[v(s')\mid s,a]\big]\). With a single sample, it is impossible to create a bias-free “max value by comparing the expected values for each action” → Section 4.2.2
The model is needed again for policy extraction. \(\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s')]\) → Section 5.3.1

Solving the two problems at once is learning the state-action value function \(Q^*\). In the Bellman equation of \(Q^*\), the max falls inside the expectation value, and policy extraction is performed without a model as \(\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a)\).






TipSignificance





Q-learning is the first and most representative of the RL algorithms we will see, and it is the foundation of many algorithms such as DQN. However, there are almost no new ideas. It is simply the application of the TD operation of “writing the Bellman equation in the form of expectations and converting expectations into samples” to the equation \(Q^*\). What is new is the choice of what to apply it to.

title: Q-Learning
text:
4.1 What is \(Q^*\)
First question to consider. \(v^*(s)\) is the “expected cumulative reward when doing one’s best, starting from state \(s\)”. If we group the first action into \(a\), what is the quantity? What if we maximize that with respect to \(a\)?
Answer. The optimal Q-function is the maximum expected cumulative reward that can be obtained starting from state \(s\) and fixing the first action to \(a\).
\[
Q^*(s,a):=\max_\pi Q^\pi(s,a)=\max_\pi\ \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\,\Big|\,s_0=s,\ a_0=a\Big].
\]
The argument is not a single state, but a (state, action) pair. Policy \(\pi\) determines only the action of \(t\ge1\), and \(a_0=a\) is enforced. Directly from the definition
\[
\boxed{\,v^*(s)=\max_{a\in A}Q^*(s,a).\,}
\]
Maximizing the optimal value with respect to the first action again results in the optimal value free up to the first action → Section 4.2.1
↓ Down: Section 4.1.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.1.1 ✍ The relationship between \(Q^\pi\) and \(v^\pi\)
Regarding the normal deterministic policy \(\pi\), it is \(Q^\pi(s,a):=\mathbb{E}^\pi[\sum_t\gamma^tr_t\mid s_0=s,a_0=a]\).
Guide Question:

What is the relationship between \(Q^\pi(s,\pi(s))\) and \(v^\pi(s)\)?
Decompose \(Q^\pi(s,a)\) into the immediate reward and the value of the next state.
Compare the sizes of the tables. How many digits are there in \(v^\pi\) and \(Q^\pi\), respectively?







NoteSolution





If the first action is fixed as the action that ZZZPH0013756ZZZ 1. If the first action is fixed as the action that \(\pi\) chooses, it is the same as following the policy exactly. \[
Q^\pi(s,\pi(s))=v^\pi(s).
\]
2. The reward for the first step, \(r(s,a)\), is determined when \((s,a)\) is determined. After that, it is \(s_1\sim p(\cdot\mid s,a)\), and since \(s_1\) follows \(\pi\), the conditional expectation of its tail is \(v^\pi(s_1)\) due to the Markov property. \[
Q^\pi(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi(s').
\] It has the same structure as value decomposition. The only difference is that the first action is not \(\pi(s)\) but an arbitrary \(a\).
3. \(v^\pi\) contains \(|S|\) samples, and \(Q^\pi\) contains \(|S||A|\) samples. \(Q\) contains more information. Accordingly, it requires more samples for training.









TipSignificance





Equation 2 is the starting point of the next node. If the optimal policy is inserted into \(\pi\), it becomes \(Q^*=r+\gamma Pv^*\) → Section 4.2.1



↑ Go Up: Section 4.1

title: Q-Learning
text:
4.2 Bellman equation of \(Q^*\)
First question to consider. If value decomposition is applied to \(Q^*(s,a)\), what fixes the immediate reward part and what becomes the remainder? Can that remainder be rewritten as \(Q^*\)?
Answer. Since action \(a\) is fixed, the immediate reward \(r(s,a)\) is fixed. The remainder is the expected value of the optimal value from the next state, and since \(v^*(s')=\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\),
\[
Q^*(s,a)=\underbrace{r(s,a)}_{\text{immediate reward}}+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}p(s'\mid s,a)\underbrace{v^*(s')}_{\text{optimal value of next state}}
=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'\in A}Q^*(s',a').
\]
Define the entire right-hand side as an operator.
\[
(TQ)(s,a):=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'\in A}Q(s',a').
\]
Then the Bellman equation is a fixed-point problem.
\[
\boxed{\,Q=TQ.\,}
\]
↓ Down: Section 4.2.1 · Section 4.2.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.2.1 ✍ Derivation: \(Q^*=r+\gamma Pv^*\) and \(v^*=\max Q^*\)
Guide Question:

Take \(\max_\pi\) from the decomposition of Section 4.1.1. Why is it \(\le r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s')\)?
Why does the equality hold? What result of MDP theory is required?
Show that maximizing the result of 1–2 for \(a\) yields \(v^*=\max_aQ^*\). Write the optimality equation \(v^*=Tv^*\).
Combine the two results to get \(Q^*=TQ^*\).







NoteSolution





1. For all \(\pi\) and \(s'\), since \(v^\pi(s')\le v^*(s')\) \[
Q^\pi(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^\pi(s')\le r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s').
\] The inequality holds even when taking \(\max_\pi\).
2. In the discounted MDP, there exists a stationary deterministic optimal policy \(\pi^*\) that is \(v^{\pi^*}=v^*\) simultaneously in all states. If we fix only the first move to \(a\) and follow \(s_1\) through \(\pi^*\), we reach the upper bound exactly. Therefore \[
Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s').
\] “Simultaneously” is the key. Regardless of the next state, the optimal value of that state must be obtainable with a single, consistent policy in order to raise each term within the expected value to \(v^*(s')\) simultaneously.
3. Maximizing the result of 2 for \(a\) \[
\max_aQ^*(s,a)=\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s')\Big]=(Tv^*)(s)=v^*(s).
\] The last equality is the optimality equation.
4. If we write 3 to \(s'\), we get \(v^*(s')=\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\). If we substitute this into 2, we get \(Q^*=TQ^*\).



↑ Go Up: Section 4.2


4.2.2 What is different from the equation \(v\): the position of the max
First question to consider. Where is \(\max\) located in each of the two equations? Why is that location critical for sample-based learning?
Answer.
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^*(s)&=\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}\big[v^*(s')\mid s,a\big]\Big]&&\text{max가 기댓값 \textbf{밖}},\\
Q^*(s,a)&=r(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\,\Big|\,s,a\Big]&&\text{max가 기댓값 \textbf{안}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The equation \(v\) covers the maximization of choosing an action from the current state. In the equation \(Q\), since the current action is already fixed as \(a\), the remaining maximization is how to optimally choose the next action from the next state. Since that choice is made after seeing the arrived \(s'\), \(\max\) falls within the expectation for \(s'\).






NoteRationale: What can be made without bias using a single sample?





Let’s assume one observation \((s,a,r,s')\) is given.

\(Q\) Page: Since \(r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) is a function of \(s'\sim p(\cdot\mid s,a)\), its conditional expectation is exactly \((TQ)(s,a)\). It is an unbiased single-sample estimate.
Page \(v\): To estimate \(\max_a\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\mid s,a]\), an expected value is needed for each action. However, only the result of a single action is observed at a time. If we take a sample for each action and substitute it with \(\max_a(\text{샘플}_a)\), then by Jensen \[
\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a X_a\big]\ \ge\ \max_a\mathbb{E}[X_a]
\] is biased upward. The order of the expected value and the max cannot be changed.










TipSignificance





Since max is within the expectation, the equation for \(Q^*\) becomes “Expectation = Sample Mean”, and Robbins–Monro can be applied directly → Section 5.1. This is the first reason for training \(Q^*\) instead of \(v^*\). The second reason is policy extraction → Section 5.3



↑ Go Up: Section 4.2

title: Q-Learning
text:
4.3 The monotoniness and contraction of \(T\)
First question to consider. What was the basis for \(T\) being monotonic and \(\gamma\) being contracted with respect to \(v\)? Does the same basis apply to \(T\) with respect to \(Q\)? What new inequality is needed?
Answer. The Bellman operator for the Q-function is also monotonic and is \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\)-contraction from \(\gamma\).
\[
Q\le Q'\ \Rightarrow\ TQ\le TQ',\qquad
\|TQ-TQ'\|_\infty\le\gamma\|Q-Q'\|_\infty.
\]
By the Banach fixed point theorem, the fixed point of \(T\) is unique, and it is \(Q^*\). Only one new inequality is required.
\[
\Big|\max_af(a)-\max_ag(a)\Big|\le\max_a|f(a)-g(a)|.
\]
↓ Down: Section 4.3.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.3.1 ✍ Proof
Guide Question:

Prove the max inequality above . Find the maximum point \(a_1\) of \(f\).
Show monotony.
Show the abbreviation . Where does \(r(s,a)\) go? Where is \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)=1\) used?







NoteSolution





If you set it as 1. \(a_1\in\arg\max_af(a)\) \[
\max_af-\max_ag\le f(a_1)-g(a_1)\le\max_a|f(a)-g(a)|.
\] If you swap the roles of \(f\) and \(g\), the opposite direction is the same.
2. If \(Q\le Q'\), then at each \(s'\)Z, it is \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\le\max_{a'}Q'(s',a')\). Since it is \(p\ge0\), the weighted sum also preserves order. Therefore, \(TQ\le TQ'\).
3. The compensation term is canceled out of the difference. \[
\big|(TQ)(s,a)-(TQ')(s,a)\big|
=\gamma\Big|\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-\max_{a'}Q'(s',a')\Big)\Big|
\le\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,\|Q-Q'\|_\infty=\gamma\|Q-Q'\|_\infty.
\] Write the triangle inequality and number 1 in the inequality sign, and finally write \(\sum_{s'}p=1\). Take the maximum for \((s,a)\) on the left side, and you are done.









TipSignificance





Concomitantness is used in two places. When the model is known, it guarantees the convergence of Q-VI → Section 4.4, and when the model is not known, it becomes the first axis of the convergence theorem when Q-learning is viewed as SA → Section 7.1.1



↑ Go Up: Section 4.3

title: Q-Learning
section: 4.4 When the model is known: Value iteration using Q-function
text:
4.4 When the model is known: Value iteration using Q-function
First question to consider. If \(Q=TQ\) is a contracted fixed-point problem, what is the simplest solution? Which part of the iteration uses transition probabilities?
Answer. Starting from an arbitrary \(Q_0\), repeatedly apply \(T\).

Initializes \(Q_0\).
For all \((s,a)\) \(Q_{k+1}(s,a)\leftarrow r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q_k(s',a')\).
\(k\leftarrow k+1\). Repeat until convergence.

Due to the conciseness of \(T\), it is \(\|Q_k-Q^*\|_\infty\le\gamma^k\|Q_0-Q^*\|_\infty\), and the converged Q-function is optimal. In every iteration, all \((s,a)\) are updated (synchronous).
The problem is that the transition probability is required for the calculation of the expected value in step 2, \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)(\cdot)\).
\[
\textbf{Q: How can we perform VI using samples?}
\]






NoteBasis: It is a repetition like the state value VI.





If you set it to \(v_k:=\max_aQ_k(\cdot,a)\) \[
v_{k+1}(s)=\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v_k(s')\Big]=(Tv_k)(s).
\] Q-VI is simply storing the “median value by action” in the state value VI.



↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Q-Learning
text:
5.1 Sample VI with Stochastic Approximation
First question to consider. In Step 2 of the Q-VI, to replace the expected value \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) with a single sample, which of the transition data \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\) should be inserted? Which cell can be modified with that sample?
Answer. Input the observed \(s_{t+1}\) as is. Weight the old estimate with \(1-\alpha\), and the new estimate (a single-sample estimate of the compensation signal \(r_t\) and the entire expectation) with \(\alpha\).
\[
Q(s_t,a_t):=(1-\alpha)\,Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha\Big[r_t+\gamma\max_{a'\in A}Q(s_{t+1},a')\Big].
\]
If you group it as \(\alpha\)
\[
\boxed{\,Q(s_t,a_t):=Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha\Big[\underbrace{r_t+\gamma\max_{a'\in A}Q(s_{t+1},a')}_{\text{new estimate}}-\underbrace{Q(s_t,a_t)}_{\text{old estimate}}\Big].\,}
\]
The part inside the parentheses is the learning direction, which is the same shape as the temporal difference of TD(0). Since only one transfer samples are required, it is completely online. The only cell to edit is \((s_t,a_t)\), where the sample appeared.






ImportantAll updates



Weights \(1-\alpha\) to the old Q estimate and \(\alpha\) to the single-sample estimate on the right-hand side of the Q-function Bellman equation.


↓ Down: Section 5.1.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

5.1.1 ✍ SA Fit to Frame
SA repetition was \(x_{k+1}(i)=(1-\alpha_k(i))x_k(i)+\alpha_k(i)\big[(Hx_k)(i)+w_k(i)\big]\)
Guide Question:

\(x\), what are the coordinates \(i\), \(H\), and \(w_t\) respectively?
How are cells that are not updated represented in the SA frame?
Show \(\mathbb{E}[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\). Why must \(a_t\) be included in the condition \(\mathcal F_t\)?
Compare with TD(0). What is the same and what is different?







NoteSolution





1. \(x=Q\in\mathbb{R}^{|S||A|}\), coordinates \(i=(s,a)\), \(H=T\) and \[
w_t:=\gamma\Big(\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')-\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s_t,a_t)\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\Big).
\] Then it is \((TQ)(s_t,a_t)+w_t=r_t+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\).
2. You just need to set the step size per cell to \(\alpha_t(s,a):=\alpha_t\,\mathbb{1}\{(s,a)=(s_t,a_t)\}\). The remaining cells are \(\alpha_t(s,a)=0\), so it is \(Q_{t+1}(s,a)=Q_t(s,a)\). Since the SA template allowed a step size per coordinate from the beginning, asynchronous updates that modify only one cell at a time also fit within the same template.
3. Given \(\mathcal F_t\), \(s_t\), \(a_t\), and the current \(Q\) are fixed, and the only random one is \(s_{t+1}\sim p(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)\). Therefore, \[
\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\,\Big|\,\mathcal F_t\Big]=\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s_t,a_t)\max_{a'}Q(s',a'),\qquad \mathbb{E}[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0.
\] \(a_t\) must be included in the condition for the distribution of \(s_{t+1}\) to be determined as \(p(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)\). Even if an action is selected via a random policy, the condition is applied using that value once it has been selected.

title: Q-Learning
text:
5.2 Algorithms and Personality
Answer.
Q-learning algorithm

Initialize to \(Q\equiv0\) and \(t\leftarrow0\). (Since it is a finite state/behavior, it can be initialized with an arbitrary table, but it is usually set to 0.)
From state \(t\) at time \(s_t\), select a random action \(a_t\) and proceed the system to \(t+1\).
Update cell \((s_t,a_t)\) with sample \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\). \[
Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha_t\Big[r_t+\gamma\max_{a'\in A}Q(s_{t+1},a')-Q(s_t,a_t)\Big].
\]
Set to \(t\leftarrow t+1\) and go to step 2.

After convergence, the policy is made into \(\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_{a\in A}Q(s,a)\) → Section 5.3
Personality:

Model-free, fully online. Updates once for each transition.
It is completely incremental. \((s_t,a_t)\) only one cell changes at a time. As the state-action space grows, it takes a very long time to sufficiently visit all cells. In large problems, this naive tabular version cannot be used, and a functional approximation is required.
There are degrees of freedom in action selection. The “random action” in step 2 is an off-policy property → Section 5.4







TipSignificance





A model-free, fully online algorithm is derived from just two steps: “Apply DP to the Q-function to obtain the Bellman equation → Apply SA to it.” The rest of the discussion (policy extraction, off-policy, search, convergence) is entirely about why and when this simple update formula works.



↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Q-Learning
text:
5.3 Policy Extraction: Why \(Q\) instead of \(v\)
First question to consider. We obtained a sufficiently good \(Q\). Is a transition probability necessary when creating a policy? What if we trained \(v^*\) in the same way?
Answer. From the current state, choose the action that maximizes \(Q\).
\[
\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_{a\in A}Q(s,a).
\]
At this stage, transition probabilities are not used. It is completely model-free up to policy extraction. This is the decisive reason for training \(Q\).
If \(v^*\) were trained, the model would need to be retrained for policy extraction → Section 5.3.1. There is a trade-off. Since \(Q^*\) contains more information with \(|S||A|\) digits than \(v^*\), training is more difficult and requires more samples.
↓ Down: Section 5.3.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

5.3.1 If you only trained ✍ \(v^*\)
Guide Question:

Write the formula to select the optimal policy from \(v^*\). Where does the model go?
What is inside the square brackets of that expression?
Show that \(\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a)\) is actually the optimal policy.







NoteSolution





1. \[
\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s')\Big].
\] Both \(r(s,a)\) and \(p(s'\mid s,a)\) are required. Even if you go to the trouble of training \(v^*\) as a model-free model, the model is needed again at the end.
2. According to result 2 of Section 4.2.1, the inside of the brackets is exactly \(Q^*(s,a)\). \(Q^*\) is a “calculation looking one step ahead with the model” that has been pre-calculated and stored.
3. Regarding the deterministic policy \(\pi(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a)\) \[
(T^\pi v^*)(s)=r(s,\pi(s))+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi(s))v^*(s')=Q^*(s,\pi(s))=\max_aQ^*(s,a)=v^*(s).
\] , that is, \(v^*=T^\pi v^*\). \(T^\pi\) is a contraction, and since the fixed point is uniquely \(v^\pi\), it is \(v^\pi=v^*\).









TipSignificance





There are two reasons for training \(Q^*\) when combined with Section 4.2.2: (i) The max is within the expected value, so the single-sample estimate is unbiased; and (ii) A model is not required for policy extraction. This is because both have absorbed the “model looking one step ahead” into \(Q\).



↑ Go Up: Section 5.3

title: Q-Learning
text:
5.4 Off-policy
First question to consider. Must the policy for selecting action \(a_t\) in Step 2 be the same as the policy targeted by learning (greedy for \(Q^*\))?
Answer. It does not have to be the same. Q-learning learns properly regardless of the policy used to generate behavior. This is called an off-policy algorithm.
\[
Q(s_t,a_t)\leftarrow Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha_t\Big[r_t+\gamma\max_{a'\in A}Q(s_{t+1},a')-Q(s_t,a_t)\Big].
\]
What goes into the target value is not the actual next action to be taken, but \(\max_{a'}\), that is, the selection of the optimal policy, which is the learning goal. Therefore, the policy that generates the action does not appear in the target value.
Result:

It has very high flexibility. You can choose any behavior, such as greedy, ε-greedy, or Boltzmann.
Already collected samples can be reused to update. Experience replay utilizes this property when scaling to larger problems (DQN), and it improves sample efficiency.

↓ Down: Section 5.4.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

5.4.1 ✍ Why is it acceptable to choose actions arbitrarily?
Guide Question:

Where does the policy that selects \(a_t\) appear under the noise condition \(\mathbb{E}[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\) of Section 5.1.1?
Then, do behavior policies have no effect on learning? What do they affect?
If the \(\max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\) of the target value is replaced with the \(Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\) of the \(a_{t+1}\) of the next action actually taken, what is the SA for which fixed-point equation?
Why is it okay to reuse \((s,a,r,s')\) collected in the past?







NoteSolution





1. It does not appear. The conditional expectation depends only on what value \(a_t\) is, and not on how that value was chosen. The distribution of \(s_{t+1}\) is only \(p(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)\), and there is no action policy in the definition of \(T\). Therefore, regardless of which action policy is used, the fixed point that SA points to is the same \(Q^*\).
2. There is an influence. The action policy determines how often a cell is updated. It does not change fixed points, but determines (i) whether the sum of the step sizes of each cell \(\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)\) diverges (infinite visit condition) → Section 7.1.1, and (ii) the convergence speed. If the action policy never selects a cell, that cell remains at its initial value. This is a search problem → Section 6.1
If you choose 3. \(a_{t+1}\sim\mu(\cdot\mid s_{t+1})\) \[
\mathbb{E}\big[Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})\mid\mathcal F_t\big]=\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s_t,a_t)\sum_{a'}\mu(a'\mid s')Q(s',a').
\] This is the Bellman operator \(T^\mu\) for the action policy \(\mu\), and the fixed point is \(Q^\mu\). In this case, the learning target becomes the value of the policy itself that generated the data (on-policy). The reason Q-learning is off-policy is precisely \(\max\) of the target value.
4. In the stored \((s,a,r,s')\), \(s'\) is still a sample of \(p(\cdot\mid s,a)\). The target value \(r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) can be recalculated using the current \(Q\), and its conditional expectation is \((TQ)(s,a)\) for the current \(Q\). It does not matter when or under what policy the data was generated.









TipSignificance





Off-policy separates “collecting data” from “what to learn.” Thanks to this, the data collection policy can be designed to be dedicated to exploration. However, separation does not mean that exploration is resolved. Even if the learning goal is independent of the action policy, learning actually occurs only in the cells visited by the action policy.



↑ Go Up: Section 5.4

title: Q-Learning
text:
6.1 Problems with Greedy policies
First question to consider. If we only use greedy actions on the current \(Q\) during training, which cells remain unupdated? If there are unupdated cells, which assumption of the Convergence Theorem is violated?
Answer. The Greedy policy chooses the action that appears most beneficial at the current \(Q\) (exploitation).
\[
\pi(s)\in\arg\max_{a\in A}Q(s,a),\qquad a_t=\pi(s_t).
\]
If \(Q\) is optimal, then the greedy policy is optimal. However, the probability that \(Q\) is near the optimal value early in training is very low.
The problem is search. If only a greedy policy is used, some state-action pairs may never be visited. In that case, the information for those cells can never be obtained, and convergence to the optimal Q-factor is not guaranteed. Even if all states are visited, certain beneficial actions may never be attempted.
↓ Down: Section 6.1.1 · Section 6.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.1.1 ✍ Two action examples
There is one state (\(s\)) and two actions. Regardless of the action taken, it returns to \(s\). The rewards are deterministically \(r(s,a_1)=1\) and \(r(s,a_2)=2\). A greedy policy is used to start at \(Q\equiv0\) and choose \(a_1\) in case of a tie. \(\alpha_t\in(0,1]\).
Guide Question:

\(Q^*(s,a_1)\), \(Q^*(s,a_2)\) and what is the optimal action?
What is the sign of \(Q(s,a_1)\) after the first update? What does the greedy policy choose from then on?
What happens to \(Q(s,a_2)\)? Where does \(Q(s,a_1)\) converge?
Is the greedy policy optimal after training?







NoteSolution





1. \(v^*=\max_aQ^*(s,a)\) and \(Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma v^*\). If you always choose \(a_2\), then \(v^*=2/(1-\gamma)\). \[
Q^*(s,a_2)=\frac{2}{1-\gamma},\qquad Q^*(s,a_1)=1+\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}.
\] Since \(Q^*(s,a_2)-Q^*(s,a_1)=1>0\), the optimal action is \(a_2\).
2. Since it is a tie, \(a_1\) is selected, followed by \(Q(s,a_1)\leftarrow0+\alpha_0(1+\gamma\cdot0-0)=\alpha_0>0\). Now that it is \(Q(s,a_1)>0=Q(s,a_2)\), the greedy continues to select \(a_1\). Afterwards, \(Q(s,a_1)\) is not decreased (the 3 updates below increase it while it is \(Q<1/(1-\gamma)\)).
3. \(a_2\) is never selected, so it remains in \(Q(s,a_2)=0\) forever. The update of \(Q(s,a_1)\) is \[
Q(s,a_1)\leftarrow Q(s,a_1)+\alpha_t\big[1+\gamma\max\{Q(s,a_1),0\}-Q(s,a_1)\big]=Q(s,a_1)+\alpha_t\big[1+(\gamma-1)Q(s,a_1)\big]
\] , and the fixed point is \(Q=1+\gamma Q\), i.e., \(1/(1-\gamma)\). At an appropriate step size, \(Q(s,a_1)\to1/(1-\gamma)\).
4. In the learned \(Q\), the greedy value is \(a_1\). It is not optimal. Furthermore, the values of already visited cells are also incorrect. It is \(1/(1-\gamma)<Q^*(s,a_1)\). This is because incorrect values from unvisited cells (\(Q(s,a_2)=0\)) are mixed within the target value \(\max_{a'}Q(s,a')\). The damage from the search failure does not stop at unvisited cells but spreads through bootstrapping.









TipSignificance





It is important to note that the off-policy property, where the policy selecting the action does not appear in the target value, is not broken in this example. The fixed point of Q-learning is still \(Q^*\). What is wrong is not the fixed point, but the assumption of the convergence theorem is broken because it is \(\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a_2)=0\) in the \((s,a_2)\) cell → Section 7.1.1



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1


6.1.2 Exploitation–exploration trade-off
Answer.

To obtain a near-optimal policy with Q-learning, we must explore all potentially beneficial state-action pairs to gather information.
If a greedy policy is used for every update, certain beneficial actions may never be attempted even if all states are explored.
To overcome this, you must sacrifice some of the immediate gains you can obtain now through greedy choices and explore thoroughly.
This trade-off arises from a lack of knowledge regarding system dynamics and compensation structures. To acquire that knowledge, one must search instead of focusing on current gains.







TipSignificance





If the model is known, no search is needed. The VI calculates every \((s,a)\) every time. The search problem is the price paid for being model-free, and it arises in all sequential decision problems where the model is unknown, not limited to RL. This problem will be addressed again later using methods such as entropy normalization.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1

title: Q-Learning
text:
6.2 ε-greedy and other methods
First question to think of. How can you make all actions continuously attempted by slightly modifying a greedy policy?
Answer.
ε-greedy. Choose a greedy action with probability \(1-\varepsilon\) and a random action with probability \(\varepsilon\). In other words, search for a probability of \(\varepsilon\).
\[
\Pr(a_t=a\mid s_t=s)=
\begin{cases}
1-\varepsilon+\dfrac{\varepsilon}{|A|}, & a=\arg\max_{a'}Q(s,a')\ (\text{유일하다면}),\\[6pt]
\dfrac{\varepsilon}{|A|}, & \text{그 밖}.
\end{cases}
\]
Another method:

Segment Switching. (i) Alternate between search segments and (ii) greedy segments. Use random actions in search segments and greedy actions in greedy segments.
Boltzmann Search. Probability of action \(a\) from state \(s\) \[
\frac{\exp\big(Q(s,a)/\tau\big)}{\sum_{a'\in A}\exp\big(Q(s,a')/\tau\big)}
\] Select . \(\tau>0\) is the temperature parameter → Section 6.2.2

ε-greedy is the most widely used in Q-learning. This is not because it is efficient, but because it is simple and allows scheduling of ε.






NoteRationale: ε-greedy attempts all actions infinitely in a visited state.





Let us assume that a state \(s\) is visited infinitely often. At each visit, the conditional probability that each action is selected, regardless of the past, is at least \(\varepsilon/|A|>0\). Since the sum of conditional probabilities diverges (a conditional version of the Borel–Cantelli lemma), each action is selected infinitely with a probability of 1.
However, this is the case if states are visited infinitely. Whether all states are visited infinitely depends on the connection structure of the MDP.



↓ Down: Section 6.2.1 · Section 6.2.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.2.1 ε scheduling
First question to consider. How does the quality of \(Q\) differ between the early and late stages of training? Should one start with a large ε or a small ε?
Answer. Start with a large ε and gradually decrease.

Initial: Since there is almost no known information, focus on searching to improve the quality of \(Q\).
Review: If \(Q\) becomes reliable, reduce ε and use greedy behavior more.

ε can also be fixed from beginning to end.






NoteReason: If you reduce too quickly





There is a tension in the rate at which ε is reduced, similar to the SA step size, which dictates that it “should be reduced, but not too quickly.” If the search probability at the \(k\)-th visit of a certain state is \(\varepsilon_k\), then \(\sum_k\varepsilon_k=\infty\) is required for an infinite search. For example, \(\varepsilon_k=1/k\) is sufficient, but \(\varepsilon_k=1/k^2\) allows for only a finite number of searches with a probability of 1 (Borel–Cantelli). The goal of schedule design is to ensure that the search continues infinitely while eventually approaching greediness.









TipSignificance





It is the principle that “the more information is accumulated, the more one trusts their own estimate.” It is a design in the same direction as starting with a large λ in TD(λ) and reducing it.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2


6.2.2 ✍ Two limits of Boltzmann search
Guide Question:

If \(\tau\to0^+\), what is the probability? Assume that \(\arg\max\) is unique.
\(\tau\to\infty\) If?
Does the probability change when the same constant \(c\) is added to all \(Q(s,\cdot)\)? How is it different compared to ε-greedy?







NoteSolution





If we set 1. \(a^*:=\arg\max_aQ(s,a)\) and \(\Delta_a:=Q(s,a^*)-Q(s,a)\) and divide the numerator and denominator by \(\exp(Q(s,a^*)/\tau)\) \[
\Pr(a)=\frac{e^{-\Delta_a/\tau}}{\sum_{a'}e^{-\Delta_{a'}/\tau}}.
\] If \(\tau\to0^+\), then \(a\ne a^*\), since \(e^{-\Delta_a/\tau}\to0\), \(\Pr(a^*)\to1\). It is a greedy policy.
2. Since all exponents go to 0, \(\Pr(a)\to1/|A|\). is uniformly random.
3. Since \(e^{c/\tau}\) is canceled out in the numerator and denominator, it does not change. The probability depends only on the difference \(\Delta_a\) of the \(Q\) values. ε-greedy selects all non-greedy actions with equal probability \(\varepsilon/|A|\), whereas Boltzmann selects actions with small differences (almost good) more often and actions with large differences less often. Since the probability of every action is always positive, the search continues.









TipSignificance





\(\tau\) is a handle that acts like ε. Starting with the large \(\tau\) and reducing it, it transitions from search to utilization.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2

title: Q-Learning
text:
7.1 Convergence Theorem
Answer.






ImportantTheorem (Q-learning convergence)



Each state-action pair is visited infinitely many times and \[
\sum_{t=0}^\infty\alpha_t(s,a)=+\infty,\qquad\sum_{t=0}^\infty\alpha_t^2(s,a)<+\infty
\] If , then for each \((s,a)\), \(Q(s,a)\) converges to \(Q^*(s,a)\) with probability 1.


The proof idea is the two axes of the SA convergence theorem.

\(T\) is a contraction map → Section 4.3.1
The noise term satisfies the conditional mean and conditional variance conditions.

↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 · Section 7.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

7.1.1 ✍ Proof Idea: Condensation and Noise Condition
Guide Question:

Write the four conditions of the SA Convergence Theorem. In Q-learning, is each an assumption or something to prove?
Where in the step size condition is “infinitely visiting each pair” hidden?
Show that the conditional variance of the noise is bounded in the form \(C_0+C_1\|Q\|_\infty^2\).
Does the commonly used step size \(\alpha_t(s,a)=1/N_t(s,a)\)(\(N_t(s,a)\): number of visits from \((s,a)\) up to time \(t\)) satisfy the condition?







NoteSolution





1.







condition
in Q-learning




\(H\) is contracted
\(H=T\), \(\gamma\)-contracted → Proven Section 4.3.1


\(\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)=\infty\), \(\sum_t\alpha_t^2(s,a)<\infty\)
Assumption


\(\mathbb{E}[w_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\)
prove Section 5.1.1


\(\mathbb{E}[w_t^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le C_0+C_1\Vert Q_t\Vert^2\)
Number 3 below



Since 2. \(\alpha_t(s,a)=\alpha_t\mathbb{1}\{(s_t,a_t)=(s,a)\}\), if \((s,a)\) is visited only a finite number of times, then \(\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)\) is finite as it is the sum of a finite number of terms. Therefore, \(\sum_t\alpha_t(s,a)=\infty\) imply infinite visits. The reason for mentioning infinite visits separately in the theorem is to emphasize that this condition depends on the action policy (search).
3. \(|\max_{a'}Q(s',a')|\le\|Q\|_\infty\) and since the weighted average also has the same upper bound, \[
|w_t|\le\gamma\big(\|Q_t\|_\infty+\|Q_t\|_\infty\big)=2\gamma\|Q_t\|_\infty,\qquad
\mathbb{E}[w_t^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le4\gamma^2\|Q_t\|_\infty^2.
\] \(C_0=0\), \(C_1=4\gamma^2\). If the reward is probabilistic, the variance of the reward is added to \(C_0\).
4. is satisfied. If each cell is visited infinitely, the step size sequence for that cell is \(1,\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\dots\) each time it is visited, so it is \(\sum1/k=\infty\) and \(\sum1/k^2<\infty\). However, this also presupposes infinite visits.









TipSignificance





It has the same structure as the convergence of TD(λ). The only difference is the operator (\(T^\pi\) or \(H\)Z instead of multi-step \(T\)). The unique aspect of Q-learning is point 2. The step size condition becomes a condition for the action policy. In policy evaluation, the policy was fixed and the visit distribution was predetermined, but in Q-learning, the way actions are selected directly determines convergence. This is why search is theoretically essential. → Section 6.1.1



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1


7.1.2 What organization means in reality
Answer. It is sufficient to know the fact that there is a theoretical guarantee and its structure (reduction + noise conditions). Even when running tabular Q-learning on simple problems, it is very difficult to perfectly learn \(Q^*\).

The core assumption of “visiting all state-action pairs infinitely” cannot be satisfied in reality.
Even with ε-greedy and ε-scheduling, the search problem cannot be perfectly solved. ε-greedy is a simple but not efficient search method, and it can be theoretically shown to be inefficient.
Since updates occur one cell at a time, even a slight increase in the state-action space makes the time required to sufficiently visit all cells unmanageable.







TipSignificance





The two items following are the two limitations of Q-learning: search and scalability. The scalability problem leads to approximate Q-learning, which approximates the Q-function with a parameterized structure (weight vector) and learns those weights.



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 3.1 Can the Bellman equation be directly obtained as the solution to the optimization problem?
text:
3.1 Can the Bellman equation be directly obtained as the solution to the optimization problem?
First question to consider. Which property of \(T\) did all the methods (VI, PI) used to solve \(v=Tv\) so far rely on? What does it become if that property is written as a “constraint” instead of “repetition”?
Answer. VI and PI rely on the contraction property of \(T\) and the Banach fixed-point theorem. This time, without repeatedly applying \(T\), the Bellman equation is relaxed to the inequality constraint \(v\ge Tv\) and the linear objective function is minimized. The property used here is monotonicity in addition to contraction.






TipSignificance






If converted to an optimization problem, mature optimization solvers (interior-point, simplex) can be used as is.
Optimization tools such as duality, feature approximation, and sample-based constraints can be introduced into MDPs.
At the end of this chapter, the same framework leads to improving policies with data without a model → Section 10.2




↓ Scroll Down: Section 4.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 4.1 Why is the optimal solution to \(\min_v c^\top v\) st \(v\ge Tv\) (\(c>0\)) uniquely \(v^*\)?
text:
4.1 Why is the optimal solution to \(\min_v c^\top v\) st \(v\ge Tv\) (\(c>0\)) uniquely \(v^*\)?
\[
\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ c^\top v\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad v\ge Tv\quad(\text{원소별}).
\]
The first question to think of.

Let \(v_{\rm opt}\) be the optimal solution. This satisfies the constraint \(v_{\rm opt}\ge Tv_{\rm opt}\). Where do we go if we continue to apply \(T\) to both sides?
Where is \(v^*\) located in this problem (is it feasible)?
What are the directions of the inequalities derived from the two facts?

Answer. It is three lines.

\(v_{\rm opt}\ge Tv_{\rm opt}\ge T^2v_{\rm opt}\ge\cdots\to v^*\), therefore \(v_{\rm opt}\ge v^*\).
Since \(v^*=Tv^*\), \(v^*\) is feasible, and therefore \(c^\top v^*\ge c^\top v_{\rm opt}\).
1 and \(c>0\) \(c^\top v_{\rm opt}\ge c^\top v^*\). For the two inequalities to hold simultaneously, \(v_{\rm opt}=v^*\).

↓ Down: Section 4.1.1 Proof · Section 4.1.2 Tool ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.1.1 Proof: Three inequalities one by one






NoteProof





We take \(v_{\rm opt}\) as the arbitrary optimal solution.
(i) \(v_{\rm opt}\ge v^*\). \[
\begin{aligned}
v_{\rm opt}&\ge Tv_{\rm opt} &&(\text{제약})\\
Tv_{\rm opt}&\ge T^2v_{\rm opt} &&(\text{윗줄 양변에 }T\text{, 단조성})\\
&\ \ \vdots\\
v_{\rm opt}&\ge T^kv_{\rm opt}\ \ \forall k &&(\text{이어 붙이기})\\
v_{\rm opt}&\ge\lim_{k\to\infty}T^kv_{\rm opt}=v^* &&(\text{Banach: 임의 초기값에서 }T^k\cdot\to v^*,\ \text{원소별 부등식은 극한에서 유지})
\end{aligned}
\]
(ii) \(c^\top v^*\ge c^\top v_{\rm opt}\). Since \(v^*=Tv^*\), \(v^*\ge Tv^*\) satisfies the equality. That is, \(v^*\) is feasible. \(v_{\rm opt}\) is the point where \(c^\top v\) is the smallest among the feasible points, so \(c^\top v_{\rm opt}\le c^\top v^*\).
(iii) \(v_{\rm opt}=v^*\). From (i), it is \(d:=v_{\rm opt}-v^*\ge0\). Rewriting (ii), it is \(c^\top d\le0\). However, \[
c^\top d=\sum_sc(s)\,d(s),\qquad c(s)>0,\ d(s)\ge0
\] Since , each term is nasal, and for the sum to be less than or equal to \(0\), all terms must be \(0\). Since \(c(s)>0\), it is \(d(s)=0\), i.e., \(v_{\rm opt}=v^*\).
Since \(v_{\rm opt}\) was chosen arbitrarily, the optimal solution is unique and is \(v^*\).









NoteAddendum: Existence of the optimal solution





The argument in (i) does not use the fact that \(v_{\rm opt}\) is the optimal solution. It only uses constraints. Therefore, for all feasible \(v\), \(v\ge v^*\) and \(c^\top v\ge c^\top v^*\). Since \(v^*\) itself is feasible, \(v^*\) actually achieves the minimum value. In other words, existence and uniqueness come together.
This is the same as the comparison lemma “\(v\ge Tv\Rightarrow v\ge v^*\)”.









TipSignificance






\(c>0\) is used only in (iii). If there is even one element \(c(s)=0\), the objective value does not change even if that element’s \(d(s)\) is positive, so uniqueness is broken.
Remember that minimization is in the direction of “pressing the Bellman equation from above.” Every point in the feasible set \(\{v\ge Tv\}\) is greater than \(v^*\), and the “bottom edge” of that set is \(v^*\).
If you want to write the problem as a maximization problem (\(\max\), \(v\le Tv\)), you must also reverse the direction of the inequality. Every point in \(\{v\le Tv\}\) is smaller than \(v^*\). If you mix the two directions (e.g., \(\min\) and \(v\le Tv\)), the objective function becomes unbounded below.




↓ Down: Section 4.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 4.1


4.1.2 Three tools used in the proof
Answer.

Monotonicity: \(v\le w\Rightarrow Tv\le Tw\). Since \(p\ge0\), it follows that \(\sum_{s'}p\,v\le\sum_{s'}p\,w\), and the inequality that holds for each \(a\) holds even when taking \(\max_a\).
Limit of iteration: Since \(T\) is a contraction of \(\gamma\), \(T^kv\to v^*\) from any starting point (Banach’s fixed point theorem). This leads to the fact that \(v^*\) is the only fixed point of \(T\).
Positive weighted sum: \(c>0\), \(d\ge0\), \(c^\top d=0\Rightarrow d=0\).







TipSignificance





The same three tools are reused in the policy evaluation LP (Section 5.1.3), Q-LP (Section 9.1), and upper limit of approximation LP (Section 7.1.1). The only thing that changes is the operator (\(T\), \(T^\pi\), \(T_Q\)).



↑ Go Up: Section 4.1.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 5.1 How does this optimization problem become a linear program?
text:
5.1 How does this optimization problem become a linear program?
The first question to think of.

Which is the problem, the objective function \(c^\top v\) or the constraint \(v\ge Tv\)?
If the constraints are expanded by state, where exactly does the nonlinearity come from?
What is the proposition equivalent to “\(x\ge\max_a y_a\)” written without max?

Answer. The objective function is linear. The problem is \(v(s)\ge\max_a[\cdots]\) and \(\max\). However, this constraint is equivalent to “\(a\) for all \(v(s)\ge[\cdots]\)”. When written this way, both sides of each constraint become affine for \(v\). \[
\boxed{\ \min_{v\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ c^\top v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad v(s)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\quad\forall(s,a)\in S\times A\ }
\] The number of variables remains \(n\), and the number of constraints has increased from \(n\) to \(nm\).






TipSignificance






LP is the simplest class of optimization problems, and solvers are a mature technology.
The cost is the number of constraints. In a large-scale MDP, \(nm\) constraints become a burden. The two directions to reduce this burden are dual(Section 6.1) and approximation(Section 7.1).
To summarize, it is an LP version of the same problem as the original, at the cost of increasing the number of constraints. The solution is still \(v^*\).




↓ Down: Section 5.1.1 Equivalence · Section 5.1.2 \(c\) · Section 5.1.3 Policy Evaluation ↑ Up: Section 4.1

5.1.1 “\(x\ge\max_ay_a\) ⇔ Two directions of \(x\ge y_a\) for all \(a\)”






NoteProof





(\(\Rightarrow\)) For all \(a\)Z \(y_a\le\max_by_b\le x\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(a\) for all \(y_a\le x\), then \(x\) is an upper bound of \(\{y_a\}\). Since the maximum value of a finite set is the smallest of the upper bounds, \(\max_ay_a\le x\).
If we set \(x=v(s)\), \(y_a=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\) and write for all \(s\), it becomes the LP of Section 5.1.









TipSignificance: Conditions under which this equivalence holds






This solution works only when max is on the larger side (right side) of the inequality and the inequality is “\(\ge\max\)”. “\(\le\max\)” becomes an existential statement “for some \(a\)” and cannot be used as the intersection of linear constraints.
It is also important to note that max is outside the sum. The same method does not apply to the Bellman equation for Q where max is inside the sum → Section 9.1.1




↑ Go Up: Section 5.1


5.1.2 What is the role of \(c\)
First question to consider. \(c\) has only the condition that “all elements are positive.” If you were designing the problem yourself, how would you determine \(c\)? Does changing \(c\) change the solution?
Answer. \(c(s)\) is the weight assigned to the \(s\)-th element of the value. If \(c(s)\) is increased, the search proceeds in the direction of further lowering \(v(s)\). If prior knowledge about the optimal value (which state has a lower value) exists, it can be reflected; otherwise, it is set to \(c=\mathbf{1}\).






TipSignificance: Different from exact LPs and approximate LPs






Exact LP: According to Section 4.1.1, if \(c>0\) is the case, the optimal solution is always \(v^*\). \(c\) does not change the solution. It only affects the solver’s search path and numerical efficiency.
Approximation LP: If \(v^*\) cannot be expressed exactly, \(c\) replaces the solution. In this case, \(c\) becomes the weight of the state-specific approximation error → Section 7.1.1
In dual: \(c\) acts as the initial state distribution. Since it is \(c>0\), positive mass is entered into all states, so the policy can be restored in all states → Section 6.1.3, Section 6.1.4




↑ Go Up: Section 5.1


5.1.3 Why are there only \(n\) constraints on policy evaluation LP?
\[
\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ c^\top v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad v\ge T^\pi v
\ \Longleftrightarrow\
\min_{v}\ c^\top v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad v(s)\ge r(s,\pi(s))+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi(s))\,v(s')\quad\forall s.
\]
Answer. There is no max in \(T^\pi\). Therefore, the constraint is linear from the start, and one per state, \(n\), is sufficient. The solution is \(v^\pi\). The proof can be done by replacing \(T\) with \(T^\pi\) in Section 4.1.1. This is because \(T^\pi\) is also monotonic and \(\gamma\)-reduction, and the only fixed point is \(v^\pi\).






TipSignificance






It is efficient because it is a small LP in which the behavioral dimension \(m\) has disappeared. It serves as the basis for using LP in the evaluation phase of PI.
In the optimal solution, all constraints hold as equals (\(v^\pi=T^\pi v^\pi\)). That is, this LP is another method for finding the solution to the system of linear equations \((I-\gamma P^\pi)v=R^\pi\).




↓ Down: Section 4.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 5.1, Section 10.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 6.1 What is the dual LP, and why can it be computationally preferred?
text:
6.1 What is the dual LP, and why can it be computationally preferred?
The first question to think of.

One dual variable is assigned to each constraint. How many primal constraints are there, and what indices do they have?
When minimizing the Lagrangian for ZZZPH0013200ZZZ \(v\), when does a finite value other than \(-\infty\) occur?
What does that “condition making it finite” become of the dual?

Answer. Since there is one primal constraint for every \((s,a)\), there are \(\lambda(s,a)\ge0\), that is, \(n\times m\). If we organize the Lagrangian by the coefficients of \(v(s')\), it is \(\min_vL=-\infty\) when at least one coefficient is not \(0\). Therefore, “coefficient \(=0\)” becomes the equality constraint of the dual, and the remaining term becomes the objective function of the dual. \[
\boxed{\ \max_{\lambda\ge0}\ \sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad c(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,p(s'\mid s,a)-\sum_a\lambda(s',a)=0\quad\forall s'\in S\ }
\]






TipSignificance






dual is also an LP. Both the objective function and the constraints are linear with respect to \(\lambda\).
There is no duality gap. If both the primal and dual are feasible, the LP satisfies strong duality. For the primal, \(v^*\) is feasible, and for the dual, the occupancy measure of an arbitrary policy is feasible (Section 6.1.3). Therefore, the dual optimal value is \(=c^\top v^*\).
Sizes are swapped: variable \(n\to nm\), constraint \(nm\to n\) (equation). In LP, dual may be preferred because having fewer constraints is usually computationally advantageous.




↓ Down: Section 6.1.1 Derivation · Section 6.1.2 weak duality · Section 6.1.3 Measure of possession · Section 6.1.4 Policy restoration ↑ Up: Section 5.1

6.1.1 From Lagrangian to Dual Function: Reordering the Sum






NoteInduction





Step 1: Change the constraint to the form \(g\le0\). The primal constraint is \[g_{s,a}(v):=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')-v(s)\ \le\ 0.\]
Step 2: Lagrangian. The Lagrangian of \(\min f\) st \(g\le0\) is \(f+\sum\lambda g\), \(\lambda\ge0\). \[
L(v,\lambda)=\underbrace{\sum_sc(s)\,v(s)}_{\text{(a)}}+\underbrace{\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a)}_{\text{(b)}}+\underbrace{\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')}_{\text{(c)}}-\underbrace{\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,v(s)}_{\text{(d)}}.
\]
Step 3: Collect all \(v\) terms into the coefficients of \(v(s')\).

(a): Renames only the indices of the junction. \(\sum_{s'}c(s')\,v(s')\).
(c): Since it is a finite sum, the order is changed. \(\sum_{s'}v(s')\cdot\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,p(s'\mid s,a)\).
(d): \(\sum_s v(s)\sum_a\lambda(s,a)\) Groups and renames to \(s'\). \(\sum_{s'}v(s')\sum_a\lambda(s',a)\).

Therefore \[
L(v,\lambda)=\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a)+\sum_{s'}v(s')\underbrace{\Big[c(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,p(s'\mid s,a)-\sum_a\lambda(s',a)\Big]}_{=:\,\kappa_\lambda(s')}.
\]
Step 4: Minimize for \(v\). \(L\) is affine for \(v\). For any \(s'\), if \(\kappa_\lambda(s')\ne0\), send to \(v(s')\to\mp\infty\) and \(L\to-\infty\). Therefore \[
g(\lambda):=\min_vL(v,\lambda)=\begin{cases}\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a), & \kappa_\lambda(s')=0\ \ \forall s',\\ -\infty, & \text{그 외}.\end{cases}
\]
Step 5: dual. Since \(\max_{\lambda\ge0}g(\lambda)\) becomes \(-\infty\)Z, \(\lambda\) is not useful for maximization, if we set \(\kappa_\lambda=0\) as a constraint, it becomes the dual LP of Section 6.1.









TipSignificance






What has changed in (c) is the perspective of counting “where starts to go to \(s'\)”. The flow out of \(s\) was recounted as the flow entering \(s'\). This shift in perspective is the starting point of the flow-preserving interpretation (Section 6.1.3).
In (d), the coefficient of \(v(s)\) is the sum of \(\lambda\) of all actions applied to \(s\). Therefore, there is one dual constraint per state, resulting in \(n\).




↑ Go Up: Section 6.1


6.1.2 ✍ weak duality: primal objective value ≥ dual objective value
Guide Question:

We define primal feasible \(v\) and dual feasible \(\lambda\). Why does the inequality remain when multiplying the constraint \(r(s,a)\le v(s)-\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,v(s')\) by \(\lambda(s,a)\ge0\)?
Add for all \((s,a)\), and then group the right-hand side into the form \(\sum_{s'}v(s')[\cdots]\), what are the square brackets? (This is the same operation as step 3 of Section 6.1.1.)
What does the square bracket change to when the dual constraint is applied?







NoteSolution





\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a)
&\le\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\Big[v(s)-\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\Big] &&(\lambda\ge0,\ \text{primal 제약})\\
&=\sum_{s'}v(s')\Big[\sum_a\lambda(s',a)-\gamma\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,p(s'\mid s,a)\Big] &&(\text{합의 순서 바꾸기})\\
&=\sum_{s'}c(s')\,v(s') &&(\text{dual 제약}).
\end{aligned}
\] equality holds only when the primal constraint is equality for all \((s,a)\) such that \(\lambda(s,a)>0\). This is the complementary slack condition → Section 6.1.4



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1


6.1.3 Why is the dual constraint flow-preserving, and what does \(\lambda\) count?
Guide Question:

dual constraint is rewritten as \(\sum_a\lambda(s',a)=c(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}p(s'\mid s,a)\,\lambda(s,a)\). What do the left side, the first term on the right side, and the second term on the right side each count, respectively?
Given a stationary policy \(\pi\) and an (unnormalized) initial mass \(c\), let \(d_t(s,a):=\Pr^\pi(s_t=s,a_t=a)\). What is the one-step recursion that writes \(\sum_ad_{t+1}(s',a)\) to \(d_t\)?
Let \(\lambda:=\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^td_t\). What is the result when you multiply the recursion by \(\gamma^{t+1}\) and add them?
What is \(\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)\,r(s,a)\) in this case?







NoteSolution





1. The left side represents the total (discounted) amount remaining at \(s'\), the first term on the right side represents the mass placed at \(s'\) from the beginning, and the second term represents the amount flowing into \(s'\), one step after the other state, multiplied by the discount. “Amount remaining = Initial amount + Discounted inflow”.
2. The next state is determined by the transition, and the next action by the policy. \[\sum_ad_{t+1}(s',a)=\Pr(s_{t+1}=s')=\sum_{s,a}p(s'\mid s,a)\,d_t(s,a).\]
3. \(t=0\) Remove the term. \[
\sum_a\lambda(s',a)=\underbrace{\sum_ad_0(s',a)}_{=c(s')}+\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^{t+1}\sum_ad_{t+1}(s',a)
=c(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}p(s'\mid s,a)\underbrace{\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^td_t(s,a)}_{=\lambda(s,a)}.
\] That is, the discount share measure of all stationary policies is dual feasible.
4. \(\sum_{s,a}\lambda r=\sum_t\gamma^t\,\mathbb{E}^\pi_c[r(s_t,a_t)]=\sum_sc(s)\,v^\pi(s)=c^\top v^\pi\). Therefore, the dual is read as the problem of “maximizing the discounted cumulative reward \(c^\top v^\pi\) starting from the initial mass \(c\) with respect to the policy”. The optimal value is \(\max_\pi c^\top v^\pi=c^\top v^*\), which is equal to the primal optimal value.
Verification. Adding all dual constraints for \(s'\) gives \(\sum_{s,a}\lambda(s,a)=\sum_sc(s)/(1-\gamma)\). This is the total mass of the discounted sum.









TipSignificance






primal examines the same problem in the value space (which \(v\) satisfies the Bellman inequality), while dual examines it in the visit frequency space (how often a policy visits a state-behavior).
Since \(c>0\), \(\sum_a\lambda(s',a)\ge c(s')>0\). All states have positive mass, so policies can be defined in all states → Section 6.1.4




↑ Go Up: Section 6.1


6.1.4 Complementary slack: How to extract a policy from a dual solution
Answer. For the primal optimal solution \(v^*\) and the dual optimal solution \(\lambda^*\), the following holds. \[
\lambda^*(s,a)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ v^*(s)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s').
\] , that is, the mass-based behavior of \(\lambda^*\) is a greedy behavior toward \(v^*\). Therefore, \[
\pi^*(a\mid s)=\frac{\lambda^*(s,a)}{\sum_b\lambda^*(s,b)}
\] is the optimal policy. Since the denominator is greater than or equal to \(c(s)>0\), it is always defined.






NoteBasis





In the chain of inequalities Section 6.1.2, substituting \(\lambda^*\) and \(v^*\) results in a duality gap of \(0\), so the first line must be equal. The difference in the first line is \(\sum_{s,a}\lambda^*(s,a)\cdot(\text{제약의 여유})\), and since each term is non-negative, all terms are \(0\). If it were \(\lambda^*(s,a)>0\), the constraint margin would be \(0\).









TipSignificance





Solving primal yields \(v^*\), and for the policy, we must solve argmax again (model needed). If we solve dual, the policy is already contained within the solution. Verify this in the manual calculation example Section 11.2.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 7.1 What decreases and what remains when approximating with a linear architecture
text:
7.1 What decreases and what remains when approximating with a linear architecture
First question to consider. Whether primal or dual, the size is proportional to \(n\) and \(m\). If \(n\) is very large, what can be made small?
Answer. Constrain the value function to a linear combination of the given features. \[
v_\theta(s)=\sum_{k=1}^K\phi_k(s)\,\theta_k=\phi(s)^\top\theta,\qquad v_\theta=\Phi\theta,\quad\Phi=[\phi_1\ \cdots\ \phi_K]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times K}\ (s\text{번째 행이 }\phi(s)^\top).
\] Assign \(v=\Phi\theta\) to the LP of Section 5.1. \[
\boxed{\ \min_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^K}\ c^\top\Phi\theta\quad\text{s.t.}\quad(\Phi\theta)(s)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,(\Phi\theta)(s')\quad\forall(s,a)\ }
\] Since \(\Phi\) is fixed, both the objective function and the constraints are linear with respect to \(\theta\). It is still an LP.

(+) Decision variable: \(n\to K\).
(−) Constraint number: \(nm\) as is.
If (−) \(v^*\notin\{\Phi\theta\}\), it loses optimality.







TipSignificance: Note the direction of the inequality sign






The direction paired with \(\min\) is \(\Phi\theta\ge T\Phi\theta\). As seen in the significance of Section 4.1.1, mixing \(\min\) and \(\le\) results in the objective function becoming unbounded below.
In literature using the cost minimization convention (ZZZPH0013268ZZZ, \(J\), \(\min_\mu\)), the form \(\max c^\top\Phi r\) st \(\Phi r\le T\Phi r\) is obtained. When switching between reward maximization and cost minimization, the objective \(\min/\max\) and the constraint \(\ge/\le\) are inverted together.
Problems where the number of constraints remains are handled using constraint sampling. The error limit of approximate solutions is also analyzed within this framework.




↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 ↑ Up: Section 5.1

7.1.1 Why is the approximate solution above \(v^*\), and what does \(c\) weigh?
Answer. Since the feasible \(\Phi\theta\) satisfies \(\Phi\theta\ge T\Phi\theta\), it is \(\Phi\theta\ge v^*\) by (i) of Section 4.1.1. Then \[
c^\top\Phi\theta=c^\top v^*+c^\top(\Phi\theta-v^*)=c^\top v^*+\sum_sc(s)\,\big|\Phi\theta(s)-v^*(s)\big|.
\] Since \(c^\top v^*\) is a constant, the approximation LP minimizes the \(c\)-weighted \(\ell_1\) error \(\|\Phi\theta-v^*\|_{1,c}\) within the feasible set.






NoteDoes a feasible \(\theta\) exist?





constant feature \(\mathbf{1}\) needs to be in the column space of \(\Phi\). If we set it to \(\Phi\theta=\kappa\mathbf{1}\), the constraint is \(\kappa\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\kappa\), i.e., \(\kappa\ge\max_{s,a}r(s,a)/(1-\gamma)\). Such a \(\kappa\) always exists.









TipSignificance






In the exact LP, \(c\) did not change the solution(Section 5.1.2). In the approximate LP, \(c\) becomes a weight that determines “which state’s error to reduce further” and changes the solution.
The approximate solution is always the upper bound of \(v^*\). This means that when estimating policy performance with approximate values, it tends to be skewed toward overestimation.




↓ Down: Section 4.1.1 ↑ Up: Section 7.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 8.1 What is the Q-function, and what is its relationship to \(v^*\)?
text:
8.1 What is the Q-function, and what is its relationship to \(v^*\)?
\[
Q^*(s,a):=\max_\pi Q^\pi(s,a)=\max_\pi\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\ \Big|\ s_0=s,\ a_0=a\Big].
\]
The first question to think of. The difference between \(v^*(s)\) and \(Q^*(s,a)\) is “what is fixed.” What must be added to \(v^*(s)\) to obtain \(Q^*(s,\cdot)\)?
Answer. \(Q^*(s,a)\) is the maximum expected cumulative reward after fixing the first action at \(a\). Since \(v^*(s)\) requires even the first action to be chosen optimally, \[
v^*(s)=\max_aQ^*(s,a),\qquad\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a).
\] In the infinite discount setting, the starting point is not important, so it was set to start at \(t=0\).






NoteThe basis of \(v^*=\max_aQ^*\)





If you use ZZZPH0013286ZZZ Section 8.1.2 to see \(Q^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s')\) \[\max_aQ^*(s,a)=\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,v^*(s')\Big]=(Tv^*)(s)=v^*(s).\] The last equality sign is because \(v^*\) is a solution to the Bellman equation.



↓ Scroll down: Section 8.1.1 Why Q · Section 8.1.2 Bellman Equation · Section 8.1.3 Properties of \(T_Q\) ↑ Scroll up: Section 3.1

8.1.1 What is the advantage of knowing \(Q^*\) compared to knowing only \(v^*\)?
First question to consider. If you write the equations for extracting the optimal policy for the two cases side by side, which side contains \(r\) and \(p\)?
Answer. \[
\begin{aligned}
v^*\text{를 알 때}:&\quad\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s')\Big] &&\leftarrow\ r,\ p\ \text{필요}\\
Q^*\text{를 알 때}:&\quad\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a) &&\leftarrow\ \text{모델 불필요}
\end{aligned}
\] \(Q^*\) is a table where the entire set of brackets is pre-calculated for each \((s,a)\). Therefore, it contains more information, and a model is not needed when retrieving policies.






TipSignificance






Even if ZZZPH0013294ZZZ is trained perfectly on \(v^*\) in a model-free configuration, a model is still needed to create a policy. Therefore, most RL algorithms train on \(Q\). The name Q-learning also comes from this.
The cost is that the size of the learning target increases from \(n\) to \(nm\).




↑ Go Up: Section 8.1, Section 10.1


8.1.2 How is the Bellman equation for Q derived?
\[
Q^*(s,a)=\underbrace{r(s,a)}_{\text{즉각 보상}}+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\underbrace{v^*(s')}_{\text{다음 상태의 최적 가치}}
=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a').
\]
First question to consider. If \((s,a)\) is currently fixed, the immediate reward is determined. Where does the remaining optimization go?






NoteInduction





If you set it to \(G_1:=\sum_{t\ge1}\gamma^{t-1}r(s_t,a_t)\), it is \(\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tr_t=r(s_0,a_0)+\gamma G_1\).
(≤) \[
\begin{aligned}
Q^\pi(s,a)&=r(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_1\mid s_0=s,a_0=a]\\
&=r(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_1\mid s_0,a_0,s_1]\ \big|\ s_0=s,a_0=a\big] &&(\text{tower})\\
&=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_1\mid s_0,a_0,s_1=s'] &&(s_1\text{의 분포는 }p(\cdot\mid s,a))\\
&\le r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s') &&(s'\text{부터의 누적 보상} \le v^*(s')).
\end{aligned}
\] Since this holds for all \(\pi\), it also holds for \(\max_\pi\).
(≥) We consider a policy where the first move is \(a\), and thereafter follows the stationary optimal policy \(\pi^*\). Due to Markov properties and stationarity, the value of the tail starting from \(s_1=s'\) is \(v^{\pi^*}(s')=v^*(s')\). Since this is an acceptable policy, \[Q^*(s,a)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s').\]
Combining the two directions yields the first equality, and substituting \(v^*=\max_{a'}Q^*\) yields the second equality.



Define the right side of this expression as an operator. \[
(T_QQ)(s,a):=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q(s',a'),\qquad Q^*=T_QQ^*.
\]






TipSignificance: The formula and structure are different from \(v\)






\(T\): max is outside the sum. Select the current action \(a\).
\(T_Q\): max is not sum. For every next state \(s'\), select the next action \(a'\) separately.

Due to this difference, the linearization of the Q-LP is not as simple as in the case of \(v\) → Section 9.1.1



↓ Down: Section 8.1.3 ↑ Up: Section 8.1


8.1.3 Why is \(T_Q\) monotonous and \(\gamma\) a contraction?






NoteProof





Monotonic. If \(Q\le Q'\), then for each \(s'\)Z, \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\le\max_{a'}Q'(s',a')\), and the weighted sum of \(p\ge0\) preserves order. Therefore, \(T_QQ\le T_QQ'\).
Abbreviation. \[
\begin{aligned}
|(T_QQ)(s,a)-(T_QQ')(s,a)|
&=\gamma\Big|\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\Big(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-\max_{a'}Q'(s',a')\Big)\Big|\\
&\le\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,\max_{a'}|Q(s',a')-Q'(s',a')| &&(\text{max 차이 부등식})\\
&\le\gamma\|Q-Q'\|_\infty\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)=\gamma\|Q-Q'\|_\infty.
\end{aligned}
\] It ends by taking the max for \((s,a)\).
max difference inequality: For all \(a\), \(x_a\le y_a+|x_a-y_a|\le\max_by_b+\max_b|x_b-y_b|\). Take \(\max_a\) on the left side, and swap \(x\) and \(y\) once more.









TipSignificance





Since it possesses the same two properties as \(T\), the argument in Section 4.1.1 is transferred directly to Q-LP (Section 9.1). The same property is used in the convergence proof of Q-learning.



↑ Go Up: Section 8.1.2, Section 9.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 9.1 What is Q-function LP and why is it inefficient
text:
9.1 What is Q-function LP and why is it inefficient
\[
\min_{Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}}\ \sum_{s,a}c(s,a)\,Q(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Q\ge T_QQ,\qquad c>0.
\]
The first question to think of.

In the proof that the solution to is \(Q^*\), which part of Section 4.1.1 needs to be changed?
To remove max, for which indices should “all” be added this time? Then, how many constraints are there?

Answer.

We just need to replace \(T\) with \(T_Q\). Since \(T_Q\) is also monotonic and contracted, and the unique fixed point is \(Q^*\) (Section 8.1.3), the unique optimal solution with the same three lines is \(Q^*\).
Since max is bound to the next action \(a'\), increase the constraint for \(a'\) as well. \[
Q(s,a)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',a')\qquad\forall(s,a,a').
\] There are \(n\times m\times m=nm^2\) constraints. It is rare to use this LP directly when finding the optimal Q.







TipSignificance





\(v\)-LP had variables \(n\) and constraints \(nm\). Q-LP had variables \(nm\) and constraints \(nm^2\). Since it amounts to solving the same information into a larger problem, there is no advantage for calculating optimal value. Q-LP is useful when the policy is fixed and the max disappears. → Section 10.1



↓ Down: Section 9.1.1 ↑ Up: Section 8.1

9.1.1 Fixed \(a'\) Is linearization equivalent to the original constraint?
First question to consider. The equivalence of Section 5.1.1 was when max was outside the sum. Under the linearization constraints above, can \(a'\) depend on \(s'\)?
Answer. They are not equivalent. Under the above constraint, \(a'\) is a single action common to all \(s'\). Therefore, the entire above constraint is \[
Q(s,a)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',a')
\] is equivalent to |||. However, generally \[
\max_{a'}\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',a')\ \le\ \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\max_{a'}Q(s',a')
\] Since (on the right, the best \(a'\) is selected separately for each \(s'\)), the linearized constraint is loose compared to \(Q\ge T_QQ\). As the feasible set grows, the optimal objective value can become smaller than that of \(Q^*\), and the solution differs from \(Q^*\).






NoteExact linearization: auxiliary variables





Set an auxiliary variable \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) to represent the value of the next state. \[
\min_{Q,u}\ \sum_{s,a}c(s,a)\,Q(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\begin{cases}
Q(s,a)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,u(s') & \forall(s,a)\\
u(s')\ge Q(s',a') & \forall(s',a')
\end{cases}
\] - If (\(\Rightarrow\)) \((Q,u)\) is feasible, then \(u(s')\ge\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\), and since \(p\ge0\), \(Q\ge r+\gamma\sum p\,u\ge T_QQ\). - (\(\Leftarrow\)) If \(Q\ge T_QQ\), then setting it to \(u(s'):=\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\) feasible.
Since the feasible set for \(Q\) is the same as the original, the solution is \(Q^*\). There are \(nm+nm=2nm\) constraints.
Numerical verification. For 200 randomly generated \(n=3\), \(m=2\), and \(\gamma=0.9\) MDPs, the auxiliary variable LPs all returned \(Q^*\) exactly. The fixed \(a'\) LP returned a solution different from \(Q^*\) (in one example, all elements were 0.04–0.06 smaller than \(Q^*\), and the maximum error out of 200 was approximately 2.7).









TipSignificance





The trick that “to get rid of a max, increase the constraint for every indices it is bound by” is only accurate when the max is outside the sum. To accurately linearize a max inside the sum, one must express “\(a'\) chosen for every \(s'\),” and the cleanest way is to keep that max value separately as a variable \(u(s')\). This \(u\) is effectively \(v\).



↑ Go Up: Section 9.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 10.1 To what extent can Q-based PI be performed without a model?
text:
10.1 To what extent can Q-based PI be performed without a model?
The first question to think of.

If policy \(\pi\) is fixed, what does the max of \(T_Q\) change to? Then, how many constraints are there in the Q-LP?
In the enhancement step \(\pi_{k+1}(s)\in\arg\max_a[r+\gamma\sum p\,v^{\pi_k}]\) of the existing PI, what is the entire bracket equal to?

Answer.

Evaluation: Since \(\pi(s')\) is placed in the max position, the constraint is linear, and there is one \((s,a)\) and \(nm\) solutions. The solution is \(Q^\pi\). \[
\min_{Q}\ \sum_{s,a}c(s,a)\,Q(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Q(s,a)\ge r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',\pi(s'))\quad\forall(s,a).
\]
Enhancement: \(\pi(s)\in\arg\max_aQ(s,a)\). No model needed.







NoteReason why the enhancement stage is Model Free





The Bellman equation of \(Q^{\pi_k}\) is \[
Q^{\pi_k}(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q^{\pi_k}(s',\pi_k(s'))=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^{\pi_k}(s').
\] This is because the final equality sign is \(v^{\pi_k}(s')=Q^{\pi_k}(s',\pi_k(s'))\) (act according to policy in the next state). In other words, the brackets of the existing enhancement stage are exactly \(Q^{\pi_k}(s,a)\). If \(Q^{\pi_k}\) has already been calculated, there is no need to recreate those brackets, and only \(\arg\max_aQ^{\pi_k}(s,a)\) needs to be done.









TipSignificance






The PI structure alternating between evaluation and enhancement remains the same. Monotonic enhancement and convergence arguments are also transferred as they are.
Now, the only place where a model remains is \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',\pi(s'))\) in the evaluation LP. If only this is changed to data, the entire thing becomes model-free → Section 10.2




↓ Down: Section 5.1.3, Section 8.1.1, Section 10.2 ↑ Up: Section 9.1

title: Linear Programming Approach
section: 10.2 Data-Driven PI: How to Eliminate Expectations in the Evaluation Phase
text:
10.2 Data-Driven PI: How to Eliminate Expectations in the Evaluation Phase
First question to consider. On the right-hand side of the evaluation LP constraint, the work done by \(p\) is the “expected value for the next state.” If we do not know \(p\) but can we sample the next state?
Answer. Collect transition samples \((s,a,r,s')\) from each \((s,a)\). These four elements constitute one unit of a transition sample in RL. Let \(D_{s,a}\) be the collection of the next states observed from \((s,a)\), and replace the expected value with the sample mean. \[
\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',\pi(s'))\ \approx\ \frac1{|D_{s,a}|}\sum_{s'\in D_{s,a}}Q(s',\pi(s')).
\] The algorithm repeats the following two steps.

Evaluation (Data-based): \[\min_{Q}\ \sum_{s,a}c(s,a)\,Q(s,a)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Q(s,a)\ge\hat r(s,a)+\gamma\,\frac1{|D_{s,a}|}\sum_{s'\in D_{s,a}}Q(s',\pi(s'))\quad\forall(s,a)\] (\(\hat r(s,a)\): Average of observed rewards. If the reward is deterministic, that value.)
Enhance: \(\pi(s)\in\arg\max_aQ(s,a)\).

Since neither step uses \(p\), it is model free.






NoteWhy is normalization of necessary for \(1/|D|\)





For the sample mean to approximate the expected value, the sum of the weights must be 1. If only \(\sum_{s'\in D}\) is used without \(1/|D|\), the right-hand side grows proportionally to the number of samples. Then, the “effective discount rate” of \(\gamma\sum_{s'\in D}\) becomes \(\gamma|D|\), which can exceed 1, and the conciseness of the operator is broken, resulting in no solution or a meaningless solution.









NoteWhat is the solution to this LP?





If we set the empirical transition probability \(\hat p(s'\mid s,a):=\#\{s'\text{가 }D_{s,a}\text{에 나타난 횟수}\}/|D_{s,a}|\) \[\frac1{|D_{s,a}|}\sum_{s'\in D_{s,a}}Q(s',\pi(s'))=\sum_{s'}\hat p(s'\mid s,a)\,Q(s',\pi(s')).\] Since \(\hat p(\cdot\mid s,a)\) is a probability distribution, the data-driven evaluation LP is the policy evaluation LP of the empirical MDP \((\hat p,\hat r)\) itself. The solution is \(Q^\pi_{\hat p}\) in that MDP. As the sample size of each \((s,a)\) increases, by the law of large numbers it becomes \(\hat p\to p\), and since \(Q^\pi\) is continuous in finite dimensions to \(p\), it becomes \(Q^\pi_{\hat p}\to Q^\pi\).









TipSignificance






It is the first algorithm to perform both evaluation and improvement without a model. The trade-off is that samples are required from every \((s,a)\), and the LP size is proportional to \(nm\). It is sufficient for small problems.
The idea of “replacing expected values with samples” is the starting point for the next steps (probabilistic approximation, TD, Q-learning). In that case, instead of collecting samples and solving LP again, the estimate is updated little by little whenever a sample comes in.




↓ Down: Section 10.1 ↑ Up: Section 10.1

✍ Try solving this first.

Write the four constraints of primal LP, and find \(v^*\) using the Bellman equation.
Write the two equation constraints of dual LP.
Determine which \(\lambda\) is 0 using complementary margins, and solve the remainders.
Check if the two target values are the same.







NoteSolution





1. primal. \[
\begin{aligned}
v(0)&\ge1+0.9\,v(0), & v(0)&\ge0+0.9\,v(1),\\
v(1)&\ge2+0.9\,v(1), & v(1)&\ge0+0.9\,v(0).
\end{aligned}
\] Bellman Equation: In State 1, repeating stay results in \(2/(1-0.9)=20\). Moving results in \(0.9\,v(0)\), but since \(v(0)\le20\), staying is better. \(v^*(1)=20\). In State 0, staying results in \(1/(0.1)=10\), and moving results in \(0.9\times20=18\). \(v^*(0)=18\).
\(v^*=(18,20)\), \(c^\top v^*=38\). The constraints for which equality holds are \((0,\text{move})\) and \((1,\text{stay})\).
2. dual constraint (\(\sum_a\lambda(s',a)=c(s')+\gamma\cdot\text{유입}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
s'=0:&\quad\lambda(0,\text{st})+\lambda(0,\text{mv})=1+0.9\big[\lambda(0,\text{st})+\lambda(1,\text{mv})\big],\\
s'=1:&\quad\lambda(1,\text{st})+\lambda(1,\text{mv})=1+0.9\big[\lambda(0,\text{mv})+\lambda(1,\text{st})\big].
\end{aligned}
\]
3. Complementary Lack. For non-equality constraints \((0,\text{stay})\) and \((1,\text{move})\), it must be \(\lambda=0\). The remaining expression is \[
\lambda(0,\text{mv})=1,\qquad\lambda(1,\text{st})=1+0.9\,(1+\lambda(1,\text{st}))\ \Rightarrow\ 0.1\,\lambda(1,\text{st})=1.9\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda(1,\text{st})=19.
\]
4. Objective value. dual: \(\sum\lambda r=19\times2=38\). primal: \(38\). Equal.
Verification. Total mass \(1+19=20=\sum_sc(s)/(1-\gamma)=2/0.1\).
Restore policy. Since \(\lambda(0,\cdot)=(0,1)\), move from state 0; since \(\lambda(1,\cdot)=(19,0)\), stay from state 1. Same as greedy policy.
Analysis of the occupancy measure. Mass 1, starting in state 0, immediately moves to state 1 (0.9 after discounting), combines with the 1 that was in state 1 from the beginning, and stays at every step. The total discount amount of state 1 is \((1+0.9)/(1-0.9)=19\).
(The above values are also confirmed with the LP solver as primal \(v=(18,20)\), dual \(\lambda=(0,1,19,0)\), and target value 38.)

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
2.1 Autoregressive dynamic system
The simplest form in which a state evolves without external input:
s^{(t)} = f(s^{(t-1)}; \theta)
If you unfold this along the time axis, all past states can be explicitly expressed.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
2.2 Dynamic system with external signal
Given external input x^{(t)}:
s^{(t)} = f(s^{(t-1)}, x^{(t)}; \theta)
In this case, s^{(t)} becomes a compressed representation of information about the entire past sequence. If we call this state the hidden state h^{(t)} and implement it as a learnable function f, that is precisely the Recurrent Neural Network:
\boxed{\;h^{(t)} = f(h^{(t-1)}, x^{(t)}; \theta)\;}






TipStatistical Intuition



This can be viewed as a neural network generalization of the HMM (Hidden Markov Model). While HMMs assume discrete states and linear transition probabilities, RNNs learn continuous states and non-linear transitions.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
4.1 Three Key Reasons

4.1.1 Bounded output: (-1, +1)
\tanh(z) = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}} \in (-1, +1)
In RNNs, the hidden state is repeatedly applied along the time axis:
h^{(t)} = \tanh(W_h \cdot \tanh(W_h \cdot \tanh(\cdots)))
If the activation were unbounded (e.g., ReLU), the value could diverge exponentially in the direction of \|W_h\| > 1. The saturation property of Tanh acts as a soft limiter that prevents state divergence.


4.1.2 Zero-centered



Activation
Output Range
Zero-centered




Sigmoid
(0, 1)
✗


tanh
(-1, +1)
✓


ReLU
[0, \infty)
✗



Since Sigmoid always produces a positive output, the gradient passed to the next layer always has the same sign, causing the zigzag update problem. Tanh can represent both positive and negative values, allowing the hidden state to naturally move in both directions.


4.1.3 Superiority over sigmoid in gradient propagation
\frac{d}{dz}\tanh(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z) \in (0, 1]
In BPTT (Backpropagation Through Time), the hidden state gradient is
\frac{\partial h^{(t)}}{\partial h^{(k)}} = \prod_{\tau=k+1}^{t} W_h^\top \cdot \mathrm{diag}(1 - (h^{(\tau)})^2)
If we compare the maximum values of the derivatives here:

\tanh Maximum derivative: 1
Maximum value of sigmoid derivative: 0.25

→ vanishing occurs approximately 4 times slower with tanh than with sigmoid.






WarningStill, limits exist



In the saturation region, it becomes 1 - \tanh^2(z) \to 0, and vanishing still occurs. This is the direct motivation for the emergence of LSTM/GRU, and they do not completely discard tanh but add a separate gradient highway through a gate.








NoteWireless communication analogy



The saturation characteristics of Tanh are similar to the saturation curve of a Power Amplifier (PA). It exhibits linear behavior when the input is small, but non-linear behavior where the output clamps to \pm V_\text{sat} when the input is large, which is the same in both cases. If we view an RNN as a system with a feedback loop, Tanh is a natural limiter that prevents divergence.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
5.1 Type 1: Hidden-to-Hidden Recurrence
h^{(t)} = \tanh(W h^{(t-1)} + U x^{(t)} + b) o^{(t)} = V h^{(t)} + c
Output at every time step + connection between hidden states. Most common and powerful form.

Advantage: h^{(t)} can form a sufficient statistic for the entire past, so it has high expressive power.
Disadvantage: Essentially, sequential calculation is forced.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
5.2 Type 2: Output-to-Hidden Recurrence (Teacher Forcing)
h^{(t)} = \tanh(W o^{(t-1)} + U x^{(t)} + b)
There is no direct connection between the hidden elements, and only the previous output o^{(t-1)} is passed to the next hidden element. Teacher Forcing is injecting the correct answer y^{(t-1)} instead of o^{(t-1)} during training.

5.2.1 Advantage: Parallelization possible during training
The reason parallelization is possible is due to data dependency decoupling.
Type 1 dependency chain:
h^{(1)} \to h^{(2)} \to h^{(3)} \to \cdots
To calculate → h^{(t)}, h^{(t-1)} must be completed first. No matter how many GPUs there are, the process must proceed sequentially one step at a time.
Dependency of Type 2 + Teacher Forcing:
h^{(t)} = \tanh(W \cdot \underbrace{y^{(t-1)}}_{\text{ground truth}} + U x^{(t)})
Since y^{(0)}, y^{(1)}, \ldots, y^{(T)} are all already given in the training data, all hidden states can be calculated simultaneously.
훈련 시 (병렬):
    h^(1), h^(2), h^(3), ..., h^(T)  ←─ 한 번에 계산
                                         (모든 y가 이미 알려짐)

Since h^{(t)} is not directly connected to h^{(t-1)}Z and must pass through a low-dimensional bottleneck called o^{(t-1)}, history information is lost if the dimension of o is small.
In addition, the exposure bias problem occurs, where the distributions of training (using correct answers) and inference (using self-outputs) differ.
