Teacher Forcing is essentially the same as pilot-aided channel estimation.

text:
5.3 Type 3: Sequence-to-One
Reads the entire sequence and generates only a single output at the end. Suitable for classification problems (sentiment analysis, document classification). The structure is similar to Type 1, but the output terminal is located only at the last point in time.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
section: 6.1 Why RNNs Collapse in Long Sequences
text:
6.1 Why RNNs Collapse in Long Sequences
Let’s simplify by assuming a linear RNN: h^{(t)} = W h^{(t-1)}
→ h^{(t)} = W^t h^{(0)}
If we write W as the eigenfactory W = Q \Lambda Q^{-1}:
h^{(t)} = Q \Lambda^t Q^{-1} h^{(0)}
Looking at the behavior of \Lambda^t here:







Condition
Result




\|\lambda_i\| < 1
\lambda_i^t \to 0 → Gradient Vanishing


\|\lambda_i\| > 1
\lambda_i^t \to \infty → Gradient Exploding


\|\lambda_i\| = 1
Stable (but very narrow range)



Since it is virtually impossible to keep it exactly on top of \|\lambda_i\| = 1, almost all RNNs go vanishing or exploding.
Even if nonlinear \tanh is added, vanishing worsens because the derivative becomes 0 at saturation.






TipWireless communication analogy: System stability



This is the same logic as the BIBO stability of an LTI system. If a pole is inside the unit circle, the response dampens (\to 0), and if it is outside, it diverges (\to \infty). The W_{hh} eigenvalues of an RNN play exactly the same role.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
6.2 The Duality of Expressiveness
There is another perspective. Deep composition of non-linear functions results in highly expressive composite functions — but at the cost of a harsh gradient landscape. In other words, the trade-off between expressiveness and learnability is the fundamental problem inherent in RNN depth.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
7.1 The core idea of gating
f(x) = a \cdot x (a \in [0,1], simple damping)
f(x) = a \cdot x + (1-a) \cdot m
Let’s change it to . Here, m is memory, and a is gate (the value being learned).
→ It is possible to separate the memory path that passes the past as is and the path that fuses new information. This is the key solution to the long-term dependency problem.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
7.2 LSTM: Long Short-Term Memory
LSTM has two types of states:

c_t (cell state): long-term memory
h_t (hidden state): short-term memory and output


7.2.1 4 Gates
f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) \quad \text{(forget gate)} i_t = \sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i) \quad \text{(input gate)} o_t = \sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o) \quad \text{(output gate)} g_t = \tanh(W_g [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_g) \quad \text{(candidate cell)}


7.2.2 Update Cell state and hidden state
c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)
Here, \odot is the element-wise product.






ImportantKey Point: Cell state is a separate Gradient Highway



In c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t, when it becomes f_t \approx 1, c_{t-1} remains almost unchanged.
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx f_t
is not multiplication but can be selectively kept close to 1 by a forget gate. This is the core of LSTM that enables long-term gradient flow.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
7.3 GRU: Gated Recurrent Unit
r_t = \sigma(W_r [h_{t-1}, x_t]) \quad \text{(reset gate)} z_t = \sigma(W_z [h_{t-1}, x_t]) \quad \text{(update gate)} \tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W [r_t \odot h_{t-1}, x_t]) \quad \text{(candidate hidden)} h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t
GRU does not have a separate cell state and handles both long and short-terms with a single h_t. The number of gates has also been reduced from 4 to 2.

text:
9.1 Bidirectional RNN
When information from not only the previous point in time but also the subsequent point in time needs to be utilized (e.g., determining word meaning after viewing the entire sentence). Use a bidirectional hidden state:
\overrightarrow{h}^{(t)} = f(\overrightarrow{h}^{(t-1)}, x^{(t)}) \overleftarrow{h}^{(t)} = f(\overleftarrow{h}^{(t+1)}, x^{(t)}) y^{(t)} = g(\overrightarrow{h}^{(t)}, \overleftarrow{h}^{(t)})






NoteWireless communication analogy: Forward-Backward Smoothing



If the Kalman filter is a forward-only estimator, the Bidirectional RNN is a neural network version of the Rauch-Tung-Striebel (RTS) smoother. It is identical to the method of combining forward and backward estimates after viewing all observations to obtain a more accurate state estimate.

title: Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU
text:
9.2 Seq-to-Seq (Encoder-Decoder)
A general-purpose structure that converts variable-length input to variable-length output.
입력 시퀀스 → [Encoder RNN] → context c → [Decoder RNN] → 출력 시퀀스

Encoder: Reads the entire input and compresses the last hidden state c into a semantic summary
Decoder: Generate output one token at a time starting from c

Application: - Machine translation (Input: English, Output: Korean) - Q&A - Chatbot






WarningSeq-to-Seq bottleneck



Since the entire input is compressed into a single fixed-size c, there is severe information loss for long inputs. This is the direct motivation for the emergence of the Attention mechanism and the subsequent Transformer.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
Deep learning training is ultimately an optimization problem. The key is to find the parameters \theta to minimize the loss, but two levels must be strictly distinguished.
Ideal Goal — Risk (Expected Risk)

J^*(\theta) = \min_\theta \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim p_{\text{data}}} \big[L(f(x;\theta), y)\big]

Here, p_{\text{data}} is the actual distribution that generates “all the data in the world.” Minimizing this value is the goal of true generalization.
Realistic Alternative — Empirical Risk

J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \hat{p}_{\text{data}}} \big[L(f(x;\theta), y)\big] = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} L(f(x^{(i)};\theta), y^{(i)})

Here, \hat{p}_{\text{data}} is the empirical distribution generated by the training dataset. J(\theta) is merely a proxy for J^*(\theta).






TipWireless communication analogy



In channel estimation, we want to minimize the MMSE of the entire channel environment (all locations, all times), but in reality, we only have a finite sample measured with pilot symbols. J(\theta), created from training data, can be thought of as a pilot-based estimate, while J^*(\theta), from the real world, can be thought of as a real channel.


This is Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM).



By definition, ERM is designed to overfit the training set. However, even if overfitting is intended, it is often difficult to efficiently optimize the ERM itself. For this reason, surrogate loss is used in practice.
The most representative example is the classification problem. The real goal is to minimize the 0-1 loss, but since it is not differentiable, the cross-entropy loss is used as a surrogate. This is a function that is easy to estimate and has a similar optimal solution.



In pure optimization, the objective itself is the problem, but deep learning optimization is different. We do not want to reduce J(\theta), but rather J^*(\theta), yet we are in a situation where we can only use J(\theta) as a tool. This subtle difference creates the inherent difficulty of deep learning optimization.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
Deep learning training is ultimately an optimization problem. The key is to find the parameters \theta to minimize the loss, but two levels must be strictly distinguished.
Ideal Goal — Risk (Expected Risk)

J^*(\theta) = \min_\theta \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim p_{\text{data}}} \big[L(f(x;\theta), y)\big]

Here, p_{\text{data}} is the actual distribution that generates “all the data in the world.” Minimizing this value is the goal of true generalization.
Realistic Alternative — Empirical Risk

J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \hat{p}_{\text{data}}} \big[L(f(x;\theta), y)\big] = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} L(f(x^{(i)};\theta), y^{(i)})

Here, \hat{p}_{\text{data}} is the empirical distribution generated by the training dataset. J(\theta) is merely a proxy for J^*(\theta).






TipWireless communication analogy



In channel estimation, we want to minimize the MMSE of the entire channel environment (all locations, all times), but in reality, we only have a finite sample measured with pilot symbols. J(\theta), created from training data, can be thought of as a pilot-based estimate, while J^*(\theta), from the real world, can be thought of as a real channel.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
By definition, ERM is designed to overfit the training set. However, even if overfitting is intended, it is often difficult to efficiently optimize the ERM itself. For this reason, surrogate loss is used in practice.
The most representative example is the classification problem. The real goal is to minimize the 0-1 loss, but since it is not differentiable, the cross-entropy loss is used as a surrogate. This is a function that is easy to estimate and has a similar optimal solution.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text: In pure optimization, the objective itself is the problem, but deep learning optimization is different. We do not want to reduce J(\theta), but rather J^*(\theta), yet we are in a situation where we can only use J(\theta) as a tool. This subtle difference creates the inherent difficulty of deep learning optimization.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
4.1 principle
If we expand J(\theta) around \theta_0, we get:

J(\theta) \approx J(\theta_0) + (\theta - \theta_0)^\top \nabla J + \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \theta_0)^\top H (\theta - \theta_0)

By differentiating with respect to \theta and setting it to 0, a single update step is obtained in a closed form:

\theta^* = \theta_0 - H^{-1} \nabla J(\theta_0)

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
4.2 Failure condition of Newton’s Method
If the Hessian is indefinite (containing a mix of positive and negative eigenvalues), the Newton step can converge to a saddle point. This situation is very common in the high-dimensional space of deep learning.
There are also practical problems.

If there are n parameters, H is the n \times n matrix — calculating the inverse matrix is virtually impossible with hundreds of millions of parameters.
Memory requirement O(n^2), computation amount O(n^3)
For this reason, deep learning relies on quasi-Newton methods (such as L-BFGS) or first-order methods

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
5.1 Batch Training Algorithm

W \leftarrow W - \lambda \cdot \frac{1}{m} \Delta W

Here, \Delta W = \sum_{i=1}^m \nabla_W \text{loss}^{(i)}(W), sum the gradients of all m samples.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
5.2 Characteristic Analysis

GD trade-off






Characteristics
Result




Use all data → Stable gradient
Descent in the correct direction


No noise
Some important gradients may be canceled out


Large datasets → Rapid increase in memory/computation costs
Reduced practicality



The core problem is that the larger the dataset, the more the entire data must be traversed for a single update. This is not practical at the scale of modern deep learning datasets.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
6.1 Mini-batch Training algorithm
By splitting the data into n mini-batches (each batch size k, total m = n \cdot k):

W_{l,j} \leftarrow W_{l,j} - \frac{\lambda}{k} \Delta W_{l,j}

Update immediately for each mini-batch.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
section: 6.3 Arguments in favor of SGD — Noise is actually an advantage
text:
6.3 Arguments in favor of SGD — Noise is actually an advantage

Local minimum escape: GD definitely gets stuck in a local minimum, but the stochastic noise of SGD causes it to escape.
Saddle point escape: Newton’s method attempts to converge to the saddle point, but SGD avoids this with noise.
Easy to Parallel: Each mini-batch can be processed independently → Advantageous for distributed learning.







NoteImportant Insight



The structure of the solution space is determined by the data distribution, not the convexity of the loss function. Even when using a convex loss, the landscape created by the data can be non-convex.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.1 Ill-conditioning
Hessian H occurs when the condition number \kappa is very large.

\kappa = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} \gg 1

The ideal step is \theta \leftarrow \theta - H^{-1} \nabla J, but with ill-conditioning, the general gradient direction deviates significantly from the optimal direction, following a zigzag path, and convergence becomes extremely slow.






TipWireless Communication Intuition



If the channel matrix H is ill-conditioned (if some singular values are very small), noise is amplified even when calculating the pseudo-inverse H^+. For the same reason, gradient updates on the ill-conditioned Hessian are also very unstable.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.2 Local Minima
The loss landscape of deep learning has numerous local minimums. There are various reasons why optimization fails to converge.

If the function has no local minimum → does not stop
If gradient noise is too large → diverge
Overfitting → Extreme values that fit only the training data
Deterministic: Stops before reaching the critical point in most cases

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.3 Saddle Points — Key Challenges
Let’s think of the sign of the Hessian eigenvalue at each parameter dimension as a coin toss.

heads = positive (local minimum direction)
tails = negative (local maximum direction)

The probability that all are heads (pure local minimums) in the dimension n is 2^{-n}. Since the n of deep learning ranges from millions to billions, there are overwhelmingly many saddle points.
Correction for Random Matrix Theory: The lower the loss value J, the higher the probability that the eigenvalue is positive. Therefore:

Low-J critical point → mostly local minimum (good solution)
High-J critical point → mostly saddle point (to avoid)

This theoretically supports the empirical observation in deep learning that “a good local minimum is good enough.”

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.4 Cliffs and Exploding Gradients
In deep or time-stretched networks like RNNs, when the same weight matrix is repeatedly multiplied, the gradient increases exponentially.

\nabla J \sim W^\top \cdot W^\top \cdots W^\top \cdot \delta

The solution is Gradient Clipping.

\hat{g} = \frac{g}{\|g\|} \cdot \tau \quad \text{if } \|g\| > \tau

Limits only the magnitude while maintaining the direction of the gradient.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.5 Long-Term Dependencies (Vanishing Gradient)
As the hidden layer deepens, the Jacobian is cumulatively multiplied according to the chain rule.

\frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial h^{(n)}} \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{n-1} \frac{\partial h^{(k+1)}}{\partial h^{(k)}}

If the Jacobian of each layer is less than 1, the product decreases exponentially → vanishing gradient. The gradient of the initial layer becomes virtually zero, making learning impossible.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.6 Inexact Gradients
The mini-batch gradient of SGD is merely a stochastic estimate of the true gradient.

g_{\text{batch}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in \text{batch}} \nabla_\theta L^{(i)} \approx \nabla_\theta J(\theta)

Optimization is more difficult because it is not an exact gradient. The solution is to use a surrogate loss instead of the actual loss.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
section: 7.7 Poor Local vs. Global Structure Correspondence
text:
7.7 Poor Local vs. Global Structure Correspondence
Occurs when local gradient information does not represent the global landscape. SGD must diagnose which of the following situations applies.

Is it trapped in a local minimum?
Are you wandering at the saddle point?
Are you wasting time navigating global obstacles?
Does it vibrate between multiple local bumps?
Does it move along the winding canyon?

This can be diagnosed through visualization.

1D subspace visualization: loss landscape between two points
2D subspace visualization: landscape in a plane spanned by two direction vectors

Empirical Lesson: In most problems, there exists a linear subspace with monotonically decreasing values. This is why SGD actually works well.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
7.8 Theoretical Limits
Theoretical analysis of deep learning optimization is extremely difficult. What we actually want is:

Exact global minimum ❌
Sufficiently good generalization performance ✓

This subtle difference makes deep learning theoretically difficult.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
10.1 Why is it necessary?
Vanilla SGD has two structural problems.
Problem 1 — ill-conditioning (poor Hessian conditioning)
If the contours of the loss function are very long ellipses (shaped like narrow canyons), the gradient oscillates back and forth along the walls of the canyon in the narrow direction, while moving slowly in the deeper direction. This occurs when the condition number of the Hessian is large.

\kappa = \max_{i,j} \left|\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}\right|

Problem 2 — Variance of Stochastic Gradient
Since the mini-batch gradient is a noisy estimate of the true gradient, the direction fluctuates at every step.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
10.2 Momentum Algorithm [Polyak, 1964]
The core idea is to accumulate past gradients using an exponentially decaying moving average to create velocity \mathbf{v}, and to move the actual parameters in the direction \mathbf{v}.

\mathbf{v} \leftarrow \alpha \mathbf{v} - \epsilon \nabla_\theta \left(\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} L(f(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\boldsymbol{\theta}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)})\right)


\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} + \mathbf{v}


\alpha \in [0,1): momentum hyperparameter, determines the exponential decay rate of the previous gradient contribution
\epsilon: learning rate
If \alpha = 0, it is the same as vanilla SGD; \alpha = 0.9 or 0.99 are common.







TipWireless communication analogy



\alpha is a type of low-pass filter coefficient. Instead of using the noisy gradient of each step as is, it exponentially weights and averages past signals to suppress stochastic noise and amplify signals in a consistent direction. This is the same principle as how the MMSE estimator filters out noise.


Magnitude of the steady-state value of velocity: If the continuous gradient g is fixed, the velocity is

\mathbf{v}_\infty = \frac{\epsilon \|\mathbf{g}\|}{1-\alpha}

converges to |||. That is, it moves \frac{1}{1-\alpha} times faster than vanilla SGD. If it is \alpha = 0.9, it is 10 times faster, and if it is \alpha = 0.99, it is 100 times faster.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
10.3 Nesterov Momentum
It is an improved version of Ordinary Momentum. The key difference is that it calculates the gradient not at the current position, but at the position where velocity is applied one step ahead.

Ordinary vs. Nesterov Momentum








Ordinary Momentum
Nesterov Momentum




gradient calculation location
\boldsymbol{\theta}
\boldsymbol{\theta} + \alpha\mathbf{v}


Formula
\mathbf{v} \leftarrow \alpha\mathbf{v} - \epsilon\nabla_\theta L(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\mathbf{v} \leftarrow \alpha\mathbf{v} - \epsilon\nabla_\theta L(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \alpha\mathbf{v})



The entire update rule is:

\mathbf{v} \leftarrow \alpha\mathbf{v} - \epsilon\nabla_\theta\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} L\left(f(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\boldsymbol{\theta}+\alpha\mathbf{v}),\mathbf{y}^{(i)}\right)\right]


\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} + \mathbf{v}







NoteWhy is it good?



Since we already know the direction of movement due to inertia is \alpha\mathbf{v}, we calculate the gradient at that position and add the correction factor. For convex functions, it has been theoretically proven that the convergence speed improves from O(1/T) to O(1/T^2).

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
11.1 Why is initialization important?
Since deep learning optimization is non-convex, where you start significantly influences where you converge. In particular:

If the initial value is too large → activation saturates → gradient vanishing
If the initial value is too small → the signal does not propagate
All units have the same value → No symmetry breaking occurs

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
11.2 Reset Weight

11.2.1 Naive method

W_{i,j} \sim U\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\right)

It is a scale inversely proportional to the fan-in m. The idea is to maintain a constant variance of the activation by reducing the contribution of each weight as the input increases.


11.2.2 Xavier / Glorot Initialization [Glorot and Bengio, 2010]

W_{i,j} \sim U\left(-\sqrt{\frac{6}{m+n}}, \sqrt{\frac{6}{m+n}}\right)

Here, m is the fan-in (number of inputs) and n is the fan-out (number of outputs).
The core idea is to achieve two goals simultaneously.

Forward pass: Activation variance is kept equal across all layers
Backward pass: Gradient variance of all layers is kept equal

The geometric mean of the scale that simultaneously satisfies these two conditions in a linear network (no activation) is \sqrt{\frac{2}{m+n}}, and if the range is set accordingly in a uniform distribution, the above equation is derived.






WarningLimitations of the assumption



Xavier’s derivation assumes a “matrix multiplication chain without non-linearity.” Since real networks contain non-linear activations such as ReLU and sigmoid, this is not a completely accurate assumption. Nevertheless, it works very well in practice.




11.2.3 He Initialization [He et al., 2015] — Version for ReLU

W \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \sqrt{\frac{2}{m}}\right)

Since ReLU makes half of the input (negative region) zero, the variance is multiplied by 2 to compensate for the reduction of the effective variance by half.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
11.3 Bias Initialization
In most cases, even if you initialize to 0, the weights break symmetry. The exceptions are as follows.

Output unit bias: The value obtained by converting the marginal statistics (mean) of the training set output into the inverse of the activation function.
ReLU bias: Set to around 0.1 → Prevent ReLU saturation during initialization
Gate/switch unit (LSTM forget gate, etc.): Set close to 1 → Allow information to pass through initially

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
12.1 AdaGrad [Duchi et al., 2011]
Adjust the learning rate by accumulating the sum of squares of past gradients \mathbf{r} for each parameter.

\mathbf{r} \leftarrow \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{g} \odot \mathbf{g}


\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \frac{\epsilon}{\delta + \sqrt{\mathbf{r}}} \odot \mathbf{g}


\delta: Small constant for numerical stability (\sim 10^{-7})
\odot: element-wise product

Effect: Parameters with large and frequent gradients → \mathbf{r} increases → effective learning rate decreases. Conversely, sparse parameters maintain large steps.






WarningProblem



Since \mathbf{r} is monotonically increasing, the effective learning rate converges to 0 as training lengthens → training stops prematurely. For this reason, it does not work well in non-convex deep learning.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
12.2 RMSProp [Hinton, 2012 — unpublished]
Solves the monotonically increasing problem of AdaGrad. Uses the exponential moving average instead of the sum of squares.

\mathbf{r} \leftarrow \rho\mathbf{r} + (1-\rho)\mathbf{g} \odot \mathbf{g}


\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{\delta + \mathbf{r}}} \odot \mathbf{g}


\rho: decay factor (usually 0.9 or 0.99)

Intuition: It reflects only the magnitude of the recent gradient, so it forgets old information. It has a sliding window effect. It is superior to AdaGrad in non-stationary objectives.
RMSProp with Nesterov momentum version also exists.

\mathbf{r} \leftarrow \rho\mathbf{r} + (1-\rho)\nabla_\theta L(\boldsymbol{\theta}+\alpha\mathbf{v}) \odot \nabla_\theta L(\boldsymbol{\theta}+\alpha\mathbf{v})

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
12.3 Adam [Kingma and Ba, 2014]
It is currently the de facto standard optimizer for deep learning. It integrates RMSProp + Momentum and adds bias correction.
(1) 1st moment estimate (mean): 
\mathbf{s} \leftarrow \rho_1 \mathbf{s} + (1-\rho_1)\mathbf{g}

(2) 2nd moment estimation (uncentered variance): 
\mathbf{r} \leftarrow \rho_2 \mathbf{r} + (1-\rho_2)\mathbf{g} \odot \mathbf{g}

(3) Bias correction: 
\hat{\mathbf{s}} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{s}}{1-\rho_1^t}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{r}} \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{r}}{1-\rho_2^t}

(4) Parameter update: 
\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \epsilon \frac{\hat{\mathbf{s}}}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{r}}} + \delta}







ImportantWhy is bias correction necessary?



It starts initially as \mathbf{s}_0 = 0, \mathbf{r}_0 = 0. In the first step, it is \mathbf{s}_1 = (1-\rho_1)\mathbf{g}_1, which is underestimated by a factor of (1-\rho_1) compared to the actual expected gradient value, \mathbf{g}_1. This is corrected by dividing by \frac{1}{1-\rho_1^t}. As t increases, it becomes \rho_1^t \to 0, so the effect of the correction disappears.


Recommended hyperparameter:

\rho_1 = 0.9 (momentum decay)
\rho_2 = 0.999 (RMSProp decay)
\epsilon = 10^{-3} (learning rate)
\delta = 10^{-8} (numerical stability)

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
12.4 Optimizer Comparison Summary
SGD          : θ ← θ - ε·g
Momentum     : θ ← θ + v,  v ← αv - ε·g
AdaGrad      : θ ← θ - ε/√r · g,  r 단조증가
RMSProp      : θ ← θ - ε/√r · g,  r 지수이동평균
Adam         : θ ← θ - ε·ŝ/√r̂,  both moments + bias correction






NoteWhich optimizer should be used?



According to the No Free Lunch Theorem, the optimal optimizer varies for each problem. Even in the extensive comparative study by Schaul et al. (2014), no clear superiority was determined. Generally, Adam is used as the default, and in vision tasks, momentum + SGD sometimes shows better generalization.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
14.1 Coordinate Descent
is a method that optimizes each dimension of the vector input \mathbf{x} independently. It repeats the process of freezing other variables and optimizing only one variable. Optimizing a subset of dimensions together results in block coordinate descent.
It is valid only when dimensions are truly independent, so it is not suitable for general deep learning parameters. However, it is useful for problems where dimensions are clearly distinct (e.g., the color dimension and edge dimension of an image).

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
14.2 Polyak Averaging
In the optimization process, the average of visited points is used as the final parameter.

\bar{\theta} = \frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t} \theta^{(i)}

In convex optimization, there is a strong guarantee of convergence. In non-convex neural networks, it is a heuristic but works well in practice. For non-convex problems, the running average (averaging only recent points) is commonly used.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
15.1 Batch Normalization [Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015]
Strictly speaking, it is not an optimization algorithm but an adaptive reparameterization method, yet it has a significant impact on optimization.
Normalize the activation of each layer in mini-batch units.

\hat{x}^{(k)} = \frac{x^{(k)} - \mu_\mathcal{B}}{\sqrt{\sigma_\mathcal{B}^2 + \epsilon}}


y^{(k)} = \gamma^{(k)}\hat{x}^{(k)} + \beta^{(k)}

\gamma, \beta is a learnable scale/shift parameter. If it is \gamma = \sigma_\mathcal{B}, \beta = \mu_\mathcal{B}, the original activation can be restored, so there is no loss of expressiveness.
Why is this necessary? Looking at the second-order term \epsilon^2 g_i g_j \prod_{k=i}^{j-1} w_k of the neural network output, if \prod w_k is greater than 1, an exponentially large term is created, making it very difficult to select a learning rate. BN alleviates this problem by stabilizing the activation distribution of each layer.
Effect:

Allow higher learning rate
Less sensitive to initialization
Regularization effect (mini-batch noise acts as a kind of noise injection)

Test: Use \mu, \sigma, the running average accumulated during training.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
15.2 Pretraining
Uses parameters pre-trained on large datasets or related tasks as initial values. Allows starting in a good area of the loss landscape.
Greedy supervised pretraining: When it is difficult to directly optimize a complex model, this is a method of training a simpler model on a simpler task and then gradually increasing the complexity.
MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning) [Finn et al., 2017]: meta-pretrains on multiple tasks to learn initial values that enable fast adaptation to new tasks.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
15.3 Knowledge Distillation [Hinton et al., 2015]
Train a small student model using the soft prediction of a large teacher model as the target. Pass the “dark knowledge” contained in the teacher’s prediction distribution.
This topic is very important, so it will be covered in detail in a separate section.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
15.4 Continuation Methods
Optimize by starting with an easy cost function J^{(0)} and moving to increasingly difficult cost functions J^{(k)}. The initial point is well-set to ensure that local optimization spends most of its time in the well-behaved region.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
15.5 Curriculum Learning [Bengio et al., 2009]
It trains by starting with easy examples and gradually moving to more difficult ones. It can be viewed as a data version of the Continuation method. It accelerates convergence by making the optimization landscape smoother. It is particularly useful in weakly supervised tasks like reinforcement learning.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
15.6 Better Architecture (ResNet)
Strictly speaking, it is an architectural design rather than an optimization algorithm, but it is a key element that aids in optimization. Residual connections (highway connections) preserve the gradients of later layers down to the initial layers, mitigating vanishing gradients.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
section: 16.1 Why are soft labels helpful for training?
text:
16.1 Why are soft labels helpful for training?
This is the core mechanism of Knowledge Distillation and can be analyzed from three perspectives: Information Theory + Optimization Landscape + Generalization.

16.1.1 Hard Label vs. Soft Label
The hard label (one-hot) is y = [0, 0, 1, 0, 0, \ldots, 0], which assigns a probability of 1 only to the correct class. The only information given to the model is “what the correct answer is”.
Soft label (teacher’s softmax output) shows that the correct answer class has the highest value, as in q = [0.01, 0.05, 0.85, 0.06, 0.02, \ldots, 0.01], but there is also a meaningful probability distribution in the incorrect answer class.


16.1.2 Information Theory Perspective — “Dark Knowledge”
This is a concept named by Hinton et al. (2015). The output of Teacher implicitly encodes the inter-class similarity structure. For example, for the MNIST digit “8” image, teacher:

Teacher distribution contains dark knowledge


Class
Soft Label




8 (Answer)
0.87


3
0.07


0
0.04


1
0.01


remainder
\approx 0



If you printed , this contains the information that “8 is visually similar to 3 and somewhat similar to 0.”
When comparing entropy, the one-hot distribution is H(p) = 0 bits, but the soft label is H(q) > 0. This means that additional information is contained.


16.1.3 Gradient Perspective — Maintaining Learning Signals
Let’s directly compare the gradients of the cross-entropy loss.
Hard label: 
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{hard}}}{\partial z_c} = p_c - y_c

A meaningful gradient flows only for the correct class (c). For the incorrect class j \neq c: 
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{hard}}}{\partial z_j} = p_j \quad \text{(매우 작음)}

If the model is already highly confident in the correct answer (p_c \approx 1), the gradient converges to nearly 0 and the learning signal vanishes.
Soft label: 
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{soft}}}{\partial z_j} = p_j - q_j

Since the incorrect class is also q_j > 0, a continuous gradient is supplied to allow the model to learn the relative relationship between the incorrect classes.


16.1.4 Normalization Effect — Generalization of Label Smoothing
Label smoothing (Szegedy et al., 2016): 
y_{\text{smooth}} = (1-\epsilon) \cdot y_{\text{hard}} + \frac{\epsilon}{K}

Distributes \epsilon/K evenly across all incorrect answer classes. Soft labels refine this further: 
y_{\text{soft}} = (1-\lambda) \cdot y_{\text{hard}} + \lambda \cdot q_{\text{teacher}}

Smooths the distribution to reflect actual similarity, even unevenly among incorrect answer classes. Both suppress the model’s over-confident prediction.


16.1.5 The role of Temperature
In KD, temperature T is introduced to softmax: 
q_c^{(T)} = \frac{\exp(z_c/T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}


Temperature distribution shape effect


Temperature T
Effect




T = 1
Original softmax (sharper)


T \gg 1
Distribution approaches uniform (softer)


T \to \infty
Perfectly uniform distribution



The higher the T used, the higher the probability of incorrect answer classes, and similarity information between classes becomes clearer. Hinton et al. recommend that both teacher and student use the same T.


16.1.6 Cleanup
Soft Label이 학습에 도움이 되는 이유:

1. 정보량 증가    → 클래스 간 유사도 구조(dark knowledge) 전달
2. Gradient 유지  → 정답에 confident해도 학습 신호가 소멸하지 않음
3. Landscape 개선 → Loss surface가 더 smooth, flat minimum 형성
4. 정규화 효과    → Over-confident prediction 억제, generalization 향상






TipWireless communication analogy



Training solely with hard labels is akin to performing channel estimation using only binary decisions (0/1). Soft labels convey confidence information, such as the Log-Likelihood Ratio (LLR), enabling the student model to make more accurate and robust estimates.

title: Optimization for Deep Learning
text:
16.2 What exactly is “Loss Landscape”?
In a word, it is the “topographic map” generated by the loss function in the parameter space.

16.2.1 Intuitive understanding
If we simplify the model to have only two parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \theta_2), the loss L(\theta_1, \theta_2) can be visualized in 3D space. Since actual deep learning models have millions to billions of parameters, direct visualization is impossible, but we can cut a 2D cross-section or conceptually imagine this terrain.


16.2.2 Major features of the landscape

Main structures of Loss landscape







Terrain
Meaning
Problem




Global minimum
L is the lowest point in the whole
hard to find


Local minimum
Lower than surroundings but not the global minimum
Can get stuck here


Saddle point
Some directions are minimum, other directions are maximum
Difficult to escape because gradient = 0


Flat region
Flat region with gradient \approx 0
Training appears to have stopped


Sharp valley
A canyon that is steep in one direction and gentle in the other
ill-conditioning problem





16.2.3 What Optimization Techniques Do in Landscapes
Gradient descent is ultimately a search process of walking over this terrain. Each technique plays the following role on the terrain.

Momentum → Use inertia to escape the canyon
Adaptive LR → Adjust stride based on terrain slope
Good initialization → Select a good starting location
Batch normalization → Makes the terrain itself smoother
Soft label → Reshape terrain to make it smoother



16.2.4 Flat Minimum vs Sharp Minimum
The statement that “flat minimums provide good generalization” also stems from this context. If the range converges to a wide, flat valley, the loss does not change significantly even if the parameters fluctuate slightly, making it stable on test data. In contrast, with a sharp minimum, the loss increases explosively with even a slight deviation (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Keskar et al., 2017).






TipWireless communication analogy



The landscape of the cost function in channel estimation is a familiar concept. The MMSE estimator has a convex quadratic landscape, so it has only one global minimum and converges easily. On the other hand, ML estimation in non-linear channel models has a non-convex landscape, leading to local minimum problems — exactly the same situation as in deep learning.

title: Machine Learning Basics - Part II
text:
The goal of linear regression is to learn the mapping from the input \(\mathbf{x}\) to the continuous target \(t(\mathbf{x})\). The core structure is the weighted sum of basis functions:
\[
\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{K} w_i h_i(\mathbf{x})
\]
where \(H = \{h_1, \dots, h_K\}\) is a predetermined set of basis functions and \(\mathbf{w} = \{w_1, \dots, w_K\}\) is the parameter to be learned.






ImportantMeaning of “Linear”



Even if non-linear basis functions like \(h_i(x) = x^2\) are used, this is still linear regression. This is because “linear” refers to linearity with respect to the coefficients (parameters) \(w\), not linearity with respect to the input \(x\).
\[
\hat{y} = w_0 + w_1 x + w_2 x^2
\]
There is a non-linear transformation \(x^2\), but it is a linear regression because \(w_0, w_1, w_2\) is a linear equation.







Hypothesis space \(\mathcal{H}\) is the set of all possible functions that we assume “the correct answer will be in here.” In linear regression:
\[
\mathcal{H} = \left\{ f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{K} w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) \;\middle|\; w_i \in \mathbb{R} \right\}
\]
When the basis function \(\{h_1, \dots, h_K\}\) is fixed, all possible weight combinations form the hypothesis space. The basis function defines the “coordinate axes” of the hypothesis space, and the weights are the coordinate values in that coordinate system.



The selection of the basis function itself is an inductive bias:







Basis function selection
Inductive bias




\(\{h_1(x) = x,\; h_2(x) = 1\}\)
“The answer will be a straight line”


\(\{h_1(x) = x^2,\; h_2(x) = x,\; h_3(x) = 1\}\)
“The answer will be a quadratic curve”


\(\{\sin(nx),\; \cos(nx)\}\)
“The answer is likely a periodic function”









TipWireless Communication Perspective



The choice of whether to use a delay spread-based basis, a Fourier basis, or a polynomial basis when estimating channels corresponds to this inductive bias. The selection of the basis function determines “how we view the structure of the world,” and this is the prior knowledge that humans inject prior to learning.
The reason deep learning is innovative is that it learns the basis functions themselves from the data. This is handled in the MLP (Multi-layer Perceptron).






Minimize the sum of squares of residuals:
\[
\text{total error} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_i \left( y_i - \sum_k w_k f_k(x_i) \right)^2
\]
This is the sum of the squared residual \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) at each data point. The reason for using squaring is to prevent positive and negative residuals from canceling each other out and to apply a larger penalty to large errors.





Design matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) is the \(N \times K\) matrix, and the elements are:
\[
H_{ji} = h_i(\mathbf{x}^j)
\]






WarningEach row of the Design Matrix has a different value



The definition of the basis function is that \(h_i(\cdot)\) is fixed (the form of the function depends only on \(i\)), but since the input value substituted into the function differs for each \(\mathbf{x}^j\), the output value depends on all \((i, j)\).
Example: 1D input, parabola basis \(\{h_1(x) = x^2,\; h_2(x) = x,\; h_3(x) = 1\}\), if data \(x^1=2, x^2=3, x^3=5\):
\[
\mathbf{H} = \begin{bmatrix} h_1(x^1) & h_2(x^1) & h_3(x^1) \\ h_1(x^2) & h_2(x^2) & h_3(x^2) \\ h_1(x^3) & h_2(x^3) & h_3(x^3) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \\ 25 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Just as in OFDM \(H_{ji}\) represents the contribution of the \(i\) tap to the \(j\) subcarrier, here \(H_{ji}\) represents the contribution of the \(i\) basis function to the \(j\) data.





If we define weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\) (\(K \times 1\)) and target vector \(\mathbf{t}\) (\(N \times 1\)):
\[
\mathbf{w}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} (\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})^T(\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})
\]
\((\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})\) is the residual vector, and its inner product with itself is the sum of squared residuals.






\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = (\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})^T(\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})
\]



Apply the distributive law of transposition \((A - B)^T = A^T - B^T\):
\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = (\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T - \mathbf{t}^T)(\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})
\]
Create 4 terms using the distributive property:
\[
= \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{t}
\]






NoteTranspose property of a scalar



\(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}\) and \(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}\) are both scalars, and since the transpose of a scalar is itself:
\[\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} = (\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w})^T = \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}\]
Therefore, the two terms can be combined.


\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{t}
\]



Two matrix differentiation formulas needed:
Rule 1 (Scalar version: Vector expansion of \(\frac{d}{dw}(aw) = a\)):
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{a}
\]
Rule 2 (Scalar version: Vector expansion of \(\frac{d}{dw}(aw^2) = 2aw\), when \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric):
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}
\]
Here, \(\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\) is always symmetric: \((\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^T = \mathbf{H}^T(\mathbf{H}^T)^T = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\)



\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} F(\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} + \mathbf{0}
\]
\(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{t}\) is a constant independent of \(\mathbf{w}\), so its derivative is 0.



\[
2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{0}
\]
\[
\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{w}^* = (\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}}
\]






ImportantInverse matrix existence condition



For \((\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1}\) to exist, \(\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\) must be invertible. This holds when the columns of \(\mathbf{H}\) are linearly independent, that is, when the basis functions are independent of each other. If \(N < K\) (number of data points < number of basis functions), it is not invertible, so the solution is not unique. This is one of the reasons why regularization is necessary.








TipConnection with MIMO ZF receiver



This Normal Equation has exactly the same structure as a zero-forcing receiver in a MIMO system:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{H}^H\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^H\mathbf{y}
\]
The only difference is that in the complex channel, the Hermitian transpose (\(H\)) is used instead of the transpose (\(T\)).








The observation model is assumed as follows:
\[
t(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) + e, \quad e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]
Under this assumption, the likelihood of a single observation is:
\[
P(t \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{[t - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x})]^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
\]



The log-likelihood of the entire data under the iid assumption is:
\[
\ln P(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \ln\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^N + \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{-[t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(x_j)]^2}{2\sigma^2}
\]
Maximizing for \(\mathbf{w}\), since the first term is a \(\mathbf{w}\)-independent constant:
\[
\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \ln P(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{-[t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(x_j)]^2}{2\sigma^2}
\]
If we convert the negative sign of the numerator and max to min, and remove the \(2\sigma^2\) constant:
\[
= \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} [t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(x_j)]^2
\]






ImportantLeast-Squares = Gaussian Noise MLE



Under the assumption of Gaussian noise, least-squares linear regression is equivalent to MLE.
If the noise distribution changes, the corresponding loss function also changes:

Gaussian noise → L2 loss (MSE)
Laplace noise → L1 loss (MAE) → robust regression

\(\{h_1(x) = x,\; h_2(x) = 1\}\)
“The answer will be a straight line”


\(\{h_1(x) = x^2,\; h_2(x) = x,\; h_3(x) = 1\}\)
“The answer will be a quadratic curve”


\(\{\sin(nx),\; \cos(nx)\}\)
“The answer is likely a periodic function”









TipWireless Communication Perspective



The choice of whether to use a delay spread-based basis, a Fourier basis, or a polynomial basis when estimating channels corresponds to this inductive bias. The selection of the basis function determines “how we view the structure of the world,” and this is the prior knowledge that humans inject prior to learning.
The reason deep learning is innovative is that it learns the basis functions themselves from the data. This is handled in the MLP (Multi-layer Perceptron).






Minimize the sum of squares of residuals:
\[
\text{total error} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_i \left( y_i - \sum_k w_k f_k(x_i) \right)^2
\]
This is the sum of the squared residual \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\) at each data point. The reason for using squaring is to prevent positive and negative residuals from canceling each other out and to apply a larger penalty to large errors.





Design matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) is the \(N \times K\) matrix, and the elements are:
\[
H_{ji} = h_i(\mathbf{x}^j)
\]






WarningEach row of the Design Matrix has a different value



The definition of the basis function is that \(h_i(\cdot)\) is fixed (the form of the function depends only on \(i\)), but since the input value substituted into the function differs for each \(\mathbf{x}^j\), the output value depends on all \((i, j)\).
Example: 1D input, parabola basis \(\{h_1(x) = x^2,\; h_2(x) = x,\; h_3(x) = 1\}\), if data \(x^1=2, x^2=3, x^3=5\):
\[
\mathbf{H} = \begin{bmatrix} h_1(x^1) & h_2(x^1) & h_3(x^1) \\ h_1(x^2) & h_2(x^2) & h_3(x^2) \\ h_1(x^3) & h_2(x^3) & h_3(x^3) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & 1 \\ 9 & 3 & 1 \\ 25 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Just as in OFDM \(H_{ji}\) represents the contribution of the \(i\) tap to the \(j\) subcarrier, here \(H_{ji}\) represents the contribution of the \(i\) basis function to the \(j\) data.





If we define weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\) (\(K \times 1\)) and target vector \(\mathbf{t}\) (\(N \times 1\)):
\[
\mathbf{w}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} (\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})^T(\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})
\]
\((\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})\) is the residual vector, and its inner product with itself is the sum of squared residuals.






\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = (\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})^T(\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})
\]



Apply the distributive law of transposition \((A - B)^T = A^T - B^T\):
\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = (\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T - \mathbf{t}^T)(\mathbf{Hw} - \mathbf{t})
\]
Create 4 terms using the distributive property:
\[
= \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{t}
\]






NoteTranspose property of a scalar



\(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}\) and \(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}\) are both scalars, and since the transpose of a scalar is itself:
\[\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} = (\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w})^T = \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w}\]
Therefore, the two terms can be combined.


\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} + \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{t}
\]



Two matrix differentiation formulas needed:
Rule 1 (Scalar version: Vector expansion of \(\frac{d}{dw}(aw) = a\)):
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{a}
\]
Rule 2 (Scalar version: Vector expansion of \(\frac{d}{dw}(aw^2) = 2aw\), when \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric):
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}
\]
Here, \(\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\) is always symmetric: \((\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^T = \mathbf{H}^T(\mathbf{H}^T)^T = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\)



\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} F(\mathbf{w}) = 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} + \mathbf{0}
\]
\(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{t}\) is a constant independent of \(\mathbf{w}\), so its derivative is 0.



\[
2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - 2\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{0}
\]
\[
\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathbf{w}^* = (\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}}
\]






ImportantInverse matrix existence condition



For \((\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1}\) to exist, \(\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\) must be invertible. This holds when the columns of \(\mathbf{H}\) are linearly independent, that is, when the basis functions are independent of each other. If \(N < K\) (number of data points < number of basis functions), it is not invertible, so the solution is not unique. This is one of the reasons why regularization is necessary.








TipConnection with MIMO ZF receiver



This Normal Equation has exactly the same structure as a zero-forcing receiver in a MIMO system:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{H}^H\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^H\mathbf{y}
\]
The only difference is that in the complex channel, the Hermitian transpose (\(H\)) is used instead of the transpose (\(T\)).








The observation model is assumed as follows:
\[
t(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) + e, \quad e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]
Under this assumption, the likelihood of a single observation is:
\[
P(t \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left( -\frac{[t - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x})]^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
\]



The log-likelihood of the entire data under the iid assumption is:
\[
\ln P(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \ln\left(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^N + \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{-[t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(x_j)]^2}{2\sigma^2}
\]
Maximizing for \(\mathbf{w}\), since the first term is a \(\mathbf{w}\)-independent constant:
\[
\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \ln P(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{-[t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(x_j)]^2}{2\sigma^2}
\]
If we convert the negative sign of the numerator and max to min, and remove the \(2\sigma^2\) constant:
\[
= \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} [t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(x_j)]^2
\]






ImportantLeast-Squares = Gaussian Noise MLE



Under the assumption of Gaussian noise, least-squares linear regression is equivalent to MLE.
If the noise distribution changes, the corresponding loss function also changes:

Gaussian noise → L2 loss (MSE)
Laplace noise → L1 loss (MAE) → robust regression

title: Machine Learning Basics - Part II
text:
2 Logistic Regression

2.1 Regression for classification
Although “regression” is in the name, Logistic regression is a classification model. The core idea: the regression output is passed through a logistic function (sigmoid) to convert it into a probability.


2.2 Logistic Function and Sigmoid
General logistic function:
\[
f(x) = \frac{L}{1 + e^{-k(x - x_0)}}
\]

\(x_0\): mid-point
\(L\): Maximum value of the curve (height)
\(k\): Curve slope (steepness)

standard sigmoid (\(L=1, k=1, x_0=0\)):
\[
\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
\]






Note\(\sigma\) Note on notation



In the ML/DL field, the sigmoid function is conventionally denoted as \(\sigma(\cdot)\). This has a completely different meaning from the standard deviation of a Gaussian distribution, \(\sigma\).

\(\sigma(\cdot)\): sigmoid function
\(\sigma^2\): Variance of Gaussian noise (in linear regression MLE)

This is notational overloading that must be distinguished by context.



2.2.1 Advantageous properties of Sigmoid

Output is in the \([0, 1]\) interval → Can be interpreted as probability
Smooth & continuous → Differentiable (Suitable for gradient-based optimization)
Mirror symmetric → \(\sigma(-x) = 1 - \sigma(x)\)
Derivative is cheap: \(\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))\) — Differentiation can be calculated using only the output value




2.3 Generative Model vs. Discriminative Model

2.3.1 Generative Model
Learn the Joint distribution \(P(X, Y)\). Decomposing it using Bayes’ rule:
\[
P(X, Y) = P(X|Y) \cdot P(Y)
\]
Model two things for each class \(Y\):

\(P(X|Y)\) (likelihood): “What does the data of this class look like”
\(P(Y)\) (prior): “How often this class appears”

Apply Bayes’ rule when classifying:
\[
P(Y|X) = \frac{P(X|Y) \cdot P(Y)}{P(X)}
\]
Examples: Gaussian Naive Bayes, HMM, GMM


2.3.2 Discriminative Model
Directly train on \(P(Y|X)\). Do not model \(P(X|Y)\) or \(P(X)\).
Examples: Logistic Regression, SVM, Neural Network


2.3.3 Key Comparison









Generative
Discriminative




Training Target
\(P(X,Y)\) or \(P(X|Y), P(Y)\)
\(P(Y|X)\) Direct


Data generation possible?
Possible (Origin of name)
Impossible


Number of parameters
High (describes input distribution)
Low


Classification Accuracy
Falls behind discriminative when data is large
Usually higher


Advantages
Missing data processing, outlier detection
Focus on classification, efficient









TipWireless communication analogy




Generative: For each transmitted symbol \(s_k\), fully describe the received signal distribution \(P(\mathbf{y}|s_k)\) using a channel model and perform MAP/ML detection.
Discriminative: Learns received signal → transmitted symbol mapping directly from data without a channel model (learned MIMO detector)






2.4 Probabilistic model of Logistic Regression
Logistic regression is a discriminative model that directly trains \(P(Y|\mathbf{X})\). In binary classification (\(y \in \{0, 1\}\)):
\[
P(Y=1 \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}}}
\]


2.5 MCLE: Maximum Conditional Likelihood Estimation

2.5.1 Problem situation
Traditional MLE attempts to maximize joint likelihood:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{MLE} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \prod_{j=1}^{n} P(x^j, y^j | \mathbf{w})
\]
However, since logistic regression is a discriminative model, it does not know \(P(X, Y | \mathbf{w})\) and only modeled \(P(Y|X, \mathbf{w})\). In other words, there is no usable tool.


2.5.2 Decomposition of Data Likelihood
Product rule of joint probability:
\[
P(x^j, y^j | \mathbf{w}) = P(x^j | y^j, \mathbf{w}) \cdot P(y^j | \mathbf{w})
\]
This comes from the definition of conditional probability \(P(A,B|C) = P(A|B,C) \cdot P(B|C)\). If we take the logarithm and sum it over all the data:
\[
\ln P(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w}) = \underbrace{\sum_j \ln P(x^j | y^j, \mathbf{w})}_{\text{(A): 입력 분포 모델링}} + \underbrace{\sum_j \ln P(y^j | \mathbf{w})}_{\text{(B): 클래스 prior}}
\]






Noteiid assumption



In the decomposition above, to decompose the joint likelihood into the product, the iid assumption is required for the data pair \(\{(x^j, y^j)\}_{j=1}^N\). Under the independence assumption, it is decomposed into \(P(y^1, \dots, y^N | x^1, \dots, x^N, \mathbf{w}) = \prod_j P(y^j | x^j, \mathbf{w})\), and taking the logarithm changes the product into a sum.




2.5.3 MCLE Solution
We define likelihood based only on what we have. Use Conditional data likelihood as the objective function:
\[
\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{MCLE} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \prod_{j=1}^{N} P(y^j | x^j, \mathbf{w})
\]
If you take the log:
\[
l(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \ln P(y^j | x^j, \mathbf{w})
\]
Since \(P(y|x, \mathbf{w}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x})^y \cdot (1 - \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}))^{1-y}\):
\[
l(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_j \left[ y^j \ln \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}^j) + (1-y^j) \ln(1 - \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}^j)) \right]
\]
This is the prototype of binary cross-entropy loss.


2.5.4 MCLE’s Philosophy: What is the benefit of only estimating \(P(Y|X)\)
Efficiency: The distribution \(X\) of the input \(P(X)\) is typically very high-dimensional and complex. In image classification, \(P(X)\) represents the “distribution of natural images,” and accurately modeling this is incredibly difficult. This information is not needed for classification. To distinguish between a cat and a dog, there is no need to know “what distribution the natural image follows.”
Accuracy: When training resources are limited, since parameters are not wasted on modeling \(P(X|Y)\) , but rather focused on \(P(Y|X)\), which is unnecessary for classification, classification performance tends to be better with the same amount of data.


2.5.5 Justification for MCLE replacing MLE
In the data log-likelihood decomposition above:

(A) \(P(X|Y, \mathbf{w})\): In logistic regression, \(\mathbf{w}\) is the parameter of the decision boundary. Since the distribution of the input data \(X\) is mostly not dependent on \(\mathbf{w}\), this term does not contribute to the optimization of \(\mathbf{w}\).
(B) \(P(Y|\mathbf{w})\): The prior probability of the class is usually independent of \(\mathbf{w}\), or is already given as a ratio in the data.

Therefore, (A) and (B) act as constant terms in the optimization for \(\mathbf{w}\) and:
\[
\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \ln P(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w}) \approx \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_j \ln P(y^j | x^j, \mathbf{w})
\]
While Generative MLE may be theoretically better, performance actually deteriorates if \(P(X|Y)\) is mismodeled (model misspecification). The Discriminative approach avoids this risk.



2.6 Gradient Ascent Optimization
Regarding the optimization of \(l(\mathbf{w})\):

\(l(\mathbf{w})\) has a concave function for \(\mathbf{w}\) → a globally optimal solution exists
No closed-form solution (Key difference from linear regression!)
The concave function can be optimized relatively easily using gradient ascent.

Gradient and update rules:
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} l(\mathbf{w}) = \left[ \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_0}, \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial l}{\partial w_n} \right]
\]
\[
w_i^{(t+1)} \leftarrow w_i^{(t)} + \eta \frac{\partial l(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_i}
\]






NoteAscent vs. Descent




maximize the objective function → gradient ascent (sign \(+\))
Minimize Loss → Gradient Descent (Sign \(-\))

The two are essentially the same algorithm, differing only in sign.

title: Machine Learning Basics - Part II
text:
3 Support Vector Machine (SVM)

3.1 Geometric intuition
In binary classification, a linear classifier divides the space into hyperplanes:
\[
\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + w_0 = 0
\]
\(\mathbf{w}\) is the normal vector of the hyperplane, and \(w_0\) is the bias. The label is \(y^j \in \{+1, -1\}\).


3.2 distance from point to hyperplane
Signed distance from data point \(\mathbf{x}^j\) to hyperplane:
\[
d^j = \frac{\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0}{\|\mathbf{w}\|_2}
\]
Multiplying \(y^j\) results in a positive number for correctly classified points:
\[
y^j \cdot \frac{\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0}{\|\mathbf{w}\|_2} > 0
\]


3.3 Margin Definition and Maximization
Margin = Distance to the nearest data point from the hyperplane:
\[
\text{margin} = \min_j \frac{y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0)}{\|\mathbf{w}\|_2}
\]
SVM maximizes this margin. If we fix it to \(\min_j y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0) = \gamma\) using scaling degrees of freedom, the margin becomes \(\frac{\gamma}{\|\mathbf{w}\|_2}\), and margin maximization is \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(\|\mathbf{w}\|_2\) minimization.


3.4 Final optimization problem
\[
\min_{\mathbf{w}, w_0} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2
\] \[
\text{s.t.} \quad \forall j, \quad y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0) > \gamma
\]
Meaning of each element:







Element
Meaning




\(\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2\)
\(\mathbf{w}\) Minimize size → Maximize margin. \(\frac{1}{2}\) is differentiation bias, squaring ensures convexity


\(y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0)\)
Functional margin. Positive for correct classification by multiplying \(y^j\)


\(> \gamma\)
Not a simple classification (\(>0\)), but requires a margin of at least \(\gamma\)



Conventionally, if set to \(\gamma = 1\), it is the standard form:
\[
\min_{\mathbf{w}, w_0} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \forall j, \; y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0) \geq 1
\]


3.5 Support Vector
The points where equality holds under the constraint —that is, the data points \(y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0) = \gamma\)— are support vectors. Only these points determine the location of the hyperplane, and the remaining points do not affect the result.


3.6 Connection with Lagrangian/KKT
This problem is a Quadratic Programming (QP) problem because it involves quadratic objectives + linear constraints. Lagrangian:
\[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, w_0, \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 - \sum_j \alpha_j \left[ y^j(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}^j + w_0) - \gamma \right]
\]
By the KKT condition, only the points \(\alpha_j > 0\) are support vectors, and the rest are \(\alpha_j = 0\).






TipWireless Communication Analogy: Constellation Design



Margin maximization in SVM follows the same philosophy as minimum distance maximization in telecommunications. Just as maximizing the minimum Euclidean distance between symbols in QAM constellation design minimizes BER, SVM reduces misclassification by maximizing the minimum distance between classes.

title: Machine Learning Basics - Part II
text:
4 K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) Classifier

4.1 algorithm

Given a new data point, find the \(K\) neighbors closest to the training data
Determine class by majority voting
No separate parameter learning step (lazy learning)

The definition of “closeness” depends on the distance metric (Euclidean, Manhattan, etc.).


4.2 No Training Phase?
“No training” means there is no parameter optimization process:

“Training” Step: Save training data. End.
Prediction Step: When a new \(\mathbf{x}\) comes in, calculate the distance to all stored training data, and Find the closest \(K\) and vote by majority

Calling fit() in scikit-learn internally stores data and builds index structures (KD-tree, Ball-tree, etc.) for efficient searching. It is not parameter learning.



Attribute
Value




Training time
\(O(1)\) — Just save


Prediction Time
\(O(N \cdot d)\) — Proportional to Data Size, Slow


Hyperparameter
\(K\) Value or ball radius (tuned with validation)









TipWireless Communication Perspective



KNN is actively used in RF fingerprinting-based location estimation. It is natural to assume that locations with similar received signal patterns will have similar coordinates.

title: Machine Learning Basics - Part II
text:
5 Decision Tree and Random Forest

5.1 Decision Tree
This is a method that recursively partitions data based on feature conditions. Each internal node checks the condition for a single feature, and the leaf node makes the final decision.


5.2 Limitations of Decision Trees

Easily overfitting on training data
High variance problem where the tree structure changes significantly even with slight changes in data



5.3 Random Forest
Create multiple decision trees and ensemble them. The key is two types of randomness that intentionally make each tree different:
Creates a different training set for each tree using bootstrap sampling from the original data . When \(N\) data points are sampled with replacement (\(N\)) of them, on average, only about 63.2% of the unique data is included.
Feature randomness: When splitting at each node, the optimal split is found only from randomly selected \(\sqrt{d}\) (classification) or \(d/3\) (regression) features, rather than from all \(d\) features.


5.4 Prediction method

Category: Majority vote on predictions for all trees
Regression: Average the predictions of all trees



5.5 Why it works well
Individual trees have high variance and low bias. Averaging trees created with different randomness reduces variance and maintains bias.






TipWireless Communication Analogy: Diversity Combining



Just as combining multiple independent fading channels increases overall confidence, combining independent trees increases prediction stability.

These are all representative algorithmic paradigms of supervised learning and demonstrate the core axes of ML through their contrasting characteristics.

that starts with linear regression, applies the sigmoid function to logistic regression, and extends to SVM by introducing the concept of margin. This lineage is the foundation of neural networks.






ImportantConnection to the next step



Linear regression and logistic regression are actually 1-layer neural networks. If you stack layers on top of them and add non-linear activation, they become MLPs (Multi-layer Perceptrons). This is the key point of the next chapter.

title: Introduction to DL
text:
3.1 Embedding

3.1.1 Mathematical Definition
“When Object \(X\) is embedded in \(Y\), the embedding is given by the injective and structure-preserving function \(f: X \to Y\).”
In deep learning, it is specified as follows.
\[f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}^d, \quad d \ll D\]
Two conditions are important.
① Injective:
\[x_1 \neq x_2 \implies f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)\]
Discriminability of information is preserved.
② Structure-preserving:
\[d_{\text{원공간}}(x_1, x_2) \approx d_{\text{임베딩}}(f(x_1), f(x_2))\]
Relationships in the original space are maintained in the embedding space as well. A representative example is the relationship preservation in Word2Vec.
\[\vec{\text{king}} - \vec{\text{man}} + \vec{\text{woman}} \approx \vec{\text{queen}}\]

title: Introduction to DL
text:
3.2 Manifold

3.2.1 Mathematical Definition
“In mathematics, a \(n\)-dimensional manifold is a topological space in which the neighborhood of each point is homeomorphic to the \(n\)-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\).”
Simply put, it is a space that looks like a flat Euclidean space when viewed from a sufficiently close distance (locally).
The image of a person standing on the Earth on the slide conveys this intuition well. The Earth is a sphere existing in three-dimensional space, but its surface is two-dimensional. A location on the Earth’s surface can be completely described using only two coordinates: latitude and longitude.
전체적으로(Globally):  구부러진 표면  (지구)
가까이서(Locally):     평평한 평면  (내 발 앞 땅)


3.2.2 Manifold Hypothesis
This is one of the theoretical grounds on which deep learning works.

Actual data is not evenly distributed in high-dimensional space, but, It is concentrated on a much lower-dimensional manifold.

Mathematically:
\[p_{\text{data}}(x) \text{ is concentrated near a manifold } \mathcal{M} \subset \mathbb{R}^D\]
\[\dim(\mathcal{M}) = d \ll D\]
Example: In a 28×28 = 784-dimensional image space, “natural handwriting images” exist only in a very small part (low-dimensional manifold) of this 784-dimensional space.


3.2.3 Relationship with the Curse of Dimensions
The Curse of Dimensionality discussed in Goodfellow Ch. 5.11 is overcome by the manifold hypothesis.
If the input dimension is \(d\) and Z\(v\) values are distinguished on each axis, the number of required regions increases exponentially with the dimension, reaching \(O(v^d)\). Deep learning utilizes the Manifold Hypothesis to learn the fact that real data is concentrated on a low-dimensional manifold within a high-dimensional space.
The Autoencoder is a representative model for learning this manifold.
\[\text{Encoder: } \mathbb{R}^D \xrightarrow{f_\phi} \mathbb{R}^d, \quad
\text{Decoder: } \mathbb{R}^d \xrightarrow{g_\theta} \mathbb{R}^D\]
\[\min_{\phi, \theta} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}} \|x - g_\theta(f_\phi(x))\|^2\]

3.3 Latent Space

3.3.1 Intuition
The puppeteer controls the entire complex movement of the puppet using only a few strings. What is visible (puppet movement, high dimension) is determined by what is invisible (string pulling, low dimension). The space of these invisible strings is precisely Latent Space.


3.3.2 Mathematical Definition
\[\underbrace{x}_{\text{관측 가능}} = g(\underbrace{z}_{\text{잠재 변수}}) + \epsilon\]
\(z \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are the hidden causes that generate data, and \(g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D\) converts it into an observable form.


3.3.3 Subspace vs Latent Space




Subspace
Latent Space




Origin

PCA (Linear Subspace):
\[z = W^\top x, \quad W \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d} \text{ (직교 기저)}\]
VAE (Non-linear Latent Space):
\[q_\phi(z \mid x) \approx \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x),\, \sigma^2_\phi(x))\]
Linear interpolation between two points \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) in a well-learned Latent Space generates meaningful intermediate data (continuity).

4.3 Why is a Validation Set necessary?
Goodfellow states the key point in Chapter 5.3. If hyperparameters controlling the model’s capacity are trained on the training data, the algorithm will always select the maximum possible capacity, which leads directly to overfitting.
\[\lambda^* = \arg\min_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}\bigl(\theta^*(\lambda)\bigr)\]






WarningTest Set No Contamination



During the hyperparameter tuning process through validation, repeatedly examining the test set effectively turns it into a second validation set. The final performance estimate becomes optimistically biased. “It’s a crime!” — Lecture slides

text:
6.3 Why Traditional ML Fails: The Local Smoothness Assumption
According to Goodfellow Ch. 5.11, traditional ML relies on the local smoothness assumption. It estimates the output of a new input as the output of the nearest training point.
In high-dimensional space, this assumption is broken because there is not enough “near” training data (curse of dimensionality) . Deep learning overcomes this through hierarchical representation learning.

Classical theory predicts that as model complexity (capacity) increases, bias decreases and variance increases, causing the test error to follow a U-shaped curve.

section: 7.4 Reasons why it becomes generalized in Modern Regimes
text:
7.4 Reasons why it becomes generalized in Modern Regimes

7.4.1 Implicit Regularization of SGD
SGD implicitly favors the minimum norm solution among the infinitely many solutions that satisfy the training data.
Set of solutions satisfying the training data in a linear model:
\[\{\theta : X\theta = y\}\]
tends to converge to the solution with the minimum of \(\|\theta\|_2\) in this set, i.e., the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse solution.
\[\theta^* = X^\top(XX^\top)^{-1}y\]


7.4.2 Smooth Interpolation
With a much larger number of parameters, one can find a function that smoothly passes between training points. In the critical zone, the function must bend sharply, but in the Modern Regime, slack degrees of freedom lead to a smooth solution.






NoteEpoch-wise Double Descent



There is also a phenomenon that occurs the longer the same model is trained. Initially, it learns useful patterns (first-order descent), then memorizes noise (ascending), and after training long enough, it converges back to meaningful patterns (second-order descent). This is also the reason why Early Stopping is not always the best option.








TipWireless Network Perspective



in the same context as the distribution shift problem in channel estimation, where performance drops sharply when a trained model goes out of the SNR range . Also, just as Compressed Sensing finds a sparse solution for an underdetermined system \(M < N\) by minimizing the \(\ell_1\) norm, SGD also induces implicit sparsity.

title: Latest Deep Learning Techniques: RLHF · PEFT · RAG · Agents · World Models
text: One-line Map: A well-prepared LLM is (1) aligned to human preferences (RLHF·Alignment), (2) efficiently adapted with few parameters (PEFT), (3) reduced illusions using external knowledge (RAG), (4) task completion using external tools/behaviors (Agents), and (5) planned/simulated by modeling the world itself (World Models). This note organizes these five axes using mathematical formulas, intuition, and wireless communication analogies.

title: Latest Deep Learning Techniques: RLHF · PEFT · RAG · Agents · World Models
section: 1.1 Motivation: Why instruction finetuning alone is insufficient
text:
1.1 Motivation: Why instruction finetuning alone is insufficient
Direct Answer. Instruction finetuning optimizes the language modeling objective function, but what we actually want is to satisfy human preferences. There is an objective mismatch between the two.






NoteRecap — Instruction Finetuning



When a pre-trained LLM is further fine-tuned by grouping various tasks into “instruction–answer” pairs, zero-shot performance is improved even on unseen tasks that were not directly used for training (Wei et al., Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners, ICLR 2022). Although formally called “fine-tuning,” in reality it is closer to a procedure of pre-training the model with a wide range of tasks to improve generalized response capabilities.


Two inherent limitations of instruction finetuning:









#
Limit
Description
Example




1
Task with no correct answer
Open-ended generation has no single correct answer or single metric → Cannot generate instruction–answer pairs themselves
“Write a story about a puppy and its pet grasshopper”


2
Equal Punishment for Token Errors
Language modeling loss punishes all token errors equally, but some errors are more fatal
In “The current US president is ___“, errors in the name token are much more fatal than errors in particles or conjunctions



Key Insight: The objective of language modeling (\(\max \log p(\text{next token})\)) does not directly care about “user satisfaction.” It merely outputs the next token with high probability, and how much that response satisfies humans is not included in the objective function. → “Can’t we include human preference as an explicit objective?” is the starting point of RLHF.

title: Latest Deep Learning Techniques: RLHF · PEFT · RAG · Agents · World Models
text:
1.2 3-stage structure of RLHF
Direct Answer. RLHF = Establish a starting point with SFT → Train a reward model with preference data → Fine-tune LLM to RL using that reward.





flowchart LR
    A["Step 1<br/>Instruction-tuned LM<br/>(SFT 시작점)"] --> B["Step 2<br/>인간 피드백 수집<br/>(선호 쌍, Likert/랭킹)"]
    B --> C["Step 3<br/>보상 모델(RM) 학습<br/>+ PPO로 LLM 미세조정"]
    C -. "정책이 base에서<br/>너무 벗어나지 않게 KL 제약" .-> C







Step 1 — SFT Starting Point: Build a base model that produces a plausible response using instruction finetuning.
Step 2 — Feedback Collection: When the LLM generates two responses for a single prompt, a human evaluates which one is preferred using a Likert scale (strongly better ↔︎ slightly better) or ranking. (There is an anecdote that OpenAI hired a large number of linguistics and humanities majors, rather than engineering majors, and paid them high wages to perform labeling.)
Step 3 — Reward Model + RL: Train a reward model with preference data, and fine-tune the LLM using reinforcement learning with that reward as a signal.







TipHistorical Context — Learning to summarize (NeurIPS 2020)



In initial experiments (Stiennon et al.), for the same prompt, the vanilla LM output was mechanical, such as repeating the same words, but the output of the model injected with lightweight human feedback became natural, as if written by a human. After confirming this effect, a three-stage pipeline was established to advance the GPT-3 family from InstructGPT to ChatGPT.

title: Latest Deep Learning Techniques: RLHF · PEFT · RAG · Agents · World Models
text:
1.3 Reward Model and Bradley–Terry Loss
Direct Answer. The reward model is trained with a loss that increases the difference between the two rewards so that the reward for the chosen response becomes greater than the reward for the rejected response.
Add a new final layer (preferred head) on top of the base model and minimize the following loss:
\[
L_{\text{RM}} \;=\; \log\!\Big(1 + e^{\,r_{\text{rejected}} - r_{\text{chosen}}}\Big).
\]
This is identical to the Bradley–Terry / Logistic Preference Model. If set to \(\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\)
\[
L_{\text{RM}} = -\log \sigma\!\big(r_{\text{chosen}} - r_{\text{rejected}}\big),
\]
That is, it is the negative log-likelihood (binary cross-entropy) of the “probability that ‘chosen’ beats ‘rejected’”. (In Appendix Section 8, the numerical equivalence of the two forms is verified using SymPy.)






NotePractical Details




Single 1 epoch training (intentional overfitting).
Human evaluation mutual agreement rate is typically at the 65–75% level — reward signals are inherently noisy. This leads to the need for KL normalization later on (Section 1.5).
Variations that add margin (difference in strength between options) to the loss are common.

RL Concept
Correspondence in RLHF




Agent / Policy \(\pi_\theta\)
LLM in Learning


Action
Response generated by LLM (Token string)
