title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
section: 2.1 Why can’t I handle p(x) directly
text:
2.1 Why can’t I handle p(x) directly
Given the data X=\{x_1,\dots,x_N\}, it is difficult to directly model p(x). Therefore, we bypass this by introducing the known (easy to sample) prior distribution p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I).

p(x)=\int_z p(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz .

The problem is that this integral is still difficult to handle (z integral over the entire space). So, we replace the posterior distribution p(z\mid x) with a parameterized approximation distribution q_\phi(z). This is variational inference.

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
2.2 ELBO Induction
Starting from Bayes’ rule and \log p(x)=\log p(x)\cdot\int q_\phi(z)\,dz, if we organize:

\log p(x)=\underbrace{\mathbb E_{q_\phi}\!\big[\log p(x,z)-\log q_\phi(z)\big]}_{\textstyle \text{ELBO}}
\;+\;\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q_\phi(z)\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big)}_{\textstyle \ge 0}.

The left side \log p(x) is constant for \theta,\phi. Since the KL term is always \ge 0, increasing ELBO = making the approximate posterior q_\phi closer to the true posterior p(z\mid x).
If you expand ELBO one more time, two familiar terms appear.

\mathrm{ELBO}=\mathbb E_{q_\phi}\!\big[\log p(x\mid z)\big]-\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q_\phi(z)\,\|\,p(z)\big).


First term: reconstruction — How well decoder p(x\mid z) reconstructs x
Second term: Regularization — Force the distribution of the latent z to follow \mathcal N(0,I)

Therefore, the VAE loss is

\min_{\theta,\phi}\;\; -\,\mathbb E_{q_\phi}\!\big[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)\big]\;+\;\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big).

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
2.3 Reparameterization Trick
The backpropagation path is \mathcal L \to z \to \phi, but if we sample z\sim q_\phi(z\mid x), the operation is not differentiable. We bypass this by separating randomness into external variables.

z=\mu_\phi(x)+\sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).

Now, randomness exists only in \epsilon, and since the path passing through \mu_\phi,\sigma_\phi is deterministic, a gradient flows.






ImportantWireless Communication Analogy — Reparameterization = Received Signal Model



Let’s consider the received signal y=h\,x+n,\ n\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2). If we separate the channel gain h (the deterministic part) and the noise n (the random part), derivatives with respect to system parameters flow only along the deterministic path, and randomness is isolated from the noise term. Reparameterization z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon is exactly this structure — it creates samples in the form of “mean (signal) + standard deviation (noise intensity) × standard normal”.

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
section: 3.1 Adversarial examples and adversarial training are different
text:
3.1 Adversarial examples and adversarial training are different






WarningCaution: Confusion



Adversarial example: Adding subtle perturbations to the input to trick an already trained neural network. For instance, adding a patch invisible to the human eye to an image of a cat causes it to misclassify it as a “desktop computer” with high confidence. The objective is an attack.
Adversarial training (= GAN learning paradigm): Learning in which two networks compete to deceive/not deceive each other to improve together. The goal is to make the generator better.
Both share the word “adversarial,” but their purposes are diametrically opposed. (LeCun noted in 2016 that “the most interesting idea in ML over the last decade is adversarial learning.”)

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
section: 3.2 Components: Generator G and Discriminator D
text:
3.2 Components: Generator G and Discriminator D

Generator G: Takes a d-dimensional random vector z (e.g., a sample from \mathcal N(0,I)) as input and outputs an image. The z space is the “latent space”, and G mimics the data generation distribution.
Discriminator D: Determines whether the input image is real (real-world data) or fake (created by G). Output D(x)\in[0,1] is the “probability that it is real”.

What makes a good generator? It is one that produces a high degree of “realistic appearance in the generated images.” However, humans cannot grade whether they look realistic every time. Therefore, a second network called a discriminator is introduced and used as an automated grader—this is the core idea of adversarial learning.





flowchart LR
    Z["z ~ N(0,I)"] --> G["생성기 G"]
    G --> FAKE["가짜 이미지 G(z)"]
    REAL["진짜 이미지 x ~ p_data"] --> D
    FAKE --> D["판별자 D"]
    D --> OUT["D(·) ∈ [0,1]<br/>진짜일 확률"]

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
3.3 minimax objective function

\min_G\max_D\; V(D,G)=\mathbb E_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}\big[\log D(x)\big]
+\mathbb E_{z\sim p_z}\big[\log\!\big(1-D(G(z))\big)\big].

The physical meaning of is “log probability that x is real” + “log probability that G(z) is fake”. It must be read in terms of two variables.

D Perspective (Maximization): If x is true, then D(x)\to1, so the first term \log D(x)\to0 (maximum). If G(z) is false, then D(G(z))\to0, so the second term \log(1-0)\to0. In other words, if D does well, V becomes larger → D maximizes V.
G Perspective (Minimization): If G successfully deceives D, then D(G(z))\to1, which is the second term \log(1-1)\to-\infty. That is, if G performs well, V becomes smaller → G minimizes V.

It is a zero-sum non-cooperative game (minimax problem) where players pull in opposite directions.






Notelearning = block coordinate descent (alternating optimization)



The parameters of G and D are included together within the entire parameter set. Optimization is performed alternately by fixing one side and descending or ascending (gradient) on the other. This is block coordinate descent. Instead of descending all coordinates simultaneously, variable blocks are divided and descended alternately. (The maximization term is unified into descent simply by reversing its sign.)


Update written in three steps:

D Update (Real): To make D say “Real” for real data. D(x_{\text{real}})\to1.
D Update (Fake): To make D say “fake” for fake data. D(G(z))\to0.
G Update: Update G so that D mistakes the fake for “real”. To become D(G(z))\to1.

At each step, the higher side is barely updated, while the lower side is updated significantly. When updating G, the gradient is backpropagated serially through D to G; therefore, by the time G is reached, the gradient has already decreased significantly, making it difficult to train G (connected to the three major challenges below).

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
section: 3.4 Optimal Discriminator and JSD: Why is it p_g=p_{\text{data}} if it works well?
text:
3.4 Optimal Discriminator and JSD: Why is it p_g=p_{\text{data}} if it works well?
If we fix G, we can maximize V with respect to D. Differentiating the integral interior with respect to D(x) and setting it to zero gives the optimal discriminator:

D^\*(x)=\frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x)+p_g(x)} .

Substituting this, the objective function is simplified to Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD).

V(G,D^\*)=-\log 4+2\,\mathrm{JSD}\!\big(p_{\text{data}}\,\|\,p_g\big).

Since ZZZPH0009154ZZZ \mathrm{JSD}\ge0 and p_g=p_{\text{data}}, 0, the global optimum is p_g=p_{\text{data}}, and the value therein is -\log 4\approx-1.386. (This value was numerically verified using the appendix code.)

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
section: 3.5 Why GANs are effective: hard negative
text:
3.5 Why GANs are effective: hard negative
To accurately map the “mountain ranges” of a data generation distribution, samples near the borders/envelopes are decisive. In taxonomic literature, challenging negative samples near the boundaries are referred to as hard negatives (hard samples). Typically, such samples are difficult to collect externally.
However, the generator G naturally learns to create data near the decision boundary in order to effectively fool the discriminator D. In other words, adversarial competition produces hard negatives for free, with no additional cost. As a result, GANs are sample-efficient and clearly capture the boundaries of the distribution. (The original motivation for proposing GANs in 2014 was to address data deficiency.)

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
3.6 3 Major Practical Challenges






WarningWhy GAN training is notorious




Non-convergence: Parameters oscillate or diverge and do not converge. D learns much more easily/faster than G (since it only needs to learn boundaries), resulting in a power imbalance. If D becomes excessively strong, the two models fail to improve together with each iteration and become unstable.
Mode Collapse: A phenomenon where G repeatedly generates only a few easy samples, deceiving D and settling there. Failing to learn all the various peaks (modes) of the true distribution, it creates only a few sharp peaks → Loss of diversity.
Diminished Gradient: If D performs too well, the gradient backpropagating to G disappears, so G learns nothing.

Numbers 2 and 3 essentially stem from the imbalance in learning difficulty/speed between D and G. Tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size) is “artistically” difficult.

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
3.7 Stabilization variants
Hundreds of variations have emerged targeting the two problems above (mode collapse and non-convergence).

LSGAN (Least Squares GAN): Least Squares Loss
WGAN (Wasserstein GAN): Smoother loss with Wasserstein distance
WGAN-GP: WGAN + Gradient Penalty
BEGAN (Boundary Equilibrium GAN), DCGAN, CycleGAN, etc.

The fact that GANs can freely change their loss functions (e.g., Wasserstein, Hinge loss) is a strength, but it is also a weakness in that the high degree of freedom in tuning makes stabilization difficult.






ImportantWireless Communication Analogy — GAN = Spoofing Transmitter vs. Signal Detector Game



Let G be the spoofing transmitter and D be the signal detector. D is a Neyman–Pearson-type detector that determines whether the input is a “real signal” or a “synthetic signal,” and the optimal discriminator D^\*=\tfrac{p_{\text{data}}}{p_{\text{data}}+p_g} is exactly the same form as the likelihood ratio test of the two hypotheses. From this perspective:

Mode Collapse = The transmitter loses constellation diversity and repeatedly transmits only a few symbols
Gradient Vanishing = The gradient of the likelihood ratio disappears as the detector becomes saturated deep in the high-SNR region
minimax / zero-sum = Jammer vs. Receiver, or the game structure of worst-case detection

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
3.8 Connection between VAE and GAN
Since the input z of the generator is usually modeled as \mathcal N(0,I), the VAE decoder can be used directly as the GAN generator. By adding the decoder =G and the discriminator to the VAE encoder-decoder structure, it becomes a GAN. The two are similar structures that are interchangeable. The difference lies in the learning paradigm (VAE = Variational Inference/MLE family, GAN = Adversarial Learning).

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
4.1 GAN vs Diffusion: Why Switched






TipDirect Answer



GANs are fast and have good sample efficiency but are unstable (mode collapse/non-convergence). Diffusion is slow but stable and offers excellent quality. Key difference: Diffusion is trained using a well-understood optimization called Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), and trains a single model without pitting two models against each other → the concept of mode collapse itself does not exist.











Diffusion (DDPM)
GAN




Pros
High-quality, sharp samples with vivid detail / MLE = Well-understood Optimization / Both Image & Audio
High Quality (Image & Audio) / Relatively Fast Training / Various loss functions (Wasserstein, Hinge) available


Cons
Slow and computationally expensive (T iterations) / Requires a lot of data
Difficult to train / Sensitive to hyperparameters / Mode collapse









NoteProfessor’s Intuition — Building a “Probability Tower”



While GANs draw sharp boundaries using hard negatives, Diffusion creates mountain ranges of distribution in a different way. By providing data points from every location and training the noiseization process, it learns “how high to stack probabilities at each location.” In other words, it reconstructs the entire terrain, including not only boundaries but also the heights of the peaks. However, since it requires data from every location, a large amount of data must be collected.








NoteStability Analogy — Highly Volatility Stocks vs. Steady Rising Stocks



GANs can produce a great model overnight if you’re lucky, but if things go wrong, training all night will yield useless results that have completely collapsed (resulting in massive financial losses for large-scale training). Diffusion is slow, but it produces a model that improves steadily, little by little, every day — it offers peace of mind. This is why the industry has chosen Diffusion. (Today, most image and video generation is Diffusion-based.)

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
4.2 DDPM: Two processes
DDPM(Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model, 2020) consists of two processes.





flowchart LR
    X0["x₀ (깨끗한 데이터)"] -->|"q(xₜ|xₜ₋₁) 노이즈 추가"| XT["x_T ~ N(0,I) (순수 잡음)"]
    XT -->|"pθ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) 학습된 디노이징"| X0b["x₀ (생성)"]
    X0 -. "Forward (고정)" .- XT
    XT -. "Reverse (생성/학습)" .- X0b







4.2.1 Forward (diffusion) process — fixed
A Markov chain of latent variables, progressively adding Gaussian noise with a pre-scheduled variance \beta_t.

q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal N\!\big(x_t;\ \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\big).


\beta_t: Noise Magnitude at time t
\alpha_t=1-\beta_t: Signal retention size, and \bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s

By using Markovs and Gaussian composition, an arbitrary time t can be represented in a closed-form.

\boxed{\,x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\,}

If we set \beta_t sufficiently small and increase T to take the continuous limit of \delta t\to0, it becomes a stabilistic differential equation (SDE).

dx=-\tfrac12\,\beta(t)\,x\,dt+\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t,\qquad (W_t:\text{Wiener 과정}).

Since the noise \epsilon at each t is random and uncontrollable, it is a stochastic differential equation.


4.2.2 Reverse (Denoising) Process — Learning Target
The inverse process according to Bayes’ rule is

q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\frac{q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1})}{q(x_t)}

, but q(x_{t-1}), q(x_t) is unknown (bad news). Good news: If \beta_t\ll1, then it is true. There is a theorem that the inverse process q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) is well approximated by a Gaussian. Therefore, we approximate it using a Gaussian parameterized by a neural network.

p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\mathcal N\!\big(x_{t-1};\ \mu_\theta(x_t,t),\ \sigma_t^2 I\big).

What we will learn is the average of this Gaussian, \mu_\theta (=denoiser).


4.2.3 Training: Predict “noise” instead of the mean
By organizing the true mean in the closed form of Forward, \mu_\theta can be reparameterized into noise predictor \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t).

\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\!\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right).

Then, learning becomes surprisingly simple. For each t, the real noise \epsilon is taken as the correct answer, and the neural network regresses to identify that noise.

\boxed{\;\mathcal L_{\text{simple}}=\mathbb E_{t,\,x_0,\,\epsilon}\Big[\ \big\|\,\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\ t\big)\big\|^2\ \Big]\;}

Algorithm:

Time t extraction, correct noise \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I) extraction
x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon Calculation
Slope descent to \nabla_\theta\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|^2



4.2.4 Generation(Sampling)
Starting from x_T\sim\mathcal N(0,I), it goes down to t=T,\dots,1Z and denoises step by step to the learned \epsilon_\theta.

\hat x_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}\big(x_t-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\big),\qquad
x_{t-1}=\mu_\theta(x_t,\hat x_0)+\sigma_t z,\quad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I).







WarningNote regarding the number of steps



The standard implementation of DDPM typically uses a sequential inverse process of T\approx1000 steps (default in papers). This sequentiality is the root cause of the slowness. (Some sources cite much larger figures, but the exact value depends on the noise schedule and resolution.) The key point is that “hundreds to thousands of forward passes are required to obtain a single sample,” and DDIM reduces this to dozens of steps.

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
4.3 Three Perspectives: Variation · Score · Flow






Note



Diffusion is interpreted equivalently by three mathematical tools.








Perspective
Root
Representative Method




Variational view
(VAE formula) Variational inference
DDPM


Score-based view
Energy-based models in statistical physics
NCSN / score-SDE


Flow-based view
Normalizing Flow
Flow Matching



All three perspectives converge to continuous-time formulations, and flow matching, in particular, reduces the number of iterations, becoming the de facto standard for recent generation. This theorem focuses on the most basic variational perspective (DDPM).

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
4.4 DDIM: Non-Markov + Deterministic Sampling






TipWhy DDIM?



DDPM offers good quality but (1) sampling is slow, (2) control is difficult because it is a stochastic path, and (3) every sample requires a full inverse SDE. The goal of DDIM is: fewer steps + deterministic path + maintaining the same marginal distribution as DDPM.


DDIM reinterprets the forward process as a non-Markovian deterministic mapping. It becomes non-Markovian by making x_t depend not only on x_{t-1}* but also on x_0. The key point is that the implementation is the same as DDPM, but the mathematical interpretation is different — DDPM is based on SDE, while DDIM is based on ODE.
Generalized reverse sampling:

x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)+\sigma_t z,
 
\sigma_t=\eta\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\sqrt{1-\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}},\qquad z\sim\mathcal N(0,I).


\eta=0\Rightarrow\sigma_t=0: Truly deterministic(no noise injection)
\eta=1: Identical to DDPM(Markov·Stochastic)







ImportantKey Benefit — Training remains the same, only sampling accelerated



The loss function of is exactly the same as DDPM. That is, a noise predictor \epsilon_\theta trained once can be used directly for DDIM sampling. Thanks to the deterministic process of \sigma_t=0, denoising is well-defined even at arbitrary time intervals, allowing for fast sampling with a significantly reduced number of steps.

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
text:
4.5 LDM (Stable Diffusion): Latent Space Diffusion
Learning diffusion directly in pixel space incurs too high a memory cost. LDM compresses images into a low-dimensional latent and then learns diffusion in that latent space. As a text conditional large-scale model, the sweet spot of the downsampling rate is important.

LDM-1(Uncompressed): Training time is excessively long
LDM-32(Overcompression): Quality degradation due to information loss
LDM-4 / 8 / 16: Competitive performance — Moderate compression is optimal

title: Generative Models: VAE · GAN · Diffusion
section: 4.6 ControlNet: Conditional fine-tuning of small amounts of data
text:
4.6 ControlNet: Conditional fine-tuning of small amounts of data
Efficiently fine-tunes an unconditionally trained image diffusion model for image-conditional scenarios with a relatively small (<50K) input–output pairs.

Idea: Process condition images using the pre-trained noise prediction U-Net
Encoder: Copy and initialize pre-trained U-Net parameters, then fine-tune
Decoder: Combines encoded condition information + noise image, but injects control signals using zero convolution (stable incremental learning as the influence is 0 initially)
Training data \sim100\text{K} Scale — Approximately 1/50,000 of LAION-5B

Since condition information is introduced gradually rather than suddenly, it can be generally applied to any image condition (edge, pose, depth, etc.).






ImportantWireless Communication Analogy — Diffusion = Progressive AWGN and its inverse operation



The closed form of Forward, x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon, is literally the same as the fading + AWGN channel model with signal gain \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} and noise power 1-\bar\alpha_t. As t increases, the SNR decreases monotonically, reaching SNR\to0 (pure noise) at t=T.

Training Noise Prediction \epsilon_\theta = Training MMSE Estimator for Noise Estimation
Reverse Process = Step-by-step denoising, i.e., a structure similar to Iterative Equalization/Continuous Interference Removal (SIC)
Deterministic path of DDIM(\eta=0) = Deterministic equalization path without noise reinjection
\beta_t Schedule = SNR Schedule Design

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
The content covered today is divided into two axes.

Making Transformers Cheaper — Attempts to reduce the \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) cost of Self-attention. The leading example is Mamba from the State Space Model (SSM) family.
Handling various types of data in one space — a multimodal model that combines text, images, and audio into a single embedding space. The core tools for this are CLIP and subsequent models (SigLIP, SigLIP 2).

These two are actually two faces of the same question. The first axis is “How to efficiently encode long contexts?”, and the second axis is “How to align heterogeneous information into the same coordinate system?”. From the perspective of a wireless communications major, the former naturally translates to the filter complexity-performance trade-off, and the latter to the matched filtering and diversity combining problem. This correspondence is specified in the “View via Wireless Communication” box at the end of each section.


Code
flowchart TB
  A["Transformer (Self-Attention)<br/>강력하지만 O(n²)"] --> B["효율화 계열"]
  A --> C["멀티모달 확장"]
  B --> B1["Mamba (SSM, S4→S6)"]
  B --> B2["Hybrid: Jamba / MambaVision / TransMamba"]
  C --> C1["CLIP (대조학습)"]
  C1 --> C2["SigLIP (sigmoid)"]
  C2 --> C3["SigLIP 2 (LocCa + 증류)"]

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
2.1 What was good
Self-attention densely encodes contextual information by directly connecting all token pairs within a window. Unlike RNNs, which compress information into a single hidden state and transmit it sequentially, it examines long-range dependencies all at once.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
2.2 Two essential limitations






ImportantLimit 1 — Cannot see outside the window



Attention concatenates only tokens within the consideration window. Context outside the window cannot be encoded in principle.








ImportantLimit 2 — Cost is the square of the window size



If the window size is \(n\), the time and memory complexity is because scores are calculated for all query-key pairs \[
\mathcal{O}(n^2 d)
\] . Increasing the window size allows for more context (\(\Rightarrow\) better alignment and accuracy), but the cost increases exponentially.



2.2.1 Why Squares of All Things? (3-Step Causal Chain)

Create \(Q = XW_Q,\; K = XW_K,\; V = XW_V\) from input \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\).
The moment the score matrix \(S = QK^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is created, the number of elements is \(n^2\). This single line \(\Rightarrow\) is the source of squared complexity.
\(\text{softmax}(S/\sqrt{d})\,V\) also undergoes operations of the same scale as \(n^2\). Therefore, if the window is doubled, the cost becomes four times higher.

The industry responds in two ways: (a) simply handling large Windows with more expensive hardware (H100, H200, B100/B200 …), or (b) an efficiency transformer that algorithmically lowers the cost itself. The efficiency trend seeks to reduce complexity through \(\mathcal{O}(n^2) \to \mathcal{O}(n\log n) \to \mathcal{O}(n)\). Mamba is a prime example of the latter.






TipView via Wireless Communication — Direct Convolution vs FFT



The effort to reduce \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(n\log n)\) or \(\mathcal{O}(n)\) shares the same motivation as the classic strategy in communications signal processing of replacing direct time-domain convolution (\(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\)) with FFT-based frequency-domain product (\(\mathcal{O}(n\log n)\)). The goal of “reducing the order of complexity while maintaining accuracy” is the same.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
3.1 At a glance
Mamba is an efficient model for sequence encoding named after the black mamba (a fast and deadly snake). It is based on the Structured State Space Sequence model (S4), which is simplified through S5 and adopts the selective version S6.


Code
flowchart LR
  S4["S4<br/>(2021, 구조화 SSM)"] --> S5["S5<br/>(단순화)"]
  S5 --> S6["S6<br/>(Selective)"]
  S6 --> M["Mamba<br/>(2023)"]

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
3.2 Two key ideas

3.2.1 (1) Selective mechanism (S6)

Maintain a small, fixed-size window, but keep only the highly relevant tokens inside it.
“Relevance” is measured in a manner similar to the gating mechanism of RNNs. That is, it dynamically decides which information to remember and which to discard based on the input.







NoteDetails are everything



The idea itself (“keep only important tokens”) is simple, but what is considered important (importance score function) and how the selection is made determine performance. This is the core contribution of the original paper (Gu & Dao, Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces, 2023).




3.2.2 (2) Hardware-aware parallel scan
Linear cycle \(h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t\) is essentially sequential, but it can be reconfigured into associative scan (prefix-sum) operations and parallelized on the GPU. Mamba implements this scan to match the GPU memory hierarchy (SRAM/HBM) to boost inference speed.






WarningWork Memo



Since this hardware-aware kernel is not yet natively embedded in NVIDIA hardware, the potential efficiency gains of Mamba have not been fully realized. Custom kernel/hardware optimization remains an open research and engineering opportunity.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
3.3 Variants of Mamba



Table 1: Mamba Variant Comparison










Model
Structure
Key Features




Vision Mamba (Vim)
Pure Mamba
Non-dedicated Mamba


Jamba

Mixes the two blocks in MoE form. Max 256k token window


MambaVision
Hybrid
Front end = Mamba, Back end = Transformer self-attention


TransMamba

Dynamic selection of Mamba or Transformer for each layer/token







3.3.1 One-line summary of design philosophy

Mamba: Strong in computational efficiency (fast). However, it is not that the expressiveness itself is superior.
Transformer: Strong against long-distance dependencies due to strong context encoding.

The intuition of hybrids (e.g., MambaVision) is as follows: Initial layers can afford to let some information flow, so they are processed by efficient Mamba; Later layers require more sophisticated inference, so self-attention is used to boost accuracy. In essence, the balance between efficiency and accuracy is tuned through layer placement. TransMamba makes that placement smoother and more selective.


3.3.2 Theoretical results on expressiveness
Theorems have been proposed that, from the perspective of circuit complexity, Mamba does not have greater expressive power than Transformer (Chen et al., 2025). In other words, the value of Mamba lies not in expressive superiority, but in obtaining the same or similar expressive power at a lower cost.






TipView as Wireless Communication — SSM = Linear System / IIR Filter / Kalman Filter



The core recurrence relation of SSM \[
h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t,\qquad y_t = C h_t \;(+\, D x_t)
\] is the discrete-time linear state-space system itself. That is, the backbone of Mamba is isomorphic to the state equations of an infinite impulse response (IIR) filter or (with noise added) a Kalman filter.

If the eigenvalue magnitude of \(A\) is \(|\lambda|<1\), the system is stable and past information decays exponentially (\(\Rightarrow\) finite effective memory length).
“Optional (S6)” means making \(A,B,C\) time-varying depending on the input — this is the same concept as adaptive filters (e.g., LMS/RLS) in communication. Just as tap counts change depending on the channel state, state transitions change depending on the token content.
The trick of parallelizing sequential recurrence relations using prefix-scan is identical to the parallel prefix technique in signal processing, which groups linear recurrence relations into blocks for parallel processing.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
4.1 What is “Modality”






NoteDefinition — mode and modality




Mode: The peak of a probability distribution, i.e., the point where the density is (locally) maximum.
Multimodal distribution: A distribution with multiple peaks.
Extending this to data, multimodal data refers to a situation where multiple distinct homogeneous chunks of information (=each modality) are mixed together and entered into a single decision/embedding space.



In the past, storage media differed for each type of data (audio = tape, video = videotape, etc.), so it was called multimedia. Now, since all signals are converted to digital (0/1) and stored in the same semiconductor storage, the term is called multimodal, emphasizing the “mode” rather than the “medium.” Modality can include sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell, and even extend to abstract “senses” such as attention, memory, and preference.
The two most important modalities are text and vision. This is because they are the information humans use every day (audio has been largely resolved, and video + text remains a difficult challenge).

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
5.1 CLIP’s core idea
CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training, Radford & Kim et al., OpenAI, ICML 2021) is the most widely used co-embedding method. It bridges the gap between computer vision and natural language processing by mapping images and text to the same embedding space. Once this mapping is trained, tasks such as zero-shot classification are possible without separate fine-tuning.

5.1.1 Contrastive pre-training
Let’s assume there are \(N\) (image, text) pairs in the minibatch. The image encoder creates \(\{I_i\}\) and the text encoder creates \(\{T_j\}\) embeddings. A \(N \times N\) matrix is created using the similarity of all pairs, and

Diagonal element(\(i=j\), correct pair) → Probability close to 1,
Non-diagonal element(\(i \neq j\), mismatch) → Probability close to 0

To create , apply softmax to the entire minibatch and backpropagate the two encoders together.


Code
flowchart LR
  TXT["텍스트<br/>'Pepper the aussie pup'"] --> TE["Text Encoder"]
  IMG["이미지"] --> IE["Image Encoder"]
  TE --> M["유사도 행렬 N×N<br/>(I_i · T_j)"]
  IE --> M
  M --> L["대각=양성, 비대각=음성<br/>Softmax 대조손실"]











Similarity is usually measured by cosine similarity (the inner product of \(\ell_2\) normalized embeddings). The symmetric InfoNCE loss is \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{CLIP}}
= \tfrac{1}{2}\Big(
\underbrace{-\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\log\frac{e^{\langle I_i,T_i\rangle/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{\langle I_i,T_j\rangle/\tau}}}_{\text{image}\to\text{text}}
+
\underbrace{-\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{j}\log\frac{e^{\langle I_j,T_j\rangle/\tau}}{\sum_i e^{\langle I_i,T_j\rangle/\tau}}}_{\text{text}\to\text{image}}
\Big),
\] where \(\tau\) is the temperature. This is exactly the same form as “one-hot classification for correct pairs” and therefore reduces to cross-entropy minimization.


5.1.2 Where does the data come from? — The rediscovery of alt-text
This massive (image, text) pair was collected in large quantities from HTML text alt. In the early days of the Internet, the practice of including alternative text (alt-text) to describe images because image loading was slow later became a free weak supervision signal for CLIP learning. Thanks to the vast amount of alt-text on the web, it was possible to obtain a large number of image-text pairs.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
5.2 SigLIP: sigmoid instead of softmax
SigLIP(Zhai et al., Google DeepMind Zurich, ICML 2021) improves CLIP in terms of memory efficiency and scalability. The idea itself is simple. Instead of applying softmax to the entire mini-batch, sigmoid is applied independently to each pair.
If the label of the pair ZZZPH0008748ZZZ \((i,j)\) is \(z_{ij}\in\{+1,-1\}\) (diagonal=+1, off-diagonal=−1), then \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SigLIP}}
= -\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i}\sum_{j}
\log \sigma\!\big(z_{ij}\,(t\,\langle I_i,T_j\rangle + b)\big),
\] Here, \(t\) (scale), \(b\) (bias) are learning parameters, and \(\sigma\) is sigmoid.

5.2.1 Why sigmoid is advantageous (Step 3)

softmax requires relative information of the entire mini-batch in the denominator \(\Rightarrow\) the normalization terms of the pairs from every step must be collected (synchronization cost).
sigmoid evaluates each pair independently \(\Rightarrow\) pairwise loss can be calculated in parallel and variance.
Therefore, without all-gathering between devices, only small blocks need to be loaded into memory at a time \(\Rightarrow\) Memory usage ↓, scalability ↑.







NoteEfficient Loss Implementation (parallelism)



The original paper splits the global batch across multiple devices and accumulates partial loss by swapping text representations between devices. At any given moment, only small partial blocks are loaded into memory, and after every image-text pair interacts once, it concludes with a sum across devices. The key point is that an all-gather is not required.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
5.3 SigLIP 2: Richer map signal
SigLIP 2(Tschannen et al., Google DeepMind, 2025) adds two things.

5.3.1 (1) LocCa — Location recognition captioning
The alt-text of the existing CLIP/SigLIP describes the image only at the whole level. LocCa (Wan et al., NeurIPS 2024) provides a fine-grained map signal.

Cap (Captioning): Captioning the entire image.
ARef (Automatic Referring expression): given description → Find the location of the bounding box that the description points to.
GCap (Grounded Captioning): Given bounding box → Generate caption for that area.

In other words, it links descriptions like “puffin standing on a cliff edge” to specific box coordinates of an image. Thanks to these location-based weak maps, modern LLM/VLM is able to understand even small parts of an image.


5.3.2 (2) Autodistillation for slow learners (image encoders)






NoteWhy Image Encoders Are “Slow Learners”




Text: Contains highly abstract high-level meaning → Information is compressed and rich.
Image: A pixel-level concrete realization. From a semantic perspective, it is noisy and contains information that must be selectively taken.

Therefore, image encoders learn slower than text encoders and are susceptible to noise.


The solution is the slow-fast / teacher-student concept of computer vision. By setting the weights, which are slowly updated by the Exponential Moving Average (EMA), as the teacher, \[
\theta^{\text{EMA}}_t = \alpha\,\theta^{\text{EMA}}_{t-1} + (1-\alpha)\,\theta_t,\qquad \alpha \approx 0.8\text{~}0.99,
\] Allows the student encoder to converge faster and more stably from this stable teacher through self-distillation/mask prediction (SILC/TIPS-type loss). As a result, the image encoder learns a finer and more robust representation.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
5.4 CLIP + Generated Model = Text→Image
By combining CLIP-style co-embeddings with image generators such as diffusion models, it is possible to generate long text → corresponding images/videos. Intuitively: if you replace the image encoder with an image generator and train a text encoder using the CLIP method, you obtain a generator that outputs a corresponding image when given text. This is the basic framework of today’s text-image systems (such as DALL·E).






TipView via Wireless Communication — Cosine Similarity = Matched Filter, SigLIP Loss = Detection Theory




CLIP’s cosine similarity \(\langle I,T\rangle / (\|I\|\|T\|)\) is the normalized correlation, or the matched filter output. Just as a matched filter maximizes the alignment of the received signal and the reference waveform, CLIP maximizes the alignment of correct (image, text) pairs. This is analogous to the steering vector alignment in beamforming.
Softmax (CLIP) vs. Sigmoid (SigLIP) correspond to two perspectives in detection theory. Softmax is multi-hypothesis detection that selects one of \(N\) hypotheses (requires mutual normalization), while sigmoid is independent binary detection of whether each pair is positive or negative. The latter is lightweight in implementation because each detector can be run in parallel—similar to how using independent detection per user instead of joint detection in cellular multi-user detection reduces complexity.
Temperature \(\tau\) and Scale \(t\) can be viewed as the gain that controls the logit’s SNR. If it is too large, it leads to overconfidence; if it is too small, it leads to a loss of discernment.

text:
6.1 Overview of Three Eras


Code
timeline
  title 멀티모달 연구의 세 시대
  1970s : 행동주의(Behavioral) : 인간의 다중감각 처리 연구 (McGurk 1976)
  1980s-2000 : 계산주의(Computational) : AVSR 등 계산 모델로 모방
  2010-Now : 딥러닝(Deep Learning) : 표현을 스스로 학습












6.1.1 The Age of Behaviorism — The McGurk Effect (1976)
If you play the same audio but change only the lip-sync video, the heard sound changes (e.g., auditory “ba” + visual “ga” → perceived as “da”). When you close your eyes, you hear the actual sound, but when you open them, the visual overwrites the auditory. This is an example of multimodal interference. While multimodal information is usually helpful, conflicts can actually lead to misperception. (The reason phone English is difficult: because it uses only partial information without visual data.)


6.1.2 The Age of Computationalism — AVSR and SNR
In Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR), adding visual information achieves the same Word Error Rate (WER) even at much lower Acoustic SNR. Qualitatively:

Audio Only: Relatively high SNR (e.g., ~10) is required to achieve a certain WER.
Audio+Visual: Since visual signals assist, pseudo-WER can be achieved even at nearly 0 SNR.







TipView as wireless communication — Multimodal fusion = diversity combining



This is not a metaphor, but almost identical mathematics. Increasing the effective SNR by adding an independent (quasi-independent) observation branch called time is based on the exact same principle as Maximal Ratio Combining (MRC) in receive diversity, which obtains array gain by summing the branch-specific SNRs.

\(L\) independent modalities ≈ \(L\)-order diversity → Even if one channel falls into deep fading (=noise/ambiguity), the other channel compensates.
The fact that AVSR “operates even near 0 dB” means that the required SNR has been significantly lowered due to diversity gain.

Therefore, multimodal fusion design translates into the problem of designing combining rules in communication: with what weights should branches be merged (=fusion).

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
section: 6.2 5 Key Challenges of the Deep Learning Era
text:
6.2 5 Key Challenges of the Deep Learning Era






Note5 Core Challenges




Representation — Represents/summarizes multimodal data using complementarity and redundancy.
Alignment — Find direct correspondences between (child) elements of two or more modalities.
Fusion — Combines information from multiple modalities to perform prediction.
Translation — Transforms one modality into another (can be open/subjective).
Co-Learning — Transfer of knowledge (representation/prediction models) between modalities.




6.2.1 Task 1: Representation — Joint vs Coordinated



Table 5: Comparison of expression styles











Method
Definition
Advantages
Disadvantages




Joint Representation
All modalities in a single shared space
Alignment is implicitly embedded at training time → Reduced concerns about future alignment
Difficult to train that space


Coordinated Representation
Individual Space per Modality + Post-alignment
Reflects the Unique Characteristics of Each Modality
Postpones the Difficult Problem of Alignment






Deep learning generally moves toward joint representations. Thanks to the advantage of deep learning that it learns representations on its own, alignment is automatically achieved by simply combining and computing inputs by modality to integrate them into a single joint embedding.


6.2.2 The Magic of Joint Representations — Vector Space Arithmetic
In a well-trained joint multimodal space, images, texts, and audio with similar meanings are placed closely together. Furthermore, vector arithmetic holds (Kiros et al., 2014). \[
\text{image}(\text{파란 차}) - \mathbf{v}_{\text{blue}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{red}} \;\approx\; \text{image}(\text{빨간 차})
\] That is, if you look up the vicinity of the location where blue vector is subtracted and red vector is added in the “blue car” embedding, red car images appear. Changing one word in a sentence to another corresponds to vector addition/subtraction in the embedding space, and as a result, the images in the vicinity of the embedding change (“Draw an Iron Man” → “Draw a cat”).


6.2.3 Assignment 2~5 Summary

Alignment: If you choose the alignment representation, you must explicitly solve the element correspondence between modalities (difficulty). The joint representation absorbs this into the learning process.
Fusion: Combines multiple modalities to produce a single prediction (see AVSR/Diversity Combination above).
Translation: One modality → another (e.g., video → sound, text → image). Since the relationship can be open and subjective, there is not a single correct answer.
Co-Learning: Transferring knowledge from one modality to another (e.g., the slow-fast distillation mentioned above). It is deeply connected to alignment.

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
text:
7.1 CNN’s Limitations Revealed in VQA
Let’s consider “How many birds are in this image?” (Visual Question Answering, VQA). CNNs assume spatial stationarity and locality. That is, each filter response has the same meaning regardless of location, and only strong responses are retained while the rest are treated as noise (max pooling).






WarningWhy Counting Fails (Causal Chain)




CNN is designed to extract position-invariant features → It captures “novelty” well.
However, max pooling sends the one strongest response to the next layer → count information is lost.
“Three animals” implies that each position must have a different meaning (different individual), which conflicts head-on with the assumption of normality → failure to count.



When birds of the same species are located in the bottom-left and top-right corners of the screen, the question “Are they the same species?” requires long-distance relationships and information on behaviors that vary by location. CNNs are weak at such long-distance and context-dependent relationships. (Theoretically, locally-connected networks are an alternative, but they are not practical because the number of parameters explodes, causing them to lose the advantages of CNNs.)

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
section: 7.2 Attention = Weights that change depending on the input
text:
7.2 Attention = Weights that change depending on the input






ImportantCore Intuition



The general weight \(W\) is fixed regardless of the input (learned from data but remains invariant during inference). The Attention weight \(a\) takes the input itself as input, changes the weight, and applies the changed weight back to the input. \[
\text{고정: } y = Wx \qquad\text{vs}\qquad \text{Attention: } y = a(x)\,x
\] Thanks to , even the same input is encoded into different roles and meanings depending on the context.


To implement the idea of “calculating weights from inputs,” we introduce the Query, Key, Value concept (it does not necessarily have to be three elements, but this is the standard implementation of the Transformer). In the next lecture, we will complete attention using QKV, and then take the midterm exam (the Transformer exam will focus on high-level concepts).

title: Transformer Efficiency and Multimodal Model
section: 7.3 Gating Review — A Matter of Memory
text:
7.3 Gating Review — A Matter of Memory
In cyclic structures, memory over time is handled by gating. It takes the weighted sum of the current input and the moving average of past memory. \[
f(x) = g(x)\odot x + \big(1-g(x)\big)\odot m,\qquad g(x)\in(0,1),
\] Here, \(m\) represents memory (past accumulation), and \(g\) represents the gate. Representative implementations are LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) and GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit). GRU achieves similar performance to LSTM while simplifying it (reducing parameters).






NoteOne-line memo



“Remembering over time” remains a major challenge that has not yet been fully solved. Mamba’s selective mechanism is also a new answer to the same problem, which ultimately determines what to remember and what to discard through gating.








TipView as wireless — Gate = 1st order IIR smoother / Adaptive gain



\(f = g\odot x + (1-g)\odot m\) is an Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA), which is a first-order IIR low-pass filter. If the gate \(g\) is time-varying, it becomes an adaptive smoother. This is the same structure as using an adaptive forgetting factor to suppress noise in channel estimation.

def siglip_loss(I, T, t=10.0, b=-10.0):

10.3 Linear SSM scan (\(\mathcal{O}(n)\) sequential recurrence relation)


Code
def ssm_scan(x, A, B, C):
    """h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t,  y_t = C h_t  (IIR/칼만 상태식과 동형)"""
    n = A.shape[0]; h = np.zeros(n); ys = []
    for xt in x:
        h = A @ h + B * xt
        ys.append(C @ h)
    return np.array(ys)

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
2.1 Direct answer
The data dealt with so far was fixed-length ‘snapshots’ — images (numbers, objects), graphs, etc. On the other hand, sequence modeling aims to learn from data of variable length. Representative example:

Language (Text) — Variable-length sequence of words/characters
Time Series (Stocks) — Values on the time axis
Video — Sequence of frames
Audio — Waveform/Spectrogram

Major applications include computer vision (image analysis, e.g., YOLO), natural language processing (text analysis, e.g., GPT), and speech recognition (e.g., voice assistants), and sequence modeling is particularly key in NLP.






TipWireless communication perspective analogy



Sequence modeling is like a receiver processing a variable-length symbol stream. Each packet has a different length, and the meaning of a single symbol depends on the preceding and succeeding symbols (channel state, preamble). Just as a memoryless detector that only sees the “current symbol” cannot demodulate a channel with ISI (inter-symbol interference), a sequence model must carry past states.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
3.1 Direct answer
RNN is a dynamic system that recursively updates the state over time. By reusing the same function \(f\) and the same parameters \(\theta\) at every time step, it compresses variable-length inputs into a fixed-size state.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
3.2 Mathematical expansion
Classical form of a dynamical system without external signals:
\[
s^{(t)} = f\!\left(s^{(t-1)};\, \theta\right)
\]
When external input \(x^{(t)}\) is received:
\[
s^{(t)} = f\!\left(s^{(t-1)},\, x^{(t)};\, \theta\right)
\]
In this case, state \(s^{(t)}\) contains information of the entire past sequence. If we call this state the hidden state \(h^{(t)}\), then that is the RNN:
\[
\boxed{\,h^{(t)} = f\!\left(h^{(t-1)},\, x^{(t)};\, \theta\right)\,}
\]

Input: Current data \(x^{(t)}\) and past hidden state \(h^{(t-1)}\)
Output: Model output at the current time point and hidden state to be passed to the next time point

The essence of a one-step RNN is revealed when contrasted with a non-recursive form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{비재귀:}\quad & f(x_t) = w x_t + b\\
\text{슬라이딩 윈도(이동평균):}\quad & f(x_t, x_{t-1}) = w_1 x_t + w_2 x_{t-1} + b\\
\text{한 스텝 재귀:}\quad & f(x_t, x_{t-1}) = w_1 x_t + w_2\, f(x_{t-1}, x_{t-2}) + b
\end{aligned}
\]
The recursive term \(f(x_{t-1},x_{t-2})\) makes this go back infinitely far into the past.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
3.3 Two gains of recursive structures






NoteWhy Recursion Is Good




The input size is always the same regardless of the sequence length. The trained model handles arbitrary lengths.
Parameters such as the same transfer function \(f\) can be reused at every time step (parameter sharing).

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
3.4 Three types of RNNs








Type
Structure
Features




Type 1
Output at every time step + recursive connection between hidden states
Most common · Highly expressive


Type 2
Output at every time step + Output → Next Hidden State connection (Teacher forcing)
Easy to parallelize / No hidden state connection, so past is forgotten more easily


Type 3
Hidden state recursion + Read entire sequence and single output at the end
Classification/Summary type









ImportantPrecise definition of Teacher forcing (Type 2)




During training: Feed the correct answer output \(y^{(t)}\) (extracted from the train set) as the input to the next step’s hidden state \(h^{(t+1)}\).
During inference: Since the correct answer is unknown, approximate \(o^{(t)}\) with the model output \(y^{(t)}\) and feed it back.

This is precisely where the exposure bias between the learning and inference distributions occurs. The advantage is that by breaking output dependencies, it is possible to separate learning by time point → parallelize.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
4.1 Direct answer
When simple non-linear functions are combined multiple times, the resulting composite function becomes extremely non-linear. The time progression of an RNN is precisely this composition, and as a result, gradients vanish (mostly) or explode (rare but fatal), making it difficult to incorporate information from the distant past into learning.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
4.2 Mathematical expansion (Eigenvalue decomposition perspective)
Let’s look at the linearly approximated RNN transition \(h^{(t)} = W^\top h^{(t-1)}\). If we perform eigenvalue decomposition \(W = Q\,\Lambda\, Q^{-1}\) on \(W\):
\[
h^{(t)} = \left(W^\top\right)^{t} h^{(0)} = Q\, \Lambda^{t}\, Q^{-1} h^{(0)}
\]
Since \(\Lambda^{t} = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1^t, \dots, \lambda_n^t)\) here,
\[
\boxed{\;|\lambda_i| < 1 \Rightarrow \lambda_i^{t}\to 0 \ (\text{소실}), \qquad |\lambda_i| > 1 \Rightarrow \lambda_i^{t}\to \infty \ (\text{폭발})\;}
\]
, that is, for time depth \(t\), the contribution is exponentially attenuated/amplified. Only the boundary at exactly \(|\lambda_i|=1\) preserves information, but it is virtually impossible to maintain this during learning.






TipWireless communication perspective analogy



This is equivalent to the cumulative channel gain in a multi-hop relay. If the gain of each hop is \(\lambda\), the signal after \(t\) is \(\lambda^t\). If \(|\lambda|<1\), the signal sinks below the noise (\(\to\) information loss), and if \(|\lambda|>1\), it clips and diverges due to non-linear amplification (\(\to\) explosion). Just as the gain is grouped near 1 using AGC (Automatic Gain Control) for stable transmission, the RNN must also control the spectral radius near 1.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
4.3 Key Prescription: Gating

Let’s create a direct connection between the past and the present (or future).

The representative implementation is gating. Replace the simple product \(f(x)=a\cdot x,\ a\in[0,1]\) with the following:
\[
f(x) = a\cdot x + (1-a)\cdot m
\]
where \(m\) is memory. This is an intuition similar to momentum/moving averages — it retains information for a long time by weighting the current input with past memory. Two representative implementations: LSTM (1997) and GRU (2014).

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
5.1 Direct answer
LSTM is an explicit memory cell \(c_t\) and three gates (forget, input, output) + gate gate**, which maintains long-term information by softly controlling how much of the cell contents to forget, how much to rewrite, and how much to send out.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
5.2 Mathematical expansion
Combine the previous hidden state \(h_{t-1}\) and the current input \(x_t\) as input. All gates are sigmoid \(\sigma(\cdot)\in(0,1)\), and the candidate is \(\tanh\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_f\,[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f\right) && \text{(망각 gate)}\\
i_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_i\,[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i\right) && \text{(입력 gate)}\\
o_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_o\,[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o\right) && \text{(출력 gate)}\\
g_t &= \tanh\!\left(W_g\,[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_g\right) && \text{(gate gate / 후보 메모리)}\\[4pt]
c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t && \text{(셀 상태 갱신)}\\
h_t &= o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) && \text{(은닉상태 출력)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Role of each gate:

\(f_t\)(Forgetting): How long to retain previous cell content \(c_{t-1}\) — Throttling the cell’s self-loop connection.
\(i_t\)(Input): How much current information to write to the cell.
\(g_t\)(Gate Gate): The candidate content itself to be used in the cell.
\(o_t\)(Output): How much of the cell content to output/hide.







ImportantLSTM has two streams



While vanilla RNNs propagate only one hidden state \(h\) over time, LSTMs propagate two cell states \(c\) (dedicated memory) and hidden states \(h\) together. The key point is that the cell state path is updated only by multiplication by the forget gate plus the addition of the input, so it can flow along a path where the gradient is close to 1** (the Jacobian of \(c_{t-1}\to c_t\) is \(\mathrm{diag}(f_t)\)). This is the mechanism for preserving long-term information.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
5.3 Geometry/Intuition
When the forget gate is close to 1, the cell state becomes a ‘conveyor belt’ where data flows almost unchanged. Since information is processed and stored via gates rather than stored as is, it retains data longer than a vanilla RNN, but still cannot retain data infinitely. (It is like eating sausage instead of raw meat—the original flavor is partially lost due to processing.)






TipWireless communication perspective analogy



The cell state \(c_t\) is a leaky integrator-based channel estimator/trace filter. The forget gate \(f_t\) is an adaptive version of RLS (Recursive Least Squares) with a forgetting factor \(\lambda\): if the channel is static, it averages for a long time with \(f_t\to1\), and if it is volatile, it discards the past quickly with \(f_t\downarrow\). The input gate corresponds to the confidence (Kalman gain) of the new observation.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
6.1 Direct answer
GRU is a gating unit that implements almost the same idea as LSTM in a simpler way, has 3 gates (update, reset, and candidate), and has no separate cell state. It achieves equivalent performance with fewer parameters compared to LSTM.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
6.2 Mathematical expansion
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_r\,[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_r\right) && \text{(reset gate)}\\
z_t &= \sigma\!\left(W_z\,[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_z\right) && \text{(update gate)}\\
\tilde{h}_t &= \tanh\!\left(W_h\,[\,r_t \odot h_{t-1},\, x_t\,] + b_h\right) && \text{(후보 상태)}\\[4pt]
h_t &= (1 - z_t)\odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t && \text{(상태 갱신)}
\end{aligned}
\]

reset gate \(r_t\): How much to reflect the previous state in the candidate calculation (reset degree).
update gate \(z_t\): The ratio for mixing past states and new candidates — a form combining the forget and input gates of an LSTM into one.

Note that the last diet is exactly in the form of the gating prescription \(f(x)=z\cdot(\text{새것}) + (1-z)\cdot(\text{메모리})\).

text:

WarningPrecise attention to ‘parameter half’



If we count only the gate-specific weight matrices, 4 LSTMs vs 3 GRUs results in \(3/4\). The commonly cited “about 1/2” is a loose approximation that includes cell state path elimination and practical simplification, while the strict gate-weight ratio is closer to \(3/4\). Either way, the conclusion is the same: GRU achieves equivalent performance with fewer parameters.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
8.1 Direct answer
To interpret information, one must look at the context. Since the role and meaning of even the same word change depending on the context, using fixed weights results in converting the same word into the same vector every time, making it impossible to encode different meanings.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
8.2 Classic example: “Buffalo buffalo …”
Grammatically correct sentence in English:

Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo.

Here, Buffalo alternates between three roles: (1) a city name in New York State, (2) an animal ‘buffalo (American bison)’, and (3) a verb ‘to scare/to harass’. Without context, it is impossible to know whether a buffalo is a noun or a verb. The same problem applies to homonyms in Korean — the same spelling of “gamda” plays completely different roles depending on the context, such as (to close eyes) / (to wind thread) / (to wash hair).

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
section: 8.3 Why can’t fixed weights be used
text:
8.3 Why can’t fixed weights be used
Deterministic functions like word2vec always assign the same word to the same vector. If you multiply that by fixed weights \(W\), the result is always the same. If so, how do we distinguish the different roles of the same word?

What if you use a stabilistic function? The weights change every time, but it is uncontrollable — you cannot control what meaning it will produce.
Solution: Change weights based on the input itself → Attention, and stack them into Transformers.







TipWireless communication perspective analogy



Fixed weight = Fixed equalizer. It is ineffective when the channel (context) changes. Attention = Adaptive equalizer: Estimates and applies tap coefficients from the received symbol (input) itself every time. This is equivalent to demodulating the same transmitted symbol differently depending on the channel state.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
9.1 Contextual Conditional RNN (Type 4)
Idea: Looking at past outputs improves future prediction. It performs sequential prediction using a single input as context and establishes a reverse connection from the future.
To encode the context for the sequence input, use both the backward hidden state output and the backward output as inputs for the current hidden state.






ImportantDecisive difference from Type 2 (teacher forcing)



Type 2 breaks the chain to the output connection for computational efficiency (parallelization). On the other hand, context-conditional RNNs use hidden state connections as well for better output — so they forgo parallelization (serial cascade) but carry the context better. In other words, although they look the same, their purposes are the exact opposite.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
9.2 Bidirectional RNN (Type 5)
Idea: Reading twice—forward to backward and backward to forward—enhances the context of each word. Introduce a forward hidden state and another hidden state for the reverse direction. Although the number of parameters increases because dedicated weights are required for each hidden state, the context at each time point becomes richer.


Code
flowchart LR
    subgraph fwd["정방향"]
      f1["→h₁"] --> f2["→h₂"] --> f3["→h₃"]
    end
    subgraph bwd["역방향"]
      b3["←h₃"] --> b2["←h₂"] --> b1["←h₁"]
    end
    f1 & b1 --> y1["y₁"]
    f2 & b2 --> y2["y₂"]
    f3 & b3 --> y3["y₃"]

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
10.1 Direct answer
Seq2Seq is a general-purpose sequence modeling architecture consisting of two RNNs (encoder and decoder). An encoder (Type 3) reads the entire input and summarizes it into a fixed-size context vector \(C\), and a decoder receives \(C\) to generate an output sequence.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
10.2 Structure and Learning

Encoder (Type 3): Reads the input to the end and creates a context variable \(C\), which is a semantic summary.
Decoder (Type 4): Receives \(C\) and the current input and produces output at every time step. \(C\) affects all output timestamps.



Code
flowchart LR
    x1 --> E1["인코더"] --> E2["인코더"] --> E3["인코더"] --> C(("C\n문맥벡터"))
    C --> D1["디코더"] --> y1["y₁"]
    C --> D2["디코더"] --> y2["y₂"]
    D1 --> D2 --> D3["디코더"] --> y3["y₃"]
    C --> D3











Learning: In the case of machine translation (e.g., French → English), the source text is fed into the encoder, and the loss is reduced by targeting the correct answer (gold standard) of the decoder output. The gradient of the loss is backpropagated in reverse time from decoder → context → encoder. Because the path is long, it is vulnerable to gradient vanishing and forgetting.
Inference: Since the answer is unknown, the decoder starts from the start token (<sos>) and generates one token at a time by feeding its own output back as the next input.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
10.3 Application

QA System: Input=Question, Output=Answer
Conversational System (Chatbot): Input=User Utterance, Output=Response
Machine Translation: Input=Language A, Output=Language B







NoteInsights into Bottlenecks



Compressing the entire variable-length input into a single fixed size \(C\)** is both the elegance and the weakness of Seq2Seq. The longer the sentence, the more severe the information bottleneck \(C\) becomes — this limitation later becomes the direct motivation for attention (where the decoder directly references all hidden states of the encoder).








TipWireless communication perspective analogy



Encoder = Source encoder compressing a message into a fixed-length codeword \(C\). Decoder = A decoder that restores the message from that codeword. The dimension of \(C\) is the rate of rate-distortion, and if it is too short, it cannot contain a long sequence, so the distortion increases.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
11.1 Deep RNN
If \(f\) inside Seq2Seq is replaced with a multilayer MLP (or CNN/diffusion, etc.) instead of a single matrix multiplication, expressiveness increases. Deep operations placed inside recursion are called Deep RNNs.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
11.2 Recursive Neural Network
As another generalization of RNN, it uses a computational graph of a tree structure instead of a chain structure.

Search complexity reduced to \(\tau \to \log(\tau)\) (since it is a tree).
Call the same architecture recursively, but expect it to perform different roles at each point/node.
Application: Scene parsing — Each hidden node corresponds to an object in the scene, forming a tree that decomposes and synthesizes images into semantic units.







WarningTerminology Note (Two types of RNN)



The abbreviation RNN is typically reserved for Recurrent Neural Networks (chain structure). Recursive Neural Networks (tree structure) are a generalization of this; while theoretically feasible, practical implementation is difficult because each node must learn a different role (it often fails due to capacity limitations, etc.).

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
13.1 Direct answer
The Transformer is a Seq2Seq model that changes weights for each word and context. Even for the same word, it analyzes its neighbors (context) and transforms it into different embeddings for each situation to distinguish its role and meaning. The name ‘Transformer’ comes from the weights that change their form (transform) depending on the input.
The meaning of each word’s embedding is determined by looking at neighboring words (context). Therefore, the two buffaloes in Buffalo buffalo have different embeddings as city/bison, respectively.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
13.2 Three Key Ideas


Code
flowchart TB
    T["Transformer"] --> A["1. 토큰 (Tokens)"]
    T --> B["2. 어텐션 (Attention)"]
    T --> C["3. 포지셔널 인코딩 (Positional Encoding)"]

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
14.1 Direct answer
A token is a vector of neurons, that is, a bundle that encapsulates information. Transformers perform operations at the token level rather than on individual neurons.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
14.2 Tokenization
Split the input into chunks and project each chunk onto a vector. Performance is determined by how tokens are defined (tokenization method) — a form of input engineering.



Input Type
Tokenization Method




Image
Divided into patch units and vectorized (ViT)


Language
Character / Syllable / Word / Byte-Pair Encoding etc.


Audio
Time interval division, or waveform → spectrogram → patch









NoteEmpirical Conclusions of Language Tokenization



As a result of trying various units such as characters, syllables, BPEs, and words, there was no significant intrinsic superiority among them. Therefore, the word unit, which is the simplest and has the fewest tokens, is widely used. Non-linearity is not introduced during the tokenization stage, and that role is delegated to Transformer encoding — tokenization is simple, and non-linear encoding is handled by the Transformer.


Operations on a set of tokens consist of linear combinations of tokens + token-wise nonlinearity. (The “node attributes/feature descriptors” of GNNs are also effectively tokens.)

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
15.1 Direct answer
Attention is a weighted sum method that dynamically determines weights based on the input. Unlike fixed weights, it takes the input itself as input, modifies the weights, and then applies those modified weights to the input. Therefore, even the same input can encode different roles or meanings depending on the context.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
15.2 Motivation: Limitations of CNN (VQA Example)
Let’s look at VQA (Voice Question Answering) like “How many birds are in this image?” CNNs are built on the assumptions of spatial stationarity and locality, where each filter responds to the same pattern regardless of location. However:

Counting requires different meanings (first bird vs. second bird) at each position — max-pooling loses counts by passing only the strongest reaction to the next layer.
Long-distance relationships (Are the two birds at opposite ends of the image the same species?) are difficult to capture with local filters.
Selective focus (answer by looking only at this area) is needed, but CNNs treat all locations equally.

In other words, the locality and stationarity of CNNs are unsuitable for long-distance relationships and context-dependent processing.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
15.3 Fixed Weights vs. Self-Attention









Fixed weights
(Self) Attention




Weight
Fixed regardless of input
Varies depending on input (Trigger = Input)


Training Target
\(W\) (Trained with data, fixed)
Attention Function \(a(\cdot)\) — Trained with data but takes input and applies to input


Context processing
Impossible
Possible

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
15.4 Implementing with Query–Key–Value
The idea of “taking input and calculating weights” is implemented using three elements: Query \(Q\), Key \(K\), Value \(V\). (These three elements are fully integrated into the Transformer, and while it does not necessarily have to be in this form, it has become the standard.)






TipWireless communication perspective analogy



Attention is a beamforming/spatial match filter. While fixed weights are fixed beams (receiving only in a specific direction), attention estimates the channel from the received signal (input) and adapts the beam weights every time. Query = desired direction, Key = direction each antenna faces, Value = signal in that direction — greater weight is given to values with a higher degree of match (correlation) between the Query and Key. This is the same principle as a matched filter, which weights based on correlation with the signal.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
16.1 Direct answer
Self-attention refines the representation of each patch/token by taking into account neighbors, by weighting the values by weights determined by the query-key match.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
16.2 Scaled Dot-Product Attention
Create three projections from the input token matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\):
\[
Q = X W_Q,\qquad K = X W_K,\qquad V = X W_V
\]
Attention output:
\[
\boxed{\;\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \underbrace{\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)}_{A:\ \text{어텐션 행렬}\ (n\times n)} V\;}
\]

\(QK^\top\): Similarity (Dot Product) of all token pairs — How well the query of token \(i\) and the key of token \(j\) match.
\(\sqrt{d_k}\) Scaling: If \(d_k\) is large, the variance of the inner product increases proportionally to \(d_k\), causing the softmax to saturate (vanishing of gradients). This is to normalize the variance to 1.
\(\mathrm{softmax}\): each row as a probability distribution — attention weights distributed by token \(i\) to other tokens.
\(A V\): Dynamic pooling (query-based) of values with those weights.

This is a “query-based dynamic pooling operation” that refines the semantic representation of a patch by considering neighboring patches. (An example is a visualization in self-supervised ViTs like DINO where related patches are highlighted together when a specific patch is labeled ‘dog’.)

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
16.4 Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA)
A single \(Q,K,V\) projection set is insufficient to encode all aspects of the data. Let’s place multiple sets of attention in parallel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{head}_h &= \mathrm{Attention}(X W_Q^h,\, X W_K^h,\, X W_V^h)\\
\mathrm{MHSA}(X) &= \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\dots,\mathrm{head}_H)\, W_O
\end{aligned}
\]
Each head has its own \(Q,K,V\) function, which is executed in parallel and then combines the output token vectors. It is particularly useful for language context encoding (capturing multiple types of relationships simultaneously).






TipWireless communication perspective analogy



Multihead = Multi-spatial streams of MIMO. A single head (single beam) captures only one type of relationship, but multiple heads separate and receive signals in parallel into different subspaces. Each head observes different directions/relationships with different antenna weights (different \(Q,K,V\)) and combines them at the end.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
17.1 Direct answer
Self-attention is permutation equivariant, so it does not know the order of tokens. To inject positional information, a different code value is added to the input for each position.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
section: 17.2 Why it is necessary: Permutation equivariance
text:
17.2 Why it is necessary: Permutation equivariance
Attention \(A=\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})\) treats tokens like sets. Changing the input order simply changes the output to the same order (equivariance), but it does not distinguish the order itself. However, “Cheolsu saw Younghee” and “Younghee saw Cheolsu” are different — the order changes the meaning.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
17.3 Implementation: Positional code addition
Add codes for position \(pos\) and dimension \(i\) so that patches at different locations have different inputs (sine/cosine form):
\[
\begin{aligned}
PE_{(pos,\,2i)} &= \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d}}\right)\\
PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} &= \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d}}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]
Then \(\tilde{x}_{pos} = x_{pos} + PE_{pos}\). This makes the model not permutation invariant and allows it to recognize order.






TipWireless communication perspective analogy



Positional encoding is equivalent to a position pilot created with orthogonal frequency tones. Just as OFDM distinguishes symbols using subcarriers (frequencies), different frequency components of sine and cosine assign a unique ‘fingerprint’ to each position. Thanks to the exponential frequency spectrum (\(10000^{2i/d}\)), a phase pattern is created where nearby positions are similar and far positions are distinctly different.

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
19.1 Language Model (LM)
LM is a probabilistic model that predicts the next word given a previous word sequence (assuming a fixed-size window). On a large scale, it becomes an LLM (e.g., GPT).
\[
p(w_1,\dots,w_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p\!\left(w_t \mid w_{1:t-1}\right)
\]

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
19.2 Autoregressive Transformers and GPT
When trained using causal attention (future token masking), each position predicts the next token by looking only at the past. GPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer) is a Transformer trained with this structure. A small implementation example is minGPT (karpathy).






NoteLearning = massive teacher forcing



Autoregressive LM training performs “guessing the next token” in parallel at every position — it is parallelizing the teacher forcing of a Type 2 RNN with masked self-attention. Unlike RNNs, there is no serial dependency between time points, so it calculates all positions at once (the core advantage of Transformers).

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
section: 22.1 A. Vanishing/Explosion by Vanilla RNN and Eigenvalues
text:
22.1 A. Vanishing/Explosion by Vanilla RNN and Eigenvalues


Code
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)

def rnn_state_norms(W, T=40, h0=None):
    n = W.shape[0]
    h = np.ones(n) if h0 is None else h0
    norms = []
    for _ in range(T):
        h = W @ h
        norms.append(np.linalg.norm(h))
    return np.array(norms)

# |lambda| < 1 -> 소실
W_decay = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.0, 0.5]])
print("eig(W_decay) =", np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(W_decay), 3))
nd = rnn_state_norms(W_decay)
print(f"||h|| : {nd[0]:.3f} -> {nd[-1]:.4f}  (소실)")

# |lambda| > 1 -> 폭발
W_explode = np.array([[1.2, 0.0], [0.0, 1.05]])
ne = rnn_state_norms(W_explode)
print(f"||h|| : {ne[0]:.3f} -> {ne[-1]:.1f}  (폭발)")

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
22.2 B. LSTM cell forward


Code
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1)
sigmoid = lambda x: 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))

def lstm_step(x, h, c, P):
    z = np.concatenate([h, x])
    f = sigmoid(P['Wf'] @ z + P['bf'])   # 망각
    i = sigmoid(P['Wi'] @ z + P['bi'])   # 입력
    o = sigmoid(P['Wo'] @ z + P['bo'])   # 출력
    g = np.tanh (P['Wg'] @ z + P['bg'])  # gate gate
    c = f * c + i * g                    # 셀 상태
    h = o * np.tanh(c)                   # 은닉상태
    return h, c

H, X = 3, 2
mk = lambda a, b: np.random.randn(a, b) * 0.1
P = {k: mk(H, H + X) for k in ['Wf', 'Wi', 'Wo', 'Wg']}
P.update({k: np.zeros(H) for k in ['bf', 'bi', 'bo', 'bg']})

h, c = np.zeros(H), np.zeros(H)
for t in range(5):
    h, c = lstm_step(np.random.randn(X), h, c, P)
print("LSTM h =", np.round(h, 3))

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
section: 22.3 C. GRU cell forward + parameter count comparison
text:
22.3 C. GRU cell forward + parameter count comparison


Code
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(2)
sigmoid = lambda x: 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x))

def gru_step(x, h, P):
    z_in = np.concatenate([h, x])
    r = sigmoid(P['Wr'] @ z_in + P['br'])         # reset
    u = sigmoid(P['Wu'] @ z_in + P['bu'])         # update
    hh = np.tanh(P['Wh'] @ np.concatenate([r * h, x]) + P['bh'])  # 후보
    return (1 - u) * h + u * hh                   # 갱신

H, X = 3, 2
mk = lambda a, b: np.random.randn(a, b) * 0.1
Pg = {k: mk(H, H + X) for k in ['Wr', 'Wu', 'Wh']}
Pg.update({k: np.zeros(H) for k in ['br', 'bu', 'bh']})

h = np.zeros(H)
for t in range(5):
    h = gru_step(np.random.randn(X), h, Pg)
print("GRU h =", np.round(h, 3))

n_lstm = 4 * (H * (H + X) + H)
n_gru  = 3 * (H * (H + X) + H)
print(f"게이트 가중치 비율 GRU/LSTM = {n_gru / n_lstm:.2f}")  # ~0.75

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
section: 22.4 D. Scaled Dot-Product Attention (+ causal mask)
text:
22.4 D. Scaled Dot-Product Attention (+ causal mask)


Code
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(3)

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def attention(Q, K, V, causal=False):
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)
    if causal:
        n = Q.shape[0]
        mask = np.tril(np.ones((n, n), dtype=bool))
        scores = np.where(mask, scores, -1e9)
    A = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return A @ V, A

n, d = 4, 8
Q, K, V = (np.random.randn(n, d) for _ in range(3))

out, A = attention(Q, K, V)
print("어텐션 행 합 = 1 :", np.allclose(A.sum(1), 1.0))

out_c, A_c = attention(Q, K, V, causal=True)
print("causal 상삼각 ~ 0 :", np.allclose(np.triu(A_c, 1), 0.0, atol=1e-6))

title: Sequence Modeling and Transformers
text:
22.5 E. Sine/Cosine Positional Encoding


Code
import numpy as np

def positional_encoding(L, d):
    pos = np.arange(L)[:, None]
    i = np.arange(d)[None, :]
    angle = pos / np.power(10000.0, (2 * (i // 2)) / d)
    pe = np.zeros((L, d))
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angle[:, 0::2])
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angle[:, 1::2])
    return pe

pe = positional_encoding(50, 16)
print("PE shape =", pe.shape, "| 값 범위 =", round(pe.min(), 2), "~", round(pe.max(), 2))
# 서로 다른 위치는 서로 다른 코드를 가짐 (행벡터가 모두 구별됨)
print("위치 0 vs 1 코드가 다른가 :", not np.allclose(pe[0], pe[1]))
