TipHow to use this note



Each section is structured to be read in the order of Direct Definition → Mathematical Derivation → Geometric/Statistical Intuition → Analogies for Wireless Communication and Signal Processing. It is recommended to copy the formulas by hand once and then verify them by running them directly using the NumPy code in the final Section 11.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
2.1 Convolution is actually cross-correlation
The operation called “convolution” in deep learning is not the true convolution of signal processing (flipping the kernel), but cross-correlation. The output \((i,j)\) component in a single channel is
\[
y[i,j] \;=\; \sum_{m=0}^{k_h-1}\sum_{n=0}^{k_w-1} x[\,i\,s + m,\; j\,s + n\,]\;w[m,n],
\]
is the inner product of the input patch and the filter. Since the kernel is not flipped, the learned \(w\) can be viewed as learning an “already flipped kernel,” and consequently, there is no difference from a learning perspective.






NoteThe fact that inner product equals similarity (determines the pooling type later)



\[
\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x}\rangle = \|\mathbf{w}\|\,\|\mathbf{x}\|\cos\theta
\] The cross-correlation value between filter \(\mathbf{w}\) and input patch \(\mathbf{x}\) measures the directional alignment (angular distance). If the value is \(\theta\to 0\), it is maximum → a strong response indicating “this pattern is at this location.” This perspective serves as the criterion for distinguishing between max and min pooling in Section 2.6.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
section: 2.2 Stride: Decimation from a multirate perspective
text:
2.2 Stride: Decimation from a multirate perspective
Stride \(s\) applies the filter by skipping \(s\) pixels. Since adjacent responses are highly correlated (redundant), for high-resolution (4K, 8K) inputs, redundant calculations are reduced and downsampling is performed to \(s>1\).

e.g.: \(7\times7\) input + \(3\times3\) filter.

\(s=2\) → Prints \(\{0,2,4\}\) neatly aligned with one axis at position \(3\times3\).
It matches only up to \(s=3\) → \(\{0,3\}\), and information is truncated at the boundary (compensated by padding below).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
2.3 Padding: Preservation of boundary information
Adding virtual values to the edges so that the filter extends beyond the boundaries. Three types are common.








Method
Fill Value
Effect/Remarks




Zero padding
\(0\)
Most common. Effectively “turns off” the weights multiplied at boundaries → No noise injection. (Black border if value range \([0,255]\))


Replicate(repeat) padding
Duplicate boundary pixels
Extend boundary values as they are (\(\dots,0.5,0.5\,|\,\)image\(\,|\,0.5,0.5,\dots\))


Reflect(mirror) padding
Boundary-based mirror reflection
Symmetric reflection like \(\dots,1,0.5\,|\,\)image\(\,|\,0.5,1,\dots\)



Zero padding is based on exactly the same concept as zero-padding in FFT / boundary processing for linear convolution. With appropriate padding, the output size can be matched to the input (“same” padding).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
2.4 Output Size Formula
\[
\boxed{\;o = \left\lfloor \dfrac{i - k + 2p}{s} \right\rfloor + 1\;}
\]
where \(i\) input size, \(k\) filter size, \(p\) one-sided padding, \(s\) stride. The library handles this automatically, but manual calculation will appear on the exam.






ImportantRepresentative Example (Must be done by hand)



Input \(32\times32\), Filter \(5\times5\), Stride \(1\), Padding \(2\), Filter \(10\). \[
o = \frac{32 - 5 + 2\cdot2}{1} + 1 = 31 + 1 = 32.
\] → The output tensor is \(32\times32\times10\) (number of filters = number of output channels).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
2.5 Counting parameters (CNN vs MLP)
One filter parameter = (kernel volume) + (1 bias). \(5\times5\) If you apply the filter to a 3-channel input
\[
\underbrace{5\times5\times3}_{=75}\;+\;\underbrace{1}_{\text{bias}} \;=\; 76 \quad\text{(필터당)}, \qquad 76 \times 10\ \text{filters} = \boxed{760}.
\]






NoteCommon pitfall: The filter depth automatically matches the input channels



When saying “‘\(5\times5\) filter’,” usually only the spatial size is mentioned. If the input is 3 channels, the filter automatically becomes \(5\times5\times3\). The bias is one scalar per filter (\(\,W\!*\!x + b\,\)’s \(b\)). Therefore, it is \(760\), not \(250\).


If you process and \(32\times32\times3\) inputs using MLP, each output neuron is connected to every pixel \[
32\times32\times3 = 3072 \ (\,+1\ \text{bias} = 3073\,)\quad\text{(뉴런 1개당)}
\] weights are required. As the number of output neurons increases, it explodes through multiplication. On the other hand, convolution shares all locations with \(10\) filters and creates \(32\times32\times10\) feature maps even after training only \(760\).
The nature of this gap is two inductive biases.

Weight Sharing: Reuse the same filter at all locations → Automatic encoding of location-invariant patterns, drastic reduction in parameters.
Local connectivity: Views only at the patch level → No need to “learn inter-pixel relationships individually,” simultaneously securing data efficiency + computational efficiency.

During training, backpropagation updates the filter not at a single location, but by summing the gradients of all locations where the filter has slid (a direct consequence of weight sharing): \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w[m,n]} \;=\; \sum_{i,j} \frac{\partial L}{\partial y[i,j]}\; x[\,i s+m,\; j s+n\,].
\]






TipWireless Communication & Signal Processing Analogy — Matched Filters and LTI Systems



A convolutional layer is a linear time-invariant (LTI) filter bank for an input signal. Each filter is a matched filter for a specific pattern, and the larger the correlation (inner product) with the patch, the larger the output — this is the same principle as correlation with known templates (pilot/preamble) at the receiver maximizing the SNR. Weight sharing is the time-invariance itself, meaning “tap coefficients do not change over time.”

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
section: 2.6 Pooling: An operation to select a number from a pool
text:
2.6 Pooling: An operation to select a number from a pool
“Pooling” is an operation that selects a single number from a pool of numbers (English noun pool → verb pooling). It selects a representative value from a pool of responses obtained by applying filters to multiple locations.








Type
Operation
When is it suitable




Max pooling
\(\max_k x_k\)
When the filter response is similarity (inner product). Keep only the best fit


Average(mean) pooling
\(\frac1n\sum_k x_k\)
When you want to preserve background/global statistics. Low-pass (smoothing)


Min pooling
\(\min_k x_k\)
When the filter response is distance (dissimilarity), the closest (smallest) response is the best match









WarningTerminology Note: mean vs min



mean = average, min = minimum. The pronunciation is confusing, but they are completely different. average pooling = mean pooling, minimum pooling = min pooling.


Why the types differ (statistical and geometric basis). As seen in Section 2.1, cross-correlation measures similarity \(\langle\mathbf w,\mathbf x\rangle=\|\mathbf w\|\|\mathbf x\|\cos\theta\). Therefore, the “strongest pattern match” is the max value → max pooling. However, if the filter produces dissimilarity such as Euclidean distance \(\|\mathbf w-\mathbf x\|_2\), the best match is the minimum value → min pooling. The nature of the operation determines the pooling.
Statistically speaking, average pooling estimates the expected value (low variance, bias toward the background) of the response, while max pooling estimates the extreme value (high variance, detection of prominent activity), which is a kind of bias-variance trade-off.
Three benefits and one loss of max pooling.

Expanding the receptive field — without increasing parameters. Stacking conv-pools allows the same \(3\times3\) filter to see a wider area in the input coordinate system (Section 2.6.1).
Removal of redundant/noise responses. Since responses at adjacent locations are strongly correlated (almost redundant), only the maximum value is passed to the next layer → suppression of unnecessary noise, saving computation.
Local translation invariance.
Disadvantage: Some accurate location information is lost. This is acceptable for classification, but for tasks where location is important (detection/segmentation), average pooling or pooling omission is chosen.

Because of this balance of “positive effects ≫ negative effects,” pooling is widely used not only in CNNs but also in MLP and Transformer families.

2.6.1 Recurrence relation
The reception area of ZZZPH0007803ZZZ layer \(l\) \(r_l\)Z and “jump” \(J_l\) is \[
r_l = r_{l-1} + (k_l - 1)\,J_{l-1}, \qquad J_l = J_{l-1}\, s_l, \qquad r_0=1,\ J_0=1.
\]



Configuration
\(r\) (Area of Reception)




conv3(s1)
\(3\)


conv3(s1) → conv3(s1)
\(5\)


conv3(s1) → pool2(s2) → conv3(s1)
\(8\)


conv3 → pool2 → conv3 → pool2 → conv3
\(18\)









NoteWhat “pooling gives a wider view” really means



Intuitively, it is said that if \(3\times3\) conv is followed by \(2\times2\) pooling, the next conv will look at the \(6\times6\) degree of the input, but the recurrence relation provides the exact value considering overlap (\(8\) in the table above). The key point is that pooling multiplicatively increases the jump \(J\) to rapidly expand the receptive range. By expanding the receptive range with pooling instead of using large filters, a wide context is obtained without parameter or data cost.








TipWireless Communication & Signal Processing Analogy — Decimation and Envelope Detection in Multirate Systems



Pooling corresponds to decimation in multirate DSPs. Redundancy is eliminated by lowering the sample rate through stride/pooling. In particular, max pooling is equivalent to envelope detection after rectification, and average pooling is equivalent to low-pass averaging. “Large filter = long tap for narrow bandwidth selectivity,” and by lowering the resolution through pooling and then reusing the same short filter, wider frequency and spatial selectivity are obtained with the same number of taps.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
3.1 Definition and effective kernel size
For dilation rate \(d\), place filter tabs at \(d\) cell intervals. \(k\times k\) The effective size of the filter is \[
k_{\text{eff}} = k + (k-1)(d-1) = d(k-1)+1.
\] Example: \(k=3,\ d=2 \Rightarrow k_{\text{eff}} = 2\cdot2+1 = 5\). That is, the parameters are still \(3\times3=9\), but they cover the \(5\times5\) region in the input coordinate system. The output size is \[
o = \left\lfloor \frac{i - k_{\text{eff}} + 2p}{s}\right\rfloor + 1.
\]

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
section: 3.2 What is the difference from Stride?
text:
3.2 What is the difference from Stride?

flowchart LR
    subgraph Stride["Stride=2 (계산을 건너뜀)"]
      direction LR
      s["픽셀 일부는 합성곱 계산에서 제외됨"]
    end
    subgraph Dilated["Dilated rate=2 (계산은 모두 보되 성기게)"]
      direction LR
      di["모든 픽셀이 어느 출력엔가 기여, 단 탭은 성기게 샘플링"]
    end











Stride: Decimates output positions → Some input pixels may be discarded as they do not contribute to any output.
Dilated: Maintain output resolution but sparse tabs → Expand the receptacle area without discarding entire pixels.

Therefore, dilated is suitable when you “want to skip (view a wide area) but do not want to remove any entire pixels.” It is particularly useful in high resolutions, such as 4K and satellite imagery, where adjacent pixels contain nearly identical geometric information (choose between large max pooling or dilated).






TipWireless Communication & Signal Processing Analogy — Sparse Tap FIR / Comb Filter



A dilated conv is a zero-stuffed / sparse-tap filter with zeros inserted between the taps. It has a structure similar to a filter upsampled in polyphase decomposition or a comb filter with a periodic response, and increases spatial selectivity by expanding the support of the impulse response without increasing the number of taps (=parameters).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
4.1 Why “transposed” — Transposition of Linear Transformations
Since convolution is a linear operation, for the input vector \(\mathbf{x}\), to the sparse (Toeplitz) matrix \(C\) \[
\mathbf{y} = C\,\mathbf{x}, \qquad C \in \mathbb{R}^{(\text{작은 출력})\times(\text{큰 입력})}
\] It can be written as . Transposed convolution applies \(C^\top\) created with the same weights \[
\mathbf{z}' = C^\top \mathbf{z}, \qquad C^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{(\text{큰 입력})\times(\text{작은 출력})}
\] , that is, it returns from small (output) space → large (input) space. The name is natural given that the gradient of the forward convolution is exactly the product of \(C^\top\). If there is no information loss (e.g., max pooling), the original space can be (theoretically) restored using appropriate inverse weights.






NoteMathematical Reinforcement (Linear Algebra)



If the matrix of a linear transformation \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is \(C\), then the matrix of its adjoint \(T^\ast\) is \(C^\top\) (\(\langle C\mathbf x,\mathbf z\rangle = \langle \mathbf x, C^\top \mathbf z\rangle\)). A transposed conv is the application of the adjoint of a convolution operator, which corresponds exactly to the analysis–synthesis pair in signal processing.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
section: 4.2 Transposed conv with stride and its uses
text:
4.2 Transposed conv with stride and its uses
Downsampled by the stride in the forward direction, zeros are inserted between the inputs in the transposed direction, and then convolution is performed to upsample. A typical use case is pixel-to-pixel learning.

4.2.1 Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) and Semantic Partitioning
When the goal is to produce a “semantic map of the same size as the input, where each pixel has a class label”:

flowchart LR
    I["입력 H×W×3"] --> E["인코더<br/>conv+pool (다운샘플)"]
    E --> Z["병목: 작고 의미적·잡음제거된 표현"]
    Z --> D["디코더<br/>transposed conv (업샘플)"]
    D --> O["출력 H×W×C<br/>픽셀별 라벨"]











You can stack convolutions of the same size all the way to the end, but this fails to compress information in the middle, resulting in carrying noise all the way to the end and causing the side effect of having to enlarge the filter to see a wide context.
Instead of , if you compress with an encoder (reducing dimensions + removing noise through pooling) → restore to the original resolution via transposed convolution with a decoder, intermediate parameters are reduced and data efficiency improves. In this case, each pixel location no longer has RGB values but semantic values.







TipWireless Communication & Signal Processing Analogies — Intermediate Filter / Synthetic Filter Bank / DAC Reconstruction



Transposed convolution is the upsampling (zero insertion) + interpolation filter itself. It corresponds to the synthesis side of an analysis-synthesis filter bank or the reconstruction filter of a DAC. It is a structure where the encoder (analysis) decomposes and compresses into subbands, and the decoder (synthesis) combines them again to restore the original signal dimension.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
5.1 Separable Convolution
One-line definition: A technique to reduce the number of multiplications by decomposing a 2D convolution into cascade operations of two 1D convolutions.
If the kernel is separable (rank-1), i.e., \(K = \mathbf{u}\,\mathbf{v}^\top\), then \[
K * x = \mathbf{u} *_{\text{row}}\!\big(\mathbf{v} *_{\text{col}} x\big).
\] The number of multiplications per output position decreases from \(k\times k\) to \(2k\) (if it is \(k=3\), it becomes \(9 \to 6\)).






WarningWhy isn’t it widely used? — Parallelization cost



Every efficiency improvement comes at a cost. Separable operations are dependent operations (first a 1D convolution → then another 1D convolution on the output), so even with 9 cores, they cannot all be used simultaneously and must wait for the output of the first stage. In other words, although the amount of computation (FLOPs) decreases, parallelization efficiency is poor, resulting in a loss in wall-clock time. In the GPU era, parallelism equals speed, so it is not widely adopted.








NoteTerm distinction (accuracy)



Here, “separable” refers to spatially separable: decomposing \(k\times k\) into \(k\times1\) and \(1\times k\). This is a different concept from depthwise separable, which is common in MobileNet and the like — channel-wise spatial conv + \(1\times1\) pointwise conv —. The latter is much more widely used in practice.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
5.2 Group Convolution
One-line definition: A technique that divides input channels into \(g\) groups, concatenates each group independently, and then concatenates them. Advantageous for parallelization.
If the \(C_{\text{in}}\) channels are split into \(g\) groups, each filter only examines the \(C_{\text{in}}/g\) channel, so the kernel term parameter FLOPs are reduced to approximately \(1/g\). Since the groups are independent of each other, they can be parallelly deployed across multiple cores/GPUs (the original example used by AlexNet for 2-GPU splitting).
\[
\text{full: } (k^2 C_{\text{in}}+1)C_{\text{out}}
\;\xrightarrow{\ g\text{ groups}\ }\;
\Big(k^2 \tfrac{C_{\text{in}}}{g}+1\Big)C_{\text{out}}.
\]
e.g.: \(k=3,\ C_{\text{in}}=C_{\text{out}}=64,\ g=4 \Rightarrow 36{,}928 \to 9{,}280\) (approx. \(\times\tfrac14\)).






WarningCost — Inter-group interaction loss



Cross-channel interaction is interrupted by the extent that the groups are divided. When combining group outputs, some information is lost with simple averaging/connection, so unlike separable, the operations are not equivalent. To mitigate this, channel shuffling (ShuffleNet) or interleaved group conv (Zhang et al., ICCV 2017) have been proposed.











Separable conv
Group conv




Decomposition Axis
Spatial Axis (\(k\times1,\,1\times k\))
Channel Axis (Group Split)


Operational Equivalence
Equivalent (no information loss)
Non-equivalent (loss of inter-group interaction)


Parallelization
Bad (Dependent Operations)
Good (Group Independence)


Main Gain
FLOPs Decrease
Parallelization + Parameter Reduction









TipWireless Communication & Signal Processing Analogy — Separated 2D Filter vs. Subband/Antenna-based Processing



Separable convolution is isomorphic to the separable 2D filter (row-column decomposition, separable FFT) in image processing. Group convolution corresponds to creating parallel branches in a block-diagonal structure, similar to parallel processing per antenna/stream in MIMO or per-subcarrier processing in OFDM (parallel gain at the cost of breaking inter-branch coupling).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
6.1 Structured outputs
The structure of the CNN output varies depending on the task.








Output Format
Assignment
Example




Single Label
Classification
Image Classification


Labels by pixel
Semantic segmentation
FCN (Section 4.2.1)


Graph (Matrix)
Graph Prediction
Structure represented by an adjacency matrix



The graph output is represented in 2D as an adjacency matrix. However, since the rows and columns of the adjacency matrix contain the semantic relationships of nodes, the structural information is broken if handled with a standard \(3\times3\) conv → Filter and output design must be done differently, like a Graph Neural Network (GCN/GNN).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
6.2 Various input types (Input data types)
CNN can receive “anything arranged in 2D”.

Spectrogram: Processing the time-frequency representation (STFT) of a voice or communication signal as a 2D image.
AlphaGo Input: \(19\times19\) A \(17\) tensor stacking \(19\times19\times17\) feature planes on a Go grid. The planes encode the current and past stone arrangements and turn colors: \[
[\,X_t,\,Y_t,\,X_{t-1},\,Y_{t-1},\,\dots,\,X_{t-7},\,Y_{t-7},\,C\,]\quad(\text{8+8+1}=17).
\] This tensor is encoded into a CNN like a single “image” and then combined with MCTS and reinforcement learning to estimate the winning probability of the next move.







TipWireless Communication & Signal Processing Analogy — Time-Frequency Image



Spectrograms are a core tool for wireless signal analysis. In modulation recognition, interference detection, and radar processing, viewing STFT/scalograms as 2D images and applying CNNs is essentially the task of detecting local patterns with matched filters in the time-frequency plane.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
9.1 ImageNet — Large image dataset

Built by Fei-Fei Li (currently at Stanford) in 2009 while at Princeton. Inspired by WordNet (Princeton’s word ontology tree), it collected images corresponding to each word node.
Scale: Approx. 14M images, 24k categories. Collected via search and noise refined via crowdsourcing (e.g., “apple” contains fruit/company).
Challenge subset (ImageNet-1K): Approx. 1.2M images, 1000 categories. The competition was held, explosively boosting vision research.







NoteImageNet Challenge Stagnation (2009~2011)



The error rate of the initial best algorithm appeared to stagnate, improving slowly by 1–3 percentage points annually from \(\sim35\%\) (accuracy \(\sim64\%\)). There was even skepticism that this was due to label noise — soon CNNs were on the verge of turning the tables.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
9.2 LeNet → AlexNet → Deeper

timeline
    title CNN 아키텍처의 흐름
    1998 : LeNet (Yann LeCun) — 손글씨 숫자(MNIST)·우편번호 인식
    2012 : AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Hinton) — ImageNet 오류율 급감, 부흥의 시작
    2014 : GoogLeNet (Inception) — 매우 깊은 망
    2015 : ResNet (Kaiming He) — 잔차연결로 초심층 학습
    2017 : DenseNet — 조밀 연결
    2021~ : ViT / gMLP — Transformer·MLP 계열로 전환











LeNet (1998): Proposed by LeCun for handwritten digit recognition. \(5\) convolutional layers + a final MLP structure. Classified digits using MNIST and utilized for zip code recognition. (The name comes from Le in LeCun.)
AlexNet (2012): Krizhevsky, under the supervision of Hinton (Toronto), constructed a 7-layer structure (5 convolutional layers + 2 fully connected layers) similar to LeNet, and dropped the error rate by about 10%p in just one year on the ImageNet challenge (a drop that would have taken more than 5 years under existing trends). A signal of revival.
GoogLeNet (2014, Inception): An Inception module combining filters of various sizes in parallel. Trained for over a week on multiple high-performance GPUs. (Typically counted as a depth of 22 layers.)
ResNet (2015, Microsoft Research Asia, Kaiming He): Stably trained up to 152 layers (experimentally over 1000 layers) using skip connections. Rated as “ultra deep” by LeCun.
DenseNet (2017): Densely connects all front layers to back layers.







NoteWhy Residual Connections Enable Deep Networks (Causal Chains)



The Jacobian of the residual block \(y = x + f(x)\) is \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = I + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\). Due to the identity term \(I\), gradients are preserved during backpropagation rather than being multiplied and vanished → very deep networks can be learned → improved expressiveness and accuracy. (In other words, a chain of identity Jacobian term → gradient preservation → learnability.)


The software ecosystem also exploded: DeCaf → Caffe(Yangqing Jia) → TensorFlow(Google) / Torch(LeCun) → PyTorch(current PyTorch Foundation).

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
9.3 What’s next? Transformer / ViT / gMLP

Transformer (Vaswani et al., NeurIPS 2017): The standard architecture of modern NLP. Attention Is All You Need.
Vision Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., ICLR 2021): Views the image as a \(16\times16\) patch token sequence and processes it with a Transformer. “An image is worth 16×16 words.”
gMLP (Liu et al., NeurIPS 2021): Pay Attention to MLPs — Competitiveness without attention with gated MLPs. “Attention may not be everything.”

ViT is now largely replacing CNN in many 2D encoding tasks.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
11.1 Output size·Parameters·Area
import numpy as np

def out_size(i, k, s=1, p=0, d=1):
    """conv 출력 크기. d>1이면 dilated."""
    k_eff = d * (k - 1) + 1
    return (i - k_eff + 2 * p) // s + 1

def conv_params(kh, kw, c_in, c_out):
    """필터당 (kh*kw*c_in + 1), 총 *c_out."""
    return (kh * kw * c_in + 1) * c_out

def receptive_field(layers):
    """layers: [(k, s), ...]  반환: 입력 좌표계 수용영역."""
    r, J = 1, 1
    for (k, s) in layers:
        r = r + (k - 1) * J
        J = J * s
    return r

print(out_size(32, 5, s=1, p=2))                 # 32
print(out_size(7, 3, s=2, p=0))                  # 3
print(out_size(7, 3, s=1, p=0, d=2))             # 3 (k_eff=5)
print(conv_params(5, 5, 3, 10))                  # 760
print(32 * 32 * 3 + 1)                           # 3073  (MLP 뉴런 1개)
print(receptive_field([(3,1),(2,2),(3,1)]))      # 8

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
11.2 2D cross-correlation using im2col method (including dilated)
def conv2d(x, w, stride=1, pad=0, dilation=1):
    H, W = x.shape
    kh, kw = w.shape
    kh_e = dilation * (kh - 1) + 1
    kw_e = dilation * (kw - 1) + 1
    xp = np.pad(x, pad, mode='constant')
    Hp, Wp = xp.shape
    oh = (Hp - kh_e) // stride + 1
    ow = (Wp - kw_e) // stride + 1
    y = np.zeros((oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            r0, c0 = i * stride, j * stride
            patch = xp[r0:r0+kh_e:dilation, c0:c0+kw_e:dilation]
            y[i, j] = np.sum(patch * w)        # 패치와 필터의 내적
    return y

x = np.arange(1, 26).reshape(5, 5).astype(float)
w = np.ones((3, 3))
print(conv2d(x, w).shape)                  # (3, 3)
print(conv2d(x, w, dilation=2).shape)      # (1, 1)
print(conv2d(x, w, stride=2, pad=1).shape) # (3, 3)

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
section: 11.3 Transposed convolution = Transpose of the convolution matrix
text:
11.3 Transposed convolution = Transpose of the convolution matrix
# 1D 예시: 순방향 conv를 행렬 C로 쓰고, 전치 C^T로 업샘플
x_in = np.array([1., 2., 3., 4.])
ker  = np.array([1., 0., -1.])
n_out = len(x_in) - len(ker) + 1
C = np.zeros((n_out, len(x_in)))
for i in range(n_out):
    C[i, i:i+len(ker)] = ker

y  = C @ x_in            # 순방향(다운): 4차원 -> 2차원
up = C.T @ np.array([1., 1.])   # 전치(업): 2차원 -> 4차원
print(y)                 # [-2. -2.]
print(up)                # [ 1.  1. -1. -1.]

title: Convolutional Neural Networks — Part II
text:
11.4 Separable / Group / Pooling
# spatially separable: K = u v^T 이면 2D conv = (1D row) o (1D col)
u = np.array([1., 2., 1.]); v = np.array([1., 0., -1.])
K = np.outer(u, v)
full = conv2d(x, K)
sep  = conv2d(conv2d(x, u.reshape(3, 1)), v.reshape(1, 3))
print(np.max(np.abs(full - sep)))          # ~0.0 (동치)

# group conv 파라미터: g배 절감
def params(kh, kw, c_in, c_out, g=1):
    return (kh * kw * (c_in // g) + 1) * c_out
print(params(3, 3, 64, 64, g=1))           # 36928
print(params(3, 3, 64, 64, g=4))           # 9280

# max / average pooling
def pool(x, k=2, mode='max'):
    H, W = x.shape
    oh, ow = H // k, W // k
    out = np.zeros((oh, ow))
    for i in range(oh):
        for j in range(ow):
            blk = x[i*k:(i+1)*k, j*k:(j+1)*k]
            out[i, j] = blk.max() if mode == 'max' else blk.mean()
    return out

xp = np.arange(1, 17).reshape(4, 4).astype(float)
print(pool(xp, 2, 'max'))   # [[ 6.  8.] [14. 16.]]
print(pool(xp, 2, 'avg'))   # [[ 3.5  5.5] [11.5 13.5]]

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
ImportantOne-line summary of the key points of this note



The solution space of a neural network is ill-conditioned, full of saddle points and cliffs, and even the gradients we use are noisy. Therefore, we give up on finding the global optimum and instead employ practical devices such as momentum, good initialization, and learning rate scheduling to find a sufficiently good local minimum. This is the essence of first-derivative-based deep learning optimization.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
3.1 Idea: 2nd-order Taylor approximation
If we Taylor expand loss \(f(x)\) to the second order and discard the higher-order terms, the optimal step can be obtained in a closed form.
\[
f(x) \approx f(x_0) + (x - x_0)^\top g + \frac{1}{2}(x - x_0)^\top H (x - x_0)
\]

\(g\): 1st derivative (gradient)
\(H\): 2nd derivative matrix (Hessian)

Differentiate this with respect to \(x\) and set it to 0 to get an update.
\[
x^{\ast} = x_0 - H^{-1} g
\]
In other words, the curvature information indicates the optimal stride length without the need to tune the step size separately. For a convex objective, the global optimal point is reached with fewer iterations.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
section: 3.2 Why isn’t it used in deep learning?
text:
3.2 Why isn’t it used in deep learning?






WarningThree reasons why Newton’s method fails




Computation Cost: If there are \(n\) parameters, the Hessian is \(n \times n\). For hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, computation, storage, and inverse matrix operations are nearly impossible.
The surface is not smooth: For very complex loss surfaces, the second-order approximation itself does not provide a meaningful step. Even if calculated expensively, it is not the optimal step.
Dragged toward saddle points: Newton’s method points toward critical points where the gradient is zero. However, most critical points on high-dimensional surfaces are saddle points (see Section 4.3 below). If the signs of the eigenvalues of the Hessian are mixed, the extremum can be a minimum, a maximum, or a saddle point.



The classification of critical points is determined by the Hessian eigenvalue sign.



Hessian eigenvalue
type of critical point




All positive (positive definite)
local minimum


All negative (negative definite)
local maximum


Mixed positive and negative numbers
saddle point

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
4.1 1. Ill-conditioning
Condition number is the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix \(A\).
\[
\kappa(A) = \max_{i,j}\left|\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}\right| = \frac{|\lambda_{\max}|}{|\lambda_{\min}|}
\]
Here, \(A\) is typically considered the covariance matrix of the feature space (or the Hessian of the loss surface). Eigenvalues indicate how spread the data is in the direction of each eigenvector.

\(\kappa \approx 1\): Data spreads isotropically → Similar step sizes work in either direction → Easy optimization
\(\kappa \gg 1\) (e.g., \(10^4\)): Wide distribution in some directions, dense distribution in others → step size becomes extremely sensitive

Mechanism of step size sensitivity:

If the step is large relative to the dense (high curvature) direction → oscillates by skiping the minimum
If the step is small relative to the spreading (small curvature) direction → stops before reaching the minimum

A situation where two directions cannot be satisfied simultaneously with a single learning rate is ill-conditioning.






ImportantThe higher the dimension, the default ill-conditioning



As dimensionality increases, the number of eigenvalue combinations increases, making it highly likely that the ratio \(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) will grow. Since most real-world data is high-dimensional, it is safe to assume that the solution space in practice is almost always ill-conditioned.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
section: 4.2 2. Local minima — Difficult to determine convergence
text:
4.2 2. Local minima — Difficult to determine convergence
Deep neural networks may not converge. The reasons:

There may be no local minimums at all. If there is a single global minimum and the rest is a series of plateaus, optimization wanders without a reference point to stop and eventually stops.
“stuck” state: A state where parameters continue to move even though the loss is not decreasing. Candidate causes are ① poor conditioning, ② excessive gradient noise (SGD), ③ overfitting (especially with small training data), and ④ other unknown causes.
It is common to stop before reaching a critical point. When using scheduling that gradually reduces the learning rate, if the learning rate becomes too small before entering a local minimum, training ends at an intermediate point. This happens very frequently in practice.







WarningYou cannot tell “whether it has converged well” based solely on the training loss curve



Even by examining the loss value and the optimization trajectory, it is impossible to determine whether the current stopping point is a good minimum. Whether the training was effective is ultimately revealed only when evaluated on test/validation data. It is difficult to know during training.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
section: 4.3 3. Saddle point, plateau — are they common? Unfortunately, yes.
text:
4.3 3. Saddle point, plateau — are they common? Unfortunately, yes.
Coin Toss Argument: Let us toss a coin for each eigenvalue of the Hessian.

Heads → Its eigenvalue is positive
Back side → Negative

For it to be a local minimum, all eigenvalues must be positive (all heads). As the dimension \(n\) increases, the probability of all heads becomes exponentially rare as \(\sim (1/2)^n\). Saddle points where one direction is a minimum and another is a maximum become the overwhelming majority of critical points.
Correction for Random Matrix Theory: In fact, this coin is not fair and is weighted. The lower the loss value \(J\), the higher the probability of getting heads (positive eigenvalues). Therefore:

Critical point with low \(J\) → Likely a local minimum
critical point with high \(J\) → mostly saddle point







TipPractical Implications



The worry about “getting stuck in a local minimum” is less fatal than expected. This is because reachable local minimums are clustered in areas with low losses anyway. The real problem is the saddle points scattered across high-loss regions, and Newtonian methods are dragged into these very things — this is another reason why first-order methods (+noise) are preferred.
Behavior near the saddle point: It appears to converge by showing a minimum in one direction, but the moment the gradient in the other direction increases, it rolls down into a different valley. At this point, one can observe the loss suddenly soaring.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
section: 4.4 4. Cliff and exploding gradient → gradient clipping
text:
4.4 4. Cliff and exploding gradient → gradient clipping
On the loss surface, there exists a cliff — a point where the loss drops or spikes. If the step size is sufficiently large, it jumps over the cliff and falls into an absurdly high loss region, causing the loss to spike significantly in just a single iteration, making it appear as though the training is broken.

Simple solution: Reduce the learning rate → However, overall training slows down. An unwanted trade-off.
Heuristic Solution: Gradient Clipping. Clips the gradient if its norm exceeds a threshold.

\[
g \leftarrow g \cdot \min\!\left(1,\; \frac{\tau}{\lVert g \rVert}\right)
\]
It interprets an abnormally large gradient as a signal that one is currently traversing highly irregular terrain, forcibly restricts stride length, and descends cautiously. Although it started as an absurdly simple heuristic, its excellent practical performance has made it a standard technique.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
4.5 5. Long-term dependency (vanishing gradient)
As the number of hidden layers increases, the magnitude of the gradient backpropagated from the output to the input decreases exponentially (vanishing gradient). The learning signal generated in the output layer is diluted as it passes through multiple layers, so the parameters of the layer closest to the input are not effectively learned. Separate mechanisms (skip connection, normalization, etc.) are required to preserve information or reduce noise.






NoteSame name, different axis: long-term dependency of the time axis



What is being referred to here is the dependency (depth axis) between the input and output layers within a single MLP. In sequence data, a separate long-term dependency exists along the time axis — to understand a long paragraph, one must remember and connect the meanings of the preceding words and sentences.
Modern Transformers store this contextual information in the KV cache, but this consumes GPU memory explosively as the sequence becomes longer. While compression typically results in information loss, recent techniques have emerged that compress data by approximately six times without (or with minimal) loss, significantly improving cache efficiency. This topic will be covered again in the section on sequence modeling.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
4.6 6. Inexact gradient → surrogate loss
The stochastic gradient used by SGD is not a true gradient. It is a noisy estimate that has only “tasted” a portion of the data called a mini-batch. This noise can lead optimization astray.
Solution: surrogate loss. Instead of the original complex loss surface, define a surrogate loss that is ① similar to it and ② much smoother and easier to optimize, and optimize on it.

The minimum of the surrogate is slightly different from the original minimum, but it stably reaches a point sufficiently close to the original solution with fewer iterations.
Since the surface itself is smooth, it eventually converges near the minimum even if the gradient is noisy.







ImportantOpen problem



The core question is “how to design a surrogate loss that is close to the original surface and whose minimum is close to the original solution.” The answer depends on the dataset and the objective function, and there is no general solution. If a good surrogate is found, optimization becomes dramatically easier, even when using noisy gradients. (Using cross-entropy instead of 0-1 loss in classification is a typical example of a surrogate loss.)

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
section: 4.7 7. Inconsistency between local and global structures
text:
4.7 7. Inconsistency between local and global structures
1-Dimensional Thought Experiment: Let’s assume that the loss is increasing locally in a certain parameter range. From the perspective of looking only at the gradient, there are various possible interpretations.

“The current valley is a good local minimum, and we must not go over the hill” → Stop here
“Overfitting has started” → Stop training
“There is a much deeper minimum beyond the hill” → A better year if you bravely cross over

The problem is that local observations alone cannot distinguish the three. Because local information provides poor correspondence regarding the global structure, the decision to stop or continue while monitoring the learning curve is inherently difficult.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
4.8 8. Theoretical Limitations of Optimization
In neural network learning, we give up on finding the exact minimum of a function. This is because the surface is too complex to be virtually impossible. Instead, we change our goal:

Reduce the loss value sufficiently to obtain good generalization performance.

Theoretical analysis of “which optimization algorithms can achieve the objective (finding the global minimum)” is extremely difficult. Therefore, deriving a realistic performance bound—for example, a theoretical tool that guarantees the gap between the surrogate optimization result and the true optimal solution—remains an important goal of machine learning research. Creating such a guarantee would represent a meaningful advance in learning on complex surfaces.

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
5.1 Lessons Learned from Visualization

In most problems, there exists a linear subspace where the loss decreases monotonically. Even a seemingly insanely complex surface can have a simple and even linear underlying subspace.
In some problems, there are obstacles between this subspace and the SGD path. Local ups and downs where the learning curve temporarily stagnates or spikes can often be ignored, and a decreasing trend can eventually be confirmed by observing for a sufficient period.
Factored linear models capture many qualitative aspects of deep neural network learning. Factoring \(W\) of the linear model \(y = Wx + b\)Z into eigenvectors and eigenvalues reveals the linear subspace beneath the complex surface and serves as a tool for analyzing the optimization process.







TipThis section’s punchline



Even if the surface appears complex, the latent space can be simple. This is why learning is possible even though the surface becomes more complex as the model grows larger. Based on the same philosophy, finding a good surrogate loss—since it leverages the simple underlying structure—works very well in practice. (The ripples on the surface are merely caused by data noise and inclusivity, while the fundamental structure is often simple.)

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
6.1 Momentum
Everyday definition: The force gained by motion (or a series of events) — the momentum in physics \(M = m \cdot v\), i.e., inertia.
Intuition in Machine Learning: At some point, due to bad mini-batch luck, the stochastic gradient may point in the wrong direction. However, it is rare for the downhill direction of a surface to change abruptly in a single step. In that case, instead of relying 100% on the current noisy gradient, let’s trust the direction (history) we have come down so far more — let’s give the gradient inertia.
Momentum algorithm [Polyak, 1964] accumulates the exponentially decaying moving average of past gradients and continues moving in that direction.
\[
\begin{aligned}
v &\leftarrow \alpha\, v \;-\; \epsilon\, \nabla_\theta J(\theta) \\
\theta &\leftarrow \theta + v
\end{aligned}
\]

\(v\) (velocity): The direction and speed of a parameter as it passes through the parameter space. It is defined as the exponentially damped mean of the negative gradient.
\(\alpha \in [0,1)\): hyperparameter. Determines how quickly the contribution of past gradients decays. For example, \(\alpha = 0.8\) implies that 80% of the weight is given to accumulated past velocity and the remainder to new gradients — trusting history more than the current “noisy” gradients.
Note: \(\alpha\) is another hyperparameter that must be specified when using momentum, and the results are quite sensitive to this value. It determines “how much inertia to use.”

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
6.2 Nesterov Momentum
One inefficiency of ordinary momentum: the gradient is calculated at a previous (old) parameter point. However, if it is certain that the vehicle will move to velocity anyway, that gradient is already outdated the moment it is calculated.
Nesterov momentum adds a correction factor — it calculates the gradient at the lookahead point where velocity is applied first.
\[
\begin{aligned}
v &\leftarrow \alpha\, v \;-\; \epsilon\, \nabla_\theta J(\theta + \alpha v) \\
\theta &\leftarrow \theta + v
\end{aligned}
\]
In online training scenarios where parameters are updated live whenever a mini-batch arrives, the gradient is less worn out because it previews the gradient of the “space to be actually evaluated in the next iteration.” In practice, it usually performs better than standard momentum and is used as the default choice.









Ordinary Momentum
Nesterov Momentum




gradient evaluation point
current \(\theta\)
lookahead \(\theta + \alpha v\)


Interpretation
Past Average + Current Slope
Past Average + Slope of Future Prediction Point


Real-world performance
Standard
Generally better

title: Challenges in Neural Network Optimization and First Derivative-Based Techniques (Momentum, Initialization)
text:
6.3 Parameter initialization strategy (excluding bias)
If you start in a good valley, you don’t have to worry about escaping it — initialization is one of the most important elements in machine learning optimization. However, there is no single silver bullet, and there is a collection of heuristics known to work well.

6.3.1 Default options and the “magnitude” problem

From which distribution is sampling? A Gaussian distribution or a Uniform distribution of a certain range is the standard.
Does magnitude matter? Yes. The magnitude of the initial values affects both ① the results of the optimization procedure and ② the network’s generalization ability. However, there is no single trend like “larger is always better” or “smaller is always better” — it depends on the surface (i.e., the data and the objective function).
Prescription for MLP: If there are \(m\) layers of inputs and \(n\) layers of outputs, the following uniform distribution is known to provide a good starting point.

\[
W_{ij} \sim U\!\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}},\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\right)
\]


6.3.2 Xavier (Glorot) initialization [Glorot & Bengio, 2010]
Another prescription, normalized initialization (commonly known as Xavier init):
\[
W_{ij} \sim U\!\left(-\sqrt{\frac{6}{m+n}},\; \sqrt{\frac{6}{m+n}}\right)
\]
The core design philosophy is compromise between two goals.

Initialize all layers to have the same activation variance (preserve forward signal)
Initialize all layers to have the same gradient variance (backward signal preservation)







ImportantWhy Variance Equilibrium Saves Optimization — Causal Chain



If the layer-by-layer activation variance and gradient variance are maintained within a certain range → signals do not explode or vanish in any layer → local cliffs and explosions on the loss surface are suppressed → allowing for a stable descent that skips local bends, much like optimizing a smooth surrogate loss. Regularizing variance within a range effectively constrains the learning process.


Assumptions and Limitations: This derivation is based on the assumption that “the network consists only of a chain of non-linear matrix products.” Of course, real-world networks have numerous non-linear activations between inputs and outputs. It is used as a standard because it works quite well in practice despite the assumption being broken.


6.3.3 Gain factor — Correction for nonlinearity [Saxe et al., 2013]
Let’s assume we use ReLU. If about half of the activations are negative, that half will drop to zero, and the activation variance will drop by that proportion. The activation–gradient variance balance established by Xavier is broken.
Correction: Restores the magnitude lost through a gain factor. In the case of ReLU, since the variance is halved, a correction of \(\times 2\) (based on weighted standard deviation \(\times\sqrt{2}\)) is applied — generally, a scale adjusted to the rate at which negative activations occur is multiplied. By “simulating” nonlinearity in this way and restoring variance balance, a good local minimum is reached with fewer iterations. The importance of the gain factor was also confirmed in subsequent research [Sussillo, 2014]. (The He initialization family formalized the gain for ReLU.)


6.3.4 Sparse initialization [Martens, 2010]
Another approach proposed at the same time: the method of initializing a majority of parameters to 0 can also provide a good initial point and is widely used in various applications.








Initialization
Distribution

\(U(-1/\sqrt{m}, 1/\sqrt{m})\)

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
text:
2 Classic Classifier Finish

2.1 k-Nearest Neighbor (k-Nearest Neighbor)
Key Idea: When inferring the label of a new sample, we look at the labels of the closest training samples in the feature space. The concept of “closeness” is determined by a distance metric defined in the space.
Four terms are used interchangeably to refer to the point of testing — testing, inference, prediction, and evaluation. Of these, inference is the most widely used.
There are two variations:








Variation
Definition of Neighbor
Determination Method




k-NN
Nearest \(k\) samples
Majority voting


ball(radius) based
all samples that fall inside a ball with radius \(r\)
majority









ImportantkNN’s Essential Trade-off




There is no training phase. There is no model or model prototype. Therefore, model bias is 0, and the VC dimension is infinite — the variance can be infinitely large.
In return, for every sample to be inferred, the distance to all training samples must be calculated. If there are \(N\) training samples, then \(O(N)\) per inference — accuracy increases as the data grows, but at the same time, the computation becomes unmanageable.

It is a classifier that is beautiful in theory and intuition, but lacks practicality.




2.2 Decision Tree
A decision is obtained by traversing the tree to the leaf nodes, starting from the root node and following the decision criteria of each node. Since the leaf nodes are countable, it is suitable for discrete label classification but is inherently unsuitable for regression requiring continuous value prediction (although it can be used by assigning a value range to each leaf, it is not precise regression). Classical algorithms such as C4.5 are used for training.






TipThe decisive strength of decision trees: Explainability



In most models, including neural networks, parameters are merely weight values for each dimension, making it difficult to interpret their meaning in themselves. On the other hand, decision trees allow for back-tracing the nodes through which a decision was reached. In other words, the path can explain “why a particular decision was reached.” This property is the reason why tree-based models survive even in the current era dominated by deep learning.
In addition, the VC dimension of the tree is larger than that of a linear model, so it can capture non-linear relationships between input and output.




2.3 Random Forest
When multiple trees come together, they form a forest. A classifier composed of multiple decision trees, each trained on a random subset of data is called a Random Forest. It is a representative example of ensemble learning, and this concept leads to the modern Mixture of Experts (MoE). Microsoft Kinect’s motion recognition is a famous application of Random Forests.






NoteClassic Classifier Summary



Linear regression is the foundation of numerous modern models, such as logistic regression, neural networks, and SVMs. kNN, decision trees, and random forests can be remembered by the keywords “classification without a model,” “explainable classification,” and “the power of ensembles,” respectively.

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
text:
3 Perceptron

3.1 Artificial Neural Networks vs. Human Neurons
Neural networks (original name: artificial neural network — omitted because attaching ‘artificial’ to every artifact is meaningless) are inspired by human neurons, but their mode of operation is completely different.








Item
Human Brain
Artificial Neural Network




Switching time
~0.001 sec
Varies by hardware


Number of neurons
~\(10^{10}\)
Modern LLMs have hundreds of billions of parameters (more)


Connections per neuron
\(10^4 \sim 10^5\), Sparse connections between modules + Dense connections within modules
Connections only between adjacent layers (almost no connections skipping layers)


Scene Recognition
~0.1 sec, approx. 100 cycles of iteration/feedback
Typically 1 single forward pass



The reason we cannot conclude that something is “smarter” even if the number of parameters exceeds that of human neurons is precisely the difference in connectivity scheme. In the human brain, functional compartments such as the hippocampus are sparsely connected while the interiors of these compartments are densely connected, whereas artificial neural networks have a single, monolithic structure without compartments, connecting only between adjacent layers.


3.2 Structure of a perceptron
The perceptron proposed in the 1950s is a single neuron:
\[
y = g\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b\right) = g(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b)
\]

Multiply each input \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) by the weight \(w_i\)Z, sum the results, and add the bias \(b\).
The result is passed through the activation function \(g\).







ImportantIf there is no activation function?



Weighted sum and biased addition are both linear operations. If only linear operations are stacked, the input-output relationship remains linear forever and cannot encode complex non-linear relationships. The device that injects non-linearity is the activation function \(g\), which was also called a gating function in the sense that it passes or blocks signals like a gate.


The activation of the original perceptron is the Heaviside step function: if the weighted sum is greater than 0, \(+1\) (fire signal), otherwise \(-1\) (do not fire). Then, to change the output range to \([0,1]\) — values that look like probabilities — it was replaced with a sigmoid, and the resulting sigmoid neuron is essentially the same form as logistic regression.
\[
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}, \qquad y = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b)
\]


3.3 What a perceptron can solve: AND, OR — and what it cannot solve: XOR
Let’s consider the logical operation on the binary input \(x_1, x_2 \in \{0,1\}\).



\(x_1\)
\(x_2\)

XOR

AND, OR, NOT: Two classes can be perfectly separated by a single straight line on a 2D plane → Solved with a single perceptron (= linear decision boundary). Remember that even when using a sigmoid, the decision boundary itself is ultimately linear (same as logistic regression).
XOR: \((0,1), (1,0)\) is class 1, \((0,0), (1,1)\) is class 0 — cannot be separated by any straight line. Even if the activation function is non-linear, a single perceptron is not sufficient.

In Boolean algebra, all logical operations can be expressed using only AND, OR, and NOT. However, the fact that XOR cannot be solved means that a single perceptron lacks logical completeness. It is widely accepted that the first AI slump began around 1969 when Marvin Minsky pointed out this limitation.


3.4 XOR Solution: Stack Perceptrons
XOR is decomposed into combinations of basic operations:
\[
x_1 \oplus x_2 = (x_1 \lor x_2) \land \lnot(x_1 \land x_2)
\]
Since AND, OR, and NOT can each be implemented with a single perceptron, XOR is solved by cascade perceptrons in two stages. The two units of the first stage produce \(v_1 = \text{OR}(x_1,x_2)\) and \(v_2 = \text{NAND}(x_1,x_2)\), and the second stage calculates \(y = \text{AND}(v_1, v_2)\), and that is it.






NoteHidden Layer



The layer sandwiched between the input layer and the output layer is called a hidden layer. We see the input and the output, but the intermediate representation is usually not looked at, so it is called “hidden.” A neural network with one or more hidden layers is a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP).
With this, AND/OR/NOT/XOR can all be expressed → Boolean algebra becomes complete → Arbitrary logical input-output relationships can be represented by neural networks.


However, it is not free. As the sigmoid is composited into two layers, the loss function is no longer convex. Although logistic regression did not have a closed solution, thanks to its convexity, it was possible to find the global minimum using gradient descent; however, starting with MLPs with only one hidden layer, even that guarantee disappears. This is the starting point where optimization becomes inherently difficult.


3.5 Universal Approximation Theorem

A feed-forward neural network with a single hidden layer and a finite number of neurons can approximate a continuous function on a compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with arbitrary precision under weak assumptions about the activation function.


First proof: George Cybenko, 1989 — for the sigmoid activation function. The proof was subsequently extended to other activations such as ReLU.
Implication: There is no need to model the form of the function (polynomial? exponential? sigmoid?) in advance. As long as there is enough data, the neural network approximates it automatically — the theoretical basis for neural networks emerging as a general-purpose tool.







WarningWhat the Organization Doesn’t Tell You



This theorem guarantees only existence. It does not tell us at all whether (1) the weights can be found by gradient descent, (2) the number of neurons required is realistic, or (3) whether it generalizes to unseen data. “Being able to express” and “being able to learn” are separate issues.

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
text:
4 MLP Inference and Learning
There is two directions of information flow in an MLP:

Forward Pass = Inference: Starting from the input layer, it proceeds to the output layer by repeating (weight multiplication → passing through the activation function) at each layer. Since it only moves forward without a feedback loop, it is called a feed-forward network.
Backward pass = Learning: Updates all weights by propagating the error (target vs. prediction) calculated from the output from right to left.


4.1 Why the Chain Law?
To train using Gradient Descent, the gradients of all weights \(\partial L / \partial w\) for the loss \(L\) is required. The problem is that the influence of a single weight close to the input on the loss is transmitted through numerous subsequent paths. Calculating this all at once is nearly impossible.
The solution is the chain rule of composite function differentiation:
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial h^{(K)}} \cdot \frac{\partial h^{(K)}}{\partial h^{(K-1)}} \cdots \frac{\partial h^{(2)}}{\partial h^{(1)}} \cdot \frac{\partial h^{(1)}}{\partial w^{(1)}}
\]
Each layer calculates only its own local gradient, multiplies it by the gradient flowing from behind, and passes it forward. Since it propagates backward from output to input, it is back-propagation. The library automatically performs this by constructing a computational graph.


4.2 Minimal example of backpropagation
\[
f(x, y, z) = (x + y)\,z, \qquad x = -2,\; y = 5,\; z = -4
\]
If we introduce the intermediate variable \(q = x + y\), it becomes \(f = qz\).
Forward propagation: \(q = -2 + 5 = 3\), \(\;f = 3 \times (-4) = -12\).
Backpropagation (from output to input):








Step
Calculate
Value




Starting Point
\(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial f}\)
\(1\)


\(z\) direction
\(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = q\)
\(3\)


\(q\) direction
\(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial q} = z\)
\(-4\)


\(x\) direction
\(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial q}\cdot\dfrac{\partial q}{\partial x} = z \cdot 1\)
\(-4\)


\(y\) direction
\(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial q}\cdot\dfrac{\partial q}{\partial y} = z \cdot 1\)
\(-4\)



Each node only needs to know its own local derivative and multiply it by the gradient coming from upstream. The GPU processes these multiplications in parallel.


4.3 Three ways to calculate gradients








Method
Idea
Limitations




Symbolic Differentiation
Deriving the derivative as a formula like \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\)
Complex composite functions must be derived/implemented manually by humans. In early deep learning libraries (~2012), derivatives also had to be coded by hand when defining loss functions.


Numerical Differentiation (numeric)
\(\frac{f(x+\epsilon)-f(x)}{\epsilon}\), observe output change by slightly shaking the input
If \(\epsilon\) is too small, it gets buried by the floating-point precision limit, and if it is too large, the limit approximation breaks. Cannot provide an accurate gradient


Automatic Differentiation (automatic, autograd)
Decomposes complex functions into atomic operations and embeds the derivatives of each atomic operation in a library. Compounds the total gradient by multiplying local gradients along the computation graph
Modern Standard (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX)









TipAutomatic differentiation in one sentence



“Complex function → Decompose into a composition of atomic functions → The derivative of each atom is already known → Reassemble using the chain rule.” For example, if you define \(\tanh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\), the library creates a computation graph of atomic operations—exponentiation, division, subtraction, and addition—multiplies them by their respective built-in derivatives, and returns the value \(\tanh'(x)\).

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
text:
5 Loss function for classification: cross-entropy

5.1 Settings: One-hot encoding
\(n\)-class In supervised learning, target labels are encoded as one-hot vectors rather than scalar \(1\sim n\):
\[
\mathbf{p} = [0, 0, \dots, 0, 1, 0, \dots, 0] \in \{0,1\}^n
\]
Only the correct class dimension is 1, and all others are 0. (The name “hot” comes from the convention of representing hot=1 and cold=0 in thermodynamic heatmaps.) The model’s predicted probability vector is denoted as \(\mathbf{q}\).


5.2 Definition and Decomposition
Cross Entropy (CE) — Also called multinomial logistic loss:
\[
H_p(q) = H(p, q) = \sum_{x \in \{1,\dots,n\}} p(x)\,\bigl(-\log q(x)\bigr) = \mathbb{E}_{p}\bigl[-\log q\bigr]
\]
If entropy \(H(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)\) is “encoding itself with its own distribution,” then cross-entropy is “taking the expectation of the distribution \(p\) with the sign length of the distribution \(q\).” The following identity is key:
\[
H(p, q) = H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q)
\]
Proof (One line):
\[
H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
= -\sum_x p\log p + \sum_x p\log\frac{p}{q}
= \sum_x p\,(-\log p + \log p - \log q)
= \sum_x p\,(-\log q) = H(p,q). \;\blacksquare
\]






ImportantIf it is a one-hot target, CE = KL divergence



The one-hot vector \(p\) is a deterministic distribution — the probability of one class is 100%, and the rest is 0. Therefore, \(H(p) = 0\) is, and
\[
H(p, q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\|\, q)
\]
, that is, minimizing cross-entropy = minimizing KL divergence that pulls the predicted distribution \(q\) toward the target distribution \(p\).




5.3 Reducing to binary classification: Logistic Loss, and MLE
When \(n=2\), if set to \(p = [y, 1-y]\), \(q = [q(x), 1-q(x)]\):
\[
H(p,q) = y\bigl(-\log q(x)\bigr) + (1-y)\bigl(-\log(1 - q(x))\bigr)
\]
This is exactly the negative log-likelihood of logistic regression. Therefore:
\[
\text{CE 최소화} \;\equiv\; \text{최대 가능도 추정(MLE)}
\]
This is the biggest reason why cross-entropy has established itself as the standard loss for classification—because it is equivalent to a statistically well-grounded MLE formulation. (Additional advantages—benefits from a gradient perspective—are covered in the next note.)


5.4 Cost functions other than CE








Cost Function
Definition
Meaning of Optimal Solution \(f^\ast(x)\)




Mean Squared Error (MSE)
\(\mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_\text{data}}\|y - f(x)\|^2\)
\(f^\ast(x) = \mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(y|x)}[y]\) — Conditional Average


Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
\(\mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_\text{data}}\|y - f(x)\|_1\)
Conditional Median



MSE trains a function to predict the mean of each \(x\)Z to \(y\), while MAE trains a function to predict the median. Although they can be used instead of CE in classification, CE is the standard choice.


5.5 Output Units
The output unit of the last layer of the neural network is selected according to the assumed output distribution:









Output Unit
Type
Corresponding Distribution
Application




Linear
\(\hat{y} = W^\top h + b\)
Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(y;\hat{y}, I)\)
Regression


Sigmoid
\(\hat{y} = \sigma(w^\top h + b)\), \(z = w^\top h + b\) are called logits
Bernoulli
Binary classification


Softmax
\(\text{softmax}(z)_i = \dfrac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\)
Multinulli (Multinoulli; Extension of Bernoulli’s Multiclass)
Multiclass



If you apply the sigmoid function separately for each class, the sum of the outputs does not equal 1 — it merely looks like unnormalized probability. The softmax function is the result of normalizing the values by applying an exponent.


5.6 Softmax is “More than normalization”
argmax(picking the maximum) is a non-linear operation, so it is not differentiable and cannot be expressed as a simple matrix multiplication (since the selection vector to be multiplied changes depending on which input is the maximum). From a learning perspective, what we want is: to amplify the gap** between the maximum class and the rest so that the prediction \(q\) converges quickly to the one-hot target \(p\).
The exponential function of softmax does exactly this job. Let’s compare it to L1 regularization:



Input
L1 Normalization
Softmax




\([1, 2]\)
\([0.333, 0.667]\)
\([0.269, 0.731]\)


\([10, 20]\)
\([0.333, 0.667]\)
\([0.0000454, 0.99995]\)



L1 normalization preserves only the ratio of the input, so it is insensitive to magnitude. Softmax is sensitive to magnitude thanks to the exponent, so the larger the logit gap, the closer the output becomes to one-hot. In other words, it is an operation that performs “maximum selection” in a soft and differentiable way—true to its name, soft + max.






NoteThe boundary up to here



The full properties of softmax (Gumbel-Softmax, reparameterization trick, general activation functions, vanishing gradients, etc.) will be continued in the next note.

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
section: 6 Intuition from a Wireless Communication Perspective
text:
6 Intuition from a Wireless Communication Perspective
If this content is read again in the Signal Processing/Wireless Communication background, the following correspondence is established.








Deep Learning Concepts
Wireless Communication Support
Connecting Link




kNN Classification
Minimum Distance Decoding / Nearest Codeword Decoding
Identical structure to ML detection, which determines the received signal based on the nearest symbol on a constellation. Accuracy increases as the codebook (=training set) grows, but search costs skyrocket — the same problem awareness that led to the emergence of sphere decoding.


Weighted sum of a perceptron \(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}\)
MRC (Maximum Ratio Synthesis) / Matched Filter
The structure is exactly the same in that it combines multiple antenna (input dimension) signals by weights to produce a single decision statistic. The activation function corresponds to the slicer.


Linear Inseparability of XOR
Limitations of Linear Equalizers
Channel nonlinear distortion (amplifier saturation, etc.) cannot be compensated for by linear equalizers → Nonlinear equalizers/high-dimensional lifting are required. Kernel tricks and hidden layers are two forms of the same prescription


Backpropagation Chain Law
Sensitivity Analysis of Cascade Linear Systems
The structure is identical in that the sensitivity of the final output stage gain in a multistage amplifier chain is obtained by multiplying the gain product of subsequent stages by the local response to obtain the overall response


Cross-entropy / KL
MCS Mismatch Cost in AMC
The efficiency loss when operating the actual channel distribution \(p\) as the assumed distribution \(q\) is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\). CE minimization is a goal like link adaptation, which is “fitting the assumed distribution to reality”


One-Hot Encoding
Orthogonal Signaling
Loading \(n\) classes into mutually orthogonal \(n\)-dimensional standard basis vectors. Representation without “interference” between classes


Softmax vs. argmax
Soft Decision vs. Hard Decision
Hard decisions (argmax) discard information and are non-differentiable, whereas soft decisions (LLR-based) preserve confidence and are continuous — just as soft decisions provide a ~2dB gain in channel decoding, softmax preserves gradients in learning. Logit size corresponds to SNR: just as soft decisions converge to hard decisions as SNR increases, softmax converges to one-hot decisions as the logit gap increases.


Random Forest
Diversity Synthesis
A structure that combines multiple independently fading paths (trees trained on random subsets) to increase confidence compared to a single path



In particular, the softmax = soft judgment correspondence is also valid when understanding the temperature parameter \(\tau\) of the next note: if \(\tau \to 0\), it is hard judgment (argmax), and if \(\tau\) is large, it is uniform distribution — it plays exactly the same role as SNR scaling.

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
text:
7 cleanup

kNN has zero model bias, infinite variance, and inference cost \(O(N)\) — theoretically beautiful and practically heavy. The distinguishing feature of decision trees is explainability, random forests are ensembles and their lineage continues to MoE.
Single perceptron = linear decision boundary → Solves AND/OR/NOT but cannot solve XOR. With a 2-stage perceptron cascade (hidden layer), XOR is solved and Boolean algebra becomes complete.
Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko, 1989): A single hidden-layer MLP approximates a continuous function over a compact set—provided that only existence is guaranteed, while learnability and generalization are separate. Also, the moment a hidden layer is introduced, the convexity of the loss is broken.
Backpropagation = Systematic application of the chain rule. Each node calculates only the local gradient, multiplies it by the upstream gradient, and passes it downstream. Modern frameworks perform this using automatic differentiation (atomic operation decomposition + built-in derivatives + computational graphs).
Cross-entropy \(H(p,q) = H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\). Since \(H(p)=0\) at the one-hot target, CE minimization = KL minimization = MLE. When reduced to binary, it is the logistic loss itself.
Softmax is not simple normalization but a size-sensitive, differentiable max — it exponentially amplifies the gap to accelerate convergence to a one-hot target.

title: Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Backpropagation, and Cross-Entropy
text:
8 Appendix: Executable Code

8.1 A. Minimal Backpropagation Example — \(f = (x+y)z\) Manual Calculation vs. PyTorch

import torch

x = torch.tensor(-2.0, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.tensor( 5.0, requires_grad=True)
z = torch.tensor(-4.0, requires_grad=True)

q = x + y          # 중간 노드
f = q * z          # 순전파: f = -12
f.backward()       # 역전파 (autograd가 계산 그래프를 역순회)

print(f"f = {f.item()}")                      # -12.0
print(f"df/dx = {x.grad.item()}")             # z * 1 = -4
print(f"df/dy = {y.grad.item()}")             # z * 1 = -4
print(f"df/dz = {z.grad.item()}")             # q     =  3



8.2 B. Checking the Limits of Numerical Differentiation

import numpy as np

def f(x, y, z):
    return (x + y) * z

# 해석적 정답: df/dx = z = -4
for eps in [1e-1, 1e-5, 1e-9, 1e-13]:
    num_grad = (f(-2 + eps, 5, -4) - f(-2, 5, -4)) / eps
    print(f"eps={eps:.0e}: 수치 그래디언트 = {num_grad:.10f}  (오차 {abs(num_grad + 4):.2e})")
# eps가 너무 크면 근사 오차, 너무 작으면 부동소수점 반올림 오차가 지배



8.3 C. XOR — A single perceptron fails, but a single hidden layer succeeds

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

X = torch.tensor([[0.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,0.],[1.,1.]])
Y = torch.tensor([[0.],[1.],[1.],[0.]])   # XOR

def train(model, steps=5000, lr=0.5):
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    loss_fn = nn.BCELoss()
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X), Y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    return loss.item(), model(X).detach().round().flatten()

single = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 1), nn.Sigmoid())                       # 단일 퍼셉트론
mlp    = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 2), nn.Sigmoid(), nn.Linear(2, 1), nn.Sigmoid())  # 은닉층 1개

l1, p1 = train(single)
l2, p2 = train(mlp)
print(f"단일 퍼셉트론: loss={l1:.4f}, 예측={p1.tolist()}  (정답 [0,1,1,0] 불가)")
print(f"은닉층 MLP   : loss={l2:.4f}, 예측={p2.tolist()}")



8.4 D. CE = H(p) + KL(p‖q) Numerical Verification

import numpy as np

def H(p):            return -np.sum(p * np.log(p + 1e-12))
def CE(p, q):        return -np.sum(p * np.log(q + 1e-12))
def KL(p, q):        return  np.sum(p * np.log((p + 1e-12) / (q + 1e-12)))

# 일반 분포: CE = H + KL
p = np.array([0.7, 0.2, 0.1]); q = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
print(f"CE={CE(p,q):.6f}, H(p)+KL={H(p)+KL(p,q):.6f}")

# 원-핫 타깃: H(p)=0 이므로 CE = KL
p_onehot = np.array([0., 1., 0.])
print(f"H(p_onehot)={H(p_onehot):.6f}, CE={CE(p_onehot,q):.6f}, KL={KL(p_onehot,q):.6f}")



8.5 E. Softmax vs. L1 Normalization — Size Sensitivity

import numpy as np

def softmax(z): e = np.exp(z - z.max()); return e / e.sum()
def l1norm(z):  return z / z.sum()

for v in [np.array([1., 2.]), np.array([10., 20.])]:
    print(f"입력 {v}:  L1 = {np.round(l1norm(v), 4)},  softmax = {np.round(softmax(v), 6)}")
# L1은 비율만 보존 → 두 경우 동일. softmax는 크기가 클수록 원-핫에 수렴
