title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
This summarizes the statistical inference and generalization theories essential for a deep understanding of deep learning. There are two main pillars.

Theory of Generalization — capacity, bias–variance tradeoff, VC dimension, inductive bias, Occam’s razor, No Free Lunch.
Parameter Estimation — Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), Maximum a Posteriori (MAP), and the Bayesian perspective connecting them.







NoteOne-line summary



A “good model” is not a model that fits training data well, but a model that works well on unseen data (test). Almost every concept in this note is a variation of this single sentence.


Intuition for Wireless Communications Majors: The estimation theory in this note corresponds one-to-one with detection/estimation theory in receiver design. MLE ↔︎ ML detection, MAP ↔︎ MAP detection, prior ↔︎ a priori symbol probability or channel statistics, bias–variance ↔︎ estimator MSE decomposition. Connect in the Wireless Communications Correspondence box at the end of each section.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
2.1 Three errors: training / true / test
Let’s consider the linear basis model \(f(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{w}) = \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x})\). If we use squared error (L2) in regression, the training error is
\[
\mathrm{error}_{\text{train}}(\mathbf{w}) \;=\; \frac{1}{N_{\text{train}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{train}}}\Big(t(\mathbf{x}_j) - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}_j)\Big)^2 .
\]
What we obtain through learning is the parameter that minimizes this training error.
\[
\mathbf{w}^{*} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_j \Big(t(\mathbf{x}_j) - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}_j)\Big)^2 .
\]
However, what we really care about is the true error (prediction error) for all possible inputs.
\[
\mathrm{error}_{\text{true}}(\mathbf{w}) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},t)\sim p}\Big[\big(t(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{w})\big)^2\Big]
\;=\; \int \big(t(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{w})\big)^2 \, p(\mathbf{x})\, d\mathbf{x}.
\]
The integral is generally uncalculable. This is because \(t(\mathbf{x})\) is unknown for all \(\mathbf{x}\), and the input distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is also unknown. Therefore, we approximate with Monte Carlo using the iid sample \(\{\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_M\}\sim p(\mathbf{x})\).
\[
\mathrm{error}_{\text{true}}(\mathbf{w}) \;\approx\; \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\big(t(\mathbf{x}_m) - f(\mathbf{x}_m;\mathbf{w})\big)^2 .
\]

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
section: 2.2 Why does training error underestimate true error?
text:
2.2 Why does training error underestimate true error?
The equation for the training error and the equation for the true error approximated by Monte Carlo are almost identical in form. Nevertheless, the reason why the training error is a poor estimate of the true error is key.






ImportantOptimistically biased estimate




For a single fixed \(\mathbf{w}\), the training error is the unbiased estimate of the true error.
However, we optimized \(\mathbf{w}\) for that very training set. In other words, we selected \(\mathbf{w}^{*}\), which best fits that sample.
Therefore, the training error measured with the same data is optimistically biased. It is as if the model “took the test with the correct answer already seen.”



The solution is to separate the data into a training set and a test set. By obtaining \(\mathbf{w}^{*}\) as the training set and measuring the error on the test set, which has never been used for optimization, we obtain an unbiased estimate of the generalization error.








Error Estimator
Characteristics
Application




Ground truth (true error)
Ideal standard (uncalculable)
The value we truly want


Training error
Optimistically biased
Learning objective function


Test error
Final measurement (unbiased)
Reported value of generalization performance

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
2.3 Bias–Variance Tradeoff
The act of selecting a hypothesis class itself introduces learning bias.

More complex classes → Reduced bias: With more functions to represent, we can get closer to the true function.
More complex classes → Increased variance: The solution fluctuates significantly even with small variations (noise) in the data.

As model complexity increases, training error decreases monotonically, but true/test error follows a U-shaped curve. The left side represents underfitting (high bias), the right side represents overfitting (high variance), and the valley represents optimal complexity.






TipFormal definition of overfitting



Given a data distribution \(D(X,Y)\) and a hypothesis space \(H\), if the hypothesis \(h\in H\) has a \(h'\in H\) satisfying the following, then \(h\) overfits. \[
\mathrm{error}_{\text{train}}(h) < \mathrm{error}_{\text{train}}(h') \quad\text{이면서}\quad \mathrm{error}_{\text{true}}(h) > \mathrm{error}_{\text{true}}(h').
\] In other words, it means that there exists another hypothesis that is better in training but worse in true.








NoteBenign overfitting (recent phenomenon)



From a traditional bias–variance perspective, performance should deteriorate if the number of parameters is excessive. However, severely overparameterized deep neural networks achieve near-optimal generalization error on unseen data while perfectly interpolating noisy data (zero training error). This is called benign overfitting and challenges the traditional tradeoff. Contrasting concepts include tempered overfitting and catastrophic (traditional) overfitting.



Wireless communication support






Tip📡 Bias–Variance ↔︎ Estimator MSE Decomposition



The mean squared error of the estimator \(\hat\theta\) follows exactly the same decomposition. \[
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat\theta) = \underbrace{\big(\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta]-\theta\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)}_{\text{variance}}.
\]

LS Channel Estimator vs. MMSE Channel Estimator: LS is unbiased but has high variance. MMSE reduces variance by intentionally introducing bias using channel statistics as a prior — the same principle as regularization to lower model complexity.
Diagonal loading of MVDR beamforming: The variance of covariance estimation explodes when there are few snapshots. Diagonal loading \(\hat{\mathbf{R}}+\epsilon\mathbf{I}\) is a normalization that suppresses variance at the expense of bias.
Select AR/Channel Tap Order: Increasing the number of taps (model order) improves training fit but models noise as well, leading to overfitting. Selecting order = selecting capacity.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
3.1 Definition: shattering
The VC dimension \(h\) of classifier \(f\) is the maximum number of points that \(f\) can shatter. Here, “shatter” means that \(f\) can realize all possible binary label assignments for those points without error. In other words, \(h\) = the maximum number of training points that can be classified accurately.

2D Plane Linear Classifier: \(h = 3\) (All 8 ± assignments are possible for any 3 points at any position, but generally 4 points are not possible).

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
3.2 Generalization boundary (Vapnik, 1971)
Assumption: All training/test samples are drawn from the same distribution as iid. Then with probability \(1-\eta\)
\[
\underbrace{\mathrm{TESTERR}}_{\text{일반화 오차}} \;\le\; \mathrm{TRAINERR} \;+\; \sqrt{\dfrac{h\big(\log(2R/h)+1\big) - \log(\eta/4)}{R}},
\]
Here, \(h\) is the VC dimension, and \(R\) is the number of training samples. The second term is the capacity penalty, which increases when \(h\) is large (complex model) and decreases when \(R\) is large (large amount of data). This is the mathematical basis for the intuition that the more data there is, the safer one can use complex models.



Classifier
VC dimension




\(d\) Dimensional Linear Classifier (+ Constant Term \(b\))
\(d+1\)


Neural Network
\(\approx\) Number of Parameters


1-nearest neighbor
\(\infty\)









The fact that the VC dimension of a 1-NN is infinite means that it can memorize any label assignment with always 0 training error — a typical overfitting machine.




Wireless communication support






Tip📡 VC bound ↔︎ Model order selection / Sample complexity



The \(R\) (sample size) of the generalization boundary plays the same role as the number of training symbols in channel estimation. In massive MIMO, as the channel dimension \(h\) to be estimated increases, the number of training symbols \(R\) required for the same performance increases proportionally — this is the curse of dimensionality and sample complexity.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
4.2 Occam’s Razor

“Pluralitas non est ponenda sine necessitate” — Do not complicate things unnecessarily.


Argument for favoring short hypotheses: Short hypotheses have a low probability of fitting the data by chance (long hypotheses have a high chance of fitting by chance).
Counterargument: It is merely an assumption that the hypothesis space is small; there is nothing inherently special about the length of the hypothesis itself.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
4.3 No Free Lunch Theorem






ImportantSummary (Wolpert & Macready, 1997)



If you average over all possible data generation distributions, all classification algorithms have the same error rate when classifying unseen points. \(\Rightarrow\) Generally, there is no machine learning algorithm that is superior to all other algorithms.


Therefore, we must design algorithms to operate well on specific tasks. Since the most suitable model varies for each task, we design and build a model tailored to it whenever we encounter a new task.






NoteDoes the Foundation model violate the NFL?



The trend of reusing a single massive foundation model across multiple tasks may seem like a contradiction to the NFL, but it is not. To use a foundation model effectively for a specific task, it must also undergo a process called fine-tuning (or sophisticated modifications) to regulate and adapt it to that task. The NFL is a mathematically proven theorem, and in practice, foundation models are practically effective because “their mean” differs from the distributions we encounter.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
5.1 Parameter vs Hyperparameter

Parameter: Value learned from data (e.g., weight \(\mathbf{w}\), coin example \(p\)). training = parameter tuning.
Hyperparameter: Controls the model/training with values specified by a user. Examples: Regularization coefficient \(\lambda\), learning rate, number of layers, layer width (plane/space size), etc.

Key Question: How do you choose hyperparameters? Since the goal is to generalize as much as possible to the model on unseen data, you must select them by evaluating them on data that was not used for training.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
5.2 Held-out(validation/development) data
Separate data not used during training is set aside (held-out) and used to sneak peek at the model’s generalization performance during training. There are several names for the same data.



Name
Emphasis




Held-out set
The point that it was set aside from training


Validation set
The point that generalization validates


Development set
The point of viewing the model while developing









WarningDisadvantages of Held-out



This data is not used for training. When data is expensive and scarce, setting aside a portion for validation is a waste of valuable resources.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
5.3 k-fold Cross-Validation
Cross-validation is a technique that verifies without explicit held-outs to mitigate waste issues.

Divide the training data into \(k\) subsets (folds). Example: \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\).
Round 1: Train with fold \(\{2,3,4,5\}\) and validate with fold \(\{1\}\) → Evaluate one hyperparameter candidate.
Round 2: Train with fold \(\{1,3,4,5\}\) and validate with fold \(\{2\}\) → Another candidate.
Rotate so that every fold becomes a validation set once.
The hyperparameter is determined by combining the \(k\) results using majority voting/average.

This way, all data is used for training while maintaining the benefits of held-out validation.

Wireless communication support






Tip📡 Validation ↔︎ Pilot/Data Symbols, CV ↔︎ Resource Reuse



The channel is estimated (=trained) using the frame’s pilot symbols, and performance is evaluated using data symbols. As pilots become more expensive (overhead), a trade-off identical to the “wasting data on validation” problem arises. The fold rotation in CV is analogous to the idea of maximizing the recycling of limited pilot resources.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
6.1 What is Likelihood
Likelihood is the amount of “how well your theoretical model fits the observations (data).” We want to adjust the model’s parameters so that the model fits the observations as closely as possible (this adjustment is learning).
Regression Intuition: When fitting a linear model to data points, if we define the goodness of fit between the data and the model probabilistically and maximize it, the shape of the model becomes as similar as possible to the shape of the data. “Measuring the amount of fit by probability” is the essence of likelihood.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
6.2 Coin Toss Example
There is a biased coin. \(p\) = the probability of getting heads. It was tossed \(n\) times and got heads \(k\) times. Intuitively, it is \(\hat p = k/n\), but justifying this mathematically is MLE.
Modeling: Assume each throw is iid and treat it as Bernoulli/binomial.
\[
P(\text{Head}) = p,\qquad P(\text{Tail}) = 1-p,\qquad \text{flips are i.i.d.}
\]
The probability (=likelihood) of the sequence \(\mathcal{D}\), observed as heads \(\alpha_H=k\) and tails \(\alpha_T=n-k\), is
\[
P(\mathcal{D}\mid p) \;=\; \binom{n}{\alpha_H}\, p^{\alpha_H}(1-p)^{\alpha_T}.
\]






NoteLikelihood vs Posterior — Pay attention to the direction of the condition




Likelihood \(P(\mathcal{D}\mid p)\): Assuming a model (parameters), how well that model explains the data. A partial plot of “Model → Data”.
Posterior \(P(p\mid \mathcal{D})\): Give data and view the entire distribution of parameters. It is a complete picture of the entire parameter space, from which data can also be generated → generative perspective.

If the direction of the condition variable changes, the meaning changes completely. MLE maximizes likelihood, while MAP/Bayesian maximizes posterior.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
6.3 Why log-likelihood?
Maximize log-likelihood instead of ||| likelihood.
\[
\ell(p) \;=\; \log P(\mathcal{D}\mid p) \;=\; \alpha_H\log p + \alpha_T\log(1-p) + \text{const}.
\]
There are three reasons.

Argmax Invariant: \(\log\) is a monotonically increasing function. Composing monotonically increasing functions does not change the locations of the extrema. Therefore, \(\arg\max_p P(\mathcal{D}\mid p) = \arg\max_p \ell(p)\). (Although the magnitudes of the values change, the optimal \(p\) remains the same.)
Product → Sum: If iid, the likelihood is product, but if we take \(\log\), it becomes sum. Addition is computationally cheaper and more stable than multiplication.
Underflow/Overflow Prevention: The product of small probabilities results in a very small number that exceeds the computer’s floating-point range (underflow). \(\log\) provides numerical stability by “saturating” such values into a manageable range.







\(p\to 0\) has the side effect of \(\log p \to -\infty\), but in realistic estimation, cases where the probability becomes exactly 0 are rare, so it is not a big problem.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
6.4 MLE Solution Derivation
Since the objective function is concave (in this example) for \(p\), we set the first derivative to 0 to find the maximum.
\[
\frac{d\ell}{dp} = \frac{\alpha_H}{p} - \frac{\alpha_T}{1-p} = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\; (1-p)\,\alpha_H = p\,\alpha_T
\;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{\;\hat p_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\alpha_H}{\alpha_H + \alpha_T} = \frac{k}{n}\;}
\]
The intuitive guess \(k/n\) is derived. (This is also a common interview question.)






ImportantIn reality, there are almost no closed suns



This coin example is a rare case where a closed-form solution exists. In reality, 99% of the time the objective function is neither convex nor concave, so it cannot be solved simply by setting the derivative to zero. Therefore, an approximate optimal solution is found using gradient descent.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
section: 6.5 Conditional Log-Likelihood (Generalized form of supervised learning)
text:
6.5 Conditional Log-Likelihood (Generalized form of supervised learning)
Most supervised learning models the probability \(y\) of the label \(P(y\mid x;\theta)\) given the input \(x\). If the sample is iid
\[
\theta^{*} = \arg\max_\theta \prod_{i=1}^{N} P(y_i\mid x_i;\theta)
= \arg\max_\theta \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P(y_i\mid x_i;\theta).
\]






NoteSemicolon notation \(P(y\mid x;\theta)\)



\(\theta\) is both a condition and a model parameter. To highlight this duality, a semicolon is sometimes used instead of a comma: \(P(y\mid x;\theta)\). The meaning is the same.



6.5.1 Why model \(p(y\mid x)\) instead of \(p(x)\)
This is because the label space \(y\) is much simpler semantically than the input space \(x\).

Example: One 4K image ≈ \(3840\times2160\times3 \approx 2.4\times10^7\) pixels. Video is 60–120 frames per second. The dimensions of the input space \(x\) are astronomical.
On the other hand, \(y\) is a concept of prime numbers like “cat/dog”. Solving \(P(y\mid x)\) is much easier to handle (discriminative).

Conversely, if \(p(x)\) itself (the complete distribution of the input) is modeled, images, video, and audio can be generated → generative model. (This is the branch leading to generative models in subsequent lectures.)


Wireless communication support






Tip📡 MLE ↔︎ ML detection, log-likelihood sum ↔︎ MRC




ML Symbol Detection: \(\hat{s}_{\text{ML}}=\arg\max_s p(\mathbf{y}\mid s)\). Maximizing only the likelihood under the implicit prior that symbols have equal probability — this is exactly MLE.
Product → Sum = Diversity Combination: The combination likelihood of independent receiving branches \(L\) is a product, and taking the logarithm gives a sum. Maximizing this sum of log-likelihoods in AWGN is structured the same as the decision statistics of MRC (maximal-ratio combining).
Discriminative vs Generative: A detector that only makes decisions \(p(s\mid \mathbf{y})\) (discriminative), while modeling the entire distribution of the received signal \(p(\mathbf{y})\) corresponds to generative modeling of channel interference.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
7.1 Motivation: Let’s use prior knowledge
Let’s assume we have prior knowledge that the coin is approximately “50–50”. MLE is risky when observations are scarce. If we toss the coin 10 times and get heads 3 times, MLE says \(\hat p=0.3\), but we know this is inaccurate. The more limited the observations, the more we want to stabilize the estimate using already known knowledge.

Don’t be hooked solely on observation; weigh what I believe against what I see to make better decisions — this is the philosophy of MAP/Bayesian.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
7.2 Bayes’ Theorem
Instead of a single \(p\) value, obtain the entire distribution for \(p\).
\[
\underbrace{P(p\mid\mathcal{D})}_{\text{Posterior}}
= \frac{\overbrace{P(\mathcal{D}\mid p)}^{\text{Likelihood}}\,\overbrace{P(p)}^{\text{Prior}}}{\underbrace{P(\mathcal{D})}_{\text{Evidence (normalization)}}},
\qquad
P(\mathcal{D}) = \int P(\mathcal{D}\mid p)\,P(p)\,dp .
\]

Likelihood \(P(\mathcal{D}\mid p)\): Usually easily obtained (reads data probabilities from PDF when model parameters are provided).
Prior \(P(p)\): Expert knowledge. Often easy to obtain.
Evidence \(P(\mathcal{D})\): Integration over the entire data space/Monte Carlo is required, so it is very difficult. (e.g., how do you calculate the “probability of dog image data”?)

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
7.3 MAP avoids Evidence
Fortunately, all we want is \(\hat p\) which maximizes the posterior. Since the evidence \(P(\mathcal{D})\) is not a function of \(p\) but merely a constant, it cancels out of \(\arg\max\).
\[
\hat p_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_p P(p\mid\mathcal{D})
= \arg\max_p P(\mathcal{D}\mid p)\,P(p).
\]






ImportantCase where MAP reduces to MLE



If there is no prior (=unknown), set the prior to uniform. Since the uniform distribution is a constant, it does not affect \(\arg\max\). \[
P(p)=\text{const}\;\Longrightarrow\; \arg\max_p P(\mathcal{D}\mid p)P(p) = \arg\max_p P(\mathcal{D}\mid p).
\] In other words, MLE is a special case of a “MAP that assumes uniform priors.” (It is more accurate to say that MLE assumes uniform priors, rather than ignoring them.)

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
7.4 Conjugate Prior and Beta Distribution
To obtain a posterior in a closed form, one must choose the prior carefully. A conjugate prior is a prior that makes the posterior belong to the same distribution family as the prior.

Advantage: Algebraic convenience — The posterior comes out in a closed form.
Educational Advantage: Clearly demonstrates how likelihood updates the prior (the distribution family remains the same, only the parameters change).

The conjugate prior of binomial likelihood is the Beta distribution (Beta belongs to the exponential family).
\[
P(p) = \frac{p^{\beta_H-1}(1-p)^{\beta_T-1}}{B(\beta_H,\beta_T)} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\beta_H,\beta_T).
\]
Shape Intuition: \(\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)\) is a uniform distribution, \(\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)\)·\(\mathrm{Beta}(3,2)\) have peaks, and \(\mathrm{Beta}(30,20)\) looks like a skewed Gaussian with a narrow, pointed shape.

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
7.5 Posterior and MAP Estimators
When the Beta prior is multiplied by the binomial likelihood, the exponents are added so that the posterior becomes Beta again (conjugation).
\[
P(p\mid\mathcal{D}) = \frac{p^{\alpha_H+\beta_H-1}(1-p)^{\alpha_T+\beta_T-1}}{B(\beta_H+\alpha_H,\ \beta_T+\alpha_T)} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\beta_H+\alpha_H,\ \beta_T+\alpha_T).
\]
Maximizing this posterior (the same differentiation trick as before) yields the MAP estimator.
\[
\boxed{\;\hat p_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_p P(p\mid\mathcal{D}) = \frac{\alpha_H+\beta_H-1}{\alpha_H+\beta_H+\alpha_T+\beta_T-2}\;}
\]






TipPrior = “Imaginary additional observation”



When comparing the MAP equation with the MLE equation \(\frac{\alpha_H}{\alpha_H+\alpha_T}\), the prior \(\beta_H,\beta_T\) acts like a fictitious number of throws (extra/pseudo tosses) held through experience, which were not actually thrown. In other words, the prior adds “experience from a previous life” to the observation.

Data explosion(\(N\to\infty\)): \(\alpha_H,\alpha_T \gg \beta_H,\beta_T\) becomes prior is forgotten → MAP \(\to\) MLE.
Small Sample: For example, if there are 10 observations vs. 1,000 prior observations, the prior dominates the estimation → stable estimation.









NoteConnection with large-scale learning



When observations are virtually infinite (e.g., large models learning with billions of tokens), we forget about priors and rely on the data. Conversely, in early stages with limited data and small-scale problems, relying on priors is necessary for stability. The principle of “use data when data is sufficient, and prior knowledge when data is scarce” forms the philosophical basis of modern large-scale learning.



Wireless communication support






Tip📡 MAP ↔︎ MAP detection, Beta pseudo-count ↔︎ Bayesian channel estimation




MAP Symbol Detection: \(\hat{s}_{\text{MAP}}=\arg\max_s p(\mathbf{y}\mid s)\,P(s)\). The a-priori probability of the symbol \(P(s)\) is the prior. If the symbol has equal probability, \(P(s)\) becomes a constant, so MAP = ML — Exactly the same structure as “uniform prior → MAP = MLE” in the text.
Prior ↔︎ Channel Statistics: MMSE/Bayesian channel estimation obtains stable estimates with a small number of pilots by using the channel’s prior statistics \(\mathbf{R}_h\) as a prior. Just as the pseudo-count of Beta is a “virtual observation,” MMSE attracts estimates using the prior covariance as a “virtual measurement.”
Small Sample ↔︎ Few Snapshots: The fewer the pilot/snapshots, the greater the weight of the prior (channel statistics); the more there are, the more the measurement data dominates — equivalent to the prior being forgotten in \(N\to\infty\).

title: Machine Learning Basics — Part I
text:
8.2 Conclusion at a Glance

The Bias-variance tradeoff is a central concept in understanding generalization.
Inductive bias (especially Occam’s razor) is a common tool for preventing overfitting.
VC dimension is a quantitative measure of classifier capacity and explains the relationship between data volume and model complexity as a generalization boundary.
No Free Lunch: There is no universally best algorithm — design for the task.
Hyperparameters must be tuned (via cross-validation, etc.).
MLE is a widely used estimation tool, and MAP is a generalization more widely used in practice that provides better estimates with the help of priors.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
To understand deep learning, three mathematical foundations are essential.

Probability Theory: A language for dealing with the uncertainty of data and models
Information Theory: A tool for quantifying differences between probability distributions
Numerical Optimization: A mechanism for learning model parameters

A core challenge called overfitting lies upon these three pillars, and overcoming it is the central task of deep learning research.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
To understand deep learning, three mathematical foundations are essential.

Probability Theory: A language for dealing with the uncertainty of data and models
Information Theory: A tool for quantifying differences between probability distributions
Numerical Optimization: A mechanism for learning model parameters

A core challenge called overfitting lies upon these three pillars, and overcoming it is the central task of deep learning research.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.1 Random Variable
There are two levels to understanding random variables.
Simple Definition: A variable that can take various values randomly. For example, when rolling a die, the result \(X\) takes one of \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\).
Strict Definition: A random variable is a mapping that maps elements of a sample space \(\Omega\) to a measurable space, usually real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\).
\[\text{Real world event} \xrightarrow{\text{Random variable}} \text{Probability (a measurable value)}\]






TipAnalogy in Wireless Communication



The Channel State Information (CSI) \(\mathbf{h}\), which represents the state of the channel, is the random variable. It maps a “real-world event”—the channel environment—to a “measurable value”—a complex vector.


Random variables are classified as discrete or continuous, and the functions describing each are different.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
section: 1.2 Probability Distribution of Discrete Random Variables — PMF
text:
1.2 Probability Distribution of Discrete Random Variables — PMF
A discrete random variable is described by a Probability Mass Function (PMF) \(P(x)\). A representative example is the Bernoulli distribution (resulting in \(\{0, 1\}\) outcomes such as coin tosses).
PMF must satisfy three axioms.

The domain of \(P(\cdot)\) must be the set of all possible states of \(x\).
\(\forall x \in \mathbf{x},\; 0 \le P(x) \le 1\)
\(\sum_{x \in \mathbf{x}} P(x) = 1\) (Normalization condition)

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
section: 1.3 Probability Distribution of Continuous Random Variables — PDF
text:
1.3 Probability Distribution of Continuous Random Variables — PDF
Continuous random variables are described by a Probability Density Function (PDF) \(p(x)\). The Gaussian (normal) distribution is typical, \(\mu\) represents the mean, and \(\sigma^2\) represents the variance.
Three axioms of continuous rv:

The domain of \(p(\cdot)\) must be the set of all possible states of \(x\).
\(\forall x \in \mathbf{x},\; 0 \le p(x)\) — However, it does not have to be \(p(x) \le 1\)!
\(\int p(x)\,dx = 1\)







ImportantKey Differences Between PMF and PDF



In PMF, it is \(P(x) \le 1\), but in PDF, \(p(x)\) can be greater than 1. For example, in the case of a Gaussian of \(\sigma^2 = 0.2\), it is \(p(0) \approx 0.89\), and as the variance becomes smaller, the peak exceeds 1. This is because in PDF, the probability is defined not by the value of \(p(x)\) itself, but by the integral \(\int_a^b p(x)\,dx\).


The concept of measure zero is also important. In a continuous distribution, the probability of a specific point is \(P(\mathbf{x} = x) = 0\). Nevertheless, integrating the entire distribution yields 1. This is the property of “zero almost everywhere, but integrating equals 1” as described in measure theory.






TipAnalogy in Wireless Communication



The PDF of the AWGN channel noise \(n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) is the Gaussian PDF. As the variance \(\sigma^2\) decreases (as the SNR increases), the PDF becomes sharper and the peaks become higher, but the integral remains 1.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.4 Joint Probability Distribution
is the probability that two random variables \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) simultaneously take a specific value.
\[P(\mathbf{x} = x, \mathbf{y} = y)\]
It is also simply written as \(P(x, y)\). In joint probability, the order of variables does not matter. It is \(P(A, B, C) = P(B, A, C) = P(C, A, B)\). The intuition regarding “probability of simultaneous occurrence” is accurate.






TipAnalogy in Wireless Communication



The combined distribution of the transmitted signal \(x\) and the received signal \(y\) describes the entire channel model.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.5 Marginal Probability
It is the process of “summing out” one variable from a joint distribution to obtain the distribution of only the remaining variables.

Discrete: \(P(\mathbf{x} = x) = \displaystyle\sum_{y} P(\mathbf{x} = x, \mathbf{y} = y)\)
Consecutive: \(p(x) = \displaystyle\int p(x, y)\,dy\)

This process is called marginalization.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.6 Conditional Probability
\[P(\mathbf{y} = y \mid \mathbf{x} = x) = \frac{P(\mathbf{y} = y, \mathbf{x} = x)}{P(\mathbf{x} = x)}\]
Here, \(\mathbf{x}\) is the conditioning variable, and \(\mathbf{y}\) is the conditioned variable.






NoteP(y=y|x=x) is a function of some variable?



Strictly speaking, \(P(\mathbf{y} = y \mid \mathbf{x} = x)\) is a function of both \(x\)Z and \(y\)Z. However, to highlight the essential characteristics of conditional probability, it is often emphasized as a “function of \(x\).” This is because, while the general \(P(\mathbf{y} = y)\) is a function of \(y\) alone, the novel aspect is that when a condition is applied, the entire distribution for \(y\) changes whenever \(x\)Z changes. It is obvious that \(y\) is a variable, so it is not emphasized separately.
Specifically, it is divided as follows.

If we fix \(y\) and vary \(x\) → likelihood function \(\mathcal{L}(x) = P(\mathbf{y}=y_0 \mid \mathbf{x}=x)\): “With the observation \(y_0\) fixed, which \(x\) best explains this observation?”
If we fix \(x\) and vary \(y\) → Conditional Distribution \(P(\mathbf{y}=y \mid \mathbf{x}=x_0)\): “What is the shape of the probability distribution of \(y\) under the condition \(x_0\)?”

To use a wireless communication analogy, in the channel model \(p(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(y - hx)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\), fixing the transmitted signal \(x\) results in a Gaussian distribution for the received signal \(y\), while fixing the received signal \(y\) results in a likelihood representing the probability of observing \(y\) when a specific \(x\) is transmitted. The interpretation of the same function differs depending on which variable is viewed.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.7 Conditional Probability Chain Rule

1.7.1 Basic form: 2 variables
From the definition of conditional probability:
\[P(\mathbf{y} = y \mid \mathbf{x} = x) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x} = x, \mathbf{y} = y)}{P(\mathbf{x} = x)}\]
Multiplying both sides by \(P(\mathbf{x} = x)\):
\[P(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}) \cdot P(\mathbf{x})\]
This is the most basic form of the chain rule. “joint = conditional × marginal”.


1.7.2 Expansion to 3 variables
Let’s decompose \(P(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})\). Treat \((\mathbf{a})\) and \((\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})\) as a single unit and apply the 2-unit rule:
\[P(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) = P(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) \cdot P(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})\]
Now apply the 2-character rule again to \(P(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})\):
\[P(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) = P(\mathbf{b} \mid \mathbf{c}) \cdot P(\mathbf{c})\]
Combine:
\[\boxed{P(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) = P(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) \cdot P(\mathbf{b} \mid \mathbf{c}) \cdot P(\mathbf{c})}\]


1.7.3 \(n\) Generalization of variables
If you repeat the same “peeling”:
\[P(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) = P(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}) \prod_{i=2}^{n} P(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(i-1)})\]
This is called a chain rule or product rule.






NoteDerivation process of the generalized formula



If you first remove ZZZPH0006279ZZZ \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\) from \(P(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)})\):
\[= P(\mathbf{x}^{(1)} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) \cdot P(\mathbf{x}^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)})\]
If you remove \(\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\) from \(P(\mathbf{x}^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)})\):
\[= P(\mathbf{x}^{(1)} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) \cdot P(\mathbf{x}^{(2)} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(3)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}) \cdot P(\mathbf{x}^{(3)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)})\]
Repeating this until only \(P(\mathbf{x}^{(n)})\) remains yields the final formula. Regardless of the direction from which the decomposition begins (the method above leaves \(\mathbf{x}^{(n)}\) as the last marginal, while the formula form places \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\) as the first marginal), the result is the same.








NoteIntuitive interpretation



You can think of “Probability of \(\mathbf{a}\), \(\mathbf{b}\), \(\mathbf{c}\) occurring simultaneously” as sequential decision:

First, \(\mathbf{c}\) occurs → then, with \(\mathbf{c}\) given, \(\mathbf{b}\) occurs → finally, with all \(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}\) given, \(\mathbf{a}\) occurs.

The order of joint probabilities does not matter, but the form of the equation changes depending on the order of condition application when decomposing using the chain rule. This choice becomes an important design decision in modeling.








TipDeep Learning Connection: Autoregressive Model



Autoregressive models like GPT utilize this very chain rule when generating sequences.
\[P(w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n) = P(w_1) P(w_2|w_1) P(w_3|w_1, w_2) \cdots\]
Sequentially generating tokens is a direct application of the chain rule.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
section: 1.8 Independence and Conditional Independence (Independence & Conditional Independence)
text:
1.8 Independence and Conditional Independence (Independence & Conditional Independence)

1.8.1 Independence
If \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) are independent, the joint distribution is decomposed into the product of the marginal distributions:
\[p(\mathbf{x} = x, \mathbf{y} = y) = p(\mathbf{x} = x)p(\mathbf{y} = y)\]


1.8.2 Conditional Independence
Given \(\mathbf{z}\), if \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) are conditionally independent:
\[p(\mathbf{x} = x, \mathbf{y} = y \mid \mathbf{z} = z) = p(\mathbf{x} = x \mid \mathbf{z} = z)p(\mathbf{y} = y \mid \mathbf{z} = z)\]






WarningIndependence and conditional independence do not imply each other



Two independent variables can become conditionally dependent if a common outcome is observed (explaining away), and conversely, two dependent variables can become conditionally independent if a certain variable is given.




1.8.3 Explaining Away Phenomenon
Explaining away is a classic example of conditional dependency. The key point is: Two independent variables become conditionally dependent if a common outcome is observed.
Let’s take an example from wireless communication. Suppose the received signal suddenly weakens (\(Y = \text{weak}\)). There are two possible causes:


Transmitter failure


Shadowing by buildings


Since A and B are physically independent events, it is \(P(A, B) = P(A)P(B)\).
However, the situation changes after observing \(Y = \text{weak}\). If someone confirms that “it was due to building shadowing” (\(B = \text{true}\)), one infers, “Then the probability of a transmitter failure is low.” In other words:
\[P(A \mid Y, B = \text{true}) < P(A \mid Y)\]
If one cause explains away the result, the probability of the other cause decreases. In a formula:
\[P(A, B \mid Y) \neq P(A \mid Y) P(B \mid Y)\]
\(A\) and \(B\) were originally independent, but became conditionally dependent when the common result \(Y\) was observed.
There is also an example in the opposite direction. The throughput of two users at the same base station is dependent (sharing the same base station load), but they can be conditionally independent given the base station load \(Z\).

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.9 Expectation
is an operator representing the “most likely occurring value” of a random variable.

Discrete: \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim P}[f(x)] = \displaystyle\sum_x P(x)f(x)\)
Consecutive: \(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p}[f(x)] = \displaystyle\int p(x)f(x)\,dx\)

As a key property, expectation is a linear operator:
\[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}[\alpha f(x) + \beta g(x)] = \alpha \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}[f(x)] + \beta \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}[g(x)]\]

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.10 Dirac Delta Function
It is a “function” (strictly speaking, a distribution) that is 0 everywhere except the origin, but becomes 1 when integrated.

1.10.1 The reason the integral is 1
Strictly speaking, the Dirac delta is not an ordinary function. A function that is “zero everywhere and integrates to 1” does not exist in the classical sense. The Dirac delta is a generalized function, defined as an operator acting on other functions:
\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x) f(x)\,dx = f(0)\]
This is the definition of Dirac delta. If you substitute \(f(x) = 1\), it becomes \(\int \delta(x)\,dx = 1\). The fact that the integral is 1 is not a proof, but derived from the definition.






NoteIntuitive Understanding: Dirac delta as an extreme process



Let’s imagine a Gaussian where the variance gradually decreases:
\[\delta(x) = \lim_{\sigma \to 0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
No matter how small \(\sigma\) becomes, the integral of the Gaussian is always 1. Although the peaks become infinitely high and the width becomes infinitely narrow, the area (integral) is always conserved. This limit is the Dirac delta.




1.10.2 Empirical Distribution
Dirac delta is used when constructing the empirical distribution of continuous random variables:
\[\hat{p}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \delta(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^{(i)})\]
This is a method of representing continuous rv discretely by assigning equal weights \(1/m\) to \(m\) observations. This concept of empirical distribution serves as the starting point for Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE).

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.11 Mixture of Distributions
\[P(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i P(\mathbf{c} = i) P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c} = i)\]
Here, \(P(\mathbf{c})\) represents the multinoulli distribution (which component to select), and \(\mathbf{c}\) is the latent variable. The most representative mixture distribution is the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), where each component \(P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c} = i)\) is Gaussian.
GMM is called the universal approximator of densities. By using a sufficient number of Gaussian components, any continuous density can be approximated with desired precision.

1.11.1 Why is \(c\) called a “latent variable”?
The only one actually observed is \(\mathbf{x}\). \(\mathbf{c}\) is a variable indicating “which component this data point came from,” but it cannot be directly observed. “Latent” is Latin for “hidden” and refers to a variable that is unobservable but necessary to explain the data generation process.






TipAnalogy in Wireless Communication



Let’s assume we have Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) data collected from various base stations in a city. Looking at the overall distribution, it is a complex shape with multiple peaks. In fact, each peak originates from a measurement point close to a different base station, but the data does not record “which base station the data came from.” This “which base station” is precisely the latent variable \(\mathbf{c}\).

\(P(\mathbf{c} = i)\): Probability of measuring near the \(i\)th base station
\(P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c} = i)\): RSSI distribution near the \(i\)-th base station





1.11.2 Importance in Deep Learning
The idea of a mixture of distributions is the foundation of core generative models in deep learning.
VAE(Variational Autoencoder): \(\mathbf{c}\) is extended to a continuous latent vector \(\mathbf{z}\) instead of a discrete one.
\[P(\mathbf{x}) = \int P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{z}) P(\mathbf{z})\,d\mathbf{z}\]
It is a continuous mixture of infinitely many components.
GAN: Passing random noise \(\mathbf{z}\) through a generator to produce \(\mathbf{x} = G(\mathbf{z})\) is a generalization of mixture, which generates a complex data distribution from a latent variable \(\mathbf{z}\).
Softmax Output: The classification model outputting \(P(\mathbf{c} = i \mid \mathbf{x})\) is solving the inverse problem of the mixture using Bayes’ rule. “From which component is it most likely that this data \(\mathbf{x}\) to have come?”

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
1.12 Bayes’ Rule
\[P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{x})P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})}{P(\mathbf{y})}\]
is a formula that swaps the roles of \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) in conditional probability. The names of each term are as follows.

Names and Meanings of Each Clause in Bayes’ Rule







Item
Name
Meaning




\(P(\mathbf{x})\)
Prior (Prior Probability)
Belief in \(\mathbf{x}\) prior to observation


\(P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})\)
Likelihood
Probability of observing \(\mathbf{y}\) under \(\mathbf{x}\)


\(P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})\)
Posterior (Posterior Probability)
Updated belief in \(\mathbf{x}\) after observation


\(P(\mathbf{y})\)
Evidence
Total probability of observation \(\mathbf{y}\) (normalization constant)









TipAnalogy in Wireless Communication



The MAP(Maximum a Posteriori) detector uses exactly this Bayes’ rule. After observing the received signal \(\mathbf{y}\), it maximizes the posterior probability of the transmitted signal \(\mathbf{x}\):
\[\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{x}} P(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{y})\]

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
2.1 Origins of Information Theory
Information theory was born in 1948 when Shannon studied the problem of transmitting discrete alphabet messages over a noisy channel.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
2.2 Self-Information
\[I(x) = -\log P(x)\]
The unit is nat (when using natural logarithm).

2.2.1 Intuitive Understanding: “Degree of Surprise (Surprise)”
If you think of your amount of self-information as the degree of surprise, your intuition becomes clearer.
The probability that the sun will rise tomorrow is almost 1. What is your reaction if someone says, “They say the sun will rise tomorrow!”? “So what?” — Not surprising at all, and there is no new information. Since \(P \approx 1\), it is \(I = -\log(1) = 0\).
On the other hand, if someone says, “They say it’s going to snow 3 meters in Seoul tomorrow!”, you are extremely surprised, and your behavior changes drastically after hearing this information (canceling appointments, preparing, etc.). Since \(P \approx 0\), it is \(I = -\log(\epsilon) \to \infty\).






ImportantKey Insights into Information Theory



Value of Information = Amount of change in belief before and after hearing it. There is no information when hearing about a certain event because belief does not change, and there is a large amount of information when hearing about the outcome of an uncertain event because belief changes significantly.




2.2.2 Why \(\log\) of all things?
Reason 1: Additive nature of independent events. The information of independent events must be additive. If they are independent, it is \(P(x_1, x_2) = P(x_1)P(x_2)\), and the function that converts this product into a sum is \(\log\):
\[-\log(P(x_1)P(x_2)) = -\log P(x_1) - \log P(x_2) = I(x_1) + I(x_2)\]
Reason 2: Origin in communication. To transmit one of \(n\) messages of equal probability, \(\log_2 n\) bits are required. Since the probability of each message is \(1/n\), it is \(-\log_2(1/n) = \log_2 n\).

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
2.3 Shannon Entropy (Shannon Entropy)
The expected value of self-information is Shannon entropy:
\[H(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim P}[I(x)] = -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim P}[\log P(x)]\]
Entropy measures the amount of uncertainty contained in a probability distribution.
If \(\mathbf{x}\) is a continuous random variable, it is called differential entropy. It should be noted that, unlike discrete entropy, continuous entropy can be negative.

2.3.1 The reason why entropy is maximum in the Bernoulli variable when \(p = 0.5\)






WarningCaution against confusion between self-information and entropy



Self-information \(I(x) = -\log P(x)\) is the information amount of a specific event one, and as \(P(x)\) increases, it monotonically decreases. This is correct.
However, entropy is the expected value of self-information:
\[H = -\sum_x P(x) \log P(x)\]
This is the weighted average of \(I(x)\) and \(P(x)\), so it is not monotonically decreasing.


Since Bernoulli(\(p\)) variable \(\mathbf{x} \in \{0, 1\}\):
\[H = -p \log p - (1-p) \log(1-p)\]
The key point is that there are two terms for . If you increase \(p\), the size of \(\log p\) in the first term decreases, but the weight \(p\) increases; simultaneously, in the second term, \((1-p)\) decreases, but the size of \(\log(1-p)\) increases. It is a structure where these two effects compete.
Specifically calculated:

Entropy values according to the probability of Bernoulli variables


\(p\)
\(H\)




0.1
\(\approx 0.33\)


0.5
\(\approx 0.69\) (max)


0.9
\(\approx 0.33\)



The reason it reaches a maximum at \(p = 0.5\) is that at this point, both events are in a “moderately surprising” state. If it is \(p = 0.99\), \(x = 1\) is almost certain (no surprise), and \(x = 0\) is very surprising but rarely occurs, so the average surprise is small. Average surprise is maximized when both events are equally uncertain.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
2.4 KL Divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence)
\[D_{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_x p(x)(\log p(x) - \log q(x))\]
It is a “kind of distance” between two probability distributions \(p\) and \(q\), but it is not a true distance metric.

2.4.1 The 4 Axioms of Metrics and KL Divergence
For the distance function (metric) ZZZPH0006379ZZZ to be \(d(x, y)\), four axioms must be satisfied:

KL Divergence metric axiom satisfaction







Axiom
Formula
Whether KL divergence is satisfied




Nasal
\(d(x, y) \ge 0\)
Satisfied


Identity of the unidentifiable
\(d(x, y) = 0 \leftrightarrow x = y\)
Satisfaction


Symmetry
\(d(x, y) = d(y, x)\)
Dissatisfaction


Triangle Inequality
\(d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z)\)
Dissatisfied









ImportantKL Divergence does not satisfy the triangle inequality either.



Not only symmetry but also the triangle inequality is broken. As a specific counterexample, consider the three Bernoulli distributions \(p = (0.1, 0.9)\), \(q = (0.5, 0.5)\), and \(r = (0.9, 0.1)\):
\[D_{KL}(p \| r) \approx 1.76 > D_{KL}(p \| q) + D_{KL}(q \| r) \approx 0.51 + 0.51 = 1.02\]
Therefore, since KL divergence satisfies only 2 of the 4 metric axioms, it is called “divergence” and not “distance”. On the other hand, the square root of the Jensen-Shannon divergence \(\sqrt{D_{JS}}\) becomes a true metric.


KL divergence has directionality, so it is read as “from \(p\) to \(q\)”. There are also symmetric variations:

Symmetric KL divergence: \(D_{KL}(p, q) + D_{KL}(q, p)\)
Jensen-Shannon divergence: \(D_{JS}(p, q) = \frac{D_{KL}(p \| m) + D_{KL}(q \| m)}{2}\), where \(m = \frac{p+q}{2}\)

JS divergence appears in the original objective function of GAN (Generative Adversarial Network).


2.4.2 Asymmetry of KL Divergence — Intuitive Understanding
The key to understanding asymmetry is which distribution acts as the “weight” in the KL divergence formula.
\[D_{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_x p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\]
Here, since \(p(x)\) is the weight of the sum, the difference where \(p(x)\) is large is dominant.




2.4.2.1 Forward KL: \(q^* = \arg\min_q D_{KL}(p \| q)\)
Let \(p\) be a bimodal (two peaks), and let \(q\) be constrained to a single Gaussian.
Since the weight of is \(p(x)\), if \(q(x) \approx 0\) occurs where \(p(x) > 0\), it becomes \(\log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} \to +\infty\), causing KL to explode. Therefore, \(q\) must cover all places where \(p\) is positive. To cover both peaks, \(q\) must spread widely.
Result: Wide and flat \(q^*\) → “mean-seeking” or “zero-avoiding” behavior.


2.4.2.2 Reverse KL: \(q^* = \arg\min_q D_{KL}(q \| p)\)
From \(D_{KL}(q \| p) = \sum_x q(x) \log \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\), the weight is now \(q(x)\). At \(q(x) > 0\), if it becomes \(p(x) \approx 0\), KL explodes.
Therefore, \(q\) should not have mass placed where \(p\)Z is 0. Since \(p \approx 0\) is in the valley between the two peaks, the safest strategy is to concentrate on only one peak.
Result: Narrow and pointed \(q^*\) → “mode-seeking” or “zero-forcing” behavior.






TipUnderstanding Forward KL vs Reverse KL via Wireless Communication Analogy



Let’s consider a situation where there are signals in two frequency bands.

Approximation as Forward KL(\(p \| q\)): “The band containing the signal must never be missed” → Design a broadband filter that covers both bands. The cost of missing is high.
Approximation by Reverse KL(\(q \| p\)): “Filters should not be placed in bands containing only noise” → Design a narrow-band filter that focuses on only one band. The cost of false alarms is high.









NoteMeaning in Deep Learning




Training a model with MLE (Maximum Likelihood Estimation) is equivalent to minimizing the forward KL \(D_{KL}(\hat{p}_{\text{data}} \| p_{\text{model}})\) → the model attempts to cover all modes of the data.
In Variational Inference, optimizing the ELBO minimizes the reverse KL \(D_{KL}(q \| p)\) → the approximate distribution is concentrated in one mode of the posterior.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
3.1 Basic Concepts of Gradient-based Optimization
Optimization is the process of minimizing or maximizing a function.

The function to be minimized or maximized is called the objective function or criterion.
When minimizing, it is called the cost function, loss function, and error function.
The optimal solution is denoted as \(\hat{x} = x^* = \arg\min_x f(x)\). \(\hat{\ }\)(hat) represents the estimated value, and \(*\)(star) represents the optimal value.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
3.2 Gradient Descent
The key principle is that moving in the opposite direction of the gradient reduces the function value:
\[x_{t+1} = x_t - \epsilon \nabla_x f(x_t)\]
Here, \(\epsilon\) is the learning rate.
In the example of \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^2\):

Moving from \(x < 0\) to \(f'(x) < 0\) → to the right decreases \(f\)
If you move from \(x > 0\) to \(f'(x) > 0\) → left, \(f\) decreases
Gradient descent stops at the point \(f'(x) = 0\) (here, \(x = 0\)) → global minimum

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
3.3 Convex Optimization
If the function is convex, then local minimum = global minimum, so gradient descent can definitely find the global optimal solution.






WarningThe loss landscape of deep learning is non-convex.



In deep learning, gradient descent cannot guarantee a global minimum and can get stuck in local minimums or saddle points. Nevertheless, the reason SGD actually works well is due to its unique structure in high-dimensional spaces (most critical points are saddle points), implicit regularization, etc.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
3.4 Constrained Optimization
General form of a constrained optimization problem:
\[\min f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad g_i(\mathbf{x}) = c_i \;\text{(등식)},\quad h_j(\mathbf{x}) \ge d_j \;\text{(부등식)}\]
It is much more difficult than unconstrained optimization.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
section: 3.5 Lagrangian — Converting equation constraints into unconstrained problems
text:
3.5 Lagrangian — Converting equation constraints into unconstrained problems

3.5.1 Basic Idea
Original constraint problem:
\[\text{maximize } f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{subject to } g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\]
Transform this into a new unconstrained objective function (Lagrangian):
\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda g(\mathbf{x})\]
Here, \(\lambda\) is the Lagrange multiplier.






NoteReason for expanding to 2D



In optimization problems, when \(\mathbf{x}\) is a vector, there are cases where the components are explicitly expanded into \(\mathbf{x} = (x, y)\) for visualization. In this case, it is denoted as \(\mathcal{L}(x, y, \lambda) = f(x, y) - \lambda g(x, y)\), but this does not mean that a new variable \(y\) has been added; rather, it is explicitly expanding the components of the vector \(\mathbf{x}\). This is because it must be written in 2D to draw contour lines.




3.5.2 Why can it only be used for equation constraints?
The equation constraint \(g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\) defines a surface in space. The task is to move along this surface and find the point where \(f\) no longer increases.
Geometric intuition: At the optimal point, the contour line of the objective function is tangent to the constraint curve, i.e., \(\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g\).
This means that “the change in \(f\) is zero in all directions that can move on the surface.” That is, \(\nabla f\) must be perpendicular to the constraint plane, and since the vector perpendicular to the constraint plane is \(\nabla g\), \(\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g\) holds.
The inequality constraint \(h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0\) defines a region rather than a surface. The optimal point may be inside the region (inactive constraint) or on the boundary (active constraint). To handle these two cases integrally, the KKT condition is required.


3.5.3 Why the Lagrangian guarantees optimality
The stationary point condition of Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda g(\mathbf{x})\) is:
\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \nabla f = \lambda \nabla g\] \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\]
The second condition automatically satisfies the constraint. If you add \(\lambda\) as a variable and find the stationary point of \(\mathcal{L}\), the constraint is automatically embedded.






NotePhysical meaning of \(\lambda\): Shadow Price



\(\lambda\) is the shadow price. If the constraint is slightly relaxed from \(g(\mathbf{x}) = 0\) to \(g(\mathbf{x}) = \epsilon\), the value of the optimal objective function changes by approximately \(\lambda \epsilon\).
In wireless communication, the Lagrange multiplier of power constraints represents “a capacity increase of 1 unit of additional power,” and the water level \(\frac{1}{\lambda}\) in waterfilling is derived from this Lagrange multiplier.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
3.6 KKT conditions — including inequality constraints
Including inequality constraints, the generalized Lagrangian is:
\[L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = f(\mathbf{x}) + \boldsymbol{\mu}^\top \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}) + \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{x})\]
\(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) are called KKT multipliers (named after Karush, Kuhn, and Tucker).
In KKT, the condition \(\mu_i g_i(\mathbf{x}) = 0\) (complementary slackness) is added, and it automatically handles “\(\mu > 0\) if the constraint is active, and \(\mu = 0\) if it is inactive”.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
3.7 Example: Linear Least Squares

3.7.1 Non-constrained problem
Objective function:
\[f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|_2^2\]
Gradient:
\[\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A}^\top(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b}\]
Gradient descent algorithm:

Set step size \(\epsilon\) and tolerance \(\delta\)
Repeat while \(\|\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b}\|_2 > \delta\):

\(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} - \epsilon(\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b})\)




3.7.2 Added constraint: \(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x} \le 1\)
Lagrangian:
\[L(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}\|_2^2 + \lambda(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{x} - 1)\]
If we differentiate with \(\mathbf{x}\) and set it to 0:
\[\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b} + 2\lambda\mathbf{x} = 0\]
\[\boxed{\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A} + 2\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{b}}\]






TipConnection with Wireless Communication: MMSE Estimator and Ridge Regression



The form of this result has exactly the same structure as a wireless communication MMSE estimator:
\[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\text{MMSE}} = (\mathbf{H}^H\mathbf{H} + \sigma^2\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^H\mathbf{y}\]
\(\lambda\) acts as regularization and corresponds to \(\sigma^2\) (noise power). In other words, constraint optimization ↔︎ regularization is equivalent through the Lagrangian. Adjusting the strength of the constraint to \(\lambda\) is equivalent to adjusting the strength of regularization.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
4.1 Definition of Overfitting
data is generated from the distribution \(D(X, Y)\), and when finding the hypothesis \(h\) within the hypothesis space \(\mathcal{H}\), the hypothesis \(h\) is said to be overfitted if there exists another hypothesis \(h' \in \mathcal{H}\):
\[\text{error}_{\text{train}}(h) < \text{error}_{\text{train}}(h')\]
but
\[\text{error}_{\text{true}}(h) > \text{error}_{\text{true}}(h')\]
It refers to the state where . In other words, it is a state where the training error is lower but the actual error is higher.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
text:
4.2 Neural Network and Lipschitz Continuity
Neural networks are susceptible to overfitting. This is because small changes in input can cause dramatic changes in output.
Lipschitz continuity is a tool for controlling this:
\[\forall \mathbf{x}, \forall \mathbf{y},\; |f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})| \le \mathcal{L}\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|_2\]
The smaller the Lipschitz constant \(\mathcal{L}\), the smoother the function’s changes relative to input changes, and therefore, the less overfitting occurs. In practice, regularization techniques such as spectral normalization and gradient penalty stabilize the model by limiting the Lipschitz constant. WGAN (Wasserstein GAN) is a representative model that utilizes the Lipschitz constraint.

title: Foundation of Deep Learning
section: 4.3 Why use Neural Networks despite this?
text:
4.3 Why use Neural Networks despite this?
The purpose of ML is generalization, so why use neural networks that are susceptible to overfitting? This is a core question, and the answer is found through the double descent phenomenon, along with various techniques such as regularization, dropout, batch normalization, early stopping, and data augmentation.

NoteUser Guide




This is a collection of predicted questions reflecting actual exam trends (statistical calculations, concept accuracy, understanding of deep learning structures).
Click the collapsed box below each question to view the answers and explanations.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 1
Assume that a call center receives an average of 10 calls per hour. When call arrivals follow a Poisson process, which is the correct method to calculate the probability that the next call will arrive after 5 minutes?

Calculate the Poisson distribution \(P(X=0)\) in time units.
Calculates the exponential distribution \(P(T > 5/60)\), which is equal to \(e^{-10 \cdot 5/60}\).
Approximate to the binomial distribution \(B(10, 5/60)\)
Calculate the \(z\)-value by approximating with a normal distribution







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2
In a Poisson process, the waiting time between events follows an exponential distribution of the parameter \(\lambda\). If there are 10 cases per hour, it is \(\lambda = 10\) (in hours), and since 5 minutes = \(1/12\) hours,
\[P(T > 1/12) = e^{-10/12} \approx 0.4346\]
For reference, the same applies when approaching it as “the probability of zero calls in 5 minutes”: the average over 5 minutes is \(10/12\), so \(P(N=0) = e^{-10/12}\). The fact that both perspectives yield the same value is the essence of the Poisson–exponential relationship.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 2
Factory A follows a Poisson distribution with a mean of 2 for the number of defective items per hour, and Factory B follows a binomial distribution with a production rate of 10 items per hour and a defect rate of 0.3 for each product. Assuming the two factories are independent, what is the value closest to the probability that a total of 5 defects occur in both factories in one hour?

0.124
0.155
0.194
0.231







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 3 (approx. 0.194)
Since it is the sum of two independent random variables, it is calculated using convolution.
\[P(A+B=5) = \sum_{k=0}^{5} P(A=k) \, P(B=5-k)\]
from scipy import stats
p = sum(stats.poisson.pmf(k, 2) * stats.binom.pmf(5-k, 10, 0.3)
        for k in range(6))
# 0.1944
For each \(k\), multiplying the probabilities of cases (\(k\) in Poisson and \(5-k\) in binomial) and adding them all up gives approximately 0.1944.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 3
In the exponential distribution, when \(\lambda = 1\), which all are correct?

When \(x \to \infty\), it converges to \(f(x) \to 0\).
The average is 1.
The variance is \(1/2\).
\(\int_0^1 e^{-x}\,dx = 1\) is







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1, 2

The mean of the exponential distribution is \(1/\lambda = 1\), and the variance is \(1/\lambda^2 = 1\). Therefore, 3 is incorrect.
The probability density function \(f(x) = e^{-x}\) converges to 0 at \(x \to \infty\) (1 correct).
The interval where the total integral is 1 is \([0, \infty)\). Since the integral for the interval \([0, 1]\) is \(1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632\), 4 is incorrect. Beware of the trap of subtly changing the integration interval.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 4
Two people, A and B, each consecutively draw one toy without replacement from a box containing 3 toys worth 1,000 won, 4 toys worth 500 won, and 3 toys worth 100 won. Let the prices of the toys each person drew be \(X\) and \(Y\). What is \(E[X + Y]\)?

1030
1040
1050
1060







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 4 (1060)
The linearity of the expectation \(E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y]\) holds regardless of independence. Even with sampling without replacement, due to symmetry, the marginal distribution of \(Y\) is identical to that of \(X\).

Total Price Sum: \(1000 \times 3 + 500 \times 4 + 100 \times 3 = 5300\)
Expected value per draw: \(5300 / 10 = 530\)
\(E[X+Y] = 530 \times 2 = 1060\)

This is a problem type that induces the misconception that “since it is sampling without replacement, isn’t linearity impossible because it is dependent?”

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 5
When the joint probability density function \(f(x, y) = c\) is defined in the region \(0 < x < 1,\; 0 < y < 1 - x\), what is \(P(X < Y)\)?

1
1/2
1/4
1/8







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2 (1/2)
Since the support region is a triangle with a base and height of 1, the area is \(= 1/2\), therefore \(c = 2\).
The region \(X < Y\) is the part above the line \(y = x\)Z and below \(y < 1 - x\). Since the two lines meet at \((1/2, 1/2)\),
\[P(X<Y) = 2 \int_0^{1/2} \big[(1-x) - x\big]\,dx = 2\left[x - x^2\right]_0^{1/2} = 2 \times \tfrac{1}{4} = \tfrac{1}{2}\]
It can also be solved using symmetry logic: since the support region is symmetric to the commutative \(x \leftrightarrow y\) and \(P(X=Y)=0\), \(P(X<Y) = 1/2\).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 6
When the joint probabilities of two random variables \(A\) and \(B\) are as follows, which of the following is a correct explanation for the calculation of mutual information \(I(A;B)\)?




\(b_1\)
\(b_2\)




\(a_1\)
1/4
1/2


\(a_2\)
1/4
0




Calculate as \(I(A;B) = \sum_{a,b} p(a,b) \log \dfrac{p(a,b)}{p(a)p(b)}\), and exclude cells with a joint probability of 0 from the sum.
Calculate as \(I(A;B) = \sum_{a,b} p(a)p(b) \log p(a,b)\)
It can be calculated using only marginal probabilities
If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, then it is \(I(A;B) = 1\).







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
Marginal Probabilities: \(p(a_1) = 3/4\), \(p(a_2) = 1/4\), \(p(b_1) = p(b_2) = 1/2\).
\[I(A;B) = \tfrac{1}{4}\log_2\tfrac{1/4}{3/8} + \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2\tfrac{1/2}{3/8} + \tfrac{1}{4}\log_2\tfrac{1/4}{1/8} \approx 0.3113 \text{ bits}\]
The term \(p(a,b) = 0\) is treated as \(0 \log 0 = 0\) (excluded from the sum). If independent, it is \(p(a,b) = p(a)p(b)\), so all log terms become 0, resulting in \(I(A;B) = 0\) (4 is incorrect).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 7
Which of the following is not a correct description of the probability vector \(X = (X_1, X_2)\) that follows a bivariate normal distribution?

In a probability density function, the set of points with the same function value forms an ellipse.
The marginal distribution of \(X_2\) follows a normal distribution.
Conditional distribution \(X_1 \mid X_2\) follows a normal distribution.
Even if the covariance between \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) is 0, they may not be independent.







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 4
In general, “covariance 0 ≠ independence,” but under the condition that the joint distribution is a bivariate normal distribution, if the covariance is 0, they are independent. Since the premise of this problem is “bivariate normal distribution,” 4 is an incorrect explanation.
1~3 are standard properties of the multivariate normal distribution: contour lines are ellipses, and both marginal and conditional distributions are normal. (However, a reverse trap is often presented stating that just because “each marginal distribution is normal” does not mean the joint distribution is bivariate normal.)

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 8
A population of 100 follows a normal distribution. We want to calculate the probability that the value in this population is less than or equal to a specific value, denoted as scipy.stats.norm.cdf(x, loc, scale). What value should be entered into scale?

Population standard deviation \(\sigma\)
Standard Error \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\)
Variance \(\sigma^2\)
Sample size \(n\)







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1

Probability that an individual observation is less than or equal to a specific value → Use the population distribution as is → scale = 표준편차(σ)
Probability for the distribution of the sample mean → Use the sampling distribution of the sample mean → scale = 표준오차(σ/√n)

The key point is that scale changes depending on what distribution is being asked (individual values or sample means). If it is the CDF for the population itself, then the standard deviation is correct.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 9
Which of the following is not a correct description of the \(t\)-distribution?

Thicker tails than the standard normal distribution
As the degrees of freedom increase, it approximates the standard normal distribution.
For independent \(X \sim t(n_1)\) and \(Y \sim t(n_2)\), \(X + Y\) follows a \(t\)-distribution with degrees of freedom \(n_1 + n_2\).
Non-central \(t\)-The mean of a distribution may not be 0







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 3
Unlike the normal or chi-square distribution, the \(t\)-distribution does not satisfy additivity. The sum of two \(t\)-distribution random variables is not a \(t\)-distribution.

1, 2 are basic properties of the \(t\)-distribution.
4: The mean of the commonly encountered (central) \(t\)-distribution is 0 (degrees of freedom > 1), but the mean of the \(t\)-distribution with a non-central parameter is not 0. It appears in power calculations, etc.

Problem 10
Which is the most appropriate activation function to use when you need to output a probability value between 0 and 1, like the output of logistic regression?

ReLU
Leaky ReLU
tanh
Sigmoid







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 4

Sigmoid: \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\), Output range \((0, 1)\) → Probability interpretation possible
tanh: \((-1, 1)\) → Unsuitable as probability
ReLU / Leaky ReLU: \([0, \infty)\) or \((-\infty, \infty)\) → Unsuitable as a probability

To make the sum of class probabilities equal to 1 in multi-class classification, use softmax.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 11
A die was rolled 60 times, and the observations for each face were 9, 13, 12, 9, 6, and 11. When performing a test of goodness of fit to determine if the die is fair (expected frequencies of each face are 10), what are the test statistic and degrees of freedom?

\(\chi^2 = 3.2\), degrees of freedom 5
\(\chi^2 = 3.2\), degrees of freedom 6
\(\chi^2 = 5.4\), degrees of freedom 5
\(\chi^2 = 6.4\), degrees of freedom 6







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
\[\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i} = \frac{1 + 9 + 4 + 1 + 16 + 1}{10} = \frac{32}{10} = 3.2\]
Degrees of freedom are the number of categories \(- 1 = 6 - 1 = 5\).
from scipy import stats
stats.chisquare([9,13,12,9,6,11], [10]*6)
# statistic=3.2, pvalue=0.669
When directly calculating the p-value for , use 1 - chi2.cdf(3.2, df=5) or chi2.sf(3.2, df=5). Be careful, as the mistake of calculating only cdf and failing to subtract it from 1 is common.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 12
A coin was tossed 200 times, resulting in 115 heads and 85 tails. Which of the following is the correct test to verify if the coin is fair, and what is the correct result?

Test of independence, p ≈ 0.34
Goodness of fit test, \(\chi^2 = 4.5\), p ≈ 0.0339
Homogeneity test, \(\chi^2 = 2.25\), p ≈ 0.13
Goodness of fit test, \(\chi^2 = 9.0\), p ≈ 0.003







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2
Since this checks whether the observed frequency distribution matches the theoretical distribution (100 times each), it is a goodness-of-fit test.
\[\chi^2 = \frac{(115-100)^2}{100} + \frac{(85-100)^2}{100} = 2.25 + 2.25 = 4.5\]
At 1 degree of freedom \(p = P(\chi^2_1 > 4.5) \approx 0.0339\). At a significance level of 0.05, the null hypothesis (fair coin) is rejected.

Goodness of fit: Distribution of one variable vs. Theoretical distribution → scipy.stats.chisquare
Independence: Association between two categorical variables (cross-tabulation) → scipy.stats.chi2_contingency

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 13
To verify that the birthday distribution is 25% each for spring, summer, autumn, and winter, 96 for spring, 120 for summer, 104 for autumn, and 80 for winter were obtained from a sample of 400. What is the chi-square goodness-of-fit test statistic? (Rounded to the first decimal place)

6.4
7.5
8.3
9.2







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 3 (8.3)
The expected frequency is each \(400 \times 0.25 = 100\).
\[\chi^2 = \frac{16 + 400 + 16 + 400}{100} = \frac{832}{100} = 8.32 \approx 8.3\]
Since \(p \approx 0.040\) at 3 degrees of freedom, the “seasonally uniform distribution” hypothesis is rejected at a significance level of 0.05.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 14
Which analysis uses a contingency table?

Correlation analysis of two continuous variables
Test of independence of two categorical variables
Single sample mean test
Significance test of regression coefficients







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2
The contingency table is a table summarizing the frequencies of two categorical variables by combination and serves as the input for the chi-square test of independence (chi2_contingency). Expected frequencies are calculated as row sum × column sum / total sum, and the degrees of freedom are \((r-1)(c-1)\).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 15
The sleep duration of 3 students changed from 6, 6, and 8 hours before treatment to 8, 7, and 8 hours after treatment. What is the test statistic for the paired-sample \(t\)-test?

1.00
1.34
1.73
2.45







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 3 (√3 ≈ 1.73)
Difference \(d = (2, 1, 0)\), \(\bar{d} = 1\), \(s_d = 1\) (divided by sample standard deviation, \(n-1\)).
\[t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{1}{1/\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732\]
from scipy import stats
stats.ttest_rel([8,7,8], [6,6,8])   # statistic ≈ 1.7321
Since this is a comparison of the same subjects before and after, you must use the paired samples test (ttest_rel) instead of the independent samples test (ttest_ind).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 16
Before-and-after data for the same group is available. The p-value for the normality test of the difference was found to be 0.03 (significance level 0.05). Which test should be used in this case?

Paired-samples t-test
Independent Samples t-Test
Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Mann–Whitney U test







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 3
Judges in two steps:

Matching Status: Comparison of before and after of the same object → Paired design
Normality: p = 0.03 < 0.05 → Reject normality → Non-parametric test

Corresponding + Nonparametric = Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test(scipy.stats.wilcoxon).
Mann–Whitney U (= Wilcoxon rank-sum, mannwhitneyu) is unsuitable here because it is for two independent groups. The key pitfall is distinguishing between the two Wilcoxon tests with similar names (signed-rank vs. rank-sum).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 17
Which of the following is a correct description of the Mann–Whitney U test?

The assumption of independence between the two samples is necessary.
Normality assumption is required
Used in paired-sample design
Do not use ranking information







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
Mann–Whitney U is a nonparametric test that compares the distribution locations of two independent groups.

No normality assumption is needed (2 Incorrect) — Rather, it is an alternative when normality is broken.
Wilcoxon signed-rank is used for paired samples (3 incorrect).
Convert data to rank and calculate (4 incorrect).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 18
Which of the following descriptions of the characteristics of the testing method is not correct?

Spearman rank correlation is a parametric method
Kendall’s tau is a rank-based nonparametric correlation coefficient.
Pearson correlation coefficient measures linear relationships
Spearman correlation measures monotonic relationships







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
Spearman rank correlation is a non-parametric method that calculates data by converting it into ranks. The statement “Spearman is parametric” is a frequently appearing incorrect answer choice.

Pearson: Linear relationship, assumptions of normality and interval scale (parametric)
Spearman: monotonic relation, rank-based (non-parametric)
Kendall: Rank pair matching/mismatching based (non-parametric), df.corr(method='kendall')

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 19
Which of the following is not a correct explanation of the Spearman and Kendall correlation coefficients?

Spearman measures the relationship between ranks
Kendall directly measures the linear relationship between two variables.
Both are more robust to outliers than Pearson
Both are non-parametric methods.







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2
Kendall’s tau measures the concordance of rank pairs, not the linear relationship. Pearson measures the linear relationship directly. Since both are rank-based, they are relatively robust to outliers.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 20
Which is not an assumption of one-way ANOVA?

The population variances of each group are equal.
The error follows a normal distribution.
The observations are independent of each other.
The sample size of each group must be the same







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 4
The three main assumptions of ANOVA are normality, homogeneity of variances, and independence. Although equal sample sizes (balanced design) make it more robust against violations of homogeneity of variances, equal sample sizes are not a mandatory assumption. Only these three assumptions are specified in the scipy.stats.f_oneway document as well.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 21
When there are 20 samples in each of the 5 groups, what are the between-group degrees of freedom and within-group degrees of freedom in the one-way ANOVA?

(4, 95)
(5, 99)
(4, 99)
(5, 95)







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1

Between groups: \(k - 1 = 5 - 1 = 4\)
Within group: \(N - k = 100 - 5 = 95\)
All: \(N - 1 = 99 = 4 + 95\)

\(F = \dfrac{\text{MSTr}}{\text{MSE}} = \dfrac{\text{SSTr}/(k-1)}{\text{SSE}/(N-k)}\), and as \(F\) increases, the p-value becomes smaller (saying it increases is incorrect).

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 22
Which of the following is an incorrect description of interaction in two-way ANOVA?

It means that the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor.
If the p-value of the interaction is 0.05 or less and is significant, the lines in the interaction plot appear parallel.
If the interaction is significant, caution is required in interpreting the main effects.
The interaction term is included in the model as the product of two factors.







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2
It is the other way around. If the interaction is significant, the lines are not parallel (they intersect or have different slopes). Lines being parallel is a visual signal that there is no interaction. “If significant, they are parallel” is a typical trap of contradictory statements.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 23
Which is the most appropriate meaning of “the result is significant” in hypothesis testing?

p-value is smaller than the significance level
The test statistic is not included in the rejection region
The null hypothesis was proven true.
The sample size is sufficiently large







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
