TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 3
1, 2, and 4 are descriptions of the underfitting (high bias) series. 3 is a signal of overfitting (high variance) where learning is good but generalization is poor.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 122
In LOOCV (Leave-One-Out Cross Validation), how many times is the model trained (and evaluated) when there are 9,000 data points?

10
100
8,999
9,000







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 4
LOOCV trains by keeping 1 for validation and using the remaining \(n-1\) for training, so it trains a total of \(n\) = 9,000 times. This is an extreme case of K-fold (\(k = n\)), and the computational cost is very high.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 123
Which of the following evaluation methods can overestimate a model’s performance?

Measure performance directly using the data used for training
Use stratified K-fold cross-validation
Use time-ordered backtest splits for time series data
Do not use the holdout test set for training at all







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
Reusing training data is a typical error that inflates generalization performance. Similar cases include data leakage, where scaling and oversampling are applied to the entire data before splitting, and splitting that makes future data predict the past in time series, which also leads to overestimation.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 124
Which is the correct explanation of Cross Entropy Loss?

This is the standard loss function for regression problems.
Measures the difference between the predicted probability distribution and the actual distribution, and the lower the predicted probability of the correct class, the greater the loss.
always has a value between 0 and 1
It is not differentiable, so it cannot be used for gradient descent







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2
\(L = -\sum_c y_c \log \hat{p}_c\). If the probability of the correct class is close to 0, the loss diverges to infinity (3 incorrect — no upper bound). It is the standard loss for classification and is differentiable, so it is used for backpropagation.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 125
In the problem of finding the optimal threshold by calculating FRR and FAR while varying the classification threshold in increments of 10, which of the following definitions is correct?

\(FRR = \dfrac{FP}{FP + TN}\), \(FAR = \dfrac{FN}{FN + TP}\)
\(FRR = \dfrac{TP}{TP + FN}\), \(FAR = \dfrac{TN}{TN + FP}\)
FRR and FAR are always the same value.
Increasing the threshold reduces both FRR and FAR.







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 1
(From the perspective of authentication where normal=0 is accepted and abnormal=1 is rejected) The false rejection rate FRR is the ratio of normal (actual 0) rejected, and the false acceptance rate FAR is the ratio of abnormal (actual 1) accepted, with the denominators being “total actual 0” and “total actual 1”, respectively. When moving the threshold, there is a trade-off where if one side decreases, the other side increases (4 incorrect), so the point where the two values are equal (EER) or the threshold where the weighted sum is minimized is found.
Practical Tip: Select only the rows where true == 0 and calculate directly using Boolean indexing of the formula for the ratio pred == 1.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 126
Which is the correct explanation for the Weighted F1 score?

Simple average of F1 values for all classes
Weight the F1 of each class by the number of samples (support) of that class.
Defined only in binary classification
Always larger than macro F1







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2

macro F1: Simple average of F1 by class (prime classes treated equally)
weighted F1: support weighted average (majority classes have a large influence)
micro F1: Calculate by summing all TP/FP/FN

A practical problem has also been presented in a variation type where the inverted weighted F1 (emphasizing prime classes), weighted by the reciprocal of support, is provided as a formula and calculated directly — in this case, one simply needs to calculate the recall and F1 for each class separately and then combine them exactly as given in the formula.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 127
Which of the following is not a correct description of regression evaluation metrics?

MAE is the average of the absolute values of the errors, and the penalty for large errors is weaker than MSE.
RMSE is the square root of MSE and can be interpreted in units of won.
MAPE becomes unstable if the actual value is close to 0.
MAE is differentiable at every point, so it is most advantageous for gradient-based optimization.







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 4
MAE is not differentiable at the point where the error is zero. The key point regarding the disadvantages of MAE is that “there is a point of non-differentiability, and it penalizes large errors relatively less.” In problems requiring RMSE, the mistake of calculating only the MSE and omitting the square root (resulting in a different number of decimal places) is also a common pitfall in the practical exam.

title: DS Level 3 Written Exam Predicted Question Bank
text:
Problem 128
When creating a derived variable from the conditional mean by group, what is the method that broadcasts the result groupby to each row of the original DataFrame sorted by index?

agg
transform
filter
describe







TipAnswer and Explanation





Answer: 2

agg: Abbreviated to 1 row per group
transform: broadcast group statistics to the same length as the original → Map conditional expectations \(E[Y|\text{group}]\) to each row and use them to create missing value imputations and derived variables

Matching the result groupby().mean() to map yields the same result. This is the most frequently occurring pattern in the practical preprocessing test.









ImportantFinal Study Points



The types of traps that are repeatedly asked are summarized as follows.

Reversing the Definition: “Minimizing margins”, “direction of increasing slope”, “parallel if significant”, “C discriminant axes” — A passage with only one word changed from the correct definition
Changing Range/Conditions: Exponential distribution integration interval \([0,1]\), decimal scaling \(j\), adding minor conditions such as changing MinMax to 0~100
Similar Concepts Cross-Track: Wilcoxon signed-rank vs Mann–Whitney U, Goodness of Fit vs Test of Independence, Feature Extraction vs Selection, Macro vs Weighted F1, Standard Deviation vs Standard Error
Absolute Expressions: For examples containing “always,” “completely,” “unconditionally,” or “must,” think of a counterexample first
Calculation Problem: Chi-square goodness of fit, degrees of freedom, number of parameters (including bias), feature map size, gradient descent iterations, linearity of expectation — manual calculation speed equals the score

Fit a simple regression explaining Rings from df_abalone to Whole_weight and OLS from statsmodels and output summary().
Check each of the following in the output table and answer their meanings.

from statsmodels.api import OLS, add_constant

# TODO: OLS로 Rings ~ Whole_weight 단순 회귀를 적합하고 summary()를 출력하세요.







TipExplanation 1-1






Why the difference between R^2 and Adj. R^2 is minimal
\[R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{(1-R^2)(n-1)}{n-p-1}\]

Since there are only \(p=1\) and \(n \approx 4177\) is very large, the penalty term \(\frac{n-1}{n-p-1} \approx 1\) becomes \(\frac{n-1}{n-p-1} \approx 1\), making the two values nearly identical. As more variables are included, the gap between the two values widens, and this gap itself serves as a signal that “unnecessary variables are mixed in.”

Interpretation of coef

When Whole_weight increases by 1 (unit: gram-based scale), the conditional expected value of Rings increases by coef. Since this is simple regression, it is a marginal effect, not an effect that controls for other variables.

Df Residuals

\(n - (p + 1) = 4177 - 2 = 4175\). Degrees of freedom were consumed to estimate a total of 2 parameters, 1 intercept and 1 slope.

Null hypothesis of Prob (F-statistic)

\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) (All regression coefficients except the intercept are 0). In simple regression, it yields the same conclusion as the t-test of the slope, and in fact, the \(F = t^2\) relationship holds.

print(lm.summary())

# F = t^2 관계를 확인합니다.
t_stat = lm.tvalues['Whole_weight']
print(f'\nt^2 = {t_stat ** 2:.4f}, F = {lm.fvalue:.4f}')

from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

X_cols = [i for i in df_abalone.columns if i != 'Rings']
cont_val = [i for i in df_abalone.columns if i not in ['Sex', 'Rings']]

# TODO: passthrough 버전과 StandardScaler 버전의 MSE를 각각 구하고 비교하세요.







TipExplanation 1-2





Key Point: Gradient descent is sensitive to scale, while the normal equation is not.
SGDRegressor moves down the loss surface in the gradient direction. If the scales between variables differ significantly, the loss surface becomes a severely elongated ellipse, bouncing excessively along the large-scale axis and barely moving along the small-scale axis.
abalone shows a large scale difference, as HeightZ is around 0.1, whereas Whole_weight exceeds 2. Since the same learning rate \(\eta\) is applied to all variables:
\[\beta_j \leftarrow \beta_j - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta_j}\]
Since is \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta_j} \propto x_j\), the gradient of the larger scale variable becomes dominant, causing divergence or extremely slow convergence.
If you change it to LinearRegression?
Since the normal equation \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) is solved in a closed form, the same optimal solution is obtained regardless of scale. Standardization does not affect prediction performance.
However, in the regularized Ridge/Lasso, the penalty \(\lambda\sum\beta_j^2\) directly punishes the magnitude of the coefficients; thus, the coefficients of the small-scale variable automatically increase, resulting in an unfairly large penalty. In other words, standardization is mandatory even for closed solutions if regularization is present.

from sklearn.linear_model import SGDRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

X_cols = [i for i in df_abalone.columns if i != 'Rings']
cont_val = [i for i in df_abalone.columns if i not in ['Sex', 'Rings']]

results = {}
for name, scaler in [('passthrough', 'passthrough'), ('standardized', StandardScaler())]:
    ct = ColumnTransformer([
        ('std', scaler, cont_val),
        ('ohe', OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), ['Sex'])
    ])
    reg = make_pipeline(ct, SGDRegressor(max_iter=100, random_state=123))
    reg.fit(df_abalone[X_cols], df_abalone['Rings'])
    results[name] = mean_squared_error(df_abalone['Rings'], reg.predict(df_abalone[X_cols]))

print('SGDRegressor')
for k, v in results.items():
    print(f'  {k:14s} MSE = {v:,.4f}')

# LinearRegression은 스케일에 무관합니다.
print('\nLinearRegression')
for name, scaler in [('passthrough', 'passthrough'), ('standardized', StandardScaler())]:
    ct = ColumnTransformer([
        ('std', scaler, cont_val),
        ('ohe', OneHotEncoder(drop='first'), ['Sex'])
    ])
    reg = make_pipeline(ct, LinearRegression())
    reg.fit(df_abalone[X_cols], df_abalone['Rings'])

TipExplanation 1-3





Result Pattern: Ridge has zero zero coefficients in any alpha, whereas Lasso has zero zero coefficients as alpha increases until they all become zero.
Why Is There Such a Difference — Gradient Perspective
It is clear if you look at the derivative of the penalty.
\[\frac{d}{d\beta}\left(\beta^2\right) = 2\beta \quad\text{(L2)}, \qquad \frac{d}{d\beta}|\beta| = \operatorname{sign}(\beta) \quad\text{(L1, } \beta \neq 0)\]

L2: If \(\beta \to 0\), the penalty gradient is also \(\to 0\). As it approaches 0, the repulsive force disappears, so there is no incentive to reach exactly 0.
L1: No matter how small \(\beta\) is, the gradient magnitude is always constant at \(1\). Even near 0, it continues to push with the same intensity, so it reaches 0 and stays there.

In \(\beta = 0\), L1 is not differentiable, and the subgradient becomes the interval \([-\lambda, \lambda]\). If the gradient of the data loss falls within this interval, \(\beta = 0\) becomes the stopping point, so 0 becomes the positive measure solution.
Geometric Interpretation: The L1 constraint region \(\sum|\beta_j| \le t\) is a diamond (an intersecting polytope in higher dimensions) with vertices on the axes. The point where the loss contour first meets this region is likely to be a vertex, and a vertex is a point where some coordinates are zero. The L2 sphere is smooth, so the probability of it touching a single point on the axis is virtually zero.

TipExplanation 2-1





1. Maximum value

Entropy: \(p = 0.5\) when in binary classification \(H = 1\). Generally, \(c\) when the classes are equal \(\log_2 c\).
Genie: In binary classification, when it is \(p = 0.5\), it is \(G = 0.5\). Generally, it is \(1 - 1/c\).

Both curves are convex upwards with peaks at \(p=0.5\), but the entropy is sharper and steeper at the extremes.
2. Genie’s Probabilistic Interpretation
Let’s calculate the probability that two samples drawn from the same node are of different classes with sampling with replacement.
\[P(\text{같은 클래스}) = \sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i \cdot p_i = \sum_i p_i^2\]
Therefore
\[P(\text{다른 클래스}) = 1 - \sum_i p_i^2 = G(t)\]
The same value is obtained in the form \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\). Since it is \(\sum_i p_i = 1\).
\[\sum_i p_i(1-p_i) = \sum_i p_i - \sum_i p_i^2 = 1 - \sum_i p_i^2\]
Implementation Note: Since \(p_i = 0\) becomes \(\log_2 0 = -\infty\), replace it with np.where(p > 0, p, 1) to make it \(0 \cdot \log_2 1 = 0\).

def entropy(p):
    """클래스 비율 배열 p에 대한 엔트로피를 반환합니다."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    return -np.sum(p * np.log2(np.where(p > 0, p, 1)))


def gini(p):
    """클래스 비율 배열 p에 대한 지니 불순도를 반환합니다."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    return 1 - np.sum(p ** 2)

Creating Branch Point Candidates
The branch point for a continuous variable is taken as the adjacent midpoint of the sorted eigenvalues. When the eigenvalue is \(a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k\), there are \(b_i = \frac{a_i + a_{i+1}}{2}\), making \(k-1\) candidates.
The reason for using the center point instead of \(a_i\) as a candidate is that selecting the most central value among the threshold interval \((a_i, a_{i+1}]\) where the split yields the same result is advantageous for generalization.
Efficient Calculation
If we iterate through the data twice at every branch point, it becomes \(O(nk)\). By using pd.cut + crosstab + cumsum, we obtain the class distribution of the left node in one go using cumulative frequency, and for the right, we subtract the left from the total, so it is reduced to \(O(n + k)\).
Match with sklearn
Since DecisionTreeClassifier is the base criterion='gini', it optimizes the same objective function. However, since sklearn’s tree_.threshold has a slightly different floating-point processing method, there may be a difference in the last digit; therefore, it is safer to check whether it creates the same partition rather than whether the values are exactly the same.
Note: sklearn weights the impurity reduction by N(t)/N * IG(t) and accumulates it in feature_importances_. The variable importance of the entire tree is the normalized value of this.

    index=pd.cut(df_titanic[col], bins=b, right=True),
    columns=df_titanic['Survived']

Key: min_samples_leaf is not the “leaf size” but the “splitting condition”.
min_samples_leaf = k is a constraint stating that “For any partition to be performed, both resulting children must be at least \(k\)”. Since partitions that do not satisfy this condition are not even attempted, the partition is stopped prematurely.

Cause of Confusion: It is easy to think of the “number of samples in one leaf” and the “number of leaves” as being in the same direction, but with the total \(N\) fixed, these two are inversely proportional. # TODO: alpha를 변화시키며 train/test AUC를 기록하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 3-1





1. alpha \(\to 0\): Zero-frequency problem
Estimating conditional probability without smoothing
\[P(w_i \mid c) = \frac{N_{w_i, c}}{N_c}\]
The word that has never appeared with class \(c\) in the training data is \(P(w_i \mid c) = 0\). Since Naive Bayes multiplies these,
\[P(c \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto P(c)\prod_i P(w_i \mid c) = 0\]
A single non-appearing word invalidates all other evidence. Even if there are ten words strongly suggesting spam, the probability becomes 0 because of one word never seen in ham.
Laplace(ad-one) smoothing prevents this.
\[P(w_i \mid c) = \frac{N_{w_i, c} + \alpha}{N_c + \alpha |V|}\]
2. When alpha is too large: Excessive smoothing
If \(\alpha \to \infty\), then \(P(w_i \mid c) \to \frac{1}{|V|}\), and the conditional probability of all words becomes equal regardless of class. The signal obtained from the data is completely buried in the prior distribution, resulting in a state where prediction is made using only prior probabilities, and the AUC converges to 0.5.
\(\alpha\) can be interpreted as the concentration parameter of the Dirichlet prior distribution and acts as a regularization parameter that controls the bias-variance trade-off.
3. The Reason for Using Log Probability — Underflow
If there are 20 words in one message and each probability is at the \(10^{-3}\) level
\[\prod_{i=1}^{20} 10^{-3} = 10^{-60}\]
Since the minimum normalized number of a float64 is approximately \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\), it actually underflows to zero in documents with hundreds of words. If you take the logarithm, the product becomes the sum.
\[\log P(c\mid\mathbf{x}) \propto \log P(c) + \sum_i \log P(w_i \mid c)\]
It is numerically stable. Since only the order is required for class comparison, taking the logarithm, which is a monotonic transformation, does not change the conclusion.

The Curse of Dimensions — The Disappearance of Distance Contrast
As the dimension \(d\) increases, the distances between any two points all become similar. Under certain conditions:
\[\lim_{d \to \infty} \frac{\max_i \|x_i - q\| - \min_i \|x_i - q\|}{\min_i \|x_i - q\|} \to 0\]
In other words, the distance difference between the “nearest neighbor” and the “farthest point” relatively disappears. KNN relies entirely on the premise that “closer things are similar,” but this premise becomes meaningless.
Intuition: In \(d\) dimensions, Euclidean distance
\[\|x - q\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{d} (x_j - q_j)^2\]
Since it is the sum of \(d\) terms, it clusters around the mean according to the law of large numbers. The average of the distances increases to \(O(\sqrt{d})\), but the standard deviation remains at \(O(1)\), resulting in relative variation \(\sigma/\mu \to 0\).
Additional Issues in Text Data — Sparsity
Even when applying min_df=5, the vocabulary size is typically 1000 to 2000 dimensions, and individual messages contain only 10 to 30 words. If two messages share almost no words, the Euclidean distance effectively only reflects the lengths of the two documents, resulting in the selection of neighbors unrelated to the content.
Why Naive Bayes Is Advantageous
Since each word is treated independently to individually estimate \(P(w_i \mid c)\), the number of estimated items increases only linearly as the dimensionality increases. Although the assumption of conditional independence is practically incorrect, it works well in text classification because classification decisions only require the incremental relationship between classes to be correct, rather than the absolute value of the probability.
Improvement Direction: To use KNN, you must first apply dimensionality reduction using cosine distance (document length normalization), TF-IDF weighting, or SVD.

TipExplanation 4-1





1. Weight Vector
In the dual solution of the SVM, \(\mathbf{w}\) is a linear combination of the support vectors.
\[\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i\]
Since sklearn’s dual_coef_ already contains \(\alpha_i y_i\), we obtain it directly as dual_coef_ @ support_vectors_. Points that are not support vectors are \(\alpha_i = 0\) and do not contribute — this is the sparsity of SVM.
2. Margin Range
The two margin boundaries are \(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = \pm 1\). The distance between the two parallel hyperplanes is
\[\text{margin} = \frac{|1 - (-1)|}{\|\mathbf{w}\|} = \frac{2}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\]
Therefore, margin maximization \(\equiv\) \(\|\mathbf{w}\|\) minimize. This is why the original problem of SVM is \(\min \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\).
3. Function value in support vector = 1
The constraint of the hard margin SVM is for all \(i\)
\[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) \ge 1\]
KKT complementarity condition by \(\alpha_i\left[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) - 1\right] = 0\):

\(\alpha_i > 0\) (Support Vector) \(\Rightarrow\) Constraints are activated by equality \(\Rightarrow\) \(y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) = 1\)
\(y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) > 1\) (Out of Margin) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\alpha_i = 0\)

That is, the support vectors lie exactly on the margin boundary. In a soft margin where \(C\) is finite, points that cross the margin (\(\xi_i > 0\)) can also be support vectors, so the value can be less than 1; therefore, \(C\) is made very large (\(10^5\)) to be close to a hard margin.

If \(C\) is small: Since the encroachment penalty is low, the margin is widened to contain many points within the margin. Since all points inside or above the margin are support vectors, the number increases. \(\|\mathbf{w}\|\) becomes smaller (because the margin \(= 2/\|\mathbf{w}\|\) is wide).

Bias-Variance Interpretation
A small number of support vectors means that the decision boundary depends on only a few points. Since the boundary fluctuates significantly if those few points change, the variance is large. Derivation of Theoretical Value
The probability that a specific sample is not drawn in a single extraction is \(1 - \frac{1}{n}\). Since it is sampling with replacement, \(n\) trials are independent and

Why \(n\) is smaller than \(1/e\)
If you take the log of \(f(n) = \left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^n\)
\[\ln f(n) = n\ln\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right) = n\left(-\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{2n^2} - \frac{1}{3n^3} - \cdots\right) = -1 - \frac{1}{2n} - \frac{1}{3n^2} - \cdots\]
Since the right-hand side of is smaller than \(-1\), it is \(f(n) < e^{-1}\), and as \(n\) increases, it monotonically increases from the bottom rather than from the top and converges to \(1/e\).

TipExplanation 5-2





The term that bagging reduces is variance.
In bias-variance decomposition
\[\mathbb{E}\left[(y_0 - \hat{f}(x_0))^2\right] = \underbrace{\left(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x_0)] - f(x_0)\right)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\hat{f}(x_0) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x_0)]\right)^2\right]}_{\text{Variance}} + \sigma^2\]
When the average of the \(T\) models is \(\hat{f}_{bag}(x) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_t \hat{f}_t(x)\), and the variance of each model is \(\sigma_f^2\) and the pairwise correlation is \(\rho\),
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{f}_{bag}\right) = \rho\,\sigma_f^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{T}\sigma_f^2\]

If \(T \to \infty\), the second term disappears and only \(\rho\sigma_f^2\) remains.
Bias hardly changes: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}_{bag}] = \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}_t]\), so the average prediction remains the same.

This equation is also the reason for the existence of Random Forest. With bagging alone, the trees become similar to each other, leaving a large \(\rho\), but if the variable is randomly restricted at each split (max_features), \(\rho\) decreases, and the lower bound \(\rho\sigma_f^2\) itself decreases.
Reasons why growing individual trees deeply is reasonable
Bagging reduces variance but not bias. Therefore, a low-bias (=high-variance) model is suitable as the base learner.

Unconstrained deep tree: low bias, high variance \(\to\) Bagging handles variance \(\to\) Good combination
Shallow tree (stump): High bias, low variance \(\to\) Bias remains even after bagging \(\to\) Bad combination

Shallow trees are actually suitable as the base learners for boosting. Boosting has the exact opposite requirements because it is a method that reduces bias by learning residuals sequentially.

# TODO: hard/soft voting의 정확도를 비교하고, 예측이 갈린 샘플을 분석하세요.







TipExplanation 5-3





Definition of the two methods

Hard voting: \(\hat{y} = \operatorname{mode}\left(\hat{y}_1, \ldots, \hat{y}_M\right)\) — Each model gets one vote
Soft voting: \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_k \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} P_m(y=k \mid \mathbf{x})\) — Average of probability

Conditions where results diverge
This is when the model on the losing side in the majority vote has much stronger conviction. For example, three models



Model
\(P(y=1)\)
Hard Vote




A
0.95
Class 1


B
0.45
Class 0


C
0.48
Class 0




Hard: Class 0 wins with 2 votes
Soft: Since the average is \(P(y=1) = (0.95+0.45+0.48)/3 = 0.627 > 0.5\), it is Class 1

Hard voting treats 0.95 and 0.51 as equally 1 vote. It discards information called “strength of conviction” while compressing probabilities into binary values. Soft voting preserves this information.
Is soft voting always better?
No. The superiority of soft voting depends on the premise that the probabilities of individual models are well corrected.

Unconstrained decision tree purifies the leaves and outputs \(P\) as only 0 or 1 — Unfounded extreme confidence
Naive Bayes pushes probabilities to the extremes due to the assumption of conditional independence

If models like are mixed in, soft voting can give that model excessive influence, potentially making it worse than hard voting. Countermeasures include correcting with CalibratedClassifierCV or lowering the weights of low-confidence models with VotingClassifier(weights=...).
Note: To use soft voting, all models must support predict_proba. SVC requires probability=True, and since cross-validation-based Platt scaling is performed internally, training becomes noticeably slower.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor

# TODO: 두 앙상블의 max_leaf_nodes별 MSE를 비교하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 5-4





The two ensembles target different terms of bias-variance decomposition.









Bagging / Random Forest
Boosting




Learning Method
Parallel · Independent
Sequential · Residual Learning


Term that mainly reduces
Variance
Bias


Required base learner
Low bias · High variance (Deep tree)
High bias · Low variance (Shallow tree)


If you increase the base learner
almost no overfitting
overfitting possible



Random Forest
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{f}_{bag}\right) = \rho\sigma_f^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{T}\sigma_f^2\]
Since the mean only reduces variance while leaving bias unchanged, the bias of the base tree must be low from the start. Therefore, max_leaf_nodes=None (unconstrained) is close to optimal. If the tree is made shallow, bias remains and cannot be recovered no matter how much averaging is done.
Gradient Boosting
\[F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu \cdot h_m(x), \qquad h_m \approx -\frac{\partial L}{\partial F}\bigg|_{F=F_{m-1}}\]
The next model fills in the parts (residuals) that the previous model missed, gradually reducing bias. The contribution of each step must be small (=the basis tree must be simple) to achieve fine convergence, whereas if the basis tree is deep, it absorbs all residuals at once, leading to immediate overfitting.
As a rule of thumb, max_depth of GBM is commonly used for 3 to 8, and max_leaf_nodes for 4 to 32. If learning_rate \(\nu\) is lowered, the stride length of each step decreases, requiring more n_estimators, but there is a trade-off where generalization improves.
Summary: Bagging stabilizes “already smart but volatile” learners, while boosting makes “dull but consistent” learners smarter little by little. The requirements are opposite.

# TODO: 각 모델을 교차검증하고 결과를 표로 정리하세요.







TipExplanation 6-1





1. The learning-evaluation gap = A proxy for variance
\[\text{gap} = \text{AUC}_{train} - \text{AUC}_{valid}\]
A large value indicates that the model has learned patterns specialized for the training folds, signaling that the variance term in the bias-variance decomposition is large.
Typically, the gap is largest in unconstrained Random Forests, which yield a training AUC close to 1.0. However, this gap is less problematic in Random Forests — because individual trees only look at 63.2% of the training data due to bootstrapping, a high training score for the entire ensemble does not immediately mean overfitting. The judgment should be made based on the absolute value and standard deviation of the evaluation scores.
A large standard deviation is also an important signal. It means that performance fluctuates when the fold changes, and this is a more direct measure of variance.
2. Voting Does Not Always Win
The premise of ensemble theory is that constituent models produce different errors. When the error correlation is \(\rho\), the ensemble variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{f}_{ens}\right) = \rho\sigma_f^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{M}\sigma_f^2\]
When Voting fails:

When performance variance is large: The weak model drags down the strong model. This is because the simple average gives equal weight to all models. weights= You must adjust with the factor or subtract the weak model.
When models are similar: If \(\rho \approx 1\), averaging does not reduce variance. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, which are already ensembles, are both tree-based, so they have a high correlation.
When probability correction is poor: Since soft voting averages probabilities as they are, models that generate extreme probabilities without basis dominate the results.

In the discrimination of ZZZPH0003930ZZZ abaloneZ and I, the signals are relatively clear, resulting in small performance differences between individual models; in this case, it is natural for the Voting to be similar to or only slightly better than the best single model. Ensembles win only when there is diversity.

TipExplanation 1-1






Why the difference between R^2 and Adj. R^2 is minimal
\[R^2_{adj} = 1 - \frac{(1-R^2)(n-1)}{n-p-1}\]

Since there are only \(p=1\) and \(n \approx 4177\) is very large, the penalty term \(\frac{n-1}{n-p-1} \approx 1\) becomes \(\frac{n-1}{n-p-1} \approx 1\), making the two values nearly identical. As more variables are included, the gap between the two values widens, and this gap itself serves as a signal that “unnecessary variables are mixed in.”

Interpretation of coef

When Whole_weight increases by 1 (unit: gram-based scale), the conditional expected value of Rings increases by coef. Since this is simple regression, it is a marginal effect, not an effect that controls for other variables.

Df Residuals

\(n - (p + 1) = 4177 - 2 = 4175\). Degrees of freedom were consumed to estimate a total of 2 parameters, 1 intercept and 1 slope.

Null hypothesis of Prob (F-statistic)

\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) (All regression coefficients except the intercept are 0). In simple regression, it yields the same conclusion as the t-test of the slope, and in fact, the \(F = t^2\) relationship holds.

TipExplanation 1-2





Key Point: Gradient descent is sensitive to scale, while the normal equation is not.
SGDRegressor moves down the loss surface in the gradient direction. If the scales between variables differ significantly, the loss surface becomes a severely elongated ellipse, bouncing excessively along the large-scale axis and barely moving along the small-scale axis.
abalone shows a large scale difference, as HeightZ is around 0.1, whereas Whole_weight exceeds 2. Since the same learning rate \(\eta\) is applied to all variables:
\[\beta_j \leftarrow \beta_j - \eta \frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta_j}\]
Since is \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \beta_j} \propto x_j\), the gradient of the larger scale variable becomes dominant, causing divergence or extremely slow convergence.
If you change it to LinearRegression?
Since the normal equation \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\) is solved in a closed form, the same optimal solution is obtained regardless of scale. Standardization does not affect prediction performance.
However, in the regularized Ridge/Lasso, the penalty \(\lambda\sum\beta_j^2\) directly punishes the magnitude of the coefficients; thus, the coefficients of the small-scale variable automatically increase, resulting in an unfairly large penalty. In other words, standardization is mandatory even for closed solutions if regularization is present.

# TODO: alpha별로 Ridge와 Lasso의 0인 계수 개수를 세어 비교하세요.







TipExplanation 1-3





Result Pattern: Ridge has zero zero coefficients in any alpha, whereas Lasso has zero zero coefficients as alpha increases until they all become zero.
Why Is There Such a Difference — Gradient Perspective
It is clear if you look at the derivative of the penalty.
\[\frac{d}{d\beta}\left(\beta^2\right) = 2\beta \quad\text{(L2)}, \qquad \frac{d}{d\beta}|\beta| = \operatorname{sign}(\beta) \quad\text{(L1, } \beta \neq 0)\]

L2: If \(\beta \to 0\), the penalty gradient is also \(\to 0\). As it approaches 0, the repulsive force disappears, so there is no incentive to reach exactly 0.
L1: No matter how small \(\beta\) is, the gradient magnitude is always constant at \(1\). Even near 0, it continues to push with the same intensity, so it reaches 0 and stays there.

In \(\beta = 0\), L1 is not differentiable, and the subgradient becomes the interval \([-\lambda, \lambda]\). If the gradient of the data loss falls within this interval, \(\beta = 0\) becomes the stopping point, so 0 becomes the positive measure solution.
Geometric Interpretation: The L1 constraint region \(\sum|\beta_j| \le t\) is a diamond (an intersecting polytope in higher dimensions) with vertices on the axes. The point where the loss contour first meets this region is likely to be a vertex, and a vertex is a point where some coordinates are zero. The L2 sphere is smooth, so the probability of it touching a single point on the axis is virtually zero.

    rows.append(row)

df_result

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# TODO: 임계값을 바꾸며 precision / recall / F1을 계산하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 1-4





1. Lowering the threshold increases recall, decreases precision
Lowering the threshold \(\tau\) causes the set of positive cases to monotonically grow. Since \(\tau_1 < \tau_2\) is \(\{x: p(x) \ge \tau_2\} \subseteq \{x: p(x) \ge \tau_1\}\) when \(\tau_1 < \tau_2\):

\(TP\) does not decrease and \(FN\) does not increase \(\Rightarrow\) \(\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\) is monotonically increasing
\(FP\) also increases, and since the newly incorporated samples are those with a low probability (=low likelihood of being positive), the positive rate of the incorporated group is lower than before. \(\Rightarrow\) \(\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\) is trending to decrease

The precision is not strictly monotonic. If the actual positive rate of a newly incorporated section happens to be higher than the current precision, it may rise locally, causing the actual curve to exhibit a sawtooth shape.
2. F1 Optimal Threshold
For the F/M classification of abalone, the two class ratios are nearly balanced and the separability is low (AUC near 0.6), so the F1 optimal threshold does not deviate significantly from 0.5. On the other hand, in problems where the classes are severely imbalanced or the misclassification cost is asymmetric (fraud detection, disease diagnosis), the optimal threshold shifts significantly from 0.5.
Caution: The threshold must be explored from the validation data. If the optimal threshold is selected from the evaluation data, the performance will be optimistically biased.

# TODO: df_titanic['Survived']의 불순도를 구하고, p에 따른 두 지표를 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 2-1





1. Maximum value

Entropy: \(p = 0.5\) when in binary classification \(H = 1\). Generally, \(c\) when the classes are equal \(\log_2 c\).
Genie: In binary classification, when it is \(p = 0.5\), it is \(G = 0.5\). Generally, it is \(1 - 1/c\).

Both curves are convex upwards with peaks at \(p=0.5\), but the entropy is sharper and steeper at the extremes.
2. Genie’s Probabilistic Interpretation
Let’s calculate the probability that two samples drawn from the same node are of different classes with sampling with replacement.
\[P(\text{같은 클래스}) = \sum_{i=1}^{c} p_i \cdot p_i = \sum_i p_i^2\]
Therefore
\[P(\text{다른 클래스}) = 1 - \sum_i p_i^2 = G(t)\]
The same value is obtained in the form \(\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)\). Since it is \(\sum_i p_i = 1\).
\[\sum_i p_i(1-p_i) = \sum_i p_i - \sum_i p_i^2 = 1 - \sum_i p_i^2\]
Implementation Note: Since \(p_i = 0\) becomes \(\log_2 0 = -\infty\), replace it with np.where(p > 0, p, 1) to make it \(0 \cdot \log_2 1 = 0\).

def entropy(p):
    """클래스 비율 배열 p에 대한 엔트로피를 반환합니다."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    return -np.sum(p * np.log2(np.where(p > 0, p, 1)))


def gini(p):
    """클래스 비율 배열 p에 대한 지니 불순도를 반환합니다."""
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    return 1 - np.sum(p ** 2)

print(f'Gini    = {gini(p_surv):.4f}')

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# TODO: Fare의 모든 분기점에서 지니 불순도 감소량을 계산하고 최댓값을 찾으세요.
# TODO: DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1) 결과와 대조하세요.







TipExplanation 2-2





Creating Branch Point Candidates
The branch point for a continuous variable is taken as the adjacent midpoint of the sorted eigenvalues. When the eigenvalue is \(a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_k\), there are \(b_i = \frac{a_i + a_{i+1}}{2}\), making \(k-1\) candidates.
The reason for using the center point instead of \(a_i\) as a candidate is that selecting the most central value among the threshold interval \((a_i, a_{i+1}]\) where the split yields the same result is advantageous for generalization.
Efficient Calculation
If we iterate through the data twice at every branch point, it becomes \(O(nk)\). By using pd.cut + crosstab + cumsum, we obtain the class distribution of the left node in one go using cumulative frequency, and for the right, we subtract the left from the total, so it is reduced to \(O(n + k)\).
Match with sklearn
Since DecisionTreeClassifier is the base criterion='gini', it optimizes the same objective function. However, since sklearn’s tree_.threshold has a slightly different floating-point processing method, there may be a difference in the last digit; therefore, it is safer to check whether it creates the same partition rather than whether the values are exactly the same.
Note: sklearn weights the impurity reduction by N(t)/N * IG(t) and accumulates it in feature_importances_. The variable importance of the entire tree is the normalized value of this.

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

col = 'Fare'
n = len(df_titanic)

# 1. 분기점 후보: 정렬된 고유값의 인접 중점
u = pd.Series(df_titanic[col].unique()).sort_values()
b = np.array([-np.inf] + ((u + u.shift(1)) / 2).dropna().tolist() + [np.inf])

# 2. 구간별 클래스 빈도의 누계 -> 좌측 노드 분포
df_cnt = pd.crosstab(
    index=pd.cut(df_titanic[col], bins=b, right=True),
    columns=df_titanic['Survived']
).cumsum()

vcnt = df_cnt.iloc[-1].values          # 전체 클래스 빈도
imp_t = gini(vcnt / n)                 # 분기 전 불순도
df_cnt = df_cnt.iloc[:-1]              # 마지막(전체) 행 제외


def weighted_imp(x):
    s = x.sum()
    return gini(x / s) * s / n if s > 0 else 0.0


imp_left = df_cnt.apply(weighted_imp, axis=1)
imp_right = (vcnt - df_cnt).apply(weighted_imp, axis=1)
ig = (imp_t - imp_left - imp_right).rename('IG')

best_interval = ig.idxmax()
best_threshold = best_interval.right
print(f'분기 전 Gini      = {imp_t:.6f}')
print(f'최대 IG           = {ig.max():.6f}')
print(f'직접 계산 분기점  = {col} <= {best_threshold:.4f}')

# 3. sklearn 결과와 대조
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, criterion='gini', random_state=123)
clf.fit(df_titanic[[col]], df_titanic['Survived'])
sk_threshold = clf.tree_.threshold[0]
sk_ig = clf.tree_.impurity[0] - (
    clf.tree_.weighted_n_node_samples[1] / n * clf.tree_.impurity[1]
    + clf.tree_.weighted_n_node_samples[2] / n * clf.tree_.impurity[2]
)
print(f'sklearn 분기점    = {col} <= {sk_threshold:.4f}')
print(f'sklearn IG        = {sk_ig:.6f}')
print(f'\n같은 분할인가? {np.isclose(best_threshold, sk_threshold, atol=1e-6)}')

ig.sort_values(ascending=False).head()

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# TODO: 두 파라미터 각각에 대해 리프 개수와 정확도를 기록하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 2-3





Key: min_samples_leaf is not the “leaf size” but the “splitting condition”.
min_samples_leaf = k is a constraint stating that “For any partition to be performed, both resulting children must be at least \(k\)”. Since partitions that do not satisfy this condition are not even attempted, the partition is stopped prematurely.
It is clear when looking at the upper bound on the number of leaves. Since every leaf must have at least \(k\) when the total number of samples is \(N\):
\[\text{리프 개수} \le \frac{N}{k}\]
Since \(k\) is in the denominator, \(k \uparrow \Rightarrow\) number of leaves \(\downarrow \Rightarrow\) complexity \(\downarrow\).
Cause of Confusion: It is easy to think of the “number of samples in one leaf” and the “number of leaves” as being in the same direction, but with the total \(N\) fixed, these two are inversely proportional. It is like applying the rule that “one slice must be at least 200g” when cutting a cake, which reduces the number of slices.
Remembering by Prefix








Parameter
If you increase the value
Complexity




max_depth
Allow deeper tree
increment


max_leaf_nodes
Allow more leaves
increase


min_samples_leaf
Strengthen splitting conditions
Decrease


min_samples_split
Strengthen splitting conditions
Decrease


min_impurity_decrease
Strengthen splitting conditions
Decrease



The prefix max_ relaxes the upper bound, so the value \(\uparrow\) = complexity \(\uparrow\), and the prefix min_ raises the minimum requirement, so the value \(\uparrow\) = complexity \(\downarrow\).

from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

# TODO: alpha를 변화시키며 train/test AUC를 기록하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 3-1





1. alpha \(\to 0\): Zero-frequency problem
Estimating conditional probability without smoothing
\[P(w_i \mid c) = \frac{N_{w_i, c}}{N_c}\]
The word that has never appeared with class \(c\) in the training data is \(P(w_i \mid c) = 0\). Since Naive Bayes multiplies these,
\[P(c \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto P(c)\prod_i P(w_i \mid c) = 0\]
A single non-appearing word invalidates all other evidence. Even if there are ten words strongly suggesting spam, the probability becomes 0 because of one word never seen in ham.
Laplace(ad-one) smoothing prevents this.
\[P(w_i \mid c) = \frac{N_{w_i, c} + \alpha}{N_c + \alpha |V|}\]
2. When alpha is too large: Excessive smoothing
If \(\alpha \to \infty\), then \(P(w_i \mid c) \to \frac{1}{|V|}\), and the conditional probability of all words becomes equal regardless of class. The signal obtained from the data is completely buried in the prior distribution, resulting in a state where prediction is made using only prior probabilities, and the AUC converges to 0.5.
\(\alpha\) can be interpreted as the concentration parameter of the Dirichlet prior distribution and acts as a regularization parameter that controls the bias-variance trade-off.
3. The Reason for Using Log Probability — Underflow
If there are 20 words in one message and each probability is at the \(10^{-3}\) level
\[\prod_{i=1}^{20} 10^{-3} = 10^{-60}\]
Since the minimum normalized number of a float64 is approximately \(2.2 \times 10^{-308}\), it actually underflows to zero in documents with hundreds of words. If you take the logarithm, the product becomes the sum.
\[\log P(c\mid\mathbf{x}) \propto \log P(c) + \sum_i \log P(w_i \mid c)\]
It is numerically stable. Since only the order is required for class comparison, taking the logarithm, which is a monotonic transformation, does not change the conclusion.

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# TODO: NB와 KNN의 정확도를 비교하고, 쌍별 거리 분포를 확인하세요.







TipExplanation 3-2





The Curse of Dimensions — The Disappearance of Distance Contrast
As the dimension \(d\) increases, the distances between any two points all become similar. Under certain conditions:
\[\lim_{d \to \infty} \frac{\max_i \|x_i - q\| - \min_i \|x_i - q\|}{\min_i \|x_i - q\|} \to 0\]
In other words, the distance difference between the “nearest neighbor” and the “farthest point” relatively disappears. KNN relies entirely on the premise that “closer things are similar,” but this premise becomes meaningless.
Intuition: In \(d\) dimensions, Euclidean distance
\[\|x - q\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{d} (x_j - q_j)^2\]
Since it is the sum of \(d\) terms, it clusters around the mean according to the law of large numbers. The average of the distances increases to \(O(\sqrt{d})\), but the standard deviation remains at \(O(1)\), resulting in relative variation \(\sigma/\mu \to 0\).
Additional Issues in Text Data — Sparsity
Even when applying min_df=5, the vocabulary size is typically 1000 to 2000 dimensions, and individual messages contain only 10 to 30 words. If two messages share almost no words, the Euclidean distance effectively only reflects the lengths of the two documents, resulting in the selection of neighbors unrelated to the content.
Why Naive Bayes Is Advantageous
Since each word is treated independently to individually estimate \(P(w_i \mid c)\), the number of estimated items increases only linearly as the dimensionality increases. Although the assumption of conditional independence is practically incorrect, it works well in text classification because classification decisions only require the incremental relationship between classes to be correct, rather than the absolute value of the probability.
Improvement Direction: To use KNN, you must first apply dimensionality reduction using cosine distance (document length normalization), TF-IDF weighting, or SVD.

TipExplanation 3-3





Result Direction: Optimal threshold in Structure B (FP cost 10x) shifts up.
Reason
A high FP cost means that “you must be more cautious when determining something as spam.” Raising the threshold reduces the set of positive (spam) judgments, decreasing FP, and in return, increases FN. Since the cost of FN is relatively low, this trade-off is advantageous.
Theoretical Optimal Threshold
The decision rule that minimizes expected cost is when \(p = P(\text{spam} \mid \mathbf{x})\)
\[\text{스팸으로 판정} \iff c_{FP}(1-p) < c_{FN} \cdot p \iff p > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}\]

Structure B: \(\tau^* = \frac{10}{10+1} \approx 0.909\)

Caution: This formula is accurate only when the model’s probability estimates are well-calibrated. Naive Bayes has poor calibration because it has a strong tendency to push probabilities to the extremes (near 0 or 1) due to the assumption of conditional independence. Therefore, the optimal threshold value may differ from the theoretical value, and it is safer to explore it directly from the actual data.
To improve the correction, you can apply Platt scaling or isotonic regression with CalibratedClassifierCV.

Margin width \(\frac{2}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\)

from sklearn.svm import SVC

# TODO: w, 마진 폭, 서포트 벡터의 함수값을 계산하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 4-1





1. Weight Vector
In the dual solution of the SVM, \(\mathbf{w}\) is a linear combination of the support vectors.
\[\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i \in SV} \alpha_i y_i \mathbf{x}_i\]
Since sklearn’s dual_coef_ already contains \(\alpha_i y_i\), we obtain it directly as dual_coef_ @ support_vectors_. Points that are not support vectors are \(\alpha_i = 0\) and do not contribute — this is the sparsity of SVM.
2. Margin Range
The two margin boundaries are \(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = \pm 1\). The distance between the two parallel hyperplanes is
\[\text{margin} = \frac{|1 - (-1)|}{\|\mathbf{w}\|} = \frac{2}{\|\mathbf{w}\|}\]
Therefore, margin maximization \(\equiv\) \(\|\mathbf{w}\|\) minimize. This is why the original problem of SVM is \(\min \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\).
3. Function value in support vector = 1
The constraint of the hard margin SVM is for all \(i\)
\[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) \ge 1\]
KKT complementarity condition by \(\alpha_i\left[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) - 1\right] = 0\):

\(\alpha_i > 0\) (Support Vector) \(\Rightarrow\) Constraints are activated by equality \(\Rightarrow\) \(y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) = 1\)
\(y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) > 1\) (Out of Margin) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\alpha_i = 0\)

That is, the support vectors lie exactly on the margin boundary. In a soft margin where \(C\) is finite, points that cross the margin (\(\xi_i > 0\)) can also be support vectors, so the value can be less than 1; therefore, \(C\) is made very large (\(10^5\)) to be close to a hard margin.

TipExplanation 4-2





Objective function of soft margin SVM
\[\min_{\mathbf{w}, b, \xi} \; \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i \quad \text{s.t.}\quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i+b) \ge 1 - \xi_i,\; \xi_i \ge 0\]
\(C\) is the balance between margin width and allowable margin intrusion. It is easier to understand as the reciprocal of the regulatory strength — \(C \uparrow\) = Regulation \(\downarrow\).
Observed Pattern










\(C\)
Margin

\(\|\mathbf{w}\|\)

If \(C\) is small: Since the encroachment penalty is low, the margin is widened to contain many points within the margin. Since all points inside or above the margin are support vectors, the number increases. \(\|\mathbf{w}\|\) becomes smaller (because the margin \(= 2/\|\mathbf{w}\|\) is wide).
If If \(C\) is large: Since intrusion is severely penalized, it attempts to classify all points correctly even if it means narrowing the margins. Only a small number of points right on the boundary become support vectors.

Bias-Variance Interpretation
A small number of support vectors means that the decision boundary depends on only a few points. Since the boundary fluctuates significantly if those few points change, the variance is large. Conversely, if there are many support vectors, the boundary is determined by the sum of multiple points, making it stable.
Specificity of gene data
This is a high-dimensional small sample with \(n \approx 72\), \(d \approx 7129\). In this situation, since there always exists a hyperplane that perfectly separates the training data, even if \(C\) is increased, the training accuracy cannot rise further from 1.0. The evaluation accuracy plateaus or drops when \(C\) exceeds a certain point, and in this case, it is common for the side with a smaller \(C\) (strong regularization) to be more advantageous.

Use df_abalone to perform the following.

# TODO: 이론값과 실측 OOB 비율을 비교하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 5-1





Derivation of Theoretical Value
The probability that a specific sample is not drawn in a single extraction is \(1 - \frac{1}{n}\). Since it is sampling with replacement, \(n\) trials are independent and
\[P(\text{한 번도 안 뽑힘}) = \left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^n\]
If \(x = -1\) is substituted into \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{x}{n}\right)^n = e^x\), then \(e^{-1} \approx 0.3679\).
Why \(n\) is smaller than \(1/e\)
If you take the log of \(f(n) = \left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^n\)
\[\ln f(n) = n\ln\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right) = n\left(-\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{2n^2} - \frac{1}{3n^3} - \cdots\right) = -1 - \frac{1}{2n} - \frac{1}{3n^2} - \cdots\]
Since the right-hand side of is smaller than \(-1\), it is \(f(n) < e^{-1}\), and as \(n\) increases, it monotonically increases from the bottom rather than from the top and converges to \(1/e\).
Looking at the numbers:



\(n\)
\((1-1/n)^n\)




10
0.3487


100
0.3660


1000
0.3677


\(\infty\)
0.3679



Practical Meaning of OOB
Since approximately 36.8% of the data for each base learner is not used for training, generalization performance can be estimated using this sample without separate validation data. RandomForestClassifier(oob_score=True) automates this.
If we use ZZZPH0003845ZZZ trees \(T\), the probability that a specific sample is drawn from all trees is \((1 - 1/e)^T \approx 0.632^T\); therefore, even if \(T\) increases only slightly, almost every sample becomes OOB at least once, making it possible to estimate OOB for the entire data.

Then answer. Which term of bias-variance decomposition does bagging reduce? Why is growing individual trees deep (unconstrained) rather reasonable in bagging?




from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

# TODO: n_estimators에 따른 예측 분산과 MSE를 기록하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 5-2





The term that bagging reduces is variance.
In bias-variance decomposition
\[\mathbb{E}\left[(y_0 - \hat{f}(x_0))^2\right] = \underbrace{\left(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x_0)] - f(x_0)\right)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\hat{f}(x_0) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x_0)]\right)^2\right]}_{\text{Variance}} + \sigma^2\]
When the average of the \(T\) models is \(\hat{f}_{bag}(x) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_t \hat{f}_t(x)\), and the variance of each model is \(\sigma_f^2\) and the pairwise correlation is \(\rho\),
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{f}_{bag}\right) = \rho\,\sigma_f^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{T}\sigma_f^2\]

If \(T \to \infty\), the second term disappears and only \(\rho\sigma_f^2\) remains.
Bias hardly changes: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}_{bag}] = \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}_t]\), so the average prediction remains the same.

This equation is also the reason for the existence of Random Forest. With bagging alone, the trees become similar to each other, leaving a large \(\rho\), but if the variable is randomly restricted at each split (max_features), \(\rho\) decreases, and the lower bound \(\rho\sigma_f^2\) itself decreases.
Reasons why growing individual trees deeply is reasonable
Bagging reduces variance but not bias. Therefore, a low-bias (=high-variance) model is suitable as the base learner.

Unconstrained deep tree: low bias, high variance \(\to\) Bagging handles variance \(\to\) Good combination
Shallow tree (stump): High bias, low variance \(\to\) Bias remains even after bagging \(\to\) Bad combination

Shallow trees are actually suitable as the base learners for boosting. Boosting has the exact opposite requirements because it is a method that reduces bias by learning residuals sequentially.

from sklearn.ensemble import VotingClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# TODO: hard/soft voting의 정확도를 비교하고, 예측이 갈린 샘플을 분석하세요.







TipExplanation 5-3





Definition of the two methods

Hard voting: \(\hat{y} = \operatorname{mode}\left(\hat{y}_1, \ldots, \hat{y}_M\right)\) — Each model gets one vote
Soft voting: \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_k \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} P_m(y=k \mid \mathbf{x})\) — Average of probability

Conditions where results diverge
This is when the model on the losing side in the majority vote has much stronger conviction. For example, three models



Model
\(P(y=1)\)
Hard Vote




A
0.95
Class 1


B
0.45
Class 0


C
0.48
Class 0




Hard: Class 0 wins with 2 votes
Soft: Since the average is \(P(y=1) = (0.95+0.45+0.48)/3 = 0.627 > 0.5\), it is Class 1

Hard voting treats 0.95 and 0.51 as equally 1 vote. It discards information called “strength of conviction” while compressing probabilities into binary values. Soft voting preserves this information.
Is soft voting always better?
No. The superiority of soft voting depends on the premise that the probabilities of individual models are well corrected.

Unconstrained decision tree purifies the leaves and outputs \(P\) as only 0 or 1 — Unfounded extreme confidence
Naive Bayes pushes probabilities to the extremes due to the assumption of conditional independence

If models like are mixed in, soft voting can give that model excessive influence, potentially making it worse than hard voting. Countermeasures include correcting with CalibratedClassifierCV or lowering the weights of low-confidence models with VotingClassifier(weights=...).
Note: To use soft voting, all models must support predict_proba. SVC requires probability=True, and since cross-validation-based Platt scaling is performed internally, training becomes noticeably slower.

from sklearn.ensemble import VotingClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

df_ab = df_abalone.assign(Class=lambda x: (x['Sex'] == 'I').astype(int))
df_tr, df_te = train_test_split(df_ab, train_size=0.8, random_state=123)
Xc = [i for i in df_ab.columns if i not in ['Sex', 'Class']]

estimators = [
    ('knn', make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=50))),
    ('lr', make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=100, max_iter=1000))),
    ('dt', DecisionTreeClassifier(max_leaf_nodes=8, random_state=123)),
]

preds = {}
for voting in ['hard', 'soft']:
    clf_vt = VotingClassifier(estimators, voting=voting)
    clf_vt.fit(df_tr[Xc], df_tr['Class'])
    preds[voting] = clf_vt.predict(df_te[Xc])
    print(f'{voting:5s} voting accuracy = '
          f'{accuracy_score(df_te["Class"], preds[voting]):.4f}')

# 두 방식의 예측이 갈린 샘플
disagree = np.where(preds['hard'] != preds['soft'])[0]
print(f'\n예측이 갈린 샘플 수 = {len(disagree)} / {len(df_te)}')

if len(disagree) > 0:
    rows = []
    for pos in disagree[:5]:

        for name, est in estimators:
            est.fit(df_tr[Xc], df_tr['Class'])
            x = df_te[Xc].iloc[[pos]]
            row[f'{name}_pred'] = int(est.predict(x)[0])
            row[f'{name}_prob'] = float(est.predict_proba(x)[0, 1])
        row['mean_prob'] = np.mean([row[f'{n}_prob'] for n, _ in estimators])
        row['hard'] = int(preds['hard'][pos])

    df_dis = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('idx')

else:

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor

# TODO: 두 앙상블의 max_leaf_nodes별 MSE를 비교하고 시각화하세요.







TipExplanation 5-4





The two ensembles target different terms of bias-variance decomposition.









Bagging / Random Forest
Boosting




Learning Method
Parallel · Independent
Sequential · Residual Learning


Term that mainly reduces
Variance
Bias


Required base learner
Low bias · High variance (Deep tree)
High bias · Low variance (Shallow tree)


If you increase the base learner
almost no overfitting
overfitting possible



Random Forest
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{f}_{bag}\right) = \rho\sigma_f^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{T}\sigma_f^2\]
Since the mean only reduces variance while leaving bias unchanged, the bias of the base tree must be low from the start. Therefore, max_leaf_nodes=None (unconstrained) is close to optimal. If the tree is made shallow, bias remains and cannot be recovered no matter how much averaging is done.
Gradient Boosting
\[F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu \cdot h_m(x), \qquad h_m \approx -\frac{\partial L}{\partial F}\bigg|_{F=F_{m-1}}\]
The next model fills in the parts (residuals) that the previous model missed, gradually reducing bias. The contribution of each step must be small (=the basis tree must be simple) to achieve fine convergence, whereas if the basis tree is deep, it absorbs all residuals at once, leading to immediate overfitting.
As a rule of thumb, max_depth of GBM is commonly used for 3 to 8, and max_leaf_nodes for 4 to 32. If learning_rate \(\nu\) is lowered, the stride length of each step decreases, requiring more n_estimators, but there is a trade-off where generalization improves.
Summary: Bagging stabilizes “already smart but volatile” learners, while boosting makes “dull but consistent” learners smarter little by little. The requirements are opposite.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

df_tr, df_te = train_test_split(
    pd.get_dummies(df_abalone, columns=['Sex']), train_size=0.8, random_state=123)
Xc = [i for i in df_tr.columns if i != 'Rings']

leaf_list = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, None]
results = {}
for name, Model, kw in [
    ('RandomForest', RandomForestRegressor, dict(n_estimators=200, random_state=123, n_jobs=-1)),
    ('GradientBoosting', GradientBoostingRegressor, dict(n_estimators=200, random_state=123, learning_rate=0.1)),
]:
    rows = []
    for leaf in leaf_list:
        reg = Model(max_leaf_nodes=leaf, **kw)
        reg.fit(df_tr[Xc], df_tr['Rings'])
        rows.append({
            'max_leaf_nodes': 'None' if leaf is None else leaf,
            'mse_train': mean_squared_error(df_tr['Rings'], reg.predict(df_tr[Xc])),
            'mse_test': mean_squared_error(df_te['Rings'], reg.predict(df_te[Xc])),
        })
    results[name] = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('max_leaf_nodes')
    print(f'--- {name} ---')
    print(results[name].round(4).to_string())
    best = results[name]['mse_test'].idxmin()
    print(f'최적 max_leaf_nodes = {best}\n')

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
for ax, (name, df_r) in zip(axes, results.items()):
    pos = np.arange(len(df_r))
    ax.plot(pos, df_r['mse_train'], marker='o', label='MSE of train')
    ax.plot(pos, df_r['mse_test'], marker='s', label='MSE of test')
    ax.axvline(list(df_r.index).index(df_r['mse_test'].idxmin()),
               linestyle='dotted', color='gray')

from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedStratifiedKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier, VotingClassifier

# TODO: 각 모델을 교차검증하고 결과를 표로 정리하세요.







TipExplanation 6-1





1. The learning-evaluation gap = A proxy for variance
\[\text{gap} = \text{AUC}_{train} - \text{AUC}_{valid}\]
A large value indicates that the model has learned patterns specialized for the training folds, signaling that the variance term in the bias-variance decomposition is large.
Typically, the gap is largest in unconstrained Random Forests, which yield a training AUC close to 1.0. However, this gap is less problematic in Random Forests — because individual trees only look at 63.2% of the training data due to bootstrapping, a high training score for the entire ensemble does not immediately mean overfitting. The judgment should be made based on the absolute value and standard deviation of the evaluation scores.
A large standard deviation is also an important signal. It means that performance fluctuates when the fold changes, and this is a more direct measure of variance.
2. Voting Does Not Always Win
The premise of ensemble theory is that constituent models produce different errors. When the error correlation is \(\rho\), the ensemble variance is
\[\operatorname{Var}\left(\hat{f}_{ens}\right) = \rho\sigma_f^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{M}\sigma_f^2\]
When Voting fails:

When performance variance is large: The weak model drags down the strong model. This is because the simple average gives equal weight to all models. weights= You must adjust with the factor or subtract the weak model.
When models are similar: If \(\rho \approx 1\), averaging does not reduce variance. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting, which are already ensembles, are both tree-based, so they have a high correlation.
When probability correction is poor: Since soft voting averages probabilities as they are, models that generate extreme probabilities without basis dominate the results.

In the discrimination of ZZZPH0003930ZZZ abaloneZ and I, the signals are relatively clear, resulting in small performance differences between individual models; in this case, it is natural for the Voting to be similar to or only slightly better than the best single model. Ensembles win only when there is diversity.

from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, RepeatedStratifiedKFold,
                                     cross_validate)
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier,
                              VotingClassifier)
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

df_ab = df_abalone.assign(Class=lambda x: np.where(x['Sex'] == 'I', 1, 0))
df_tr, df_te = train_test_split(df_ab, train_size=0.8, random_state=123)
Xc = [i for i in df_ab.columns if i not in ['Sex', 'Class']]

cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=123)


def eval_model(name, clf):
    r = cross_validate(clf, df_tr[Xc], df_tr['Class'], cv=cv,
                       scoring='roc_auc', return_train_score=True, n_jobs=-1)
    return pd.Series([
        '{:.4f}±{:.4f}'.format(r['train_score'].mean(), r['train_score'].std()),
        '{:.4f}±{:.4f}'.format(r['test_score'].mean(), r['test_score'].std()),
        r['train_score'].mean() - r['test_score'].mean(),
    ], index=['train', 'valid', 'gap'], name=name)


clfs = [
    ('K-Nearest neighbors',
     make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=50))),
    ('Logistic Regression',
     make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(C=100, max_iter=1000))),

                   SVC(C=10, kernel='poly', degree=2, coef0=1, probability=True))),
    ('Random Forest',
     RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_leaf_nodes=64, random_state=123)),
    ('Gradient boosting',
     GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=150, max_leaf_nodes=4,
                                random_state=123, learning_rate=0.1)),
]

results = [eval_model(name, clf) for name, clf in clfs]
results.append(eval_model('Voting (soft)', VotingClassifier(clfs, voting='soft')))

df_cv = pd.concat(results, axis=1).T
df_cv['gap'] = df_cv['gap'].astype(float).round(4)
print(df_cv.to_string())

# 평가 데이터에서 최종 확인
print('\n--- 평가 데이터 AUC ---')
for name, clf in clfs + [('Voting (soft)', VotingClassifier(clfs, voting='soft'))]:

import numpy as np

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
1.1 Bernoulli distribution
\[p(x) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x}, \quad x \in \{0, 1\}\]
Expected Value \(E(X)\)
\[E(X) = \sum_{x=0}^{1} x \cdot p(x) = 0\cdot(1-p) + 1\cdot p = p\]
Variance \(V(X)\)
First, find \(E(X^2)\). Since \(x \in \{0,1\}\) is \(x^2 = x\):
\[E(X^2) = 0^2\cdot(1-p) + 1^2\cdot p = p\]
\[V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p)\]

p = 0.3
Xb = bernoulli.rvs(p, size=100_000, random_state=1)
print("표본 평균:", np.mean(Xb).round(4), "| 이론값:", p)
print("표본 분산:", np.var(Xb).round(4), "| 이론값:", round(p * (1 - p), 4))

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
1.2 Binomial distribution
\[p(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \quad x = 0, 1, \dots, n\]
A binomial random variable can be viewed as the sum of independent Bernoulli trials. \(X = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\), each \(X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) and is independent of each other.
Expected Value \(E(X)\) — Linearity of Expected Value (Independence Not Required)
\[E(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} E(X_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p = np\]
Variance \(V(X)\) — Since they are independent, the variances are added as they are
\[V(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} V(X_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p(1-p) = np(1-p)\]
Although calculating \(\sum_x x\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\) directly from the definition yields the same result, it is much more concise to view it as a Bernoulli sum because it requires the use of the identity \(x\binom{n}{x} = n\binom{n-1}{x-1}\).

n = 100
X = binom.rvs(n, p, size=500, random_state=123)
print("표본 평균:", np.mean(X), "| 이론값:", n * p)
print("표본 분산:", np.var(X, ddof=1).round(3), "| 이론값:", n * p * (1 - p))

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
1.3 Poisson distribution
\[p(x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}, \quad x = 0, 1, 2, \dots\]
Expected Value \(E(X)\)
\[E(X) = \sum_{x=0}^{\infty} x \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}
       = \sum_{x=1}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{(x-1)!}\]
The \(x=0\) term is 0, so it cancels out. If we substitute with \(k = x-1\):
\[= \lambda \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!} = \lambda \cdot 1 = \lambda\]
The final sum is the total sum of the Poisson pmf, so it becomes 1.
Variance \(V(X)\)
The calculation is cleaner if you calculate \(E[X(X-1)]\) first. This is because it becomes \(x(x-1)/x! = 1/(x-2)!\).
\[E[X(X-1)] = \sum_{x=2}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{(x-2)!}
            = \lambda^2 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!} = \lambda^2\]
Therefore:
\[E(X^2) = E[X(X-1)] + E(X) = \lambda^2 + \lambda\]
\[V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = (\lambda^2 + \lambda) - \lambda^2 = \lambda\]

lam = 4
Xp = poisson.rvs(lam, size=100_000, random_state=2)
print("표본 평균:", np.mean(Xp).round(4), "| 이론값:", lam)
print("표본 분산:", np.var(Xp).round(4), "| 이론값:", lam)

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
1.4 Summary of three distributions









distribution
\(p(x)\)
\(E(X)\)
\(V(X)\)




Bernoulli
\(p^x(1-p)^{1-x}\)
\(p\)
\(p(1-p)\)


binomial
\(\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\)
\(np\)
\(np(1-p)\)


Poisson
\(\dfrac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}\)
\(\lambda\)
\(\lambda\)



The core of the derivation differs for each. Bernoulli is derived directly from the definition, binomial from the linearity of Bernoulli sums, and Poisson from an index shift trick of the form \(x/x! = 1/(x-1)!\).

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
3.1 scipy.stats.expon’s scale parameter
scipy accepts the exponential distribution as scale rather than rate(\(\lambda\)).
\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\text{scale}} e^{-x/\text{scale}}, \quad x \geq 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \text{scale} = \frac{1}{\lambda}\]
, that is, scipy’s scale is the reciprocal of the rate \(\lambda\) commonly used in statistics. expon.cdf(0.4, scale=1/5) means \(\lambda = 5\), and becomes \(F(0.4) = 1 - e^{-5 \times 0.4} = 1 - e^{-2}\).

print("expon.cdf(0.4, scale=1/5):", expon.cdf(0.4, scale=1/5))
print("수식 1 - exp(-2)      :", 1 - np.exp(-2))

As the scale increases, the average waiting time becomes longer and the distribution spreads more widely (\(E(X) = \text{scale} = 1/\lambda\)). Since loc and scale are factors common to most continuous distributions, they are used in the same way in Gamma, Weibull, and others.






Warning



If you enter \(\lambda\) as is, like expon.cdf(x, lambda_), an incorrect value will result. You must convert it to scale = 1/λ before entering it.

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
3.2 plt.gca().twinx()
This is a matplotlib function that creates a new y-axis while sharing the same x-axis.

plt.gca(): get current axes — Get the axis objects currently being drawn
.twinx(): Creates a new axis that shares the x-axis but is independent of the y-axis (new tick marks on the right)

The y-axis of the histogram represents frequency (tens), while the y-axis of the pmf represents probability (0 to 1), so the scales are completely different. If plotted on the same y-axis, the pmf values would be hidden at the bottom, so a separate y-axis is placed on the right to plot them overlappingly.

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
sns.histplot(X)
sns.scatterplot(
    x=np.arange(0, 101),
    y=binom.pmf(np.arange(0, 101), n, p),
    ax=plt.gca().twinx(), color="orange", label="Probability",
)
plt.show()

title: Probability Distributions: Moments and Sampling Notes
text:
3.3 alpha of fill_between
alpha is not a statistical variable but an argument that specifies the opacity of the color, receiving a value between 0 and 1.

alpha=0: Transparent, alpha=1: Opaque (default)
alpha=0.6: 60% Opaque = 40% Transparent (See-through)

The name comes from the A (alpha) channel of the RGBA color representation. It allows curves and grid lines behind filled areas to show through, and when multiple areas overlap, the overlapping parts are displayed in bold to distinguish them. It is an argument commonly received by almost all matplotlib functions, such as plot, scatter, and hist .

x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
tail = np.linspace(1.645, 4, 200)

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.plot(x, norm.pdf(x))
plt.fill_between(tail, 0, norm.pdf(tail), color="orange", alpha=0.6)
plt.title("Right tail (alpha = 0.6)")
plt.show()
