title: Distance between Vector Space and Probability Densities
text:
5.4 Chernoff Street

5.4.1 Curve \(p_s\)
About \(s\in[0,1]\)
\[
p_s(x)=\frac{p_0(x)^{1-s}\,p_1(x)^s}{J(s)},\qquad J(s)=\int p_0(x)^{1-s}p_1(x)^s\,dx
\]

\(J(s)\) is a normalization constant. Since \(J(0)=J(1)=1\), \(s=0,1\) and \(p_s\) are respectively \(p_0,p_1\).
Taking the logarithm of gives \(\log p_s=(1-s)\log p_0+s\log p_1-\log J(s)\), which is the logarithmic density linear interpolation (normalized geometric mean).
If written as \(\Lambda=\log(p_1/p_0)\), it is \(p_s=p_0\,e^{s\Lambda}/J(s)\) and \(J(s)=E_{p_0}[e^{s\Lambda}]\). It is an exponential family with sufficient statistics \(\Lambda\), natural parameters \(s\), and logarithmic partitioning functions \(\log J(s)\).

Example: Homoscedastic Gaussian. In the exponent
\[
(1-s)(x-\mu_0)^2+s(x-\mu_1)^2=(x-\mu_s)^2+s(1-s)\Delta^2,\qquad \mu_s=(1-s)\mu_0+s\mu_1
\]
, therefore
\[
J(s)=e^{-s(1-s)\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad p_s=\mathcal N(\mu_s,\sigma^2)
\]
This is the path where one peak moves from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu_1\).


5.4.2 \(J(s)\le1\)
If we set it as \(U=p_1/p_0\), it becomes \(J(s)=E_{p_0}[U^s]\), and since \(u\mapsto u^s\) is concave at \(s\in(0,1)\),
\[
J(s)\le\big(E_{p_0}[U]\big)^s=\Big(\int_{p_0>0}p_1\,dx\Big)^s\le1
\]
The equality sign applies only when \(U\) is a constant in strict concavity, i.e., \(p_1=p_0\) ae.


5.4.3 \(\log J(s)\) is convex
\(\log J(s)\) is the leakage rate generating function of \(\Lambda\).
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\log J=E_{p_s}[\Lambda],\qquad \frac{d^2}{ds^2}\log J=\mathrm{Var}_{p_s}[\Lambda]\ge0
\]
(the derivation of the first equation is Section 5.5.3). Since \(\log J(0)=\log J(1)=0\) at the end point, the minimum value is always \(\le0\).


5.4.4 Definition and Properties
\[
C(p_1,p_0)=-\min_{0\le s\le1}\log J(s)
\]

Nasal: Since \(\log J\le0\), \(C\ge0\).
Equals: \(C=0\iff\) In all \(s\) \(\log J(s)=0\iff p_1=p_0\) ae
Symmetry: \(s\to1-s\) Since the role of \(p_0,p_1\) changes due to the substitution, \(C(p_1,p_0)=C(p_0,p_1)\).
Bhattacharyya coefficient: \(J(\tfrac12)=\int\sqrt{p_0p_1}\,dx\). Generally, since \(s^\star\ne\tfrac12\), it is \(-\log J(\tfrac12)\le C\).
Gaussian homovariance: Since \(\log J(s)=-s(1-s)\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\) is minimal at \(s=\tfrac12\) \[
C=\frac{\Delta^2}{8\sigma^2}
\] is 1/4 of KL \(\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\) in the same case.



5.4.5 Error Index
The error probability of the MAP test in a binary hypothesis test with prior probability \(\pi_0,\pi_1\) and iid samples \(n\) is
\[
P_e=\int\min\big(\pi_0p_0^{(n)},\pi_1p_1^{(n)}\big)\,d\mathbf x,\qquad p_i^{(n)}(\mathbf x)=\prod_{k=1}^np_i(x_k)
\]
. Since \(a,b\ge0\) and \(s\in[0,1]\)Z, it is \(\min(a,b)\le a^{1-s}b^s\) (if \(a\le b\), then \(a=a^{1-s}a^s\le a^{1-s}b^s\)).
\[
P_e\le\pi_0^{1-s}\pi_1^s\int\big(p_0^{(n)}\big)^{1-s}\big(p_1^{(n)}\big)^s\,d\mathbf x=\pi_0^{1-s}\pi_1^s\,J(s)^n
\]
and if we minimize from \(\pi_0^{1-s}\pi_1^s\le1\) to \(s\)
\[
P_e\le\exp\big(-n\,C(p_1,p_0)\big)
\]
. The fact that this exponent is the best (\(-\frac1n\log P_e\to C\)) is Chernoff’s theorem. In equal probability BPSK, the exponent of \(P_e=Q\big(\frac{\Delta}{2\sigma}\big)\le\tfrac12e^{-\Delta^2/(8\sigma^2)}\) matches the above \(C\).
The exponent of the Neyman–Pearson setup, which places a constraint on one-sided error, is determined by KL (Stein’s Lemma), and the exponent of the Bayes setup, which is weighted by prior probability, is determined by Chernoff.

title: Distance between Vector Space and Probability Densities
section: 5.5 The relationship between KL and Chernoff
text:
5.5 The relationship between KL and Chernoff

5.5.1 Claim
If we let \(s^\star=\arg\min_sJ(s)\) (since logarithms are increasing functions, this is equal to \(\arg\min_s\log J(s)\)), then
\[
C(p_0,p_1)=D(p_{s^\star}\|p_0)=D(p_{s^\star}\|p_1)=-\log J(s^\star)
\]
The last equality sign is the definition, and the actual content is the two equality signs in the middle. The point \(p_{s^\star}\) on the curve is at the equi-KL point, which is the equidistant point from the two endpoints, and the common value is the Chernoff distance. The definition of \(C\) does not include KL, but the key point is that the conclusion is that its value is KL.
Points to note:

\(p_{s^\star}\) is the first argument of KL. It is generally different from \(D(p_0\|p_{s^\star})\) or \(D(p_0\|p_1)\).
\(s^\star=\tfrac12\) applies only in the symmetrical case.

The proof of is two steps: (i) calculate two KLs at any point on the curve, and (ii) find the first-order condition of \(\log J\) and substitute it. The two steps meet at the same quantity \(E_{p_s}[\Lambda]\).


5.5.2 Step 1: Two KLs on the curve
\[
D(p_s\|p_0)=\int\underbrace{p_s(x)}_{\text{가중치}}\log\frac{\overbrace{p_s(x)}^{\text{로그 안}}}{p_0(x)}\,dx
\]
In , \(p_s\) plays a different role in the second digit, so it is processed separately.
(A) Ratio inside the log. Since \(p_0^{1-s}/p_0=p_0^{-s}\)
\[
\frac{p_s}{p_0}=\frac{p_0^{1-s}p_1^s}{J(s)\,p_0}=\frac1{J(s)}\Big(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big)^s
\]
(B) Properties of logarithms.
\[
\log\frac{p_s}{p_0}=\log\Big(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big)^s-\log J(s)
\]
(C) Multiply by weights and integrate. \(\log J(s)\) is a constant independent of \(x\), and since \(\int p_s=1\),
\[
\int p_s\log J(s)\,dx=\log J(s)
\]
Therefore
\[
D(p_s\|p_0)=\int\frac{p_0^{1-s}p_1^s}{J(s)}\log\Big(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big)^s dx-\log J(s)
\]
(D) Move exponents forward. From \(\log u^s=s\log u\)
\[
D(p_s\|p_0)=s\int p_s\log\frac{p_1}{p_0}\,dx-\log J(s)=s\,E_{p_s}[\Lambda]-\log J(s)
\]
In the same way, \(\dfrac{p_s}{p_1}=\dfrac1{J(s)}\Big(\dfrac{p_1}{p_0}\Big)^{s-1}\), therefore
\[
D(p_s\|p_1)=(s-1)\,E_{p_s}[\Lambda]-\log J(s)
\]
The two expressions are multiplied by the same expected value with only the coefficients \(s\) and \(s-1\)Z differing, and if you subtract
\[
D(p_s\|p_0)-D(p_s\|p_1)=E_{p_s}[\Lambda]
\]
. The condition for the two KLs to be equal is \(E_{p_s}[\Lambda]=0\).
Check. If \(s=0\), it matches the definition as \(0-\log1=0=D(p_0\|p_0)\); if \(s=1\), it matches the definition as \(E_{p_1}[\Lambda]-\log1=D(p_1\|p_0)\).


5.5.3 Step 2: Differentiation of \(\log J(s)\)
(1) Differentiation of composite functions.
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\log J(s)=\frac{J'(s)}{J(s)}
\]
(2) Differentiate into integral. (Under the conditions of the Dominant Convergence Theorem)
\[
J'(s)=\int\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\Big[p_0(x)^{1-s}p_1(x)^s\Big]dx
\]
(3) Differentiation of the integrand. If \(x\) is fixed, \(p_0,p_1\) is a constant and
\[
p_0^{1-s}p_1^s=p_0\Big(\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big)^s
\]
is of the form \(a^s\). Since \(a^s=e^{s\ln a}\), it is \(\frac{d}{ds}a^s=a^s\ln a\) and
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\Big[p_0^{1-s}p_1^s\Big]=p_0^{1-s}p_1^s\,\ln\frac{p_1}{p_0}
\]
Even after differentiation, the original expression remains and \(\ln(p_1/p_0)\) is multiplied by one.
(4)–(5) Combine and take the expected value.
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\ln J(s)=\frac1{J(s)}\int p_0^{1-s}p_1^s\ln\frac{p_1}{p_0}\,dx=\int p_s\ln\frac{p_1}{p_0}\,dx=E_{p_s}\Big[\ln\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big]
\]
Since it was divided by \(J(s)\), the weight becomes the normalized density \(p_s\), which is the expected value.
Identification with Step 1. Slope of \(\log J\) = Difference between two KLs.

5.5.3.1 base of the log
In the differentiation of exponential functions, \(\ln\) always appears regardless of the base, so the logarithm appearing in the above derivation is the natural logarithm. If defined as \(\log=\log_b\)
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\log_bJ(s)=\frac1{\ln b}\,E_{p_s}\Big[\ln\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big]=E_{p_s}\Big[\log_b\frac{p_1}{p_0}\Big]
\]
As , the factor \(\frac1{\ln b}\) is absorbed by \(\frac{\ln u}{\ln b}=\log_bu\). The expansion in Step 1 is base-independent because it uses only \(\log(ab)=\log a+\log b\) and \(\log u^s=s\log u\), and the condition “\(\frac{d}{ds}\log J=0\)” used in Step 3 is also not affected by positive constant multiples. Therefore, as long as the base is unified within the same expression, the conclusion is base-independent. If the base is 2, the unit is simply bits.


5.5.3.2 The minimum value is inside and the only reason
The first-order condition can be used only when \(s^\star\) is inside the interval. Second derivative
\[
J''(s)=\int p_0^{1-s}p_1^s\,\Lambda^2\,dx>0\quad(p_0\ne p_1)
\]
In , \(J\) is strictly convex, and the slope at the endpoint is
\[
\frac{d}{ds}\log J\Big|_{s=0}=E_{p_0}[\Lambda]=-D(p_0\|p_1)<0,\qquad \frac{d}{ds}\log J\Big|_{s=1}=E_{p_1}[\Lambda]=D(p_1\|p_0)>0
\]
. Since the gradient is continuous, strictly increasing, and changes from negative to positive, there is exactly one zero in \((0,1)\), which is \(s^\star\). This is \(p_0\ne p_1\) and is the argument when the two KLs are finite, but the case where the support is different and KL is \(\infty\) is outside this argument.



5.5.4 Step 3: Substitution
From \(s^\star\), since it becomes \(E_{p_{s^\star}}[\Lambda]=0\), the first term of Step 1 disappears.
\[
D(p_{s^\star}\|p_0)=-\log J(s^\star),\qquad D(p_{s^\star}\|p_1)=-\log J(s^\star)
\]
and \(C=-\min_s\log J(s)=-\log J(s^\star)\), therefore
\[
\boxed{\,C(p_0,p_1)=D(p_{s^\star}\|p_0)=D(p_{s^\star}\|p_1)=-\log J(s^\star)\,}
\]








Step
Key Formula
Role




1
\(D(p_s\|p_0)-D(p_s\|p_1)=E_{p_s}[\Lambda]\)
the difference between two KLs as an expected value


2
\(\frac{d}{ds}\log J=E_{p_s}[\Lambda]\)
The same expected value is the slope of \(\log J\)


3
Slope at the optimal point \(=0\)
The two KLs are equal and the value is \(-\log J(s^\star)\)





5.5.5 Verification: Gaussian equal variances
\(p_s=\mathcal N(\mu_0+s\Delta,\sigma^2)\) Therefore
\[
D(p_s\|p_0)=\frac{s^2\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2},\qquad D(p_s\|p_1)=\frac{(1-s)^2\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}
\]
The two values become the same at \(s^\star=\tfrac12\), and the common value is \(\frac{\Delta^2}{8\sigma^2}=C\). The difference is
\[
\frac{(2s-1)\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}=\frac{d}{ds}\Big[-\frac{s(1-s)\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big]
\]
is consistent with the identity in Step 1–2. On the expectation side as well, if we set \(x=\mu_s+\sigma z\), it becomes \((x-\mu_0)^2-(x-\mu_1)^2=(2s-1)\Delta^2+2\Delta\sigma z\), which is equal to \(E_{p_s}[\Lambda]=\frac{(2s-1)\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}\).


5.5.6 Check numerical values of asymmetric examples
For \(p_0=\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(p_1=\mathcal N(2,2^2)\)Z with different variances, it is \(s^\star\ne\tfrac12\). The figure below shows the numerical calculation of \(-\log J(s)\), \(D(p_s\|p_0)\), and \(D(p_s\|p_1)\) on the curve. The intersection point of the two KL curves coincides with the location of the maximum value of \(-\log J\) (i.e., the minimum value of \(\log J\)).


5.5.7 Interpretation
The most plausible error path. For an error to occur, a sample from \(p_0\) must look like \(p_1\) or vice versa. In such a rare event, the experience distribution follows a \(q\), and the exponential cost of that probability is \(D(q\|\text{진짜 분포})\) (Sanov). The equilibrium point where both types of errors occur with the same exponential is \(p_{s^\star}\), where the two KLs are equal, and the common cost is \(C\). \(E_{p_{s^\star}}[\Lambda]=0\) means that “a sample from \(p_{s^\star}\) provides, on average, neither type of evidence.”
Legendre conversion. If you set it to \(\psi(s)=\log J(s)=\log E_{p_0}[e^{s\Lambda}]\), it becomes \(\psi'(s)=E_{p_s}[\Lambda]\) and
\[
D(p_s\|p_0)=s\,\psi'(s)-\psi(s)
\]
is the Legendre transformation of \(\psi\). \(C=-\min_s\psi(s)=\psi^*(0)\) is the value of the rate function of Cramér’s theorem calculated from the origin, that is, the exponent of the “event where the sample mean of LLR is greater than 0”.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
This document is composed of two branches.

Sampling: Multiplying a continuous-time signal by an impulse train replicates the spectrum in the frequency domain at intervals of \(\omega_s\). When applied to a random process, a band-limited steady-state process is represented as a discrete-time random sequence without loss.
Poisson Process: A point process that models “events whose timing is unknown.” From the small-\(\Delta t\) law, it is derived that the number of events within an interval follows a Poisson distribution.

Both topics have in common that they deal with points on the time axis. In sampling, points are placed on a deterministic lattice \(kT_s\), while in the Poisson process, the positions of the points themselves are random.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
2.1 Definition
impulse train with period \(T_s\)
\[
p_{T_s}(t)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(t-nT_s)
\]
If defined as , sampling is the product of the signal and the impulse train.
\[
x_s(t)=x(t)\,p_{T_s}(t)=\sum_{n}x(nT_s)\,\delta(t-nT_s)
\]
The second equality comes from \(x(t)\delta(t-t_0)=x(t_0)\delta(t-t_0)\). The sample value \(x(nT_s)\) is stored as the area of each impulse.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
2.2 Fourier Series Review
To obtain the Fourier transform of an impulse train, a Fourier series is required.
Orthogonality. When the periods are \(T\) and \(\omega_0=2\pi/T\), the complex exponent \(\{e^{jk\omega_0 t}\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}\) is orthogonal over one period.
\[
\int_{-T/2}^{T/2} e^{jk\omega_0 t}\,\overline{e^{jl\omega_0 t}}\,dt=\int_{-T/2}^{T/2} e^{j(k-l)\omega_0 t}\,dt=
\begin{cases}T & k=l\\ 0 & k\neq l\end{cases}
\]
If \(k\neq l\), the integral is 0 because it rotates an integer number of times during one period, and if \(k=l\), the integrand is 1.
When both sides of Coefficient. \(x(t)=\sum_k c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t}\) are multiplied by \(e^{-jl\omega_0 t}\) and integrated over one period, only the \(k=l\) term remains.
\[
\boxed{c_k=\frac{1}{T}\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}x(t)\,e^{-jk\omega_0 t}\,dt}
\]






NoteSource of \(1/T\)



\(1/T\) is the basis norm squared \(\int_{-T/2}^{T/2}|e^{jk\omega_0 t}|^2dt=T\). It has the same structure as the expanded coefficient of an orthogonal basis in finite dimensions, \(c_k=\langle x,e_k\rangle/\langle e_k,e_k\rangle\). \(c_0\) is the one-period average (DC component).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 2.3 Fourier transform of complex exponential: \(\mathcal F\{e^{j\omega_0 t}\}=2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0)\)
text:
2.3 Fourier transform of complex exponential: \(\mathcal F\{e^{j\omega_0 t}\}=2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0)\)
The transformation pair is set to the following convention.
\[
X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t}dt,\qquad
x(t)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(j\omega)e^{j\omega t}d\omega
\]
For \(x(t)=e^{j\omega_0 t}\), the defining expression \(\int e^{j(\omega_0-\omega)t}dt\) does not converge in the classical sense because the absolute value of the integrand is 1. Therefore, we consider a candidate and verify it using the inverse transform. Let \(X(j\omega)=A\,\delta(\omega-\omega_0)\).
\[
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int A\,\delta(\omega-\omega_0)e^{j\omega t}d\omega=\frac{A}{2\pi}e^{j\omega_0 t}
\;\Longrightarrow\; A=2\pi .
\]
\[
\boxed{\mathcal F\{e^{j\omega_0 t}\}=2\pi\,\delta(\omega-\omega_0)}
\]
Interpretation. The spectrum of a signal rotating forever at a single frequency exists only at that single point of frequency. The coefficient \(2\pi\) is a value that compensates for the \(1/2\pi\) convention of the inverse transform. In particular, if \(\omega_0=0\), then \(\mathcal F\{1\}=2\pi\delta(\omega)\).
Meaning as a distribution. If the integral is cut at \([-L,L]\)
\[
\int_{-L}^{L}e^{j(\omega_0-\omega)t}dt=\frac{2\sin\big((\omega-\omega_0)L\big)}{\omega-\omega_0}.
\]
This function tapers at \(L\to\infty\) with height \(2L\) and width \(\sim 1/L\), and the area is fixed at \(\int\frac{2\sin(uL)}{u}du=2\pi\). Therefore, the limit when integrating over the test function is \(2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0)\), and the equation should be understood in this sense.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 2.4 Fourier transform of an impulse train
text:
2.4 Fourier transform of an impulse train
① Fourier Series. \(p_{T_s}(t)\) has a period \(T_s\), and within one period \([-T_s/2,T_s/2)\), there is only one impulse \(t=0\). Due to the sifting property
\[
c_k=\frac{1}{T_s}\int_{-T_s/2}^{T_s/2}\delta(t)e^{-jk\omega_s t}dt=\frac{1}{T_s}\quad(\forall k),
\qquad
p_{T_s}(t)=\frac{1}{T_s}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}e^{jk\omega_s t},\quad \omega_s=\frac{2\pi}{T_s}.
\]
All harmonic components have the same magnitude and phase, so they simultaneously undergo constructive interference only at \(t=nT_s\) to create an impulse.
② Term-wise transformation. If you use linearity and the above result
\[
\boxed{P(j\omega)=\mathcal F\{p_{T_s}(t)\}=\frac{1}{T_s}\sum_k 2\pi\,\delta(\omega-k\omega_s)=\frac{2\pi}{T_s}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\delta(\omega-k\omega_s)}
\]
In general, if the series coefficient of a periodic signal is \(c_k\), then it is \(X(j\omega)=\sum_k 2\pi c_k\,\delta(\omega-k\omega_0)\). That is, the position of the impulse is \(k\omega_0\), and the area is \(2\pi c_k\).

2.4.1 Coefficient \(2\pi/T_s\) Dissection
Since \(\omega_s=2\pi/T_s\) is already in the formula, the preceding coefficient may appear redundant, but the two have different roles.








Element
Role
Source




\(\delta(\omega-k\omega_s)\) of \(\omega_s\)
Position of impulse
Period \(T_s\) → Fundamental frequency


Part of the preceding \(1/T_s\)
impulse area
Fourier series coefficients \(c_k\)


Part of the preceding \(2\pi\)
impulse area
\(\omega\) area transformation convention (\(e^{j\omega_0t}\leftrightarrow2\pi\delta\))



Since the area is numerically equal to \(\omega_s\), writing \(P(j\omega)=\omega_s\sum_k\delta(\omega-k\omega_s)\) is equivalent. In this case, the preceding \(\omega_s\) represents the area, not the location.
Assuming there are no coefficients leads to a contradiction. Letting \(P(j\omega)=\sum_k\delta(\omega-k\omega_s)\) and performing the inverse transform, by the Poisson sum formula \(\sum_k e^{jk\omega_s t}=T_s\sum_n\delta(t-nT_s)\)
\[
\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_k e^{jk\omega_s t}=\frac{T_s}{2\pi}\,p_{T_s}(t)\neq p_{T_s}(t).
\]


2.4.2 Verification

Dimension: The unit of \(p_{T_s}(t)\) is \(1/\mathrm{s}\), and passing through \(\int dt\), the transformation is dimensionless. The right-hand side \(\frac{2\pi}{T_s}[1/\mathrm s]\times\delta(\omega)[\mathrm s]\) is also dimensionless.
\(f\) Notation: \(x(t)=\int X(f)e^{j2\pi ft}df\). In the \(x(t)=\int X(f)e^{j2\pi ft}df\) convention, it is \(e^{j2\pi f_0t}\leftrightarrow\delta(f-f_0)\), so \(P(f)=\frac{1}{T_s}\sum_k\delta(f-k/T_s)\). If changed to \(\delta(f)=\delta(\omega/2\pi)=2\pi\delta(\omega)\), it matches the result of the \(\omega\) range. That is, \(2\pi\) is a product of the notation convention, and \(1/T_s\) is the intrinsic scale.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
2.5 Spectrum of the sampled signal
The product in the time domain is the convolution in the frequency domain (\(\omega\) is attached in the convention \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\)).
\[
X_s(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi}X(j\omega)*P(j\omega)
=\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac{2\pi}{T_s}\sum_k X(j\omega)*\delta(\omega-k\omega_s)
=\boxed{\frac{1}{T_s}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}X\big(j(\omega-k\omega_s)\big)}
\]
\(2\pi\) of \(2\pi/T_s\) is canceled out by the \(1/2\pi\) of the convolution, and the remaining \(1/T_s\) becomes the gain of each replica. The original spectrum is replicated at \(\omega_s\) intervals.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
2.6 Aliasing and Full Restoration
Let’s call it \(X(j\omega)=0\) for \(|\omega|>\omega_m\).

\(\omega_s>2\omega_m\) : The duplicates \([k\omega_s-\omega_m,\,k\omega_s+\omega_m]\) do not overlap. If only the baseband duplicates are selected using an ideal low-pass filter (LPF), \(x(t)\) is restored.
\(\omega_s<2\omega_m\) : Adjacent copies overlap (aliasing). Since the original component and the duplicate component are added together at the overlapping part, they cannot be separated by any filter.







TipDetailed conditions of the restoration filter



Since the gain of the replica is \(1/T_s\), the passband gain of the LPF must be \(T_s\) to accurately recover the original signal.
\[
H(j\omega)=\begin{cases}T_s & |\omega|\le\omega_c\\ 0 & |\omega|>\omega_c\end{cases},\qquad \omega_m\le\omega_c\le\omega_s-\omega_m .
\]
The cutoff frequency can be placed anywhere in the empty band between the two copies, not just \(\omega_c=\omega_m\). If set to \(\omega_c=\omega_s/2\), it becomes \(h(t)=\mathrm{sinc}(t/T_s)\) (normalized sinc) and yields the interpolation formula \(x(t)=\sum_n x(nT_s)\,\mathrm{sinc}\big((t-nT_s)/T_s\big)\).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
3.1 Random Sequence
A random sequence is a random process with integer time indices, that is, a discrete-time random process.
\[
\{X(l)\}_{l\in\mathbb Z}\quad(\text{인덱스는 정수, 값은 실수 가능})
\]
Sampling the continuous-time process \(X(t)\) at intervals \(T\) results in a random sequence.
\[
\tilde X(l)\equiv X(lT).
\]

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
3.2 Sampling Theorem for Random Processes
For deterministic signals, we examined whether the Fourier transform \(X(j\omega)\) is band-limited. Since the sample path of a random process usually has infinite energy and therefore no Fourier transform exists, we use the Power Spectral Density (PSD) as the reference.






ImportantCleanup



WSS If the process \(X(t)\) satisfies \(S_X(f)=0\) for \(|f|>W\) and the sample interval is \(T<\dfrac{1}{2W}\), then the discrete-time sequence \(X(lT)\) represents the original process.


Here, “expresses” does not mean point-by-point convergence of individual sample paths, but mean-square in the sense of
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}E\!\left[\Big|X(t)-\sum_{l=-L}^{L}X(lT)\,\mathrm{sinc}\!\Big(\frac{t-lT}{T}\Big)\Big|^2\right]=0
\]
This means that holds. The difference from the deterministic sampling theorem is that the concept of stochastic convergence is required in random processes.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 3.3 Correlation function of a sampled sequence
text:
3.3 Correlation function of a sampled sequence
For the WSS process \(X(t)\), \(R_X(\tau)=E[X(t)X(t+\tau)]\) depends only on the lag \(\tau\). The correlation function of the sampled sequence is
\[
R_{\tilde X}(k)=E\big[\tilde X(l)\tilde X(l+k)\big]=E\big[X(lT)X(lT+kT)\big]=\boxed{R_X(kT)}
\]
In the final equality, the WSS property (depending only on the lag \(kT\), independent of \(l\)) was applied. Therefore, \(\tilde X\) is also a WSS sequence, and its correlation function is the continuous correlation function sampled at intervals of \(T\).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 3.4 PSD of sampled sequence: Probabilistic version of spectral replication
text:
3.4 PSD of sampled sequence: Probabilistic version of spectral replication
The PSD of a sequence at normalized frequency \(\nu\) (cycles/sample) is defined as the discrete-time Fourier transform.
\[
S_{\tilde X}(\nu)=\sum_{k}R_{\tilde X}(k)e^{-j2\pi\nu k}.
\]
If you substitute \(R_X(kT)=\int S_X(f)e^{j2\pi fkT}df\) and use the Poisson sum formula \(\sum_k e^{j2\pi(fT-\nu)k}=\sum_m\delta(fT-\nu-m)=\frac1T\sum_m\delta\!\big(f-\frac{\nu+m}{T}\big)\)
\[
\boxed{S_{\tilde X}(\nu)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}S_X\!\left(\frac{\nu+m}{T}\right)}
\]
is exactly the same structure as the deterministic signal \(X_s(j\omega)=\frac1{T_s}\sum_kX(j(\omega-k\omega_s))\). \(S_X\) is limited to \(|f|\le W\), and if it is \(1/T>2W\), the copies do not overlap, so \(S_X\) can be read back from \(S_{\tilde X}\). This is the frequency domain meaning of the PSD reference sampling theorem.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
4.1 Point process and counting process
A point process is a mathematical model of a random event occurring at a specific point in time (or space). Examples: the arrival time of a packet in a network, the position of a star on the celestial sphere.
Taking packet arrival as an example, the arrival time is random because it is impossible to know exactly when the user will send the next request. This is described in terms of two quantities.

Counting Process \(N_t\): Start of observation. Number of events that occurred from \(t=0\) to \(t\). \(N_0=0\).
Event Time \(W_1<W_2<\cdots\) : The time when the \(i\)-th event occurred. The vector containing event times up to \(t\) is written as \(\mathbf W\in\mathbb R^{N_t}\) (the dimension itself is random).

The interval coefficient is obtained from the difference of the cumulative coefficients.
\[
N_{t_1,t_2}=N_{t_2}-N_{t_1},\qquad N_t=N_{0,t}.
\]

4.1.1 interval endpoint convention
Depending on how \(N_t\) is defined, whether the endpoint of the interval counted by \(N_{t_1,t_2}\) is included depends on the definition.
\[
N_t=\#\{i:W_i\le t\}\;\Rightarrow\;N_{t_2}-N_{t_1}=\#\{i:\,t_1<W_i\le t_2\}
\]
\[
N_t=\#\{i:W_i< t\}\;\Rightarrow\;N_{t_2}-N_{t_1}=\#\{i:\,t_1\le W_i< t_2\}
\]








\(N_t\) Definition
Continuity of the sample path
Interval counted by \(N_{t_1,t_2}\)




\(\#\{W_i\le t\}\) (“\(t\)”, standard)
accidental genus (càdlàg)
\((t_1,t_2]\)


\(\#\{W_i< t\}\)
Left Continuous
\([t_1,t_2)\)



“number of events occurring up to \(t\)” is consistent with the properties of the coincidence, and \((t_1,t_2]\) is the one that matches. Although some formulas in this document are written as \([t_1,t_2)\) by convention, since event times in a Poisson process follow a continuous distribution (\(\Pr(W_i=t_1)=0\)), the distributions of the two conventions are identical. The difference becomes an actual issue in general point processes or discrete-time models where events can be clustered at deterministic times (e.g., slot boundaries). Regardless of the convention, the interval must be standardized to a semi-open interval so that adjacent intervals are partitioned without overlap or omission, as in \((t_0,t_1]\cup(t_1,t_2]\cup\cdots=(t_0,t_n]\).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
4.2 Properties of the sample path
The sample path of \(N(t)\) (=\(N_t\)) is a step function and has the following properties.

Non-decrease: The number of events only increases or remains the same and does not decrease.
Integer value: Since it counts events \(0,1,2,\dots\)
Casual: The count is updated to a new value the very moment the event occurs. \(N(W_i)=\lim_{s\downarrow W_i}N(s)\).
Unit Jump: \(N(W_i)-N(W_i^-)=1\) at each jump time.
Between events, \(N(t)\) is constant.


4.2.1 Why Unit Jumps: Orderliness
“One event increments the count by exactly 1” is merely the definition of the counting process (weight of 1 for each event). The jump size is
\[
\text{점프 크기}=\#\{\text{그 시각에 발생한 사건 수}\}\times1
\]
Since , if two events overlap at the same time, the jump becomes 2. In fact, there exist non-simple point processes that allow batch arrival. Therefore, for a “unit jump” to hold, the property that at most one event at a time is additionally required, and the Poisson process guarantees this under the following condition.
\[
\Pr\big[N_{t,t+h}\ge 2\big]=o(h)\qquad(h\to0)
\]
Proof (Probability of simultaneous events = 0). Divide \([0,T]\) into Z\(h=T/n\) subintervals of length \(n\). By the union bound
\[
\Pr\Big(\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\{\text{소구간 }i\text{ 에 사건 }\ge2\}\Big)\le n\cdot o(T/n)=T\cdot\frac{o(T/n)}{T/n}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0.
\]
Since two events at the same time fall into the same subinterval in any partition, the probability of this happening is less than this upper bound and is 0. In other words, almost certainly (as) all event times are different.
Another perspective. As shown later, the arrival interval \(W_i-W_{i-1}\) follows an exponential distribution (continuous distribution), so it is \(\Pr(W_i=W_{i-1})=0\).
In models where co-arrival is actually important, the compound Poisson process \(\sum_{i\le N(t)}Y_i\) is used. The arrival times are Poisson, and the jump size of each arrival \(Y_i\) follows a random distribution.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
4.3 Intensity and Infinitesimal Interval Law
The probability law of a point process is defined by strength \(\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)\). For a sufficiently small \(\Delta t\)
\[
\boxed{\Pr\big[N_{t,t+\Delta t}=1\;\big|\;N_t;\mathbf W\big]=\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)\,\Delta t+o(\Delta t)}
\]







Symbol
Meaning




\(N_{t,t+\Delta t}\)
Number of events in the infinitesimal interval \((t,t+\Delta t]\)


\(N_t\), \(\mathbf W\)
Observations to date (number of events, times of events) = History of the process


\(\lambda(\cdot)\)
Instantaneous occurrence rate, unit is events/s


\(o(\Delta t)\)
\(\lim_{\Delta t\to0}o(\Delta t)/\Delta t=0\) In Hang



Intuition: Speed × Time. Just as traveling at a speed of \(v\) for a time of \(\Delta t\) results in a distance of \(v\Delta t\), if the occurrence rate is \(\lambda\) for a time of \(\Delta t\), the probability of an event is approximately \(\lambda\Delta t\) (dimensionless). For example, if \(\lambda=2\)/s, \(\Delta t=1\) ms, the probability is approximately \(0.002\).
\(\lambda\) does not determine the number of events. \(\lambda=5\) /s does not mean that exactly 10 events occur in 2 seconds. \(\lambda\) is a quantity that determines the probability in an infinitesimal interval, and the actual number is random (we will show later that the average is \(\lambda T\)).
Read as definition of intensity.
\[
\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)=\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\Pr[N_{t,t+\Delta t}=1\mid N_t;\mathbf W]}{\Delta t}
\]
The idea is similar to giving the probability of a small interval \(f(x)dx\), but since \(\lambda\) is not a density but a rate, it can be greater than 1. \(\Delta t\) must be sufficiently small so that it becomes \(\lambda\Delta t\le1\).
Why is it \(+o(\Delta t)\) and not an equal sign? In the Poisson process of constant intensity \(\lambda\), exactly
\[
\Pr[N_{t,t+\Delta t}=1]=\lambda\Delta t\,e^{-\lambda\Delta t}=\lambda\Delta t-\underbrace{(\lambda\Delta t)^2+\tfrac12(\lambda\Delta t)^3-\cdots}_{o(\Delta t)}
\]
. \(\lambda\Delta t\) is a first-order approximation, and the rest are of a higher order than \((\Delta t)^2\) and are ignored compared to \(\Delta t\).

4.3.1 Notation: ; and ,
In \(\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)\), \(\Pr[\,\cdot\mid N_t;\mathbf W]\), ; and , have mathematically the same role (all arguments/conditions), and the only difference is the notational grouping.

, : List of factors at the same level
; : The first part is the current status \((t,N_t)\), and the second part is the history \(\mathbf W\), distinguishing the roles.

That is, \(\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)=\lambda(t,N_t,\mathbf W)\) and \(\Pr[\cdot\mid N_t;\mathbf W]=\Pr[\cdot\mid N_t,\mathbf W]\). For reference, since \(N_t=\dim\mathbf W\), \(N_t\) is information determined from \(\mathbf W\).







; conventions in other fields
meaning




\(p(x;\theta)\)
\(\theta\) is a fixed parameter, not a random variable (frequency caution). \(p(x\mid\theta)\) is \(\theta\), which is a random variable (Bayesian)


\(I(X;Y)\), \(I(X;Y\mid Z)\)
Distinguishing two variables in mutual information; \mid is the condition



Here, \(\mathbf W\) is not a fixed parameter but a random history, so it differs from the \(p(x;\theta)\) convention. In point process literature, the same object is often written as the conditional strength \(\lambda^*(t)=\lambda(t\mid\mathcal H_t)\) for the history \(\mathcal H_t\).


4.3.2 Classification of point processes according to intensity function








Strength
Process
Example




\(\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)\equiv\lambda_0\)
Normal (Uniform) Poisson
Packet arrival with constant average traffic


\(\lambda(t)\)
Abnormal (Non-vehicle) Poisson
Traffic change by time of day (Day ↑, Night ↓)


\(\lambda\) depends on \(\mathbf W\)
self-excitation process (Hawkes et al.)
earthquake aftershock, burst traffic



The infinitesimal interval law is a framework that defines the intensity of not only Poisson processes but the entire point process, and a Poisson process is a case where the intensity does not depend on hysteresis.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 4.4 Normal Poisson Process and Abnormal Poisson Process
text:
4.4 Normal Poisson Process and Abnormal Poisson Process
The Poisson process is memoryless: its strength does not depend on the process history \((N_t,\mathbf W)\).

Stationary: \(\lambda(t,N_t;\mathbf W)=\lambda_0\) (Constant). Independent of time and history.
nonstationary: \(\lambda(t)\). It changes over time but is still unrelated to history.

Interpretation of Coin Toss. Divide the time axis into \(\Delta t\) squares, and for each square, toss a coin that produces an “event” with probability \(\lambda_0\Delta t\). Each toss is independent of past (and future) results. In the case of anomalies, only the probability changes to \(t\) in the square at time \(\lambda(t)\Delta t\), while the independence remains the same.






WarningDistinguish between “normal” and “independent”



The source of independence between intervals is memorylessness (hysteresis-independence), not stationarity (constant strength). Even in an anomalous Poisson process, the number of events in non-overlapping intervals is independent of each other. This is the reason why the derivation of the count statistics that follows holds true in the general form \(\lambda(t)\).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
4.5 Two Laws of Probability

count statistics: The probability that there are \(n\) events in the interval \([t_1,t_2)\) \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]\).
Time of occurrence: Joint distribution of the times of the first \(n\) events within the observation interval \((W_1,\dots,W_n)\).


4.5.1 Why the time of occurrence is important
Information inclusion relationship. The count is a function of time.
\[
N_{t_1,t_2}=\sum_i\mathbf 1\{t_1<W_i\le t_2\}
\]
If the joint distribution of event times is known, the count distribution of any interval is determined, but the count distribution alone cannot tell where the events are clustered within the interval. For example, the information that there are “2” in \([0,1)\) cannot distinguish between \(\{0.10,0.15\}\) (burst) and \(\{0.2,0.8\}\) (variance). The time distribution is a complete description of the process, and the count is a summary of it.
Meaning in communication systems.

Queueing Delay: Even if the average arrival rate is the same, a queue builds up if arrival times are concentrated.
Collision Probability (ALOHA type): Whether two transmissions overlap depends not on the number of times but on the time difference \(|W_i-W_j|\).
Estimation/Testing: The likelihood used to estimate the maximum likelihood of \(\lambda\) with the observed event times or to test the Poisson assumption is the joint density of the times.

The reason count statistics are derived first is that they are simpler summaries, not because the time of occurrence is less important. The rule of the time of occurrence is derived from the count results in the distribution of arrival times .

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
5.1 Adjacent interval decomposition
If we consider two adjacent intervals \([t_1,t_2)\), \([t_2,t_2+\delta)\)
\[
N_{t_1,t_2+\delta}=N_{t_1,t_2}+N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}. \tag{1}
\]
The goal is to express as the probability of \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2+\delta}=n]\) in two subintervals.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
5.2 Total probability decomposition
For the total to be \(n\), there must be exactly \(k\) in the next interval when there are \(n-k\). The possible \((k,n-k)\) is \((0,n),(1,n-1),\dots,(n,0)\), and since the events for different \(k\) are disjoint, the probabilities can be added.
\[
\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2+\delta}=n]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\Pr\big[N_{t_1,t_2}=k,\;N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}=n-k\big].
\]
Independence. Due to memorylessness, the intensity of the subsequent section is independent of the history of the preceding section, therefore
\[
\Pr[N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}=j\mid N_{t_1,t_2}=k]=\Pr[N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}=j]
\]
, and therefore
\[
\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2+\delta}=n]=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=k]\;\Pr[N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}=n-k]. \tag{2}
\]

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
5.3 Three cases of infinitesimal intervals
If \(\delta\) is sufficiently small, there are three possible outcomes in the following interval: “0 / 1 / 2 or more”, and the sum of the probabilities of the three is 1.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr[N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}=1]&=\lambda(t_2)\,\delta+o(\delta) &&\text{(강도의 정의)}\\
\Pr[N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}\ge2]&=o(\delta) &&\text{(단순성)}\\
\Pr[N_{t_2,t_2+\delta}=0]&=1-\lambda(t_2)\,\delta+o(\delta) &&\text{(합이 1)}
\end{aligned} \tag{3}
\]
The third equation is a simplified version of \(1-[\lambda\delta+o(\delta)]-o(\delta)\).






Note\(o(\cdot)\) notation arithmetic



\(o(\delta)\) is not a specific function, but a notation meaning “some function satisfying \(o(\delta)/\delta\to0\)”. \(o(\delta)\), appearing twice in the same equation, can be different functions (one being \(\delta^2\), the other \(\delta^3+\delta^{3/2}\), etc.). Therefore, while the exact value of \(-o(\delta)-o(\delta)\) is unknown, we know that the result is again \(o(\delta)\). The rule that holds:

\(o(\delta)\pm o(\delta)=o(\delta)\) (finite sum)
\(c\cdot o(\delta)=o(\delta)\) (\(c\) is a bounded constant independent of \(\delta\). e.g.: \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n-2]\))
\(\delta\cdot O(1)\) is not \(o(\delta)\) — the first term survives.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 5.4 From difference equation to differential equation
text:
5.4 From difference equation to differential equation
Substitute (3) into (2). If we divide the cases into \(n-k\)

\(k=n\) (\(n-k=0\)): \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]\,(1-\lambda(t_2)\delta+o(\delta))\)
\(k=n-1\) (\(n-k=1\)): \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n-1]\,(\lambda(t_2)\delta+o(\delta))\)
\(k\le n-2\) (\(n-k\ge2\)): \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=k]\cdot o(\delta)=o(\delta)\) — \(\delta\) Even when multiplied by a probability unrelated to \(o(\delta)\), and since it is the sum of a finite number (\(n-1\)), the total is also \(o(\delta)\)

\[
\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2+\delta}=n]=\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]\big(1-\lambda(t_2)\delta\big)+\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n-1]\,\lambda(t_2)\delta+o(\delta). \tag{4}
\]
If we subtract \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]\) from both sides, divide by \(\delta\), and take \(\delta\to0\), the left side becomes the definition of the derivative and is \(o(\delta)/\delta\to0\).
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t_2}\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]=-\lambda(t_2)\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]+\lambda(t_2)\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n-1],\qquad \Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=-1]\equiv0. \tag{5}
\]
Interpretation (Probabilistic Flow). The probability of state \(n\) increases by the incoming flow “\(\lambda\Pr[n-1]\)” when one event occurs in “\(n-1\)”, and decreases by the outgoing flow “\(\lambda\Pr[n]\)” when one event occurs in “\(n\)”. This is the Kolmogorov forward equation for a pure birth process.

is an infinite system of differential equations for \(n=0,1,2,\dots\). Although it can be solved sequentially starting from \(n=0\), it can be solved in one step using a generating function.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
5.5 Generator function conversion
Defines the transformation of the count distribution.
\[
P(t_2,z)\equiv\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]\,z^n. \tag{6}
\]






NoteCode convention



This is the Probability Generating Function (PGF) \(E[z^{N}]\) of probability theory. Since the z-transform in signal processing usually uses \(z^{-n}\), there is a difference \(z\leftrightarrow z^{-1}\), but the principle of reading the coefficients is the same. The advantage of this transformation is that it changes an infinite system of equations for \(n\) into a single equation with \(z\) as a parameter. The distribution that was a function of \(n\) becomes a function of \((t_2,z)\).


If we multiply (5) by \(z^n\) and add it for \(n\ge0\),
\[
\frac{\partial P(t_2,z)}{\partial t_2}=-\lambda(t_2)\sum_{n\ge0}\Pr[N=n]z^n+\lambda(t_2)\sum_{n\ge0}\Pr[N=n-1]z^n .
\]
If we shift the index to \(m=n-1\) for the second sum (the \(n=0\) term becomes \(\Pr[N=-1]=0\))
\[
\sum_{n\ge0}\Pr[N=n-1]z^n=\sum_{m\ge0}\Pr[N=m]z^{m+1}=z\,P(t_2,z).
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{\partial P(t_2,z)}{\partial t_2}=-\lambda(t_2)\,(1-z)\,P(t_2,z). \tag{7}
\]
Boundary condition. If \(t_2=t_1\), the interval length is 0, so there is no event: \(\Pr[N_{t_1,t_1}=0]=1\), the rest are 0. Therefore
\[
P(t_1,z)=1. \tag{8}
\]

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
5.6 sun

is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation for \(t_2\) when \(z\) is fixed. Separating variables

\[
\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial t_2}=-\lambda(t_2)(1-z)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\ln P(t_2,z)-\underbrace{\ln P(t_1,z)}_{=\ln1=0}=-(1-z)\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\lambda(\alpha)\,d\alpha .
\]
\[
\boxed{P(t_2,z)=\exp\{-(1-z)\,C\},\qquad C\equiv\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\lambda(\alpha)\,d\alpha} \tag{9}
\]
\(e^{-(1-z)C}=e^{-C}e^{zC}\) and if we Taylor expand \(e^{zC}\)
\[
P(t_2,z)=e^{-C}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{C^k}{k!}z^k. \tag{10}
\]

and (10) \(z^n\) (inverse transformation of the generating function)

\[
\boxed{\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]=e^{-C}\,\frac{C^n}{n!},\qquad C=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\lambda(\alpha)\,d\alpha} \tag{11}
\]
In the normal case, if \(\lambda(t)\equiv\lambda_0\), then \(C=\lambda_0(t_2-t_1)\) and
\[
\Pr[N_{t_1,t_2}=n]=e^{-\lambda_0(t_2-t_1)}\frac{\big[\lambda_0(t_2-t_1)\big]^n}{n!}.
\]
In the normal case, the distribution depends only on the length of the interval \(t_2-t_1\) and is independent of location (normal increment). In the abnormal case, since it depends only on the cumulative amount of intensity \(C\), rescaled to the time axis \(\tau(t)=\int_0^t\lambda\) results in a normal process of unit intensity.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
text:
5.7 Result Verification
Normalization. \(P(t_2,1)=\sum_n\Pr[N=n]=e^{0}=1\). ✓
Mean and Variance (Derivative of the Generating Function).
\[
E[N]=\partial_zP\big|_{z=1}=C,\qquad
E[N(N-1)]=\partial_z^2P\big|_{z=1}=C^2,\qquad
\mathrm{Var}[N]=C^2+C-C^2=C .
\]
Mean = Variance = \(C\). Since the mean in the normal case is \(\lambda_0(t_2-t_1)\), the interpretation that “\(\lambda\) = average number of events per unit time” is justified here. As the standard deviation \(\sqrt C\) decreases to \(1/\sqrt C\) relative to the mean \(C\), the number is relatively concentrated around the mean over long intervals.
Direct assignment. Since \(p_n(C)=e^{-C}C^n/n!\) in \(\frac{dC}{dt_2}=\lambda(t_2)\)
\[
\frac{\partial p_n}{\partial t_2}=\lambda(t_2)\Big(-e^{-C}\frac{C^n}{n!}+e^{-C}\frac{C^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}\Big)=-\lambda(t_2)p_n+\lambda(t_2)p_{n-1}
\]
satisfies (5). ✓

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 5.8 Extreme behavior: When the interval and \(n\) grow together
text:
5.8 Extreme behavior: When the interval and \(n\) grow together
What happens to the individual probability mass when \(C\to\infty\) (the interval is very long or the intensity is high)?

\(n\) Fixed: \(e^{-C}C^n/n!\to0\). Exponential decay beats polynomial increase.
\(n\) also increases, \(n\approx C\) (near the mode of the distribution): Stirling formula \(n!\approx\sqrt{2\pi n}\,(n/e)^n\) \[
e^{-C}\frac{C^C}{C!}\approx\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi C}}\to0 .
\]

That is, for any \(n\), the individual mass approaches 0. Since the possible values spread out widely with a width of \(\sim\sqrt C\), each mass becomes smaller. A properly standardized \((N-C)/\sqrt C\) converges to a standard normal distribution by the central limit theorem.

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 5.9 Alternative Derivation: Binomial Limit of Coin Toss
text:
5.9 Alternative Derivation: Binomial Limit of Coin Toss
Let’s directly derive the normal case using the coin toss interpretation. If we divide length \(T=t_2-t_1\) into \(m=T/\Delta t\) cells and an event occurs in each cell with probability \(p=\lambda_0\Delta t\) (independent, maximum 1 per cell)
\[
\Pr[N=n]=\binom{m}{n}p^n(1-p)^{m-n},\qquad mp=\lambda_0T\ \text{고정}.
\]
From \(m\to\infty\)
\[
\binom{m}{n}p^n=\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}{m^n}\cdot\frac{(mp)^n}{n!}\to\frac{(\lambda_0T)^n}{n!},\qquad
(1-p)^{m-n}=\Big(1-\frac{\lambda_0T}{m}\Big)^{m-n}\to e^{-\lambda_0T}
\]
Since , we obtain the same result \(e^{-\lambda_0T}(\lambda_0T)^n/n!\). The derivation of the generating function can be seen as performing this binomial limit in the form of differentiation that “increases one by one.”

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 6.1 First arrival time and arrival interval
text:
6.1 First arrival time and arrival interval
The fact that the first event occurs after \(t\) is the same as saying that there is no event in \((0,t]\).
\[
\Pr(W_1>t)=\Pr[N_{0,t}=0]=e^{-\lambda_0t}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
f_{W_1}(t)=\lambda_0e^{-\lambda_0t},\quad t\ge0 .
\]
, that is, \(W_1\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_0)\). Due to memorylessness, the interval \(W_{i-1}\) to the next event \(X_i=W_i-W_{i-1}\) is also independent of the past \(\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_0)\), and the average arrival interval \(1/\lambda_0\). The exponential distribution itself also possesses memorylessness \(\Pr(X>s+t\mid X>s)=\Pr(X>t)\).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 6.2 The combined density of the first \(n\) events
text:
6.2 The combined density of the first \(n\) events
For \(0<w_1<\cdots<w_n\), the probability of “one event for each \([w_i,w_i+dw_i)\), and no events in between” is
\[
f_{W_1,\dots,W_n}(w_1,\dots,w_n)\,dw_1\cdots dw_n
=\prod_{i=1}^n\big(\lambda_0dw_i\big)\cdot e^{-\lambda_0 w_n}
\]
\[
\Longrightarrow\quad f_{W_1,\dots,W_n}(w_1,\dots,w_n)=\lambda_0^n e^{-\lambda_0w_n},\qquad 0<w_1<\cdots<w_n .
\]
It is interesting that the density depends only on the last time \(w_n\). This is equivalent to the arrival intervals following an iid exponential distribution (\(\prod_i\lambda_0e^{-\lambda_0x_i}=\lambda_0^ne^{-\lambda_0\sum x_i}\)).

title: Stochastic Processes - II
section: 6.3 Conditional distribution when the number is given: Uniform distribution
text:
6.3 Conditional distribution when the number is given: Uniform distribution
Under the condition that exactly \(n\) events were observed in the observation interval \([0,T]\), if we multiply the event time density by “\((w_n,T]\) no events” \(e^{-\lambda_0(T-w_n)}\) and divide by \(\Pr[N_{0,T}=n]\)
\[
f(w_1,\dots,w_n\mid N_{0,T}=n)=\frac{\lambda_0^ne^{-\lambda_0T}}{e^{-\lambda_0T}(\lambda_0T)^n/n!}=\boxed{\frac{n!}{T^n}},\qquad 0<w_1<\cdots<w_n\le T .
\]
This is equal to the joint density of the order statistic of \(n\) of the uniformly distributed iid samples \([0,T]\). Given the number, the events are scattered within the interval “without any preference.” Since this result does not depend on \(\lambda_0\), the visual information does not provide more information than the number to the \(\lambda_0\) estimation (in normal Poisson, \(N_{0,T}\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\lambda_0\)). Conversely, in abnormal autoexcitation processes, the visual arrangement itself contains information about the intensity.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
This document unfolds around the following single question.

Given the PDF of the random variable (vector) \(\mathbf{X}\), what is the PDF of \(\mathbf{Y} = g(\mathbf{X})\)?

The answer is summarized in a single sentence: “Probability mass is conserved, and volume changes by a factor of \(|\det J|\)”. To accurately understand this sentence, we organize Taylor expansions, Landau notation, Jacobians, the geometric meaning of determinants, and the inverse function theorem in order, and then apply the results to Gaussian random variables and probability vectors. Finally, we conclude with the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), which explains why Gaussians appear so frequently.







Part
Key Result




1D variable transformation
\(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,/\,\lvert g'(g^{-1}(y))\rvert\)


Multidimensional variable transformation
\(f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = f_{\mathbf{X}}(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y}))\,/\,\lvert\det J(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y}))\rvert\)


Gaussian
PDF, Standardization, CF/MGF, \(\mathbb{E}[e^{aX+bX^2}]\)


Gaussian Vector
Real/Complex PDF, Linear Transformation, CF, Isserlis–Wick Theorem


CLT
Normalized iid sum \(\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
2.1 CDF method
Let \(Y = g(X)\) and assume that \(g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is strictly monotone and differentiable. It is safer to start with the CDF rather than dealing directly with the PDF. This is because the CDF is probability itself, so we only need to accurately determine the equivalence of events.
In the case of an increasing function. If \(g\) increases, then \(g(X)\le y \iff X\le g^{-1}(y)\), therefore
\[
F_Y(y) = \Pr(g(X)\le y) = \Pr\big(X\le g^{-1}(y)\big) = F_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big).
\]
Differentiating both sides with respect to \(y\) (Chain rule)
\[
f_Y(y) = f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\cdot\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y).
\]
In the case of a decreasing function. If \(g\) decreases, the direction of the inequality sign is reversed: \(g(X)\le y \iff X\ge g^{-1}(y)\). In a continuous distribution
\[
F_Y(y) = 1 - F_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f_Y(y) = -f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\cdot\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y).
\]
Since \(\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) < 0\), the right side is positive.
Integration of the two cases. Using the differentiation formula for the inverse function \(\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) = 1/g'(g^{-1}(y))\) (justified in the next section), both the increasing and decreasing cases
\[
\boxed{\,f_Y(y) = f_X\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\cdot\frac{1}{\big|g'\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\big|}\,}
\]
It can be written as . The absolute value absorbs the negative sign that occurs in a decreasing function, ensuring that the PDF is always non-negative.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
section: 2.2 Geometric interpretation: If the slope is large, the density decreases
text:
2.2 Geometric interpretation: If the slope is large, the density decreases
The smaller interval \([x, x+\Delta x]\) is moved to an interval of length \(\Delta y \approx |g'(x)|\,\Delta x\) via \(g\). The probability masses contained in the two intervals are equal:
\[
f_X(x)\,\Delta x \approx f_Y(y)\,\Delta y = f_Y(y)\,|g'(x)|\,\Delta x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f_Y(y) \approx \frac{f_X(x)}{|g'(x)|}.
\]
, that is, if \(|g'(x)|\) is large, short sections are stretched out, so the same mass is spread out more widely, resulting in lower density. The PDF is scaled by the reciprocal of the local gradient. This logic of “mass conservation + length (area, volume) scaling” is extended directly to multiple dimensions.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
section: 2.3 Differentiation of Inverse Functions and Inverse Function Theorem
text:
2.3 Differentiation of Inverse Functions and Inverse Function Theorem

2.3.1 The formula itself is the consequence of the chain rule.
Assuming that \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\) are both differentiable, by differentiating both sides of the identity \(g\big(g^{-1}(y)\big) = y\) with respect to \(y\)
\[
g'\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)\cdot\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) = 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) = \frac{1}{g'\big(g^{-1}(y)\big)}.
\]
If only the formula is needed, the chain rule is sufficient. However, there are three hidden premises in this calculation.

Does \(g^{-1}\) exist (at least locally)?
Is \(g^{-1}\) differentiable? — If it is not differentiable, differentiating both sides is impossible.
Is the denominator ZZZPH0001448ZZZ \(g'(g^{-1}(y))\neq 0\)?

These three are propositions that require proof, and the Inverse Function Theorem guarantees this.


2.3.2 Accurate statement of theorem






ImportantInverse function theorem



Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set and let \(g:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a function \(C^1\) (where the derivative is continuous). At some point \(\mathbf{x}_0\in U\)
\[
\det Dg(\mathbf{x}_0)\neq 0
\]
If , then there exist open neighborhoods \(U_0\) of \(\mathbf{x}_0\) and open neighborhoods \(V_0\) of \(\mathbf{y}_0 = g(\mathbf{x}_0)\),

\(g: U_0\to V_0\) is a bijector, and
\(g^{-1}: V_0\to U_0\) is \(C^1\),
\(D g^{-1}(\mathbf{y}) = \big[Dg\big(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)\big]^{-1}\), \(\quad\forall\,\mathbf{y}\in V_0\).



The main body of the theorem is numbers 1 and 2, namely existence and smoothness. Formula 3 is a byproduct that follows by the chain rule after numbers 1 and 2 are secured.


2.3.3 Why is it necessary?
The question that Jeong-i answers is as follows.

Can the linear algebraic information (the Jacobian is invertible) at a single point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) guarantee the much stronger property that the nonlinear function \(g\) itself is invertible in its vicinity?

In one dimension, \(g'(x_0)\neq 0\), and if \(g'\) is continuous, then in the vicinity, the sign of \(g'\) is fixed, making \(g\) monotonic, and monotonic functions automatically have inverse functions. Since existence is obtained almost for free, only the formula stands out.
However, in \(n\ge 2\), the concept of “fixed sign” does not exist. \(\det J\neq 0\) merely means that the linear approximation at that moment has not degenerated, and it is not obvious that \(g\) maps to the neighborhood without overlap. Bridging this gap is the Inverse Function Theorem, which serves as the logical foundation for the following.

Equivalent to the Implicit Function Theorem: Solving \(g(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{y}\) for \(\mathbf{x}\) is a special form of \(F(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) := g(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\). One theorem can be derived from the other.
Justification of Coordinate Transformation: When integrating by converting to polar coordinates, spherical coordinates, etc., the transformation must be a local diffeomorphism. The sufficient condition for this is the invertibility of the Jacobian.
Multidimensional variable transformation formula: \(f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = f_{\mathbf{X}}(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y}))/|\det J|\) to be used later is meaningful only if \(g^{-1}\) exists and is differentiable.



2.3.4 The core idea of the proof
Since it cannot be bypassed by monotonism like in 1D, another tool is used.

If we consider ZZZPH0001467ZZZ \(A = Dg(\mathbf{x}_0)\) instead of \(A^{-1}g\), we can set it as \(Dg(\mathbf{x}_0) = I\) without losing generality.
If we let \(h(\mathbf{x}) := \mathbf{x} - g(\mathbf{x})\), then \(Dh(\mathbf{x}_0) = 0\). \(g\in C^1\), then it can be made into \(\|Dh(\mathbf{x})\| \le \tfrac12\) in a sufficiently small vicinity.
The equation \(g(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{y}\) is equivalent to the floating point problem of \(\phi_{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x}) := \mathbf{y} + h(\mathbf{x})\): \(\phi_{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} \iff g(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{y}\).
By the mean value inequality , \(\|\phi_{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})-\phi_{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x}')\|\le\tfrac12\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'\|\), i.e., \(\phi_{\mathbf{y}}\), is a contraction. The Banach Fixed Point Theorem guarantees the existence of a unique fixed point \(\mathbf{x}(\mathbf{y}) = g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\).
From the same inequality , the Lipschitz continuity of \(g^{-1}\) is derived, and using this, differentiability and Formula 3 are obtained.

In that the engine of the proof is the fixed-point theorem, it shares the same roots as the logic showing that Newton’s method converges locally.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
section: 2.4 In the case of non-injective silk
text:
2.4 In the case of non-injective silk
If \(g\) is not monotonic, multiple inverse \(x_1(y), x_2(y),\dots\) correspond to a single \(y\). Mass conservation can be applied separately near each inverse and then added:
\[
f_Y(y) = \sum_m \frac{f_X\big(x_m(y)\big)}{\big|g'\big(x_m(y)\big)\big|}.
\]
Example: \(Y = X^2\). If it is \(y>0\), then the inverse sequences are \(\pm\sqrt{y}\) and \(|g'(\pm\sqrt y)| = 2\sqrt y\), so
\[
f_Y(y) = \frac{f_X(\sqrt y)+f_X(-\sqrt y)}{2\sqrt y}\,\mathbb{1}\{y>0\}.
\]

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
3.1 Taylor expansion

3.1.1 Derivation of Ideas and Coefficients
Differentiable functions can be approximated by a polynomial in the vicinity of a point. \(x_0\) In the vicinity
\[
f(x) \approx a_0 + a_1(x-x_0) + a_2(x-x_0)^2 + \cdots
\]
Let , and determine the coefficients by repeatedly differentiating both sides at \(x_0\).
\[
f(x_0) = a_0,\qquad f'(x_0) = a_1,\qquad f''(x_0) = 2a_2,\qquad f'''(x_0) = 3!\,a_3,\ \dots
\]
Differentiating \(n\) times, the \((x-x_0)^n\) term survives \(x=x_0\), and since the coefficient \(n!\) is attached, it becomes \(a_n = f^{(n)}(x_0)/n!\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\,f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(x_0)}{n!}(x-x_0)^n\,}
\]
(The series converges to \(f\) when \(f\) is an analytic function.) A typical example is
\[
e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{x^n}{n!},\qquad
\sin x = x - \frac{x^3}{3!}+\frac{x^5}{5!}-\cdots.
\]


3.1.2 1st-order approximation
If you write it as \(x = x_0 + s\)
\[
f(x_0+s) = f(x_0) + s\,f'(x_0) + \frac{s^2}{2}f''(x_0)+\cdots.
\]
If \(s = 0.01\), then \(s^2 = 10^{-4}\). Since the contribution of higher-order terms decreases rapidly, if \(s\) is sufficiently small, using only the first-order term results in a good approximation. This is the first-order Taylor approximation (linearization), and it is the approximation used throughout this document.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
3.2 Landau notation: \(o(s)\) and \(O(s)\)
\[
f(s) = o(s)\ \ (s\to 0) \iff \lim_{s\to 0}\frac{f(s)}{s} = 0,
\qquad
f(s) = O(s)\ \ (s\to 0) \iff \frac{|f(s)|}{|s|}\text{ 가 0 근방에서 유계}.
\]








Notation
Meaning
Intuition




\(f(s) = O(s)\)
\(\lvert f(s)/s\rvert\) bounded
\(s\) at the same speed or lower, decreasing to 0


\(f(s) = o(s)\)
\(f(s)/s\to 0\)
\(s\) strictly faster than 0



\(o(s)\) is a notation that accurately records only the fact that the specific form of the remaining terms is unknown, but they can be ignored compared to the first term.






NoteDifferentiability itself is \(o(\cdot)\) linearization



If \(f\) is twice differentiable, the remainder is \(\frac{s^2}{2}f''(x_0)+\cdots\), so naturally it is \(o(s)\). However, higher-order derivatives are not needed for the expression \(o(s)\). The definition of differentiation is
\[
f(x_0+s) = f(x_0) + s f'(x_0) + o(s)
\iff
\lim_{s\to0}\frac{f(x_0+s)-f(x_0)}{s} = f'(x_0)
\]
This is because . The (to)differentiability of the multivariable function \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is also defined in the same way:
\[
g(\mathbf{x}_0+\boldsymbol{\Delta}) = g(\mathbf{x}_0) + J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\boldsymbol{\Delta} + o(\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|).
\]
, that is, “differentiable” means “locally approximated by the linear mapping \(J(\mathbf{x}_0)\) and the error is \(o(\|\boldsymbol\Delta\|)\).”

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
section: 3.3 Jacobian Matrix: Why “Rows = Output, Columns = Input”
text:
3.3 Jacobian Matrix: Why “Rows = Output, Columns = Input”
Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\ y_1 = g_1(x_1,x_2)\), and \(y_2 = g_2(x_1,x_2)\). Note that the two inputs \(x_1, x_2\) are passed into both component functions \(g_1, g_2\).
Component-wise first-order Taylor approximation. Since each \(g_i\) is a 2-variable scalar function
\[
g_i(\mathbf{x}_0+\Delta\mathbf{x}) \approx g_i(\mathbf{x}_0)
+ \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_1}\Big|_{\mathbf{x}_0}\Delta x_1
+ \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_2}\Big|_{\mathbf{x}_0}\Delta x_2,
\qquad i = 1,2.
\]
If you stack the two expressions vertically
\[
\begin{bmatrix} g_1(\mathbf{x}_0+\Delta\mathbf{x})\\ g_2(\mathbf{x}_0+\Delta\mathbf{x})\end{bmatrix}
\approx
\begin{bmatrix} g_1(\mathbf{x}_0)\\ g_2(\mathbf{x}_0)\end{bmatrix}
+
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
\partial y_1/\partial x_1 & \partial y_1/\partial x_2\\
\partial y_2/\partial x_1 & \partial y_2/\partial x_2
\end{bmatrix}_{\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}_0}}_{J(\mathbf{x}_0)}
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_1\\ \Delta x_2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Index placement is enforced by the definition of matrix multiplication. The matrix-vector product is defined as \((J\Delta\mathbf{x})_i = \sum_j J_{ij}\Delta x_j\). Since the change amount of the \(i\)-th output must be \(\sum_j(\partial g_i/\partial x_j)\Delta x_j\)
\[
J_{ij} = \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial x_j}
\]
It must be . The row index \(i\) indicates “what kind of output it is,” and the column index \(j\) indicates “in which input direction the derivative was taken.” The \(i\)-th row is the transpose of the gradient of \(g_i\).
Column Perspective: Directional Differential. If we read the same fact as columns, the \(J\)th column of \(j\) is
\[
J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathbf{e}_j = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{g(\mathbf{x}_0+h\mathbf{e}_j)-g(\mathbf{x}_0)}{h}
\]
, that is, the direction in which the output vector moves when it moves only slightly in the \(x_j\) direction. This column perspective is used critically in the subsequent area calculation.
If \(p\) dimension, then \(J\) is the \(p\times p\) matrix \(J_{ij} = \partial y_i/\partial x_j\). Also, \(J\) is a function of \(\mathbf{x}\). For example, just as \(y = x^2\) still depends on \(dy/dx = 2x\) for \(x\), the Jacobian also depends on where it is evaluated.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
3.4 Cross product, parallelogram, determinant

3.4.1 Definition and Calculation of the Cross Product
The cross product of the 3D vectors \(\mathbf{u} = (u_1,u_2,u_3)^\top\) and \(\mathbf{v} = (v_1,v_2,v_3)^\top\) is
\[
\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}
= \det\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{e}_1 & \mathbf{e}_2 & \mathbf{e}_3\\ u_1 & u_2 & u_3\\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} u_2v_3 - u_3v_2\\ u_3v_1 - u_1v_3\\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(Placing basis vectors in the first row is a formal notation for memory purposes.) The properties are as follows.

Direction: \(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{u}\)Z and \(\mathbf{v}\). Direct calculation gives \(\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) = 0\).
Size: Lagrange Identity

\[
\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2
\]
holds (verified by expanding the components). If we substitute \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta\)
\[
\|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\| = \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|\,\sin\theta.
\]
Since \(\|\mathbf{u}\|\) is the base and \(\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta\) is the height, the magnitude of the cross product is the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.


3.4.2 2D: Area \(= |\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]|\) (Sign-independent proof)
Let \(\mathbf{v}_1 = (a,b)^\top\), \(\mathbf{v}_2 = (c,d)^\top\). Since the area of a parallelogram is base × height \(= \|\mathbf{v}_1\|\|\mathbf{v}_2\|\sin\theta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area}^2
&= \|\mathbf{v}_1\|^2\|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2\sin^2\theta
= \|\mathbf{v}_1\|^2\|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2 - (\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_2)^2\\
&= (a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2) - (ac+bd)^2\\
&= a^2d^2 + b^2c^2 - 2abcd = (ad-bc)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\,\text{Area} = |ad-bc| = \left|\det\begin{bmatrix}a & c\\ b & d\end{bmatrix}\right| = |\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]|\,}
\]
This derivation makes no assumptions about the signs of the components. (The pictorial proof of subtracting a triangle from a large rectangle is not a general proof because it holds true only in configurations where all components are positive.)
If we look at the same result through the cross product, when we map the 2D vectors \((a,b,0)^\top\) and \((c,d,0)^\top\) to 3D and take the cross product
\[
(a,b,0)^\top\times(c,d,0)^\top = (0,\ 0,\ ad-bc)^\top
\]
Since , the magnitude \(|ad-bc|\) is the absolute value of the determinant. In other words, the magnitude of the cross product and the determinant are two ways to calculate the same geometric object (the area of a parallelogram).


3.4.3 Meaning of the sign: orientation
\(\det[\mathbf{v}_2\ \mathbf{v}_1] = -\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]\). The area is the same, but the sign is reversed.

\(\det>0\): Counterclockwise from \(\mathbf{v}_1\) to \(\mathbf{v}_2\) (direction preserved)
\(\det<0\): Clockwise direction (Reverse direction, mirror image)

Since the area cannot be negative, \(|\det|\) is entered into the variable transformation formula.


3.4.4 Why “Determinant = Signed Volume” (Axiomatic View)
If we list the properties that the signed area function \(A(\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2)\) must satisfy,

Linear to each factor: If one side is \(c\) times the area, the area is also \(c\) times. The area remains constant because the base and height remain the same even when a multiple of one side is added to one side (shear).
Alternation: \(A(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}) = 0\) (flat parallelogram).
Normalization: \(A(\mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2) = 1\) (unit square).

The function satisfying these three properties is unique and is the determinant. The same applies in the dimension \(n\), where \(\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{v}_n]\) is the signed volume of a parallel body formed by \(n\) column vectors. Also, the multiplicative property \(\det(AB) = \det A\,\det B\) is the algebraic expression of the geometric fact that “the volume is \(B\) with a linear mapping \(|\det B|\), followed by \(A\) with \(|\det A|\).”

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.1 Settings
Let \(\mathbf{y} = g(\mathbf{x})\), \(\ \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^2\), and \(g\) be differentiable and locally one-to-one. In \(\mathbf{x}\)-space, take a small rectangle (cell) with \(\mathbf{x}_0 = (x_{01},x_{02})^\top\) as one vertex. The two sides are
\[
\mathbf{e}_1\Delta x_1 = \begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_1\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{e}_2\Delta x_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\\Delta x_2\end{bmatrix}
\]
. The question is this: What do these two edges become in \(g\) after passing through \(\mathbf{y}\)-space?

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.2 Variant Parameterization and Image Curve
The first side (bottom side) is fixed at \(x_2\), and only \(x_1\) is moved. With the scalar parameter \(s\)
\[
\gamma_1(s) = \mathbf{x}_0 + s\,\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}x_{01}\\x_{02}\end{bmatrix} + s\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad 0\le s\le\Delta x_1.
\]
If you apply \(g\) to all points on this line segment, the curve in \(\mathbf{y}\)-space
\[
\mathbf{y}(s) = g\big(\gamma_1(s)\big) = g(\mathbf{x}_0 + s\,\mathbf{e}_1)
\]
We obtain . \(\mathbf{x}\) was a straight line in space, but since \(g\) is nonlinear, the image is generally a curve.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.3 Tangent vector: Chain rule
\(\mathbf{y}\) is 2-dimensional, and since \(s\) is a scalar, it is \(d\mathbf{y}/ds = (dy_1/ds,\ dy_2/ds)^\top\). Applying the chain rule component-wise, let \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x}_0+s\mathbf{e}_1\).
\[
\frac{dy_i}{ds} = \sum_{j=1}^{2}\frac{\partial g_i}{\partial z_j}\,\frac{dz_j}{ds},\qquad i=1,2.
\]
Since \(\frac{d\mathbf{z}}{ds} = \mathbf{e}_1\) (\(\mathbf{x}_0\) is a constant for \(s\)), if we group into a matrix
\[
\frac{d\mathbf{y}}{ds} = J(\mathbf{x}_0+s\mathbf{e}_1)\,\mathbf{e}_1,
\qquad
\mathbf{y}'(0) = J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathbf{e}_1.
\]
\(J(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{e}_1\) is the first column of \(J(\mathbf{x}_0)\), and is the directional derivative with respect to the \(x_1\) axis. By the definition of differentiability
\[
\mathbf{y}(s) = g(\mathbf{x}_0 + s\mathbf{e}_1) = g(\mathbf{x}_0) + s\,J(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{e}_1 + o(s).
\]
Here, \(o(s)\) is the remainder that vanishes faster than \(s\) (§Landau notation: \(o(s)\) and \(O(s)\)). That is, the upper curve appears like a straight line with a slope of \(J(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{e}_1\) near the starting point.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.4 Approximation of the side vector
\(\mathbf{y}\)-space The exact displacement of the first side is by the fundamental theorem of calculus
\[
\mathbf{v}_1 = g(\mathbf{x}_0+\Delta x_1\mathbf{e}_1) - g(\mathbf{x}_0) = \int_0^{\Delta x_1} J(\mathbf{x}_0+s\mathbf{e}_1)\,\mathbf{e}_1\,ds.
\]
If the variation is very short, becomes \(J(\mathbf{x}_0+s\mathbf{e}_1)\approx J(\mathbf{x}_0)\) over the integration interval, which becomes a constant independent of \(s\).
\[
\mathbf{v}_1 \approx J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathbf{e}_1\,\Delta x_1.
\]
\(x_2\) The same applies to the direction side
\[
\mathbf{v}_2 = g(\mathbf{x}_0+\Delta x_2\mathbf{e}_2) - g(\mathbf{x}_0)\approx J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathbf{e}_2\,\Delta x_2.
\]
That is, each small side is approximately translated into a straight line vector scaled by \(J(\mathbf{x}_0)\) and \(\Delta x_1\) and \(\Delta x_2\), respectively. Even a curved line is a straight line when viewed on a sufficiently small scale.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.5 Area of the upper cell
A linear mapping maps a rectangle to a parallelogram. Therefore, the image of the small cell \(R_{\mathbf{y}}\) is approximated by the parallelogram formed by \(\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\), and its area is \(|\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]|\).
Now calculate the determinant. If we take the scalar \(\Delta x_1,\Delta x_2\) out of the column
\[
[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2]
= \big[J(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{e}_1\Delta x_1\ \ J(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{e}_2\Delta x_2\big]
= J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\underbrace{[\mathbf{e}_1\ \mathbf{e}_2]}_{I}\,
\begin{bmatrix}\Delta x_1 & 0\\ 0 & \Delta x_2\end{bmatrix}.
\]
If you apply \(\det(ABC) = \det A\det B\det C\)
\[
\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \mathbf{v}_2] = \det J(\mathbf{x}_0)\cdot 1\cdot\Delta x_1\Delta x_2,
\]
\[
\boxed{\,\text{Area}(R_{\mathbf{y}}) \approx |\det J(\mathbf{x}_0)|\,\Delta x_1\Delta x_2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
dy_1\,dy_2 = |\det J(\mathbf{x}_0)|\,dx_1\,dx_2\,}
\]
The absolute value of the Jacobian determinant is the local area scaling ratio by \(g\). The sign of \(\det J\) indicates orientation, and the absolute value is used for the area.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.6 Density transformation from mass conservation
Just as \(\Pr\{x_0\le X\le x_0+dx\}\approx f_X(x_0)\,dx\) (height × width) in 1 dimension, the probability mass contained in a small cell in 2 dimensions is (density height) × (cell area). Since the same event corresponds to the cell and its surface, the probability mass is the same:
\[
\Pr\{\mathbf{X}\in d\mathbf{x}\}\approx f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}_0)\,dx_1dx_2
= \Pr\{\mathbf{Y}\in d\mathbf{y}\}\approx f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}_0)\,dy_1dy_2,
\qquad \mathbf{y}_0 = g(\mathbf{x}_0).
\]
If you substitute \(dy_1dy_2 = |\det J(\mathbf{x}_0)|\,dx_1dx_2\) and eliminate \(dx_1dx_2\)
\[
f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}_0)\,|\det J(\mathbf{x}_0)| \approx f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}_0).
\]
If you set the cell size to 0 and substitute \(\mathbf{x} = g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\) to write the right side as an expression using only \(\mathbf{y}\)
\[
\boxed{\,f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{f_{\mathbf{X}}\big(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)}{\big|\det J\big(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)\big|}\,}
\]
Interpretation: Convert \(\mathbf{y}\) to \(\mathbf{x} = g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\) to read the original density, and scale it by the local area factor \(1/|\det J|\). All that has happened is that \(|g'|\) in the 1D formula has been changed to \(|\det J|\). Since the derivative is now a \(2\times 2\) matrix, the determinant acts as the “size” of that matrix.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
4.7 Sanity check: linear mapping \(\mathbf{Y} = A\mathbf{X}\)
A Sanity check is a procedure that verifies whether a general formula obtained through complex arguments is consistent by substituting it into the simplest case where the answer can be known independently. Since the derivation above involved several steps, such as Taylor approximation and limits, it is necessary to check for the possibility of errors occurring somewhere.
If \(g(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}\) (\(A\) is reversible \(2\times2\)), then \(J(\mathbf{x})\equiv A\) and \(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y}) = A^{-1}\mathbf{y}\), so the general formula is
\[
f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{f_{\mathbf{X}}(A^{-1}\mathbf{y})}{|\det A|}.
\]
Meanwhile, this can be verified independently using only linear algebra: \(A\) maps the unit square to a parallelogram whose column vector is the column of \(A\), thereby increasing the area exactly by \(|\det A|\). Since any region can be divided into small squares, the area of all regions becomes \(|\det A|\) (as it is a linear mapping, this is exact, not approximate). For probability mass to be conserved, the density must be \(1/|\det A|\). The answers for the two paths exactly match.
Passing simple cases does not prove a general formula, but it gives confidence that there are no obvious errors. It is a habit worth practicing after a complex derivation.

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
5.1 Local volume scaling
If \(g:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is differentiable and locally one-to-one, then a small \(p\)-dimensional cuboid \(dx_1\times\cdots\times dx_p\) is
\[
\mathbf{v}_i\approx J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\mathbf{e}_i\,\Delta x_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,p
\]
It is transferred to the parallel field formed by . With the same factorization as in 2D.
\[
\text{Vol}(R_{\mathbf{y}})\approx|\det[\mathbf{v}_1\ \cdots\ \mathbf{v}_p]|
= \Big|\det\Big(J(\mathbf{x}_0)\,I\,\operatorname{diag}(\Delta x_1,\dots,\Delta x_p)\Big)\Big|
= |\det J(\mathbf{x}_0)|\prod_{i=1}^p\Delta x_i,
\]
\[
dy_1\cdots dy_p = |\det J(\mathbf{x}_0)|\,dx_1\cdots dx_p.
\]

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
5.2 Density conversion formula
From mass conservation in small \(p\)-cells
\[
\boxed{\,f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{f_{\mathbf{X}}\big(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)}{\big|\det J\big(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)\big|}\,}
\]
Here, \(J\) is the Jacobian of \(p\times p\) and is a function of \(\mathbf{x}\). Therefore, first calculate \(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\), evaluate \(J\) at that point, take the determinant, and place it in the denominator, while placing the value of \(f_{\mathbf{X}}\) at the same point into the numerator.
In the case of silk thread. If \(g\) is in the non-overlapping region \(\{R_m\}\)Z and \(k\) is in the ratio of 1, add the contributions of each inverse branch:
\[
f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_m\frac{f_{\mathbf{X}}\big(\mathbf{x}_m(\mathbf{y})\big)}{\big|\det J\big(\mathbf{x}_m(\mathbf{y})\big)\big|},
\qquad \mathbf{x}_m(\mathbf{y})\in R_m,\ \ g\big(\mathbf{x}_m(\mathbf{y})\big) = \mathbf{y}.
\]

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
6.1 PDF and parameters
The PDF of \(X\sim\mathcal{N}(m,\sigma^2)\) is
\[
p_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-m)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad\sigma^2>0.
\]

\(m = \mathbb{E}[X]\) (Average): Shifts the center (position) of the curve.
\(\sigma^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X)\) (Dispersion): Controls spreading. If \(\sigma\) is large, it is a wide and low species; if small, it is a narrow and pointed species.
As the distance from the center increases, the density decreases rapidly to \(e^{-(x-m)^2/2\sigma^2}\), so the probability of a large deviation is very small.


6.1.1 Proof of Normalization Constant: Polar Coordinates and Jacobian
If you set it as \(I := \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2/2}dx\)
\[
I^2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}\,dx\,dy.
\]
Converts variables to \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\). The Jacobian is
\[
J = \begin{bmatrix}\partial x/\partial r & \partial x/\partial\theta\\ \partial y/\partial r & \partial y/\partial\theta\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta\end{bmatrix},
\qquad \det J = r.
\]
Therefore, \(dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta\) (as seen in the previous figure, \(r\Delta r\Delta\theta\)) and
\[
I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\Big[-e^{-r^2/2}\Big]_0^\infty = 2\pi,
\qquad I = \sqrt{2\pi}.
\]
\(u = (x-m)/\sigma\) \(\int p_X(x)dx = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{-u^2/2}du = 1\) is confirmed by substitution (\(dx = \sigma\,du\)).

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
6.2 Affine transformation and standardization
Affine transformation. If it is \(Y = aX+b\) (\(a\neq 0\)), then in the 1D variable transformation formula, since \(g^{-1}(y) = (y-b)/a\) and \(|g'| = |a|\),
\[
p_Y(y) = \frac{1}{|a|}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\big(\frac{y-b}{a}-m\big)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi a^2\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\big(y-(am+b)\big)^2}{2a^2\sigma^2}\right).
\]
, i.e., \(Y\sim\mathcal{N}(am+b,\ a^2\sigma^2)\). The Gaussian is closed under affine transformations.
If you set it to Standardized (Z-converted). \(a = 1/\sigma\), \(b = -m/\sigma\)
\[
Z = \frac{X-m}{\sigma}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).
\]
If you check directly, \(\mathbb{E}[Z] = (\mathbb{E}[X]-m)/\sigma = 0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \mathbb{E}[Z^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X-m)^2]/\sigma^2 = 1\).

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
6.3 CDF and Q-function
PDF and CDF of standard normal \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)
\[
\varphi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},\qquad \Phi(z) = \Pr[Z\le z] = \int_{-\infty}^{z}\varphi(t)\,dt
\]
It is written as . The CCDF is used particularly frequently in the field of communications, and
\[
Q(z) = \Pr[Z>z] = 1-\Phi(z) = \int_z^\infty\varphi(t)\,dt.
\]
Since \(\varphi\) is an even function, symmetry \(\Phi(-z) = 1-\Phi(z) = Q(z)\) holds. The general Gaussian is obtained through standardization
\[
\Pr[X\le x] = \Phi\!\left(\frac{x-m}{\sigma}\right),\qquad \Pr[X>x] = Q\!\left(\frac{x-m}{\sigma}\right).
\]

title: Foundations of Probability Theory - II
text:
6.4 MGF and characteristic function

6.4.1 Derivation of MGF: Perfect square
\[
M_X(s) = \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\!\left(sx-\frac{(x-m)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)dx.
\]
Complete the exponent for \(x\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
sx-\frac{(x-m)^2}{2\sigma^2}
&= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\Big[x^2-2(m+\sigma^2s)x+m^2\Big]\\
&= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\Big[\big(x-(m+\sigma^2 s)\big)^2 - (m+\sigma^2s)^2 + m^2\Big]\\
&= -\frac{\big(x-(m+\sigma^2s)\big)^2}{2\sigma^2} + ms + \frac{\sigma^2s^2}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last line utilized \((m+\sigma^2s)^2-m^2 = 2m\sigma^2s+\sigma^4s^2\). If the term irrelevant to \(x\) is removed from the integral, the remaining integral is the total integral \(=1\) of a Gaussian PDF with mean \(m+\sigma^2s\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\,M_X(s) = \exp\!\left(ms+\tfrac12\sigma^2s^2\right)\,}
\]


6.4.2 characteristic function
\[
\Phi_X(jv) = \mathbb{E}[e^{jvX}] = \exp\!\left(jmv-\tfrac12\sigma^2v^2\right).
\]
The derivation of is \(s\to jv\), which is the same as perfect squaring, but in this case, the complex number \(m+j\sigma^2v\) comes in the “mean” position. The integral of a Gaussian shifted by a complex number.
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-c)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)dx = \sqrt{2\pi}\sigma,\qquad c\in\mathbb{C}
\]
The fact that still holds is justified by Cauchy’s theorem, which states that since \(e^{-z^2/2\sigma^2}\) is an analytic function and decreases rapidly at \(|\operatorname{Re}z|\to\infty\), the value does not change even if the integration path is moved from the real axis to the horizontal line \(\operatorname{Im}z = \operatorname{Im}c\). (Alternatively, since both \(M_X(s)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[e^{sX}]\) are analytic over the entire complex plane, \(s = jv\) can be substituted as analytic continuity.)
