3 Exercise 1 — Z-test (Right-tailed, \(\sigma\) known)






Some coffee beans are labeled as 250g per bag. A consumer group claims that this company packs more than 250g (overfilling) the beans. Assume that the population standard deviation of the packaging machine is known as \(\sigma = 5\text{g}\) and is reliable. 36 samples were measured. Test whether the claim is acceptable using the p-value method. (Significance level 0.05)



Since \(\sigma\) is given, it is a \(Z\)-test. Since it claims overfilling, i.e., \(\mu > 250\), it is a right-tailed test in which the alternative hypothesis supports a large value.
\[
H_0: \mu = 250 \qquad H_1: \mu > 250
\]
Since is right-tailed, the p-value is calculated as the area to the right of the test statistic, i.e., norm.sf(Z) (\(=1 - \Phi(Z)\)).

X = [
    253.52, 246.8, 255.75, 256.7, 242.24, 245.49, 252.64, 250.42, 251.92, 247.73,
    256.4, 255.89, 252.33, 257.64, 254.34, 247.7, 253.84, 247.21, 256.39, 251.75,
    251.08, 248.6, 258.11, 251.23, 249.86, 250.24, 254.66, 253.83, 254.06, 254.15,
    262.71, 249.97, 249.44, 247.93, 255.08, 257.64
]

# TODO: mu0, sigma, n 정의 후 X_bar 계산
# TODO: Z = (X_bar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
# TODO: pvalue = norm.sf(Z)  (우측 꼬리)
# TODO: pvalue 와 0.05 비교







NoteView Solution






X = np.array([
    253.52, 246.8, 255.75, 256.7, 242.24, 245.49, 252.64, 250.42, 251.92, 247.73,
    256.4, 255.89, 252.33, 257.64, 254.34, 247.7, 253.84, 247.21, 256.39, 251.75,
    251.08, 248.6, 258.11, 251.23, 249.86, 250.24, 254.66, 253.83, 254.06, 254.15,
    262.71, 249.97, 249.44, 247.93, 255.08, 257.64
])

mu0, sigma, n = 250.0, 5.0, len(X)
X_bar = X.mean()
se = sigma / np.sqrt(n)          # 표준오차
Z = (X_bar - mu0) / se
pvalue = norm.sf(Z)             # 우측 꼬리

print(f"X_bar = {X_bar:.4f}")
print(f"Z = {Z:.4f}, pvalue = {pvalue:.5f}")
print("결론:", "H0 기각 (과충전 주장 채택)" if pvalue < 0.05 else "H0 기각 못함")

xs = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.plot(xs, norm.pdf(xs))
plt.axvline(Z, color='red', linestyle='--')
tail = np.linspace(Z, 4, 200)
plt.fill_between(tail, 0, norm.pdf(tail), color='orange', alpha=0.6)
plt.title("right tail (p-value)")
plt.show()

With \(Z \approx 2.84\), the sample mean is 2.84 times above 250g by standard error. Since the p-value is approximately 0.0022, which is less than 0.05, we reject \(H_0\) — we accept the overload claim. If \(H_0\) is true (the mean is exactly 250), it means the probability of a sample mean this heavy is only 0.22%.

section: 4 Exercise 2 — The same test using the rejection region method
text:
4 Exercise 2 — The same test using the rejection region method






Test the same data and hypothesis as in Exercise 1 using the rejection region method. The critical value is norm.ppf(0.95), and if the test statistic is greater than the critical value, reject \(H_0\).



The rejection region method, instead of calculating the p-value every time, sets a critical value corresponding to the significance level in advance and checks only whether the statistic crosses that boundary. In the right tail, the critical value \(Z_{ub}\) is the top 5% point of the standard normal distribution, i.e., norm.ppf(0.95).
The reason the two methods always yield the same conclusion is that the CDF is monotonically increasing.
\[
\text{p-value} < \alpha
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
1 - \Phi(Z) < \alpha
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
Z > \Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha) = Z_{ub}
\]
In other words, “the tail width is smaller than \(\alpha\)” and “the statistic exceeds the threshold” are completely equivalent. The p-value method simply expresses how extreme something is as a continuous numerical value, whereas the rejection region method expresses whether the boundary has been crossed as a dichotomy.

# TODO: 연습 1의 Z 를 재사용
# TODO: cv = norm.ppf(0.95)
# TODO: Z > cv 이면 기각







NoteView Solution






cv = norm.ppf(0.95)            # 우측 꼬리 임계값

print(f"Z = {Z:.4f}, 임계값 cv = {cv:.4f}")
print("결론:", "H0 기각" if Z > cv else "H0 기각 못함")

xs = np.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.plot(xs, norm.pdf(xs))
plt.axvline(Z, color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.axvline(cv, color='green', linestyle='--')
region = np.linspace(cv, 4, 200)
plt.fill_between(region, 0, norm.pdf(region), color='lightgreen', alpha=0.7)
plt.title("rejection region")
plt.show()

print("두 방법 일치:", (pvalue < 0.05) == (Z > cv))

The threshold for is approximately 1.645, and since \(Z \approx 2.84\) exceeds this, it is rejected. This is the same conclusion as the p-value method in Exercise 1, and the last line confirms that the two judgments always agree.

text:
5 Exercise 3 — t-test (left-tailed, \(\sigma\) unknown)






Some power banks are advertised as having a standby time of 500 hours on a full charge. One reviewer claims that the actual standby time falls short of 500 hours. Although the population standard deviation was not given, it was confirmed that the standby time (population) follows a normal distribution. A sample of 25 was measured. (Significance level 0.05)



This time, \(\sigma\) was not given. Under the assumption of a normal population, if we substitute \(\sigma\) with the sample standard deviation \(s\), the statistic follows a \(t\) distribution with degrees of freedom \(n-1 = 24\). Since it claims a deficit, i.e., \(\mu < 500\), it is a left-tailed test supporting the small value, and the p-value is t.cdf(t_stat, df), which calculates the left region.
\[
H_0: \mu = 500 \qquad H_1: \mu < 500
\]

X = [
    490.63, 481.92, 482.11, 499.81, 500.92, 498.52, 484.01, 494.79, 493.4, 494.62,
    502.46, 494.68, 500.15, 492.81, 495.47, 499.58, 474.51, 488.16, 486.36, 484.33,
    488.7, 509.94, 481.61, 503.62, 471.81
]

# TODO: S = np.std(X, ddof=1) 로 표본표준편차 사용
# TODO: t_stat = (X_bar - mu0) / (S / sqrt(n)),  df = n - 1
# TODO: pvalue = t.cdf(t_stat, df)  (좌측 꼬리)







NoteView Solution






X = np.array([
    490.63, 481.92, 482.11, 499.81, 500.92, 498.52, 484.01, 494.79, 493.4, 494.62,
    502.46, 494.68, 500.15, 492.81, 495.47, 499.58, 474.51, 488.16, 486.36, 484.33,
    488.7, 509.94, 481.61, 503.62, 471.81
])

mu0, n = 500.0, len(X)
df = n - 1
X_bar = X.mean()
S = X.std(ddof=1)
t_stat = (X_bar - mu0) / (S / np.sqrt(n))
pvalue = t.cdf(t_stat, df=df)   # 좌측 꼬리

print(f"X_bar = {X_bar:.4f}, S = {S:.4f}")
print(f"t = {t_stat:.4f} (df={df}), pvalue = {pvalue:.5f}")
print("결론:", "H0 기각 (미달 주장 채택)" if pvalue < 0.05 else "H0 기각 못함")

xs = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400)
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.plot(xs, t.pdf(xs, df=df))
plt.axvline(t_stat, color='red', linestyle='--')
tail = np.linspace(-5, t_stat, 200)
plt.fill_between(tail, 0, t.pdf(tail, df=df), color='orange', alpha=0.6)
plt.title("left tail t-test")
plt.show()

With \(t \approx -4.37\), the sample mean is well below 500 hours. Since the p-value is very small at approximately 0.0001, we reject \(H_0\) — we accept the underestimation claim. If we had used a Z-test here under the misconception that we know \(\sigma\), we would have assumed a thin-tailed normal distribution, resulting in an underestimation of the p-value—that is, committing the error of rejecting too easily. Using a t-test when \(\sigma\) is unknown prevents this overconfidence.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
6 Exercise 4 — t-test (two-sided)






Some bolts are manufactured with a diameter of 10mm. The Quality Control team suspects that these bolts deviate from specifications (=are not 10mm) — whether they are too large or too small is a problem. The diameters follow a normal distribution, and the population standard deviation is not given. 20 samples were measured. (Significance level 0.05)



Since “it is a problem if it deviates, whether large or small,” this is a two-sided test that considers both tails rather than looking at only one direction.
\[
H_0: \mu = 10 \qquad H_1: \mu \neq 10
\]
Since the \(t\) distribution is symmetric around 0, we can convert the statistic to \(-\lvert t \rvert\) so that it is on the left tail, calculate the one-tailed probability, and multiply by 2 to obtain the two-tailed p-value. It is good to remember that symmetry justifies this “×2”, and that this simple doubling cannot be done in asymmetric distributions.

    9.901, 9.948, 10.259, 10.181, 10.302, 10.056, 10.185, 10.288, 10.082, 10.25
]

# TODO: pvalue = t.cdf(t_stat, df) * 2               (양측이므로 2배)

X_bar = X.mean()
S = X.std(ddof=1)

pvalue = t.cdf(t_stat, df=df) * 2               # 양측 → 2배

print(f"X_bar = {X_bar:.4f}, S = {S:.4f}")

plt.title("two-sided t-test")

The sample mean is approximately 10.15 mm, which is slightly larger than the standard. \(t \approx -4.76\) (value converted to left tail) and the two-sided p-value is small at approximately 0.0001, so \(H_0\) is rejected — it is determined to be out of standard. The symmetrical coloring of both tails in the graph illustrates the meaning of a two-sided test, which “looks only at deviation without specifying the direction.”

7 Exercise 5 — scipy Cross-validation with built-in functions






Verify the manual calculation from Exercise 4 as scipy.stats.ttest_1samp. Check if the built-in functions statistic and pvalue match the manual calculation.



The most reliable way to verify if the manual implementation is correct is to compare it with a well-verified library function. Since ttest_1samp assigns the sign of the statistic based on \(\bar X - \mu_0\) (i.e., a larger sample mean is positive), it differs only in sign from the negative number we appended when converting to the left tail. When comparing using absolute values, both the statistic and the p-value must match.

# TODO: res = ttest_1samp(X, popmean=10, alternative='two-sided')
# TODO: res.statistic, res.pvalue 를 수동 계산과 np.isclose 로 비교







NoteView Solution






res = ttest_1samp(X, popmean=mu0, alternative='two-sided')

print(f"scipy   : t={res.statistic:.4f}, p={res.pvalue:.5f}")
print(f"수동계산 : t={abs(t_stat):.4f}, p={pvalue:.5f}")

The two results match down to the decimal point. Of course, built-in functions are used in practice, but breaking it down manually like this makes it clear what the function does internally — it simply divides by the standard error, measures the tails of a \(t\) distribution with \(n-1\)Z degrees of freedom, and doubles the result because it is two-sided.

title: Hypothesis Testing
section: 8 Exercise 6 (Advanced) — Checking Type I Error Rate via Simulation
text:
8 Exercise 6 (Advanced) — Checking Type I Error Rate via Simulation






Repeat sampling from the population (\(\mu = \mu_0\)) where \(H_0\) is true, perform a two-sided t-test each time, and observe whether the proportion of \(p < \alpha\) converges to \(\alpha\).



A Type-I error is the error of rejecting \(H_0\) even though it is true. The true significance of the significance level \(\alpha\) is precisely the upper limit on the long-term occurrence rate of this error. This is not an abstract promise but a measurable frequency that can be visually verified using Monte Carlo.
We create a world where \(H_0\) is true (\(\mu = \mu_0\)), draw thousands of samples, and perform the test each time to count the rejection rate. If \(\alpha = 0.05\), the rate should be about 5% — meaning that if the test works “as designed,” the true null hypothesis is incorrectly rejected only 5 out of 100 times. This experiment allows us to experience firsthand that the p-value is not a probability for a single specific data point, but a frequency defined on the thought experiment of repeated sampling.

# TODO: H0 참인 모집단(평균 mu0)에서 표본을 sim 번 추출
# TODO: 매번 양측 t-검정의 pvalue 를 구하고 p < alpha 이면 카운트
# TODO: 기각비율을 alpha 와 비교







NoteView Solution






rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

alpha, n, mu0, sim = 0.05, 30, 0.0, 20000
df = n - 1

reject = 0
for _ in range(sim):
    s = rng.normal(mu0, 1.0, n)          # H0 이 참인 모집단
    S = s.std(ddof=1)
    t_stat = -abs(s.mean() - mu0) / (S / np.sqrt(n))
    p = t.cdf(t_stat, df=df) * 2
    reject += (p < alpha)

rate = reject / sim
print(f"alpha = {alpha}, 시뮬레이션 기각 비율 = {rate:.4f}")
print("alpha 에 근접:", np.isclose(rate, alpha, atol=0.01))

In 20,000 iterations, the rejection rate is approximately 0.048, which is very close to the set \(\alpha = 0.05\). Rejection occurred in about 5% of experiments even though \(H_0\) is true, and this is the operational meaning of “setting the significance level to 0.05.” As the number of iterations increases (law of large numbers), this rate converges more stably to 0.05.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
9 cleanup

If \(\sigma\) is known, use the Z-test; if not, use the t-test. In practice, it is rare to know the population standard deviation, so the t-test is the standard, and the additional variation of \(s\) is reflected as the thick tail of the t-distribution.
The p-value method and the rejection region method are equivalent. Due to the monotonicity of the CDF, “tail width \(< \alpha\)” and “statistic exceeds the threshold” always yield the same conclusion.
Two-sided test calculates the p-value as twice the tail of one side in a symmetric distribution.
The significance level \(\alpha\) is the upper limit of the Type I error rate, which is directly reproduced by simulation as a frequency defined over repeated sampling.

The next step can be extended to two-sample comparisons (independent and paired t-tests), Type II error, power, and effect size.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
Machine learning can be summarized as the process of finding a function \(f: X \to y\) from data. This process is broken down into four elements: a model that defines a set of candidate functions, a loss that measures the quality of the candidates, training that finds candidates that minimize the loss, and evaluation and validation that check whether the found function works well on new data.


A parametric model has a fixed number of parameters regardless of dataset size. Linear regression, \(y = X\beta + \epsilon\), and logistic regression are typical examples. Its strong assumptions allow stable estimates even with little data; however, incorrect assumptions lead to persistent bias, regardless of how much data is available.
Non-parametric models have an increasing number of valid parameters depending on the data. KNN, decision trees, and random forests belong to this category. While they are flexible and capable of capturing complex relationships, they require a large amount of data and carry a high risk of overfitting.



The loss function serves to formulate the learning objective. In regression, it is the MSE based on the sum of squared residuals.
\[
L(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - f(x_i;\beta)\right)^2
\]
, in classification cross-entropy (negative log-likelihood)
\[
L(\beta) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{k} \mathbb{1}[y_i = k]\, \log p_k(x_i;\beta)
\]
is primarily used. From a statistical perspective, minimizing MSE is equivalent to Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) under the Gaussian error assumption, and minimizing cross-entropy is equivalent to MLE for categorical distributions. The roles are distinguished in that loss is the subject of learning (optimization), while the metrics below are tools for humans to interpret performance.



Supervised learning uses input-label pairs \((x, y)\). When \(y\) is categorical, the task is classification; when it is continuous, the task is regression. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, such as clusters, density, and low-dimensional representations.





In binary classification, the following is defined from the four cells (TP, FP, FN, TN) of the confusion matrix.
\[
\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}, \qquad
\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}, \qquad
F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}
\]
Precision is the “proportion of actual positives among predicted positives,” and recall is the “proportion of actual positives caught.” The two have a trade-off relationship with a threshold between them, and since \(F_1\) is the harmonic mean of the two values, the performance drops significantly if either one collapses. In multi-class systems, a distinction is made between the macro mean (treating all classes equally), which simply averages class-specific metrics, and the weighted/micro mean, which is weighted by the sample size.



MSE is sensitive to outliers by squared penalty for large errors, while MAE is robust as it responds linearly to the magnitude of the error. \(R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2}\) is interpreted as “how much variance is explained compared to a model that predicts only by the mean” and is scale-independent.



Since there is no correct answer, silhouette coefficients that reflect both within-cluster cohesion and between-cluster separation are used.




The core principle is that test data is used only once to verify generalization performance after all selections are complete. All selections, including models, hyperparameters, variables, and thresholds, are performed using validation performance generated within the training data. Repeated use of test data in the selection process can lead to overfitting, causing performance estimates to become optimistically biased.
The method of splitting data must reflect the structure of the data. Stratified ensures that class proportions are maintained after splitting, grouped prevents information leakage caused by samples from the same individual, patient, or device entering training and validation simultaneously, and time series always learns from the past and validates against the future to prevent inversions where the past is predicted by future data.
Regarding validation methods, holdout is fast as it divides only once, but the estimation is unstable depending on the luck of the split, while k-fold cross-validation (k-fold CV) utilizes all samples for validation by dividing the data into k equal parts and using each piece for validation once, thereby estimating the mean and variance of the validation performance together. The computational cost becomes k times higher.
Model selection proceeds in the order of comparing candidate models on the same validation framework, retraining the selected model on the entire training data, and finally reporting generalization performance on the evaluation data.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
2.2 Diagnosis of Overfitting and Underfitting
The diagnostic tool is the comparison of training error and validation error. If the training error is very small while the validation error is large, it indicates overfitting (variance problem); if the two errors are similar but both are large, it indicates underfitting (bias problem). For overfitting, complexity reduction, regularization, data expansion, and early stopping are prescribed, while for underfitting, complexity expansion and feature addition are prescribed. If the training/validation curve is plotted with complexity as the axis, the validation error forms a U-shape, and the minimum point is the optimal complexity.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
2.3 Hyperparameter Optimization
Hyperparameters are values (tree depth, regularization strength, number of neighbors, etc.) that are not determined by learning but are specified externally by humans. Grid Search creates a grid of candidate values, evaluates all combinations through cross-validation, and selects the best one. Although the implementation is simple and reproducible, the number of combinations increases exponentially with the number of parameters; therefore, when there are many candidates, random search or Bayesian optimization become alternatives.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
2.4 Feature Subset Selection
The purpose of reducing variables is to suppress overfitting (reduce variance), improve interpretability, and reduce computational costs. The characteristics of the three approaches are distinctly different.
The filter method filters variables by ranking them based on the statistical association (correlation coefficient, F-statistic, etc.) between each variable and the target variable, regardless of the model. While it is very fast and independent of the model, it misses interaction or combination effects between variables because it examines them one by one.
The wrapper method explores subsets based on the validation performance of the actual model. Since examining all subsets (\(2^p\)) is nearly impossible, it employs greedy search methods such as forward selection, which adds variables with the greatest performance improvement one by one from empty sets, and backward elimination, which removes variables with the smallest contribution one by one from the whole. Although it reflects combination effects, it is costly because the model must be trained iteratively, and it does not guarantee global optimality due to being a greedy search.
Embedded methods are cases where variable selection is embedded in the training process itself. Lasso adds an L1 penalty to the loss
\[
\min_\beta \; \frac{1}{n}\lVert y - X\beta \rVert^2 + \lambda \sum_j |\beta_j|
\]
Reduces some coefficients to exactly zero. This stems from the geometric property where the solution lies on the axis (meaning the coefficients become zero) because the vertices of the L1 constraint region lie on the axis. Although it is efficient as selection and estimation are performed simultaneously in a single learning step, the selection result is dependent on the corresponding model.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
3.1 Gradient Descent
Since the gradient of loss \(L(\beta)\) is the direction in which the loss increases most rapidly locally, the parameter is shifted in the opposite direction.
\[
\beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} - \eta \, \nabla_\beta L(\beta^{(t)})
\]
The MSE loss in linear regression is \(\nabla_\beta L = -\frac{2}{n} X^\top (y - X\beta)\).
The learning rate \(\eta\) is the most important setting that determines convergence. If it is too small, convergence is slow, and if it is too large, it skips minimum points and oscillates or diverges. From the perspective of second-order approximation, the stability limit of the learning rate is inversely proportional to the curvature of the loss surface (the maximum eigenvalue of the Hessian).
The reason why variable scaling uniformity is important can be understood from the same perspective. If the scale difference between variables is large, the contours of the loss surface become elongated, distorted ellipses (due to the large condition number), and convergence in the direction of small curvature becomes extremely slow with a small learning rate tailored to the direction of large curvature. Standardization makes the surface nearly isotropic, allowing all directions to converge at a similar speed with a single learning rate.
Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) approximates gradients using random mini-batches instead of the entire dataset. Since it is an unbiased estimator of batch gradients, it moves in the same direction on average, but significantly reduces the computational load per iteration and helps to move away from local minima or saddle points where the gradient noise is shallow.
Early stopping observes the validation loss, which is set aside from the training data, during each iteration; if there is no improvement for a certain number of iterations (patience), it stops and adopts the parameters at the point where the validation loss was minimum. This can be interpreted as implicit regularization that views the number of iterations as the axis of complexity.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
3.2 EM Algorithm (Expectation-Maximization)
If there are unobserved latent variables \(z\) (e.g., which component of the mixture distribution each sample came from), the sum falls into the log-likelihood \(\log p(x;\theta) = \log \sum_z p(x, z;\theta)\), making direct maximization difficult. EM bypasses this through two iterations.
In the E-step, the posterior probability (responsibility value) of the latent variable is calculated using the current parameters. In a Gaussian mixture, the responsibility value for sample \(x_j\) belonging to component \(i\) is
\[
T_{ji} = \frac{\tau_i \,\mathcal{N}(x_j; \mu_i, \sigma_i^2)}{\sum_k \tau_k \,\mathcal{N}(x_j; \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)}
\]
In the M-step, the responsibility value is used as a weight, like the “partial ownership” of membership, to update the parameters.
\[
\tau_i = \frac{\sum_j T_{ji}}{n}, \qquad
\mu_i = \frac{\sum_j T_{ji} x_j}{\sum_j T_{ji}}, \qquad
\sigma_i^2 = \frac{\sum_j T_{ji} (x_j - \mu_i)^2}{\sum_j T_{ji}}
\]
Each iteration is equivalent to maximizing the lower bound of the log-likelihood (obtained via Jensen’s inequality), which causes the likelihood to increase monotonically and guarantees convergence. However, since the endpoint may be a local optimal, changing the initial values and trying multiple times is a practical approach.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
3.3 MCMC(Markov Chain Monte Carlo)
Monte Carlo Estimation approximates the expected value \(\mathbb{E}_p[h(X)]\) by the sample mean \(\frac{1}{N}\sum h(x_i)\) drawn from \(p\). The problem arises when it is difficult to draw a direct sample from \(p\)—particularly when the normalization constant is unknown, such as in the posterior distribution of Bayesian inference.
A Markov chain is a stochastic process in which the next state depends only on the current state, and if conditions are met, it converges to a unique stationary distribution regardless of the initial state. The idea of MCMC is to “design the transition rules of the chain such that the stationary distribution becomes the target distribution \(p\)”.
The Metropolis-Hastings (MH) algorithm implements this as follows: From the current state \(x\), candidates are selected from the proposal distribution \(q(x' \mid x)\), and the adoption probability
\[
\alpha = \min\!\left(1,\; \frac{p(x')\, q(x \mid x')}{p(x)\, q(x' \mid x)}\right)
\]
We either adopt or remain in the current state. The key point is that the normalization constant is canceled out because \(\alpha\) uses only the proportion of \(p\). In other words, we only need to be able to compute \(\tilde p\) of \(p(x) \propto \tilde p(x)\). This rule is designed to satisfy the detailed balance \(p(x)T(x\to x') = p(x')T(x'\to x)\), which guarantees that \(p\) is a normal distribution.
In practice, the initial sample (burn-in) before the chain reaches a normal distribution is discarded, the probability of acceptance is calculated on a logarithmic scale for numerical stability, and the mixing of the chain is verified using a trace plot. In Bayesian inference, setting it to \(\tilde p(\theta) = p(\text{data}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta)\) allows obtaining a sample of the posterior distribution to calculate the posterior mean, credit interval, etc.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
4.1 Why is it a problem?
If “all negative” is predicted in data where positives make up 0.2% of the total, the accuracy is 99.8%, but the model has done nothing. In imbalanced situations, accuracy distorts performance, so metrics from the minority class perspective (precision, recall, \(F_1\), PR curve) must be used, and the problem of loss minimization being dominated by the majority class is corrected using the methods below. One important principle: Resampling should be applied only to training data, and validation and evaluation data must maintain their original distribution to estimate performance in actual operating environments.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
4.2 Over sampling
Increase the sample size of the minority class to balance the ratio.
Random Over Sampling randomly duplicates the minority class. It is simple and does not lose information, but because the same samples are repeated, it is prone to overfitting to the minority class region.
SMOTE synthesizes instead of duplicating. Linearly interpolates between the prime class sample \(x\) and its k-nearest prime class neighbor \(x_{nn}\)
\[
x_{new} = x + u \cdot (x_{nn} - x), \qquad u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)
\]
Creates a new sample. This creates diversity rather than replication, but noisy samples may be generated when the distance between neighbors is actually in the majority class region.
ADASYN extends SMOTE by assigning more synthetic samples to minority samples that are surrounded by majority classes (making learning difficult). While this effectively reinforces learning intensively near the decision boundary, it is consequently more sensitive to noise.
Oversampling has the advantage of not losing information, but the disadvantage is that as the data grows, the training cost increases and there is a risk of overfitting and noise amplification.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
4.3 Under sampling
Reduce the majority class sample to balance the ratio.
Random Under Sampling randomly discards the majority of classes. It is fast and reduces training costs, but it loses potentially useful information.
Tomek’s Link finds pairs of neighbors that belong to different classes. Since these pairs are ambiguous (or noisy) samples spanning class boundaries, removing the majority class side from the pair clarifies the decision boundary. Because it cannot significantly alter ratios, it is often used in combination with other methods.
Undersampling has the advantage of faster learning and clearer boundaries, but the disadvantage that information loss is inevitable. It is practical when the data is sufficiently large.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
4.4 Adjust classification threshold
Without modifying the data, the threshold of the positive diagnosis criterion \(P(y=1\mid x) \ge 0.5\) is adjusted. Since lowering the threshold increases recall but decreases precision, the threshold at which \(F_1\) (or the cost function) is optimal in the validation data is searched for and used. Models with well-corrected probability estimations are more effective, and the cost structure can be directly reflected in problems where misclassification costs are asymmetric (fraud detection, disease diagnosis).

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
4.5 Differential data weighting
In loss calculation, greater weight is given to misclassification of minority class samples.
\[
L = \sum_i w_{y_i} \, \ell(y_i, \hat y_i), \qquad w_k \propto \frac{n}{K \cdot n_k}
\]
class_weight='balanced' uses this method to assign weights proportional to the inverse of the class frequency. Since it only changes the loss landscape without modifying the data, it avoids the side effects of resampling (replication overfitting, information loss) and is simple to implement. Conceptually, it is equivalent to oversampling in terms of expected loss, but it is efficient because it does not actually increase the sample size.

title: Summary of Core Machine Learning Concepts
text:
4.6 Perspective on Method Selection
No single method is always superior. Candidates are generated by considering data size (oversampling tends to be advantageous for small data, while undersampling is more favorable for large data), the quality of the model’s probability correction (threshold adjustment is simpler if it is good), and implementation and computational costs (weighting is the cheapest), and the final selection is always based on the indicators of the validation data that maintain the original distribution.

text:
임포트
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
1.1 Center-based clustering

1.1.1 K-Means
Objective function. For cluster partitioning \(S = \{S_1, \dots, S_k\}\)
\[
\arg\min_{S} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x \in S_i} \lVert x - \mu_i \rVert^2,
\qquad
\mu_i = \frac{1}{|S_i|} \sum_{x \in S_i} x
\]
This value is the SSE (Sum of Squared Error) and is exposed as inertia_ in scikit-learn.
Learning Algorithm (Lloyd).

Initialization — Sets \(k\) center points.

Forgy: Select \(k\) distinct data points as center points
Random Split: Assign each point to a random cluster and calculate the average

Assignment Phase — Assign each point to the cluster of the nearest centroid.
Update Phase — Update the centroid with the average of the points belonging to each cluster
Terminate when the center point no longer changes or max_iter is reached
Repeat initialization n_init times and select the result with the lowest SSE







TipWhy It Converges — K-Means as Coordinate Descent





If we view the objective function as a function of two variables \((S, \mu)\)Z \(J(S, \mu)\), the Lloyd algorithm is a coordinate descent method that fixes one variable and optimizes the other.

Assignment Phase: \(\mu\) Fixed → Assigning each point to the nearest center is the minimum value of \(J\)
Update Phase: \(S\) Fixed → \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \mu_i}\sum_{x \in S_i}\lVert x - \mu_i\rVert^2 = -2\sum_{x \in S_i}(x - \mu_i) = 0\) to \(\mu_i = \bar{x}_{S_i}\)

Both steps make \(J\) monotonically non-increasing, and since the number of possible partitions is finite (\(k^n\) or less), the algorithm must stop within a finite step.
However, global optimality is not guaranteed. Depending on the initial values, it falls into different local optima, which is why n_init is necessary.









ImportantThe reason why Euclidean distance is a premise



The reason we can use the “arithmetic mean” in the update phase is that the minimum point of the squared Euclidean distance is the mean. If we use the Manhattan distance, the minimum point becomes the median rather than the mean (→ K-Medians), and the “mean” may not be defined for arbitrary distances.
Therefore, if you simply insert different distances into K-Means, the monotonically decreasing objective function is broken and the convergence guarantee disappears.


Implicit Assumptions and Limitations

Assume the cluster is isotropic and approximately spherical.
It is implicitly assumed that the cluster size (number of points) and variance are similar.
Since it is squared loss, it is sensitive to outliers.
You must predetermine the number of clusters \(k\).


from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=100, max_iter=100, random_state=0)
km.fit(X_std)

km.labels_            # 각 포인트의 소속 군집
km.cluster_centers_   # 중심점
km.inertia_           # SSE (목적 함수 값)








Hyperparameter
Description




n_clusters
Cluster count \(k\)


n_init
Initialization iteration count (SSE minimum result accepted)


max_iter
Maximum number of center point moves per initialization





수식 확인 — SSE 는 단조 비증가한다
Xk = np.vstack([rng.normal(m, 0.5, (60, 2)) for m in [(0, 0), (4, 4), (0, 5)]])
cent = Xk[rng.choice(len(Xk), 3, replace=False)]

hist = []
for _ in range(30):
    d = cdist(Xk, cent)
    lab = d.argmin(axis=1)
    hist.append((d.min(axis=1) ** 2).sum())
    cent = np.vstack([Xk[lab == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(3)])

print("SSE 궤적 (앞 6개):", np.round(hist[:6], 2))
print("단조 비증가 여부:", bool(np.all(np.diff(hist) <= 1e-9)))




1.1.2 K-Medoids
While the representative points of K-Means are virtual points calculated as the mean (centroids), the representative points of K-Medoids are data points that actually exist within the cluster (medoids).
Objective function. Minimizes the sum of distances, not the sum of squares.
\[
\arg\min_{S} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x \in S_i} d(x, m_i),
\qquad
m_i = \arg\min_{y \in S_i} \sum_{x \in S_i} d(x, y)
\]
Learning Algorithm

Initialize random data points \(k\) into medoids
Assignment Phase — Assign each point to the cluster of the nearest medoid
Update Phase — Replace medoid in each cluster with the point that has the minimum sum of distances to other points within the cluster
Repeat until the medoid no longer changes
Adopt the best result among multiple initializations







TipWhy it is more robust than K-Means — The relationship between mean and median





This is exactly the same structure as the difference between squared loss vs. absolute loss.

\(\min_\mu \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 \Rightarrow \mu = \text{평균}\) — One outlier is dragging the average down.
\(\min_m \sum |x_i - m| \Rightarrow m = \text{중앙값}\) — Outliers only change ranks and cannot significantly change positions.

K-Medoids belong to the latter category and are therefore less sensitive to outliers.



Comparison with K-Means








Item
K-Means
K-Medoids




Representative point
Hypothetical average point
Actual data point


Loss
Sum of Squares of Distances
Sum of Distances


Distance measure
Euclidean virtually fixed
Manhattan, cosine, etc. free


Outlier
Sensitive
Robust


Calculation Cost
\(O(nkp)\) / Iteration
Distance Matrix \(O(n^2)\) Required


Interpretation

Representative point exists → Interpretation easy









Warning



The scikit-learn core does not have a K-Medoids implementation. (You must use KMedoids from the separate package scikit-learn-extraZ.)

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
1.2 Hierarchical Clustering
This is an agglomerative method that starts with each data point belonging to a single cluster and repeatedly merges the most similar pairs of clusters. A tree structure (dendrogram) is formed when the process continues until all data forms a single cluster.

1.2.1 Linkage
This is the criterion for determining whether to merge clusters \(A\) and \(B\). \(d(a,b)\) is the distance between points.








Method
Definition
Geometric Bias




Single linkage (single)
\(\min_{a \in A, b \in B} d(a,b)\)
Chaining, elongated cluster


Fully connected (complete)
\(\max_{a \in A, b \in B} d(a,b)\)
Compact spherical, sensitive to outliers


Average Connection (average)
\(\dfrac{1}{|A||B|}\sum_{a \in A}\sum_{b \in B} d(a,b)\)
Compromise between the two above


Word concatenation (ward)
Minimize increase in variance upon merging
Spherical clusters of similar size



Criteria for word linking. This is the sum of squares within clusters (MISSQ) that increases due to merging.
\[
\Delta(A, B)
= \sum_{x \in A \cup B} \lVert x - \mu_{A \cup B} \rVert^2
- \sum_{x \in A} \lVert x - \mu_A \rVert^2
- \sum_{x \in B} \lVert x - \mu_B \rVert^2
\]






Note



Word linking uses the same family of objective functions as K-Means (sum of squares within clusters). The only difference is the optimization method — K-Means uses iterative reassignment, while Word uses greedy merging. Therefore, the results of the two methods are often similar.




1.2.2 Lance–Williams recurrence relation
Calculating \(\Delta(A,B)\) according to definition every time is very expensive. The Lance–Williams recurrence relation updates new distances using only already calculated distances.
\[
d(k, i \cup j) = \alpha_i\, d(k,i) + \alpha_j\, d(k,j) + \beta\, d(i,j) + \gamma\, |d(k,i) - d(k,j)|
\]
when \(T = n_i + n_j + n_k\) based on squared Euclidean distance
\[
\alpha_i = \frac{n_i + n_k}{T}, \quad
\alpha_j = \frac{n_j + n_k}{T}, \quad
\beta = -\frac{n_k}{T}, \quad
\gamma = 0
\]
scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage is also implemented based on this recurrence relation, and the returned reference value is the square root of the squared distance.


수식 확인 — Lance–Williams 로 scipy 의 ward 를 재현한다
import itertools, heapq
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage

Xw = rng.normal(size=(30, 3))
D = squareform(pdist(Xw))
d2 = {(i, j): D[i, j] ** 2 for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(Xw)), 2)}
get = lambda a, b: d2[(a, b)] if a < b else d2[(b, a)]

clu = {i: [i] for i in range(len(Xw))}
h = [(D[i, j], (i, j)) for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(Xw)), 2)]
heapq.heapify(h)

idx, Z_manual = len(Xw), []
while h:
    crit, (i, j) = heapq.heappop(h)
    if i not in clu or j not in clu:          # 이미 병합된 군집은 건너뜀
        continue
    n_i, n_j = len(clu[i]), len(clu[j])
    new = clu[i] + clu[j]
    del clu[i], clu[j]
    for k, v in clu.items():                  # Lance–Williams 갱신
        n_k = len(v); T = n_i + n_j + n_k
        d = ((n_i + n_k) / T * get(i, k)
             + (n_j + n_k) / T * get(j, k)
             - n_k / T * get(i, j))
        d2[(k, idx)] = d
        heapq.heappush(h, (d ** 0.5, (k, idx)))
    clu[idx] = new
    Z_manual.append((i, j, crit, len(new)))
    idx += 1

Z_scipy = linkage(Xw, method="ward")
print("직접 구현 == scipy:",
      bool(np.max(np.abs(np.array(Z_manual) - Z_scipy)) < 1e-10))




1.2.3 Merge Information Matrix Z
The ZZZPH0004009ZZZ ||| Z returned by linkage is the \((n-1) \times 4\) matrix, and the \(i\)-th row is







Column
Meaning




Z[i, 0], Z[i, 1]
Index of the two merged clusters


Z[i, 2]
Distance between two clusters (connection threshold)


Z[i, 3]
Number of original data points included in the cluster after merging









Note



The cluster index is \(0 \dots n-1\), which is the original data point, and the newly created clusters from the merge are assigned starting from \(n\), increasing by 1.



from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

Z = linkage(X_std, method="ward")           # 데이터프레임 직접 입력
Z = linkage(squareform(D), method="average")  # 축약형 거리행렬 입력

dendrogram(Z)                                # 나무 구조 시각화
fcluster(Z, t=3, criterion="maxclust")       # 군집 수 3개로 절단
fcluster(Z, t=5.0, criterion="distance")     # 거리 5.0 에서 절단

agg = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, metric="euclidean", linkage="ward")
agg.fit_predict(X_std)








Function / Parameter
Description




linkage(y, method, metric)
y is a data frame or abbreviated distance matrix


fcluster(Z, t, criterion)
maxclust → t is the number of clusters / distance → t is the distance upper limit


AgglomerativeClustering
n_clusters, metric, linkage, distance_threshold









Importantfrequently occurring points




The distance argument name for AgglomerativeClustering is affinity for the old version and metric for the latest version.
linkage="ward" is defined only by Euclidean distance. Combining it with other metrics results in an error.
n_clusters and distance_threshold cannot be specified at the same time. To write distance_threshold, it must be n_clusters=None.

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
1.3 Density-based clustering — DBSCAN
DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) forms clusters based on the density around data points.

1.3.1 Key Elements

\(\epsilon\) Radius: Radius of surrounding areas to be considered as neighbors
Minimum Neighbor Count (min_samples): Minimum number of points within a \(\epsilon\) radius to become a key point



1.3.2 Three classifications of points







Category
Condition




Core Point
\(\epsilon\) Points with a minimum number of neighbors exist within the radius


Boundary point (border)
It is not a core, but is within the \(\epsilon\) radius of a core point


Noise point (noise)
Not a core and not within the radius of any core point





1.3.3 Cluster formation criteria

Reachability: It is possible to reach other points within a \(\epsilon\) radius from the core point. You cannot reach other points from non-core points. — This asymmetry is the mechanism that prevents boundary points from joining clusters.
Density-connected: If there exists a point \(o\) that is reachable to both \(p\) and \(q\), \(p\) and \(q\) are densely connected.
All densely connected points form a single cluster.



1.3.4 Learning algorithm

Initialize labels of all points to undefined, cluster number \(C = 0\), Calculate the list of \(\epsilon\) radius neighbors for each point
Select point \(P\) where label is undefined (exit if none)
If the neighbor count of \(P\) is less than the minimum neighbor count, mark the label as Noise and move to 2.
\(C \leftarrow C + 1\), \(\text{label}(P) = C\)
Define the reachable points from \(P\) as list \(S\)
Take one point \(Q\) from \(S\) (move to 2 if empty)
If \(Q\) is noise, change the label to \(C\) (becomes the boundary point), otherwise move to 6.
Set to \(\text{label}(Q) = C\), and if \(Q\) is the key point, add the neighbors of \(Q\) to \(S\) and then move to 6.







Importantmin_samples includes itself



In theoretical descriptions, it is often treated as “number of neighbors excluding itself,” but scikit-learn’s DBSCAN calculates it including itself.
Therefore, to correspond to the theoretical minimum neighbor number \(m\), you must specify min_samples = m + 1.




수식 확인 — min_samples 는 자기 자신을 포함한다
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

# eps=0.5 안에 서로 붙어 있는 포인트 3개 + 멀리 떨어진 포인트 1개
Xd = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [0.1, 0.0], [0.2, 0.0], [10.0, 10.0]])

for m in [3, 4]:
    core = DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=m).fit(Xd).core_sample_indices_
    print(f"min_samples={m} → 핵심 포인트 인덱스: {core}")
# min_samples=3 이면 3개 모두 핵심 → 자기 자신이 카운트에 포함된다는 뜻



from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

db = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=6)
labels = db.fit_predict(X)

labels                       # -1 은 잡음 포인트
db.core_sample_indices_      # 핵심 포인트의 인덱스








Hyperparameter
Description




eps
\(\epsilon\) Radius


min_samples
Minimum sample size within radius for determining key points (including itself)



Features

There is no need to predetermine the number of clusters.
You can find clusters of non-convex shapes (concentric circles, crescent moons, etc.).
Explicitly separates noise → Can be used directly for outlier detection.
On the other hand, if clusters of different densities are mixed, they are not captured well by a single \(\epsilon\).
In higher dimensions, \(\epsilon\) becomes difficult to set due to the distance concentration phenomenon.

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
section: 1.4 Mixture Model-Based Clustering — Gaussian Mixture Model
text:
1.4 Mixture Model-Based Clustering — Gaussian Mixture Model
Assume that the data was generated from a mixture of multiple probability distributions.
\[
p(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{C} \tau_j \, \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j),
\qquad \sum_{j=1}^{C} \tau_j = 1
\]
Each point is assigned to the cluster of the component with the highest membership probability. Unlike K-Means’ hard assignment, GMM provides soft assignment (membership probability).

1.4.1 EM algorithm
The parameter is \(\theta = (\mu, \Sigma, \tau)\).
E-step — Calculates the posterior probability (responsibility) that each point belongs to each component.
\[
T_{j,i}
= \frac{P(X_i = x_i \mid Z_i = j;\ \theta')\, P(Z = j)}
       {\sum_{k=1}^{C} P(X_i = x_i \mid Z_i = k;\ \theta')\, P(Z = k)}
\]
M-step — Updates parameters with responsibility as weights.
\[
\tau_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} T_{j,i},
\qquad
\mu_j = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} T_{j,i}\, x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} T_{j,i}},
\qquad
\Sigma_j = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} T_{j,i}\,(x_i - \mu_j)^{\top}(x_i - \mu_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} T_{j,i}}
\]






TipK-Means is a special case of GMM.





In GMM, if the following constraints are applied, it converges to K-Means.

Covariance of all components is fixed at \(\Sigma_j = \sigma^2 I\) (isotropic/identical).
\(\sigma^2 \to 0\)

At this point, responsibility \(T_{j,i}\) becomes 1 for the nearest center and 0 for the rest, so soft allocation collapses into hard allocation. Since the update formula \(\mu_j\) of the M-step becomes the arithmetic mean, EM becomes the Lloyd algorithm.
From this perspective, it is revealed that K-Means’ “spherical clustering assumption” was actually the isotropic covariance assumption. The reason GMM can capture elliptical clusters is also because it freely estimates \(\Sigma_j\).





수식 확인 — 등방 공분산 GMM 은 K-Means 와 같은 분할을 준다
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

Xg = np.vstack([rng.normal(m, 0.4, (80, 2)) for m in [(0, 0), (4, 4), (0, 5)]])

km = KMeans(3, n_init=20, random_state=0).fit(Xg)
gm = GaussianMixture(3, covariance_type="spherical", reg_covar=1e-9,
                     means_init=km.cluster_centers_, random_state=0).fit(Xg)

gm_lab = gm.predict(Xg)
agree = np.mean([np.max(np.bincount(gm_lab[km.labels_ == c])) / np.sum(km.labels_ == c)
                 for c in range(3)])
print("K-Means 와 등방 GMM 의 분할 일치율:", round(agree, 3))



from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture

gm = GaussianMixture(n_components=3, n_init=10, max_iter=100, random_state=0)
gm.fit(X)

gm.predict(X)        # 하드 할당
gm.predict_proba(X)  # 소프트 할당 (소속 확률)
gm.means_, gm.covariances_, gm.weights_




Hyperparameter
Description




n_components
Number of clusters (mixed components)


n_init
Initialization and training trials


max_iter
EM Repeat Count


covariance_type
full, tied, diag, spherical









Warning



If the sample size is small or the number of components is large, the covariance estimation becomes unstable, and in extreme cases, a singularity problem occurs where one component collapses to a single point and the likelihood diverges. This is prevented by adding small values to the diagonal components as reg_covar.

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
section: 1.5 Comparison of Clustering Model Pros and Cons
text:
1.5 Comparison of Clustering Model Pros and Cons








Model
Pros
Cons




K-Means / K-Medoids
Easy to understand and interpret results, fast computation
Number of clusters must be specified / Results vary depending on initial values, so there is a lack of consistency


Hierarchical Clustering
Number of clusters can be flexibly determined later and hierarchy can be viewed in a tree structure
High computational load (\(O(n^2)\) memory, \(O(n^2 \log n)\) or more)


DBSCAN
No need to specify cluster count / Detect various types of clusters / Noise separation
Difficult to apply to data with varying densities / \(\epsilon\) Sensitive


Mixed Model
Supports Elliptical Clustering and Soft Assignment / Stochastic Interpretation Possible
Unstable with Small Data Size / Requires Distribution Assumptions

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
2.1 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
PCA is a method that analyzes the amount of information (variability) contained in data through eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance matrix.

2.1.1 Covariance Matrix
For \(p\) dimension data \(X\)
\[
\operatorname{cov}(X) =
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_{11} & \sigma_{12} & \cdots & \sigma_{1p} \\
\sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22} & \cdots & \sigma_{2p} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\sigma_{p1} & \sigma_{p2} & \cdots & \sigma_{pp}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(x_{ki} - \bar{x}_i)(x_{kj} - \bar{x}_j)
\]
Key Properties

The diagonal element \(\sigma_{ii}\) is the variance of the \(i\)-th variable.
Symmetric matrix (\(\sigma_{ij} = \sigma_{ji}\)).
Positive semi-definite. , that is, for every vector \(x\), it is \(x^\top A x \ge 0\), and therefore all eigenvalues are greater than or equal to 0.



2.1.2 eigenvalue decomposition
For a square matrix \(A\), \(x\) satisfying \(Ax = \lambda x\) (\(x \ne \mathbf{0}\)) is called an eigenvector and \(\lambda\) is called an eigenvalue. Rearranging the terms
\[
(A - \lambda I)x = \mathbf{0}
\]
Since and for a solution \(x \ne \mathbf{0}\) to exist, \(A - \lambda I\) must not have an inverse,
\[
\det(A - \lambda I) = 0
\]
This is a \(p\) degree polynomial for \(\lambda\), so the eigenvalues are at most \(p\).
If we let eigenmatrix \(Q = [\,q_1\ q_2\ \cdots\ q_p\,]\) and diagonal matrix \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_p)\), then it is \(AQ = Q\Lambda\), and therefore
\[
A = Q \Lambda Q^{-1}
\]






TipThe reason why ZZZPH0004105ZZZ is a symmetric matrix and \(Q\) is an orthogonal matrix





\(A = A^\top\) so
\[
A^\top = (Q \Lambda Q^{-1})^\top = (Q^{-1})^\top \Lambda Q^\top
\]
For ZZZPH0004107ZZZ ||| \(Q \Lambda Q^{-1} = (Q^{-1})^\top \Lambda Q^\top\) to hold true in \(A = A^\top\), it must be \(Q^\top = Q^{-1}\).
A matrix such that \(Q^\top Q = I\) is called an orthonormal matrix, and at this
\[
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top
\]
It becomes . Since orthogonal matrices are rotations (and reflections), they do not change the length of the vectors. This fact serves as the basis for the conclusion later that “PCA preserves total variability.”





2.1.3 Induction of PCA
If you mean-center as \(X_c = X - \bar{X}\), the covariance matrix can be written as a Gram matrix.
\[
A = \operatorname{cov}(X) = \frac{1}{n-1} X_c^\top X_c = Q \Lambda Q^\top
\]
If you multiply both sides by \(Q^\top, Q\)
\[
\Lambda = \frac{1}{n-1}\, Q^\top X_c^\top X_c\, Q = \frac{1}{n-1}\,(X_c Q)^\top (X_c Q)
\]
Since the mean of \(X_c\) is 0, the mean of \(X_c Q\) is also 0. Therefore, component matrix
\[
C = X_c Q
\]
has the following properties.

\(\Lambda\) is the covariance matrix of \(C\).
Since \(\Lambda\) is a diagonal matrix, the covariance between the components is all 0 — they are independent (uncorrelated).
The diagonal element \(\lambda_i\) is the variance = explained volatility of the \(i\)-th component.
Since \(Q\) is an orthogonal matrix, the total variability of the data is preserved.







ImportantReasons why mean centering is necessary



For the covariance matrix to be written as a Gram matrix of the form \(X_c^\top X_c\), the mean must be 0. If not centered, the first principal component captures the “direction from the origin to the center of the data” instead of the “direction of data variance”.
Standardization (z-score) results in a mean of 0, so no separate centering is necessary.




2.1.4 Summary: PCA Procedure

\(A = \operatorname{cov}(X)\)
Eigenvalue decomposition into \(A = Q\Lambda Q^\top\) → Eigenvalue \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_p\) and eigenmatrix \(Q\)
Mean centering with \(X_c = X - \bar{X}\)
Components derived as \(C = X_c Q\) (assuming eigenvalues are sorted in descending order)

Variance Explanatory Power and Explanation Rate
\[
\text{설명력}_i = \lambda_i,
\qquad
\text{설명율}_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_{k=1}^{p}\lambda_k}
\]
\(\sum_i \lambda_i\) is the total variability of the data. Taking \(r\) variables from \(c_1\) to \(c_r\) is the choice that maximizes the explainable variability when linearly transformed into \(r\) variables.


2.1.5 Inverse transformation and information loss
Returns to the original dimension with only the selected components.
\[
X' = C' Q'^{\top}
\]

\(C'\): Matrix consisting of selected components
\(Q'\): A matrix composed of eigenvectors corresponding to the selected components

If all components are selected, it is theoretically identical to the original data (in reality, there are slight differences due to floating-point calculation errors). If only a portion is taken, volatility is lost by the sum of the discarded eigenvalues.
\[
\frac{1}{n-1}\lVert X_c - X' \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{k=r+1}^{p} \lambda_k
\]


수식 확인 — 총 변동성 보존과 절단 손실
Xp = rng.normal(size=(200, 4)) @ rng.normal(size=(4, 4))
Xc = Xp - Xp.mean(axis=0)
n = len(Xc)

lam, Q = eigh(np.cov(Xc.T))
idx = np.argsort(-lam)                 # eigh 는 오름차순 → 내림차순 재정렬
lam, Q = lam[idx], Q[:, idx]

print("총 변동성 보존:",
      np.allclose(np.trace(np.cov(Xc.T)), lam.sum()))

r = 2
Xr = (Xc @ Q[:, :r]) @ Q[:, :r].T      # 2개 성분만으로 역변환
resid = np.sum((Xc - Xr) ** 2) / (n - 1)
print("절단 손실 == 버린 고윳값의 합:",
      np.allclose(resid, lam[r:].sum()))
print("  손실 =", round(resid, 6), "/ 버린 고윳값 합 =", round(lam[r:].sum(), 6))



from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=0.98)   # 전체 변동성의 98% 를 설명하는 최소 성분 수
pca.fit(X_std)

pca.explained_variance_        # 고윳값 λ
pca.explained_variance_ratio_  # 분산 설명율
pca.components_                # Q^T (고유행렬의 전치)

C = pca.transform(X_std)       # 성분
X_inv = pca.inverse_transform(C)  # 역변환








n_components Value
Action




Integer
Select components in descending order of eigenvalue


Real number between 0 and 1
Select the minimum number of components explaining more than that proportion of total volatility


None
Select All Ingredients









Important



pca.components_ is not \(Q\) but \(Q^\top\). Therefore, the manual inverse conversion is C @ pca.components_, not C @ pca.components_.T.








WarningMeaning of standardization status




Covariance Matrix-based PCA (Centering Only): The original scale of the variables is reflected as is. The variable with the larger unit dominates the principal component.
Correlation Matrix-based PCA (Standardized): Treats all variables equally.

If the units of the variables are different, standardization is practically essential.

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
2.2 Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)
\(m \times n\) decomposes the matrix \(M\) into the product of three matrices.
\[
M = U \Sigma V^\top
\]

\(U\): \(m \times m\) Orthogonal matrix (\(U^\top U = I\)) — Left singular matrix
\(\Sigma\): \(m \times n\) Diagonal matrix, diagonal elements are called singular values.
\(V\): \(n \times n\) Orthogonal matrix (\(V^\top V = I\)) — Right singular matrix


2.2.1 Main properties
\[
M M^\top = U \Sigma V^\top V \Sigma^\top U^\top = U \Sigma \Sigma^\top U^\top
\quad\Rightarrow\quad U \text{ 는 } MM^\top \text{ 의 고유벡터}
\]
\[
M^\top M = V \Sigma^\top U^\top U \Sigma V^\top = V \Sigma^\top \Sigma V^\top
\quad\Rightarrow\quad V \text{ 는 } M^\top M \text{ 의 고유벡터}
\]


2.2.2 Relationship with PCA
If we mean-center \(X = M - E(M)\)
\[
\operatorname{cov}(X) = \frac{1}{n-1} X^\top X = \frac{1}{n-1} V \Sigma^\top \Sigma V^\top
\]
Therefore, it corresponds to the components of PCA as follows.
\[
Q = V,
\qquad
\Lambda = \frac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^\top \Sigma,
\qquad
C = XV = U\Sigma
\]






TipWhy SVD is used in practical implementations





Although mathematically it is possible to create a covariance matrix and perform eigenvalue decomposition, SVD is mostly used in actual implementations.

If you explicitly calculate Numerical Stability — \(X^\top X\), the condition number becomes squared. In the direction where the singular value is \(\sigma\), the eigenvalue becomes \(\sigma^2\), so the small singular value is buried in the rounding error. SVD avoids this problem because it acts directly on \(X\).
Memory — In the case of \(p \gg n\), you do not need to create the \(p \times p\) covariance matrix.
sklearn.decomposition.PCA is also internally SVD-based.

Sign Note: Since the signs of eigenvectors are not unique, the results of eigenvalue decomposition and SVD may have component signs that are reversed. This does not affect magnitude-based interpretations such as variance explanation.





수식 확인 — PCA 와 SVD 의 동치
U, S, VT = svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)

print("λ == S²/(n-1):", np.allclose(lam, S ** 2 / (n - 1)))
print("|X_c Q| == |UΣ| (부호 제외):", np.allclose(np.abs(Xc @ Q), np.abs(U * S)))
print("\nλ      =", np.round(lam, 4))
print("S²/(n-1) =", np.round(S ** 2 / (n - 1), 4))




2.2.3 Reduced Singular Value Decomposition (Reduced SVD)








Type
Definition
Characteristics




full SVD
\(M = U\Sigma V^{*}\)
Includes all singular vectors regardless of singular values


thin SVD
\(M = U_k \Sigma_k V_k^{*}\), \(k = \min(n,m)\)
\(\Sigma\) Reduces only as much as becomes square. Efficient when \(k \ll \max(n,m)\)


compact SVD
\(M = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^{*}\)
Keeps only non-zero singular values. Efficient when \(r \ll \min(n,m)\)


truncated SVD
\(\bar{M} = U_t \Sigma_t V_t^{*}\)
Keep only those singular values above the threshold. Approximation matrix not equal to \(M\)









TipWhy Truncated SVD is the “Optimal” Approximation — Eckart–Young Theorem





Among all matrices \(r\) and below, \(B\), \(\bar{M}_r\), which has only large singular values \(r\), is the closest approximation to \(M\) in both the Frobenius norm and the spectral norm.
\[
\lVert M - \bar{M}_r \rVert_F = \min_{\operatorname{rank}(B) \le r} \lVert M - B \rVert_F
= \sqrt{\sum_{i > r} \sigma_i^2}
\]
In other words, the greedy choice of “taking the largest singular value first” is actually the global optimal. This is the same story as “taking the largest eigenvalue first” being optimal in PCA.




from numpy.linalg import svd
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD

U, Sigma, VT = svd(M, full_matrices=False)   # thin SVD

tsvd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=100, random_state=0)
X_reduced = tsvd.fit_transform(X_sparse)     # 희소 행렬에 효율적







ImportantThe decisive difference between PCA and TruncatedSVD



TruncatedSVD does not mean center.

This is the intended design. If you center a sparse matrix like a text count matrix This is because the matrix, which was mostly 0, becomes a dense matrix, causing memory to explode.
So, for sparse matrix-based dimensionality reduction (LSA, etc.), TruncatedSVD is used.
Conversely, if you use TruncatedSVD on dense data, you get a different result from PCA.





수식 확인 — TruncatedSVD 는 중심화하지 않는다
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, TruncatedSVD

Xo = Xp + 100.0   # 평균이 0 에서 크게 벗어난 데이터

p_out = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xo)
t_out = TruncatedSVD(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xo)

print("PCA 결과의 평균          :", np.round(p_out.mean(axis=0), 6))
print("TruncatedSVD 결과의 평균 :", np.round(t_out.mean(axis=0), 4))

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
2.3 Multidimensional Scaling (MDS)
Converts \(k\) dimension data to \(m \le k\) dimension, while preserving distance information between the original data as much as possible.

2.3.1 Classical MDS (Classical MDS)
Supports only metric distances (distances satisfying non-negative, symmetric, and triangle inequalities, e.g., Euclidean distance) and minimizes the strain loss function.
\[
\text{Strain}_D(x_1, \dots, x_n)
= \sqrt{ \frac{\sum_{i,j}\left(b_{ij} - x_i^\top x_j\right)^2}{\sum_{i,j} b_{ij}^2} }
\]
Learning Algorithm

Prepare the squared distance matrix \(D^{(2)} = [\,d_{ij}^2\,]\)
Calculate \(B\) using double centering
\[
C = I - \tfrac{1}{n}J \ \ (J \text{ 는 모든 요소가 1인 } n \times n \text{ 행렬}),
\qquad
B = -\tfrac{1}{2}\, C D^{(2)} C
\]
We perform eigenvalue decomposition of \(B\) and select \(m\) with large eigenvalues Construct the eigenvector matrices \(Q_m\) and \(\Lambda_m^{1/2}\)
\(X_{\text{mds}} = Q_m \Lambda_m^{1/2}\)







TipClassical MDS = PCA in Euclidean distance





The double centering matrix \(B\) is actually the Gram matrix of the centered data.
\[
B = -\tfrac{1}{2} C D^{(2)} C = X_c X_c^\top
\]
Meanwhile, PCA decomposes \(X_c^\top X_c\). \(X_c X_c^\top\) and \(X_c^\top X_c\) have completely identical non-zero eigenvalues (both are \(\Sigma^2\) when viewed via SVD), the eigenvector of \(B\) is \(U\), and the eigenvector of PCA is \(V\).
\[
X_{\text{mds}} = U_m \Sigma_m = X_c V_m = C_{\text{PCA}}
\]
Therefore, classical MDS using Euclidean distance yields the same result as PCA. This has practical significance as it can substitute for PCA when only the distance matrix is given and the original data is unavailable.





수식 확인 — 고전적 MDS == PCA (유클리드 거리)
D2 = squareform(pdist(Xc)) ** 2
Cmat = np.eye(n) - np.ones((n, n)) / n
B = -0.5 * Cmat @ D2 @ Cmat

lamB, QB = eigh(B)
idxB = np.argsort(-lamB)[:2]
X_mds = QB[:, idxB] * np.sqrt(lamB[idxB])
X_pca = Xc @ Q[:, :2]

print("classical MDS == PCA (부호 제외):",
      np.allclose(np.abs(X_mds), np.abs(X_pca)))




2.3.2 Metric MDS and Non-metric MDS
Metric MDS — Generalizes classical MDS to various distances and minimizes stress loss.
\[
\text{stress}_D(x_1, \dots, x_n)
= \sqrt{\sum_{i \ne j} \left(d_{ij} - \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert\right)^2}
\]
Optimization uses the stress majorization algorithm.
Non-metric MDS — Maintains the rank of the distance, not the distance itself.
\[
\text{stress}_D
= \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i<j}\left(f(d_{ij}) - \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert\right)^2}
              {\sum_{i<j}\left(\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert\right)^2}}
\]
where \(f\) is a monotonically increasing function. It is suitable when distance is an ordinal scale.

from sklearn.manifold import MDS

mds = MDS(n_components=2, metric=True)   # False → non-metric MDS
X_mds = mds.fit_transform(X)
mds.stress_

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
2.4 t-SNE
This is a probabilistic method for reducing high-dimensional data to 2-3 dimensions for visualization.
Circular Space — Defines and symmetries Gaussian-based conditional probabilities.
\[
p_{j|i} = \frac{\exp\left(-\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2 / 2\sigma_i^2\right)}
               {\sum_{k \ne i}\exp\left(-\lVert x_i - x_k \rVert^2 / 2\sigma_i^2\right)},
\qquad
p_{ij} = \frac{p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}}{2n}
\]
Reduced space — Uses the \(t\) distribution with 1 degree of freedom.
\[
q_{ij} = \frac{\left(1 + \lVert y_i - y_j \rVert^2\right)^{-1}}
              {\sum_{k}\sum_{l \ne k}\left(1 + \lVert y_k - y_l \rVert^2\right)^{-1}}
\]
Loss function — Minimize the KL divergence of the two distributions using gradient descent.
\[
L = \mathrm{KL}(P \Vert Q) = \sum_{i \ne j} p_{ij} \log \frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}
\]
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_i}
= 4 \sum_j (y_i - y_j)(p_{ij} - q_{ij})\left(1 + \lVert y_i - y_j \rVert^2\right)^{-1}
\]






TipWhy is only the reduced space \(t\) distribution — crowding problem





In high dimensions, the number of “reasonably separated” points increases exponentially as the dimension increases. If you try to arrange them in 2D, space is insufficient, so points of intermediate distance are all compressed towards the center. This is the crowding problem.
The \(t\) distribution with 1 degree of freedom has thicker tails than the Gaussian.
\[
q \propto \left(1 + \lVert y_i - y_j\rVert^2\right)^{-1}
\quad\text{vs}\quad
p \propto \exp\left(-\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert^2 / 2\sigma^2\right)
\]
To obtain the same probability value \(q\), a much greater distance is required from the \(t\) distribution. As a result, there is room for intermediate distance pairs to spread out more generously in lower dimensions, and the cluster structure does not get crushed.









Warningt-SNE Caution When Interpreting Results




The distance between clusters is meaningless. Even if two clusters appear far apart, they are not actually far apart.
The size (area) of the cluster is also meaningless. High-density clusters appear magnified.
This is a non-deterministic method where the result varies significantly depending on the initial value and perplexity.
transform No method found → Cannot be applied to new data, visualization only.




from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=0)
X_tsne = tsne.fit_transform(X)   # fit_transform 만 존재 (transform 없음)

Description




n_components
Number of output dimensions (usually 2 or 3)


perplexity
Between 5 and 50, corresponds to the number of significant neighbors. Larger data corresponds to larger values.

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
2.5 Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
If PCA finds the linear transformation that “best explains the data,” LDA finds the linear transformation that “best distinguishes classes”. → Supervised learning-based dimensionality reduction

2.5.1 Idea

Maximize between-class volatility, Minimize within-class volatility

Covariance between classes
\[
\Sigma_b = \frac{1}{C}\sum_{i=1}^{C}(\mu_i - \mu)(\mu_i - \mu)^\top
\]
\(\mu_i\) is the average score of class \(i\), and \(\mu\) is the overall average score.
It is assumed that within-class covariance is the same across all classes.
\[
\Sigma = \Sigma_1 = \cdots = \Sigma_C
\]


2.5.2 Learning algorithm
The transformation that explains the maximum volatility of \(\Sigma_b\) is obtained through eigenvalue decomposition.
\[
\Sigma_b = Q_b \Lambda_b Q_b^\top
\]
At this time, the number of non-zero eigenvalues is maximum \(C-1\).
The transformation that minimizes the within-class covariance is the inverse matrix.
\[
\Sigma = Q \Lambda Q^\top
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Sigma^{-1} = Q \Lambda^{-1} Q^\top
\]
Since \(\Lambda\) becomes the reciprocal, it becomes the direction of minimization. The two processes are combined into a single eigenvalue decomposition.
\[
S = \Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_b
\]
By performing eigenvalue decomposition on \(S\), we simultaneously obtain a linear transformation that explains the variability between classes to the maximum extent and the explanatory power of each component.






Important\(S\) is not a symmetric matrix



\(\Sigma^{-1}\) and \(\Sigma_b\) are each symmetric, but the product of two symmetric matrices is generally not symmetric.
Therefore, you must use numpy.linalg.eig instead of numpy.linalg.eigh. eigh is for symmetric (Hermitian) matrices only and produces incorrect results when used for asymmetric matrices.
Since eig can return complex eigenvalues, you must take the real part as .real.








TipThe reason the upper limit of the number of ingredients is \(\min(C-1, p)\)





\(\Sigma_b\) is the sum of the cross products of \(C\) average deviation vectors \((\mu_i - \mu)\). However, there is one constraint on these \(C\) vectors.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{C} n_i (\mu_i - \mu) = \mathbf{0}
\]
Since the weighted sum of deviations of the overall mean is 0 by definition, one of the \(C\) vectors is a linear combination of the remainders. Therefore, \(\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma_b) \le C - 1\), and the rank of \(S = \Sigma^{-1}\Sigma_b\) does not exceed this.
Of course, since the number of variables \(p\) cannot be exceeded, the final upper limit is \(\min(C-1,\ p)\).





수식 확인 — LDA 성분 수의 상한
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

Xl = rng.normal(size=(300, 10))
yl = rng.integers(0, 4, 300)          # 클래스 4개, 변수 10개

out = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis().fit_transform(Xl, yl)
print("LDA 출력 차원:", out.shape[1], "= min(C-1, p) =", min(4 - 1, 10))



from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)
X_lda = lda.fit_transform(X, y)        # y 필요 (지도 학습)

lda.explained_variance_ratio_

title: Summary of Unsupervised Learning Concepts: Clustering · Dimensionality Reduction · Outlier Detection
text:
2.6 Partial Least Squares Regression (PLS)
Find the linear transformation that maximizes the covariance between the input \(X\) and the numeric target variable \(y\).

2.6.1 Induction of optimal direction
Let be the linear transformation \(t = Xw\), and assuming that \(X\) and \(y\) are mean-centered,
\[
\operatorname{cov}(t, y) = \frac{1}{n-1} w^\top X^\top y
= \frac{1}{n-1}\lVert w \rVert \cdot \lVert X^\top y \rVert \cos\theta
\]
Since \(-1 \le \cos\theta \le 1\), it is maximum when \(\cos\theta = 1\), that is, when \(w\) and \(X^\top y\) are in the same direction. If normalized to \(\lVert w \rVert = 1\)
\[
w = \frac{X^\top y}{\lVert X^\top y \rVert}
\]


2.6.2 NIPALS algorithm

Mean centering \(X\), \(y\)
\(w = \dfrac{X^\top y}{\lVert X^\top y \rVert}\)
Calculated regression coefficients by solving the normal equation using \(t = Xw\) and \(y\) \[\beta = (t^\top t)^{-1}(t^\top y)\]
Remove the part already explained in Deflation — \(y\) \[y \leftarrow y - \beta t\]
Save \(w\), \(\beta\), \(t\)
Move to 2 until the exit condition is satisfied







TipDifference from PCR — Whether or not to look at y





PCR (Principal Component Regression, PCA + Regression) extracts components starting from the direction of greater variance of \(X\). In this process, \(y\) is not considered at all.
The problem is that there is no guarantee that the “direction of large variance in \(X\)” matches the “direction that predicts \(y\) well.” If a signal strongly associated with \(y\) lies in the direction of small variance in \(X\), PCR discards that component.
PLS directly maximizes \(\operatorname{cov}(t, y)\), so this problem does not exist. It can be seen as considering variance and correlation simultaneously — \(\operatorname{cov}(t,y) = \operatorname{corr}(t,y)\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(t)}\sqrt{\operatorname{var}(y)}\)
Reason why deflation is necessary: If the part already explained in \(y\) is not removed, the same direction will continue to appear in subsequent iterations. The direction of maximum covariance must be identified again from the residuals so that components containing different information are extracted sequentially.




from sklearn.cross_decomposition import PLSRegression

pls = PLSRegression(n_components=5)
pls.fit(X_train, y_train)

X_t = pls.transform(X_train)   # 성분으로 변환
pls.predict(X_test)            # 회귀 예측까지 한 번에







Note



PLSRegression performs dimensionality reduction and regression simultaneously. Use transform if you only need components, and predict if you need prediction.
