title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
1.1 Self-information (Self-information amount)
The self-information of event x with probability p(x) is

I(x) = -\log p(x).


Common event (p large) → small amount of information, rare event (p small) → large amount of information.
It is a quantity that is not derived from deep theory but is intuitively defined (Shannon).
Unit: If natural logarithm(\ln), nats, if \log_2, bits.







NoteIntuition



A measure of “how surprising (surprise)” it is. If something obvious happens, there is little information, and if something unlikely happens, there is a lot of information.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
1.2 Entropy (Entropy)
Entropy is the expected value of magnetic information.

H(X) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\big[-\log p(x)\big] = -\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}} p(x)\log p(x).


The etymology is the degree of disorder in thermodynamics. However, there is no concept of particles/matter here, and it measures only the randomness and disorder of a random variable.
More random variable → Higher entropy / Less random → Lower entropy.
notation is usually H or \mathbb{H}.

Differential entropy for continuous random variables, where the sum is changed to an integral:

h(X) = -\int_{\mathcal{X}} p(x)\log p(x)\,dx.







Tip“Why is it differential?”



If x is continuous, it is called differential entropy because the random variable can be differentiated. When it is discrete, it is just entropy.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
1.3 KL Divergence (Coolback–Liveler Divergence)
“Distance similar” amount between two distributions p, q:

D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q) = \sum_{x} p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
= \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p}\!\left[\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right].


The name is Kullback–Leibler(two people’s names).
There is a direction. “Divergence from p to q” D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q) and “from q to p” D_{KL}(q\,\|\,p) are different.
notation uses two lines (\|) instead of an arrow (\to).
Property: D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q)\ge 0 (Gibbs inequality), equality only when p=q.







WarningCommonly Mistaken Points



KL is called “distance,” but it is not a true metric. It is asymmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality. If written in a different direction, it becomes a different quantity.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
section: 1.4 The 4 Axioms of the Metric (Distance Function)
text:
1.4 The 4 Axioms of the Metric (Distance Function)
Another name for the distance function d(\cdot,\cdot) is metric. For a function to be a distance, it must satisfy the following four axioms.









#
Axiom
Formula
Meaning




1
Non-negativity
d(s,d)\ge 0
Distance cannot be negative


2
Identity
d(s,d)=0 \iff s=d
If 0, the same point


3
Symmetry
d(s,d)=d(d,s)
Same whether going or coming


4
Triangle Inequality (triangle ineq.)
d(s,d)\le d(s,m)+d(m,d)
Direct is shorter than the intermediate route




Metric learning: Much of what we do in machine learning ultimately involves “learning the appropriate distance function (space) in a vector space.” We learn an embedding space that makes points that should be close close and points that should be far far apart.

Why KL is not a metric: It violates 3 (symmetry) and 4 (triangle inequality) among the axioms above. (Axioms 1 and 2 are satisfied.)






NoteReal-world examples of asymmetric “distance” (intuition enhancement)




Hiking Energy: Energy used to climb a mountain > Energy used to descend. Even if the route is the same, the “cost” varies depending on the direction.
Looking Beyond the Valley: When two people standing on the summits of two peaks look at each other, if there is a large lens/obstacle in between, their “visible distance” may differ.
Navigation (GPS): Due to one-way roads/traffic volume, S\to D shortest route and D\to S shortest route are different.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
1.5 Symmetricing KL: Symmetric KL & Jensen–Shannon
Since KL is asymmetrical and inconvenient, I will create a symmetrical version.
Symmetric KL: 
D_{\text{SKL}}(p,q) = D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q) + D_{KL}(q\,\|\,p).

Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD): Given the intermediate distribution m=\tfrac12(p+q) 
D_{\text{JS}}(p,q) = \tfrac12 D_{KL}(p\,\|\,m) + \tfrac12 D_{KL}(q\,\|\,m).


The value remains the same even if the order of p,q is changed → Symmetry.
In addition to this, there are various other symmetry methods (you can also define and name them yourself if you wish).

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
2.1 Cross-Entropy Decomposition
cross-entropy for correct (one-hot) distribution p, predicted distribution q:

H(p,q) = -\sum_{x} p(x)\log q(x) = \mathbb{E}_{p}[-\log q].

Core Relationship:

\boxed{\,H(p,q) = H(p) + D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q)\,}


If p is fixed (correct answer), then H(p) is a constant.
Therefore, CE Minimization = KL Minimization = Maximum Likelihood (MLE).

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
2.2 Mean-seeking vs Mode-seeking (★ emphasis)
When minimizing KL with q as the training variable and p as fixed, the nature of the solution changes completely depending on the direction.

D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q) = \sum_x p(x)\big[\log p(x) - \log q(x)\big].


Where p(x)>0, if q(x)\to 0, then -\log q(x)\to +\infty → KL explodes.
Therefore, q attempts to cover all regions where p exists → a broad solution that covers multiple modes on average.

Conversely

D_{KL}(q\,\|\,p) = \sum_x q(x)\big[\log q(x) - \log p(x)\big].


p(x)\approx 0 where q(x)>0 explodes → q avoids the place where p is 0 q makes itself 0 (zero-forcing).
Therefore, q focuses on a single mode (peak).










Forward KL D_{KL}(p\,\|\,q)
Reverse KL D_{KL}(q\,\|\,p)




nickname
mean-seeking / mass-covering
mode-seeking / peak-seeking


Behavior
Covers the entire area of p
Focused on a single peak


Mechanism
zero-avoiding (p>0, but if q=0, it diverges)
zero-forcing (p=0, but if q>0, it diverges)


Relationship with MLE
MLE is forward KL D_{KL}(\hat p\,\|\,q_\theta)
—









WarningTest Trap



“What is the KL direction used in MLE?” → D_{KL}(\hat{p}\,\|\,p_\theta) (forward). If written in reverse, a problem arises where it diverges when p_\theta has mass in the unobserved data region. (In other words, the reverse cannot penalize regions outside the data.)

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
2.3 (Supplement) Why Cross-Entropy is Popular
Two reasons why CE is preferred over MSE for classification loss:
1) Gradient vanishing is less. In sigmoid output q=\sigma(z)

MSE: \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (q-y)\,\underbrace{\sigma'(z)}_{\text{포화 시 } \to 0}\,x → Gradient vanishes when output saturates.
CE (binary): \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (q-y)\,x → \sigma'(z) The term disappears, resulting in less loss.

2) CE = Maximum log-likelihood of logistic regression (Bernoulli).

\text{Bernoulli: } P(y)=p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y},\quad
\log L(\theta)=\sum_i\big[y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\big].

The negative of this log-likelihood is the binary cross-entropy.
Interpretation of other cost functions (Reference):







Cost Function
Optimal Forecast f^{*}(x)




Mean Squared Error (MSE)
Conditional Mean \mathbb{E}[y\mid x]


Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
Conditional Median

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
section: 3.1 argmin / argmax, and the definition of ML
text:
3.1 argmin / argmax, and the definition of ML

\min_x f(x): function’s minimum value.
\arg\min_x f(x): The x value that creates that minimum value.

Example: f(x)=(x-2)^2+3 → \min = 3, \arg\min = 2.






Important



Machine learning is ultimately the task of solving \displaystyle \arg\min_{\theta} \mathcal{L}(\theta). The parameter values that minimize the loss are the “learned model (knowledge)”.








NoteParameter vs Argument (CS Terminology Summary)




Parameter: container for values — formal arguments used in the function definition.
Argument: The value actually passed when calling the function.

Example: In def D(s, d): ..., s, d is the parameter, and in D(2, 3), 2, 3 is the argument.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
3.2 Objective Function Terminology Summary



Direction
Function Name




minimize
cost / loss / error / objective function


maximize
reward / value / benefit / profit function



Notation convention:

\hat{x} : The solution to a problem.
x^{*} : Optimal solution — “The asterisk emphasizes the good/optimal”.
Like \displaystyle \min_{x} f(x,y,z), only the subscript variable is the control variable, and the rest are treated as constants.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
3.3 Convex vs Concave




Convex
Concave




Shape
\cup (e.g., (x-2)^2+3)
\cap (e.g., -(x-2)^2+3)


min/max
Global min exists
Global max exists









Important



Convex functions have a unique global minimum over the entire domain. However, most actual objective functions are non-convex (convex only locally), making it very difficult to find a global minimum.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
section: 3.4 Computational complexity perspective: Every problem is search
text:
3.4 Computational complexity perspective: Every problem is search

From a computer’s perspective, solving the problem involves searching all candidates using an evaluation function.
Therefore, the cost is proportional to the size of the solution space → If it cannot be solved in polynomial time, it is effectively unsolvable.
NP-hard / NP-complete: A set of problems that cannot be solved within a reasonable time (combinatorial explosion). Due to realistic time constraints, we are satisfied with a suboptimal solution.
Strategy: Restrict search space → Solves faster but is not guaranteed to be optimal (suboptimal).

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
3.5 Constrained Optimization

\min_x f(x)\quad \text{subject to (s.t.)}\quad g(x)=0.


Constraint expressions are attached after “subject to / such that(st)”.
If there are constraints, it is expensive because conditions must be checked at every optimization step → I want to solve it unconstrained.

Equality Constraint → Lagrange multiplier: 
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda) = f(x) - \lambda\, g(x).


Absorb the constraint into the objective function using the auxiliary variable \lambda (Lagrange multiplier).
Constraints like g(x)=10 can always be converted to the form =0 as g'(x)=g(x)-10=0 (equality constraint).
Note that this provides an approximate solution and may not be an exact solution.

Inequality Constraint → KKT Condition: 
g(x)\le 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT)} \text{ 조건으로 변환}.


The names of three mathematicians: Karush, Kuhn, and Tucker.
We introduce the KKT multiplier (a generalization of Lagrange \lambda) to transform the inequality-constrained problem into an unconstrained problem.


Deeper: Convex Optimization (Stephen Boyd, Stanford) — Although convex shapes may look easy, it is a field deep enough to be a 1,000-page book.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
3.6 Closed solution vs. Gradient descent
If it is convex like linear least squares, we set the slope to 0 to immediately obtain the closed form:

\min_w \|Xw-y\|_2^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \nabla_w = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; w^{*} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y.

If there is no closed solution or it is expensive, gradient descent:

x_{t+1} = x_t - \eta\,\nabla f(x_t).


The slope indicates the direction of the slope. If the slope is 0, the extreme point = (local) minimum/maximum.
\eta = step size / learning rate = how much to move at once.







WarningThe learning rate is “art”




\eta If too large: Wanders or diverges around the minimum point.
\eta If too small: Too slow.
Hint: Using the second derivative (Hessian) allows you to estimate the appropriate stride length (Newtonian method series) → x_{t+1}=x_t-[\nabla^2 f]^{-1}\nabla f. However, finding the optimal \eta in practice is still difficult.

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
4.1 Definition of Overfitting
Intuitive Definition: Not generalizing to unseen data because of looking at too much of the training data.
Formal Definition: Assume that data originates from the data-generating distribution \mathcal{D}. Hypothesis space \mathcal{H}, hypothesis (=model) h\in\mathcal{H}.

Training error \hat{R}(h): Error on training set (calculable).
True error R(h): Error in the true distribution (smaller indicates better generalization).


Model h is overfit: some h'\in\mathcal{H} exists \hat{R}(h) < \hat{R}(h') \quad\text{이지만}\quad R(h) > R(h'). That is, the case where the learning error is lower but the true error is higher.







NoteWhy is it difficult to diagnose overfitting?



By definition, one would have to check all h' to determine if even one satisfies the above condition → In practice, this is impossible. Therefore, papers do not make a definitive statement; instead, they write, “I assume/estimate that my model is overfit.” (Decision signals will be discussed later.)

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
section: 4.2 “Neural networks are the worst-case generalization models, so why use them?” (★ Emphasized discussion)
text:
4.2 “Neural networks are the worst-case generalization models, so why use them?” (★ Emphasized discussion)

Neural networks are notorious for being models that overfit very well to the training set, that is, do not generalize well.
In the past, models like SVM (support vector machine), which were theoretically well-guaranteed for generalization, were used.
And yet, we use neural networks now. Why?

Key Answer: Generalization is too difficult, so virtually giving up, and instead

“Let’s gather a massive training set that is almost identical to reality and fit it perfectly.” → Appears like a generalization.


This is the essence of benign overfitting, and large data + large models = large-scale (LLM) approach.
Advantages of Neural Networks: Easy to scale (capacity can be easily increased by adding parameters → can store massive amounts of information).

title: Information Theory · Optimization · Generalization — Exam Preparation Summary
text:
4.3 Capacity & Bias–Variance Trade-off






Important



The Bias–Variance Trade-off is a central concept in machine learning. With this, you can understand overfitting, underfitting, and capacity all at once.










Status
Meaning
Result




High bias
Model is too rigid/inflexible
Does not capture enough information → underfitting


High variance
Model is too flexible
Fits even the variance of the training set → overfitting




Capacity: Amount of information/complexity the model can hold.

SVM: small capacity → fails if training set becomes larger than capacity.
Neural Networks: Capacity can be easily increased (by adding parameters), making them advantageous for large-scale applications.



Next Time Preview: capacity, bias–variance, MLE / MAP, linear regression, etc.

title: ML Basics II: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVM
text:
The core of a deep learning model is ultimately a linear model. Even though neural networks include non-linear activation functions, the operations of each layer are essentially linear transformations, with non-linearity added on top of them. Therefore, a deep understanding of linear regression serves as the starting point for understanding non-linear deep networks.
The overall structure of the content covered in this note is as follows.





flowchart TD

    C --> D
    D --> E["로지스틱 회귀<br/>확률을 '회귀'하는 분류기"]

Why is logistic “regression,” a regression model, the most representative classification model?

title: ML Basics II: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVM
text:
2 Linear Regression

2.1 Problem formulation
Given the observation pairs ZZZPH0006871ZZZ \(\langle \mathbf{x}_i, t_i \rangle\) and \(i = 1, \dots, N\), learn the mapping from the input \(\mathbf{x}\) to the target value \(t(\mathbf{x})\). The hypothesis space is restricted to a linear combination of the basis functions \(\{h_1, \dots, h_K\}\) and \(h_k(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}\).
\[
\hat{y}_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k \, h_k(\mathbf{x}_i)
\]
The learning target is the coefficient vector \(\mathbf{w} = (w_1, \dots, w_K)\). There are several options for the objective function (cross-entropy, KL divergence, etc.), but the most basic form is the Mean Squared Error (MSE), and the MSE-based linear regression problem is called the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).
\[
\text{total error} = \sum_{i} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i} \Big( y_i - \sum_{k} w_k \, h_k(\mathbf{x}_i) \Big)^2
\]
Here, \(y_i - \hat{y}_i\) is called the residual. The goal is to minimize the sum of the squared vertical distances between the observed values and the model predicted values.


2.2 The precise meaning of “linear” — linearity of coefficients






ImportantThe standard for a linear model is not the input, but the parameters



If \(h_1(x) = x^2,\ h_2(x) = x,\ h_3(x) = 1\) is selected as the basis function, the relationship \(x\)–\(y\) becomes a parabola, but this model is still linear regression. This is because the model is linear with respect to parameter \(\mathbf{w}\).
\[
\hat{y} = w_1 x^2 + w_2 x + w_3 \quad \text{— } \mathbf{w} \text{에 대해 선형, } x \text{에 대해 비선형}
\]
Regardless of the non-linear transformation ZZZPH0006877ZZZ the input undergoes \(h_k(\cdot)\), as long as linearity with respect to the optimization variable \(\mathbf{w}\) is maintained, all the theories of OLS (convexity, closed solutions) hold true. For a 2D input, any basis can be freely defined as \(\{h_1 = x_1^2,\ h_2 = x_2^2,\ h_3 = x_1 x_2, \dots\}\).


The basis function \(h_k\) acts as a feature transformation that moves data into a representation space. In traditional machine learning, this \(h_k\) was handcrafted and only \(\mathbf{w}\) was trained, but modern deep learning (CNN, Transformer) places learnable parameters within \(h_k\) as well to learn the representation itself from the data (representation learning). In this case, closed solutions no longer exist and dependence shifts to iterative optimization (gradient descent) — this is the fundamental reason why deep learning optimization is difficult.


2.3 Matrix Notation and Closed Solutions
Let’s rewrite the optimization problem in matrix form.
\[
\mathbf{w}^\ast = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \Big( t(\mathbf{x}_j) - \sum_{i=1}^{K} w_i \, h_i(\mathbf{x}_j) \Big)^2
\]
The \(j\)-th row of the design matrix \(\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\) is \((h_1(\mathbf{x}_j), \dots, h_K(\mathbf{x}_j))\), \(\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{N}\) is the observation output vector, and \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}\) is the weight vector. Then
\[
\mathbf{w}^\ast = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \underbrace{(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{t})^{T} (\mathbf{H}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{t})}_{\text{residual error } F(\mathbf{w})}
\]
Derivation. \(F(\mathbf{w})\) is a quadratic expression in \(\mathbf{w}\). Expanded
\[
F(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{H} \mathbf{w} - 2\, \mathbf{t}^T \mathbf{H} \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{t}^T \mathbf{t}
\]
If we set the gradient to 0 (Matrix derivative: \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\, \mathbf{w}^T A \mathbf{w} = 2A\mathbf{w}\) for symmetric \(A\), \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\, \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{b}\))
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} F = 2\,\mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{H} \mathbf{w} - 2\,\mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{t} = 0
\]
\[
\boxed{\ \mathbf{w}^\ast = (\mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{H})^{-1} \mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{b}\ }
\qquad \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K},\quad \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{K}
\]
\((\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^T\) is the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse of \(\mathbf{H}\). \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\) can be interpreted as the \(K \times K\) matrix containing the (denormalized) covariance structure of the transformed data.






NoteWhy Closed Solutions Are Guaranteed — Convexity



\(\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H}\) is a positive semidefinite function because for any \(\mathbf{v}\)Z, it is \(\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{H}^T \mathbf{H} \mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{H}\mathbf{v}\|^2 \ge 0\), and therefore \(F(\mathbf{w})\) is a convex function. Since the point where the gradient is zero is the global minimum of a convex quadratic function, the global optimum is obtained simply by differentiating and setting it to zero. In one-dimensional intuition, it is a downward-concave parabola of the form \(F(w) = aw^2 - 2bw + c,\ a \ge 0\).
For convexity, PSD matrices, and the rigorous derivation of matrix derivatives, refer to the quadratic forms and convexity chapters in the Mathematics for Machine Learning notes.
On the other hand, in actual deep learning, \(h_k\) itself is learned, so the objective function becomes non-convex over the entire \(\mathbf{w}\) (parameters of all layers), and must be explored through iterative optimization among numerous local minima.








TipComputation Perspective: \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) and BLAS



Solving linear systems of the form \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{b}\) is the most common operation across engineering simulations, so the highly optimized library BLAS (Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms) has established itself as the standard. NVIDIA provides cuBLAS, which implements this for GPU parallel architectures, and these libraries are ultimately called at the bottom of PyTorch and TensorFlow. The performance of matrix operations in deep learning frameworks is essentially the performance of BLAS-family kernels.




2.4 Connection with MLE — Least squares is the MLE of the Gaussian noise model
Now, let’s look at the same problem again from a probabilistic perspective. Let’s model the prediction as a “linear function + Gaussian noise”.
\[
t(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i} w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}) + e, \qquad e \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
\]
Then the likelihood of a single observation is
\[
P(t \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left( \frac{-\big[t - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x})\big]^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
\]






WarningDo not omit the product of the likelihoods of the entire iid dataset



The most common mistake in deriving the MLE is stopping with only the single-sample likelihood. If the dataset \(\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_j, t_j)\}_{j=1}^N\) is iid, the total likelihood must start as the product of \(N\) terms, take the logarithm, and then become the sum. In the experiment, if you start with a single term without \(\prod_{j=1}^N\), all subsequent expansions become meaningless.


Maximizing the log-likelihood of the entire data for \(\mathbf{w}\):
\[
\ln P(\mathcal{D} \mid \mathbf{w}, \sigma) = \ln \left( \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \right)^{N} \prod_{j=1}^{N} \exp\!\left( \frac{-\big[t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}_j)\big]^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)
\]
Applying the properties of logarithms (product → sum, \(\ln e^z = z\)), the exponential function disappears and:
\[
\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \underbrace{\ln \left( \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \right)^{N}}_{\mathbf{w}\text{와 무관한 상수}} + \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{-\big[t_j - \sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}_j)\big]^2}{2\sigma^2}
\]
Since the constant term has no effect on \(\arg\max\), it is removed; and since the denominator \(2\sigma^2\) is also irrelevant to \(\mathbf{w}\), it is removed as well, and the max is flipped to min due to the negative sign.
\[
= \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} -\big[t_j - \textstyle\sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}_j)\big]^2
= \boxed{\ \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \big[t_j - \textstyle\sum_i w_i h_i(\mathbf{x}_j)\big]^2\ }
\]
This is exactly the OLS objective function. Conclusion:

Least-squares linear regression is equivalent to MLE under a Gaussian noise model.

To summarize the causal chain: ① Assume the noise is Gaussian → ② The likelihood takes the form of an exponential family, and the log-likelihood is proportional to the negative squared error → ③ Maximizing the likelihood = Minimizing the squared error. Linear regression is used so widely because many natural phenomena are well modeled as “signal + Gaussian noise.”






TipWireless Communication Perspective: ML Detection and LS Channel Estimation of AWGN Channels



This equivalence relation is a result already familiar in communication theory.

ML detection = minimum distance detection. ML detection of a transmitted symbol in AWGN channels \(r = s + n\) and \(n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) is equivalent to selecting \(\arg\max_s P(r \mid s) = \arg\min_s \|r - s\|^2\), that is, the constellation point closest to the received signal. This has the exact same structure as the derivation “Gaussian assumption → MLE = LS” above.
LS Channel Estimation. The LS channel estimate \(\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{LS} = (\mathbf{X}^H\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^H\mathbf{y}\) from the pilot matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) and the receiver \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{n}\) is the same as the OLS closed solution \(\mathbf{w}^\ast = (\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^T\mathbf{t}\). The design matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) corresponds to the pilot matrix, and the weights \(\mathbf{w}\) correspond to the channel coefficients.
The reason digital communication is possible. If we know that the channel noise is Gaussian, we can reconstruct the original signal virtually without error using ML estimation, even without knowing \(\sigma\). Knowledge of the statistical structure of the noise is the ability to reconstruct it — this is exactly the same principle as how assumptions about the noise model determine the objective function in machine learning.

The tool known as MLE itself has evolved deeply from communication/detection theory, and therefore machine learning and digital communication share the same mathematical foundation.




2.5 Why \(P(Y \mid X)\) — Benefits of Conditional Modeling
For supervised learning data \(\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}, y)\}\), the principle likelihood is the joint distribution \(P(\mathbf{x}, y \mid \theta)\); however, since the input space \(\mathbf{x}\) (e.g., images) is usually ultra-high-dimensional, direct modeling is very difficult. Therefore, most classification problems are reduced to an easier version where \(\mathbf{x}\) is set as a given condition and only \(P(y \mid \mathbf{x}, \theta)\) is modeled.
The key difference lies in the difficulty of calculating the expected value. If \(\mathbf{x}\) is treated as a random variable, the integral (expected value) over an unknown high-dimensional distribution gets involved in the likelihood calculation, making it virtually impossible to compute. On the other hand, if \(\mathbf{x}\) is fixed as a condition, the design matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) becomes a deterministic constant, and since \(y\) is low-dimensional (a finite class in the case of classification), calculating the expected value becomes as simple as counting. It is not that the modeling format itself changes, but rather that computability leads to the choice of conditional formulation.

title: ML Basics II: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVM
text:
3 Discriminant Model vs Generative Model








Classification
Generative Model
Discriminative Model




Training Target
\(P(X, Y)\) (Joint Distribution)
\(P(Y \mid X)\) (Conditional Distribution)


Ability
Data \(X\) Can generate itself
Only class determination possible


Difficulty
Requires modeling of high-dimensional \(X\) space → Difficult
Modeling only semantic (class) space → Relatively easy


Representative Examples
VAE, GAN, Diffusion
Logistic Regression, SVM



The philosophy of discriminant models is that if the goal is classification, one should not spend effort learning \(P(X \mid Y)\) but rather focus on \(P(Y \mid X)\) estimation, and logistic regression is a prime example. Generative models will be covered in detail later in VAE/GAN/Diffusion.

title: ML Basics II: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVM
text:
4 Logistic Regression

4.1 The paradox of “classifying” as “regression”
It seems contradictory at first glance that the name of the most popular discriminative classification model is logistic regression. The key to resolving this: the probability of a subject being regressed belonging to a class.
The model’s regression output is interpreted as the “probability that this sample belongs to that class,” and classification is performed by taking the maximum value of that probability. For example, if the regression probability for an image is Dog 0.8, Cat 0.7, and Flower 0.2, it is classified as a Dog. That is,
\[
\text{회귀 (확률 추정)} \;\xrightarrow{\;\arg\max\;}\; \text{분류 (결정)}
\]


4.2 Logistic function
To regress the probability , a function is needed where the output is confined to \([0, 1]\). The general logistic function is
\[
f(x) = \frac{L}{1 + e^{-k(x - x_0)}}
\]

\(x_0\): mid-point of the curve
\(L\): Curve height (upper limit)
\(k\): Curve steepness

The sigmoid function is a special case of \(L = 1,\ k = 1,\ x_0 = 0\).
\[
\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}
\]
Properties that make the logistic function preferred for classifiers:

Output is between 0–1 — Can be interpreted as a probability (not a strict probability, but the interval matches)
Smooth and continuous — Since it is based on an exponential function, it can take derivatives infinitely, making it suitable for gradient-based optimization.
Mirror Symmetry (\(\sigma(-x) = 1 - \sigma(x)\)) — Useful in some applications
Very cheap to differentiate — See derivation below

Derivative derivation. By differentiation of composite functions
\[
\sigma'(x) = \frac{e^{-x}}{(1 + e^{-x})^2}
= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} \cdot \frac{e^{-x}}{1 + e^{-x}}
= \sigma(x)\,\big(1 - \sigma(x)\big)
\]
Since the derivative is obtained using only the pre-calculated function value \(\sigma(x)\), there is almost no additional cost in backpropagation.


4.3 Probabilistic Models and Linear Decision Boundaries
The probabilistic model of logistic regression in binary classification \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\) is
\[
P(Y = 0 \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i)}, \qquad
P(Y = 1 \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}) = \frac{\exp(w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i)}{1 + \exp(w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i)}
\]
(The signs of the exponents can be set differently according to convention — if the numerator and denominator are multiplied by \(\exp\) and simplified, the signs are absorbed to become equivalent expressions, so \(-\) The signed definition and the unsigned definition are the same model.)
Decision Boundary Derivation. Let’s assume we classify as \(P(Y=1 \mid \mathbf{X}) \gtrless P(Y=0 \mid \mathbf{X})\). If we take the ratio of the two probabilities, the common denominator cancels out, and
\[
\frac{P(Y = 1 \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w})}{P(Y = 0 \mid \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w})} = \exp\Big( w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i \Big) \gtrless 1
\]
Taking the logarithm of both sides (since \(\exp\) is monotonically increasing, keep the inequality direction):
\[
\boxed{\ w_0 + \sum_i w_i X_i \ \underset{0}{\overset{1}{\gtrless}}\ 0\ }
\]
That is, the decision boundary is a linear (hyperplane) boundary of the input space. The essence of logistic regression is that while the probability output is non-linear (sigmoid), the decision rule itself is a linear classifier.






TipWireless Communication Perspective: log-odds are LLR



The \(\ln \frac{P(Y=1\mid \mathbf{x})}{P(Y=0 \mid \mathbf{x})} = w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i\) derived above is an object similar to the LLR(Log-Likelihood Ratio) used daily in communication.

The soft decision of the channel decoder (LDPC, Turbo) calculates bit-by-bit LLR \(\ln \frac{P(b=1\mid r)}{P(b=0\mid r)}\) and makes a hard decision based on the sign — this is the same structure as logistic regression classifying based on the sign of log-odds.
Sigmoid is a transformation that converts LLR back into probabilities: \(P(b=1 \mid r) = \sigma(\text{LLR})\). Just as LLR \(= 2r/\sigma^2\) in BPSK over AWGN is a linear function of the received values, logistic regression can be viewed as a learner that models LLR as a linear function of the features.





4.4 Training: MCLE (Maximum Conditional Likelihood Estimation)
We train the parameters \(w_0, w_1, \dots, w_d\) on the \(d\)-dimensional features. Ideally, we would like to use the MLE of the joint likelihood \(P(\mathcal{D}_X, \mathcal{D}_Y \mid \mathbf{w})\), but our model only has \(P(Y \mid X)\). Therefore, we maximize the conditional data likelihood.
\[
l(\mathbf{w}) = \ln P(\mathcal{D}_Y \mid \mathcal{D}_X, \mathbf{w}) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \ln P(y^j \mid x^j, \mathbf{w})
\]
(The symbol \(l\) represents the loss l, but here it is the objective function to be maximized.)
Derivation. Write the log-likelihood of the two classes in a single line using the indicator function \(\mathbf{1}(\cdot)\).
\[
l(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_j \Big[ \mathbf{1}(y^j = 1) \ln P(Y=1 \mid X^j, \mathbf{w}) + \mathbf{1}(y^j = 0) \ln P(Y=0 \mid X^j, \mathbf{w}) \Big]
\]
Thanks to the label being \(\{0, 1\}\), it can be replaced with \(\mathbf{1}(y^j = 1) = y^j\) and \(\mathbf{1}(y^j = 0) = 1 - y^j\) (this trick does not work if the label is set to \(\{-1, +1\}\)).
\[
= \sum_j \Big[ y^j \ln P(Y=1 \mid X^j, \mathbf{w}) + (1 - y^j) \ln P(Y=0 \mid X^j, \mathbf{w}) \Big]
\]
Substituting the definition of the probability model and simplifying:
\[
l(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_j \left[ y^j \Big( w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i^j \Big) - \ln \Big( 1 + \exp\big( w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i^j \big) \Big) \right]
\]






NoteGood news and bad news




Good news: \(l(\mathbf{w})\) is the concave function of \(\mathbf{w}\) → The local optimum is the global optimum.
Bad news: There is no closed solution. Even if you try to solve \(\nabla l = 0\), the exponential terms are tangled and cannot be solved algebraically.
Good news again: Concave functions are easy to optimize. Since the global optimal point is unique, as you ascend the mountain (gradient ascent), you will inevitably reach near the summit.

(Note: The absence of a closed solution or the non-uniformity of the solution does not imply non-convexity — here, it is proven that the objective function is actually concave.)




4.5 Gradient Ascent
Maximization of the concave function is performed using gradient ascent that goes up in the direction of the gradient.
Gradient Derivation (3-step causal chain):
\[
\frac{\partial l(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_i}
= \sum_j \left[ \frac{\partial}{\partial w_i} y^j \Big( w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i^j \Big) - \frac{\partial}{\partial w_i} \ln\Big( 1 + \exp\big(w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i^j\big) \Big) \right]
\]
① The first term is linear, so \(y^j x_i^j\). ② The second term follows the chain rule, so \(\dfrac{x_i^j \exp(w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i^j)}{1 + \exp(w_0 + \sum_i w_i x_i^j)} = x_i^j \, P(Y=1 \mid x^j, \mathbf{w})\). ③ When factored by the common factor \(x_i^j\):
\[
\boxed{\ \frac{\partial l(\mathbf{w})}{\partial w_i} = \sum_j x_i^j \Big( y^j - P(Y^j = 1 \mid x^j, \mathbf{w}) \Big)\ }
\]
The interpretation is beautiful: the gradient is the sum of (actual label − predicted probability) × input, i.e., a quantity weighted by the input to the prediction error. Since the label is 0/1 and the prediction probability is between 0 and 1, the error term \(y^j - P(\cdot)\) is confined to \([-1, 1]\), so all quantities naturally have a normalized scale.
Algorithm. Given a learning rate \(\eta > 0\), repeat until convergence:
\[
w_0^{(t+1)} \leftarrow w_0^{(t)} + \eta \sum_j \big[ y^j - P(Y^j = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}^j, \mathbf{w}) \big]
\]
\[
w_i^{(t+1)} \leftarrow w_i^{(t)} + \eta \sum_j x_i^j \big[ y^j - P(Y^j = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}^j, \mathbf{w}) \big] \qquad (i = 1, \dots, n)
\]
The outer loop runs on dimension \(i\), and the inner sum runs over the entire training sample \(j\). The termination conditions are ① reaching a fixed number of iterations, or ② the gradient (or the change in \(\mathbf{w}\)) becoming below a threshold—the latter is a method that guarantees a suboptimal point where it “no longer moves.”






NoteGeometric meaning of bias term \(w_0\)



\(w_0\) is a special weight that is not multiplied by the input \(x_i\), and it serves as the intercept of the linear model. Without \(w_0\), the decision hyperplane remains fixed at the origin and can only rotate; \(w_0\) is required to freely translate across the entire space. Although it is named “bias,” it is a distinct concept unrelated to the bias in the bias–variance tradeoff, so do not confuse them. In the update equation as well, it can be observed that \(w_0\) is updated solely by the error statistics, without the input \(x_i^j\).








WarningLearning Rate Scheduling — To avoid going over the top



The learning rate \(\eta\) problem is like determining the step size without knowing the terrain of the mountain (the curvature of the objective function). If the step size is too large near the summit (optimal point), an overshoot occurs where the model goes over the summit and falls to the opposite side. Therefore, learning rate scheduling, which reduces the step size as training progresses, determines the quality of convergence. What is called an “optimizer” in deep learning libraries (Adagrad, RMSProp, Adam, etc.) is essentially a combination of gradient descent/ascent and learning rate adjustment rules — the framework of the optimization algorithm is the same, but the rules regarding when and how much to reduce the learning rate differ. This is exactly the same structure as the LMS step size \(\mu\) in wireless communication adaptive filters determining the trade-off between convergence speed and steady-state error (misadjustment).

title: ML Basics II: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVM
section: 5 Support Vector Machine: Max Margin Classifier
text:
5 Support Vector Machine: Max Margin Classifier

5.1 Which linear classifier is the best
In linearly separable binary classification problems, there are infinitely many straight lines that perfectly separate the training data. Since they all have a learning error of 0, which one is better? The evaluation criterion is the goal of machine learning itself, namely generalization.
Intuition: Since points of each class are likely to be more distributed around visible samples, the boundary that maximizes the margin between the two classes is the safest for future samples. The Support Vector Machine (SVM) implements this intuition and is a model whose validity has been confirmed in intuition, theory, and practice.


5.2 Anatomy of a name

Machine = function (classifier). In machine learning, “machine” refers to a learned function.
Support Vector = A small number of data points that support (define) the decision boundary and margin. Since they are points in a vector space, they are vectors.

Key Insight: To define the boundary, only confusing samples close to the boundary are needed. The remaining distant points contribute nothing to the solution. The margin is defined by support vectors, and maximizing the margin itself becomes the objective function; expanding the formula results in a constrained linear (convex) optimization problem.


5.3 Limitations and Historical Position

Since SVM is a linear model, it cannot directly represent complex non-linear boundaries. Although non-linear boundaries can be implemented using kernel SVM, the computational cost is high, and at that level, there is no difference from using deep networks, so it has gradually been replaced by deep learning.
SVM was THE classifier of the pre-deep learning era (around 2010–2011). Remember that there was a time when neural networks were treated as “failed models” and SVMs dominated — dominant paradigms cycle.
Nevertheless, the key to remember: SVM is a linear classifier with a built-in margin concept and possesses a robust generalization theory. This margin/generalization idea extends to the regularization theory of neural networks as well.







TipWireless communication perspective: Margin = Minimum distance



The intuition of maximum margin is similar to the minimum distance design in digital modulation. Just as the probability of error due to noise decreases exponentially as the minimum Euclidean distance between symbols \(d_{\min}\) increases in constellation design (\(P_e \sim Q(d_{\min}/2\sigma)\)), the larger the margin of the classification boundary, the less likely it is for a new (noisy) sample to cross the boundary and be misclassified. Support vectors correspond to the “nearest constellation point pairs” that determine the boundaries of the decision region.

text:
6 Next Topic Preview: KNN and Decision Trees
Unlike the linear model family (linear regression → logistic regression → SVM), the following two supervised learning algorithms are non-linear and non-parametric approaches.

K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN): Classification by majority voting of “close” samples. Two variations — ① the closest \(K\) samples ② neighbors within a radius \(r\) of a ball. The definition of “close” is determined by the distance metric. There is no training phase, and the hyperparameter is \(K\) or ball radius.
Decision Tree: Partitions space into a tree of feature questions. Extended to the ensemble version, Random Forest.

Linear regression is the foundation of modern ML models. The criterion for linearity is parameters, not inputs, and non-linear relationships can also be fitted as basis functions.
OLS has a closed solution because its objective function is a convex quadratic, which is equivalent to MLE under the assumption of Gaussian noise. Since deep learning learns up to the representation (\(h_k\)), it leaves this world of closed solutions and enters the world of non-convex iterative optimization.
Logistic regression is a discriminant model that classifies by regression of probabilities. The objective function of MCLE is concave, and it reaches a global optimality through gradient ascent. The gradient has a neat form as the sum of (error × input).
SVM is a linear classifier with a built-in generalization principle called margin maximization, and was the standard in the pre-deep learning era.

title: ML Basics II: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, and SVM
text:
8 Appendix: Python Implementation
Validate OLS closed solution and logistic regression gradient ascent in NumPy.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ---- OLS: 닫힌 해 검증 ----
# 진짜 모델: y = 2*x^2 - 3*x + 1 + Gaussian noise
N = 200
x = rng.uniform(-2, 2, N)
t = 2 * x**2 - 3 * x + 1 + rng.normal(0, 0.5, N)

# 기저 함수: h1 = x^2, h2 = x, h3 = 1  (비선형 기저, 계수에 대해선 선형)
H = np.column_stack([x**2, x, np.ones(N)])     # N x K 설계 행렬

# w* = (H^T H)^{-1} H^T t   — 수치적으로는 solve가 inv보다 안정적
w_star = np.linalg.solve(H.T @ H, H.T @ t)
print("OLS closed-form w* =", np.round(w_star, 3), " (true: [2, -3, 1])")

# np.linalg.lstsq (내부적으로 LAPACK/BLAS 호출)와 일치 확인
w_lstsq, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(H, t, rcond=None)
assert np.allclose(w_star, w_lstsq)


# ---- 로지스틱 회귀: gradient ascent ----
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))

# 2D 가우시안 두 덩어리로 이진 분류 데이터 생성
N2 = 300
X0 = rng.normal([-1.5, -1.0], 1.0, (N2 // 2, 2))   # class 0
X1 = rng.normal([+1.5, +1.0], 1.0, (N2 // 2, 2))   # class 1
X = np.vstack([X0, X1])
y = np.r_[np.zeros(N2 // 2), np.ones(N2 // 2)]

Xb = np.column_stack([np.ones(N2), X])   # bias term w0 추가
w = np.zeros(3)
eta = 0.01

for step in range(2000):
    p1 = sigmoid(Xb @ w)                  # P(Y=1 | x, w)
    grad = Xb.T @ (y - p1)                # ∂l/∂w = Σ_j x^j (y^j - p1^j)
    w = w + eta * grad                    # ascent (오목 함수 최대화)
    if np.linalg.norm(eta * grad) < 1e-6: # 정지 조건: 파라미터 변화량
        break

acc = np.mean((sigmoid(Xb @ w) > 0.5) == y)
print(f"steps={step},  w = {np.round(w, 3)},  train acc = {acc:.3f}")

# 결정 경계가 선형(w0 + w1 x1 + w2 x2 = 0)임을 수치로 확인
print("decision boundary: "
      f"{w[0]:.2f} + {w[1]:.2f}*x1 + {w[2]:.2f}*x2 = 0")


# ---- "MLE = LS" 수치 검증 ----
# Gaussian 노이즈 모델의 음의 로그우도를 직접 최소화한 해가 OLS 해와 일치하는지
from scipy.optimize import minimize

sigma = 0.5
def neg_log_likelihood(w):
    r = t - H @ w
    # i.i.d. 곱 → 로그 합: N개 항 전체를 합산해야 함
    return 0.5 * np.sum(r**2) / sigma**2 + N * np.log(sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))

w_mle = minimize(neg_log_likelihood, np.zeros(3)).x
print("w_MLE =", np.round(w_mle, 3), " vs  w_OLS =", np.round(w_star, 3))
assert np.allclose(w_mle, w_star, atol=1e-4)
print("MLE (Gaussian noise) == OLS  ✓")

section: 2 Why Cross Entropy: Gradient Comparison with MSE
text:
2 Why Cross Entropy: Gradient Comparison with MSE

2.1 Problem Settings
Let’s consider a single sigmoid output unit.
\[
\hat{y} = \sigma(z), \qquad z = w^\top x + b, \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}
\]
Compare the gradients of two loss functions for the same model.


2.2 Slope of MSE
\[
L_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(y - \sigma(z)\right)^2
\]
Differentiating using the chain rule:
\[
\frac{\partial L_{\text{MSE}}}{\partial w}
= \underbrace{(\sigma(z) - y)}_{\text{오차}} \cdot \underbrace{\sigma'(z)}_{\text{문제의 항}} \cdot \, x
\]


2.3 Gradient of CE (Binary Classification)
\[
L_{\text{CE}} = -\left[ y \log \sigma(z) + (1-y)\log(1 - \sigma(z)) \right]
\]
If we use \(\frac{d}{dz}\log\sigma(z) = 1 - \sigma(z)\), \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\), the \(\sigma'(z)\) term cancels out and disappears:
\[
\frac{\partial L_{\text{CE}}}{\partial w} = (\sigma(z) - y) \cdot x
\]






WarningCausal Mechanism Chain (Essential Structure for Essay Answers)



Ending with “CE is good” will result in a deduction. You must write the entire following chain:

The derivative of the sigmoid is \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\), the maximum value is at \(z=0\) and \(0.25\), and as \(|z|\) increases, it converges exponentially to 0 (saturation).
Since \(\sigma'(z)\) remains as a multiplication factor in the MSE gradient, the gradient becomes almost 0 even if the error is large when the neuron is in the saturation region.
When stacking layers, the local gradients of each layer are multiplied sequentially during backpropagation, so the factor \(\le 0.25\) is multiplied by the number of layers, and the gradient near the input layer becomes virtually zero (vanishing gradient).
Therefore, parameters near the input layer are hardly updated from their initial values, so learning does not proceed.
On the other hand, since the \(\sigma'(z)\) factor is eliminated for CE, the gradient is directly proportional to the error \((\sigma(z)-y)\); therefore, as predictions become incorrect, it receives a larger gradient, resulting in faster learning and mitigated vanishing.





2.4 Statistical Justification of CE: Equivalence with Bernoulli MLE
The pmf of the Bernoulli distribution is \(P(y) = q^y (1-q)^{1-y}\). The log-likelihood for the iid sample \(\{y_i\}_{i=1}^N\) is:
\[
\log \mathcal{L}(q) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ y_i \log q_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-q_i) \right]
\]
Maximizing this is exactly the same as minimizing the CE. That is, CE minimization = Bernoulli maximum likelihood estimation in logistic regression.






NoteCaution regarding iid summation (prevention of floating-point pattern A)



Do not stop after writing only the single-sample form \(y\log q + (1-y)\log(1-q)\). In MLE derivation problems, you must first write the form aggregated over the entire data using \(\sum_{i=1}^N\) (log-likelihood) or \(\prod_{i=1}^N\) (likelihood).




2.5 Summary: Two reasons to prefer CE







Perspective
Content




Practical
Less slope vanishing due to the absence of the \(\sigma'(z)\) factor in the MSE slope


Theoretical
Equivalent to the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of Bernoulli / Multinoulli distributions — Statistically principled loss



MSE is natural for regression (\(f^*(x) = \mathbb{E}[y|x]\), conditional mean prediction), while MAE learns a function to predict the conditional median. It is still widely used for simple problems.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
3 Output Units
A unit that generates an output (probability or value) in the last layer. It corresponds 1:1 with the assumption of the output distribution.









Output Unit
Formula
Corresponding Output Distribution
Application




Linear
\(\hat{y} = W^\top h + b\)
Gaussian: \(p(y|x) = \mathcal{N}(y; \hat{y}, I)\)
regression


Sigmoid
\(\hat{y} = \sigma(w^\top h + b)\)
Bernoulli
Binary Classification


Softmax
\(\text{softmax}(z)_i = \dfrac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\)
Multinoulli (Multi-class extension of Bernoulli)
Multi-class



Here, \(z = w^\top h + b\) is called logit.






WarningThe Trap of Sigmoid Output



If a sigmoid is applied to each of the 10-dimensional outputs, each dimension takes on the value \([0,1]\), but the sum is not 1. In other words, it is not a probability distribution but “appears like unnormalized probability.” Normalizing it by taking the exponent results in softmax.



3.1 Softmax is more than normalization
The essence is revealed when compared to L1 normalization (values verified by direct calculation):



Input
L1 Normalization
Softmax




\([1, 2]\)
\([0.333, 0.667]\)
\([0.269, 0.731]\)


\([10, 20]\)
\([0.333, 0.667]\)
\([0.0000454, 0.99995]\)




L1 normalization preserves only ratios — \([1,2]\) and \([10,20]\) are the same.
Softmax is magnitude sensitive — the larger the absolute difference, the closer it amplifies the max to 1.
That is, softmax is an operation that takes the max softly: it is not a deterministic argmax, but amplifies the gap while maintaining it in a differentiable form.
Practical Benefit: The amplified probability gap leads to an amplified gradient, making learning easier.







TipWireless Communication Perspective: Soft Decision vs Hard Decision



The relationship between softmax and argmax is exactly the same as the relationship between a receiver’s soft decision vs. hard decision. Argmax is a hard decision that immediately confirms a symbol and discards information (reliability), whereas softmax is a soft decision that preserves the reliability of each candidate, similar to LLR. Just as passing LLR to the channel decoder improves performance, a differentiable softmax is required for backpropagation.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
4 Gumbel Softmax: Makes argmax differentiable

4.1 Synchronous: End-to-end connection between two networks
Let’s assume that we want to connect the discrete output (softmax + argmax) of neural network A as the input to neural network B.
A representative application is the Robotics Foundation Model: Network A determines high-level actions (“Go to the door,” “Go to the refrigerator”), while Network B generates fine-grained actions (maintaining an appropriate distance to grasp the doorknob, turning the handle, pulling). To perform end-to-end learning of the entire model from input to output, all intermediate operations must be differentiable for backpropagation to pass.
The problem is:

softmax: infinitely differentiable ✓
argmax: Cannot be differentiated as it is an index selection operation ✗ — Backpropagation stops here



4.2 Solution: Add noise to convert to sampling
\[
\text{(기존)} \quad p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j)}, \qquad y_i = \begin{cases} 1 & i = \text{argmax}_j\, p_j \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\]
\[
\text{(Gumbel Softmax)} \quad y_i = \frac{\exp\!\left(\dfrac{z_i + g_i}{\tau}\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{k} \exp\!\left(\dfrac{z_j + g_j}{\tau}\right)}
\]

\(g_i\): Noise sampled from a Gumbel distribution
\(\tau\): Temperature hyperparameter — The smaller the value, the closer it is to one-hot; the larger the value, the closer it is to a uniform distribution.



4.3 Why the Gumbel distribution of all things?
The PDF of the Gumbel distribution is \(f(x) = e^{-(x + e^{-x})}\) (in the form of an exponent inside an exponent). Key property:






ImportantGumbel-Max Trick (Key Properties)



If Gumbel noise is added to the logit and then argmax is applied, the result follows the distribution identical to sampling from a softmax distribution:
\[
\text{argmax}_i (z_i + g_i) \sim \text{Categorical}\left(\text{softmax}(z)\right)
\]
That is, the deterministic argmax is reinterpreted as sampling of a random variable, and if that sampling process is continuous with the softmax formula (\(y_i\) above), the whole becomes differentiable. This technique of making something non-differentiable differentiable is called the reparameterization trick, and this special case using the Gumbel distribution is called the Gumbel-Max trick.




4.4 Application

End-to-end training of a single model connecting two networks via cascade
Variational Autoencoder (VAE) control of discrete latent variables — VAE is the foundation of modern generative AI (GAN is also based on VAE architecture), and is more widely used in foundation models such as VLA (Vision-Language-Action) these days than when it was proposed in 2017 (Jang et al., Maddison et al., ICLR 2017).







TipWireless Communication Perspective: Modulators in Learnable Communication Systems



In end-to-end learned communication systems based on autoencoders, the transmitter’s constellation mapping is discrete selection and therefore non-differentiable. To directly minimize BER by combining the transmitter and receiver into a single neural network, this discrete selection must be relaxed to be differentiable, and the standard tool used for this is Gumbel Softmax. Additionally, the reparameterization trick plays the same role when making the quantization layer of CSI feedback compression (CsiNet family) learnable.

text:
5 Activation Functions

5.1 Candidates









Function
Formula
Range
Characteristics




Logistic Sigmoid
\(\sigma(z)\)
\((0,1)\)
Smooth and infinitely differentiable, but severe vanishing gradient in \(\sigma' \le 0.25\)


Hyperbolic Tangent
\(\tanh(z)\)
\((-1,1)\)
Similar to sigmoid but with different curvature; better accuracy depending on the application — the choice between the two is determined by application/experimentation, not intrinsic superiority


ReLU
\(\max(0, z)\)
\([0,\infty)\)
The standard of modern deep learning; contributes to vanishing gradient mitigation and catastrophic forgetting mitigation





5.2 First Impressions and Twist on ReLU
ReLU is a “futilely simple” function that is linear in the positive range and kills negative values to zero. In a single layer, it appears to provide almost no non-linearity between input and output. However, when stacking multiple layers, the non-linearity between input and output becomes exponentially complex. It is preferred over sigmoid/tanh because it ensures sufficient expressiveness even with simple activation if the depth is sufficient, while simultaneously having the decisive advantage of minimal vanishing gradients.


5.3 Generalizations and Variations of ReLU
There are also applications where negative input information is important. Since vanilla ReLU kills all negative numbers, a generalized formula is:
\[
h_i = \max(0, z_i) + \alpha_i \min(0, z_i)
\]








\(\alpha_i\)
Result
Remarks




\(0\)
ReLU
Completely block negatives


\(1\)
Linear unit
Activation vanished (no non-linearity)


\(-1\)
Absolute value rectification: \(h_i = |z_i|\)
Folding a negative number into a positive


\(0.01\) (small positive)
Leaky ReLU
“Leaks” negative information


Trainable Parameter
PReLU (Parametric ReLU)
\(\alpha\) Learn from itself as data — The philosophy of “Let’s learn everything we can”



Maxout is also a variation of the same spirit (taking the maximum of several linear functions).


5.4 Intuitive Justification: Space Folding
Using Absolute Value Rectification \(h = |z|\) causes the input space to fold in half. When simple (nearly linear) classification boundaries are learned in the folded space and then unfolded, they become much more complex boundaries in the original space.

Fold 1 → Double boundary complexity effect
\(n\) folds (= \(n\) hidden layer cascade) → exponentially complex classification boundary

In other words, since depth exponentially amplifies complexity even if the activation of each layer is simple, deep neural networks can encode very complex classification boundaries. This is the justification for “simple activation + deep structure”.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
6 Gradient Vanishing

6.1 mechanism (causal chain)

Backpropagation in deep neural networks is multiplying the local gradients of each layer by the chain rule.
If the magnitude of the local gradient is in the \([0,1]\) interval (especially a value sufficiently smaller than 1), the magnitude of the gradient decreases exponentially with each passing layer.
Even if the magnitude of the gradient at the output layer is sufficiently large, it becomes almost 0 by the time it reaches the input layer.
If the gradient magnitude is close to 0, the update amount in \(w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla_w L\) is close to 0.
Therefore, parameters near the input layer hardly change from the initial state, and no matter how much training progresses, that layer cannot learn → learning efficiency becomes extremely low, so a mechanism to greatly increase the number of iterations or amplify the gradient is required, but amplification amplifies even the noise in the gradient.



6.2 Effects by activation function








Activation
Local Gradient
Result




Sigmoid
Max \(0.25\) (at \(z=0\)), in the saturation region \(\approx 0\)
\(0.25\) repeatedly multiplied → severe vanishing


ReLU
Exactly in the positive range \(1\)
\(1 \times 1 \times \cdots\) → The magnitude of the gradient in the output layer is transmitted alive to the input layer



This is the biggest reason why ReLU is preferred in deep networks.






TipWireless Communication Perspective: SNR Degradation of Multi-Hop Relays



The local gradient multiplication at each layer is equivalent to the channel gain multiplied at each hop in a multi-hop relay. If the gain at each hop is less than 1 (attenuation), the received signal weakens exponentially as the number of hops increases — this corresponds exactly to how an amplify-and-forward relay amplifies noise along with the signal, and how gradient boosting amplifies gradient noise. ReLU preserves the signal magnitude like a regenerative (decode-and-forward) relay with a gain of exactly 1.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
7 Catastrophic Forgetting

7.1 Definition

Knowledge about a previously learned task (Task A) tends to be abruptly lost as information related to the current task (Task B) is integrated (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989)



7.2 Occurrence mechanism in mini-batch learning

Train a fixed-size network in mini-batches: Update parameters with Batch 1 → Update with Batch 2 → ⋯
Immediately after training Batch 1, the loss for Batch 1 is nearly 0 (well trained).
However, the slopes of subsequent batches continue to overwrite the same set of parameters. There is no barrier/protector.
Even parameters independent of a specific batch will change significantly when accumulated millions of times, as long as the slope is not exactly 0 (e.g., \(10^{-6}\)).
When looking at Batch 1 as the epoch nears its end, the loss has risen again — information from the initial batch has been forgotten. In the case of a 5,000-unit mini-batch, information from the early batches of the epoch is almost forgotten by the time of the last mini-batch.



7.3 Why It Is “Cataclysmic” — Two Causes







Cause
Explanation




Absence of Protection
A fixed set of parameters is shared and overwritten by all data; there is no mechanism to say “Do not touch this parameter”


Insufficient Capacity
If the amount of data > network capacity, old data must be deleted to insert new data. To put 2MB of data onto a 500KB storage device, the only option is to overwrite — only the last data inserted remains.





7.4 Relationship with multi-epoch learning
There is no winning theory yet regarding “why run multiple epochs?” One of the leading hypotheses is catastrophic forgetting: because reviewing the same data multiple times mitigates forgetting. In practice, it is empirically known that multiple epochs provide a better model.


7.5 Derived concept

Continual Learning: A scenario where data is viewed only once and passed through as a stream (review is impossible). It is an environment where forgetting is most severe and is a subfield of machine learning. The smaller the model (the less capacity it has), the more severe the problem.
Aspects of the Era of Large Models: Models with massive parameters, such as LLM/VLA, can “seep” information into the spare parameter space, making forgetting relatively less severe. In other words, the forgetting problem takes on a different aspect in the realm of large models.







TipWireless Communication Perspective: Time-varying Channel Tracking of Adaptive Filters



The LMS/RLS adaptive equalizer intentionally forgets past information using a forgetting factor \(\lambda\) to track time-varying channels. The catastrophic forgetting of neural networks is akin to a situation where data order is enforced without being able to control this forgetting factor. Furthermore, the logic that “if information amount > capacity, overwriting is unavoidable” can be interpreted as a stored version of Shannon’s theorem, which states that error-free transmission is impossible at transmission rates exceeding channel capacity.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
8 Two questions in network design

8.1 Q1. How deep should it be?
In multi-digit transcription tasks, increasing the number of layers raises accuracy from 92% → 95% → 96%, but the rate of increase gradually slows down. The name of this phenomenon:






NoteDiminishing Returns



A phenomenon in which marginal gain decreases as inputs (number of layers, number of parameters) increase. Most phenomena in nature follow this pattern. (Equivalent to diminishing marginal utility in Korean)




8.2 Q2. How many parameters should there be?
Increasing the number of parameters can lead to performance actually declining beyond diminishing returns, or fluctuating without a consistent trend. Causes for each:







Phenomenon
Cause




Performance degradation
If parameters are excessive relative to the amount of data, overfitting — fits the training data but fails to generalize


Irregular fluctuations
The test set is merely a sample of the world and therefore cannot perfectly represent the world → Ups and downs caused by local noise are a natural phenomenon





8.3 Conclusion
There is no general answer to the question of “how many layers and parameters are optimal.” It all depends on the application, the dataset, and the architecture. This non-obviousness is why machine learning engineers are needed.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
9 Convergence of Backpropagation

9.1 From convex to non-convex








Model
Solution Space
Convergence Guarantee




Single-layer Perceptron + Logistic Regression Loss
Convex
Gradient Descent Guarantees Reaching Global Minimum


Perceptron layer 2 or higher (from the point where XOR solving is possible)
Non-convex
Gradient descent can get stuck at a local minimum





9.2 Determinants of the solution space
The solution space is determined by the combination of loss function definition × dataset. If the loss is changed from logistic regression to CE, or if the data changes from 100 to 1000, the solution space itself changes.






WarningTest Trap: “Multiple solutions = non-convex” is not true



The basis for non-convexity is the structural fact that “the objective function loses convexity due to multilayer composition,” not the observation that there are multiple solutions (convex functions can also have multiple sets of minimums). Furthermore, since it is virtually impossible to search the entire high-dimensional solution space, gradient descent operates based solely on local information and settles at a local minimum.




9.3 Results and History

The selection of the number of hidden units and layers is a hyperparameter — since there is no guarantee of convergence, human intervention is required to find a good local solution.
Neural networks lagged behind SVMs for over 10 years due to the lack of convergence guarantees: SVMs guaranteed convergence through convex optimization, had robust generalization theory (made stronger by kernel tricks), and did not require multiple epochs of training. However, SVMs were inherently shallow models with limited capacity (even with kernels), and high-capacity neural networks defeated SVMs in 2012 with AlexNet.
The reason for using convex optimization tools (gradient-based methods) even knowing that the objective function is non-convex: Because there is no mathematically guaranteed better alternative. Convex optimization techniques remain the most reliable tools for finding good local minima, even in non-convex spaces.







NoteAs a side note, a memorable metaphor



The problem of finding a good local solution is similar to many life decisions (e.g., finding a spouse) — since exploring the entire solution space is NP-hard, we look for a good local minimum within a constrained search space (my city, my school). And if we expand the search space, a better local solution almost certainly exists — the probability that the current solution is the global optimal is very low.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
10 Regularization (Regularizer)

10.1 General form of the learning objective function
\[
\min_\theta \;\; \underbrace{L(\theta)}_{\text{Loss}} + \underbrace{\Omega(\theta)}_{\text{Regularizer}}
\]

Loss: Target for minimization. Reliability decreases if data is insufficient (coin toss example — MLE is unstable if the sample size is small).
Regularizer \(\Omega\): As an inductive bias, it acts as guidance (prior information) to prevent overfitting under the premise that training data is always insufficient.
Design Principle: Normalization terms should be designed to minimize. If a quantity is meaningful only when maximized, invert the sign and insert \(-\Omega\).



10.2 Hard Constraint vs Soft Constraint
Hard constraint — Optimization with constraints:
\[
\min_\theta L(\theta) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \theta \in \mathcal{H} \qquad \text{예: } \|\theta\|_2^2 \le r^2
\]
Since a solution is infeasible if it is outside the set, constraint satisfaction must be checked every time, and it is generally difficult to solve. Constraints can be applied to the parameter space rather than the function space (since neural networks are defined by parameters).
Soft constraint — Absorbed as penalty term:
\[
\min_\theta \; L(\theta) + \lambda \|\theta\|_2^2
\]






ImportantEquivalence of two forms (Lagrangian)



There exists a normalization parameter \(\lambda^* > 0\) such that hard-constraint optimization is equivalent to soft-constraint optimization — this is the Lagrange multiplier method. The difference: hard guarantees that the solution is inside the ball, whereas soft “guides to keep the size from becoming excessive” without such guarantee. The soft form is much easier to solve because it is an unconstrained optimization.


The name “penalty” implies that penalties are imposed to ensure the model does not have a large magnitude when optimization is finished. This principle of favoring simple models is Occam’s razor, and it is in the same context as what we saw in the 13th-order polynomial overfitting example — everything is connected.


10.3 L1, L0 Penalty and Sparsity
Sparse vector: A vector in which most of the components are zero (vs. dense vector: non-zero values in almost every dimension). “How many zeros must there be to be sparse” is somewhat subjective, like the distinction between a beautiful flower and a non-beautiful one.









Penalty
Effect
Bayesian Interpretation
Optimization Difficulty




\(\ell_2\): \(\|\theta\|_2^2\)
Size suppression (weight decay)
MAP with Gaussian prior
Easy (differentiable)


\(\ell_1\): \(\|\theta\|_1\)
encourage sparsity — not guaranteed
MAP with Laplace prior
NP-hard but approximate exists → can be solved with gradient-based tools


\(\ell_0\): Number of non-zero components
force scarcity — rarer year
—
NP-hard, combination optimization — virtually impossible to optimize directly









WarningTest Trap: encourage vs force



\(\ell_1\) only induced sparsity, not guaranteed it. \(\ell_0\) enforced sparsity, but it is difficult to solve because it is a combinatorial optimization. The reason \(\ell_1\) is the practice standard is that it is a tractable approximation of \(\ell_0\). (Caution regarding definition inversion — Real pattern C)




10.4 Bayesian perspective: Regularizer = Prior
Bayes’ Theorem:
\[
p(\theta \mid \{x_i, y_i\}) = \frac{p(\theta) \, p(\{x_i, y_i\} \mid \theta)}{p(\{x_i, y_i\})}
\]

\(p(\theta)\): prior regarding the hypothesis (parameter) — an assumption about the model/parameter, which translates to a constraint on the parameter.
\(p(\{x_i,y_i\} \mid \theta)\): likelihood
Denominator: Normalization constant (partition function)

Taking the logarithm and using MAP makes the structure transparent:
\[
\max_\theta \; \log p(\theta \mid \{x_i, y_i\}) = \max_\theta \; \underbrace{\log p(\theta)}_{\text{Regularizer}} + \underbrace{\log p(\{x_i, y_i\} \mid \theta)}_{\text{MLE loss}}
\]
That is, from a Bayesian perspective, the normalization term is the prior, and the loss term is the likelihood. The solution optimized together with the normalization term becomes the MAP solution.






TipWireless Communication Perspective: MMSE vs. Sparse Channel Estimation (Review and Integration)




\(\ell_2\) Normalization = Gaussian prior MAP ↔︎ MMSE Channel Estimation (Gaussian prior to channel coefficients; the prior suppresses noise amplification in LS estimation)
\(\ell_1\) Normalization = Laplace prior MAP ↔︎ Sparse Channel Estimation for mmWave/Massive MIMO (LASSO/OMP; prior indicating a small number of paths in the delay-angle domain)
\(\ell_0\) ↔︎ The problem of restoring accurate sparse support — even in compressed sensing, \(\ell_0\) is NP-hard, so it is exactly the same logic as using \(\ell_1\) Convex Relaxation (Basis Pursuit).
It is also the same that the role of the prior (normalization) becomes greater as the data (pilot) becomes scarce.

title: MLP Advanced: Output Units, Activation Functions, and Regularization
text:
11 Regularization techniques for deep learning
Traditional normalization was a hand-crafted prior, but deep learning with an end-to-end philosophy prefers a data-driven normalization method.

11.1 Dataset Augmentation
The fundamental motivation behind normalization is to combat the lack of training data. The easiest but most expensive solution is to “collect more data”—but if budget is limited, create new, fake data that represents the data while retaining its semantics.

Image: Affine distortion, noise injection, axis deformation, flip, translation, color change — pixels change, but same class
Text: Word Variations — Ensuring sentence diversity through synonyms/variants like “trash can” ↔︎ “recycle bin”, “chair” ↔︎ “sofa”



11.2 Adversarial Examples
Neural networks are prone to having solutions that are overfitted to the training data, so the output can be manipulated by microscopic noise invisible to the human eye.

Classic example: panda image (57.7% confidence) + fine noise → 99.3% confidence misclassification as gibbon. This is because the noise pattern triggers an internal statistical/response corresponding to a different semantic.
Safety-related case: If a few stickers are attached to a STOP sign, the autonomous vehicle’s vision model mistakes it for a speed limit sign → it does not stop. An attack actually demonstrated in early neural network-based autonomous driving.

Utilization as defense and normalization — Two methods:







Method
Content




Method 1: Noise in Input
Generate adversarial examples and retrain with correct labels (“This is also a panda”) → The model becomes robust to adversarial perturbations (adversarial training; the primary purpose is security, but it also has the effect of general regularization)


Method 2: Noise on output target = Label Smoothing
Smooth one-hot targets: \(1 \to 1-\epsilon\), \(\;0 \to \dfrac{\epsilon}{k-1}\) (\(\epsilon\): small value, \(k\): number of classes). Prevents overconfidence like “98% pandas, 2% gibbon” to induce less overfitted solutions (Szegedy et al., CVPR 2016)









WarningLabel Smoothing formula memorize



\(k\)-In class, the correct dimension is \(1-\epsilon\) and the incorrect dimension is \(\epsilon/(k-1)\). Verify that the sum is exactly \(1\): \((1-\epsilon) + (k-1)\cdot\frac{\epsilon}{k-1} = 1\).








TipWireless Communication Perspective: Minimum Power Target Jamming



Adversarial perturbation is similar to smart jamming, where an attacker who knows the receiver’s decision boundary pushes symbols beyond the boundary with minimum power — it is identical in that it is efficient to push only in a direction perpendicular to the boundary rather than using broadband noise (a waste of power). And label smoothing corresponds to techniques like LLR clipping, which gain robustness by limiting overconfidence.




11.3 Remaining Data-Driven Normalization Techniques (Detailed in the next note)
Semi-supervised learning (unlabeled data = normalized information), Multi-task learning, Early stopping, Parameter sharing/tying (\(\|B-A\|_2^2\) minimization), Bagging/Ensemble, Dropout, Tangent propagation. This is followed by optimization methodologies (Momentum, initialization, adaptive learning rate, BatchNorm, etc.).

text:
13 1-Minute Cheat Sheet

CE slope \(=(\sigma(z)-y)x\), MSE slope \(=(\sigma(z)-y)\sigma'(z)x\). \(\sigma'_{\max}=0.25\).
CE Minimize ≡ Bernoulli Log-likelihood \(\sum_i [y_i\log q_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-q_i)]\) Maximize.
Sigmoid Multidimensional output sums are not 1 → Exponential normalization results in softmax.
Softmax is size sensitive: the results of \([1,2]\) and \([10,20]\) are different (L1 regularization is the same).
Gumbel-Max trick: \(\text{argmax}(z_i+g_i)\) ~ softmax distribution; a type of reparameterization trick; temperature \(\tau\).
\(h_i=\max(0,z_i)+\alpha_i\min(0,z_i)\): \(\alpha=0\) ReLU, \(-1\) Absolute Value, \(0.01\) Leaky, Learning PReLU.
Folding \(n\) times → Boundary complexity exponential increase.
Vanishing Gradient: Local Gradient (\(\in[0,1]\)) Chain Product → Input Layer Gradient \(\approx 0\); ReLU multiplies by 1.
Catastrophic forgetting: unprotected parameter sharing + insufficient capacity; multiple epochs are a mitigation (no definitive theory); extreme scenario = continual learning.
Depth/parameter: Diminishing returns; Over-parameters → Overfitting; Fluctuations in test accuracy are because the test set is also a sample.
Perceptron (convex, global solution guaranteed) vs MLP (non-convex, local solution); Solution space = Loss × Dataset; lagging behind SVM for over 10 years → 2012 AlexNet.
\(\min L + \Omega\); hard ↔︎ soft constraints are equivalent to \(\lambda^*\) (Lagrangian); \(\ell_1\) inductive/\(\ell_0\) enforced (NP-hard).
MAP \(= \log p(\theta) + \log p(\mathcal{D}|\theta)\) = prior(normalization) + MLE.
Label smoothing: \(1\to1-\epsilon\), \(0\to\epsilon/(k-1)\).

text:
14 Appendix: Verification Code

14.1 CE vs MSE Slope Comparison

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

z = np.linspace(-8, 8, 400)
sig = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
y = 1.0  # 정답 라벨

grad_mse = np.abs((sig - y) * sig * (1 - sig))  # |∂L/∂z|, x=1 가정
grad_ce  = np.abs(sig - y)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax[0].plot(z, sig * (1 - sig))
ax[0].axhline(0.25, ls='--', c='gray')
ax[0].set_title(r"$\sigma'(z)$ — max 0.25 at z=0")
ax[0].set_xlabel("z")

ax[1].plot(z, grad_mse, label="|MSE grad|")
ax[1].plot(z, grad_ce, label="|CE grad|")
ax[1].set_title("y=1일 때 기울기 크기: 포화 영역(z≪0)에서 MSE는 죽는다")
ax[1].set_xlabel("z"); ax[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



14.2 Size Sensitivity of Softmax vs L1 Regularization

def softmax(x):
    e = np.exp(x - np.max(x))
    return e / e.sum()

for v in ([1., 2.], [10., 20.]):
    v = np.array(v)
    print(f"input={v},  L1={v/v.sum()},  softmax={softmax(v)}")



14.3 Empirical verification of the Gumbel-Max trick: The empirical distribution of argmax(logit+Gumbel) = softmax

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
logits = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.5])
N = 200_000

g = rng.gumbel(size=(N, 3))                  # 표준 Gumbel 노이즈
samples = np.argmax(logits + g, axis=1)      # Gumbel-Max 샘플링
emp = np.bincount(samples, minlength=3) / N

print("softmax(logits) :", np.round(softmax(logits), 4))
print("empirical freq  :", np.round(emp, 4))



14.4 Variations of the ReLU generalized formula

def gen_relu(z, alpha):
    return np.maximum(0, z) + alpha * np.minimum(0, z)

z = np.linspace(-3, 3, 300)
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for a, name in [(0, "ReLU"), (-1, "|z| (abs rectifier)"),
                (0.01, "Leaky ReLU"), (0.3, "PReLU (α=0.3 예시)")]:
    plt.plot(z, gen_relu(z, a), label=f"{name}, α={a}")
plt.legend(); plt.title(r"$h=\max(0,z)+\alpha\min(0,z)$"); plt.grid(alpha=.3)
plt.show()



14.5 Gradient Vanishing Simulation: Gradient Magnitude According to Number of Floors

layers = np.arange(1, 31)
sigmoid_chain = 0.25 ** layers   # 각 층 최대 기울기 0.25 가정
relu_chain = 1.0 ** layers

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.semilogy(layers, sigmoid_chain, 'o-', label="Sigmoid (×0.25/layer, 최선의 경우)")
plt.semilogy(layers, relu_chain, 's-', label="ReLU (×1/layer)")
plt.xlabel("layer depth"); plt.ylabel("gradient magnitude (log)")
plt.legend(); plt.grid(alpha=.3); plt.title("Gradient Vanishing")
plt.show()



14.6 Label Smoothing

def label_smooth(onehot, eps):
    k = len(onehot)
    return np.where(onehot == 1, 1 - eps, eps / (k - 1))

t = np.array([0, 0, 1, 0, 0])
print("original :", t)
sm_t = label_smooth(t, eps=0.1)
print("smoothed :", sm_t, "  sum =", sm_t.sum())

title: Advanced Optimization II — Modern Techniques, and Introduction to CNNs
text:
This summary consists of two parts. The first part covers modern techniques (pretraining, MAML, knowledge distillation, architecture improvement, continuation/curriculum learning) that help optimize neural networks, and the second part covers the motivation of CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) — why 2D image recognition is inefficient with MLP alone — and the basics of convolution operations (stride, padding, output size, number of parameters, pooling).
