title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
section: 8.1 Function Composition and Amplification of Nonlinearity
text:
8.1 Function Composition and Amplification of Nonlinearity
One-line summary: Even a simple non-linear function becomes extremely non-linear when composed multiple times.
When a very simple non-linear function \(f\) is applied once, it forms a smooth curve, but as it is synthesized two, three, …, ten times (\(f\circ f\circ\cdots\circ f\)), the ridges in the middle increase sharply. For a 10-word sentence, \(f\) is synthesized 10 times, and for a 300-word paragraph, it is synthesized 300 times. As a result, the function encoded by the RNN becomes an extremely complex and torsion-driven function, making optimization difficult.
\[
h^{(t)} = \underbrace{f\circ f \circ \cdots \circ f}_{t\text{ 번}}\,(h^{(0)})
\]

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
8.2 Eigenvalue Decomposition and Unit Element
In the linear approximation (or the core part ignoring the activation function), if we view the transition between time \(t-1\) and \(t\) as \(h^{(t)} \approx W\,h^{(t-1)}\),
\[
h^{(t)} = W^{t}\,h^{(0)}.
\]
If we perform eigenvalue decomposition of \(W\) \(W = Q\,\Lambda\,Q^{-1}\),
\[
W^{t} = Q\,\Lambda^{t}\,Q^{-1},
\qquad
\Lambda^{t} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^t, \dots, \lambda_n^t).
\]
Therefore, the magnitude of the eigenvalue dominates the behavior.
\[
\boxed{\;|\lambda_i| < 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \lambda_i^t \to 0\ (\text{소실})
\qquad
|\lambda_i| > 1 \;\Rightarrow\; |\lambda_i^t| \to \infty\ (\text{폭발})\;}
\]
When synthesized 300 times, values slightly less than 1 rapidly converge to 0 (gradient vanishing), and values slightly greater than 1 run wild (gradient explosion). As a result, the loss surface drops/rises like a cliff, making optimization unstable. If MLPs are stacked further as layers (deep RNN), the gradients already vanished in a single step worsen, rendering the deep RNN virtually useless.






ImportantWireless communication analogy — Stability of discrete-time LTI systems (exactly the same mathematics)



This is literally the same result as BIBO stability of discrete-time LTI systems.

Eigenvalues of the state transition matrix \(W\) = poles of the system.
All poles are inside the unit circle(\(|\lambda|<1\)): Impulse response damps exponentially → stabilizes, but the influence of the distant past disappears (= gradient vanishing).
Poles are outside the unit circle(\(|\lambda|>1\)): Response diverges → instability (= gradient explosion).
Long-term memory and stability coexist only at the boundary (\(|\lambda|=1\)), but maintaining this boundary precisely is very difficult.

In other words, wanting “long-term memory” is like trying to place the system on the edge of stability (\(|\lambda|\approx 1\)). Gating (Section 9.1) can be understood as a mechanism that adaptively shifts this pole to near 1 depending on the data.


Another limitation is memory capacity. Since the entire past is typically compressed into a single vector using only one or a few cells/gates, it is insufficient to hold all long time-series information.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
9.1 Gating: Key Idea
One-line summary: Create a “highway” from the past to the present (or future), and weight blend the current input and past memory.
\[
f(x) = a\cdot x \;\longrightarrow\; f(x) = a\cdot x + (1-a)\cdot m,
\qquad a\in[0,1],\ m=\text{memory}
\]
\(a\) is a gate value between 0 and 1. The current input \(x\) and the past memory \(m\) are mixed in a ratio of \(a\). This single line of simple mixing is the gating integer.






TipWireless communication analogy — Forgetting factor/1st order IIR low-pass



\(m_t = a\,x_t + (1-a)\,m_{t-1}\) is the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) and 1st-order IIR low-pass filter, and has the same form as the forgetting factor of RLS (Recursive Least Squares). Since the poles lie at \(1-a\), making \(a\) smaller causes the poles to approach 1 (long memory), while making it larger results in rapid forgetting (short memory). Gating is the adaptive learning of this forgetting factor for each data point and time.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
9.2 Gating 1: LSTM
Long Short-Term Memory (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). There is a separate “highway” called cell state \(c_t\), and the flow of information is controlled by three gates.
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_t &= \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f) &&\text{(forget gate)}\\
i_t &= \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i) &&\text{(input gate)}\\
o_t &= \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o) &&\text{(output gate)}\\
\tilde{c}_t &= \tanh(W_c[h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c) &&\text{(candidate)}\\
c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t &&\text{(cell update)}\\
h_t &= o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) &&\text{(hidden output)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The key is the cell state update \(c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1} + i_t\odot\tilde c_t\). If it is the forget gate \(f_t\approx 1\), the past cell state is passed almost exactly as is, so the gradients are preserved (= poles are adaptively placed near 1). This is the same spirit as ResNet’s residual connection (Section 3.2).

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
9.3 Gating 2: GRU
Gated Recurrent Unit (Cho et al., 2014). A simpler implementation of almost the same idea as LSTM. The cell state and hidden state are combined and the gate is reduced to two.
\[
\begin{aligned}
z_t &= \sigma(W_z[h_{t-1}, x_t]) &&\text{(update gate)}\\
r_t &= \sigma(W_r[h_{t-1}, x_t]) &&\text{(reset gate)}\\
\tilde{h}_t &= \tanh\!\left(W[r_t \odot h_{t-1}, x_t]\right) &&\text{(candidate)}\\
h_t &= (1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1} + z_t\odot \tilde{h}_t &&\text{(혼합)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The last line is the vector version of Section 9.1’s mixed formula \(a\cdot x + (1-a)\cdot m\).

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
9.4 LSTM vs GRU









LSTM
GRU




Number of Gates
3 (forget/input/output)
2 (update/reset)


State
Cell State \(c_t\) + Concealed \(h_t\)
Concealed \(h_t\) Only


Parameters
Many
About 1/2


Performance
Standard
Equivalent to LSTM


Strengths
Expressiveness
Risk of Overfitting ↓ (Advantageous when data is small)



GRU was an attempt to achieve similar performance with fewer parameters based on the observation that “LSTM is overparameterized” and succeeded.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
9.5 Other solutions

Idea 1 — Time skip connection: Add a direct connection to a distant view like Vision’s DenseNet.
Idea 2 — Leaky units: \(h_t = (1-\alpha)h_{t-1} + \alpha\,\sigma(W_{rec}h_{t-1} + W_{in}x_t)\). (Independent of leaky-ReLU.) Same form as the first-order IIR integrator above.
Idea 3 — Gating: LSTM/GRU (discussed above).
Idea 4 — Optimization Trick: Gradient Clipping (Explosive Correspondence) + Normalization Encouraging Information Flow (Vanishing Correspondence).
Idea 5 — Explicit Memory: External memory modules such as Memory Networks (Weston et al., ICLR 2015).

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
10.1 Buffalo Example
The English sentence “Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo” is a grammatically correct sentence in which all words have the same spelling (place name/animal/verb), but their part of speech and meaning change depending on the context. It clearly demonstrates that even with the same token, the surrounding context determines the meaning.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
10.2 Context-Conditional RNN and Bidirectional RNN

Context-Conditional RNN (Single Input): The idea that looking at past outputs helps predict the future. It establishes a backward connection from the future.
Context-Conditional RNN (Sequence Input): Uses the hidden state output from the previous time step and the output from the previous time step both as inputs for the next hidden state (unlike teacher forcing, it maintains the hidden state connection).
Bi-directional RNN: “Reading back and forth helps with memory.” By introducing a backward hidden state separate from the forward hidden state, the representation of each time step considers both past and future contexts.

\[
\overrightarrow{h}_t = f(\overrightarrow{h}_{t-1}, x_t),\qquad
\overleftarrow{h}_t = f(\overleftarrow{h}_{t+1}, x_t),\qquad
y_t = g\!\left(\overrightarrow{h}_t, \overleftarrow{h}_t\right)
\]






NoteWireless communication analogy — Filtering vs. Smoothing



A unidirectional RNN is a causal filter that uses only the past = Kalman filtering. A bidirectional RNN is a non-causal smoothing that uses future observations as well = Kalman smoothing. Estimating by looking at the entire sequence offline (smoothing) becomes more accurate than causal estimation (filtering), but it cannot be used for real-time processing. This is exactly the same trade-off as the bidirectional RNN needing to receive the entire sequence to operate.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
12.1 Deep RNN
RNN with multiple hidden layers. Expressiveness increases, but as seen in Section 8, the gradient that is already weakened in one step is added to the depth, making training more difficult.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
12.2 Recursive Neural Networks
One-line summary: A generalization of RNNs that uses a tree structured computational graph instead of a chain.

Process sequences as a tree instead of linearly.
For length \(\tau\), the search/propagation depth is reduced from \(\tau\) to \(\log(\tau)\) → This is advantageous (in principle) as it allows long-term dependencies to be connected via shorter paths.
Application: Scene parsing — Each hidden node corresponds to an object in the scene (Socher et al., ICML 2011).







NoteWireless communication analogy — Reducing the depth of the tree structure



Reducing the \(O(\tau)\) depth of sequential processing to a \(O(\log\tau)\) tree is equivalent to shortening the critical path by replacing serial accumulation with binary-tree reduction. This aligns with the spirit of divide and conquer, where FFT reduces the \(O(N^2)\) DFT to \(O(N\log N)\).

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
13.1 More to read

Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning — Ch. 9(CNN, specifically 9.10 Comparison with the Human Visual System), Ch. 10(Sequence Modeling: RNN, LSTM, GRU, BPTT, seq2seq).
Dive into Deep Learning (d2l.ai) — Ch. 9 RNN Basics (BPTT’s Vanishing/Explosion of Eigenvalues), Ch. 10 Modern RNN (LSTM/GRU/Deep/Bi-RNN/Seq2Seq/Encoder-Decoder).
The BPTT section of d2l.ai explains the mathematical details of gradient vanishing/explosion well from the eigenvalue perspective of \(W_{hh}^\top\). (For a linear algebra review, refer to the matrix eigenvalue decomposition and spectral radius sections.)

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
14.1 A. Eigenvalue Size and Disappearance/Explosion


Code
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)

def spectral_radius(W):
    return np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(W)))

# 수축 행렬 (|lambda|<1) -> 소실 / 팽창 행렬 (|lambda|>1) -> 폭발
Wc = np.array([[0.9, 0.1], [0.0, 0.8]])
We = np.array([[1.2, 0.1], [0.0, 1.1]])

print(f"rho(Wc) = {spectral_radius(Wc):.3f}   rho(We) = {spectral_radius(We):.3f}")
print(f"{'t':>4} | {'||Wc^t||':>12} | {'||We^t||':>12}")
for t in [1, 5, 20, 50]:
    nc = np.linalg.norm(np.linalg.matrix_power(Wc, t))
    ne = np.linalg.norm(np.linalg.matrix_power(We, t))
    print(f"{t:>4} | {nc:>12.3e} | {ne:>12.3e}")


If the spectral radius is less than 1, \(\|W^t\|\) goes to 0, and if it is greater, it goes to infinity — this is the nature of gradient vanishing/explosion.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
14.2 B. Vanilla RNN Forward Propagation


Code
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(1)

def rnn_step(h, x, Wxh, Whh, b):
    return np.tanh(Whh @ h + Wxh @ x + b)

T, dh, dx = 6, 3, 2
Wxh = 0.5 * np.random.randn(dh, dx)
Whh = 0.6 * np.random.randn(dh, dh)
b = np.zeros(dh)

h = np.zeros(dh)
xs = np.random.randn(T, dx)
for t in range(T):
    h = rnn_step(h, xs[t], Wxh, Whh, b)
    print(f"t={t}  h = {np.round(h, 4)}")

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
14.3 C. EMA as Gating (Forgetting Factor)


Code
import numpy as np

# m_t = a * x_t + (1 - a) * m_{t-1}   (1차 IIR 저역통과 = 적응적 망각)
a = 0.3
m, xs = 0.0, np.ones(10)   # 계단 입력
traj = []
for t in range(10):
    m = a * xs[t] + (1 - a) * m
    traj.append(round(m, 4))

print("EMA(forgetting factor) trajectory:")
print(traj)
print("steady state ->", traj[-1], "(approaches 1)")


Small \(a\) creates long memory by setting the poles close to 1, and large \(a\) creates fast forgetting. The gates of the LSTM/GRU learn this \(a\) for every data and time.

title: From the Evolution of CNNs to Sequence Modeling: History, Architecture, and RNN
text:
14.4 D. RNN Type Comparison (Conceptual Sketch)


Code
# 의사코드 수준의 개념 비교 (실제 학습 루프는 아님)
def type1_step(h, x, params):
    h = tanh(params.Whh @ h + params.Wxh @ x)   # hidden -> hidden
    o = params.Who @ h
    return h, o

def type2_step(h, x, prev_out, params, training, y=None):
    feedback = y if training else prev_out       # teacher forcing vs 자기 출력
    h = tanh(params.Wfh @ feedback + params.Wxh @ x)  # output -> hidden
    o = params.Who @ h
    return h, o

# Type 3: 전체 시퀀스를 돌린 뒤 마지막 h로만 출력
def type3_run(xs, h, params):
    for x in xs:
        h = tanh(params.Whh @ h + params.Wxh @ x)
    return params.Who @ h                         # 끝에서 단일 출력

print("Type1: 매 시각 출력, 은닉-은닉 (표준/강한 기억)")
print("Type2: teacher forcing (병렬화 쉬움 / 기억 약함)")
print("Type3: 끝에서 단일 출력 (시퀀스 분류·QA의 표준)")

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
TipKey line



A Transformer is a sequence-to-seq model that uses “input-dependent weights” instead of “fixed weights.” These weights do not directly weight the data, but are assigned to the similarity between data points.


The three pillars supporting the Transformer are as follows.








Component
One-line definition
Intuition




Token
A vector (bundle of neurons) encapsulating information
Elevating the minimum unit of processing from “neuron” to “bundle of vectors”


Attention
Dynamic pooling that assigns learned weights to similarity
Observes the input, changes the weights, and applies them back to the input


Positional Encoding
Code that adds a positional address to a token
Tells a model that does not know the order “which token it is”



Of these three, attention is the most important. The other two are more like auxiliary devices that make attention applicable to actual data.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
2.1 Two challenges in sequence modeling
The data discussed so far has been “snapshots” (images, graphs) with fixed length. However, language, time series (stock prices), video, and audio are sequences with variable length. There are two key challenges in sequence encoding.

Long-term dependency: It is difficult to remember information from a long time ago.
Context: Even the same token can have different meanings depending on the surrounding context. (e.g., as in the sentence “Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo …”, the same word can be interpreted as a noun, verb, or place name depending on the context.)

RNNs address these two difficult problems by propagating the hidden state from start to finish. The Transformer is an alternative to this and has now become the de facto standard.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 2.2 CNN Limitations: Failure Cases Seen Through VQA
text:
2.2 CNN Limitations: Failure Cases Seen Through VQA






NoteVQA(Visual Question Answering) Example



Let’s think about questions like “How many birds are in this image?”, “Are the bird in the top right and the bird in the bottom left the same species?”, and “What is the color of the sky?”


CNN stands on two design assumptions.

Locality: The filter only considers adjacent areas.
Spatial stationarity: Applies the same filter equally across the entire image (parameter sharing).

Because of this assumption, CNN does not do the following well.

Counting: max-pooling passes only the position with the strongest reaction to the next layer. This conflicts with the task of counting different “birds” at each position.
Long-distance relationship comparison: Determining the relationship between two distant objects (“Top right vs. Bottom left”) is difficult with local filters.
Selective attention based on context: CNNs scan all spatial locations equally, but there are times when they need to pay attention to “only specific regions” depending on the question.

Locally-connected networks (CNNs that eliminate weight sharing) are advantageous for counting, but the number of parameters explodes, and they lose almost all the advantages of CNNs. Therefore, a different type of encoding method is needed — that is attention.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
3.1 New data structure






TipKey point



A token is not a “single neuron” but a “vector encapsulating information.” Transformers perform operations at the token level, not the neuron level.



It is essentially the same concept as the “node attribute” of GNN — the unit of information is a vector.
If you chop the input and project each piece onto a vector, it becomes a token.




Input Type
Tokenization Method




Image
Split into patches and project each patch as a vector (ViT)


Text
Convert word/subword to embedding vector


Audio
Convert time interval (frame) to vector

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 3.2 Once tokenized, all modalities are in the same architecture
text:
3.2 Once tokenized, all modalities are in the same architecture
This is a major practical advantage of Transformer. Regardless of modality, once tokenized, the same architecture can be used as is.

CNNs are closer to “one way of encoding” information, while MLPs are closer to “one way of mixing” information. Transformers shift the burden of modality integration to the “tokenization” stage by pushing inputs into a token space.

Tokens are updated through linear combinations between tokens and token-wise nonlinearity (i.e., position-wise MLP).

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
4.1 Fixed Weights vs. Attention






ImportantThe most important distinction




Ordinary weight: A fixed value regardless of the input. It is learned from the data, but remains the same regardless of the input during inference.
Attention: Weights are a function of the input. It receives input, changes the weight values, and applies the changed weights back to the input.



Looking at the formula, the output of a normal layer is ZZZPH0008507ZZZ , where \(y = Wx\) and Z\(W\) is a constant. For attention, like \(y = A(x)\,x\), the weights themselves are a function of \(x\) \(A(x)\). Only one step is added: “take the input as input, create weights, and apply those weights back to the input.”

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
4.2 Attention as dynamic pooling
Attention can be understood as dynamic/adaptive pooling based on queries.

Max/average pooling performs fixed operations (max/average) without considering the relationships between positions.
Attention dynamically determines pooling weights based on the relationship (similarity) between the query and the key.

In other words, it is “relationship-based pooling that is neither max, min, nor average”.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
4.3 Query·Key·Value (Query, Key, Value)
Defines three roles.

Query (\(q\)): The target from which to obtain encoding (embedding). What I am “asking”.
Key (\(k\)): Other contextual information. The relative to measure similarity with the query.
Value (\(v\)): Information to actually retrieve and combine. Reflected in the output as a result of the operation.







NoteLanguage example: “I like ice cream”



If you want to obtain the embedding of “like”, “like” is the query, and all words in the sentence (“I”, “like”, “ice”, “cream”) are the keys. Measure the similarity between the query and each key, and then perform a weighted sum of the values based on that similarity.








NoteVQA Example (cross-attention)



The question sentence “What color is this impala?” serves as the query, and image patches serve as the key/value. Large weights are assigned to patches (impala regions) similar to the query, and clues to the answer are obtained from the values of those regions. When the query and the key originate from different sources, this is called cross-attention.


By simply defining “what to use as queries/keys/values” based on the problem settings (translation, VQA, video generation, etc.), various problems can be reduced to a single format.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
4.4 Why is similarity cosine similarity?
Measure the similarity between query \(q\) and key \(k\) using the dot product. Let’s explain this using high school vectors.
\[
q \cdot k = \|q\|\,\|k\|\cos\theta
\]

\(\|q\|,\|k\|\) is the magnitude, \(\theta\) is the angle between the two vectors.
If the two vectors are normalized to unit vectors (or if magnitude is ignored), the dot product is \(\cos\theta\) itself.

\[
\text{cosine similarity} = \frac{q\cdot k}{\|q\|\,\|k\|} = \cos\theta
\]
Geometrically, \(\cos\theta\) is the length of the projection of one vector in the direction of another vector. That is:

\(\theta = 90°\) (Orthogonal) → \(\cos\theta = 0\): Irrelevant.
\(\theta = 0°\) (same direction) → \(\cos\theta = 1\): maximum similarity.







TipIntuition



Cosine similarity ignores magnitude and only looks at “how much the direction points in the same direction.” This is also called angular distance**. What attention asks is “whether the query and the key point in the same direction.”

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
4.5 Softmax: Amplifying the Difference
Apply softmax to the similarity score vector \(s = [s_1, \dots, s_n]\).
\[
a_j = \frac{\exp(s_j)}{\sum_{l} \exp(s_l)}
\]
The role of the softmax is to amplify the difference between the maximum value and the remainder to create a weight distribution where the sum is 1 (smooth argmax). The \(a\) obtained in this way is the attention weight.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 4.6 Value transformation matrix \(W_v\) and training target
text:
4.6 Value transformation matrix \(W_v\) and training target
Up until now, \(q, k\) has been used to determine similarity (=attention strength). Then, what is the value that will actually be combined? Instead of using the input token \(x\) as is, it is transformed once more into a trainable matrix \(W_v\). This grants degrees of freedom to rotate/scale the value space to suit the given task.
To summarize, what attention learns are three projection matrices \(W_q, W_k, W_v\).
\[
Q = X W_q,\quad K = X W_k,\quad V = X W_v
\]






ImportantThe Essence of Attention



Attention is not “applying fixed weights to the information itself”, but “applying learned weights to the similarity between pieces of information”. Which similarity is important varies depending on the data and the task, and \(W_q, W_k, W_v\) learns this judgment.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
4.7 Scaled Dot-Product Attention (Supplement)
The entire operation can be written as a single matrix as follows. (This normalization coefficient \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is omitted in the intuitive explanation above, but is included here as it invariably appears in actual implementations — refer to the Attention Scoring Functions section of d2l.ai.)
\[
\boxed{\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\ }
\]






NoteWhy divide into \(\sqrt{d_k}\)



If each component of \(q, k\) is independent with a mean of 0 and a variance of 1, the variance of the inner product \(q\cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i\) becomes \(d_k\). If \(d_k\) is large, the magnitude of the scores increases, causing the softmax to become oversaturated on one side, and the gradient becomes nearly 0 in that region. Dividing by the standard deviation \(\sqrt{d_k}\) returns the score variance to a level of 1, stabilizing the learning.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
5.1 Matrix Operations
For \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) ( \(n\) token, dimension \(d\) ):
\[
Q=XW_q,\ K=XW_k,\ V=XW_v;\qquad
\text{Out} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\tfrac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
\]
The order of operations for is the same as cross-attention, differing only in that \(Q,K,V\) comes from the same \(X\).

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 5.2 DINO: Visualization of Patch Value Refining
text:
5.2 DINO: Visualization of Patch Value Refining
In the self-supervised learning model DINO (Caron et al., ICCV 2021), when attention scores are visualized with a small patch as a query, regions of semantically identical objects (numbers) appear bright, while irrelevant backgrounds appear dark. This demonstrates that self-attention groups patches by semantic unit.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
6.1 Why Block the Future
Let’s consider machine translation (seq-to-seq). The encoder looks at the entire input sentence, but the decoder generates words one by one. At the point \(t\), the words after \(t+1\) have not yet been generated.

If attention is allowed on future tokens, the decoder will “peek” at the correct answer (future word) during training and refer to a non-existent token during inference.
As a result, the attention score of the future position becomes a meaningless value, and during backpropagation, the garbage gradient propagates up to \(W_q, W_k\), ruining the learning.

Solution: Make the score of the future position \(-\infty\) (actually a very large negative number) so that the weight becomes 0 after softmax.
\[
s_{ij} \leftarrow
\begin{cases}
s_{ij} & j \le i \quad(\text{과거·현재})\\[4pt]
-\infty & j > i \quad(\text{미래, 마스킹})
\end{cases}
\]

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
6.2 Other uses: Optional multimodal encoding
In addition to causality, masking can be used as a general mechanism to select which tokens to exclude from the context. For example, when generating a consistent sequence of images that corresponds to a text story, an attention mask can be designed to selectively encode only relevant tokens (Ahn et al., Story visualization by online text augmentation with context memory, ICCV 2023).

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
8.1 Equivariance and Invariance








Concept
Definition
One-line Intuition




Invariance
Output remains the same even if input changes
Insensitive to change


Equivariance
Output changes as much as the input changes
Reflects change



Example: If the output rotates along with the input when rotated, it is rotationally equal; if the output remains unchanged, it is rotationally invariant.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 8.2 The necessity of permutation equivariance and positional encoding
text:
8.2 The necessity of permutation equivariance and positional encoding






Importantproblem



Attention (and MLPs) are permutation equivariant. If the order of input tokens is shuffled, the output is shuffled in the same way, but the model does not know the original positions of the tokens.


In language and images, position/order determines meaning (“dog bites person” ≠ “person bites dog”). Therefore, position information must be explicitly injected into tokens. That is the position encoding in the following section.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 9.1 Why aren’t simple integer numbers allowed?
text:
9.1 Why aren’t simple integer numbers allowed?
The simplest idea is to assign positions as integers \(0,1,2,\dots\). However, sparse codes with many zeros, like binary representations, are difficult to learn weights on (weights multiplied by zeros are effectively not learned). We need dense representations where every dimension has a meaningful value, and vectors that differ by position but are similar in size.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
9.2 Sine wave position encoding (supplement)
The most widely used implementation is to use sine/cosine of different frequencies (Vaswani et al., 2017; d2l.ai Self-Attention and Positional Encoding section).
\[
PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d}}\right),\qquad
PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d}}\right)
\]

All component sizes are uniform as \([-1, 1]\) → Advantageous for weight learning.
Unique pattern (address) for each location → Location distinguishable.
Since it is a superposition of different frequencies, relative position information can also be expressed by a linear transformation.







NoteAnalogy: Military unit numbering



Even though the value itself may appear “unconventional” (e.g., Unit 6575), it is a code designed to have good properties from the perspective of learning weights. A sine wave PE is a location address that “appears meaningless to the human eye but is useful for machine learning.”


When position encoding is added, multi-head (masked) self-attention + feedforward effectively captures the context to generate appropriate output probabilities.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
11.1 Language Model
A language model is an NLP task that predicts the probability of the next word given previous words. A common assumption is that “the probability of the next word depends only on previous words within a fixed-size window.” When the scale is very large, it is called a Large-scale Language Model (LLM) (GPT, Claude, HyperClova X, etc.).
Language modeling is, in fact, the meta-task of NLP. Training a good language model can yield numerous downstream tasks, such as sentiment analysis, Named Entity Recognition (NER), coreference resolution, and question answering. Therefore, people have continuously expanded their models.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
11.2 Autoregressive Models and GPT
GPT = Generative Pretrained Transformer. The name contains “Transformer” (GPT is not General Purpose Text).

Autoregressive: Generate the next token using the previously generated token as input, and repeat this process.
Training: Train the entire encoder-decoder (or decoder-only) model to output one word at a time. Sampling (Inference) also generates one token at a time.
Causal attention: Since it does not look at future tokens, it aligns exactly with autoregressive generation.







WarningWeakness of Autoregression



Error Propagation: If an error is made once at the beginning, that error spreads to the entire sequence thereafter. As an alternative, methods to generate word chunks all at once (e.g., some models generate chunks using CNN/Diffusion) are also being studied. However, early LLMs (such as GPT-2/3) used the Transformer directly for autoregression.








NoteTouch it yourself: minGPT



A. Karpathy’s minGPT is a minimal GPT with causal attention fully implemented. Its source is very simple, which makes it suitable for training.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
section: 12.1 1) Cannot see outside the context window
text:
12.1 1) Cannot see outside the context window
Calculates \(W_q, W_k, W_v\) only within the key window (e.g., 128,000 tokens). Information outside the window is not propagated like an RNN and is therefore lost → Asking for information from a distance can increase hallucination.

Partial Mitigation: KV Cache. It stores and reuses the Key/Value pairs of important tokens to effectively maintain long contexts. However, this is a temporary solution and not a fundamental solution.
Since it must hold the KV cache, memory demand is high (one cause of GPU memory/bandwidth bottlenecks).

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
12.2 2) Computational complexity \(O(n^2)\)
For window size \(n\), the attention is \(O(n^2)\). Two operations proportional to the square of the window size are performed: once for the inner product of all query-key pairs in \(QK^\top\), and again when applying the attention weights to \(V\). As the window increases, the cost skyrockets.

title: Transformer: Token, Attention, Position Encoding
text:
12.3 Efficient Alternative

Efficient Transformer family(Tay et al., Efficient Transformers: A Survey, 2022): \(O(n^2)\) relaxation through sparse/low-rank approximation, etc.
Mamba and other State Space Model (SSM) families: Attempts to encode long contexts with lower complexity.







TipOpen problem



The current Transformer architecture is not the optimal structure that humans can imagine. Finding a deterministic function (architecture) that encodes long contexts more efficiently remains a major research topic that is still open.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
The content covered today is broadly divided into two main axes.

Multimodal Learning — A methodology for handling data of different modalities (images, text, audio, etc.) within a single system. After briefly examining an efficient alternative to the Transformer (Mamba), we will look at the five key challenges of multimodal learning and representative techniques such as CLIP and SigLIP.
Generative model I — A model that attempts to learn the data distribution p(X) itself. Starting from autoencoders (AE), it covers VAE (variational inference + ELBO + reparameterization) and GAN (minimax game).

A single sentence connecting the two axes: “If we compress high-dimensional data into low-dimensional latent representations and transform that latent space into a distribution we can control, representation, alignment, fusion, and generation all become easier.”






TipOne-line mapping for wireless communication majors




Latent representation = Compressed representation of source coding
Force latent distribution to \mathcal N(0,I) = Gaussian codebook design
Comparative Learning (CLIP) = Matched Filter / Correlation Detection
GAN minimax = Worst-case robust design in 2-player zero-sum games with jammers

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
2.1 Two limitations of the Transformer
Self-attention is powerful but has two structural weaknesses.

It is difficult to encode context outside the window. Attention interacts directly only within a fixed length of context.
The computational complexity is O(n^2) (n is the sequence/window length). As the length increases, memory and computation increase exponentially.

Research aimed at reducing this forms a major trend known as “Efficient Transformers” (Tay et al., 2022).

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
2.2 Mamba: Optional state-space model (S6)
Mamba(Gu & Dao, 2023) views sequences as State Space Models (SSM) and processes them in linear time. The core idea is twofold.

Selective mechanism (S6) — Maintain a small window, but selectively keep only relevant tokens within it. The method of measuring relevance is similar to the gating of an RNN.
Hardware-aware parallel scan — Speed is achieved by computing sequential recursion as a parallel scan on the GPU.









Features
Transformer
Mamba




Complexity
O(n^2)
O(n) (Linear)


Advantages
Strong context encoding (long-distance dependency)
Computational efficiency, long window (256k+)


Weakness
Computational Cost
Expressiveness does not exceed Transformer [Chen et al., 2025]









NoteHybrid is the trend




Jamba: Mix Transformer + Mamba into a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE).
MambaVision: The initial layer is Mamba (efficiency), and the later layer is self-attention (long-range dependency).
TransMamba: Select one of the two based on layer/token.

From the perspective of circuit complexity, Mamba is not more expressive than Transformer. In other words, Mamba is not a “smarter” model, but a “cheaper” model.








TipWireless Communication Perspective



An optional SSM is essentially a recursive state estimator. The form of the state h_t = A h_{t-1} + B x_t and output y_t = C h_t is a framework similar to a Kalman filter / linear dynamic system. Determining how much of the past to forget through gating directly corresponds to adaptively adjusting the forgetting factor \lambda of an RLS (Recursive Least Squares).

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
3.1 Assignment 1 — Representation
Definition: A method of summarizing and representing multimodal data by utilizing complementarity and redundancy between modalities.
Expression learning is divided into two branches.









Method
Description
Difficulty
Remaining Tasks




Joint representation
Embeds all modalities in a single space
Learning is difficult
(None — once trained, it is easy)


Coordinated representation
Align after learning separate spaces for each modality
Relatively easy
How to align the two spaces



Key Insight: Tuning expressions are usually easier. This is because co-expressions attempt to solve difficult problems all at once, whereas tuning expressions defer the difficulty to an “alignment stage.”

3.1.1 Multimodal Vector Arithmetic (Vector arithmetic)
In a well-trained co-embedding space, semantics are represented as vector operations.

\text{vec}(\text{이미지: 파란 책}) - \text{vec}(\text{파랑}) + \text{vec}(\text{빨강}) \approx \text{vec}(\text{빨간 책})

If you remove “sky” and add “sea” from an airplane image, the nearest neighbor becomes a boat image. This is because semantically similar data is clustered in spatially close areas. (Multimodal version of Word2Vec’s king - man + woman ≈ queen.)

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
3.2 Assignment 2 — Alignment
Definition: Finding a direct correspondence between (sub)elements in two or more modes.







Type
Description




Explicit alignment
1:1 direct mapping of elements of one modality to elements of another modality


Implicit alignment
Instead of creating explicit correspondences, leave it to a learned function to perform the mapping









Warning



The alignment referred to here is a completely different concept from LLM alignment (human value alignment). Please be careful not to confuse them.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
3.3 Assignment 3 — Fusion
Definition: The combination of information from two or more modalities for the purpose of prediction. (Since the essence of AI is ultimately to predict something, it must combine multiple inputs into one to make a prediction.)





flowchart TB
    subgraph EF["Early Fusion (model-agnostic)"]
      a1[모달 A] --> cc[Concatenate]
      a2[모달 B] --> cc
      cc --> m1[Model] --> o1[예측]
    end
    subgraph LF["Late Fusion (model-agnostic)"]
      b1[모달 A] --> mA[Model A] --> mm[Merge]
      b2[모달 B] --> mB[Model B] --> mm
      mm --> o2[예측]
    end
    subgraph IF["Intermediate / model-based"]
      c1[모달 A] --> mid[하나의 모델 내부에서 융합<br/>예: 신경망, 그래프 모델]
      c2[모달 B] --> mid --> o3[예측]
    end







Early fusion: Combine before feeding into the model. The simplest method is to concatenate the two feature vectors.
Late fusion: Pass each model through each modality, then combine them at the output stage.
Model-based (Intermediate) fusion: Designed to fuse internal within the model (neural networks, graph models, etc.). Trained end-to-end.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
3.4 Assignment 4 — Translation
Definition: Changing data from one modality to another. The correspondence is often open-ended/subjective.

Image → Text: Captioning
Text → Image: Image generation
Text → Video: Video generation









Type
Description
Examples/Limitations




Example-based
Directly constructed using data mapping between modalities as an example
Lexicographical 1:1 mapping. Works well when word order and meaning are similar, like in language translation (English ↔︎ French). Difficult when words do not match 1:1, like in English ↔︎ Chinese


Model-driven
Uses a transformation model trained with mapping examples
Most modern translators. Primarily uses neural networks

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
3.5 Assignment 5 — Co-Learning
Definition: A learning framework that transfers knowledge (representation and predictive power) between modes.

Today’s Reality: The four tasks above have virtually all been absorbed into one massive neural network. The current mainstream paradigm is “scale up the model without worrying about representation/alignment/fusion/transformation separately.”







ImportantEfficiency is competitiveness



However, scaling is very expensive in terms of money and power. Finding a efficient method to transfer knowledge better with less data and power has significant implications for beating giant tech companies with small technology. (A message as a direction for research.)








TipWireless Communication Perspective



Fusion corresponds exactly to diversity combining.

Early fusion (concatenate) ↔︎ Combines antenna signals before combining → Combines at the raw signal stage like MRC (Maximal-Ratio Combining)
Late fusion ↔︎ Independent detection and combination at each antenna → selection / soft combining

The complementarity and redundancy of different modes are the complementarity and redundancy of spatial diversity.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
4.2 SigLIP (Google DeepMind, 2021)
CLIP’s softmax requires normalization of the entire batch, resulting in high memory/communication costs. SigLIP replaces this with sigmoid (binary classification) independent of each pair.
y_{ij} = +1 (correct pair, i=j) / -1 (incorrect pair), for scale t, bias b:

\mathcal{L}_{\text{SigLIP}}
= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}
\log \sigma\!\big(y_{ij}\,(t\, I_i^\top T_j + b)\big),
\qquad \sigma(u)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-u}}

Since each pair is an independent binary decision, batch-wide normalization is not required → Increased parallelization and memory efficiency, easy to scale to large batches.

4.2.1 Comparison Table









Features

NoteCLIP + Diffusion Model = Bridge to Generation



By mapping a random vector to a CLIP embedding and using that embedding as a condition for a diffusion model, images/videos can be generated from text. DALL·E 3, Make-A-Video, Phenaki, Sora, and Runway Gen-4.5 are multimodal generation models of this family.








TipWireless Communication Perspective — Contrast Learning = Detection Theory



CLIP’s softmax-over-batch is equivalent to Maximum-Likelihood detection (ML detection) in a codebook. It selects the codeword (correct text) most correlated with the received signal (image embedding) from N candidates — this is precisely the matched-filter bank + argmax.
SigLIP’s sigmoid-per-pair is an individual binary hypothesis test (energy/correlation detection) for each pair. That is, - CLIP = Combined ML Detection (Global normalization required, optimal but expensive) - SigLIP = Pairwise Independent Detection (Separable, Excellent Scalability)
The inner product I_i^\top T_j is the correlation, and \tau/temperature is the same as the SNR scale that controls the sharpness of the detection threshold.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
5.1 Autoencoder(Autoencoder, AE)
AE Goal: Feed input x into the model to reconstruct itself.





flowchart LR
    x[입력 x] --> E[Encoder] --> z[잠재 z<br/>저차원] --> D[Decoder] --> xh[복원 x̂]












WarningThe trap of “Can’t you just copy it?”



If we output the input exactly as is, it is a perfect solution with zero reconstruction error. So why bother using an encoder-decoder?
Answer: This is because the dimension of the latent representation z is smaller than the input. (For example, Input 7 dimensions → Latent 4 dimensions.) Reconstruction is possible only by passing information through a narrow channel, discarding noise and retaining only the core information. This forced narrow channel is precisely the information bottleneck.



Encoder: Extract key information from input (compress).
Decoder: Reconstruct input from core information.
By stacking more deeply (deep AE), more sophisticated information can be compressed/restored step by step.







TipWireless Communication Perspective — Information Bottleneck = Rate–Distortion



The information bottleneck is lossy source coding itself. Latent dimension = bit rate R, restoration error = distortion D. AE solves the rate-distortion optimization problem using neural networks to minimize distortion within a given rate budget. The fewer the “knobs” called latent dimensions, the more precisely the latent space can be controlled.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
section: 5.2 Why AE Matters Now: LeCun’s Cake Analogy
text:
5.2 Why AE Matters Now: LeCun’s Cake Analogy
Yann LeCun (Meta FAIR, NYU) likened the amount of information a machine receives during learning to a cake.





flowchart TB
    cherry["🍒 체리 (꼭대기)<br/>= 강화학습 (RL)<br/>아주 적은 정보"] --> icing
    icing["🎂 아이싱<br/>= 지도학습 (Supervised)<br/>피상적 정보"] --> bread
    bread["🍰 빵 (본체, 대부분)<br/>= 자기지도학습 (Self-supervised)<br/>대부분의 정보"]















Learning method
Cake region
Signal quantity/quality
Reason




Reinforcement Learning (RL)
Cherry
Very weak, stochastic
Rewards are given in the future, sporadically. The reward at the current time must be predicted as an expectation, and the variance is large


Supervised Learning

The label “This image = cake” does not tell you anything about color, background, shape, etc.


Self-supervised Learning (SSL)

Note



Reasons why SSL is powerful: (1) extracts almost all information from the data, (2) no human labeling required → easy data acquisition. **The only difficulty is “designing a good pretext task (self-supervised task)”. AE’s “input restoration” is the most basic pretext task.








TipWireless Communication Perspective — Weak Compensation = Low SNR Feedback



The fact that the reward signal in RL is “weak and stochastic” is equivalent to a feedback channel arriving sporadically with a very low SNR. Since the estimated variance is large, learning is slow and unstable. On the other hand, since the entire input is the correct answer in SSL, it is a high-SNR full-feedback situation.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
6.1 One-line summary
VAE = AE + “Normalization that forces the latent representation z to follow \mathcal N(0,I)”. This allows for complete control of the latent space (→ smooth generation and interpolation), and learns p(x), which cannot be directly computed, by bypassing it through variational inference.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
6.2 Goal as a Generative Model
Given the data X=\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}, we want to find the distribution p(X) that explains it. However, it is difficult to model p(X) directly. Therefore, we introduce a latent variable z.

p(x) = \sum_{z} p(x\mid z)\,p(z)
\quad\xrightarrow{\text{연속}}\quad
p(x) = \int p(x\mid z)\,p(z)\,dz

Here, the prior distribution is fixed to p(z)=\mathcal N(0,I). Interpretation: “First, we draw z from the Gaussian (z\sim p(z)), and from that, we generate x (x\sim p(x\mid z)).”

6.2.1 Why Gaussian latent, of all things?

Analytically tractable. For Gaussians, differentiation, integration, and sampling are all well-defined, and KL and others also appear in a closed form.
Sampling is easy. Almost all hardware/libraries have a Gaussian sampler.
It is sufficiently expressive. Many natural phenomena follow a Gaussian distribution (Central Limit Theorem). Therefore, it is not unreasonable to assume that the latent space is Gaussian, and natural phenomena can be modeled in a controlled manner.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
6.3 Integration is difficult to handle (intractability)
Problem: In p(x)=\int p(x\mid z)p(z)\,dz, p(x\mid z) is a decoder (non-linear neural network), so the integral does not come out in a closed form.






NoteWhen you encounter “difficult integration” — Two branches



(a) Monte Carlo Sampling. Integration = “Calculating Area”. The area of a strangely shaped region is approximated by the proportion of arrows thrown infinitely into a rectangle that land within the region (Dart Game). That is, \int f \approx \frac{1}{M}\sum_m f(z_m). Problem: The latent space of images/audio/text is too high-dimensional to approximate an integral using samples (Curse of Dimensionality).
(b) Variational Inference. A more sample-efficient alternative. → The path chosen by VAE.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
6.4 Variational Inference and ELBO Derivation

6.4.1 Key Identity
For any distribution q(z) (using \int q(z)dz=1), using Bayes’ theorem p(x)=\frac{p(x,z)}{p(z\mid x)}:

\begin{aligned}
\log p(x) &= \log p(x)\cdot 1 = \log p(x)\int q(z)\,dz = \int q(z)\log p(x)\,dz\\
&= \int q(z)\log \frac{p(x,z)}{p(z\mid x)}\,dz \qquad (\because \text{Bayes})\\
&= \int q(z)\big(\log p(x,z) - \log p(z\mid x)\big)\,dz\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{z\sim q}\big[\log p(x,z) - \log p(z\mid x)\big]
\end{aligned}



6.4.2 Introduction of variational family → ELBO + KL
Now, let q be parameterized to q_\phi(z) (this is the encoder, the inference network). If we insert \frac{q_\phi(z)}{q_\phi(z)}=1 and expand it:

\begin{aligned}
\log p(x)
&= \int q_\phi(z)\log\frac{p(x,z)}{p(z\mid x)}\,dz
= \int q_\phi(z)\log\!\left[\frac{p(x,z)}{q_\phi(z)}\cdot\frac{q_\phi(z)}{p(z\mid x)}\right]dz\\
&= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(x,z) - \log q_\phi(z)\big]}_{\textbf{ELBO}\;(\text{Evidence Lower BOund})}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\big[\,q_\phi(z)\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\,\big]}_{\ge\,0}
\end{aligned}







ImportantWhy is this decomposition decisive?




\log p(x) is a constant (a real value we cannot touch, “evidence”) for \phi.
KL is always \ge 0 (non-negativeness of KL). Therefore \log p(x) \ge \text{ELBO} → “Evidence Lower Bound”.
What we really want to reduce is \mathrm{KL}[q_\phi(z)\|p(z\mid x)] (the distance between my approximate posterior distribution and the true posterior distribution), but since we do not know the true posterior distribution p(z\mid x), we cannot directly reduce KL.
Since the left side is a constant instead of , maximizing ELBO = minimizing KL. ELBO is computable. → Let’s maximize ELBO!





6.4.3 ELBO Expansion → Restoration Term + Normalization Term
Substitute p(x,z)=p(x\mid z)p(z):

\begin{aligned}
\text{ELBO}
&= \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(x,z) - \log q_\phi(z)\big]
= \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(x\mid z) + \log p(z) - \log q_\phi(z)\big]\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(x\mid z)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(z) - \log q_\phi(z)\big]\\
&= \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(x\mid z)\big] - \mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log q_\phi(z) - \log p(z)\big]\\
&= \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(x\mid z)\big]}_{\textbf{복원(Reconstruction)}}
\;-\;
\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q_\phi(z)\,\|\,p(z)\big)}_{\textbf{정규화(Regularization)}}
\end{aligned}









Term
Meaning
Role




Recovered Term \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x\mid z)]
How well x is recovered from z (Decoder Quality)
Data Fidelity


Normalization Term \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z)\|p(z))
How well the latent z follows the prior \mathcal N(0,I)
Latent Space Control



ELBO maximization balances these two: “zZ well reconstructs x, while the distribution of z is close to \mathcal N(0,I).”

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
section: 6.5 VAE Loss Function and Reparameterization Trick
text:
6.5 VAE Loss Function and Reparameterization Trick
Since ELBO is the maximization target, the sign is flipped to write it as loss (minimization). (Decoder p_\theta(x\mid z), Encoder q_\phi(z\mid x))

\boxed{\;
\mathcal{L}_{\text{VAE}}(\theta,\phi)
= \underbrace{-\,\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\!\big[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)\big]}_{\approx\ \text{MSE/CE 복원 손실}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\!\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big)}_{\text{닫힌 형태 (가우시안)}}
\;}







NoteNotation Caution (Precision)




This note follows standard (Kingma & Welling) notation: The parameters of the encoder/inference network q_\phi are set to \phi, and the parameters of the decoder/generation network p_\theta are set to \theta.
Some data may have \theta for the encoder and \phi for the decoder (notation with reversed roles), so you must read it based on which network it refers to to avoid confusion. What is important is not the symbol, but the distinction between the roles of “inference network vs. generative network”.



Since the restoration term is defined as the difference between x and \hat x, it becomes either MSE loss (Gaussian likelihood) or cross-entropy (Bernoulli likelihood) depending on the assumption. The KL term falls into a closed form as it is between the two Gaussians (equation in the appendix below).

6.5.1 Problem: Sampling is not differentiable
To train , backpropagation must be done to \hat x \to z \to x, but z\sim q_\phi(z\mid x) is stochastic sampling, so the gradient cannot pass through.


6.5.2 Solution: Reparameterization trick
The probability is subtracted as exogenous noise on the input side \epsilon.

\boxed{\;z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x)\odot \epsilon,\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\;}

Now z is a deterministic function of \mu_\phi,\sigma_\phi (neural network output) + fixed noise. The mean \mu becomes a differentiable expression that depends on the encoder, and the variance \sigma also depends on the encoder, so we can randomize only \epsilon and backpropagate normally to \phi,\theta.





flowchart LR
    x[x] --> E[Encoder q_φ]
    E --> mu[μ_φ x]
    E --> sig[σ_φ x]
    eps["ε ~ N0,I"] --> z
    mu --> z["z = μ + σ⊙ε"]
    sig --> z
    z --> D[Decoder p_θ] --> xh[x̂]
    xh -. L_MSE .-> x
    z -. L_KL .-> prior["N0,I"]

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
6.6 VAE Results and Advantages

Generates less blurry samples than AE.
The latent space is controllable. If it is a 10-dimensional Gaussian latent, each dimension can correspond to a semantic. For example, disentangled generation and interpolation is possible, such as sweeping dimension 1 as -\infty\to+\infty to change from female to male, or sweeping dimension 2 to change the hairstyle.
The latent space is analyzable, allowing for the diagnosis of the learning process, such as what additional data is needed (in contrast to the opaque latent space of AE).







TipWireless Communication Perspective — Three Mappings of VAE




Reparameterization trick = AWGN model. z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon is exactly a signal + Gaussian noise model. It is the sum of scaled white noise (\sigma\epsilon) and the deterministic signal component (\mu). It is isomorphic to y = s + n,\ n\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2), which is commonly used in radio. Thanks to this, it is possible to capture the “pathwise derivative” of the expected value.
Gaussian latent prior = Gaussian input codebook. In the same context as the input distribution being Gaussian for achieving the capacity of an AWGN channel — Gaussian is the natural choice for “maximum entropy/optimal representation”.
ELBO = Lower bound of unmanageable likelihood. The strategy of optimizing by replacing the marginal likelihood that cannot be directly calculated with a computable lower bound is based on the same idea as solving the unmanageable likelihood in detection/estimation using the variable lower bound·EM. KL regularization acts as a power constraint that “limits the power (variance) of the latent to \mathcal N(0,I)”.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
section: 7.1 Synchronization: Beyond the blur of MSE
text:
7.1 Synchronization: Beyond the blur of MSE
MSE reconstruction in VAE/AE tends to produce blurry results by selecting average, safe pixel values. GANs add adversarial loss to create sharp images with preserved detail.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
section: 7.2 Composition: Generator G and Discriminator D
text:
7.2 Composition: Generator G and Discriminator D





flowchart LR
    z["랜덤 벡터 z ~ p(z)"] --> G[Generator G]
    G --> fake["가짜 이미지 G(z)"]
    real["진짜 이미지 x"] --> D
    fake --> D[Discriminator D]
    D --> out["Real or Fake?<br/>D(·) ∈ (0,1)"]







Generator G(z): Random vector z → Image. (Good G = Generated image looks real)
Discriminator D(x): Image → “Probability of being real”. (Good D = good at distinguishing between real and fake)
Learning through competition: G tries to deceive D, and D tries not to be deceived. They attack each other hostilely and become stronger together.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
7.3 Minimax Officialization

\boxed{\;
\min_{G}\max_{D}\;
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q_{\text{data}}(x)}\big[\log D(x)\big]
\;+\;
\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p(z)}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big]
\;}

Physical meaning: \log(\text{$x$가 진짜일 확률}) + \log(1-\text{$G(z)$가 진짜일 확률}).

As this value increases, D is better → Maximize for D.
As this value becomes smaller, G is better (deceives D well) → minimize for G.
This type of problem is called a Minimax problem, or a zero-sum non-cooperative game.







NoteAdvanced — Optimal Discriminator and JS Divergence



When G is fixed, the optimal discriminator is 
D^*(x) = \frac{q_{\text{data}}(x)}{q_{\text{data}}(x) + p_g(x)}.
 If we substitute this, the objective function is 
V(G,D^*) = -\log 4 + 2\cdot \mathrm{JSD}\big(q_{\text{data}}\,\|\,p_g\big)
 (\mathrm{JSD} = Jensen–Shannon divergence). In other words, minimizing G means aligning the generating distribution p_g to the true distribution q_{\text{data}} based on the JS divergence. The global optimal is p_g = q_{\text{data}}, at which point it becomes V=-\log 4. (Numerically verified in the appendix code.)

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
7.5 Learning difficulties
GAN training is notoriously difficult.







Problem
Symptoms




Non-convergence (Non-convergence)
Parameters are oscillatory/unstable and do not converge


Mode collapse (Mode collapse)
G mass-produces only similar samples (loss of diversity)


Diminished Gradient (Gradient Vanishing)
D becomes too strong, causing G’s gradient to disappear and learning to stagnate




The imbalance between D and G causes the above problem. Hyperparameter selection is a “work of art”.
Stabilized variants: LSGAN, WGAN, WGAN-GP, BEGAN etc.
Diffusion Models Emerge as a Fundamental Alternative: Learning is slow, but stable and of excellent quality.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
section: 7.6 Why GANs Are Effective: Hard Negative
text:
7.6 Why GANs Are Effective: Hard Negative
D constantly provides G with hard negatives. By creating “almost real fakes” near the decision boundary to pressure G, it becomes a much stronger learning signal than simple MSE.






WarningAdversarial Example ≠ Adversarial Learning



Caution: Confusion. Adversarial examples are created by applying small perturbations to the input to cause a neural network to produce an unexpected output.

Example: Adding fine patterns to stop signs causes autonomous driving AI to mistake them for “slow down” → Danger.
Example: If you insert a texture invisible to the human eye into a cat image, the CNN asserts with high probability that it is a “desktop computer.”

This is evidence that neural networks are extremely sensitive (vulnerable) to small changes in input. The “adversarial” of GANs shares only the word with this phenomenon, but holds a different philosophy that two networks compete.








TipWireless Communication Perspective — GAN = Jamming Game, Adversarial Example = Precision Interference




Minimax = A zero-sum game between a jammer and a transceiver. D (the receiver) attempts to distinguish (detect) real/fake signals, and G (the jammer) synthesizes signals to evade detection. Nash equilibrium is equivalent to the saddle point of a worst-case robust design.
Adversarial example = low-power interference aligned to the decision boundary. Misculating the detector with very small perturbations (\|\delta\| small) is equivalent to a minimum power disturbance signal aligned to the decision boundary normal direction. The sensitivity of a neural network is equivalent to the ill-conditioning of the classifier — minute changes in the input are amplified in the output.
Hard negative = High-difficulty sample near the boundary. Like the “test signal near the threshold SNR” in detection theory, it provides the most informative learning signal.

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
section: 9.1 Closed form of Gaussian KL (VAE normalization term)
text:
9.1 Closed form of Gaussian KL (VAE normalization term)
When q=\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2), p=\mathcal N(0,1), 
\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}\big(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - \log\sigma_j^2 - 1\big).


import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def gaussian_kl_closed(mu, var):
    # KL( N(mu, var) || N(0, I) ), per-dimension diagonal Gaussian
    return 0.5 * np.sum(mu**2 + var - np.log(var) - 1)

# Monte Carlo 검증
mu, sig = 0.7, 1.3
closed = gaussian_kl_closed(np.array([mu]), np.array([sig**2]))
z = rng.normal(mu, sig, size=2_000_000)
logq = -0.5*np.log(2*np.pi*sig**2) - (z-mu)**2/(2*sig**2)
logp = -0.5*np.log(2*np.pi)        - z**2/2
mc = np.mean(logq - logp)
print(f"KL closed-form = {closed:.5f}   Monte Carlo = {mc:.5f}")

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
9.2 Reparameterization trick + VAE loss (forward)

def reparameterize(mu, logvar, eps=None):
    # z = mu + sigma * eps,  sigma = exp(0.5*logvar)
    std = np.exp(0.5*logvar)
    if eps is None:
        eps = rng.normal(size=mu.shape)
    return mu + std*eps                       # AWGN 모델: 신호 mu + 잡음 std*eps

def vae_loss(x, x_hat, mu, logvar):
    recon = np.mean(np.sum((x - x_hat)**2, axis=1))      # MSE 복원항
    kl    = np.mean(0.5*np.sum(np.exp(logvar) + mu**2 - 1 - logvar, axis=1))
    return recon + kl, recon, kl

# 더미 예시 (배치 4, 잠재 3, 입력 5)
mu     = rng.normal(size=(4,3))
logvar = rng.normal(size=(4,3))*0.1
z      = reparameterize(mu, logvar)
x      = rng.normal(size=(4,5))
x_hat  = rng.normal(size=(4,5))               # 실제로는 decoder(z)
total, recon, kl = vae_loss(x, x_hat, mu, logvar)
print(f"z.shape={z.shape}  total={total:.4f}  recon={recon:.4f}  kl={kl:.4f}")

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
9.3 CLIP Symmetric Contrast Loss

def clip_loss(I, T, tau=1.0):
    I = I/np.linalg.norm(I, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    T = T/np.linalg.norm(T, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    logits = I @ T.T / tau                    # 상관(correlation) 행렬, 대각이 정답
    N = len(I)
    def ce_rows(L):
        L = L - L.max(1, keepdims=True)
        logp = L - np.log(np.exp(L).sum(1, keepdims=True))
        return -logp[np.arange(N), np.arange(N)].mean()
    return 0.5*(ce_rows(logits) + ce_rows(logits.T))   # 이미지→텍스트 + 텍스트→이미지

N, d = 8, 16
base = rng.normal(size=(N, d))
aligned = clip_loss(base, base + 0.01*rng.normal(size=(N, d)))
random_ = clip_loss(rng.normal(size=(N, d)), rng.normal(size=(N, d)))
print(f"정렬된 쌍 loss = {aligned:.4f}   무작위 쌍 loss = {random_:.4f}   (log N = {np.log(N):.4f})")

title: Multimodal Models and Generative Models (I): VAE & GAN
text:
9.4 SigLIP Sigmoid Loss

def sigmoid(u): return 1/(1+np.exp(-u))

def siglip_loss(I, T, t=10.0, b=-10.0):
    I = I/np.linalg.norm(I, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    T = T/np.linalg.norm(T, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    S = I @ T.T                                # 상관 행렬
    N = len(I)
    Y = -np.ones((N, N)); np.fill_diagonal(Y, 1.0)   # 대각=+1(정답), 나머지=-1
    logits = Y*(t*S + b)
    return -np.mean(np.log(sigmoid(logits) + 1e-12)) # 쌍별 독립 이진 결정

print(f"SigLIP loss = {siglip_loss(base, base):.4f} (완전 정렬)")

section: 9.5 GAN: Optimal Discriminator and JS Divergence Identity Verification
text:
9.5 GAN: Optimal Discriminator and JS Divergence Identity Verification
Verify V(G,D^*) = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JSD}(q_{\text{data}}\|p_g) in the text as a discrete distribution.

p = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4])   # q_data
q = np.array([0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])   # p_g
D_star = p/(p+q)                                         # 최적 판별자
V = np.sum(p*np.log(D_star)) + np.sum(q*np.log(1-D_star))
m = 0.5*(p+q)
KL = lambda a,b: np.sum(a*np.log(a/b))
JSD = 0.5*KL(p,m) + 0.5*KL(q,m)
print(f"V(G, D*)            = {V:.5f}")
print(f"-log4 + 2*JSD       = {-np.log(4) + 2*JSD:.5f}")
print(f"전역최적(p_g=q_data)일 때 V = -log4 = {-np.log(4):.5f}")
