title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
2 Recap: Diffusion Model vs. GAN
One-line answer: GANs are fast but unstable (mode collapse), while diffusion models are slow but stable (MLE-based) and of excellent quality.









Diffusion Model (DDPM)
GAN




Pros
Sharpness and high quality, Well-understood optimization called MLE, for both image and audio
Relatively fast training, various loss functions (Wasserstein, Hinge), requires less data


Disadvantages
Slow and computationally intensive, requires a lot of data
High training difficulty, hyperparameter sensitive, mode collapse









TipWhy Diffusion Instead of Hard-Negative in GANs?



GANs are adversarial games that pressure the discriminator by generating “hard negatives” near the decision boundary. On the other hand, diffusion models do not involve zero-sum games because they gradually build a probability tower at each position. Therefore, learning converges slowly but stably.


Diffusion models are broadly classified into three series based on their generation mechanisms (Review paper The Principles of Diffusion Models, arXiv 2025):





flowchart TB
    A["확산 모델 (이산 노이징 ↔ 클린)"] --> B["VAE 기반 계열<br/>(DDPM 등)"]
    A --> C["에너지 기반 / 점수 기반<br/>(score-based, NCSN)"]
    A --> D["정규화 흐름 계열<br/>(normalizing flow)"]
    C -.확장.-> E["조건부 score network<br/>연속시간(SDE) 일반화"]
    D -.해석.-> F["적은 스텝으로<br/>노이즈→데이터 사상"]






The three perspectives view the same goal of “gradually transforming a complete noise matrix into a clean image” through different mathematics, and this extends to continuous-time versions (SDE/ODE).

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
3 DDPM Details
DDPM consists of two processes.

Forward Spread (forward, fixed): Gradually adds noise to the input — no learning parameters.
Reverse noise removal (reverse, generation): Creates data by removing noise — Trained with a neural network.






flowchart LR
    x0["x₀ (데이터)"] -- "q(xₜ|xₜ₋₁) 고정" --> xt["xₜ"]
    xt -- "..." --> xT["x_T ~ N(0,I)"]
    xT -. "pθ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ) 학습" .-> xt2["xₜ₋₁"]
    xt2 -. "..." .-> x0b["x̂₀ (생성)"]







3.1 Forward process (forward)
One-line answer: It is a Markov chain that adds Gaussian noise following a predefined distributed schedule \(\beta_t\).
Organize the notation.

\(\beta_t \in (0,1)\) : Noise magnitude at time \(t\) (pre-scheduled).
\(\alpha_t = 1-\beta_t\) : Signal retention rate of one step.
\(\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t}(1-\beta_s) = \prod_{s=1}^{t}\alpha_s\) : Preserve accumulated signal up to time \(t\).

The one-step transition and its closed-form marginal distribution are as follows.
\[
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_t;\, \sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1},\, \beta_t \mathbf{I}\big),
\qquad
\boxed{\;x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\;}
\tag{1}\]






NoteWhy multiply \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\) in front of the signal — variance preservation



Since the overall signal magnitude should not increase as noise is added, the original signal is reduced by \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\) and noise is added by \(\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\) to keep \(\operatorname{Var}(x_t)\) equal to \(\operatorname{Var}(x_0)\). The fact that the sum of the squares of the two coefficients is \(\bar\alpha_t + (1-\bar\alpha_t)=1\) serves as proof of this (so-called variance-preserving). It is very convenient during training because it allows a direct jump to an arbitrary \(t\) (Food 1).




3.2 Continuous-time limit: SDE
\(\delta t \to 0\) When taking the limit, the forward process is written as a stochastic differential equation (SDE).
\[
dx = -\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(t)\,x\,dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\;dW_t
\tag{2}\]
Here, \(W_t\) is the Wiener process, which models a Gaussian random sample at each time step. The drift term \(-\tfrac12\beta(t)x\) shrinks the signal to zero, and the diffusion term \(\sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dW_t\) injects noise. (Refer to the review paper for the derivation — this note uses only the result.)






TipWireless Communication Analogy — Forward Process = “Progressive Fading Channel”



\(x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\) is exactly the same form as the channel model with AWGN added to a signal attenuated by the time-varying fading coefficient \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\). \(\bar\alpha_t\) is the channel gain that decreases monotonically over time, and \(1-\bar\alpha_t\) is the accumulated noise power. Variance-preserving is equivalent to AGC (Automatic Gain Control) that keeps the total power of the received signal constant. When the SNR drops to 0 at \(t\to T\), the received signal becomes pure noise \(x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\).




3.3 Reverse process (reverse)
One-line answer: The true inverse process \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) is unknown, but since \(\beta_t \ll 1\) is approximated as Gaussian, the average is learned using a neural network.
If you try to use inversion with Bayes’ rule
\[
q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) = \frac{q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1})}{q(x_t)}
\tag{3}\]
, but the marginal distribution \(q(x_{t-1}),\,q(x_t)\) on the right side is unknown for the entire data distribution (bad news). The good news is that if \(\beta_t\) is sufficiently small, the true posterior \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) is also well approximated by a Gaussian. Therefore, we set it as a parameterized Gaussian as follows.
\[
p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(x_{t-1};\, \mu_\theta(x_t,t),\, \sigma_t^2 \mathbf{I}\big)
\tag{4}\]






ImportantStructure of cascaded approximation




True inverse process \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) → (β small) → Approximately as Gaussian
The mean of that Gaussian \(\mu_\theta\) → Approximated by a neural network

The Gaussian is completely determined by knowing only the sufficient statistics of mean and variance. Since the variance \(\sigma_t^2\) is automatically determined by the schedule \(\beta_t\), the target of training is effectively just the mean \(\mu_\theta\).




3.4 \(\mu_\theta\) Learning: Noise Reparameterization
The posterior mean of the forward process is represented by \(x_0\) and noise \(\epsilon\). If we solve Food 1 for \(x_0\) and substitute, the mean takes the following neat form.
\[
\mu_\theta(x_t,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\right)
\tag{5}\]
In other words, instead of directly predicting the mean, we just need to train a neural network \(\epsilon\) that predicts the injected noise \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\). The core idea is:

Select one time point \(t\) and sample the correct noise \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\).
Noise image generated with \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\).
Slope descent to \(\nabla_\theta \lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2\).







NoteWhy Noise Prediction — Backward Process Average = Forward Process Average



To make the inverse process the exact inverse of the forward process, the averages of the two processes must be equal: \(\mu_\theta^{\text{(rev)}}(x_t,t) = \tilde\mu^{\text{(fwd)}}(x_t,t)\). In the forward process, we know \(x_0,\epsilon\), so we can calculate this average accurately; in the inverse process, since we do not know it, we approximate it as \(\epsilon_\theta\). Since the average is a function of \(\epsilon\) (Food 5), average fitting = noise fitting.




3.5 Loss function
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DDPM}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_0,\,\epsilon}\Big[\big\lVert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\big\rVert^2\Big],
\qquad x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon
\tag{6}\]
It starts from the original variational lower bound (ELBO), but after reparameterization, it is reduced to the simple noise regression (MSE) as shown above. Unlike the zero-sum game of GANs, the loss value decreases monotonically and converges stably.


3.6 Learning/Sampling Algorithm
Training

Data \(x_0 \sim q(x_0)\).
\(t \sim \text{Uniform}\{1,\dots,T\}\) (Learnable at any time — thanks to Food 1).
\(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\).
Update to \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\), \(\;\nabla_\theta\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2\), repeat until convergence.

Sampling (Sampling / Generation)
Starting from \(x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\), about \(t=T,\dots,1\):
\[
\hat{x}_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}}\big(x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\big),
\]
\[
\mu_\theta(x_t,\hat{x}_0) = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\hat{x}_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t,
\qquad
x_{t-1} = \mu_\theta(x_t,\hat{x}_0) + \sigma_t\,z,\;\; z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}).
\]






WarningInherent limitation of DDPM — cannot control \(\sigma_t\)



In DDPM, \(\sigma_t\) (usually \(\sigma_t^2 = \tilde\beta_t = \tfrac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\beta_t\)) is automatically calculated from schedule \(\beta_t\) and cannot be touched by the user. Since it is stochastic sampling that draws a new \(z\) at every step, the path cannot be controlled, and the entire inverse-SDE must run tens of thousands of steps to generate a single sample — this is the source of slowness.







flowchart TB
    subgraph T["학습 (단순)"]
      t1["x₀ 샘플"] --> t2["t ~ Uniform"] --> t3["ε ~ N(0,I)"] --> t4["xₜ 합성"] --> t5["∇θ‖ε−εθ‖²"]
    end
    subgraph S["샘플링 (비쌈)"]
      s1["x_T ~ N(0,I)"] --> s2["t=T..1 반복"] --> s3["εθ(xₜ,t) 예측"] --> s4["x̂₀, μθ 계산"] --> s5["xₜ₋₁ = μθ + σₜz"] --> s2
    end








3.7 Evaluation Metrics: FID
One-line answer: FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) measures the distance between the generated distribution and the actual distribution on the latent representation of an Inception neural network, and lower is better.
Images are passed through a pre-trained Inception network (Google’s GoogLeNet/Inception family) to obtain semantic latent vectors, and the difference in mean and covariance (assuming Gaussian distribution) between the set of real images and the set of generated images is measured. The closer the two distributions are (=the more the product looks “like a natural image”), the smaller the FID. Although it is an old network that is over five years old, it is still widely used as a standard comparison metric.







Method (CIFAR-10)
FID ↓




Conditional GAN
14.73


StyleGAN2 + Auxiliary Techniques
2.67 (accompanied by difficulty in avoiding mode collapse)


DDPM
3.17 (Reached stably without game theory)



DDPM is simple and stable to train, yet demonstrates quality comparable to top-tier GANs. However, the inefficiency of generation speed remains a major weakness — DDIM addresses this.

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
4 DDIM: Deterministic Accelerated Sampling

4.1 Synchronous
One-line answer: DDIM reuses the same training results as DDPM, but reinterprets the forward process as non-Markov to enable deterministic, small-step sampling.
DDPM’s Weakness:

Slow sampling (tens of thousands of steps).
Stochastic path → Difficult to control · Inefficiency.
Full inverse-SDE required for every sample.

The goal of DDIM is “Fewer steps + Deterministic path + Marginal distribution identical to DDPM”. Key idea:

Interpret the forward process as a non-Markov, deterministic event.
Deriving the inverse process based on ODE (DDPM is SDE).
Realization of non-probabilistic and efficient sampling.



4.2 Non-Markov forward process
DDPM assumes that \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) depends only on \(x_t\) (Markov assumption). DDIM additionally conditions this with \(x_0\) information.
\[
q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0) = q(x_T\mid x_0)\prod_{t=2}^{T} q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0)
\tag{7}\]
Each inversion is by Bayes’ rule
\[
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}, x_0) = \frac{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0)\,q(x_t\mid x_0)}{q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)}
\tag{8}\]
is derived from ||| and is non-Markov because \(x_t\) depends on both \(x_{t-1}\)Z and \(x_0\).






Tip\(x_0\) Why does the information reduce the number of steps?



The Markov assumption is the constraint that “only the immediate state is known.” Since DDIM utilizes additional information about the destination \(x_0\) during training, it can reach the same quality with fewer iterations. By analogy, it is the difference between moving one step at a time based only on the current position (DDPM) vs. knowing the destination and jumping along a straight path (DDIM).


Crucially, the marginal distribution of \(x_t\) remains identical to DDPM.
\[
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\,(1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I}\big),
\qquad x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_t
\tag{9}\]
Thanks to this neighborhood match, the noise predictor \(\epsilon_\theta\) trained in DDPM can be reused as is. The implementation is the same, only the mathematical interpretation differs (DDPM=SDE, DDIM=ODE).


4.3 Inverse process sampling and \(\eta\)
Following the average of the posterior \(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0)\) yields a generalized update formula.
\[
\boxed{\;x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\hat{x}_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t) + \sigma_t\,z,\quad z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\;}
\tag{10}\]
Here, the amount of probability is controlled by the hyperparameter \(\eta\).
\[
\sigma_t = \eta\,\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\sqrt{1-\frac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}}
\tag{11}\]

\(\eta = 0 \Rightarrow \sigma_t = 0\) : Completely deterministic(first term + second term only, noise \(z\) eliminated).
\(\eta = 1 \Rightarrow\) Exactly equivalent to DDPM (Markov forward reduction).







NoteVerification: When \(\eta{=}1\) \(\sigma_t^2 = \tilde\beta_t\)



If you substitute \(\beta_t = 1-\tfrac{\bar\alpha_t}{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\) into Food 11 \[
\sigma_t^2\big|_{\eta=1} = \frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\beta_t = \tilde\beta_t
\] exactly matches the posterior variance of DDPM (the difference \(=0\) confirmed by symbolic calculation). Additionally, the forward margin Food 9 was confirmed to match the closed form via Monte Carlo (Section 9).




4.4 Loss Equality
Since the fact that the neural network predicts noise \(\epsilon_t\) remains the same even if the forward and inverse processes are swapped, the loss is the same as DDPM — for any \(\sigma_t\).
\[
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\,x_0,\,\epsilon}\big[\lVert \epsilon_t - \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2\big]
\tag{12}\]
That is, both DDPM and DDIM generation can be performed with \(\epsilon_\theta\), which has been trained once. You just need to leave the training code as is and add one \(\eta\) to the sampling.


4.5 DDPM vs. DDIM

TipWireless Communication Analogy — DDIM = “Deterministic Equalizer”



The stochastic inverse process of DDPM is akin to random reconstruction, which draws a new noise realization for every symbol. DDIM reconstructs the signal using deterministic ODE integral = deterministic equalization/demodulation while maintaining the channel statistics (marginal distribution of the forward process) identically. \(\eta\) is a dial that controls the amount of residual probabilism, \(\eta=0\) corresponds to a deterministic equalizer without noise addition, and \(\eta=1\) corresponds to a simulation of the original stochastic channel. Since it is a deterministic path, it is reliably reconstructed even with a small number of large steps (subsampling), significantly reducing latency. However, large steps entail a slight loss of quality (approximation error).








WarningHonest Interpretation of Experimental Facts



In terms of FID, DDIM 50 steps may appear similar to or slightly better than DDPM 1000 steps. However, since FID is not a perfect indicator, the results of a few steps may appear somewhat inferior to the naked eye. A distinction must be made between “FID ≈ Equivalent” and “Perceptual Quality Equivalent”.

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
5 LDM: Potential Diffusion (Stable Diffusion)
One-line answer: Since diffusing in pixel space takes up too much memory, the image is compressed into a low-dimensional latent space and then diffusion is performed on it.
Training large-scale text-condition models directly in pixel space incurs massive computational and memory costs. LDM compresses images into low-dimensional latent representations using an autoencoder, performs the diffusion process in the latent space, and then restores them to pixel images using a decoder.





flowchart LR
    img["입력 이미지 (픽셀, 고차원)"] -- "인코더 E" --> z["잠재 z (저차원)"]
    z -- "잠재 공간 확산 (DDPM/DDIM)" --> z2["z' 생성"]
    z2 -- "디코더 D" --> out["출력 이미지"]
    txt["텍스트 조건"] -.크로스 어텐션.-> z2






Sweet Spot of Compression Ratio: As a result of comparing quality while changing the downsampling scale,







Settings
Result




LDM-1 (Almost no compression = pixel diffusion)
Training time is significantly long


LDM-32 (Overcompression)
Discarding too much information Quality degradation


LDM-4, 8, 16
Competitive Optimal Quality









NoteThe second advantage of LDM — Semantic control



Each dimension of the latent space captures semantics better than pixels (simple color values). Therefore, adjusting specific dimensions of the latent representation allows for better control over the meaning of generated images, such as “summer deer → winter deer.” This controllability leads to ControlNet (developed in 2023).








TipWireless Communication Analogy — LDM = “Transmit after source compression”



Pixel spatial spreading is equivalent to processing the entire original signal as is. Since LDM processes over a latent representation with redundancy removed through source coding (dimensional reduction), bandwidth and computational efficiency increase significantly. Overcompression (LDM-32) is equivalent to a situation in lossy compression where the bitrate is lowered too much, causing the restoration quality to deteriorate — it is a problem of finding the sweet spot of the rate-distortion trade-off.

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
6 U-Net structure
One-line answer: It is a “butterfly/hourglass” structure in which the encoder-decoder forms an information bottleneck and the useful information lost at the bottleneck is restored through skip connections between corresponding layers.
The noise predictors for LDM and ControlNet typically use U-Net (which can be implemented using CNN or Transformer). The input and output are high-dimensional, and the representation narrows towards the center.





flowchart TB
    i1["입력 (고차원)"] --> e1["인코더 층1"] --> e2["인코더 층2"] --> b["병목<br/>(저차원 잠재)"]
    b --> d2["디코더 층2"] --> d1["디코더 층1"] --> o1["출력 (고차원)"]
    e1 -. "스킵 연결" .-> d1
    e2 -. "스킵 연결" .-> d2







Information Bottleneck: Removes unnecessary noise information through compression (same principle as an autoencoder). It takes the shape of a “butterfly” with the narrowest point in the middle, or an “hourglass” when rotated 90°.
Skip connection: Since bottlenecks can discard useful information along with noise, information is passed directly from the encoder layer → decoder layer of the same dimension to restore the details necessary for high-quality restoration. These paths form the shape of the letter U and are called U-Net.

It was originally proposed for medical image segmentation, but it is widely used in various fields due to its excellent information preservation capabilities.






TipWireless communication analogy — Skip connection = “Side information channel”



The bottleneck is lossy compression, and skip connection is equivalent to directly delivering details missing from compression to a separate side channel. It is a structure that achieves high-fidelity restoration by combining the main compression stream (main channel) and detail preservation (side channel).

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
7 ControlNet: Controllable Generation
One-line answer: It is a fractional shot editing technique that fine-tunes a pre-trained diffusion U-Net with small input-output pairs (\(<50\text{K}\)) and controls generation with condition images (sketch, edge, etc.).
Structural Idea — Process conditional images using a pre-trained noise prediction U-Net.

Encoder: Initialize by copying pre-trained U-Net parameters and fine-tune.
Decoder: Combines encoded condition information and noise image, but injects the condition (control signal) using zero convolution.






flowchart LR
    cond["조건 이미지<br/>(스케치/엣지/깊이)"] --> enc["복사된 U-Net 인코더<br/>(미세조정)"]
    base["사전학습 확산 U-Net<br/>(고정 backbone)"] --> dec["디코더"]
    enc -- "zero convolution 주입" --> dec
    dec --> out["조건부 생성 이미지"]






Procedure: Initially, realistic images are generated without condition information, and then condition information is gradually introduced (since the initial value of zero convolution is 0, the backbone is not damaged in the early stages of training). This idea is applicable to arbitrary image conditions.






NoteData Efficiency



The training dataset size is approximately \(100\text{K}\), which is about 50,000 times smaller than LAION-5B. Achieving strong controllability with a small number of pairs is a key value.








ImportantWhy is it commercially important?



In multimodal conditional generation, the ability to precisely control the generation when slightly changing the text prompt is critical. ControlNet offers high quality, controllability, and broad applicability simultaneously, making it highly commercially valuable (ICCV 2023 Best Paper).








TipWireless Communication Analogy — ControlNet = “Pilot/Control Channel Overlay”



It is equivalent to steering the beam/transmission by leaving the existing transmitting and receiving system (pre-trained backbone) as is and gradually adding a separate control/pilot channel (condition encoder + zero convolution). The zero initialization of the zero convolution corresponds to a strategy of gradually turning on the control channel at 0 power to adapt without disturbing the existing link.

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
8 Wrap-up and Next Preview





flowchart LR
    DDPM["DDPM<br/>(원형, SDE)"] -->|효율: 결정론적 가속| DDIM["DDIM<br/>(비-마르코프, ODE)"]
    DDPM -->|어디서 확산?| LDM["LDM<br/>(잠재 공간 = Stable Diffusion)"]
    LDM -->|제어성| CN["ControlNet<br/>(소수샷 조건 편집)"]







DDPM ↔︎ DDIM: Same series sharing the same \(\epsilon_\theta\). DDIM turns off probabilism with \(\eta\) and uses the ODE deterministic path to accelerate sampling.
LDM: A different philosophy that moves to latent space to gain efficiency + semantic control.
ControlNet: Grant commercial control to LDM.

Next Session — Data-Efficient Learning
In the objective function \(\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}}_{\text{데이터 적합}} + \underbrace{\Omega(\theta)}_{\text{정규화 = 귀납 편향}}\), the traditional approach when data is scarce is to design a better inductive bias (few-shot / zero-shot / continual). However, devising a new bias for every task is very wasteful.






NoteParadigm Shift: Inductive Bias → Foundation Model



An alternative is to pre-warm up the model with irrelevant but massive data instead of the data for the given task, and then fine-tune and generalize. A model that serves as the “starting point for good performance across multiple tasks” in this way is called a frontier model. It is expensive but offers powerful generalization — leading to the next topic (few/zero-shot, continual learning).

title: Generative Model II — Diffusion Model (DDPM · DDIM · LDM · ControlNet)
text:
9 Appendix: Python/NumPy Verification
Verify the two key facts in the text with code: (1) the marginal distribution of the forward process Food 1, and (2) the variance of DDIM(\(\eta{=}1\)) matches the posterior variance of DDPM \(\tilde\beta_t\) (Food 11).


Code
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(0)
betas  = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, 1000)
alphas = 1.0 - betas
abar   = np.cumprod(alphas)        # \bar\alpha_t

x0, T, N = 3.0, 500, 200_000
# 마르코프 전방을 직접 반복하여 x_T를 몬테카를로로 추정
x = np.full(N, x0, dtype=float)
for t in range(T):
    x = np.sqrt(alphas[t]) * x + np.sqrt(1 - alphas[t]) * np.random.randn(N)

print(f"MC      mean={x.mean():.4f}  var={x.var():.4f}")
print(f"closed  mean={np.sqrt(abar[T-1])*x0:.4f}  var={1-abar[T-1]:.4f}")
# closed form: x_t ~ N( sqrt(abar_t) x0, (1-abar_t) I )




Code
import sympy as sp

abar_t, abar_tm1 = sp.symbols('abar_t abar_tm1', positive=True)
beta_t = 1 - abar_t/abar_tm1                          # \beta_t = 1 - \bar\alpha_t/\bar\alpha_{t-1}

sigma_ddim_sq = ((1-abar_tm1)/(1-abar_t)) * (1 - abar_t/abar_tm1)   # eta=1
beta_tilde    = (1-abar_tm1)/(1-abar_t) * beta_t                    # DDPM 사후 분산

print("sigma_DDIM(eta=1)^2 - beta_tilde =", sp.simplify(sigma_ddim_sq - beta_tilde))
# 0 이면 두 식이 항등적으로 동일




Code
import numpy as np
# 신호 보존 sqrt(abar_t) 와 누적 잡음 sqrt(1-abar_t), 그리고 SNR = abar_t/(1-abar_t)
betas  = np.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, 1000)
abar   = np.cumprod(1 - betas)
for t in [0, 100, 300, 600, 999]:
    snr = abar[t] / (1 - abar[t])
    print(f"t={t:4d}  sqrt(abar)={np.sqrt(abar[t]):.3f}  "
          f"sqrt(1-abar)={np.sqrt(1-abar[t]):.3f}  SNR={snr:8.3f}")
# t가 커질수록 신호 보존↓, 잡음↑, SNR→0  (수신 신호가 순수 잡음으로 수렴)








NoteVerification result




Forward margin: Monte Carlo mean and variance match closed form \(\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0,\,(1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I})\).
DDIM(\(\eta{=}1\)) Variance \(-\ \tilde\beta_t = 0\) (Identity). → DDIM is a strict generalization of DDPM.
SNR \(=\bar\alpha_t/(1-\bar\alpha_t)\) converges to 0 at \(t\to T\) → \(x_T\) is pure noise.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
The Large Language Model (LLM) can be summarized in a single sentence as follows.

“Almost every NLP problem in the world is reducible to next-token prediction, and training on this single task on a sufficiently large scale brings with it emergent abilities.”

This note breaks down how that one sentence is formed in the following order.

Why Scale Determines Performance — Scaling Laws
Why Build a Single Foundation Model — No-Free-Lunch and 80/20 Logic
How all tasks are unified into next-token prediction
How to Change Behavior Without Learning — In-Context Learning, CoT
Alignment — Instruction finetuning, RLHF







NoteOne-line mapping from a wireless communication perspective



LLM is a massive predictive source coder. It predicts the next symbol most plausibly and minimizes its negative log-likelihood. Throughout this note, we continue to use the information-theoretic equivalence that “next token prediction = entropy minimization = compression.”

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
2.1 Direct answer first
Increasing the number of model parameters \(N\), the number of data tokens \(D\), and the training computation \(C\) causes the test loss to decrease smoothly according to a power law. This is the scaling laws of Kaplan et al. (2020).

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
2.2 Formula
When the other two resources are not bottlenecks for each of the three variables:
\[
L(N) \approx \left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N},\qquad
L(D) \approx \left(\frac{D_c}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D},\qquad
L(C) \approx \left(\frac{C_c}{C}\right)^{\alpha_C}
\]
Here, the exponents \(\alpha_N,\alpha_D,\alpha_C\) are all very small at the level of \(0.05\!\sim\!0.1\). Taking the logarithm of both sides,
\[
\log L = -\alpha_N \log N + \text{const}
\]
That is, it becomes a straight line on the log–log axis.






Tip“A trick to make it look like a rule”



The reason this curve appears as a neat straight line is that (1) it is a power law, so it becomes linear in log–log, and (2) the scales on the graph axis are not evenly spaced. It is closer to a repeatedly observed empirical rule than a law of nature. It is similar in nature to Moore’s Law in semiconductors — rather than a “law,” it is the product of engineering efforts to match that trend.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
2.3 Intuition

\(\alpha\) is small = diminishing returns are very gradual. Even if you increase resources tenfold, the loss only decreases by \(10^{-\alpha}\approx 0.8\sim0.9\) times, but the key point is that it continues to decrease without stopping.
If the data covers almost the entire world, the train loss becomes \(\approx\) test loss, and the generalization performance itself is determined by the scale.







NoteWireless Communication Analogy — Capacity–Resource Trade-off



The power law of the scaling law has the same shape as the rate–distortion curve. As more bits (resources) are used, distortion (loss) decreases monotonically, but marginal utility decreases. Also, if we view \(L\) as “residual uncertainty” and \(N,D,C\) as “input SNR/bandwidth,” the power exponent \(\alpha\) plays a role similar to the channel’s diversity order—it is the slope that determines how quickly the error drops relative to the resources.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
section: 2.4 Human vs. LLM: The Data Efficiency Gap
text:
2.4 Human vs. LLM: The Data Efficiency Gap

flowchart LR
    A["13세 인간<br/>< 100M 단어"] -->|"~10^4배 격차"| B["대형 LLM<br/>1.4T+ 토큰"]
    A -.다중감각 입력.-> C["시각·청각·촉각·미각<br/>+ 상호작용"]
    B -.텍스트만.-> D["단어의 나열"]









Figure 1: 학습에 노출되는 토큰(단어) 수 비교 — 로그 스케일





While a 13-year-old human sees fewer than 100 million words in a lifetime, large models see trillions of tokens. Nevertheless, models induce hallucinations. Two interpretations of this gap:

Absence of multisensory information. Humans redundantly learn the same concept through multimodal inputs such as visual, auditory, and tactile senses in addition to words → Motivation leading to VLM/VLA thereafter.
Undiscovered inefficiency. The fact that \(10^4\) times more data is required for the same performance suggests that there is a fundamental inefficiency in the learning algorithm.







ImportantThe precise definition of Hallucination



LLMs do not lie with intention. The objective function of an LLM is merely to “output the most plausible next word under the learning distribution.” The output is incorrect only from a human perspective; it is not incorrect from the perspective of the model’s own statistical objective. Therefore, hallucinations are not “lying” but a natural byproduct of a statistical word predictor.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
3.1 Direct Answer
Training a single large-scale model costs tens of billions of won. To persuade a financial officer, an argument is needed that “This single model can solve numerous tasks”. A model that serves as the foundation for other models is called a foundation model.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
section: 3.2 Conflict with No-Free-Lunch, and its resolution
text:
3.2 Conflict with No-Free-Lunch, and its resolution
According to the No-Free-Lunch theorem, there is no single model that is simultaneously optimal for all tasks. If so, is the foundation model a contradiction? The logic for resolving it is as follows.
\[
\underbrace{\text{단일 사전학습 모델}}_{\sim 80\text{–}90\%\ \text{커버}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\text{과제별 fine-tuning}}_{\text{나머지 }10\text{–}20\%}
\;=\;
\text{과제별 전문가 모델}
\]

The core task (language modeling) is a general metatask shared by almost all subtasks of NLP → 80~90% is handled by a single model.
The final touch (maximum performance) is filled in with task-specific fine-tuning → Not contradictory to NFL.

    P --> F2["Fine-tune: QA"]

    P --> F4["Fine-tune: 번역"]

4.1 Key Insights
Seemingly completely different NLP tasks are actually unified into a single format — fill-in-the-blank (predict next token)**.

TipWhy was this a revolution?



“Answering questions = predicting the next word”, “Action plan = predicting the next action token”, “Writing code = predicting the next code token”, “Diagnosis = predicting the prescription token that follows the symptom text”. Since almost all assessments measuring intelligence are ultimately “answering questions”, they are all reduced to a single next-token prediction.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
section: 4.2 Formula: Objective function of Language Modeling
text:
4.2 Formula: Objective function of Language Modeling
The joint probability of the sentence \(x = (x_1,\dots,x_T)\) is decomposed into autoregressive using the chain rule.
\[
p_\theta(x) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})
\]
Learning is the minimization of negative log-likelihood (NLL) = cross-entropy.
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})
\]
softmax for vocabulary \(V\) at each step:
\[
p_\theta(x_t = v \mid x_{<t}) = \frac{\exp(z_v)}{\sum_{v'\in V}\exp(z_{v'})}
\]
The evaluation metric perplexity is \(\mathrm{PPL} = \exp(\mathcal{L})\).






NoteReconfirmation of Cross-Entropy = KL = MLE



Minimizing \(\mathcal{L}\) is identical to minimizing the forward KL \(\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text{data}}\Vert p_\theta)\) between the data distribution \(p_{\text{data}}\) and the model \(p_\theta\), except for the sign and constant; this is precisely MLE. In other words, the essence of LLM pre-training is the equivalence chain we already know — MLE = forward-KL minimization = cross-entropy minimization — itself. Since it is forward KL, mean-seeking (zero-avoiding): probability mass must be applied to every mode the data takes, and this is the reason why it absorbs all diverse representations in massive data.








NoteWireless Communication Analogy — Predictive Encoding and Entropy Rate



Next-token prediction is exactly the same as predictive coding (DPCM/entropy coding) in communication. It predicts the next symbol of the source using a conditional distribution, and the mean of that NLL is an estimate of the source’s entropy rate \(H(\mathcal{X})\). The cross-entropy \(\ge H\) and the equality holds when \(p_\theta = p_{\text{data}}\) — that is, a perfect language model is equivalent to an optimal lossless compressor. Perplexity is the “effective branching factor,” which is the effective alphabet size indicating how many symbols are selected on average.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
5.1 Direct Answer
In-Context Learning is a prompt engineering technique that modifies model behavior by inputting a task demonstration in natural language into a prompt, without updating any parameters (no gradient, no parameter update).

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
5.2 “How is that learning?”
If we view the operational definition of learning as a change in input–output mapping:
\[
\text{학습 전: } x \mapsto y_{\text{before}}, \qquad
\text{학습 후: } x \mapsto y_{\text{after}}, \qquad y_{\text{before}} \neq y_{\text{after}}
\]
In ICL, the weights \(\theta\) remain the same, but the output changes when the context (demonstration/system prompt) changes. Since the output changes for the same core input, it is called “learning.”

flowchart LR
    U["사용자 입력 x"] --> AUG["+ system prompt<br/>+ demonstrations(context)"]
    AUG --> LLM["LLM (θ 고정)"]
    LLM --> Y["출력 y (context에 의해 달라짐)"]









Figure 3: 입력 증강(system prompt + context)이 출력을 바꾼다











NoteWireless Communication Analogy — Pilot-based Adaptive Equalization



A demonstration example of ICL is like pilot symbols. The receiver (LLM) does not retrain the weights (hardware) but estimates the channel from the pilots in the preamble and adapts the detection rule on the fly. A few-shot example from the prompt allows the “current task channel” to be estimated, and the main question (data symbol) is decoded accordingly. The fact that the decision boundary changes but the circuit remains the same accurately captures the essence of ICL.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
6.1 Definition
Emergent ability is the ability that suddenly appears when the model size exceeds a certain threshold, even without intentional training.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
6.2 Evidence: Word unscrambling task
If you look at string restoration tasks such as cyclic-letter, anagram, random-insertion, and reversed-word in the GPT-3 family:

Most tasks: Gradual performance increase with scale (consistent with scaling law).
Random insertion: \(\sim\) Up to 6.7B, in the range of almost 0 → 6.7B → 13B → 175B, suddenly jumps to the 70% range.

This discontinuous jump is a typical sign of emergent ability.






NoteWireless Communication Metaphor — Waterfall Area



Let’s recall the BER–SNR curve of the LDPC/Turbo sign. Below the critical SNR, the error hardly decreases, but the moment it exceeds the threshold, the BER plummets like a waterfall. The sharp jump in emerging ability is a phase transition phenomenon similar to this waterfall transition. When the magnitude (SNR) exceeds the critical point, the ability (reliability) turns on non-linearly.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
7.1 Few-shot CoT
If intermediate reasoning steps are solved and presented as a demonstration instead of just showing the answer, the model mimics that reasoning chain and the accuracy rate increases (Wei et al., 2022).
Q: ... (문제)
A: 먼저 ...이므로 ... 따라서 ... = 11.  답은 11.    ← 중간 단계를 펼친 시연
Q: ... (새 문제)
A: (모델이 단계별로 따라 생성)

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
section: 7.2 Zero-shot CoT: “Let’s think step by step”
text:
7.2 Zero-shot CoT: “Let’s think step by step”
Step-by-step reasoning is induced simply by adding the line “Let’s think step by step” to the prompt without even needing a demonstration (Kojima et al., 2022). Such a sentence is called a trigger prompt.



Table 2: Performance changes based on trigger prompt









Method
MultiArith Accuracy (Example)




Zero-shot (Just a question)
~17%


Few-shot (Standard)
~33%


Zero-shot CoT (“Let’s think step by step”)
~78.7%


Optimized trigger (“Let’s work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer”)
~82%












TipKey Implications



It is possible to gain +60%p with a single line of prompt, without a dataset, GPU, or parameter updates. Inference capability is already latent within the model; the trigger prompt merely draws it out. It is also possible to let the model explore the optimal trigger prompt on its own.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
7.3 Self-Consistency CoT
The same question is asked multiple times to the same model. Since the model performs stochastic sampling, it produces slightly different inference paths \(r^{(m)}\) and answers \(a^{(m)}\) each time. The majority vote of those answers is selected as the final answer (“sample-and-marginalize”).
\[
\hat{a} = \arg\max_{a}\ \sum_{m=1}^{M} \mathbb{1}\!\left[a(y^{(m)}) = a\right]
\;\approx\;
\arg\max_{a}\ \sum_{r} p_\theta(a, r \mid x)
\]
That is, the latent inference path \(r\) is marginalized in Monte Carlo to collect probability masses that reach the same answer even if the paths are different.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
7.4 Tree of Thoughts (ToT)
Inference is executed as a tree rather than a linear chain. At each node, the model is asked “What is the confidence level for this answer?” to assign weights, and the tree is traversed to synthesize the final answer.

flowchart LR
    subgraph IO["I/O"]
        a1["입력→출력"]
    end
    subgraph CoT["CoT"]
        b1["입력→단계1→단계2→답"]
    end
    subgraph SC["Self-Consistency"]
        c1["경로1→답A"]
        c2["경로2→답A"]
        c3["경로3→답B"]
        c1 & c2 & c3 --> cv["다수결→A"]
    end
    subgraph ToT["Tree of Thoughts"]
        d0["루트"] --> d1["분기1"]
        d0 --> d2["분기2"]
        d1 --> d3["평가/confidence"]
        d2 --> d4["평가/confidence"]
    end









Figure 4: 추론 구조의 진화: 단일 → 사슬 → 다수결 → 트리











NoteWireless Communication Analogy — Diversity Combination



Self-consistency is repetition coding + majority combining, or more precisely, diversity combining (MRC/selection) of multiple independent paths. A single decoding (inference path) is susceptible to noise, but combining independent trials increases the effective SNR and averages out errors, thereby improving confidence. The confidence weighting in ToT corresponds to MRC (maximal-ratio combining), which weights based on the confidence of each path.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
7.5 (Note) Jailbreaking / Trigger Prompt
By inserting specific trigger phrases (e.g., code header patterns), it is possible to induce an output close to the training data, thereby causing training-data retrieval. This phenomenon arises from the nature of next-token prediction reproducing the training distribution exactly, and is treated as a risk in terms of security and privacy.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
8.1 Direct Answer
**If you fine-tune a pre-trained model by collecting (instruction, answer) pairs from various tasks, it generalizes zero-shot to tasks that were not in training (Wei et al., 2022, FLAN). This is a method of alignment.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
8.2 structure
\[
\mathcal{D}_{\text{IFT}} = \big\{(\text{instruction}_i,\ \text{output}_i)\big\}_{i=1}^{K\ \text{tasks}}
\]
Example) “Answer the following question: What is the boiling point of nitrogen? → −320.4 °F”. Even after fine-tuning with numerous tasks not directly related to the goal task to be solved, the performance of the target task improves — another emergent phenomenon.
Definition (Wei et al.): Instruction tuning is the process of fine-tuning an instruction model with a set of tasks described by instructions to improve the zero-shot performance of unseen tasks.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
8.3 limit

Tasks with no single correct answer. Open-ended generation, such as “Write a story about a puppy and its pet grasshopper,” has no unique correct answer, making the supervised learning signal ambiguous.
Penalty all token errors equally. Language modeling uses token-level cross-entropy, which penalizes all incorrect tokens with the same weight. However, some tokens (“Yes/No”) are much more important than others → Mismatch between the objective function (LM) and the true goal (satisfying human preferences).

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
9.1 Synchronous
To bridge the discrepancy above, human preference must be incorporated as an explicit signal. One can evaluate whether “this conversation was satisfactory” only after the entire conversation has concluded; this is not a token-based map but a delayed scalar reward. This structure is solved using reinforcement learning → RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback).

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
9.2 Pipeline

flowchart LR
    G["GPT-3<br/>(사전학습 LM)"] --> SFT["Instruction FT<br/>(InstructGPT의 SFT)"]
    SFT --> RM["보상모델 r_φ 학습<br/>(인간 선호 비교 데이터)"]
    RM --> RL["정책 최적화 (PPO)<br/>r_φ 최대 + KL 제약"]
    RL --> C["ChatGPT"]









Figure 5: GPT-3 → ChatGPT로 가는 정렬 파이프라인

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
9.3 Formula: KL-Normalized Reward Maximization
Policy \(\pi_\theta\) maximizes the expected reward of the reward model \(r_\phi\), but a KL penalty is applied so that it does not deviate too far from the reference policy \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (usually an SFT model).
\[
\max_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\, y\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
\Big[\, r_\phi(x, y) \;-\; \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\!\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\,\Vert\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\big) \Big]
\]






NoteDirectionality of KL term (Connected to HW#4)



Here, KL is \(\mathrm{KL}(\pi_\theta \Vert \pi_{\text{ref}})\) — the policy being learned is the first argument. This is in the form of reverse KL, implying a mode-seeking / zero-forcing tendency: it strongly suppresses the policy from leaking into regions where the reference distribution is near zero (preventing reward hacking), but is not obligated to cover all modes of the reference. PPO/GRPO reliably optimizes this objective with clipped policy gradients.








NoteWireless Communication Analogy — Closed-loop Feedback Adaptation



RLHF is equivalent to closed-loop adaptive control. Pre-training is the open-loop transmitter, and human feedback is the feedback channel that updates the transmission strategy, such as the receiver’s ACK/quality report. The KL penalty acts as a power constraint or trust-region—limiting the update width to prevent the system from diverging. Just as closed-loop power control aligns the SINR to a target value, RLHF aligns the model output to human preference.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
section: 11.1 A.1 Next-token softmax and cross-entropy / perplexity
text:
11.1 A.1 Next-token softmax and cross-entropy / perplexity

import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max()                      # 수치 안정화 (overflow 방지)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

# 어휘 크기 5에 대한 한 스텝 로짓과 정답 토큰
logits = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0, 0.2])
target = 0                                # 정답 토큰 인덱스

p = softmax(logits)
ce = -np.log(p[target])                   # 단일 스텝 cross-entropy (NLL)
print("p:", np.round(p, 4))
print("cross-entropy:", round(float(ce), 4))

# 시퀀스 평균 NLL과 perplexity
nlls = np.array([0.31, 1.20, 0.05, 2.10])  # 토큰별 NLL 예시
avg_nll = nlls.mean()
ppl = np.exp(avg_nll)                       # PPL = exp(평균 NLL) = 유효 분기계수
print("avg NLL:", round(float(avg_nll), 4), "| perplexity:", round(float(ppl), 4))

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
text:
11.2 A.2 Check Forward-KL = cross-entropy − entropy

import numpy as np

p_data  = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])   # 데이터 분포
p_model = np.array([0.4, 0.3, 0.2,  0.1])    # 모델 분포

H_data = -(p_data * np.log(p_data)).sum()                 # 데이터 엔트로피 (하한)
CE     = -(p_data * np.log(p_model)).sum()                # cross-entropy
KL_fwd =  (p_data * np.log(p_data / p_model)).sum()       # forward KL

print("H(data) :", round(float(H_data), 4))
print("CE      :", round(float(CE), 4))
print("KL_fwd  :", round(float(KL_fwd), 4))
print("CE - H  :", round(float(CE - H_data), 4), "(== KL_fwd 이어야 함)")
# 결론: cross-entropy 최소화 == forward KL 최소화 == MLE  (상수 H(data) 차이)

title: Large Language Models (LLMs)
section: 11.3 A.3 Self-consistency: Valid accuracy increases with majority vote
text:
11.3 A.3 Self-consistency: Valid accuracy increases with majority vote

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def single_pass_correct(p_correct):
    """한 번의 추론 경로가 정답일 확률 p_correct 인 베르누이 시도."""
    return rng.random() < p_correct

def self_consistency_accuracy(p_correct, M, trials=20000):
    """M개 경로 다수결의 정확도를 몬테카를로로 추정.
       오답은 여러 잘못된 답으로 분산된다고 단순 가정."""
    wins = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        correct_votes = sum(single_pass_correct(p_correct) for _ in range(M))
        # 오답표는 (M - correct_votes)표가 서로 다른 답으로 흩어진다고 가정
        # => 정답표가 1표 이상이면서 최다이면 승리 (보수적 근사)
        wins += 1 if correct_votes * 2 > M else 0
    return wins / trials

p = 0.40                                  # 단일 경로 정확도 40%
for M in [1, 3, 5, 11, 21]:
    acc = self_consistency_accuracy(p, M)
    print(f"M={M:2d}: majority-vote accuracy ≈ {acc:.3f}")
# 직관: 단일 경로가 우연보다 낫기만 하면, 경로 수 M↑ 에 따라 정확도가 향상
#       (다이버시티 결합으로 유효 신뢰도 상승)

section: 11.4 A.4 Log–log Linearity of Scaling Law
text:
11.4 A.4 Log–log Linearity of Scaling Law

import numpy as np

# L(N) = (Nc / N)^alpha  형태의 멱법칙
Nc, alpha = 1e8, 0.076
N = np.array([1e6, 1e7, 1e8, 1e9, 1e10])
L = (Nc / N) ** alpha

logN, logL = np.log10(N), np.log10(L)
slope = (logL[-1] - logL[0]) / (logN[-1] - logN[0])   # log-log 기울기
print("log-log slope:", round(float(slope), 4), " (이론값 -alpha =", -alpha, ")")
# 결론: 멱법칙은 log-log 축에서 기울기 -alpha 의 직선으로 나타난다.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
TipKey One-Line Summary



Reinforcement learning (RL) is a problem of finding a policy \(\pi\) that maximizes the expected cumulative value of rewards on a mathematical framework called MDP. If the policy is directly parameterized as \(\theta\), the policy gradient theorem becomes the fundamental equation of learning, and from this, algorithms evolve in the direction of reducing variance (baseline, advantage, actor-critic) and controlling the update range (TRPO, PPO, GRPO).


The algorithms discussed today all lie on a single lineage. The starting point is REINFORCE, which uses the policy gradient as is; Actor-Critic emerged to reduce its variance; TRPO appeared to address the problem of learning becoming unstable due to overly large updates by binding the confidence domain; PPO approximated that complex second-order optimization with simple clipping; and GRPO is a version of PPO that completely removed the critic (value network) and replaced the advantage with group statistics.

flowchart LR
    A["MDP<br/>(상태·행동·보상)"] --> B["가치함수<br/>v_π, q_π"]
    B --> C["벨만 방정식<br/>(재귀 관계)"]
    C --> D["GPI<br/>(정책반복)"]
    D --> E["정책 경사 정리<br/>∇J(θ)"]
    E --> F["REINFORCE<br/>(Monte Carlo PG)"]
    F -->|"분산 ↓<br/>baseline/critic"| G["Actor-Critic"]
    G -->|"갱신 폭 통제<br/>KL 제약"| H["TRPO"]
    H -->|"클리핑으로 근사"| I["PPO"]
    I -->|"critic 제거<br/>그룹 정규화"| J["GRPO"]
















NoteEntry Point for Wireless Communication Majors



The core formulas of RL have exactly the same form as the tools familiar in signal processing. Discounted cumulative reward corresponds to IIR accumulation with a forgetting factor, Bellman recursion to Recursive Filter (RLS) update, baseline subtraction to DC removal / control variate, GRPO normalization to CFAR/AGC normalization, and TRPO·PPO update constraints to Normalized step size control in NLMS. Match them in the Wireless Communication Correspondence box at the end of each section.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
2.1 Direct Answer: What RL solves
RL is a problem in which an agent interacting with an environment and receiving a numerical reward signal learns action choice rules (policies) to maximize the accumulation of expected future rewards.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
2.2 Four components









Element
Symbol
Definition
Role




Policy
\(\pi(a\mid s)\)
Mapping from state to action (probability)
Defines the agent’s action itself


Reward
\(r\)
A single number given by the environment at each time point
The signal to be maximized **


Value Function (Value)
\(v_\pi, q_\pi\)
Accumulation of Expected Future Rewards
Tool for Estimating Which Action Is Good


Model (Model, Optional)
\(p(s',r\mid s,a)\)
Simulation of Environment Dynamics
Environment Proxy (Learning possible without)









Important



The key point is that the reward is an exogenous signal from the environment, and the value function is a proxy created by the agent. The policy is updated using the value function as a guide, and while the model simulates the environment to improve sampling efficiency if present (model-based), it learns even without one (model-free). All algorithms discussed today belong to the model-free family.


The name “reinforcement” comes from the fact that good state-behavior pairs become increasingly reinforced and distinct through repeated interactions. Historically, RL originated from optimal control theory, and with Bellman introducing the states of dynamical systems and value functions (optimal return functions), the Bellman equations and dynamic programming as their solution emerged. MDP is a generalization of this into a discrete, probabilistic version.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
3.1 Direct Answer: Why MDP?
To define a learnable agent, a mathematical framework is required to define the behavior of the agent and the environment. Assuming the Markov property, the analysis becomes decisively simple because the probability of the next state and reward depends only on the immediately preceding state and action.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
3.2 Definition and Markov properties
For time \(t\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}\), state \(s\in S\), action \(a\in A(s)\), and reward \(r\in R\), the environment dynamics are
\[
p(s', r \mid s, a) = \Pr\big(S_{t+1}=s',\, R_{t+1}=r \mid S_t=s,\, A_t=a\big).
\]
Here, the Markov property is that the right-hand side is conditional on only one \(S_t, A_t\). In other words, the future statistics are determined by looking only at the present point in time, rather than the entire past \((S_0,A_0,\dots,S_{t-1},A_{t-1})\).






NoteEpisode = Data point



A set of interactions from time point 1 to \(T\) \((R_1, R_2, \dots, R_T)\) is called an episode, and this is a point of data for training. If the ends are naturally divided, it is an episodic task, and if it is a single long flow, it is a continuing task.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
3.3 Discounted return and goal
\[
G_t = \sum_{k=t+1}^{T} \gamma^{\,k-t-1} R_k
    = R_{t+1} + \gamma R_{t+2} + \gamma^2 R_{t+3} + \cdots,
\qquad 0 \le \gamma \le 1.
\]
Since uncertainty is greater for future rewards, the weight is reduced using the discount factor \(\gamma\). From here, the recursive form emerges immediately:
\[
\boxed{\,G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\, G_{t+1}\,}
\]
The goal of learning is to maximize the expected return on the policy:
\[
\max_{\pi}\; \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t].
\]






TipWireless communication compatibility — IIR accumulation with forget factor



\(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\) has the same structure as a first-order IIR/exponentially weighted accumulation with a forgetting factor \(\lambda\). The closer \(\gamma\) is to 1, the further into the future it remembers (long time constant), and the closer it is to 0, the more short-sighted it becomes (short time constant). This plays exactly the same role as the forgetting factor in RLS, which determines how long past errors are reflected.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
4.1 Two value functions
\[
v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s],
\qquad
q_\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \mid S_t = s,\, A_t = a].
\]
The state value \(v_\pi\) takes state only as input, while the action value \(q_\pi\) takes both state and action as input. Since it is very difficult to calculate both exactly, they are approximated.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
4.2 Optimal Policy
\[
v_*(s) = \max_\pi v_\pi(s),
\qquad
q_*(s,a) = \max_\pi q_\pi(s,a).
\]
The optimal policy is usually obtained using the action value \(q_*\). This is because \(q\) takes an action as input, allowing for a direct comparison of which action increases value in that state, whereas \(v\) cannot directly capture the effect of an action. In deterministic policies,
\[
\pi_*(s) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_a q_*(s,a).
\]






Important



It appears to optimize to \(v\), but internally it uses \(q\). Since the two are connected as \(v_\pi(s)=\sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\,q_\pi(s,a)\) in the Bellman equation that follows, the apparent optimization of \(v\) is actually reduced to a comparison of \(q\).

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
5.1 Direct Answer: What is recursion?
The Bellman equation is a recursive formula that expresses the value function at the current time step in terms of the value function at the next time step. This recursion is necessary to convert policy iterations into iterative updates.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
5.2 \(v_\pi\) and \(q_\pi\) connection
Marginalize state values with respect to behavior:
\[
v_\pi(s) = \sum_{a\in A(s)} \pi(a\mid s)\, q_\pi(s,a)
        \;\le\; \max_a q_\pi(s,a).
\]
The inequality represents the fact that “the expected value cannot exceed the maximum value,” and sets an upper limit on policy improvement.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
5.3 Recursive expansion of \(q_\pi\)
Insert the recursion \(G_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\) returning into the action value definition. The key step is that \(G_{t+1}\) can be replaced with \(v_\pi(S_{t+1})\) inside the expectation (the two are different outside but are the same in terms of conditional expectation):
\[
\mathbb{E}_\pi[v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid S_t=s, a] = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_{t+1}\mid S_t=s, a].
\]
Therefore
\[
q_\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}\mid s,a\big]
           = \sum_{s',r} p(s',r\mid s,a)\,\big[\,r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\,\big].
\]
Substituting this into the \(v_\pi\) equation completes the Belleman expectation equation:
\[
\boxed{\;
v_\pi(s) = \underbrace{\sum_{a}\pi(a\mid s)}_{\text{에이전트가 하는 일(정책)}}
           \underbrace{\sum_{s',r} p(s',r\mid s,a)}_{\text{환경의 반응(전이·보상)}}
           \big[\,r + \gamma\, v_\pi(s')\,\big]
\;}
\]






Note



Structural Analysis (3-step causal chain): Policy determines the behavior distribution → Environment responds with transitions and rewards → The immediate reward \(r\) and the future value of the next state \(\gamma v_\pi(s')\) combine to become the present value. The fact that it splits into two separable terms (policy term / environment term) is crucially used in the subsequent Policy Gradient Theorem — the environment term is independent of \(\theta\) and is excluded from differentiation.








TipWireless Communication Support — Recursive Filter (RLS) Update



\(v_\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}[\,r + \gamma v_\pi(s')\,]\) is in the form “current estimate = new observation + discounted next estimate,” and is a framework similar to the predict–update recursion of the RLS Kalman filter. It is intuitive if you view \(\gamma\) as a stable first-order recursion acting as the state transition gain.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
6.1 Policy Improvement Summary
If we define the new greedy policy as the behavioral value of the current policy \(\pi\)
\[
\pi'(s) = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_a q_\pi(s,a)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_\pi(s) \le v_{\pi'}(s).
\]
In other words, if you change the policy to “action that maximizes the current value function,” the value never deteriorates.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
6.2 Generalized Policy Iteration (GPI)

flowchart LR
    P["정책 π"] -->|"평가<br/>(가치 추정)"| V["가치함수 v_π"]
    V -->|"개선<br/>(탐욕적 갱신)"| P










By alternately repeating evaluation (value estimation) and improvement (policy update), the optimal policy \(\pi_*\) and the optimal value \(v_*\) converge. The two processes are a cooperative iteration in which they lift each other.






WarningMotivation to transition from GPI limitations to policy gradient



GPI uses a non-differentiable greedy operation \(\arg\max\). Furthermore, greedy updates can abruptly change the policy distribution, causing agent behavior to change drastically in a single step and the learning curve to fluctuate. To train a neural network in a differentiable way, instead of \(\arg\max\), the policy must be parameterized as \(\theta\) and updated slowly using gradients. This is the motivation behind the policy gradient method.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
7.1 Direct Answer: Policy Gradient Theorem
If we set the policy to \(\pi(a\mid s;\theta)\) and define the objective function as the state value of the starting state \(J(\theta)=v_{\pi_\theta}(s_0)\), then (assuming \(\gamma=1\)) the gradient is
\[
\boxed{\;\nabla J(\theta) \;\propto\; \sum_s \mu(s) \sum_a q_\pi(s,a)\, \nabla \pi(a\mid s,\theta)\;}
\]
where \(\mu(s)\) is the state distribution induced by the policy (average time ratio of staying in state \(s\)).

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
7.2 Meaning of theorem
The gradient of the objective function is decomposed into the product of three elements: the state distribution \(\mu(s)\), the action value \(q_\pi(s,a)\), and the gradient of the policy itself \(\nabla\pi\). The key point is that the derivative applies only to the policy term, and the environment transition probability \(p(s'\mid s,a)\) is independent of \(\theta\) and vanishes.






NoteProof Framework (Overview)




Substitute the defined ZZZPH0010032ZZZ \(\nabla v_\pi(s)\) into \(v_\pi(s)=\sum_a \pi(a\mid s)q_\pi(s,a)\) and apply the product derivative: \(\nabla(\pi\,q) = (\nabla\pi)q + \pi(\nabla q)\).
Since the reward/transition probability within \(\nabla q_\pi(s,a)\) is an independent constant \(\theta\), the derivative recursively passes to the next state \(\nabla v_\pi(s')\).
If this recursion is expanded repeatedly, it is organized into the form \(\nabla v_\pi(s)\) \(s\) \(x\) \(x\) \(k\) \(\Pr(s\to x,k,\pi)\) \(\times\ \nabla\pi(\cdot\mid x)\, q_\pi(x,\cdot)\)“.
Normalizing \(\sum_k \Pr(s\to x,k,\pi)\) gives the state distribution \(\mu(x)\) — “the average number of times spent in state \(s\) in one episode”. Substituting this closes the proportion.









TipWireless communication support — Adapt only the differentiable part



The environment transition is a channel (fixed probability) that we cannot control, and the policy is the weight that we adapt. The structure in which the channel is excluded from the derivative and only the weight update term remains is a separation configuration similar to an adaptive filter that adapts only the equalizer coefficients while keeping the channel fixed.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
8.1 Log-derivative trick and update formula
If we rewrite the policy gradient theorem in terms of expectation
\[
\nabla J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\!\Big[\sum_a q_\pi(s,a)\,\nabla\pi(a\mid s,\theta)\Big].
\]
Applying the score function trick \(\nabla_\theta \ln f = \dfrac{\nabla_\theta f}{f}\) to this results in a sampleable form:
\[
\boxed{\;\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t + \alpha\, G_t\, \nabla \ln \pi(A_t\mid S_t, \theta_t)\;}
\]
Return \(G_t\) updates in a direction that increases the log probability of the action that produced a large (good) trajectory.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
8.2 algorithm






NoteREINFORCE procedure




Set the function \(\pi(a\mid s;\theta)\) (normal neural network), initial \(\theta\), and step size \(\alpha\).
Iteration: Randomly generate one episode with the current policy → Calculate \(G_t\) at each time point → Update all time points to \(\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha G_t \nabla\ln\pi(A_t\mid S_t,\theta)\) → Repeat with a new episode.
Since the gradient is estimated using sample trajectories, it is called Monte Carlo policy gradient control.









WarningWeakness of REINFORCE



Because the episodes are rolled randomly until the end to create \(G_t\), sample variance is very large. Learning is unstable (large policy updates), and sample efficiency and robustness are poor. This is why the learning curve fluctuates and the agent frequently exhibits erratic behavior (falling, stumbling). Reducing this variance is the consistent motivation for the next steps.








TipWireless communication support — Noise-heavy slope estimation



\(G_t\) is a noisy gradient with large variance, as it is an estimate obtained from a single random realization. Estimating a channel from a single snapshot is equivalent to having large variance, and the baseline subtraction in the next section corresponds to a preprocessing step that reduces the variance of the estimator.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
section: 9.1 Baseline reduces only variance without bias
text:
9.1 Baseline reduces only variance without bias
The expected value of the gradient does not change even if the state-only dependent baseline \(b(S_t)\) is subtracted from the expected value (uncomfortable):
\[
\nabla J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\big[(G_t - b(S_t))\,\nabla\ln\pi(A_t\mid S_t,\theta)\big].
\]
The reason is \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[\,b(S_t)\nabla\ln\pi\,]=b(S_t)\sum_a \nabla\pi = b(S_t)\nabla\!\sum_a\pi = 0\) (\(\sum_a\pi=1\)).

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
9.2 Advantage function
The natural baseline is the state value \(v_\pi(S_t)\). Approximating \(G_t\) with a one-step expansion without rolling it all the way results in a TD error, and this is precisely the advantage:
\[
\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\, v_\pi(S_{t+1}) - v_\pi(S_t)
\;\approx\; G_t - v_\pi(S_t) \;=\; A_\pi(S_t, A_t),
\qquad
\nabla J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[\delta_t\,\nabla\ln\pi].
\]
Advantage measures “how much better that action is than the average of that state” and reduces variance by converting large fluctuations in absolute rewards into relative values compared to the average.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
9.3 Actor-Critic








Configuration
Role
Formula




Actor(Policy Network)
Decide what action to take
\(\pi_\theta(s)\)


Critic(Value Network)
Estimate the quality of the behavior
\(Q(s,a)\) or \(v(s)\), \(\delta_t\)









Note



The critic does not directly command the actor but assists them. Initially, since the policy is immature, the critic is noisy and offers almost no control; however, as iterations progress and the policy improves, the critic’s feedback becomes more accurate. This then better constrains the actor’s updates, leading to faster and more stable convergence. However, this is merely indirect normalization, and there is no guarantee that the policy will not change abruptly in a single step. The following confidence domain method is designed to directly provide that guarantee.








TipWireless communication support — DC removal / Control variable



Baseline subtraction is a control variate technique that reduces variance by subtracting the mean (DC) before estimation. It is equivalent to estimating only the variation after removing the mean of the signal, which reduces the estimated variance; this effect is evident in the approximately 7-fold reduction (21.8→3.1) in the text verification.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
section: 10.1 Direct Answer: What does it restrict?
text:
10.1 Direct Answer: What does it restrict?
Even a single step can cause actor parameters to change rapidly, potentially leading to the breakdown of training. The solution is to bind the update domain using KL divergence to prevent the new policy from deviating too far from the previous one:
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}} \,\|\, \pi_\theta\big) \le \epsilon.
\]

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
section: 10.2 Surrogate Objective Function and Probability Ratio
text:
10.2 Surrogate Objective Function and Probability Ratio
Approximate the \(\nabla\ln\pi\) term with a probability ratio (a first-order expansion from \(\theta_{\text{old}}\) gives the same slope):
\[
r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}.
\]
TRPO is for surrogate purposes under constraints
\[
\max_\theta\; \mathbb{E}_t\big[r_t(\theta)\,\hat{A}_t\big]
\quad \text{s.t.}\quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}\le \delta
\]
Maximize . In the unconstrained form, add the KL penalty \(-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) to the objective.






WarningLimitations of TRPO



To accurately handle KL constraints, it is a complex quadratic method that requires a second-order approximation of KL (including Hessian), and it is difficult to set the KL penalty coefficient \(\beta\) as a fixed value applicable to all problems. This weakness of being computationally heavy is the motivation for moving toward PPO.








TipWireless Communication Compatibility — Normalized Step Size Control (NLMS)



KL constraints are analogous to the NLMS concept of normalizing/limiting step sizes to prevent divergence in adaptive updates. Just as steps are reduced to maintain stability when input energy is high, KL constraints pull updates back when the policy is about to jump far, keeping them within a “trusted” area.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
11.1 Direct Answer: Clipped line
PPO replaces TRPO’s complex KL calculations with a simple operation that clips the probability ratios to \([1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon]\):
\[
\boxed{\;
L^{\text{CLIP}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\Big[\min\big(r_t(\theta)\,\hat{A}_t,\;\operatorname{clip}(r_t(\theta),\,1-\epsilon,\,1+\epsilon)\,\hat{A}_t\big)\Big]
\;}
\]

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
11.2 Clipping behavior
\(r_t\) penalizes updates that deviate from 1 (=significant policy changes). Reading the behavior as a result of the body numerical validation:









Situation
\(r_t\) Small
\(r_t=1\)
\(r_t\) Large




\(\hat A>0\) (Good behavior)
Reflected as is
1.0
Upper limit at \(1+\epsilon\) (Block excessive amplification)


\(\hat A<0\) (Bad Behavior)
Lower limit at \(1-\epsilon\)
\(-1.0\)
Penalty points as is (Suppression)



In other words, it prevents the policy from jumping out from both sides by pushing good behavior too hard or pulling bad behavior too hard. Since a KL penalty variation \(L - \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) can also be used instead of clipping, PPO can be viewed as a general framework that includes the KL penalty method.






NoteAdvantages of PPO




Reusing the same data through stochastic gradient elevation over multiple epochs → Sample efficiency ↑
Maintain the stability and reliability of the confidence domain method
Simple implementation (first-order method, calculates only ratio + clip; KL Hessian unnecessary)

Thanks to this simplicity, PPO became the standard tool of RLHF and was used as a key tool for fine-tuning instructions in the GPT → InstructGPT → ChatGPT family.








Warning



There are also clear limitations. It can get stuck in a local optimum, and as clipping accumulates, there remains the possibility that the new policy will eventually become too far from the previous policy.








TipWireless Communication Support — Feedback Loop Limiter/Grid Clipping



Cutting \(r_t\) to \([1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]\) is equivalent to the amplitude limiter and slope clipping of a feedback loop. It is a protection device that saturates the output to prevent the loop gain from becoming excessive and oscillating, and it is similar in that it is a practical method that ensures stability without complex stability analysis.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
section: 12.1 Direct Answer: Remove critic + Group normalization
text:
12.1 Direct Answer: Remove critic + Group normalization
In PPO, advantage calculation (GAE) is expensive because it requires training a separate critic (value network) for the baseline. GRPO discards the critic entirely and replaces the advantage with the relative position of rewards within the group:
\[
\boxed{\;\hat{A}^{\text{GRPO}}_t = \frac{R - \mu_g}{\sigma_g + \delta}\;}
\]
\(R\): Compensation for the corresponding output, \(\mu_g\): Group mean compensation, \(\sigma_g\): Group standard deviation, \(\delta\): A small constant that prevents the denominator from becoming zero.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
12.2 Idea
For the same prompt, multiple outputs (groups/batches) are generated, and the reward of each output is normalized to its relative value relative to the group mean and used as the advantage. The advantage is calculated solely from the group statistics of the current reward, without the need for cumulative estimates of future rewards or critics. The clipping and (optional) KL terms of the objective function are nearly identical to the PPO, with only the definition of advantage being different.

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
12.3 PPO vs GRPO








Item
PPO
GRPO




Core Structure
Policy Gradient (Actor-Critic)
Policy Gradient (Critic-Free)


Advantage
\(\hat A_t = R_t - V(s_t)\) (GAE)
\(\hat A_t = \dfrac{R-\mu_g}{\sigma_g+\delta}\)


Value Network (critic)
Required (Separate \(V(s)\) training)
Unnecessary (Replaced by group statistics)


advantage focus
critic value of action versus predicted state value
value of result versus current batch average result \(\mu_g\)


Advantages
Precise value estimation → Low variance & stability
Memory & computational efficiency (critic elimination)


Fitting Region
General RL requiring precision value and low variance
Large-scale LLM RLHF (Memory bottleneck, sparse/binary reward)









Note



Although the advantage is not as precise as PPO, it offers greater computational efficiency, and as iterations progress, it generally converges to a level similar to or intermediate to PPO. It has been used as a core component in modern LLM training, such as DeepSeek-Math/V3, and is well-suited for LLM environments where memory is a bottleneck and rewards are sparse and binary.








TipWireless Communication Support — CFAR / AGC Normalization



\(\hat A=\dfrac{R-\mu_g}{\sigma_g+\delta}\) is based on the same concept as CFAR detection in radar. Just as the power of a test cell is divided by noise statistics (mean and standard deviation) estimated from surrounding cells to create detection statistics independent of absolute scale, GRPO normalizes the compensation of a single output by the mean and standard deviation of the group to create an advantage of being insensitive to the compensation scale. This is similar to how AGC normalizes signal levels by group statistics, and corresponds exactly in that it normalizes using neighbor/batch statistics without a separate critique.

text:
15.1 Log-derivative identity and baseline unbiasedness

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# softmax 정책: pi(a) = softmax(theta)_a, grad_theta log pi(a) = e_a - pi
theta = rng.normal(size=4)
pi = np.exp(theta) / np.exp(theta).sum()
grad_logpi = np.eye(4) - pi[None, :]            # 행 a = grad log pi(a)

# (1) score function 항등식: E_{a~pi}[ grad log pi ] = 0
E_score = (pi[:, None] * grad_logpi).sum(0)
print("E[grad log pi]      :", np.round(E_score, 12))   # ~ 0

# (2) 상수 baseline b 는 경사를 편향시키지 않음: E[ b * grad log pi ] = 0
b = 3.7
print("E[b * grad log pi]  :", np.round((pi[:, None] * b * grad_logpi).sum(0), 12))

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
15.2 Baseline Variance Reduction Effect

# 반환 G ~ N(5, 2), 행동을 pi에서 샘플 → G*score 대 (G - mean)*score 의 분산 비교
N = 100_000
G = rng.normal(5.0, 2.0, size=N)
a = rng.integers(0, 4, size=N)
score = grad_logpi[a]                            # (N, 4)

est_no = G[:, None] * score                       # baseline 없음
est_bl = (G - G.mean())[:, None] * score          # baseline = 평균

print("trace Var (no baseline):", round(np.cov(est_no.T).trace(), 3))
print("trace Var (w/ baseline):", round(np.cov(est_bl.T).trace(), 3))
# baseline 차감으로 분산이 크게 감소 (약 7배)

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
15.3 GRPO Group relative advantage

# 그룹 내 이진 보상 → (R - mu)/(sigma + delta) 로 정규화
R = np.array([0., 1., 1., 0., 1., 0., 0., 1.])
mu, sd = R.mean(), R.std()
A_grpo = (R - mu) / (sd + 1e-8)
print("GRPO advantage:", np.round(A_grpo, 3))
print("mean ~ 0:", round(A_grpo.mean(), 6), "| std ~ 1:", round(A_grpo.std(), 4))

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
text:
15.4 PPO Clipping Proxy Purpose

def ppo_clip(r, A, eps=0.2):
    """L^CLIP = min( r*A , clip(r,1-eps,1+eps)*A )"""
    return np.minimum(r * A, np.clip(r, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * A)

ratios = np.array([0.5, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.5])
print("A>0 (좋은 행동) r:", ratios, "-> L:", np.round(ppo_clip(ratios, +1.0), 3))
print("A<0 (나쁜 행동) r:", ratios, "-> L:", np.round(ppo_clip(ratios, -1.0), 3))
# A>0: r가 1+eps=1.2 위로 가면 상한에서 포화 (과한 증폭 차단)
# A<0: r가 1-eps=0.8 아래로 가면 하한에서 포화

title: From Reinforcement Learning to PPO·GRPO: Policy Gradient-Based Optimization
section: 15.5 Small REINFORCE training demo (similar to 2-state bandit)
text:
15.5 Small REINFORCE training demo (similar to 2-state bandit)

# 단순 2행동 문제: 행동 1의 기대보상이 더 높음 → 정책이 행동 1로 수렴하는지 확인
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
theta = np.zeros(2)                 # softmax 로짓
alpha = 0.1
true_reward = np.array([0.2, 0.8])  # 행동별 기대 보상

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max()
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

for step in range(2000):
    p = softmax(theta)
    a = rng.choice(2, p=p)                          # 현재 정책에서 행동 샘플
    G = rng.normal(true_reward[a], 0.1)             # 보상(반환) 샘플
    grad_logpi = (np.eye(2)[a] - p)                 # grad log pi(a)
    theta += alpha * G * grad_logpi                 # REINFORCE 갱신

print("최종 정책 분포:", np.round(softmax(theta), 3))  # 행동 1 확률이 1에 근접
