title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
2.1 Core

Artificially increase the training data using a label-preserving transformation to make the model invariant to that transformation. “If you cannot obtain more real data, synthesize fake data.”

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
2.2 Formatting
For the transformation distribution \(T(\cdot\mid\bm{x})\) (e.g., rotation, translation, chromatic transformation), replace the loss with the expectation of the transformed input.
\[
\tilde{L}(\bm{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\bm{x},y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{\bm{x}}\sim T(\cdot\mid\bm{x})}\big[\ell\big(f_{\bm{\theta}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}),\,y\big)\big]
\tag{4}\]
This has the effect of smoothing decision boundaries by “spreading” the data distribution along the transformation orbit.






TipNoise injection = \(\ell_2\) Normalization (for small Gaussians)



If we add small Gaussian noise \(\tilde{\bm{x}}=\bm{x}+\bm{\epsilon},\ \bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma^2 I)\) to the input and perform a second-order Taylor expansion of the regression loss, the expected value is approximately
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\epsilon}}[\ell] \approx \ell(\bm{x}) + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\|\nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x})\|^2\big]
\]
, which acts as a penalty for the Jacobian norm (inducing flatness of the function). In other words, data augmentation is equivalent to adding an implicit normalization term.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
2.3 Intuition and Caution

The transformation must be label invariant. Rotation augmentation is dangerous because rotating the handwritten ‘6’ by 180° results in ‘9’.
Domain knowledge determines good augmentation — this is why augmentation is called “manual inductive bias.”







NoteWireless communication analogy



This is equivalent to training the equalizer/receiver on multiple channel realizations. By sampling the fading channel using Monte-Carlo and training under various \(\bm{h}\) conditions, the receiver becomes robust to the entire channel distribution without overfitting to a specific channel. \(T\) in Equation Food 4 is the channel distribution \(p(\bm{h})\).

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
3.1 Core

We intentionally create and train with adversarial perturbations that are almost identical to the human eye but trick the model. The primary purpose is robustness, but it also helps with generalization by making decision boundaries insensitive to changes in input.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
3.2 Adversarial example generation: FGSM
If the loss \(J(\bm{\theta},\bm{x},y)\) is linearized first-order with respect to the input, the perturbation that maximizes the loss under the \(\ell_\infty\) constraint is the sign of the gradient (Fast Gradient Sign Method).
\[
\bm{x}_{\text{adv}} = \bm{x} + \epsilon \cdot \mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_{\bm{x}} J(\bm{\theta},\bm{x},y)\big)
\tag{5}\]
In high dimensions, even very small \(\epsilon\) perturbations accumulate across numerous dimensions and significantly shake the output (linearity hypothesis). A classic example illustrating this is when invisible perturbations are added to a panda image, causing it to be misclassified as a gibbon with 99% certainty.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
3.3 Two learning strategies

Injecting perturbation into input (Adversarial training): Add \(\bm{x}_{\text{adv}}\) from Food 5 to the training set. If written in minimax form
\[
\min_{\bm{\theta}}\ \mathbb{E}_{(\bm{x},y)}\Big[\max_{\|\bm{\delta}\|\le\epsilon} J(\bm{\theta},\bm{x}+\bm{\delta},y)\Big]
\]

— Robust optimization for the worst-case.

Injecting noise into output target (Label smoothing): Smooths the one-hot target. For class count \(k\), small \(\epsilon\)
\[
y_c^{\text{smooth}} =
\begin{cases}
1-\epsilon & (\text{정답 클래스}) \\[4pt]
\dfrac{\epsilon}{k-1} & (\text{나머지 클래스})
\end{cases}
\tag{6}\]

Prevents softmax from running into infinite logits (prevents overconfidence) and mitigates gradient vanishing in high-confidence predictions.






NoteWireless communication analogy



minimax adversarial learning is exactly the same structure as a receiver design robust against jamming/worst-case interference. In the transmitter-jammer game, robust beamforming designed to guarantee performance even when the jammer pours power in the worst direction in the signal space corresponds to the internal max of Food 5.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
4.1 Core

Combines labeled data (small amount) and unlabeled data (large amount). The distribution \(p(\bm{x})\) of the unlabeled data itself becomes normalization information, inducing the decision boundary to be placed in a low-density region rather than a dense region.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
4.2 Formatting
The objective function is a combination of supervised terms and unsupervised (normalized) terms.
\[
L = \underbrace{\sum_{(\bm{x}_i,y_i)\in\mathcal{D}_L}\ell(f(\bm{x}_i),y_i)}_{\text{레이블 정보}}
+ \lambda\underbrace{\sum_{\bm{x}_j\in\mathcal{D}_U}\mathcal{R}(f,\bm{x}_j)}_{\text{분포 정보}}
\]
Representative selection of non-guided item \(\mathcal{R}\):

Consistency Normalization (consistency): \(\mathcal{R}=\|f(\bm{x})-f(\tilde{\bm{x}})\|^2\), i.e., \(\bm{x}\), and its augmentation \(\tilde{\bm{x}}\) must have the same prediction (cluster assumption).
Entropy Minimization: \(\mathcal{R}=H(f(\bm{x}))\), to ensure the prediction is confident in one class — push the boundary into a low-density region.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
4.3 Two scenarios

When labeled and unlabeled data are in the same representation domain: standard semi-map.
When it is a different representation domain: It aligns with transfer/self-supervised methods that learn shared representations.







NoteWireless communication analogy



It is isomorphic to semi-blind channel estimation. It roughly defines the channel using a small number of pilot symbols (=labels) and reduces the estimation variance by utilizing the statistics of a large number of data symbols (received signal distribution, stationarity, structures such as finite alphabets = non-label distribution information).

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
5.1 Core

Train multiple tasks simultaneously with a single model, but share the sub-representation \(\bm{h}^{\text{shared}}\). Each task acts as a data-dependent prior to the others, preventing the shared representation from overfitting to any single task.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
5.2 structure


Code
flowchart BT
    x["입력 x"] --> hs["h(shared): 공유 표현"]
    hs --> h1["h(1): 과제1 전용"]
    hs --> h2["h(2): 과제2 전용"]
    hs --> h3["h(3): 추가 인자"]
    h1 --> y1["y(1)"]
    h2 --> y2["y(2)"]





flowchart BT
    x["입력 x"] --> hs["h(shared): 공유 표현"]
    hs --> h1["h(1): 과제1 전용"]
    hs --> h2["h(2): 과제2 전용"]
    hs --> h3["h(3): 추가 인자"]
    h1 --> y1["y(1)"]
    h2 --> y2["y(2)"]






The objective function is the weighted sum of the losses per task.
\[
L_{\text{MTL}}(\bm{\theta}_{\text{shared}}, \{\bm{\theta}_t\})
= \sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_t\, L_t\big(\bm{\theta}_{\text{shared}}, \bm{\theta}_t;\ \mathcal{D}_t\big)
\]

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
5.3 Why Normalization?
Since the shared parameter \(\bm{\theta}_{\text{shared}}\) must simultaneously satisfy the gradients of all tasks, the explorable hypothesis space is significantly narrowed. This acts as an implicit constraint imposed on the expression in Food 2 even without an explicit \(\Omega\). The effect is greater the more the assumption that tasks share a common generative factor holds true.






NoteWireless communication analogy



Joint Estimation — When a single receiver performs channel estimation, frequency offset compensation, and noise power estimation simultaneously based on a common statistic (shared representation), each estimation normalizes the other, thereby reducing the total estimation variance.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
6.1 Core

Stop training when the validation error no longer decreases. The most common, efficient, and almost free regularization. Since the longer training is done, the more the model overfits to the training set, the moment when generalization is optimal is used as a hyperparameter to control the “effective capacity”.



Code
flowchart LR
    A["훈련 시작"] --> B["train↓ val↓<br/>(과소적합 탈출)"]
    B --> C["val 최저점<br/>= Early Stopping"]
    C --> D["train↓ val↑<br/>(과적합 시작)"]





flowchart LR
    A["훈련 시작"] --> B["train↓ val↓<br/>(과소적합 탈출)"]
    B --> C["val 최저점<br/>= Early Stopping"]
    C --> D["train↓ val↑<br/>(과적합 시작)"]

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
6.2 Deep Insight: Early Stopping ≈ \(\ell_2\) Normalization
When gradient descent with a learning rate \(\epsilon\) is \(\tau\) step over the second-order approximated loss \(L(\bm{\theta})\approx L(\bm{\theta}^*) + \tfrac12(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^*)^\top H (\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}^*)\), each component shrinks as follows based on \(H=Q\Lambda Q^\top\) eigendecomposition.
\[
\theta^{(\tau)}_i = \big(1-(1-\epsilon\lambda_i)^{\tau}\big)\,\theta^*_i
\]
Comparing this to the \(\ell_2\) normalized solution \(\theta^{\ell_2}_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i+\alpha}\theta^*_i\), in the small \(\epsilon\lambda_i\) approx.
\[
\boxed{\;\alpha \approx \frac{1}{\tau\epsilon}\;}
\tag{7}\]
In other words, the fewer the step count \(\tau\) (=the earlier it stops), the greater the \(\ell_2\) regularization strength \(\alpha\). Early stopping learns the direction of large curvature (large \(\lambda_i\)) first and stops before the direction of small curvature is fully learned; this has exactly the same effect as weight decay suppressing the direction of small eigenvalues.






TipPractical advantages



If you were to manually explore \(\alpha\) of Food 7, you would have to retrain multiple times, but early stopping automatically selects the optimal regularization strength by following the validation curve in a single training iteration. So it is practically free.








NoteWireless communication analogy



It is similar to the iteration limit of iterative decoding (LDPC/Turbo). If it is run indefinitely, it can become unstable by being overly tailored to the realization of specific noise, so it is optimal to stop at the number of iterations where the verification BER is lowest.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
7.1 Core

Reduces degrees of freedom by forcing multiple parameters to be equal to or close to each other. For two similar tasks A and B, a penalty is applied to make \(\bm{w}^{(B)}\) closer to the already learned \(\bm{w}^{(A)}\).

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
7.2 Two variants
Soft tying (parameter tying): Adds a distance penalty to the loss.
\[
\Omega(\bm{w}^{(A)},\bm{w}^{(B)}) = \big\|\bm{w}^{(A)} - \bm{w}^{(B)}\big\|_2^2
\tag{8}\]
This is equivalent to the MAP of “\(\bm{w}^{(B)}\), where the prior mean is \(\bm{w}^{(A)}\)” (@see eq-map).
Hard sharing (parameter sharing): It forcibly shares identical parameters. CNN convolutional kernels are a prime example — by applying the same filter to every location in the image, it injects powerful prior knowledge of “translation invariance” and dramatically reduces the number of parameters and memory.









Soft tying
Hard sharing




Format
\(+\lambda\|\bm{w}^A-\bm{w}^B\|^2\)
\(\bm{w}^A \equiv \bm{w}^B\)


Degrees of freedom
Partially reduced
Fully coupled


Representative Case
Transfer Learning Fine-tuning
CNN Kernel, RNN Time-shifting Sharing









NoteWireless communication analogy



This is equivalent to the time-invariant or stationarity assumption. Assuming that the channel is constant within a block and applying the same channel coefficient to all symbols is the same kind of statistical assumption as hard sharing, where CNNs share the same kernel at all locations.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
8.1 Core

Multiple models are trained independently on different data subsets, and then the predictions are averaged (voted). The diversity of the dataset created by Bootstrap decorrelates errors between models, thereby directly reducing variance. A form of ensemble and model averaging.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
8.2 Quantitative proof of variance reduction
Let \(k\) be the prediction error of the models, \(\epsilon_i\), let \(v=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_i^2]\) be the variance of each error, and let \(c=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_i\epsilon_j]\,(i\ne j)\) be the covariance between models. The variance of the mean prediction error \(\bar\epsilon=\tfrac1k\sum_i\epsilon_i\) is
\[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bar\epsilon^{\,2}\right]
= \frac{1}{k^2}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Big(\sum_i \epsilon_i\Big)^2\right]
= \frac{1}{k}v + \frac{k-1}{k}c
\tag{9}\]
When looking at the two extremes:

Perfectly Correlated(\(c=v\)): \(\mathbb{E}[\bar\epsilon^2]=v\) — Averaging does not decrease at all.
Completely uncorrelated (\(c=0\)): \(\mathbb{E}[\bar\epsilon^2]=\dfrac{v}{k}\) — Variance decreases inversely proportional to the number of models!

Therefore, the effectiveness of bagging depends on “making each model sufficiently strong while making them different (uncorrelated) from one another.”






ImportantThe effect of Bagging on bias



Food 9 only deals with variance. Since the bias shared by each model remains even after averaging, bagging is most effective for low-bias, high-variance models (e.g., deep decision trees, large neural networks).








NoteWireless Communication Analogy — The Most Accurate Correspondence



Food 9 is identical to the gain formula for diversity combining (e.g., MRC). When combining \(k\) receiving branches undergoing independent fading, the effective noise variance is reduced to \(1/k\) when the noise of the branches is uncorrelated (\(c=0\)), yielding a diversity order \(k\). The communication intuition that “the more independent branches, the better” is the ensemble intuition that “the more uncorrelated models, the better.”

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
9.1 Core

In every mini-batch, each unit is randomly removed with probability \(p\) for training. This is exponentially efficient bagging that trains \(2^n\) sub-networks simultaneously with shared weights in a single training session.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
9.2 Training: Bernoulli mask
Multiply the mask ZZZPH0011658ZZZ for the hidden unit \(\bm{h}\) by \(\bm{m}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(1-p)\) (elementally independent).
\[
\tilde{\bm{h}} = \bm{m}\odot\bm{h}, \qquad m_j\in\{0,1\}
\]
Different masks define different subnetworks, and all subnetworks share weights. This is the decisive difference from bagging — in bagging, models are independent, whereas in dropout, they share parameters.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
9.3 Inference: Weight Scaling Inference Rule
During inference, the predictions of all subnetworks must be averaged (ensemble), but it is not possible to run all \(2^n\) units. Instead, it is approximated by the weight scaling rule. Since the unit was turned on with probability \(1-p\) during training, the weight (or activation) is multiplied by \((1-p)\) during inference to fit the expected input.
\[
\mathbb{E}_{\bm{m}}[\tilde{\bm{h}}] = (1-p)\,\bm{h}
\]
This single forward propagation approximates the geometric mean ensemble of exponential subnetworks well (accurate for softmax output).






TipInverted Dropout (Practical Standard)



To avoid touching the inference, the surviving activations are usually pre-scaled by dividing them into \(1/(1-p)\) during training. Then, the inference can be used as is without scaling.
\[
\tilde{\bm{h}}_{\text{train}} = \frac{\bm{m}\odot\bm{h}}{1-p}
\]

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
9.4 Why Generalization Improves
Each unit becomes unable to rely on the presence of specific peer units (co-adaptation), allowing each unit to learn robust features that are useful in themselves. This can also be interpreted as normalization that injects multiplicative noise into the input.






NoteWireless communication analogy



It is similar to random antenna selection or a distributed system robust to node failure. If trained to operate with only a random subset of antennas, it learns a robust coupling strategy that does not over-depend on a specific antenna.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
10.1 Core

is an explicit normalization that directly brings the directional derivative in a direction close to zero so that the output \(f(\bm{x})\) becomes locally invariant with respect to a “known variation direction”. Example: The output should not change when moving along a manifold formed by the same class examples.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
10.2 Formatting
Let \(\bm{v}^{(i)}\) be the tangent vector of the class-invariant transformation in data \(\bm{x}\). If the gradient of the output is orthogonal to this tangent, it becomes insensitive to changes in direction. The normalization term is the sum of squares of the directional derivatives in the tangent direction.
\[
\Omega(f) = \sum_{i}\Big(\big(\nabla_{\bm{x}} f(\bm{x})\big)^\top \bm{v}^{(i)}\Big)^2
\tag{10}\]
Minimizing Food 10 \(\nabla_{\bm{x}} f \perp \bm{v}^{(i)}\), that is, the rate of change of output in the tangential direction disappears.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
10.3 Relationship with data augmentation









Dataset Augmentation
Tangent Propagation




Method
Explicitly generate and learn modified inputs
Implicitly penalize modification effects


Variation Size
Large perturbations possible
Very small (local) perturbations only


Cost
Data growth
Jacobian calculation



Essentially, both pursue the same goal (deformation invariance), but TP directly regulates infinitesimal deformations with first-order derivative information.






WarningTP’s Two Weaknesses




Modeling only local deformation — Food 10 is a first-order approximation, so it cannot handle large deformations (dataset augmentation is superior in this respect).
Poor compatibility with ReLU — When you need to make the gradient small, ReLU kills it to zero. Since TP assumes “shrunken” gradients, it works better with smooth activation than ReLU, which cuts off to zero.









NoteWireless communication analogy



This is equivalent to invariance design to known impairment. Making the receiver insensitive to “known deformation directions,” such as small carrier phase rotation or fine Doppler shift, is isomorphic to regulating the output sensitivity to that deformation direction to zero, as in Food 10.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
11.3 Key Message

All normalization can be understood within the big picture of Food 2 — Loss + Inductive Bias —.
The three forms, Hard, Soft, and Bayesian-prior, are equivalent to each other through KKT and MAP (Food 3).
Seemingly different techniques converge to the same effect: input noise, early stopping, and tangent prop all induce function flatness (Jacobian suppression) in some sense, and bagging and dropout are grouped into variance reduction ensemble.
Wireless communication intuition — diversity coupling (=bagging), robust beamforming (=adversarial), semi-blind estimation (=semi-supervised), and stationarity assumption (=parameter sharing) — runs throughout this normalization.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
section: 12.1 A. Bagging Variance Reduction (Food 9 numerical validation)
text:
12.1 A. Bagging Variance Reduction (Food 9 numerical validation)


Code
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def ensemble_var(k, v=1.0, rho=0.0, trials=200_000):
    """k개 모델, 오차분산 v, 상관계수 rho일 때 평균오차의 분산을 추정."""
    c = rho * v
    # 공분산행렬 Sigma: 대각 v, 비대각 c
    Sigma = np.full((k, k), c) + np.eye(k) * (v - c)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)
    eps = rng.standard_normal((trials, k)) @ L.T   # 상관된 오차 샘플
    ebar = eps.mean(axis=1)
    return ebar.var()

for k in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]:
    emp = ensemble_var(k, rho=0.0)
    theory = 1.0 / k            # c=0이면 v/k
    print(f"k={k:2d} | empirical={emp:.4f} | theory(v/k)={theory:.4f}")


It can be observed that the mean error variance decreases to \(1/k\) when is uncorrelated (\(\rho=0\)). Increasing \(\rho\) converges to \(\frac1k v+\frac{k-1}{k}c\) of Food 9.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
section: 12.2 B. Dropout Forward Propagation and Weight Scaling
text:
12.2 B. Dropout Forward Propagation and Weight Scaling


Code
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def dropout_forward(h, p, training=True, inverted=True):
    """Bernoulli dropout. p = drop 확률."""
    if not training:
        return h if inverted else h * (1 - p)     # 표준 추론
    mask = (rng.random(h.shape) > p).astype(h.dtype)
    out = h * mask
    if inverted:
        out /= (1 - p)        # inverted dropout: 추론 무수정
    return out

h = np.ones(10_000)           # 모든 활성=1
p = 0.5
train_out = dropout_forward(h, p, training=True, inverted=True)
print(f"훈련 시 평균 활성(inverted) ≈ {train_out.mean():.3f}  (목표 1.0)")
print(f"실제 drop된 비율 ≈ {(train_out==0).mean():.3f}  (목표 {p})")


Inverted dropout preserves expected activity during training, so it does not require manipulation of inference.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
12.3 C. Early Stopping ↔︎ \(\ell_2\) Equivalence (Food 7)


Code
import numpy as np

# 이차 손실 L(theta) = 0.5 (theta-theta*)^T H (theta-theta*), H=diag(lams)
lams = np.array([5.0, 1.0, 0.1, 0.01])   # 곡률(고유값)
theta_star = np.ones_like(lams)
eps = 0.05                                # 학습률

def gd_solution(tau):
    # 성분별 closed-form: theta_tau = (1-(1-eps*lam)^tau) theta*
    return (1 - (1 - eps * lams) ** tau) * theta_star

def l2_solution(alpha):
    # theta = lam/(lam+alpha) theta*
    return lams / (lams + alpha) * theta_star

tau = 40
alpha_equiv = 1.0 / (tau * eps)          # 식 (early-l2)
print(f"tau={tau}, eps={eps}  ->  등가 alpha ≈ {alpha_equiv:.3f}\n")
print("성분 | early-stopping |  L2(alpha_equiv)")
for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(gd_solution(tau), l2_solution(alpha_equiv))):
    print(f"  {i}  |    {a:.4f}     |     {b:.4f}")


The direction of high curvature converges quickly to \(\theta^*\) (both close to 1), while the direction of low curvature is suppressed and stays at small values — early stopping and \(\ell_2\) normalization produce the same contraction.

title: Regularization for Deep Learning
text:
12.4 D. FGSM Hostile Perturbation (Food 5)


Code
import numpy as np

def fgsm(grad_x, eps):
    """입력 그래디언트로부터 FGSM 섭동을 만든다."""
    return eps * np.sign(grad_x)

x = np.array([0.2, -0.5, 0.9, -0.1])
grad = np.array([1.3, -0.4, 0.8, -2.1])   # dJ/dx (가정)
x_adv = x + fgsm(grad, eps=0.1)
print("원본 x      :", x)
print("적대적 x_adv:", np.round(x_adv, 3))
print("섭동 노름(∞):", np.abs(x_adv - x).max(), "= eps")


\(\ell_\infty\) under constraint, the perturbation that increases the loss the most is in the sign direction of the gradient, and its magnitude is exactly uniform \(\epsilon\).

title: Transformers
text:
Since being proposed in Attention is All You Need by Vaswani et al. in 2017, the Transformer has become the standard backbone in almost every area of deep learning, ranging from NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning . This document breaks down the Transformer into three core ideas — token, attention, and positional encoding — and organizes the information by answering the structural question of “why this structure is superior to RNN/CNN.”






TipWireless Communication Intuition One-Line Summary



Attention is adaptive beamforming, Positional Encoding is pilot symbols, and Multi-head is MIMO multi-beam. This correspondence is explained in detail throughout the text.

title: Transformers
text:
2.1 From neuron to token
The basic unit of existing neural networks was the neuron, which has a scalar value. The Transformer elevates the unit by one level and treats vectors as the unit.

\text{Neuron: } x \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad \text{Token: } \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}

A token is an “encapsulated bundle of information.” A single token contains all multidimensional attributes, such as meaning, location, and context.






NoteRelationship with GNN



a node feature or node attribute in Graph Neural Networks is a token in the Transformer world. They are essentially the same data structure.

title: Transformers
text:
2.2 How to tokenize input







Input Type
Tokenization Method




Image
Cropped into 16×16 patches and projected each patch as a vector (ViT)

Audio

project each chunk onto a fixed-dimensional vector **.

title: Transformers
section: 2.3 Linear combination of tokens and .z notation

title: Transformers
text:
3.1 Limitations of CNN: Locality Bias
CNNs are built on the locality assumption. k \times k kernels always look only at adjacent pixels:
y_{ij} = \sum_{p=-k}^{k}\sum_{q=-k}^{k} w_{pq} \cdot x_{i+p,\, j+q}
This causes inherent difficulties in two tasks:

Global Counting: “How many birds are in the image?” — The entire patch must be integrated
Long-distance relationship: “Are the bird in the bottom left and the bird in the top right the same species?” — Two far apart area must be directly compared

To establish long-distance relationships, you must stack layers deeply to expand the receptive field, but information becomes diluted in this process.






TipWireless Communication Intuition



The locality of CNN is equivalent to local cooperation where only nearby antennas cooperate. On the other hand, attention is cooperative MIMO where the entire cell shares CSI — any two nodes directly exchange information without distance constraints.

title: Transformers
section: 3.2 Weight vs. Attention: Static vs. Dynamic
text:
3.2 Weight vs. Attention: Static vs. Dynamic
The structural core of Transformer excellence can be summarized in a single line:






ImportantCore



General weights are fixed after training, but attention weights are generated in real-time based on the input.


When compared using the formula:

\text{일반 Weight: } y = \sum_i \underbrace{w_i}_{\text{고정}} \cdot x_i
\qquad
\text{Attention: } y = \sum_i \underbrace{\alpha_i(\mathbf{x})}_{\text{입력의 함수}} \cdot v_i

w_i is a point in the parameter space \Theta, but \alpha_i is the output of the function produced by the parameters . This one-step meta-fication gives rise to all the superiority of the Transformer.

3.2.1 Three capabilities created by dynamic weights

3.2.1.1 Context-dependent representation
Even the same token must have different expressions depending on the context.
"배가 고프다"  → 배 = 복부
"배가 떠난다"  → 배 = 선박
"배를 먹었다"  → 배 = 과일
With a fixed weight, “pear” always produces the same output. Since Attention changes \alpha_j depending on surrounding tokens (“hungry”, “leaves”, “ate”), the representation itself changes. This is the essence of contextual embedding.


3.2.1.2 Adaptive receptive field
operates flexibly as follows depending on the data :



Situation
Attention Behavior




Simple declarative
Focus on adjacent tokens (effectively local)


long-range demonstrative pronoun
long-range jump as antecedent


Counting task
Reference all tokens evenly



Same model, same parameters, but behavior changes depending on the data.


3.2.1.3 Learned routing
The separation of Q, K, and V makes “who asks what to whom” learnable:

\underbrace{Q}_{\text{무엇을 찾나?}} \cdot
\underbrace{K^\top}_{\text{무엇을 갖고 있나?}}
\;\to\; \underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{누구한테 얼마나?}}
\;\to\; \underbrace{\alpha V}_{\text{수집 결과}}







TipWireless Communication Intuition




Fixed weight = Fixed beamforming: Beam direction is predetermined
Attention = Adaptive Beamforming: Readjusts the beam direction at every moment based on the channel state (input).

Just as the beamforming weights \mathbf{w}^*(\mathbf{h}) are a function of the channel \mathbf{h}, the attention score \alpha_i(\mathbf{x}) is a function of the input \mathbf{x}.

title: Transformers
text:
3.3 Self-Attention: View as Matrix Operation
For the input token matrix \mathbf{T}_\text{in} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} (N tokens, each dimension d):

\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{T}_\text{in}\mathbf{W}_q^\top, \quad
\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{T}_\text{in}\mathbf{W}_k^\top, \quad
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{T}_\text{in}\mathbf{W}_v^\top

Split each token into query/key/value vectors using three trainable projection matrices \mathbf{W}_q, \mathbf{W}_k, \mathbf{W}_v .
The attention matrix and output are:

\mathbf{A} = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{m}}\right), \qquad
\mathbf{T}_\text{out} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}

where m = d_k (dimension of the key vector).






NoteWhy divide into \sqrt{d_k}



If the variance of \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top increases in proportion to d_k, the softmax shifts toward extreme values and the gradient disappears. Dividing by \sqrt{d_k} to keep the variance near 1 is the key to learning stability.



3.3.1 Meaning Interpretation
Self-attention is “an operation that refines its own representation by considering neighboring tokens”. It can be viewed as a process where a patch looks at its surrounding patches and re-determines “which part of the dog I am.”
Let’s look at a VQA (Visual Question Answering) example:







Query
Where Attention Focuses




“How many animals?”
All patches containing animals (uniformly distributed)


“What color is the impala?”
Focus only on the Impala patch



Even with the same image, the attention distribution changes dynamically depending on the query. This is why attention is called “query-based dynamic pooling.”

title: Transformers
text:
3.4 Masked Attention
A variant that blocks a specific token from seeing other tokens:

\text{MaskedAttn}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{V}) =
\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top + \mathbf{M}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\mathbf{V}

Mask \mathbf{M} inserts -\infty at the location to be blocked — after softmax it becomes 0 and is completely blocked.
Most common use: causal mask in decoders. Since looking at future tokens in autoregressive generation is cheating, all positions j > i are masked.
M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & j \leq i \\ -\infty & j > i \end{cases}

title: Transformers
text:
3.5 Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA)
With a single (Q, K, V) projection, it is easy to learn only one relationship pattern. Therefore, multiple heads are operated in parallel:
\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\mathbf{W}^O
Each head has its own (\mathbf{W}_q^{(i)}, \mathbf{W}_k^{(i)}, \mathbf{W}_v^{(i)}) and calculates attention in a different subspace.






TipWireless Communication Intuition: MIMO Beamforming



The h heads are h independent beams. Each beam is beamformed in a different direction (subspace) to simultaneously capture various channel states. The reason why multi-head attention is more expressive than general attention is exactly the same as the reason why multi-beams have higher angular diversity than single beams .


It is also interesting in terms of interpretability — analyzing the learned heads reveals specialization where some heads establish grammatical relationships, others semantic relationships, and still others positional relationships .

title: Transformers
text:
4.1 The trap called Permutation Equivariance
Pure self-attention is permutation equivariant:
F_\theta(\text{permute}(\mathbf{T}_\text{in})) = \text{permute}(F_\theta(\mathbf{T}_\text{in}))
In other words, shuffling the token order simply shuffles the output in the same way, without any loss of information. Put another way, attention alone ignores order information.
This means that the result of shuffling the image patch and the original are encoded with the same expression , which is a fatal problem in languages where “I love you” and “I love you” have the same expression.

title: Transformers
section: 4.2 Solution: Directly inject location information into the input
text:
4.2 Solution: Directly inject location information into the input
Add a unique vector for each position pos:
\text{PE}_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_\text{model}}}\right), \quad
\text{PE}_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_\text{model}}}\right)
Final input: \mathbf{x}_\text{input} = \mathbf{x}_\text{embed} + \text{PE}.

4.2.1 Advantages of Sinusoidal PE

Extrapolability: Provides reasonable positional representations even for long sequences never seen during training
Relative Position Encoding: \text{PE}_{pos+k} as a linear transformation of \text{PE}_{pos} Representable → Model easily learns relative distance
Scale Variety: Vibrating at different frequencies per dimension → From short distances to long distances Capturing various patterns







TipWireless Communication Intuition: Pilot Symbol



is essentially the same as the receiver in OFDM inserting pre-agreed pilot symbols into a specific subcarrier to estimate the channel .

Pilot = A pre-known pattern that differs for each location
PE = Deterministic sin/cos pattern that varies by location

Just as the receiver estimates the channel with a pilot, the Transformer estimates “where this token came from” with a PE.

title: Transformers
text:
5.1 Data Flow
Inputs
  └→ Input Embedding + Positional Encoding
       └→ [Encoder Block × N]
            ├ Multi-Head Self-Attention → Add & Norm
            └ Feed Forward          → Add & Norm
            ⇒ Encoder Output (다른 모든 디코더 블록의 K, V 공급원)

Outputs (shifted right)
  └→ Output Embedding + Positional Encoding
       └→ [Decoder Block × N]
            ├ Masked MH Self-Attention   → Add & Norm
            ├ Cross-Attention (Q←dec, K,V←enc) → Add & Norm
            └ Feed Forward               → Add & Norm
            ⇒ Linear → Softmax → Output Probabilities

title: Transformers
text:
5.2 Meaning of Nx: Deep stacking
\mathbf{h}^{(l)} = \text{TransformerBlock}(\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}), \quad l = 1, \ldots, N
The original paper was N=6, but modern LLMs have increased to N=96 (GPT-3) or higher. As the layers deepen, the representation becomes increasingly abstract:



Layer
Representation being learned




Sub- (1~2)
Lexical, Grammatical Patterns


Infix (3~5)
Syntactic dependency, cross-reference


Upper (6~N)
Semantics, Inference, Task-Specific Patterns

title: Transformers
section: 5.3 Add & Norm: Residual Linking and Normalization
text:
5.3 Add & Norm: Residual Linking and Normalization
Each sublayer is wrapped in the following form:
\mathbf{x}' = \text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x} + \text{SubLayer}(\mathbf{x}))

Residual connection (\mathbf{x} +): acting as a gradient highway Enables the learning of deep networks (ResNet principle). Also guarantees that original information is not lost.
Layer Normalization: Ensures training stability by normalizing at the token level. Unlike batch norm, it does not rely on inter-sample statistics, so it is suitable for variable-length sequences and RNN-like processing.

\text{LayerNorm}(\mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\gamma} \odot \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mu}{\sigma + \epsilon} + \boldsymbol{\beta}

title: Transformers
text:
5.4 Feed Forward Network (FFN)
2-layer MLP applied independently to each token:
\text{FFN}(\mathbf{x}) = \max(0, \mathbf{x}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2
Dimensional change: d_\text{model} \to d_{ff} \to d_\text{model} (usually d_{ff} = 4 d_\text{model}).






NoteDivision of roles between Attention and FFN




Attention: Information exchange between tokens — whose information to retrieve and how much
FFN: Non-linear transformation inside the token — how to process the imported information

The essence of a Transformer block is that these two are stacked alternately.

title: Transformers
text:
5.5 Cross-Attention: Legs of Encoder ↔︎ Decoder
The decoder’s second attention takes the query from the decoder, and the key/value from the encoder:
\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{H}_\text{dec}\mathbf{W}_q, \quad
\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{H}_\text{enc}\mathbf{W}_k, \quad
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{H}_\text{enc}\mathbf{W}_v
This single line determines “where in the input sequence the decoder will refer when generating output tokens.” In translation, the mechanism automatically learns a natural soft alignment, such as attending to the English word “love” when producing the corresponding target word.

title: Transformers
text:
5.6 Meaning of “Outputs (shifted right)”
Teacher forcing method learning:
Target:  <BOS>  나는  밥을  먹었다  <EOS>
입력:    <BOS>  나는  밥을  먹었다       (마지막 제외)
출력:    나는   밥을  먹었다  <EOS>      (첫 토큰 제외)
During training, the decoder predicts the next token by taking previous correct answer tokens as input. During inference, since there are no correct answers, it feeds back the previous predicted token (autoregressive).

title: Transformers
text:
7.1 Definition of Language Model
Modeling the probability distribution of the next word given the previous words:
P(w_t \mid w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{t-1})
Approximately fixed window assumption:
P(w_t \mid w_{t-n}, \ldots, w_{t-1})
As the scale increases, Large Language Model (LLM) — GPT, Claude, HyperCLOVA X, etc.

title: Transformers
text:
7.2 GPT: Decoder-only Transformer
GPT(Generative Pretrained Transformer) is a structure that uses only the decoder part of the original paper.

Remove Encoder, Remove Cross-attention
Use only causal masked self-attention
Pre-training with next token prediction

\mathcal{L} = -\sum_t \log P(w_t \mid w_{<t}; \theta)
The key finding of the GPT series is that training a massive corpus with this simple learning objective leads to emergent zero-shot/few-shot generalization ability.






NoteminGPT



Andrej Karpathy’s minGPT is an educational implementation of GPT in about 300 lines. It is useful for seeing how the concepts in the text map to code.

title: Transformers
text:
8.1 Computational complexity
The time/space complexity of self-attention for sequence length n is:
O(n^2 \cdot d)
This is because it calculates the similarity of all token pairs. If the length is n=10{,}000, 100 million pairs are required.

title: Transformers
text:
8.2 Absence of external Windows information
Information outside the window (context length) is completely invisible. While RNNs can theoretically handle infinite lengths (though in practice they cannot due to vanishing), Transformers have hard constraints.

title: Transformers
text:
8.3 Direction of follow-up research








Classification
Representative Technique
Key Idea




Sparse Attention
Longformer, BigBird
Calculate only some token pairs


Linear Attention
Performer, Linformer
O(n) with kernel tricks


Long-context
FlashAttention
Practical acceleration with memory IO optimization


RNN-Transformer Hybrid
Mamba (SSM)
State-space model O(n) + Infinite Context

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
NoteOne-sentence summary



The finite interval MDP is a difficult problem that requires optimizing \(T\) functions (decision rules) simultaneously, but since the terminal condition \(v_T = r_T\) is known, the optimal value and optimal policy can be accurately obtained by solving the Bellman equations one time step at a time from the back (backward induction).


The core flow is as follows.

Problem Formula: \(\max_\pi \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1} r_t(s_t,a_t) + r_T(s_T)\big]\)
Policy Evaluation: Define the value function \(v^\pi_t\) and decompose it into “Immediate Reward + Next State Value” → Backward Calculation
Optimization: Proof that the optimal value function \(v^*_t\) is a solution to the Bellman equation (Optimality Principle)
Policy Construction: Bellman Proving induction that the deterministic Markov policy constructed from the argmax on the right-hand side is optimal
Algorithm: Calculate \(v^*_t\) and \(\pi^*_t\) simultaneously in a single loop using DP (backward induction).
Extensions and Limitations: Continuous Control → \(\sup\)/Integral, Absence of argmax, Curse of Dimensionality → Connected to Approximation (Deep RL)

Philosophical Significance of the Bellman Equation: Optimal decision-making in the present is an action that balances the two by considering not only immediate gains but also long-term benefits to maximize their sum.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
2.1 Sequential Decision Making and Uncertainty

Instead of performing an action once and finishing, decisions are made sequentially.
Since there is uncertainty in the system, instead of a method that predetermines the sequence of actions (open-loop), it is optimized in the form of a policy (state → action rule) so that the correct action can be taken even if an unexpected state is reached.
Immediate rewards measure only the gains of the current state or action and cannot measure long-term gains. Therefore, supervised learning cannot be applied directly, and it becomes a separate problem known as reinforcement learning.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
2.2 Component








Element
Notation
Meaning




Status
\(s_t \in S\)
System status (location, speed, inventory, etc.)


Behavior
\(a_t \in A\)
Adjustable input (acceleration, order quantity, etc.)


Reward
\(r_t(s,a)\)
Immediate gain. Future gain not measured


Transition Probability
\(p(s'\mid s,a) := \Pr(s_{t+1}=s'\mid s_t=s,a_t=a)\)
Stochastic Dynamics. \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)=1\)




Reward design is important. In complex problems, reward tuning is as difficult as policy learning (reward engineering). Although LLMs can assist with reward design, manual tuning may still be necessary to precisely match desired system specifications.
In finite intervals, transition probabilities and rewards may depend on time (non-stationary). Therefore, a subscript \(t\) is attached, as in \(r_t\).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
2.3 Decision Rules vs. Policy

Decision Rule \(\pi_t: S\to A\) — A mapping that sends a state to an action at a single point in time (snapshot)
Policy \(\pi = (\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_{T-1})\) — A collection of decision rules from all points in time
Type: deterministic / stochastic(randomized), Markov / history-dependent
Stationary Policy: \(t\) has the same policy for all \(\pi_t\)







ImportantWhy distinguish decision rules and policies in finite intervals



This is because, in finite intervals, using different decision rules at each time step is actually optimal. On the other hand, in an infinite interval discounting MDP, using the same decision rule every time is optimal (stationary policy), so the two are not strictly distinguished and are simply referred to as “policies.”



2.3.1 Why is the same decision rule sufficient for infinite intervals?
This is because there is no clock. In an infinite interval, the remaining time is always infinite, so the problem in state \(s\) at time \(t\) and the problem in state \(s\) at time 0 are identical. The same problem yields the same answer.
\[
v^*_t(s) = \sup_\pi \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau=t}^\infty \gamma^{\tau-t} r(s_\tau,a_\tau)\,\Big|\, s_t=s\Big] = v^*_0(s) =: v^*(s)
\]
(when \(p, r, \gamma\) is time-invariant.) Therefore, both sides of the Bellman equation become the same function (fixed-point problem), and
\[
v^*(s) = \max_a\Big[r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s')\Big],\qquad \pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a[\cdots]
\]
Since \(t\) does not appear in argmax, the same \(\pi^*\) can be used at every time step. For the proof of optimality, since there is no terminal condition, uniqueness of fixed points of the contraction mapping is used instead of induction: \(T^{\pi^*}v^* = Tv^* = v^*\) and since the unique fixed point of \(T^{\pi^*}\) is \(v^{\pi^*}\), \(v^{\pi^*}=v^*\).
Example where policy changes at different times over a finite interval (Investment vs. Consumption)

State 1: Consume → Reward 1, Maintain State 1 / Invest → Reward 0, Move to State 2
State 2: Reward 5 per step (Absorption State), \(r_T\equiv 0\)




\(t\)
\(v_t(1)\)
\(v_t(2)\)
Optimal action for state 1




\(T\)
0
0
–


\(T-1\)
\(\max\{1+0,\,0+0\}=1\)
5
Consumption


\(T-2\)
\(\max\{1+1,\,0+5\}=5\)
10
Investment


\(T-3\)
\(\max\{1+5,\,0+10\}=10\)
15
Investment



Just before the deadline, consumption is optimal because there is no time to recover an investment. The remaining time \(T-t\) creates a time dependency on the decision rule. (This time dependency does not disappear even if a discount of \(r_t=\gamma^t r\) is applied. Since \(\gamma^t\) is multiplied commonly to all action candidates at time point \(t\), this factor itself does not change argmax, and the cause of the change in the decision rule is still the remaining time. Of course, since the value of \(\gamma\) changes the relative weight of future rewards, a different policy than in a problem without a discount may be optimal.)






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. Why is the behavioral sequence optimized in the form of a policy rather than being predetermined in a system with uncertainty?
A. Since the next state is determined probabilistically, the state → action rule must be optimized to produce an action appropriate to that state even if an unexpected state is reached.
Q2. Why cannot this be solved like supervised learning by looking only at immediate rewards?
A. This is because immediate rewards only measure the gains of the current state or behavior and fail to measure long-term gains.
Q3. Why are decision rules and policies distinguished in finite intervals?
A. This is because using different decision rules at each time point is actually optimal for finite intervals (the remaining time is different).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
3.1 Difference from infinite interval

Time does not flow infinitely and stops at \(T\).
Reward and transition probabilities can depend on time.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 3.2 Why is terminal compensation \(r_T(s_T)\) instead of \(r_T(s_T,a_T)\)?
text:
3.2 Why is terminal compensation \(r_T(s_T)\) instead of \(r_T(s_T,a_T)\)?
The action to be taken at time \(T\) is not of interest. If \(s_0\) is taken, \(a_0\) becomes \(s_1\), and by repeating this, if \(s_{T-1}\) is taken, \(a_{T-1}\) reaches \(s_T\). If an action is taken at \(T\), \(s_{T+1}\) becomes \(s_T\), but interest is limited to exactly \(s_T\). Therefore, the last term does not consider the effect of the action. This is the first characteristic of a finite horizon.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
3.3 Number of entries: \(T\) vs \(T+1\)
The terms of the objective function are \(T+1\): stage reward \(T\) (\(t=0,\dots,T-1\), action present) + terminal reward 1 (\(t=T\), action absent).
You can remember it as a fence post structure.

State \(s_0, s_1, \dots, s_T\) → Point → \(T+1\) Items
Action \(a_0, \dots, a_{T-1}\) → Interval between states (transition) → \(T\) items
Policy \(\pi=(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1})\) → \(T\) decision rules
e.g.: If \(T=3\), then \(r_0(s_0,a_0)+r_1(s_1,a_1)+r_2(s_2,a_2)+r_3(s_3)\)

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 3.4 Why is it difficult to solve (Difficult to solve — Why?)
text:
3.4 Why is it difficult to solve (Difficult to solve — Why?)
The optimization target is not a number, but \(T\) functions, and the number of candidates explodes combinatorially.
When \(|S|=n\), \(|A|=m\), even if only deterministic Markov policies are counted
\[
|\Pi_{\text{det-Markov}}| = (m^n)^T = m^{nT}
\]









Policy Enumeration \(m^{nT}\)
Number of \(Q\) values of DP \(T\cdot n\cdot m\)




\(n=m=2,\ T=3\)
64
12


\(n=10,\ m=5,\ T=10\)
\(\approx 8\times10^{69}\)
500



Also, \(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1}\) is coupled. Changing \(\pi_0\) alters the distribution of \(s_1\), which changes the importance of \(\pi_1\) in each state. Therefore, they cannot be optimized separately for each term.
DP breaks this combination from the back: Since \(v^*_{t+1}\) serves as summary information indicating that “the rest has already been handled best,” at time step \(t\), only one action needs to be chosen. This is possible because (i) the reward is the sum of terms per time step, and (ii) due to Markov properties. (The actual computational complexity of DP, including the sum of the next state, is \(\mathcal{O}(Tn^2m)\).)






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. How is this different from the infinite interval problem?
A. Time stops at \(T\), and reward/transition probabilities can depend on time.
Q2. Why is the last term \(r_T(s_T)\) instead of \(r_T(s_T,a_T)\)?
A. The action at time point \(T\) only affects \(s_{T+1}\), because interest extends exactly up to \(s_T\).
Q3. Why is this problem difficult to solve?
A. This is because the optimization targets are \(T\) functions \((\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1})\), and since they are coupled to each other through state distributions, they cannot be optimized separately.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
4.1 State·Behavior·Reward

\(S = \{0,1,\dots,M\}\) (\(M\): Storage capacity)
\(A_s = \{0,1,\dots,M-s\}\) — The set of actions depends on the state. If ordered further, there is no place to store it. Thanks to this constraint, \(s+a\le M\) is guaranteed.
\(r_t(s,a) = \underbrace{F(s+a)}_{\text{수익}} - \underbrace{O(a)}_{\text{주문비}} - \underbrace{h(s+a)}_{\text{보관비}}\) — Rewards can be set in various ways and are not the core of this example.







TipReference



It is natural for actual profit to be proportional to the sales volume \(\min\{s+a, D\}\), and thus \(D\) comes into the reward. At this point, if \(\mathbb{E}_D[\text{수익}]\) is calculated in advance and inserted into \(F\), the MDP form is maintained where \(r_t\) is a function unique to \((s,a)\).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
4.3 General Principle
When encountering a stochastic dynamics system \(s_{t+1}=f(s_t,a_t,w_t)\), transition probabilities can be mechanically constructed.
\[
p(s'\mid s,a) = \sum_{w:\ f(s,a,w)=s'} p_w(w)
\]
The inventory problem applies to the cases \(f=\max\{s+a-D,0\}\) and \(w=D\), and these three cases are the result of expanding this sum. This perspective leads to the subsequent extension of continuous control.






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. Why is the transition probability 0 when \(s+a<s'\le M\)?
A. This is an impossible event because the next stock cannot be greater than the current stock \(s+a\) after the order.
Q2. Why is the sum \(\sum_{j\ge s+a}p_j\) taken only when \(s'=0\)?
A. This is because \(\max\{\cdot,0\}\) is a many-to-one event that sends all cases where demand \(D\ge s+a\) is one \(s'=0\). \(D=s+a\) also includes an equality sign because the inventory becomes exactly 0.
Q3. Why does the behavior set depend on the state as \(A_s=\{0,\dots,M-s\}\)?
A. This is because if you order more than that, you will exceed the storage capacity \(M\) and there will be no place to store it.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
5.1 Difference from infinite interval

The starting point is important. In an infinite interval, the value function had no time dependency because “the horizon is infinite, so it does not matter when it starts.” In a finite interval, even in the same state, the value differs depending on the remaining time, so \(v^\pi_t\) is a different function at each time point.
There is a terminal condition.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
5.2 Q) \(v^\pi_T(s)\) is?
\[
v^\pi_T(s) = r_T(s)
\]
Since the start is \(T\), \(\sum_{\tau=T}^{T-1}\) is an empty sum (0), and the only remaining thing is \(r_T(s_T)\) because the condition is \(s_T=s\).






ImportantTwo characteristics of a finite interval value function




The value function is time-dependent. (2) It has terminal conditions and its value is equal to the terminal compensation function.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 5.3 Relationship between definition (sum form) and recursion
text:
5.3 Relationship between definition (sum form) and recursion
The definition is in the form of a sum, and the recursion is an expression derived by breaking down the definition one step at a time. This structure is equivalent to an infinite interval.









Definition (Sum form)
Recursion




Infinite interval
\(v^\pi(s)=\mathbb{E}^\pi[\sum_{\tau=t}^\infty\gamma^{\tau-t}r\mid s_t=s]\)
\(v^\pi = R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v^\pi\) (Fixed point problem)


Finite interval
\(v^\pi_t(s)=\mathbb{E}^\pi[\sum_{\tau=t}^{T-1}r_\tau + r_T\mid s_t=s]\)
\(v^\pi_t = \cdots v^\pi_{t+1}\) (backward calculation)



In the finite interval, the left side \(v^\pi_t\) and the right side \(v^\pi_{t+1}\) are different functions, so there is no self-referencing. Starting from \(v^\pi_T=r_T\), the process is completed by calculating each step once. In the infinite interval, \(v^\pi\) is present on both sides, so the linear equation \((I-\gamma P^\pi)v^\pi=R^\pi\) must be solved or converged iteratively.






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. What is the meaning of \(v^\pi_t(s)\) in words without a definition?
A. Expected value of future cumulative reward (return) when starting from state \(t\) at time \(s\) and following policy \(\pi\).
Q2. What is \(v^\pi_T(s)\)? What is the reason?
A. \(r_T(s)\). The sum \(\sum_{\tau=T}^{T-1}\) is empty, the remainder is \(r_T(s_T)\), and the condition is set to \(s_T=s\).
Q3. What are the two characteristics of a finite interval value function compared to an infinite interval value function?
A. (1) Depends on the starting time. (2) Has a terminal condition, and its value is equal to the terminal compensation function.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
6.1 Optimal Policy
\[
v^{\pi^*}_0(s) \ge v^\pi_0(s)\qquad \forall s,\ \forall\pi
\]
It is a policy that is of greater than or equal value to any other policy, regardless of the starting state. It can be considered the solution to the previous optimization problem.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
6.2 ε-optimal policy
An optimal policy does not always exist (it always exists for finite \(S\) and \(A\)). When it does not exist, using an ε-optimal policy poses no practical problem.
\[
v^{\pi^*_\epsilon}_0(s) + \epsilon > v^\pi_0(s)\qquad\forall s,\ \forall\pi
\]

Meaning: If you add ε, it beats all policies ⇔ Within ε of the optimal value. It is a policy that arbitrarily approaches the optimal performance.
ε must hold for all \(s\).

Example without optimal policy: \(T=1\), \(A=[0,1)\), \(r(a)=a\). No matter which \(a\) is chosen, there is no maximum value because there is a larger \(a'<1\). \(\sup=1\) is unattainable. If we set it to \(a_\epsilon = 1-\epsilon/2\), it becomes \(a_\epsilon+\epsilon = 1+\epsilon/2 > a\) (\(\forall a\)), so it is ε-optimal.
Situations where the optimal policy disappears: the action space is not closed, rewards and transitions are discontinuous at boundaries, and the argmax selection problem is measurable in a continuous space.

6.2.1 sup and max

\(\max\): The largest element of the set (may not exist)
\(\sup\) (supremum, least upper bound): ① an upper bound of every element, and ② for any \(\epsilon>0\), there exists an element greater than \(M-\epsilon\). If finite, it always exists.
Example: In \([0,1)\), \(\max\) does not exist but \(\sup=1\). If \(\max\) exists, then \(\sup=\max\).
② is the basis for the existence of the ε-optimal policy. The question of the existence of the optimal policy ultimately boils down to “\(\sup\) is achieved”.
Pair: \(\inf\)(infimum) is a generalization of \(\min\). It appears in cost minimization problems.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
6.3 Optimum value function






NoteDefinition (Optimal Value Function)



\[
v^*_t(s) := \max_{\pi\in\Pi} v^\pi_t(s) = \max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau=t}^{T-1} r_\tau(s_\tau,a_\tau) + r_T(s_T)\ \Big|\ s_t=s\Big]
\]








WarningNotation caution



The consensus start must be \(\tau=t\). If written as \(\tau=0\), (i) \(v^*_T=r_T\) is broken, (ii) the past reward \(r_0,\dots,r_{t-1}\) is not determined solely by the \(s_t=s\) condition (it is an inverse conditional probability dependent on the initial distribution), and (iii) actions after time point \(t\) cannot change the past, so there is no reason to include them in the optimization target.



The maximum value of the cumulative reward expectation that maximizes the policy at each time point.
\(\max_\pi\) is effectively the maximization of the remaining time decision rule \((\pi_t,\dots,\pi_{T-1})\).
\(v^*_0\) represents the best possible performance. If the initial state is input, it is the maximum expected cumulative reward that the MDP can obtain in that state.
If an optimal policy exists, by definition \(v^{\pi^*}_0 = v^*_0\).


6.3.1 Q) \(v^*_T(s)\) is?
\[
v^*_T(s) = r_T(s)
\]
No action is taken at the last point in time \(T\). Since the policy only includes up to \(\pi_{T-1}\), the last state is fixed even if \(\max_\pi\) is attached, so this term is not affected by any policy.






ImportantOrganize



Whether for policy evaluation or the optimal value function, the terminal condition is given by the terminal compensation function.




6.3.2 Subtle point
The definition of takes \((t,s)\) for each \(\max_\pi\) separately. Therefore, it is not self-evident that “a single \(\pi^*\) is simultaneously optimal in all \((t,s)\),” and showing this is the deterministic Markov policy optimality theorem that follows.
Numerical Example (Two-State MDP, \(t=1\), \(s=1\)):







Policy
\(v_1(1)\)




Always action 1
\(2+0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot0 = 3\)


Optimal (including \(\pi_2(2)=2\))
\(2+0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot1 = 3.5 = v^*_1(1)\)



The difference of 0.5 is the effect of choosing action 2 in future state 2 (\(v_2(2): 0\to1\)) reflected as a probability of 0.5. \(v^*_t\) is the value when the choice of the entire remaining time is optimal, not just the current action.






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. What is \(v^*_T(s)\)? What is the reason?
A. \(r_T(s)\). Since the policy includes only up to \(\pi_{T-1}\) and there is no action at time \(T\), this term is not affected by any policy even if \(\max_\pi\) is attached.
Q2. What does \(v^*_0\) represent?
A. The maximum expected cumulative reward that an MDP can obtain when starting from the initial state given at time 0, i.e., the best performance.
Q3. How would you define an ε-optimal policy in words?
A. If ε is added to the value of that policy, it is greater than any other policy in all states. That is, it is a policy that arbitrarily approaches optimal performance.
Q4. What is a simple example where an optimal policy does not exist?
A. \(A=[0,1)\), \(r(a)=a\), \(T=1\). \(\sup=1\) but there is no \(a\) to achieve.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 7.1 Idea: Immediate reward + Expected value of the next state
text:
7.1 Idea: Immediate reward + Expected value of the next state
\[
v^\pi_t(s) = \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\underbrace{r_t(s_t,a_t)}_{\text{immediate reward}} + \underbrace{v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1})}_{\text{value of next state}}\ \big|\ s_t=s\big]
\]
The timing is important. The current reward is that of time point \(t\), and for the next state value to be accurately decomposed, the value function of time point \(t+1\) must be used. The condition applies at time point \(t\).
\[
v^\pi_t(s) =
\begin{cases}
r_t(s,\pi_t(s)) + \displaystyle\sum_{s'} p(s'\mid s,\pi_t(s))\,v^\pi_{t+1}(s') & \text{deterministic}\\[2ex]
\displaystyle\sum_a \pi_t(a\mid s)\Big(r_t(s,a) + \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi_{t+1}(s')\Big) & \text{stochastic}
\end{cases}
\]

deterministic: There is no randomness in the behavior, so it is determined as \(a=\pi_t(s)\). The expected value falls only on \(s_{t+1}\), and the distribution is \(p(\cdot\mid s,\pi_t(s))\).
stochastic: Since the behavior is also given by a distribution, we must take the expected value by multiplying by the behavior distribution one more time in addition to the randomness of the next state. It is important not to forget this part.


7.1.1 The reason why there is no action sum in the deterministic equation
The action term has not disappeared; rather, the sum has collapsed into a single term. Since the deterministic policy is the Dirac delta \(\pi_t(a\mid s)=\mathbf{1}\{a=\pi_t(s)\}\), substituting it into the stochastic equation leaves only the \(a=\pi_t(s)\) term. What has disappeared is the average of actions \(\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\), and the action is substituted as \(\pi_t(s)\) in the place of \(a\).
Derivation: Conditional decomposition into \(a_t\) using the Total Probability Law \[
\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid s_t=s] = \sum_a \underbrace{\Pr(a_t=a\mid s_t=s)}_{\pi_t(a\mid s)}\ \mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid s_t=s, a_t=a]
\]
Numerical example (\(t=1\), \(s=1\), \(v_2=(2,1)\)): \(Q(1,1)=3.5\), \(Q(1,2)=2.7\)



Policy
Value




Deterministic \(\pi_1(1)=1\)
\(3.5\)


Dirac delta notation
\(1\cdot3.5 + 0\cdot2.7 = 3.5\)


Stochastic \((0.6, 0.4)\)
\(0.6\cdot3.5+0.4\cdot2.7 = 3.18\)



The value of the probabilistic policy is the weighted average (convex combination) of the \(Q\) values.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
7.2 Proof of recursion
Prove the above recursion for the stochastic Markov policy \(\pi=(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{T-1})\). The deterministic policy is a special case where \(\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\) is the Dirac delta.






NoteClaim



\[
v^\pi_t(s)=\sum_{a\in A}\pi_t(a\mid s)\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi_{t+1}(s')\Big],\qquad v^\pi_T(s)=r_T(s)
\]


Proof. If we set \(G_{t+1}:=\sum_{\tau=t+1}^{T-1}r_\tau(s_\tau,a_\tau)+r_T(s_T)\), by the linearity of the definition and expectation
\[
v^\pi_t(s)=\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t(s_t,a_t)\mid s_t=s\big]+\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s\big].
\]

First term. Given \(s_t=s\), the distribution of \(a_t\) is \(\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\), therefore \[
\mathbb{E}^\pi[r_t(s_t,a_t)\mid s_t=s]=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\,r_t(s,a).
\]
Second term, tower rule. If you apply a condition one more time to \((s_t,a_t,s_{t+1})\) \[
\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s]=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}]\ \Big|\ s_t=s\Big].
\]
Markov property. Since transition probabilities depend only on the current state and action and the policy is also Markov, given \(s_{t+1}\), the distribution of the subsequent trajectory is independent of \((s_t,a_t)\). Therefore, the inner expectation is the value from time \(t+1\), starting from \(s_{t+1}\). \[
\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}]=v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1}).
\]
Outer Expectation Expansion. Since the probability of \((a_t,s_{t+1})=(a,s')\) when \(s_t=s\) is \(\pi_t(a\mid s)\,p(s'\mid s,a)\), \[
\mathbb{E}^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s]=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi_{t+1}(s').
\]
Adding 1 and 4 and grouping them into \(\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\) results in the claim expression. The terminal condition \(v^\pi_T=r_T\) was shown in Section 5. \(\blacksquare\)







WarningEasy to miss




Step 3 is the key to this proof. The policy must be Markov for the inner expectation to be a function of only \(s_{t+1}\). If it is a history-dependent policy, the traversed path must also be included as an argument.
If it is a probabilistic policy at step 4, the action distribution \(\pi_t(a\mid s)\) is multiplied to both terms. It is common to make the mistake of multiplying it only to the reward and omitting it in the next state term.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
7.3 Algorithm: backward calculation

How do you calculate \(v^\pi_t\)? → Reverse time. This is because we know the value of the last point in time, \(T\).

초기화:  v_T^π(s) := r_T(s)   ∀s
for t = T−1 : −1 : 0
    v_t^π(s) := Σ_a π_t(a|s) ( r_t(s,a) + Σ_{s'} p(s'|s,a) v_{t+1}^π(s') )   ∀s

T−1 : −1 : 0 = “Starting from \(T-1\), decreasing by \(-1\) to \(0\) (inclusive)”. If it is \(T=3\), it becomes \(t=2,1,0\), exactly \(T\) times.
In Python, it is range(T-1, -1, -1) (\(-1\) because the end value is not included). If you write it as range(T-1, 0, -1), \(t=0\) is omitted.
Reason for reversing: \(v_t\) calculation requires \(v_{t+1}\), and the only known value is the terminal \(v_T\).







WarningPrecautions



To move from one point in time to the previous point in time, calculations must be completed for all states. The point in time \(T-1\) must be calculated in all states to ensure the necessary information for point \(T-2\) is available. The computational burden increases as the number of states increases.








TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. When splitting a value function into two parts, at which point in time should the value be used for each part?
A. The immediate reward is \(t\) at time point \(r_t\), and the next state value is the value function \(v^\pi_{t+1}\) at time point \(t+1\). The condition falls on time point \(t\).
Q2. What is the difference in evaluation formulas between deterministic and stochastic policies?
A. If it is stochastic, multiply by the action distribution \(\pi_t(a\mid s)\) and average once more over the action. If it is deterministic, the sum collapses into a single term \(a=\pi_t(s)\).
Q3. Why is \(v^\pi_t\) calculated in reverse chronological order?
This is because \(v^\pi_{t+1}\) is needed for the \(v^\pi_t\) calculation, and the only place where the value is known is the terminal \(v^\pi_T=r_T\).
Q4. What precautions should be taken when moving to a new point?
A. Calculations for all states must be completed to ensure the information required for the previous point in time calculation is complete. A large number of states places a heavy burden on the system.
Q5. Where is the Markov property used in proofs of recursion?
A. Step to change the inner expectation \(\mathbb{E}[G_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t,s_{t+1}]\) generated by the tower rule to \(v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
8.1 Bellman equation
\[
v_t(s) = \max_{a\in A}\Big(r_t(s,a) + \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v_{t+1}(s')\Big)\quad\forall s,\qquad v_T(s)=r_T(s)
\]

Reward at time \(t\), the next state uses the value at time \(t+1\).
The characteristic of a finite interval is that it has a terminal condition attached.

Uses of the Bellman Equation (An equation studied for over 70 years):

By finding the solution for , the optimal value function is obtained.
Verify which policy is optimal.
efficiently calculates the optimal value function and the optimal policy.
Analyzes the structural properties of the optimal policy and value functions.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
8.2 Principle of Optimality






NoteTheorem (Bellman equation)



The optimal value function \(v^*_t\) is a solution to the Bellman equation. \[
v^*_t(s) = \max_{a_t\in A}\mathbb{E}\big[\underbrace{r_t(s_t,a_t)}_{\text{immediate}} + \underbrace{v^*_{t+1}(s_{t+1})}_{\text{optimal value of next state}}\ \big|\ s_t=s\big]
= \max_{a\in A}\Big(r_t(s,a) + \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big),\quad v^*_T=r_T
\]








WarningDiscount rate γ is not used



\(\gamma\) is not attached to the finite interval Bellman equation. This is because the discount rate can be included within the compensation definition since time-dependent compensation is being used. \[
r_t(s,a) := \gamma^t r(s,a)
\] If you want to use discounting over a finite interval, you can do it like this.


Key Meaning: The original problem was optimization for policies (\(T\) functions), but it has now changed to optimization for a single current action — “what action to take at time \(t\), state \(s\)” —.

8.2.1 Why is \(\pi(a\mid s)\) not in the formula?
In policy evaluation, \(\pi\) is given, so the average (\(\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)\)) is calculated using that probability. In optimization, \(\pi\) is the target to find, so \(\max_a\) is selected instead of the average. Originally, maximization takes place on the action distribution \(q\), but
\[
\max_{q\in\Delta(A)}\sum_a q(a)\,Q^*_t(s,a) = \max_{a\in A} Q^*_t(s,a)
\]
This is because maximizing a linear function over simplex for \(q\) results in a solution at the vertex (Dirac delta). Additionally, since the optimal choice of the future policy is absorbed within \(v^*_{t+1}\), the future policy does not appear in the equation either.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
8.3 Proof of the Optimality Principle
Symbol: \(Q^*_t(s,a) := r_t(s,a) + \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\) — “Expected value when doing \(a\) now and doing the best thereafter”. The proof goal is \(v^*_t(s)=\max_a Q^*_t(s,a)\).
Intuition: If the action at time \(t\) is fixed, the value is split into (now reward) + (later value), and the subsequent policy can be chosen independently of the current action. Therefore, it is advantageous to do the best possible thing after the first action, and thus the value of the first action becomes \(Q^*_t(s,a)\).

8.3.1 (≤) direction
For any \(\pi\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^\pi_t(s) &= \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[r_t(s_t,a_t) + \sum_{\tau=t+1}^{T-1} r_\tau(s_\tau,a_\tau) + r_T(s_T)\ \Big|\ s_t=s\Big]\\
&\overset{(1)}{=} \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[r_t(s_t,a_t) + \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau=t+1}^{T-1}r_\tau + r_T\ \Big|\ s_{t+1}\Big]\ \Big|\ s_t=s\Big]\\
&\overset{(2)}{=} \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t(s_t,a_t) + v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s\big]\\
&\overset{(3)}{\le} \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r_t(s_t,a_t) + v^*_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\mid s_t=s\big]\\
&\overset{(4)}{=} \sum_a \pi_t(a\mid s)\,Q^*_t(s,a)\ \overset{(5)}{\le}\ \max_a Q^*_t(s,a)
\end{aligned}
\]

(1) tower rule: Decomposition into two-step expectations passing through \(s_{t+1}\).
(2) Inside is “value from point \(t+1\) starting from \(s_{t+1}\)” \(= v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\). Up to here is the equals sign.
(3) \(v^\pi_{t+1}\le v^*_{t+1}\) (The following may not be optimal).

and (3) are parts where two steps are combined into one line and are easy to write. Originally, an equal sign appears as \(v^\pi_{t+1}\), and \(v^*_{t+1}\ge v^\pi_{t+1}\) is written there.

(5) Weighted average ≤ maximum value.
Since \(\pi\) is arbitrary, taking \(\max_\pi\) on the left side gives \(v^*_t(s)\le\max_a Q^*_t(s,a)\).







WarningNotation caution



The value inside the sum of the first line of the decomposition is \(r_\tau(s_\tau,a_\tau)\) (not \(r_t\)). \(r_t(s_t,a_t)\) outside the sum is the reward at the current time point, so \(t\) is correct, while the value inside the sum is the reward at the moving time point, so it must be \(\tau\). This is not apparent in time-invariant rewards because the values are the same, but the result differs in time-dependent rewards such as \(r_t=\gamma^t r\).




8.3.2 (≥) direction
For any \(\pi\), it is \(v^*_t\ge v^\pi_t\), and if we expand \(v^\pi_t\) in the same way (tower rule) (since \(\pi\) can be randomized, we also multiply by the action probability)
\[
v^*_t(s) \ge \sum_a \pi_t(a\mid s)\Big(r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^\pi_{t+1}(s')\Big)
\]

The inequality holds for any \(\pi\), where \((\pi_{t+1},\dots,\pi_{T-1})\) on the right-hand side is involved starting from \(t+1\). Even if that part is replaced with the optimal one (\(v^\pi_{t+1}\to v^*_{t+1}\)), the inequality holds. This step is possible because the optimal policy exists, and if it does not exist, it would be much more difficult to prove using the ε-optimal policy and the ε-argument.
Now, all that remains is the action distribution at time \(t\). Since this holds for any distribution, we take all Dirac deltas (distribution with mass concentrated on the first action, distribution with mass concentrated on the second action, …). Then

\[
v^*_t(s) \ge \max_a\Big(r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big)
\]
Since both directions hold, the equality sign.
Constructive Interpretation: For any \(a\), if we create \(\pi^a\) such that “at time \(t\), \(a\), and thereafter the optimal policy”, then \(v^{\pi^a}_t(s)=Q^*_t(s,a)\le v^*_t(s)\). Since this holds for all \(a\), \(v^*_t(s)\ge\max_a Q^*_t(s,a)\).

Q1. What does the Optimality Principle say in one sentence?
A. The optimal value function \(v^*_t\) is a solution to the Bellman equation with the terminal condition \(v^*_T=r_T\).
Q2. Why is \(\gamma\) not in the finite interval Bellman equations?
This is because the discount can be included in the reward definition as ZZZPH0012373ZZZ A. Since the reward can depend on time, the discount can be included in the reward definition as \(r_t(s,a):=\gamma^t r(s,a)\).
Q3. What changed from what to what using the Bellman equation?
A. From optimization for policies (\(T\) functions), changed to optimization for one action at time \(t\) · state \(s\).
Q4. Which two steps are combined into one line in the (≤) direction?
A. An equality step where the inside becomes \(v^\pi_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\) using the tower rule, and an inequality step using \(v^\pi_{t+1}\le v^*_{t+1}\).
Q5. Where is the existence of an optimal policy used in the (≥) direction?
A. The step of replacing \(v^\pi_{t+1}\) on the right side of the inequality with \(v^*_{t+1}\). Afterwards, it must be possible to select the optimal decision rule. If it does not exist, the ε-argument is required.
Q6. Why is the Dirac delta used at the end of the (≥) direction?
Since the inequality A. holds for any action distribution at time point \(t\), if we apply a distribution where mass is distributed to each action, it holds for all \(a\), and therefore also holds for \(\max_a\).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
9.1 Fundamental Question

Under what conditions is it optimal to use deterministic Markov decision rules at each time point?

Answer: Finite MDP(\(S\), \(A\) finite) — more precisely, when the maximizer(argmax) on the right-hand side of the Bellman equation exists. Finiteness is a sufficient condition to guarantee the existence of argmax.

Why Determinism Is Sufficient: The value of the probabilistic decision rule \(q\) is \(\sum_a q(a)Q^*_t(s,a)\le\max_a Q^*_t(s,a)\). Randomization offers no benefit as it is merely a convex combination of \(Q\) values. Equality applies only when \(q\) places mass only on the argmax set. (e.g., \(t=1\), shuffling action 2 from state 1 with probability \(q\) results in \(3.5-0.8q\), a strictly loss.)
Why Markov is Enough: Once you reach \(s_{t+1}\), future rewards depend solely on your current state and future actions. How you got there does not affect \(v^*_{t+1}(s_{t+1})\) (the past is sunk).

Cases where conditions are broken: absence of a maximizer (continuous action space), when the objective function is not a sum of expectations (risk-sensitive objective, constrained MDP), when the state is not fully observable (POMDP), when there is an adversary (mixed strategies in games).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 9.2 Basic assumption: Why is it a finite MDP?
text:
9.2 Basic assumption: Why is it a finite MDP?
This is to show a mathematically clean result. If it is not a finite set, there is no guarantee that argmax exists, and then we have to deal with the ε-optimal policy (arbitrary precision approximation), which leads to focusing on technical details rather than the idea.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
9.3 Cleanup






NoteTheorem (Optimality of Deterministic Markov Policies)



\[
\pi^*_t(s)\in\arg\max_{a\in A}\Big(r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big)\qquad\forall s\in S
\] The deterministic Markov policy \(\pi^*\) defined by is the optimal policy, and for all \(t\) it is \(v^{\pi^*}_t = v^*_t\).
Conclusion: In finite MDPs, the optimal policy can be found by considering only deterministic Markov policies.



deterministic: Maps one state to one action. Markov: Uses only current state information.
“Optimal” means that no matter when it starts or what state it starts in, \(\pi^*\) always delivers maximum performance.
\(\in\) Symbol: Used for set membership because there can be multiple (ties) maximization actions.
While deterministic policies are sufficient, there are cases where randomized policies are advantageous from a learning perspective (discussed in reinforcement learning).


9.3.1 What this theorem means

There is a way to make it. Even if you do not optimize \(T\) functions at once, an optimal policy is assembled by selecting argmax for each cell from the back.
Optimal for all \((t,s)\). The latter part of the optimal policy \((\pi^*_t,\dots,\pi^*_{T-1})\) is also optimal for the remaining problem (the remainder of the optimal path is also optimal).
A policy is a reaction rule. Even if things do not go according to plan due to uncertainty, applying \(\pi^*_t\) again from the destination state restores it to optimality.

Why one step argmax is the overall optimal: This is because argmax contains not only \(r_t\) but also \(v^*_{t+1}\). Since \(v^*_{t+1}\) represents the “value when the subsequent steps are optimized,” the current choice is the best under the assumption that “the subsequent steps are optimized.” And since \(\pi^*\) is defined in the same way at all subsequent points in time, the assumption becomes reality. (e.g., \(t=T-2\) in the investment-consumption problem; looking only at the current reward in state 1, it is consumption, but since \(Q^*(1,\text{소비})=2 < Q^*(1,\text{투자})=5\), \(\pi^*\) is an investment.)
What is not said: that the optimal policy is unique (multiple if tied), that the action is the same at every time step, that argmax needs to be done at only one time step (it must be argmax at all times steps), and that the predetermined order of actions is optimal.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
9.4 Proof (Mathematical Induction)
① \(v^{\pi^*}_t \le v^*_t\) — Definition of the optimal value function. No policy can exceed the optimal value.
② \(v^{\pi^*}_t \ge v^*_t\) by induction. Where do we start? Since we know the terminal condition, we start from \(T\).

Base \(t=T\): For any policy, the terminal value function is equal to the terminal reward and the optimal value is also equal. \(v^{\pi^*}_T = r_T = v^*_T\) (equality).
Inductive Assumption: \(v^{\pi^*}_{t+1}\ge v^*_{t+1}\) (in all \(s'\)).

First inequality (using inductive hypothesis) \[
\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^{\pi^*}_{t+1}(s') \ \ge\ \sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^*_{t+1}(s') \tag{1}
\] Why? The transition probability is a weight greater than or equal to 0, and since \(v^{\pi^*}_{t+1}\ge v^*_{t+1}\) under the same weight.
Second inequality (using the definition of \(\pi^*\)) — Since \(\pi^*_t\) is defined as the argmax of the right-hand side of the Bellman inequality, for all \(a\in A\) \[
r_t(s,\pi^*_t(s))+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^*_{t+1}(s') \ \ge\ r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s') \tag{2}
\]
Combination: If we add \(r_t(s,\pi^*_t(s))\) to both sides of (1) and connect it to (2) (connection is possible because the middle term uses the same behavior \(\pi^*_t(s)\)), for all \(a\) \[
r_t(s,\pi^*_t(s))+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^{\pi^*}_{t+1}(s') \ \ge\ r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')
\]
Maximize for action: \(a\) is not on the left side.

Left side = Time point \(\pi^*\) \(t\) Policy Evaluation Formula = \(v^{\pi^*}_t(s)\)
\(\max_a\) on the right side = Bellman Equation = \(v^*_t(s)\) (Optimality Principle)

Therefore, \(v^{\pi^*}_t(s)\ge v^*_t(s)\). If it holds in \(t+1\), it also holds in \(t\), and since it holds at the end, induction is complete. Combined with ①, \(v^{\pi^*}_t = v^*_t\).

9.4.1 View as a single-line chain
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^{\pi^*}_t(s)&\overset{(a)}{=}r_t(s,\pi^*_t(s))+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^{\pi^*}_{t+1}(s')\\
&\overset{(b)}{\ge}r_t(s,\pi^*_t(s))+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi^*_t(s))\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\\
&\overset{(c)}{=}\max_a\Big(r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big)\overset{(d)}{=}v^*_t(s)
\end{aligned}
\]

Deterministic policy evaluation (b) Inductive assumption + non-negative weights (c) \(\pi^*\) is argmax (d) Optimality principle



9.4.2 Check Value (Two-State, \(t=1\), \(s=1\))

\(0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot1\ \ge\ 0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot1\)
\(1.5\ge1.5\)


(2), \(a=2\)
\(2+1.5\ \ge\ 1+0.7\cdot2+0.3\cdot1\)
\(3.5\ge2.7\)


Conclusion
