\(v^{\pi^*}_1(1)=3.5=v^*_1(1)\)





9.4.3 Why is the inductive hypothesis necessary?
\(t=1\) is argmax, but \(t=2\) is a policy that was incorrectly chosen (\(\pi_1(1)=1\), \(\pi_2(2)=1\)): \(v^\pi_2(2)=0<1=v^*_2(2)\), and \(v^\pi_1(1)=2+0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot0=3<3.5\). We must be greedy at every point in time. The greedy at one point in time combines with the greedy at subsequent points to become the overall optimal.


9.4.4 Points to note

Reason the conclusion is equal: Since (≤) already holds by definition, the inductive assumption can be set as equal from the beginning.
Roles of the two theorems: The Optimality Principle is a fact about the value (\(v^*\) is the Bellman solution), and this theorem is a fact about the achievability of a policy (the argmax policy achieves \(v^*\)).
The converse holds: If \((t,s)\) is \(v^\pi_t=v^*_t\) for all \(v^\pi_t=v^*_t\), then argmax must be selected from each cell. That is, selecting argmax ⇔ optimality. This is used for “policy optimality verification”.
The place where the finite set assumption is used is (c) (argmax exists). If we change to ε-argmax in continuous space, the error accumulates at each step to \(v^\pi_t\ge v^*_t-(T-t)\epsilon'\). To make the total error less than or equal to \(\epsilon\), the step \(\epsilon'=\epsilon/T\).

Q1. What is the exact meaning of “\(\pi^*\) is optimal”?
A. \(t\) and \(s\)Z at all \(v^{\pi^*}_t(s)=v^*_t(s)\). Achieves maximum performance regardless of the starting point or state.
Q2. Why is a finite MDP assumed?
This is because the existence of argmax is guaranteed, allowing the idea to be presented neatly without the technical details of the ε-optimal argument.
Q3. Where does induction begin? Why?
A. \(t=T\). This is because the terminal condition \(v^{\pi^*}_T=r_T=v^*_T\) is known.
Q4. What are the sources of the two inequalities combined in the proof?
A. (1) Inductive assumption + the fact that transition probabilities are non-negative weights. (2) Definition that \(\pi^*_t\) is the argmax of the right-hand side of the Bellman equation.
Q5. If both sides of the combined inequality are maximized with respect to the action, what do each side become?
A. Since the left side does not have \(a\), it is the policy evaluation formula \(\pi^*\)Z \(v^{\pi^*}_t(s)\), and the right side is \(v^*_t(s)\) by the Bellman equation.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 10.1 Proof: A stochastic policy on the argmax set is optimal
text:
10.1 Proof: A stochastic policy on the argmax set is optimal
Let \(A^*_t(s):=\arg\max_{a}\big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\big]\), and let \(Q^*_t(s,a)\) be the value inside the square brackets.






NoteClaim



If a stochastic Markov policy \(\bar\pi\) satisfies \(\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow a\in A^*_t(s)\) for all \(t,s\), then \(v^{\bar\pi}_t=v^*_t\) for all \(t\).


Proof. Back induction for \(t\).

Base \(t=T\): \(v^{\bar\pi}_T=r_T=v^*_T\).
Inductive Step: Assume \(v^{\bar\pi}_{t+1}=v^*_{t+1}\). By policy evaluation recursion (Section 7.2) and the inductive assumption \[
v^{\bar\pi}_t(s)=\sum_a\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)\Big[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*_{t+1}(s')\Big]=\sum_{a\in A^*_t(s)}\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)\,Q^*_t(s,a).
\] If \(a\in A^*_t(s)\), then it is \(Q^*_t(s,a)=\max_{a'}Q^*_t(s,a')\) and \(\sum_{a\in A^*_t(s)}\bar\pi_t(a\mid s)=1\), therefore \[
v^{\bar\pi}_t(s)=\max_{a'}Q^*_t(s,a')=v^*_t(s)
\] is. The last equal sign is the Optimality Principle (Section 8). \(\blacksquare\)

Conversely, if a positive probability \(q\) is given to \(a\) in \(Q^*_t(s,a)<\max_{a'}Q^*_t(s,a')\) from some \((t,s)\), the value of that cell is strictly reduced by the product of \(q\) and the difference. Example: Two-State \(t=1\), shuffling Action 2 from State 1 with probability \(q\) results in \(3.5-0.8q\).






TipRelationship with Deterministic Theorems



The deterministic theorem in this argument is the case where \(\bar\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\) has a mass of 1 for one argmax element. The probabilistic version is equal sign induction, so the proof is actually shorter. This is because we already know from the Optimality Principle that \(v^*\) is a Bellman solution.








TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. How is a stochastic optimal policy created?
A. When there are two or more sets of argmax(optimal actions), assign probabilities to only those actions such that their sum is 1.
Q2. What if argmax assigns probability to actions outside the set?
A. The value in that cell is smaller than the maximum value, so it is not optimal.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
11.1 Properties and the reason







Properties
Basis




Find the optimal value function at each time step
The update equation is literally equal to the right-hand side of the Bellman equation, and each step is accurate (no error accumulation) through induction on \(t\) starting from the basis \(v_T=r_T=v^*_T\)


Find the optimal policy
\(\pi^*\) is the argmax, and the Deterministic Markov Policy Optimality Theorem guarantees \(v^{\pi^*}=v^*\)


There can be multiple optimal policies
Since argmax is a set, an option arises in case of a tie









ImportantThe optimal value function is unique, but there is no reason for the optimal policy to be unique.



Tie selection does not change \(v^*\), so it does not affect the argmax set of other cells. Therefore, it is independent per cell and \[
\#\{\text{최적 결정론적 Markov 정책}\} = \prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\prod_{s\in S}\big|\arg\max_a Q^*_t(s,a)\big|
\] If there are no ties, it is 1 (unique). If there are ties, there are infinitely many optimal policies that are probabilistically mixed.


Tie Example: In Two-State, if only \(r(1,2)\) is changed to \(1\to2\), it results in \(t=2\), and in State 1, it is a tie with \(Q(1,1)=Q(1,2)=2\) → \(\pi_2(1)\in\{1,2\}\). Either way is optimal, and all \(q\in[0,1]\) that are \(\pi_2(1\mid1)=q\) are also optimal.
(Note: If the optimal policy is defined as \(t=0\) only as \(v^{\pi^*}_0\ge v^\pi_0\), the number of optimal policies increases because the action in the \((t,s)\) cell, which is not reached by any policy, does not matter. The product formula above counts the optimal policies in the strong sense, which are \(v^\pi_t=v^*_t\) across all cells.)






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. Why can \(v^*_t\) and \(\pi^*_t\) be calculated simultaneously in a single loop?
A. The only information needed for both is \(t+1\) at point \(v^*_{t+1}\), and this has already been calculated in the previous iteration. In a single \(\max\), the maximum value is stored as \(v^*_t\), and the maximization action is stored as \(\pi^*_t\).
Q2. Which is the only optimal value function and optimal policy?
A. The optimal value function is unique. There can be multiple optimal policies if argmax is tied.
Q3. Where does the computational burden of DP come from?
A. At every time step, the action maximization problem must be solved for all states. If the state and action space is large, it does not expand well.

State 1 is a good state with a large reward, and State 2 is a bad state.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
12.2 Calculation Instructions
\(p(2\mid s,a) = 1-p(1\mid s,a)\) so
\[
Q_t(s,a) = r(s,a) + v_{t+1}(2) + p(1\mid s,a)\cdot\underbrace{\big(v_{t+1}(1)-v_{t+1}(2)\big)}_{\Delta_{t+1}}
\]
Since \(v_{t+1}(2)\) is common and therefore excluded from the comparison, only the immediate reward difference and \(p(1\mid s,a)\) difference × \(\Delta_{t+1}\) need to be compared.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
12.3 Step-by-step solution
\(t=3\): \(v_3(1)=v_3(2)=0\) (End-end compensation 0)
\(t=2\) (\(\Delta_3=0\) → No future value, compare only immediate rewards, convert to greedy):

State 1: \(\max\{2,\ 1\}=2\) → \(\pi_2(1)=1\)
State 2: \(\max\{0,\ 1\}=1\) → \(\pi_2(2)=2\)

The first term inside \(\max\) is the “immediate reward + subsequent cumulative reward expected value” when performing action 1 and action 2. At time 3, the reward is 0, so there is nothing to be gained regardless of which state is reached, and therefore the transition probability does not affect the choice.
\(t=1\) (\(v_2=(2,1)\), \(\Delta_2=1\)):

State 1: \(\max\{2+0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot1,\ 1+0.7\cdot2+0.3\cdot1\} = \max\{3.5,\ 2.7\} = 3.5\) → \(\pi_1(1)=1\)
State 2: \(\max\{0+0.2\cdot2+0.8\cdot1,\ 1+0.6\cdot2+0.4\cdot1\} = \max\{1.2,\ 2.6\} = 2.6\) → \(\pi_1(2)=2\)

\(t=0\) (\(v_1=(3.5,2.6)\), \(\Delta_1=0.9\)):

State 1: \(\max\{2+0.5\cdot3.5+0.5\cdot2.6,\ 1+0.7\cdot3.5+0.3\cdot2.6\} = \max\{5.05,\ 4.23\} = 5.05\) → \(\pi_0(1)=1\)
State 2: \(\max\{0+0.2\cdot3.5+0.8\cdot2.6,\ 1+0.6\cdot3.5+0.4\cdot2.6\} = \max\{2.78,\ 4.14\} = 4.14\) → \(\pi_0(2)=2\)

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 12.5 Why is such a policy being introduced?
text:
12.5 Why is such a policy being introduced?

State 1 → Action 1: Switching to Action 2 reduces the reward by 1 and increases the probability of returning to State 1 by 0.2, resulting in \(0.2\Delta\). Since \(\Delta\le1\), what is gained < what is lost. (It must be \(\Delta>5\) for it to flip.)
State 2 → Action 2: Reward increases by 1 and the probability of going to State 1 increases by 0.4, so Benefit in both aspects.
In this example, the policy is the same regardless of the time point, but it is a coincidence of numbers (compared to the investment-consumption example).
There are no ties, so the optimal policy is unique.







TipIf there is terminal compensation, even the final decision looks to the future.



If \(r_T(1)=10\), \(r_T(2)=0\), then \(t=2\), in state 1 action 1 is \(2+0.5\cdot10=7\), and action 2 is \(1+0.7\cdot10=8\), so it flips to \(\pi_2(1)=2\). \(t=2\) was reduced to greedy because the terminal value was 0.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
12.6 Check with code
Manual calculation is for practice; in reality, you can solve it immediately by simply coding and inputting the problem data.

import numpy as np

# P[s, a, s'] : 전이확률, R[s, a] : 보상 (상태·행동은 0-index)
P = np.array([[[0.5, 0.5], [0.7, 0.3]],
              [[0.2, 0.8], [0.6, 0.4]]])
R = np.array([[2.0, 1.0],
              [0.0, 1.0]])
T = 3

v = np.zeros(2)                      # v_T = r_T ≡ 0
for t in range(T - 1, -1, -1):       # t = T-1, ..., 0
    Q = R + P @ v                    # Q[s, a] = r(s,a) + Σ_{s'} p(s'|s,a) v_{t+1}(s')
    v = Q.max(axis=1)                # v_t*(s)
    pi = Q.argmax(axis=1) + 1        # π_t*(s), 1-index로 표시
    print(f"t={t}: Q={Q.round(3).tolist()}  v={v.round(3).tolist()}  pi={pi.tolist()}")







TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. Why did the transition probability not affect the choice in \(t=2\)?
This is because there is nothing gained regardless of which state is reached, as A. \(v_3\equiv0\). It becomes a greedy choice that compares only immediate rewards.
Q2. \(t=1\), What are the two candidate values for state 1 and the optimal action?
A. Action 1: \(2+0.5\cdot2+0.5\cdot1=3.5\), Action 2: \(1+0.7\cdot2+0.3\cdot1=2.7\). Therefore, \(v_1(1)=3.5\), \(\pi_1(1)=1\).
Q3. \(t=1\), What are the two candidate values for state 2 and the optimal action?
A. Action 1: \(0+0.2\cdot2+0.8\cdot1=1.2\), Action 2: \(1+0.6\cdot2+0.4\cdot1=2.6\). Therefore, \(v_1(2)=2.6\), \(\pi_1(2)=2\).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
text:
13.1 System Model
\[
s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, w_t),\qquad w_t \sim p_w(\cdot)\ \text{(알려져 있음)}
\]

Example: Vehicle dynamics, electrochemical model approximation of Battery Management System (BMS)
Haves Markov properties: The next state depends only on the previous state, behavior, and uncertainty.
In inventory management, transition probabilities were explicitly derived for \(s\)=Inventory Quantity, \(a\)=Order Quantity, and \(w\)=Demand. In continuous control, we examine whether the optimal value and policy can be calculated directly without explicitly deriving transition probabilities.

The problem is identical: \(\max_\pi \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}r(s_t,a_t)+r(s_T)\big]\)

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 13.2 Q) What is the transition probability?
text:
13.2 Q) What is the transition probability?
\(p(s'\mid s,a)\) is the probability that the next state is \(s'\), and for it to be meaningful, it must be \(s'=f(s,a,w)\). By introducing an indicator function
\[
p(s'\mid s,a) = p_w(w)\,\mathbf{1}\{s'=f(s,a,w)\}
\]






NoteStrictly speaking, if written



The above expression is an abbreviated notation for “collecting the probabilities of \(w\) that make \(s'=f(s,a,w)\)”. Since \(w\) remains as a free variable on the right side, in reality, we must collect for \(w\). \[
p(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{w}p_w(w)\,\mathbf{1}\{s'=f(s,a,w)\}\quad(\text{이산 }w),\qquad
\Pr(s_{t+1}\in B\mid s,a)=\int\mathbf{1}\{f(s,a,w)\in B\}\,p_w(dw)\quad(\text{연속})
\] The three cases of inventory management are the expanded form of this sum (Section 4). The Bellman equation of the form \(p_w\) below is this integral written for \(v_{t+1}\).

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 13.3 Q) What is the Bellman equation?
text:
13.3 Q) What is the Bellman equation?
Since is continuous, the expected value is an integral rather than a sum, and we write \(\sup\) instead of \(\max\).
\[
v_t(s) = \sup_{a\in A}\Big[r(s,a) + \int_{s'\in S} v_{t+1}(s')\,p(ds'\mid s,a)\Big]
\]

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 13.4 Q) If you write it again as \(p_w\)?
text:
13.4 Q) If you write it again as \(p_w\)?
Since it survives only when \(s'=f(s,a,w)\), substitute \(f(s,a,w)\) for \(s'\)Z and integrate over \(w\).
\[
v_t(s) = \sup_{a\in A}\Big[r(s,a) + \int_w v_{t+1}\big(f(s,a,w)\big)\,p_w(dw)\Big]
\]
The Bellman equation can be defined without directly writing transition probabilities.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 13.5 Q) What is the optimal policy?
text:
13.5 Q) What is the optimal policy?
\[
\pi^*_t(s)\in\arg\max_{a\in A}\Big[r(s,a)+\int_w v_{t+1}(f(s,a,w))\,p_w(dw)\Big]
\]






WarningThe existence of an optimal policy is not guaranteed



In continuous problems, argmax may not exist. In such cases, an ε-optimal policy is used. In fact, when solving continuous problems with reinforcement learning, errors larger than ε occur. Most, and virtually all, reinforcement learning algorithms fail to find an optimal policy, and the very purpose of reinforcement learning is to find a sufficiently good approximation policy.

section: 13.7 New problems arising in continuous control
text:
13.7 New problems arising in continuous control

Maximum value may not exist.
Optimization is difficult because the action space is wide. Although there are algorithms for cases such as when the objective function is concave, it is generally difficult to find a maximizing action.
If the state space is continuous, initialization can be done in the form of a function, but updates must hold for all real numbers.

title: Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes
section: 13.8 Dioxide and the Curse of Dimensions
text:
13.8 Dioxide and the Curse of Dimensions
If the state space is \([0,1]\), discretize. If discretized to \(N=3\) points, the optimal value and policy are calculated only at those three points, and discretization error is introduced (perfect information is not transmitted at every step).
Generalized: 1-dimensional \(3\) point → 2-dimensional \(3^2=9\) point → \(n\)-dimensional \(3^n\) point. Computational load and memory increase exponentially.






ImportantCurse of Dimensionality



DP breaks down difficult problems into many easy problems, but the number of these easy problems can become too large. If continuous control is simply discretized, this exponential increase is immediately felt. The location of the difficulty has shifted from an “explosion of policy numbers (\(m^{nT}\))” to an “explosion of state numbers.”


Solution Approach: Instead of discretization, define a function architecture of the value function (or policy) and learn and optimize its weights. Approximating the value function and policy with a neural network is deep reinforcement learning (deep RL).






TipBlock Check (Expand to check answer)





Q1. How can the Bellman equation be written in continuous control without explicitly deriving the transition probability?
A. Substitute \(f(s,a,w)\) into the next state and integrate over \(w\): \(v_t(s)=\sup_a[r(s,a)+\int v_{t+1}(f(s,a,w))p_w(dw)]\).
Q2. Why use \(\sup\) instead of \(\max\)?
A. This is because in a continuous action space, there may not be an action that achieves the maximum value. In this case, the existence of an optimal policy is not guaranteed.
Q3. What are three new problems that arise when transitioning to continuous control?
A. (1) A maximum value may not exist. (2) The action space is wide, making maximization itself difficult. (3) The update must hold for all real number states.
Q4. What are the limitations of discretization and directions for their resolution?
A. If there are \(N\) points per dimension, \(N^n\) points are required, causing computational load and memory to increase exponentially (curse of dimensionality). The solution is to define the functional approximation structure of the value function and policy and learn the weights; using a neural network results in deep reinforcement learning.
Q5. Is what reinforcement learning algorithms generally find the optimal policy?
A. No. In continuous problems, an error greater than ε occurs, and the purpose itself is a sufficiently good approximation policy.

text:
2.1 Discrete State·Behavior
After initializing \(v_T^*(s) := r_T(s)\), perform backward induction on \(t = T-1, \dots, 0\).
\[
v_t^*(s) := \max_{a\in A}\Big(r_t(s,a) + \sum_{s'} p(s'|s,a)\,v_{t+1}^*(s')\Big),\qquad
\pi_t^*(s) \in \arg\max_{a\in A}\Big(\cdots\Big)
\]

Find the optimal value function and the optimal policy at each time point exactly.
There can be multiple optimal policies. This is because there can be multiple argmaxes.
Hidden Complexity: For every state, there is a behavior maximization for every operation. If the state and behavior space is large, it does not scale up.

2.2 Extension to continuous control
About \(s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t, w_t)\), \(w_t \sim p_w\)
\[
v_t^*(s) := \sup_{a\in A}\Big[r(s,a) + \int_w v_{t+1}^*(f(s,a,w))\,p_w(dw)\Big].
\]

Use sup instead of max. An optimal policy may not exist (find the optimal policy only when a maximizer exists).

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
3.1 Definition






NoteDefinition (Discounted MDP)



tuple \(\langle S, A, p, r, \gamma\rangle\)

\(S\): State set, \(A\): Behavior set
\(p(s'|s,a) := \Pr(s_{t+1}=s' \mid s_t=s, a_t=a)\): Probability that the next state is \(s'\) when the current state is \(s\) and the current action is \(a\).
\(r(s,a)\): Scalar reward function measuring the gain of the current state/action
\(\gamma \in (0,1)\): Discount rate determining how much future rewards will be discounted

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
3.2 Assumption

Stationary reward and transition probability: \(r(s,a)\) and \(p(s'|s,a)\) do not change over time.

In the finite horizon, the reward \(r_t\) could be time-dependent, and the transition probability could also be set to be time-dependent.
In the infinite horizon, the function itself does not directly depend on time.

Finite set of states and actions: \((s,a)\). Since the combinations are finite, the rewards are bounded. That is, for some constant \(M\), \(|r(s,a)| < M\), \(\forall s, a\).
Discount: \(0 \le \gamma < 1\).

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 3.3 Result: Cumulative rewards are always boundless
text:
3.3 Result: Cumulative rewards are always boundless
\[
\Big|\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)\Big|
\le \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\,|r(s_t,a_t)|
\le \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t M = \frac{M}{1-\gamma}.
\]
By combining finite states and actions with discounting, any value falls within the same upper bound. It is a neat setup where there is no need to worry about the divergence of cumulative rewards.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
4.1 Value function






NoteDefinition (Value function)



\[
v^\pi(s) := \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau=t}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau-t}\,r(s_\tau,a_\tau)\;\Big|\; s_t = s\Big]
\] Expected value of cumulative reward when using policy \(\pi\) starting from state \(s\).



Practice until this meaning comes to mind automatically. Intuitive understanding is much more important than mathematical definition.
The starting point \(t\) is irrelevant. Since we add up to infinity and shift the discount weight by the starting point, the value is the same regardless of what \(t\) is.
If the value function is calculated, the policy evaluation is completed by simply inserting the initial state into the state position.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
4.2 Stationary Policy
Generally, the policy is \(\pi := (\pi_0, \pi_1, \pi_2, \dots)\). \(\pi_t\) is the decision rule written at time \(t\), i.e., the state → action transition. In the finite horizon, different optimal decision rules actually emerged at each time step.
A policy being stationary means that the same decision rule is used at every point in time. \[
\pi_i = \pi_j \quad \forall i, j.
\]
Since there is no need to distinguish between decision rules and policies, write it simply as follows.

Deterministic stationary: \(\pi(s_t) = a_t\)
Stochastic stationary: \(\pi(a_t|s_t)\) (Probability distribution of actions by state)







TipQ) If it is a stationary policy, does it perform the same action at every point in time?



No. Although the event is fixed, the input (state) changes at every time step, so the output (action) also changes. Most reinforcement learning algorithms assume a stationary policy. The fact that considering only a stationary policy is sufficient is justified by the existence of an optimal policy].

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
5.1 Bellman expectation equation
Decompose the value function into (i) immediate reward and (ii) discounted next state value.
\[
v^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\underbrace{r(s_t,a_t)}_{\text{즉각 보상}} + \gamma\,\underbrace{v^\pi(s_{t+1})}_{\text{다음 상태의 가치}} \;\big|\; s_t = s\big]
= \sum_{a\in A}\pi(a|s)\Big(r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'\in S}p(s'|s,a)\,v^\pi(s')\Big).
\]
Since actions are involved in both rewards and transition probabilities, randomized policies take the expected value of actions as the outer sum.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
5.2 Proof (tower rule)
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^\pi(s) &= \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[r(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\sum_{\tau=t+1}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau-t-1}r(s_\tau,a_\tau)\;\Big|\; s_t=s\Big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[r(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau=t+1}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau-t-1}r(s_\tau,a_\tau)\;\Big|\; s_{t+1}\Big]\;\Big|\; s_t=s\Big] \\
&= \mathbb{E}^\pi\big[r(s_t,a_t) + \gamma\,v^\pi(s_{t+1}) \;\big|\; s_t=s\big] \\
&= \sum_{a}\pi(a|s)\Big[r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v^\pi(s')\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]

Line 1: Separate the infinite sum into the \(t\) point term and the \(t+1\) term thereafter.
Row 2: Apply conditional expectation to \(s_{t+1}\) one more time (tower rule)
Line 3: By definition, the inner part is a value function \(v^\pi(s_{t+1})\) with an initial state of \(s_{t+1}\) (thanks to stationarity)
Row 4: The distribution of \(a_t\) is a weighted sum of the distributions of \(\pi\) and \(s_{t+1}\) with transition probabilities

Why use conditional expectation twice? Instead of calculating the total probability all at once, we calculate the expected reward by assuming the next state \(s_{t+1}\) is determined first, and then take the average over the uncertainty of \(s_{t+1}\) itself. This is the intuition behind the tower rule \(\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[\mathbb E[X\mid Y]]\). Here, the fact that future rewards can be expressed as a function \(s_{t+1}\) \(v^\pi(s_{t+1})\) is due to Markov properties and a time-independent stationary policy.






TipVerification Question: Why does \(\gamma\) remain only once in the sum?



This is because it was separated into \(\gamma^{\tau-t}=\gamma\cdot\gamma^{\tau-(t+1)}\) in the future reward section. The inner sum becomes \(v^\pi\) ‘starting from the next state’, leaving only one \(\gamma\) for starting one step late.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 5.3 What is different from Finite Horizon?
text:
5.3 What is different from Finite Horizon?

There is no concept of time. Since stationary compensation and transitions are assumed, the equation is the same at every time point. The influence of time is hidden within the definition of the value function.
Therefore, the calculation method changes. In the finite horizon, since the left side is the value at time \(t\) and the right side is \(t+1\), it was possible to calculate one by one backward from the terminal condition. In the infinite horizon, since the same function \(v^\pi\) exists on both the left and right sides, it is impossible to calculate starting from the terminal point. → A method to “solve” the equation is required.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 7.1 (A) Reason why the eigenvalue is 1 or less
text:
7.1 (A) Reason why the eigenvalue is 1 or less
Intuition: Continuously multiplying transition probabilities means a continuous multiplication of probabilities. \(P^\pi v\) is the weighted average of the next state values from each state, and since the average cannot exceed the largest value, the magnitude of the vector does not increase. The eigenvalue is “how many times it becomes when multiplied,” so it is \(|\lambda|\le 1\).
Since eigenvalues can be complex numbers, the exact proposition is \(|\lambda| \le 1\).
Proof: Let \(P^\pi v = \lambda v\) and \(v \ne 0\) (\(v\in\mathbb{C}^n\)). If we take \(i^*\), which is \(|v_{i^*}| = \|v\|_\infty > 0\),
\[
|\lambda|\,|v_{i^*}| = \Big|\sum_j P^\pi_{i^*j}\,v_j\Big|
\le \sum_j P^\pi_{i^*j}\,|v_j|
\le \|v\|_\infty\sum_j P^\pi_{i^*j} = \|v\|_\infty.
\]

First inequality: Triangle inequality
Second inequality: \(|v_j| \le \|v\|_\infty\), \(P^\pi_{i^*j} \ge 0\)
Last equal sign: row sum is 1

Since the left side is \(|\lambda|\,\|v\|_\infty\), \(|\lambda| \le 1\). \(\blacksquare\)
Also, since \(P^\pi\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\), \(\lambda = 1\) is always an eigenvalue. That is, the upper bound of 1 is actually achieved.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
7.2 (B) Eigenvalue of \(I - \gamma P^\pi\)
If \((I-\gamma P^\pi)x = \mu x\) (\(x \ne 0\)), then \(\gamma P^\pi x = (1-\mu)x\), that is \[
P^\pi x = \frac{1-\mu}{\gamma}\,x.
\] Therefore, \(\lambda := \frac{1-\mu}{\gamma}\) is the eigenvalue of \(P^\pi\), which is \(\mu = 1 - \gamma\lambda\). Since the same calculation holds for the reverse direction, the eigenvalue of \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) is exactly \(\{1-\gamma\lambda : \lambda \text{는 } P^\pi\text{의 고유값}\}\). (The eigenvectors remain unchanged.)

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
7.3 (C) Reversibility
The matrix is not invertible \(\iff\) \(Ax = 0\)Z exists \(x \ne 0\) \(\iff\) \(0\) as eigenvalues.
\[
\mu = 1 - \gamma\lambda = 0 \iff \lambda = \frac{1}{\gamma}.
\]
If \(0<\gamma<1\), then \(1/\gamma > 1\), but by (A), there is no such eigenvalue. Therefore, \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) is always invertible. Writing it out in one step using the inverse triangle inequality \[
|1-\gamma\lambda| \ge 1 - \gamma|\lambda| \ge 1-\gamma > 0.
\]









Condition for the eigenvalue to be 0
Is it possible




\(\gamma<1\)
\(\lambda = 1/\gamma > 1\)
Impossible


\(\gamma=1\)
\(\lambda = 1\)
Always available (\(P^\pi\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\))



Why \(\gamma < 1\) is important: It pushes \(1/\gamma\) out of the upper bound of eigenvalues 1. Since \(\gamma = 1\) is \((I-P^\pi)\mathbf 1 = 0\), \(I - P^\pi\) must be singular.

7.3.1 Method of appearing without eigenvalues (Norm logic)
If \((I-\gamma P^\pi)x = 0\), then it is \(x = \gamma P^\pi x\) and \(\|P^\pi x\|_\infty \le \|x\|_\infty\), therefore \[
\|x\|_\infty = \gamma\|P^\pi x\|_\infty \le \gamma\|x\|_\infty \;\Longrightarrow\; (1-\gamma)\|x\|_\infty \le 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 0.
\] Since the null space is trivial, it is invertible. This calculation is the same as the \(T^\pi\) abbreviated proof that follows.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
7.4 Neumann series representation
is the matrix version of the scalar geometric series \(\frac{1}{1-x} = \sum_t x^t\) (\(|x|<1\)).
(a) Convergence. Since \((P^\pi)^t\) is also stochastic, it follows \(\|(\gamma P^\pi)^t\|_\infty = \gamma^t\) and \(\sum_t\gamma^t < \infty\), so it converges absolutely.
(b) The limit is the inverse matrix. For the partial sum \(S_n = \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(\gamma P^\pi)^t\), by telescoping \[
(I-\gamma P^\pi)\,S_n = I - (\gamma P^\pi)^n \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} I.
\] Therefore \(S = \lim S_n = (I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\).
(c) Meaning. By Markov properties, it is \(\mathbb{E}^\pi[r(s_t,a_t)\mid s_0 = i] = ((P^\pi)^t R^\pi)_i\).

\(R^\pi\): Expected rewards you are currently receiving
\(P^\pi R^\pi\): Expected reward one step ahead
\((P^\pi)^t R^\pi\): \(t\) Expected rewards behind the step
\(\gamma^t\): Discount to present value

, that is, the series is the sum of the discounted expected rewards of time \(0, 1, 2, \dots\), and is the definition of \(v^\pi\) itself. The inverse matrix formula is a rewriting of the definition in matrix form, and it can be verified that it is consistent with the value function originally intended to be calculated.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
7.5 Numerical Example
\(P = \begin{pmatrix}0.5 & 0.5\\ 0.2 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}\), \(\gamma = 0.9\).

Eigenvalues of \(P\): trace \(= 1.3\), det \(= 0.3\) → \(\lambda = 1,\ 0.3\)
Eigenvalues of \(I - 0.9P\): \(1 - 0.9 = 0.1\), \(1 - 0.27 = 0.73\) → Both are not 0
\((I-0.9P)^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.073}\begin{pmatrix}0.28 & 0.45\\ 0.18 & 0.55\end{pmatrix}\)
Verification: If \(R = \mathbf 1\), then \(v = \sum_t \gamma^t = 1/(1-\gamma) = 10\). Actually, the sum of each row is \(0.73/0.073 = 10\).

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 7.6 Why Inverse Matrices Are Not Often Used
text:
7.6 Why Inverse Matrices Are Not Often Used
The problem of interest usually has a very large number of states.

Operational amount: \(n\times n\) Solving linear systems \(O(n^3)\)
Memory: \(P^\pi\) stores \(O(n^2)\). If \(n = 10^6\), then \(10^{12}\) elements
Even if \(P^\pi\) is sparse, the inverse matrix is generally dense

→ We need a precise method rather than an approximation, but one that avoids the inverse matrix. This is the operator form and fixed-point iteration.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
9.1 Definition






NoteDefinition (γ-contraction)



The fact that the ||| operator \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is a γ-contraction with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\) is \[
\|Tv - Tv'\| \le \gamma\|v - v'\| \qquad \forall v, v' \in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]


Intuition: The distance between any two points after passing them through an operator is reduced to \(\gamma\) times less than before. This contractility plays a very important role in reinforcement learning.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
9.2 \(T^\pi\) is γ-contraction






Noteproposition



\(T^\pi\) is a γ-contraction with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) for any stationary policy \(\pi\).



9.2.1 Intuition: The error is reduced through three steps
What \(T^\pi\) does is “my reward + γ × (average of next state values)”. We only need to track the difference (error between the two estimates \(v, v'\).








Step
What happens
Effect on error




① Add reward \(R^\pi\)
Added equally to both \(v, v'\)
Canceled out, no effect


② Average as \(P^\pi\)
Probability-weighted average of the next state values
Since the average cannot exceed the maximum value, it does not increase


③ Multiply by \(\gamma\)
\(\gamma<1\)
Reduced by a factor of γ





9.2.2 Induction
Step 1. The reward disappears. \[
T^\pi v - T^\pi v' = \gamma P^\pi(v - v') =: \gamma P^\pi d.
\]
Step 2. Look only at one state \(s\). \((\gamma P^\pi d)(s) = \gamma\sum_j P^\pi_{sj}\,d(j)\) is the weighted average of \(d\).
Step 3. The average cannot exceed the maximum value. \[
\Big|\sum_j P^\pi_{sj}\,d(j)\Big| \le \sum_j P^\pi_{sj}\,|d(j)| \le \|d\|_\infty\underbrace{\sum_j P^\pi_{sj}}_{=1} = \|d\|_\infty.
\]
Step 4. Attach γ and max for \(s\). \[
\|T^\pi v - T^\pi v'\|_\infty \le \gamma\|v - v'\|_\infty. \qquad\blacksquare
\]
It is one line in matrix norms: \(\|\gamma P^\pi d\|_\infty \le \gamma\|P^\pi\|_\infty\|d\|_\infty = \gamma\|d\|_\infty\).


9.2.3 Numerical Example
\(P^\pi = \begin{pmatrix}0.5 & 0.5\\ 0.2 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}\), \(\gamma = 0.9\), \(v = (10, 0)\), \(v' = (0,0)\).

Input difference \(d = (10, 0)\), \(\|d\|_\infty = 10\)
Average \(P^\pi d = (5, 2)\)
\(\gamma P^\pi d = (4.5, 1.8)\) → Output difference \(4.5 \le 0.9\times 10 = 9\)



9.2.4 Supplement

Why sup-norm: \(\|d\|_\infty\) is the error of the state with the largest error, and the probability mean cannot increase the largest error. The norm for which \(\|P^\pi\|_\infty = 1\) holds is the \(\infty\)-norm. In the general \(P^\pi\), \(\|P^\pi\|_2\) can exceed 1, so the \(\|\cdot\|_2\) reduction is not guaranteed.
Constant γ is tight: If \(d = c\mathbf 1\), then \(P^\pi\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\), so equality holds.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
9.3 Banach Fixed Point Theorem






NoteBanach fixed point theorem



If \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is a contraction concept

\(T\) has the unique fixed point \(v^*\) (\(v^* = Tv^*\)).
Starting from an arbitrary \(v_0\) and defined as \(v_{k+1} := Tv_k\), then \(v_k \to v^*\).



(\((\mathbb{R}^n, \|\cdot\|_\infty)\) is a fully equipped street space.)
Convergence Rate: If the fixed point is \(v^*\), \[
\|v_{k+1} - v^*\|_\infty = \|Tv_k - Tv^*\|_\infty \le \gamma\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \le \gamma^k\|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty \to 0.
\] With each iteration, the distance from the fixed point decreases by a factor of γ, and converges exponentially regardless of where it starts.
Direct Proof of Uniqueness: If there are two fixed points, then \(\|v_1 - v_2\| = \|Tv_1 - Tv_2\| \le \gamma\|v_1 - v_2\|\), so \(\|v_1-v_2\| = 0\).






TipQ) Why is uniqueness important?



If there are multiple fixed points, when a fixed point is reached through iteration, it is impossible to know if it is the true \(v^\pi\) that was intended. Thanks to uniqueness, as long as convergence is achieved, it is guaranteed that the convergence point is \(v^\pi\). This is important not only theoretically but also practically.


Reasons why the fixed point can be called \(v^\pi\): (1) Since the Bellman expectation equation \(v^\pi=T^\pi v^\pi\) was derived from the definition of cumulative reward, \(v^\pi\) is actually the fixed point. (2) By Banach’s theorem, that fixed point is unique. Therefore, the fixed point found through iteration is not another candidate, but exactly \(v^\pi\)**.
Conclusion: The policy evaluation equation has a unique solution, and \(v^\pi\) can be obtained through fixed-point iteration.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
9.4 Value iteration for policy evaluation






Notealgorithm




Input: stationary policy \(\pi\)
Initialization: \(v_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n\) Random (if continuous, a random function)
Repeat until convergence: \(v_{k+1} := T^\pi v_k\)



\[
v_0 \xrightarrow{T^\pi} v_1 \xrightarrow{T^\pi} v_2 \xrightarrow{T^\pi}\cdots \to v^\pi
\]
Hidden Complexity: Although written concisely in operator form, in reality, one iteration is completed only after updating all states. If it is a Deterministic policy \[
v_{k+1}(s) = r(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,\pi(s))\,v_k(s') \qquad\forall s.
\] However, there is no action maximization. This is because the action is fixed as \(\pi(s)\). Action maximization is added when calculating the optimal value.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
10.1 Optimum value function
The goal is to solve the following problem. \[
\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\;\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)\Big]
\]






NoteDefinition (Optimal value function)



\[
v^*(s) := \max_{\pi\in\Pi} v^\pi(s) = \max_{\pi\in\Pi}\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{\tau=t}^{\infty}\gamma^{\tau-t}r(s_\tau,a_\tau)\;\Big|\; s_t = s\Big]
\] The maximum expected value of cumulative rewards obtainable from the starting state \(s\). Since it is an infinite horizon, the starting point does not matter.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
10.2 Bellman operator
Maximize the sum of the immediate reward and the expected cumulative reward from the next state, in accordance with the idea of dynamic programming.






Notedefinition (Bellman operator)



\[
Tv := \max_\pi\{R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v\},\qquad
(Tv)(s) := \max_\pi\sum_{a}\pi(a|s)\Big[r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v(s')\Big].
\] This can be rewritten as follows. \[
\boxed{\,(Tv)(s) = \max_{a\in A}\Big[r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v(s')\Big]\,}
\]


(In some notations, the Bellman operator is written as \(T^*\). They are the same operator.)

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 10.3 Q) Why is the maximum for policy the same as the maximum for action?
text:
10.3 Q) Why is the maximum for policy the same as the maximum for action?
\[
q_v(s,a) := r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v(s')
\] If we let , then \((T^\pi v)(s) = \sum_a\pi(a|s)\,q_v(s,a)\) is the weighted average of \(q_v(s,\cdot)\). What needs to be proven is \[
\max_\pi\sum_a\pi(a|s)\,q_v(s,a) = \max_a q_v(s,a).
\]
(≤) The average cannot exceed the maximum value. For any \(\pi\), since \(\pi(a|s) \ge 0\) \[
\sum_a\pi(a|s)\,q_v(s,a) \le \max_{a'}q_v(s,a')\sum_a\pi(a|s) = \max_{a'}q_v(s,a').
\] No policy can be found that gives a value greater than the maximum for the action.
(≥) A policy exists that achieves the upper bound. If we use the Dirac distribution \(\pi^\delta(a|s) = \mathbb{1}\{a = a^*(s)\}\) which concentrates the probability mass on \(a^*(s) \in\arg\max_a q_v(s,a)\), \[
\sum_a\pi^\delta(a|s)\,q_v(s,a) = q_v(s,a^*(s)) = \max_a q_v(s,a). \qquad\blacksquare
\]
The Bellman operator is typically defined and written in a form that maximizes the action \(a\), and most literature follows this convention.

10.3.1 Meaning of vector max
\(\max_\pi\{R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v\}\) is read as componentwise max.

The \(s\)-th element depends only on \(\pi(\cdot|s)\). A policy is a collection of distributions that can be determined independently for each state.
Therefore, state-specific maximizations do not interfer with each other.
\(\pi^\delta\) One achieves the maximum value simultaneously in all states.

Intuition: Randomly selecting is mixing the values of each action by probability. Since mixing cannot make the result better than the best action, randomness offers no benefit from an optimization perspective. This is the root of the idea that “deterministic optimal policies exist.”

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 10.4 Affine vs. Nonlinear: Why Inverse Matrices Work Only in Policy Evaluation
text:
10.4 Affine vs. Nonlinear: Why Inverse Matrices Work Only in Policy Evaluation

Policy Evaluation Operator: \(T^\pi v=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v\). It is affine with respect to \(v\) and is a linear operator in the strict sense only in the special case where the reward is \(R^\pi=0\). Nevertheless, it is called ‘linear’ in the sense that \(v^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi\) is a system of linear equations. Therefore, it can be solved as \((I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi\).
Optimal Bellman Operator: \(Tv=\max_a\{r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)v(s')\}\) is generally non-linear as it involves the maximum value for the action. Therefore, \(v^*\) cannot be directly obtained by moving to a single fixed matrix and taking the inverse.







TipThe single difference between ‘policy evaluation’ and ‘optimization’



If policy \(\pi\) is fixed, the values of the next states are probabilistically averaged. For optimization, a max is added to select the action itself to take that average. The two operators have the same dynamic programming structure, but the meaning of the fixed point is different.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
11.1 Proof of Abbreviation
In a method like \(T^\pi\), an additional step is added to process the max.
Auxiliary Inequality: \[
\Big|\max_a f(a) - \max_a g(a)\Big| \le \max_a|f(a) - g(a)|.
\] If we take \(\max_a\) on both sides of \(f(a) \le g(a) + |f(a)-g(a)| \le \max g + \max|f-g|\), we get \(\max f - \max g \le \max|f-g|\). If we swap the roles of \(f, g\), the opposite side also appears.
If you use this \[
|(Tv)(s) - (Tv')(s)| \le \max_a|q_v(s,a) - q_{v'}(s,a)|
= \gamma\max_a\Big|\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)(v-v')(s')\Big|
\le \gamma\|v - v'\|_\infty.
\] The last inequality is the weighted average argument. Take the maximum for \(s\) and you’re done. \(\blacksquare\)

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
11.2 Proof of Monotonicity
If \(v \le v'\), then \(p(s'|s,a) \ge 0\) in each \((s,a)\), so \[
q_v(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v(s') \le r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v'(s') = q_{v'}(s,a).
\] Taking \(\max_a\) on both sides gives \((Tv)(s) \le (Tv')(s)\). \(\blacksquare\)
For the same reason, \(T^\pi\) is also monotonous (the elements of \(P^\pi\) are \(\ge 0\)).

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 12.1 Q1) Why does it have a unique solution?
text:
12.1 Q1) Why does it have a unique solution?
Since \(T\) is a γ-contraction, by the first property of the Banach fixed point theorem, it has a unique fixed point. Therefore, \(v = Tv\) has exactly one solution.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
12.2 Q2) Why is that year \(v^*\)
Banach’s theorem states only that “there is a unique fixed point.” The key to showing that it is \(v^*\) is the following proposition.






Noteproposition




\(v \ge Tv\) if \(v \ge v^*\)
\(v \le Tv\) if \(v \le v^*\)



Fact of use:

(F1) For all \(\pi\), \(Tv \ge R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v\) (\(T\) is the maximum for \(\pi\))
(F2) Since the element of \(P^\pi\) is \(\ge 0\), \(x \le y \Rightarrow P^\pi x \le P^\pi y\) (preserving inequality direction)


12.2.1 (a) \(v \ge Tv \Rightarrow v \ge v^*\)
Fix an arbitrary \(\pi\). \(v \ge Tv \ge R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v\) as (F1). If this is substituted recursively, the direction is maintained thanks to (F2). \[
v \ge R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v \ge R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi(R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v) \ge \cdots \ge \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(\gamma P^\pi)^t R^\pi + (\gamma P^\pi)^n v.
\] Since \(\|(\gamma P^\pi)^n v\|_\infty \le \gamma^n\|v\|_\infty \to 0\), in \(n\to\infty\) \[
v \ge \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}(\gamma P^\pi)^t R^\pi = v^\pi.
\] Since this holds for all \(\pi\), maximizing both sides for \(\pi\) gives \(v \ge v^*\).


12.2.2 (b) \(v \le Tv \Rightarrow v \le v^*\)
The opposite direction appears in the same way as (a), but care must be taken regarding which policy is chosen. If an arbitrary \(\pi\) is used, combining \(v \le Tv\) and \(Tv \ge R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v\) does not determine the relationship between \(v\) and \(R^\pi + \gamma P^\pi v\). Instead, a policy that achieves \(Tv\) is used.
If we take the greedy policy \(\pi_g(s) \in\arg\max_a q_v(s,a)\) for \(v\), we get \(Tv = T^{\pi_g}v = R^{\pi_g} + \gamma P^{\pi_g}v\). Therefore, it is \(v \le R^{\pi_g} + \gamma P^{\pi_g}v\), and with iterative substitution like (a) \[
v \le \sum_{t=0}^{n-1}(\gamma P^{\pi_g})^t R^{\pi_g} + (\gamma P^{\pi_g})^n v \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} v^{\pi_g} \le v^*. \qquad\blacksquare
\]




Visible
Usage Policy




(a)
All policies are less than or equal to \(v\)
Any \(\pi\)


(b)
Some policy \(v\) more than
greedy policy \(\pi_g\)





12.2.3 Conclusion
The fixed point \(\bar v = T\bar v\) satisfies both \(\bar v \ge T\bar v\) and \(\bar v \le T\bar v\) simultaneously, so it is \(\bar v \ge v^*\) and \(\bar v \le v^*\), i.e., \(\bar v = v^*\).






ImportantCleanup



The Bellman equation has a unique solution, and that solution corresponds to the optimal value function. \[
v^* = Tv^*.
\] This is the fundamental theorem of optimal control and reinforcement learning.


Intuition

Uniqueness: \(T\) reduces the distance between two candidates, so if there are two solutions, the distance becomes 0 and they become the same.
Optimality: \(v \ge Tv\) indicates that “even with a one-step improvement, it cannot exceed \(v\),” meaning that \(v\) is the upper bound of the achievable value. \(v \le Tv\) indicates that “\(v\) is the lower bound of the actually achievable value.” The point where the two meet is \(v^*\).

text:

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 13.2 What does the number of repetitions depend on?
text:
13.2 What does the number of repetitions depend on?
depends on initialization. If \(v_0\) happens to be near \(v^*\), it converges in very few iterations, and if it is taken far away, many iterations are required (\(\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \le \gamma^k\|v_0 - v^*\|_\infty\)).
However, the shape of the optimal value function is very difficult to intuitively understand. This is one of the reasons why reinforcement learning has developed slowly. Therefore, it is usually initialized with a zero vector, an approximate estimate of the accumulated reward, or just an arbitrary vector.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
14.1 Proof
\[
T^{\pi^*}v^* = Tv^* = v^*.
\]

First equality (by construction): Since \(\pi^*\) contains an action that maximizes what is inside the brackets, applying \(T^{\pi^*}\) is equivalent to applying \(T\). \[
(T^{\pi^*}v^*)(s) = q^*(s,\pi^*(s)) = \max_a q^*(s,a) = (Tv^*)(s).
\]
Second Equals: \(v^*\) is the only fixed point of \(T\).
If we connect the beginning and the end, \(v^*\) is the fixed point of \(T^{\pi^*}\). Since \(T^{\pi^*}\) is also a contraction, it has a unique fixed point, which by definition is \(v^{\pi^*}\). Therefore \[
v^* = v^{\pi^*}.
\]
If the policy evaluation result of a policy is equal to the optimal value, then that policy is optimal. \(\blacksquare\)

(\(T^{\pi^*}\) is the policy evaluation operator \(T^\pi\), with \(\pi^*\) substituted for \(\pi\), and \(T\) is the Bellman operator that maximizes the action. Do not confuse these two.)

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 14.2 Proof Method: Constructive Proof + Fixed Point Identification
text:
14.2 Proof Method: Constructive Proof + Fixed Point Identification
“By construction”: This means that the property automatically holds because of the way it is defined. Since the property was intentionally included when constructing the object, there is no need to prove it separately. Here, “\(\pi^*\) was made into argmax” is the basis for the first equality.

Constructive Proof: To show that something “exists,” the object is directly constructed. Conversely, proof by contradiction or compactness arguments only demonstrate existence without physically holding the object. Since it is a constructive proof, one also obtains an algorithm stating “this is how it can be obtained.”
Identifying Fixed Points: Since \(v^\pi\) is the unique fixed point of \(T^\pi\), if we show that a vector is the fixed point of \(T^\pi\), then that vector is \(v^\pi\).

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
14.3 Points to note

Where finiteness is used: argmax must not be empty to form \(\pi^*\). If \(A\) is finite, the max is always achieved. This corresponds exactly to the fact in continuous control that “without a maximizer, an optimal policy may not exist.”
Simultaneously Optimal in All States: Since \(v^*(s) = \max_\pi v^\pi(s)\) is the maximum value for each state, the optimal policy may differ for each state. This proof shows that a single \(\pi^*\) is simultaneously optimal for all \(s\). This is because state-specific maximizations do not interfere with each other.
Why it is not a circular argument: To create \(\pi^*\), \(v^*\) is required, and \(v^*\) appears to depend on a policy by definition. However, \(v^*\) is first determined without a policy as a fixed point of \(T\), and \(\pi^*\) is created on top of it.
\(\pi_g\), which is the greedy policy \(v = v^*\) written in (b) of the Bellman equation, is \(\pi^*\).

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
15.1 Idea
Value iteration updates information only in the value space to calculate the optimal value before moving on to the policy space. The ultimate goal is the optimal policy, but can’t we also utilize information from the policy space?
Policy iteration is a method that optimally converges values and policies simultaneously by alternately utilizing information from the value space and the policy space.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
15.2 algorithm






NoteAlgorithm (Policy iteration)




Initialization: Random deterministic stationary policy \(\pi_0\) (Initialize policy, not value)
Repeat until convergence:

Policy Evaluation: Solve the fixed-point problem \(v^{\pi_k} = T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\) to calculate \(v^{\pi_k}\)
Policy improvement: \[
\pi_{k+1}(s) \in\arg\max_{a\in A}\Big[r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\,v^{\pi_k}(s')\Big]
\]









flowchart LR
    P0["π₀"] -->|평가| V0["v^π₀"]
    V0 -->|향상| P1["π₁"]
    P1 -->|평가| V1["v^π₁"]
    V1 -->|향상| P2["π₂"]
    P2 --> D["⋯ → π*"]






The policy enhancement phase assumes that \(v^{\pi_k}\) is the optimal value and adopts the action that maximizes the current reward plus the expected cumulative reward when \(\pi_k\) is used as the new policy.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 15.3 Comparison of computational amounts between VI and PI
text:
15.3 Comparison of computational amounts between VI and PI









Where action maximization is
Iterative structure




VI
Every iteration, all states
\(v_{k+1} = Tv_k\)


PI
Policy Improvement Phase Only
Evaluation (Inner Iteration) + Improvement




If you use fixed-point iteration for PI policy evaluation, there will be a lot of iterations inside, and you will have to do it again for every policy.
However, there is no action maximization in the iteration of policy evaluation. When comparing the same state updates, a single sweep of policy evaluation is usually lighter than VI. Conversely, PI has the cost of performing policy evaluation multiple times, so the overall superiority of the algorithms cannot be determined.
The total computational cost depends on the implementation of policy evaluation (linear system solving or iteration), the number of states and actions, and initialization; therefore, depending on the problem, it is different which approach is faster. For PI, the speed difference is significant depending on whether the initial policy is close to the optimal policy, while for VI, it depends on whether the initial value is close to the optimal value.
It is a strong theoretical result that both converge to the optimal value and optimal policy.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 16.1 First to distinguish in the proof: Current policy · New policy · Input value
text:
16.1 First to distinguish in the proof: Current policy · New policy · Input value
\[
q_k(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)v^{\pi_k}(s').
\]
\(q_k(s,a)\) is the expected value when assuming that only the first action from the current state is set to \(a\), and from the next state onwards, the existing policy \(\pi_k\) is followed.








Formula
Action used in the first step
Standard of value after the first step




\(T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\)
Existing \(\pi_k\)
Existing \(v^{\pi_k}\)


\(T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}\)
New \(\pi_{k+1}\)
Still Existing \(v^{\pi_k}\)


\(Tv^{\pi_k}\)
Maximize all \(a\)
Existing \(v^{\pi_k}\)


\(v^{\pi_{k+1}}\)
Use the new \(\pi_{k+1}\) forever
The actual value of the new policy itself



It is important to note that the first three are a single Bellman update, and the last one is a fixed point for policy evaluation.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 16.2 Step 1. Proof that ‘changing only the first step results in no loss’
text:
16.2 Step 1. Proof that ‘changing only the first step results in no loss’
(a) Policy evaluation — The value of the existing policy is the fixed point of the operator evaluating itself.
\[
\underbrace{v^{\pi_k}}_{\text{기존 정책의 실제 가치}}
=\underbrace{T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}}_{\text{기존 정책으로 한 스텝 평가}}.
\]
(b) Policy improvement — The new policy selects the action that maximizes \(q_k(s,a)\). Therefore, when the input value is \(v^{\pi_k}\), the following equation holds.
\[
\begin{aligned}
(T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k})(s)
&=q_k(s,\pi_{k+1}(s)) \\
&=\max_a q_k(s,a) \\
&=(Tv^{\pi_k})(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
(c) Definition of Bellman operator — The value of an existing action cannot exceed the maximum value among those actions.
\[
T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\le Tv^{\pi_k}.
\]
If you connect the three above in order
\[
\boxed{
v^{\pi_k}
=T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}
\le Tv^{\pi_k}
=T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}
}.
\]
Intuition: This means that rather than acting in the existing way, it cannot be a loss to take the best action based on the existing \(v^{\pi_k}\), even if only once.






WarningThe most confusing equation



\(T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}=Tv^{\pi_k}\) is true because the new policy was chosen greedily with respect to the existing value. However, \(T^{\pi_{k+1}}w=Tw\) is not true for any \(w\). In particular, \(v^{\pi_k}\) and \(v^{\pi_{k+1}}\) must not be swapped arbitrarily.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 16.3 Step 2. Extend ‘One Step Improvement’ to ‘Use New Policy Permanently’
text:
16.3 Step 2. Extend ‘One Step Improvement’ to ‘Use New Policy Permanently’
If we set it to \(u:=v^{\pi_k}\), \(F:=T^{\pi_{k+1}}\), we obtained \(u\le Fu\) from the front.

Monotonicity: Applying the same operator \(F\) to \(u\le Fu\) results in \(Fu\le F^2u\). Repeat this process.
Coordinateness: The value of continuously applying the operator \(F\) of the new fixed policy goes to the unique fixed point \(v^{\pi_{k+1}}\) of \(F\).
Limits and Inequalities: The \(\le\) relationship that holds in each state also holds in the limit.

\[
\underbrace{v^{\pi_k}}_{u}
\le \underbrace{T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}}_{Fu}
\le (T^{\pi_{k+1}})^2v^{\pi_k}
\le \cdots
\xrightarrow{\ell\to\infty}
\underbrace{v^{\pi_{k+1}}}_{\text{새 정책의 실제 가치}}.
\]
Therefore \[
\boxed{v^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}}\qquad\blacksquare
\]
Roles assigned by property in the proof: (i) Maximization shows that there is no loss in the first step, (ii) Monotonicity preserves the direction of the inequality even when the operator is applied multiple times, and (iii) Reducibility guarantees that the limit of the iteration is the value of the new policy.






Tip3 lines of proof framework



\[
\begin{aligned}
v^{\pi_k} &=T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\le Tv^{\pi_k}=T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k},\\
v^{\pi_k} &\le (T^{\pi_{k+1}})^\ell v^{\pi_k}\qquad(\text{monotonicity}),\\
v^{\pi_k} &\le \lim_{\ell\to\infty}(T^{\pi_{k+1}})^\ell v^{\pi_k}=v^{\pi_{k+1}}\quad(\text{contraction}).
\end{aligned}
\] If you can state the basis for the first equality/inequality/equality, the rest leads to monotonicity and conciseness.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
17.1 Monotone convergence theorem






NoteCleanup



A bounded and component-wise monotonically non-decreasing sequence of real vectors \(\{x_k\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) has component-wise finite limits. \[
x_0\le x_1\le\cdots,\quad \sup_k\|x_k\|_\infty<\infty
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_k\to \bar x.
\]


Why does this hold for vectors as well? If \(x_k=(x_k(1),\ldots,x_k(n))\), then it is a sequence of real numbers where each component is bounded above and monotonically non-decreasing over time. This is because the monotonic convergence theorem for real numbers can be applied to each component.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 17.2 Summary: Policy iteration reaches the optimal policy
text:
17.2 Summary: Policy iteration reaches the optimal policy






ImportantConvergence of Policy Iteration



In a discounted MDP with finite states and actions, \(0\le\gamma<1\), performing exact policy evaluation and greedy improvement causes \(v^{\pi_k}\) to converge to \(v^*\). For a finite set of deterministically stationary policies, the optimal value is reached with finite improvements. If the existing action is maintained in case of ties and stopped upon reaching the optimal state, the policy itself also stops at the optimal policy.



17.2.1 Step 1. Compensation is bounded → Values of all policies are also bounded
Since \(S,A\) is finite, for all \((s,a)\), we can choose \(M\), which is \(|r(s,a)|\le M\). By \(0\le\gamma<1\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
|v^\pi(s)|
&=\left|\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)\mid s_0=s\right]\right|\\
&\le \mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t |r(s_t,a_t)|\mid s_0=s\right]\\
&\le \sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^t M=\frac{M}{1-\gamma}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Meaning: No matter how the policy changes, the value cannot grow beyond a certain upper limit.


17.2.2 Step 2. Monotonic enhancement + Bounded → Converges to some \(\bar v\)
We have already proven \(v^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}\) above. Therefore, by the monotonic convergence theorem
\[
\boxed{v^{\pi_0}\le v^{\pi_1}\le \cdots \to\bar v}.
\]
Up to this point, we only knew of the existence of extremes, but did not verify optimality.


17.2.3 Step 3. Key Connection: Why does \(\bar v\) satisfy the Bellman optimality equation?
When policy improvement and monotonic improvement are used together, the following relationship holds.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{v^{\pi_k}}_{\text{기존 정책의 가치}}
&=T^{\pi_k}v^{\pi_k}\\
&\le \underbrace{Tv^{\pi_k}}_{\text{기존 가치에 대한 최적 한 스텝}}\\
&=T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_k}\\
&\le T^{\pi_{k+1}}v^{\pi_{k+1}}\\
&=\underbrace{v^{\pi_{k+1}}}_{\text{새 정책의 가치}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Reason for each symbol:

First equal sign: Policy evaluation, \(v^{\pi_k}\) is the fixed point of \(T^{\pi_k}\).
First \(\le\): \(T\) maximizes the action, so it is not smaller than the fixed policy.
Second equality: Policy improvement, \(\pi_{k+1}\) is selected greedily with \(v^{\pi_k}\) as input.
Second \(\le\): Forward forging improvement \(v^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}\) and forging of \(T^{\pi_{k+1}}\).
End equal sign: Evaluation equation of the new policy.

In other words, the key inequality is
\[
\boxed{v^{\pi_k}\le Tv^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}.}
\]
Why is this important? Both ends converge to \(\bar v\). The middle \(Tv^{\pi_k}\) also converges to \(\bar v\) by the Sandwich Theorem. Meanwhile, \(T\) is a contraction, so it is continuous. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{k\to\infty}Tv^{\pi_k}&=\bar v &&(\text{샌드위치 정리}),\\
\lim_{k\to\infty}Tv^{\pi_k}&=T\!\left(\lim_{k\to\infty}v^{\pi_k}\right)=T\bar v &&(\text{$T$의 연속성}).
\end{aligned}
\]
If you compare the two expressions
\[
\boxed{\bar v=T\bar v.}
\]
Since we previously showed that the Bellman optimality operator \(T\) has exactly one fixed point, and that it is \(v^*\),
\[
\boxed{\bar v=v^*.}
\]
This is the core logic that bridges the gap between ‘simply converged’ and ‘converged to the optimal value’.


17.2.4 Step 4. Create the actual optimal policy from the converged value
Let’s construct a greedy policy \(\bar\pi\) using the limit \(\bar v\).
\[
\bar\pi(s)\in\arg\max_a\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'|s,a)\bar v(s')\right].
\]
Because \(\bar\pi\) was configured like this, regarding \(\bar v\)
\[
\underbrace{T^{\bar\pi}\bar v}_{\text{greedy 행동으로 한 스텝}}
=\underbrace{T\bar v}_{\text{행동 최대화}}
=\underbrace{\bar v}_{\text{Step 3에서 구한 고정점}}.
\]
Therefore, \(\bar v\) is also the fixed point of \(T^{\bar\pi}\). However, since the only fixed point of \(T^{\bar\pi}\) is \(v^{\bar\pi}\),
\[
\boxed{v^{\bar\pi}=\bar v=v^*.}
\]
Therefore, \(\bar\pi\) is the optimal policy. \(\blacksquare\)






WarningPay attention to the order of the equation chain



If you compress this step into a single line \[
v^{\bar\pi}=T^{\bar\pi}\bar v=T^{\bar\pi}v^{\bar\pi}=Tv^{\bar\pi}
\] I am tempted to write it like . However, the first equation \(v^{\bar\pi}=T^{\bar\pi}\bar v\) does not hold simply because \(\bar\pi\)Z was defined greedily. We must show \(\bar v=v^{\bar\pi}\) before it.
Therefore, when writing strictly, in Step 3 above, first prove \(\bar v=T\bar v\), and then \[
\boxed{T^{\bar\pi}\bar v=T\bar v=\bar v=v^{\bar\pi}}
\] It is safer to understand it by changing the order to . The idea is the same, but it is arranged so that the basis for each equation is already secured in the previous step.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
section: 17.3 Why does it finish in a finite number of moves? (Using a finite policy set)
text:
17.3 Why does it finish in a finite number of moves? (Using a finite policy set)
The proof up to this point has demonstrated the convergence and optimality of the value sequence. We can go a step further regarding the policy iteration of a finite MDP.

If the number of states is \(n\) and there are at most \(m\) actions per state, then there are at most \(m^n\) deterministic stationary policies. Therefore, the number of possible \(v^\pi\) vectors is also finite.
\(v^{\pi_k}\) takes only a finite set of values while being monotonically non-decreasing. Therefore, at some point, two continuous values become equal: \(v^{\pi_{K+1}}=v^{\pi_K}\).
If both ends are the same in the sandwich relationship of Step 3 \[
v^{\pi_K}\le Tv^{\pi_K}\le v^{\pi_{K+1}}=v^{\pi_K}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad v^{\pi_K}=Tv^{\pi_K}=v^*.
\]
Therefore, \(\pi_K\) is already the optimal policy, and it reaches the optimal value with a finite number of exact improvements. Even if there is a tie in the optimal actions, maintaining the existing action and stopping at the optimal state guarantees the convergence (stopping) of the policy itself.

Caution: If implemented to continuously switch to a different optimal action instead of the existing one in case of a tie, oscillation between different optimal policies may occur even in the state \(v^{\pi_k}=v^*\). Therefore, strictly speaking, value convergence and policy sequence convergence must be distinguished, and tie-breaking/termination conditions must be specified when referring to the cessation of a policy sequence.

title: Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP (Infinite-Horizon Discounted MDP)
text:
17.4 Proof 6-Line Summary

Limited rewards and discounts: \(|v^\pi(s)|\le M/(1-\gamma)\).
Forging Enhancement: \(v^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}\).
Monotonic convergence: \(v^{\pi_k}\to\bar v\).
Enhancement definition + operator monotonality: \(v^{\pi_k}\le Tv^{\pi_k}\le v^{\pi_{k+1}}\).
sandwich + \(T\) continuity: \(\bar v=T\bar v\); with fixed point uniqueness \(\bar v=v^*\).
The greedy policy \(\bar\pi\) for \(\bar v\) satisfies \(T^{\bar\pi}\bar v=T\bar v=\bar v\), so it is \(v^{\bar\pi}=v^*\), which is the optimal policy.

text:
18.2 Value iteration (\(v_0 = (0,0)\))
\[
v_1 = (0, 1),\quad v_2 = (0.9, 1.9),\quad v_3 = (1.71, 2.71),\quad \dots \to (9, 10)
\]
Since \(\|v_k - v^*\|_\infty \le 0.9^k\times 10\), the error decreases exponentially, but in this example, PI, which performed accurate policy evaluation, reached the optimal state with 3 policy evaluations, whereas VI converges asymptotically. However, since each policy evaluation of PI requires internal calculation, it cannot be concluded from this single example that the overall execution time of PI is faster.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
The theorem in this article assumes a finite set of states \(S\), a non-empty finite set of actions \(A_s\), complete state observations, and expected cumulative reward maximization. All action sums and maximums are taken for \(a\in A_s\). Rewards are real and bounded.







Symbol
Meaning




\(s_t,a_t\)
State of time \(t\) and selected action


\(p_t(s'\mid s,a)\)
Distribution of the next state; non-negative and \(\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)=1\)


\(r_t(s,a)\)
Rewards for this period or their conditional average


\(h_t=(s_0,a_0,\ldots,s_t)\)
History to date


\(\pi_t(a\mid h_t)\)
Probability of action selection in general policy


\(\mu_0\)
Initial state distribution


\(\mathbb P^\pi,\mathbb E^\pi\)
Policy-induced path distribution and its expected value


\(P^\pi,R^\pi\)
Transition matrix and reward vector averaged by normal Markov policy


\(\|v\|_\infty=\max_s|v(s)|\)
Maximum absolute value norm; \(v\le w\) is a component inequality



The Markov nature of the model is the following condition.
\[
\mathbb P^\pi(s_{t+1}=s'\mid h_t,a_t=a)
=p_t(s'\mid s_t,a).
\]
In other words, if you know the current state and behavior, older records are not needed to predict the next state. Whether policies use the past is a separate issue.
If \(\rho_t(s,a,s')\) the reward also depends on the next state, then based on the expected total reward
\[
r_t(s,a)=\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)\rho_t(s,a,s')
\]
can be written by averaging it as |||. \(\rho_t(s,a,s')\) is the reward for this period, and \(v_{t+1}(s')\), which appears later, is the total reward from the next point in time.



Decision rules are guidelines to use at a given point in time, and a policy is a sequence of those rules. Deterministic rules specify a single action, while probabilistic rules specify the distribution of actions.



Class
Input
Output




MD
Current Status \(s_t\)
\(d_t(s_t)\in A_{s_t}\)


MR
Current Status \(s_t\)
\(\pi_t(\cdot\mid s_t)\)


HD
History \(h_t\)
\(d_t(h_t)\in A_{s_t}\)


HR
History \(h_t\)
\(\pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)\)



Deterministic choice is a probabilistic choice in which an action is assigned a probability of 1. Therefore, MD is included in MR and HD respectively, and MR and HD are included in HR. There is no general inclusion relationship between MR and HD.
A stationary Markov policy uses the same rule \(\pi(a\mid s)\) at every point in time. A stationary deterministic policy can also choose a different action if the state changes.






WarningMarkov policy and normal policy are different



\(\pi_t(a\mid s)\) uses only the current state, so it is a Markov policy, but it can vary depending on the time point. In a finite horizon, even for the same state, the optimal action can differ depending on the remaining time. Stationarity does not automatically follow.


The pre-fixed sequence of actions \((a_0,a_1,\ldots)\) is a special policy that does not react to observed states. Therefore, in settings using a common set of actions, the value of policy optimization is not smaller than the value of fixed sequence of actions optimization. Choosing only the current highest reward is also generally not optimal, because actions change the distribution of the next state.
The reason for optimizing the policy. The reward is the immediate gain of the current choice, not the correct label itself, which is the optimal action. Therefore, it cannot be directly transformed into a supervised learning problem that maximizes only the immediate reward. Once a policy is derived, the action to be taken in a given state is specified, even if a state different from the expectation occurs.
The difficulty of policy optimization lies in the fact that the actions determined for each state influence each other through future transitions. Even in finite models with a common set of actions, there are \(|A|^{|S|}\) policies that are not ZZZ deterministic. Dynamic programming (DP) solves this problem using value functions. It does not generalize to mean that “policies are functions and therefore cannot be differentiated under any circumstances.”

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
2.1 Path probability and Markovity
The probability of the finite path \((s_0,a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1},s_N)\) is the chain rule
\[
\mathbb P^\pi(s_0,a_0,\ldots,s_N)
=\mu_0(s_0)\prod_{t=0}^{N-1}
\pi_t(a_t\mid h_t)p_t(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t).
\]
This formula is the probability of a finite path. We apply this formula to each finite-length path event even over an infinite horizon. We do not inadvertently equate the infinite product with the probability of an individual infinite path.
Proposition. If a Markov policy is used, the sequence of states is a Markov process.
Proof. If you sum the actions
\[
\mathbb P^\pi(s_{t+1}=s'\mid h_t)
=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s_t)p_t(s'\mid s_t,a).
\]
The right-hand side depends only on \(t,s_t\), not the entire past. Since the equation remains the same even if only the past of the state is given as a condition, the state column is Markov. If both the model and the policy are time-invariant, the transition matrix is also time-independent. \(\square\)
Intuition: If the environment moves based only on the current state and behavior, and policies also act based only on the current state, the past cannot provide additional information for the future.






WarningWhen the denominator of the conditional probability is 0



When calculating conditional probability as a ratio of probabilities, the probability of the conditional event must be positive. If the entire conditional distribution is set to zero because the denominator is zero, it does not become a probability distribution. To define the value of an unvisited state, define it as a new problem starting from that state. It is not necessary to visit that state in the original initial distribution.


Since history-dependent policies can alter the distribution of behavior based on the past, the Markovity of the state sequence cannot be concluded solely from the Markovity of the model. However, this does not mean that all history policies necessarily produce non-Markov state sequences.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
3.1 Summary: Deterministic choice is sufficient
The optimal value in state \(s\) is \(\max_aw(s,a)\), and selecting the one action that gives the maximum value is optimal.
Proof. For a random action distribution \(q\)
\[
\sum_aq(a)w(s,a)
\le\sum_aq(a)\max_bw(s,b)
=\max_bw(s,b).
\]
In a finite and non-empty \(A_s\), there exists an action that achieves a maximum value. If that action is given a probability of 1, the upper bound is achieved. \(\square\)
Equality condition: All actions that are \(q(a)>0\) must yield the maximum value. Randomizing among the best actions is harmless, but it does not produce a better value either.
Proof Structure: First, find the upper bound for an arbitrary policy, and then construct a policy that achieves that upper bound. Subsequently, the proof of finite-infinite horizon optimality also follows this structure.
Adding the constant \(c\) to the total terminal reward increases all \(w(s,a)\) by \(c\). This is because the sum of the transition probabilities is 1. Therefore, the optimal action does not change. What is important for comparing actions is the difference in value between terminal states.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
4.1 Objective function and boundary conditions
The decision point is \(0,\ldots,N-1\), and at \(N\), no action is taken and only the terminal reward \(g(s_N)\) is received. This section deals with finite horizons without discounting.
\[
J_s(\pi)=\mathbb E_s^\pi\left[
\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}r_t(s_t,a_t)+g(s_N)\right].
\]
The remaining value of the Markov policy is
\[
v_t^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_{t,s}^\pi\left[
\sum_{k=t}^{N-1}r_k(s_k,a_k)+g(s_N)\right].
\]
Here, \(\mathbb E_{t,s}^\pi\) means that the state at time point \(t\) is set to \(s\), and the policy is applied thereafter. Policy evaluation is also calculated using a one-step decomposition.
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_N^\pi(s)&=g(s),\\
v_t^\pi(s)&=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid s)
\left[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)v_{t+1}^\pi(s')\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 4.2 Summary: Bellman Recursion and Optimal Policy
text:
4.2 Summary: Bellman Recursion and Optimal Policy
Define the candidate value \(V_t\) from the back as follows.
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_N(s)&=g(s),\\
Q_t(s,a)&=r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}(s'),\\
V_t(s)&=\max_a Q_t(s,a),\\
d_t^*(s)&\in\arg\max_a Q_t(s,a).
\end{aligned}
\]
Then \(\pi^*=(d_0^*,\ldots,d_{N-1}^*)\) is optimal even when compared to all HR policies. Each \(V_t(s)\) is the optimal remaining value possible at that point in time and state.

4.2.1 Proof: Inductively derives the upper bound and attainment together
1. Basic Phase \(t=N\). Since there are no more actions, the remaining reward for any policy is \(g(s_N)=V_N(s_N)\).
2. Induction to the Upper Bound. Fix an arbitrary HR policy and use \(U_t^\pi(h_t)\) as the expected remaining reward after history \(h_t\). From \(t+1\)
\[
U_{t+1}^\pi(h_t,a,s')\le V_{t+1}(s')
\]
Let’s assume . Using iterative expectation and the Markov nature of the model
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_t^\pi(h_t)
&=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid h_t)
\left[r_t(s_t,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s_t,a)
U_{t+1}^\pi(h_t,a,s')\right]\\
&\le\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid h_t)Q_t(s_t,a)\\
&\le\max_aQ_t(s_t,a)=V_t(s_t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first inequality is the assumption of induction and non-negative probability, and the second inequality is mean ≤ maximum. In a history where the reach probability is 0, the same recursion can be used by defining \(U_t^\pi\) with a specified follow-up policy and transition instead of the ratio of conditional probabilities.
3. Induction on Achieving the Upper Limit. Let us assume that if \(d_{t+1}^*,\ldots,d_{N-1}^*\) is used after time \(t+1\), \(V_{t+1}\) is achieved. If \(d_t^*(s)\) is chosen at time \(t\),
\[
v_t^{\pi^*}(s)
=r_t(s,d_t^*(s))+
\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,d_t^*(s))V_{t+1}(s')
=V_t(s).
\]
Therefore, the same policy \(\pi^*\) achieves the upper bound for all points in time and states. \(\square\)






TipThe core of the proof



“Starting from the terminal condition, we constrain the residual value of any history-dependent policy to \(V_t(s_t)\) above. Since the state-specific argmax rule inductively achieves its upper bound, a deterministic Markov policy is sufficient.”


Intuition: Solve the last problem and use the answer as the terminal value from the immediately previous time step. Even if the past is different, if the current state and remaining time are the same, the optimal strategy to be used going forward can be shared.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
5.1 Definition of Return and Value
\[
G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k r(s_{t+k},a_{t+k}),
\qquad v^\pi(s)=\mathbb E_s^\pi[G_0],
\qquad J(\pi)=\sum_s\mu_0(s)v^\pi(s).
\]
\(|r(s,a)|\le R_{\max}\) so
\[
|G_t|\le\frac{R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}.
\]
Therefore, the return converges absolutely and is integrable. The exchange of the expectation value and the infinite sum can also be justified by this upper bound. In the time-invariant model and stationary policy, since the future distribution observed from the same state is independent of the starting time, the \(v^\pi\) \(t\) subscript is not needed.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
5.2 Monte Carlo Policy Evaluation
Fix the policy and create multiple trajectories from the same starting state, then calculate the average of each cumulative reward.
If you can observe an independent full return \(G^{(1)},\ldots,G^{(m)}\) starting from the same state
\[
\hat v_m=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mG^{(i)},\qquad
\mathbb E[\hat v_m]=v^\pi(s),\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\hat v_m)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(G)}m.
\]
Linearity of the expected value is used for unbiasedness, and sample independence is used for the variance formula. If the infinite horizon is cut at the \(T\) step and replaced with \(G_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tr_t\), the sample mean is unbiased at \(\mathbb E[G_T]\), but is generally biased at \(v^\pi\).
\[
|\mathbb E[G_T]-v^\pi(s)|
\le\frac{\gamma^T R_{\max}}{1-\gamma}.
\]
Averaging many trajectories and observing each trajectory for a long time reduce other errors. There is no theorem that MC variance is always large. However, large variance can occur due to the randomness of long trajectories.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
5.3 Summary: Bellman Policy Evaluation Equation
\[
v^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)
\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^\pi(s')\right].
\]
Proof Flow.

Decomposes the return into \(G_t=r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma G_{t+1}\).
Apply iterative expectation to \(a_t,s_{t+1}\).
Using a Markov model and Markov policy, remove previous states and actions from future conditions.
Due to the time invariance of the model and policy, the remaining value at the next time step is written as \(v^\pi(s_{t+1})\).

If you connect this as an expression
\[
\begin{aligned}
v^\pi(s)
&=\mathbb E^\pi[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s]\\
&=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)
\left[r(s,a)+\gamma v^\pi(s')\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
If you use \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)=1\) in the compensation term, it is the desired expression. \(\square\)
Note: The past is not erased solely by iteration expectation. To remove the past, Markovity of the model and policy is required, and to erase time indices, stationarity is also required.

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 5.4 Matrix Representation and the Existence of Inverse Matrices
text:
5.4 Matrix Representation and the Existence of Inverse Matrices
\[
R^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)r(s,a),\qquad
P^\pi(s,s')=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)p(s'\mid s,a).
\]
Then it is \(v^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi\). Since \(P^\pi\) is a non-negative matrix where the sum of each row is 1, it is \(\|P^\pi u\|_\infty\le\|u\|_\infty\). Therefore, the matrix series converges and
\[
(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k(P^\pi)^k,
\qquad
v^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi.
\]
The inverse matrix expression is not a simple formal transposition. Multiplying the partial sum of the series by \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) results in \(I-\gamma^{m+1}(P^\pi)^{m+1}\), and since the last term goes to 0, it is confirmed to be the inverse matrix.
Example Verification: If \(\gamma=0.9\) is applied to the previous two state models, it is \(v^\pi(s_2)=-10\) in all policies. If \(s_1\) is always used with \(a_{11}\)
\[
v^\pi(s_1)=5+0.9\left[\tfrac12v^\pi(s_1)-5\right]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v^\pi(s_1)=\frac{10}{11}.
\]
If you always use \(a_{12}\), it is \(v^\pi(s_1)=10+0.9(-10)=1\).
