title: Markov Decision Process
text:
6.2 Summary: The two operators are \(\gamma\)-contraction
Policy evaluation operator. If you cancel out the reward term and limit the weighted average of the probabilities
\[
\|\mathcal T^\pi v-\mathcal T^\pi w\|_\infty
=\|\gamma P^\pi(v-w)\|_\infty
\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty.
\]
Optimal operator. First, for two finite sequences
\[
|\max_ax_a-\max_ay_a|\le\max_a|x_a-y_a|
\]
Verify that . If we select \(a_x\in\arg\max_ax_a\), it becomes \(\max x-\max y\le x_{a_x}-y_{a_x}\le\max|x-y|\), and by swapping \(x,y\), we also obtain the opposite direction. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\mathcal T v(s)-\mathcal T w(s)|
&\le\max_a\left|\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)(v(s')-w(s'))\right|\\
&\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the maximum value for the state yields contractility. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 6.3 Banach Fixed Point Theorem: Necessary Parts and Proof
text:
6.3 Banach Fixed Point Theorem: Necessary Parts and Proof
In a complete metric space, if \(T\) is a contraction with coefficient \(\gamma<1\), then a unique fixed point exists, and \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\) converges from any starting point to that fixed point.
Existence: Since \(d(x_{k+1},x_k)\le\gamma^k d(x_1,x_0)\), when \(m>n\)
\[
d(x_m,x_n)\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}\gamma^k d(x_1,x_0)
\le\frac{\gamma^n}{1-\gamma}d(x_1,x_0)\longrightarrow0.
\]
It is \(x_k\to x^*\) due to completeness, and \(Tx^*=x^*\) due to the continuity of contraction events.
Uniqueness: If there are two fixed points \(x^*,y^*\), then \(d(x^*,y^*)\le\gamma d(x^*,y^*)\), so the two are equal.
Error: If contractility is repeated \(d(x_k,x^*)\le\gamma^k d(x_0,x^*)\). \(\square\)
Here, since \((\mathbb R^{|S|},\|\cdot\|_\infty)\) is complete, it can be applied. Therefore, \(\mathcal T^\pi\) and \(\mathcal T\) each have a unique fixed point. By the policy evaluation formula, the fixed point of the former is \(v^\pi\). The fact that the latter fixed point is the optimal value still needs to be proven.

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 7.1 Summary: The fixed point is the optimal value
text:
7.1 Summary: The fixed point is the optimal value
For all HR policies, the value starting from the state at time point 0 \(s\) is defined as \(v^\pi(s)\), and
\[
v^*(s)=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi^{HR}}v^\pi(s)
\]
Let . Then \(v^*\) is the only fixed point of \(\mathcal T\), and a single deterministic steady-state Markov policy achieves this in all states. Therefore, the above \(\sup\) can be written as \(\max\).

7.1.1 Proof Step 1: Achievable Candidate Configurations
Let \(\hat v\) be the fixed point obtained through contractility. In each state
\[
d^*(s)\in\arg\max_a q_{\hat v}(s,a)
\]
If you select , it becomes \(\mathcal T^{d^*}\hat v=\mathcal T\hat v=\hat v\). Since the fixed point of the policy evaluation operator is unique,
\[
\hat v=v^{d^*}.
\]
In other words, the candidate can be achieved through actual policies.


7.1.2 Proof Step 2: Upper bound for an arbitrary policy
Since \(\hat v=\mathcal T\hat v\), for all \((s,a)\)
\[
r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\hat v(s')\le\hat v(s).
\]
Averaging behaviors with an arbitrary HR policy and applying iterative expectations
\[
\mathbb E^\pi[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma\hat v(s_{t+1})\mid h_t]
\le\hat v(s_t).
\]
Multiplying both sides by \(\gamma^t\) and taking the expected value, then adding it for \(t=0,\ldots,n-1\), the intermediate value terms are canceled out.
\[
\mathbb E_s^\pi\left[
\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\gamma^t r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma^n\hat v(s_n)
\right]\le\hat v(s).
\]
In finite state space, \(\hat v\) is bounded, so \(|\gamma^n\mathbb E_s^\pi[\hat v(s_n)]|\le\gamma^n\|\hat v\|_\infty\to0\). Since the complementary series can also pass the limit through the bounded supreme bound, it is \(v^\pi(s)\le\hat v(s)\).


7.1.3 Proof Step 3: Conclusion
For all policies, it is \(v^\pi\le\hat v\), and \(d^*\) achieves \(\hat v\). Therefore, it is \(v^*=\hat v=v^{d^*}\) and
\[
v^*(s)=\max_a\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^*(s')\right].
\]
The same \(d^*\) is optimal in all states. \(\square\)






WarningOrder to avoid circular reasoning



When proving that “the optimal value is a Bellman fixed point,” do not write it as if it were already a definition. Write it in the order of existence of a candidate due to contractility → Greedy policy achieves the candidate → Upper bound of all policies → Candidate is the optimal value. Do not conclude the optimality of all HR policies based on a proof that compares only normal policies.

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 7.2 Exact conditions of stochastic optimal policy
text:
7.2 Exact conditions of stochastic optimal policy
Let \(q^*(s,a)=q_{v^*}(s,a)\), \(A^*(s)=\arg\max_aq^*(s,a)\). The necessary and sufficient condition for the normal Markov policy \(\pi\) to be optimal in all states is
\[
\pi(a\mid s)>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\in A^*(s).
\]
Sufficientity: Since we average only the maximum actions \(\mathcal T^\pi v^*=v^*\). Due to fixed-point uniqueness \(v^\pi=v^*\).
Necessity: If \(v^\pi=v^*\), then \(\mathcal T^\pi v^*=v^*\). Therefore, in each state
\[
0=v^*(s)-\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)q^*(s,a)
=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\big[v^*(s)-q^*(s,a)\big].
\]
Since all terms are non-negative, the difference between actions with positive probabilities must be 0. \(\square\)
Deterministic policies are also included in the probabilistic policy class. The absence of ties does not mean that there are no optimal policies within the probabilistic policy class, but rather that non-degenerate randomization is impossible. Furthermore, the above condition applies to optimality in all states. When maximizing only \(J(\pi)\) of a specific initial distribution, the selection of unreached states does not need to be optimal.

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
7.3 Fixed point repetition
\[
v_{k+1}=\mathcal T v_k
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\|v_k-v^*\|_\infty\le\gamma^k\|v_0-v^*\|_\infty.
\]
That is, the fixed-point iteration converges to the optimal value. In policy evaluation, \(\mathcal T\) is iterated over instead of \(\mathcal T^\pi\).

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.1 Problem 1. One-period randomization and equality condition
text:
9.1 Problem 1. One-period randomization and equality condition
Prove that the expectation of any action distribution in the finite set \(A_s\) is less than or equal to \(\max_aw(s,a)\). Also explain the necessary and sufficient condition for equality and the location where the finiteness of the action set is written.






TipHint





Look at \(\sum_aq(a)[\max_bw(s,b)-w(s,a)]\). Each term is non-negative. You must write up to the existence of the maximum value and the part that it is achieved by giving it a probability of 1.









NoteSOLUTION





Let \(s\) be fixed and \(M=\max_{a\in A_s}w(s,a)\). Since \(A_s\) is not empty and is finite, \(M\) and the action to achieve it exist. For any probability distribution \(q\)
\[
M-\sum_aq(a)w(s,a)
=\sum_aq(a)[M-w(s,a)]\ge0.
\]
The last inequality is derived from \(q(a)\ge0\) and \(w(s,a)\le M\). Therefore, the randomized expected value cannot exceed \(M\).
The equality holds when and only when all non-negative terms are 0. That is
\[
q(a)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ w(s,a)=M
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{supp}q\subseteq\arg\max_aw(s,a).
\]
If we assign a probability of 1 to each \(a^*\in\arg\max_aw(s,a)\), the expected value is \(M\). Therefore, the optimal value is achieved through deterministic choice. Finiteness was used to guarantee the existence of the maximum value and argmax. Although the inequality that the mean cannot exceed the upper bound holds even in situations more general than finiteness, the existence of the optimal action must be verified separately. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.2 Problem 2. MD policy is better than HR policy in a finite horizon
text:
9.2 Problem 2. MD policy is better than HR policy in a finite horizon
Let’s define \(V_N=g\), \(V_t(s)=\max_a[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}(s')]\). Prove the attainment of the upper bound for an arbitrary HR policy and the upper bound for an MD policy, respectively, by reverse induction.






TipHint





The remaining value of the HR policy should not be treated as a function of \(s_t\) alone from the beginning. Start with \(U_t^\pi(h_t)\) and substitute \(V_{t+1}(s')\) using inductive assumptions. If only the upper bound is observed, it is half, and it is also necessary for the state-specific argmax policy to be achieved at all time points.









NoteSOLUTION





Assume finite \(S,A_s\), finite rewards, and terminal rewards. For any HR policy \(\pi\), let \(h_t\) be the expected remaining reward after history \(U_t^\pi(h_t)\). For a history with a probability of 0, this value is defined by a specified subsequent policy and transition instead of the ratio of conditional probabilities.
1. Upper bound of the random policy. At the end, it is \(U_N^\pi(h_N)=g(s_N)=V_N(s_N)\). Assuming it is \(U_{t+1}^\pi(h_t,a,s')\le V_{t+1}(s')\) for all subsequent histories, with respect to iterational expectation and the Markov nature of the model
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_t^\pi(h_t)
&=\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid h_t)\left[r_t(s_t,a)
+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s_t,a)U_{t+1}^\pi(h_t,a,s')\right]\\
&\le\sum_a\pi_t(a\mid h_t)\left[r_t(s_t,a)
+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s_t,a)V_{t+1}(s')\right]\\
&\le\max_a\left[r_t(s_t,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s_t,a)V_{t+1}(s')\right]
=V_t(s_t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first inequality is the assumption of induction, and the second is the fact that the mean does not exceed the maximum value. By inverse induction, the upper bound holds for all \(t\).
2. Policy to achieve the upper limit. In each \((t,s)\)
\[
d_t^*(s)\in\arg\max_a\left[r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}(s')\right]
\]
Choose . Since this is a finite set of actions, it is a possible choice. If \(v_N^{\pi^*}=g=V_N\) and \(v_{t+1}^{\pi^*}=V_{t+1}\)
\[
v_t^{\pi^*}(s)=r_t(s,d_t^*(s))+
\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,d_t^*(s))V_{t+1}(s')=V_t(s).
\]
Therefore, a single MD policy ZZZPH0013593ZZZ Therefore, a single MD policy \(\pi^*=(d_0^*,\ldots,d_{N-1}^*)\) achieves the upper limit at all points in time and states. No HR policy can yield a better value than this. \(\square\)

section: 9.3 Problem 3. Finite horizon where normal policies may not be sufficient
text:
9.3 Problem 3. Finite horizon where normal policies may not be sufficient
In the basic two-state example, assume that there are two decisions remaining and the terminal reward is 0. Find the optimal action at each time step and explain whether a single stationary deterministic policy can simultaneously achieve the optimal values at all time steps and states.






TipHint





For the last \(s_1\), \(a_{12}\) is the only optimal, and for the two remaining \(s_1\), \(a_{11}\) is the only optimal. These two choices cannot be specified simultaneously by a single rule.









NoteSOLUTION





Let’s set the time point to \(0,1\) and denote it as \(V_2=0\). Since only immediate rewards are compared at time point 1
\[
V_1(s_1)=\max\{5,10\}=10,\qquad V_1(s_2)=-1.
\]
Therefore, it is \(d_1^*(s_1)=a_{12}\) and \(d_1^*(s_2)=a_{21}\). At time point 0, \(s_1\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_0(s_1,a_{11})&=5+\tfrac12(10)+\tfrac12(-1)=9.5,\\
Q_0(s_1,a_{12})&=10+(-1)=9.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, it is \(d_0^*(s_1)=a_{11}\) and \(V_0(s_1)=9.5\). In \(s_2\), since there is only one option, it is \(d_0^*(s_2)=a_{21}\) and \(V_0(s_2)=-2\).

The two optimal actions for \(s_1\) are each unique and distinct. Since a normalized deterministic policy must assign the same action to the identical \(s_1\), it is impossible to achieve the optimal values for all time points and states simultaneously. It is advantageous to receive a large immediate reward at the end, and before that, secure the opportunity to remain in \(s_1\). \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
9.4 Problem 4. Bellman Policy Evaluation Formula
Derive the Bellman evaluation formula for a stationary Markov policy from the return definition of . Indicate separately where iterative expectation, Markovity, and stationarity are used. Also, explain why \(I-\gamma P^\pi\) is invertible.






TipHint





Start from \(G_t=r_t+\gamma G_{t+1}\). Distinguish between past elimination and time index elimination. The inverse matrix can be verified as the product of a convergent matrix series and partial sums.









NoteSOLUTION





Assuming a time-invariant model and a steady-state Markov policy \(\pi\), \(0<\gamma<1\), \(|r|\le R_{\max}\). The return is \(R_{\max}/(1-\gamma)\), which is integrable with the absolute value restricted.
Return Decomposition and Iteration Expected Value: Since \(G_t=r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma G_{t+1}\)
\[
v^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)
\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb E^\pi[G_{t+1}\mid s_t=s,a_t=a,s_{t+1}=s']\right].
\]
Markovity: Since both the model and the policy are Markov, \(s_t,a_t\) is not needed when predicting the future after \(s_{t+1}\). Stationality: Since the model and the policy are time-invariant, the expected return viewed from the state \(s'\) at time point \(t+1\) is the same function \(v^\pi(s')\). Therefore,
\[
v^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^\pi(s')\right].
\]
When the probability of the conditional event is 0, the above equation is interpreted as a new process starting from that state. In matrix notation, it is \(v^\pi=R^\pi+\gamma P^\pi v^\pi\).
Existence of Inverse: Since \(P^\pi\) is a row probability matrix, at the derived maximum norm, \(\|(P^\pi)^k\|_\infty=1\). Accordingly, \(S_m=\sum_{k=0}^m\gamma^k(P^\pi)^k\) converges to some matrix \(S\). Multiplying from both sides
\[
(I-\gamma P^\pi)S_m=S_m(I-\gamma P^\pi)
=I-\gamma^{m+1}(P^\pi)^{m+1}\longrightarrow I.
\]
Therefore, \(S=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}\) and \(v^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi\). This confirms not only the transposition of the terms but also the existence of the inverse matrix. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.5 Problem 5. Contractility of Optimal Operators and Fixed Points
text:
9.5 Problem 5. Contractility of Optimal Operators and Fixed Points
Prove starting from \(|\max x-\max y|\le\max|x-y|\), then show the contractility of \(\mathcal T\). Write down the completeness of the application space, and prove the fixed point uniqueness and the error boundary of the iteration.






TipHint





Compare the difference of maximum values in the same operation, but obtain both-way inequalities. Let \(D\) be the distance between two fixed points, then \(D\le\gamma D\). If existence is also required, the Cauchy property and completeness of iteration sequences must be used.









NoteSOLUTION





1. max inequality. If you choose \(a_x\in\arg\max_ax_a\)
\[
\max_ax_a-\max_ay_a\le x_{a_x}-y_{a_x}\le\max_a|x_a-y_a|.
\]
By changing \(x,y\) to obtain the opposite direction, it is \(|\max x-\max y|\le\max|x-y|\).
2. Contractility of the Bellman Operator. Due to the above inequality, the non-negative nature of transition probabilities, and the fact that the sum is 1
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\mathcal T v(s)-\mathcal T w(s)|
&\le\max_a\left|\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)[v(s')-w(s')]\right|\\
&\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the maximum value for each state gives \(\|\mathcal T v-\mathcal T w\|_\infty\le\gamma\|v-w\|_\infty\). The application space is a finite-dimensional normed space \((\mathbb R^{|S|},\|\cdot\|_\infty)\) and is complete.
3. Fixed point exists. If we set it to \(v_{k+1}=\mathcal T v_k\), then it becomes \(\|v_{k+1}-v_k\|_\infty\le\gamma^k\|v_1-v_0\|_\infty\). Therefore, for \(m>n\)
\[
\|v_m-v_n\|_\infty\le\frac{\gamma^n}{1-\gamma}\|v_1-v_0\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\]
It is \(v_k\to\hat v\) with completeness, and \(\mathcal T\hat v=\hat v\) with continuity of contraction events.
4. Uniqueness and Error. If there is another fixed point \(w\), then \(\|w-\hat v\|_\infty\le\gamma\|w-\hat v\|_\infty\). Since \(\gamma<1\), it is \(w=\hat v\). Also
\[
\|v_k-\hat v\|_\infty\le\gamma^k\|v_0-\hat v\|_\infty.
\]
Up to this point are the results for the fixed point. That this fixed point is the optimal value is verified by comparing it with the policy in the next problem. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.6 Problem 6. From Fixed Point to Optimal Policy
text:
9.6 Problem 6. From Fixed Point to Optimal Policy
Let \(\hat v=\mathcal T\hat v\) and its greed policy \(d\) be given. Show \(\hat v=v^d\) and prove that for all HR policies \(\pi\), \(v^\pi\le\hat v\) holds.






TipHint





The first part is \(\mathcal T^d\hat v=\hat v\) and the uniqueness of policy evaluation. The second part combines one-step inequalities to leave only \(\gamma^n\mathbb E[\hat v(s_n)]\). Specify the reason why this term disappears. It does not stop at comparing only normal policies.









NoteSOLUTION





Assumes a finite set of states and actions, bounded rewards, a time-invariant model, and \(0<\gamma<1\).
1. Achievement of the Greed Policy. Definition of \(d\) and from \(\hat v=\mathcal T\hat v\)
\[
\mathcal T^d\hat v=\mathcal T\hat v=\hat v.
\]
The fixed point of \(\mathcal T^d\) is unique, and since \(v^d\), it is \(\hat v=v^d\).
2. Upper bound for arbitrary HR policy. The fixed-point expression is at all \((s,a)\)
\[
r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\hat v(s')\le\hat v(s)
\]
Gives . Averaging behavior with an arbitrary HR policy \(\pi\)
\[
\mathbb E^\pi[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma\hat v(s_{t+1})\mid h_t]\le\hat v(s_t).
\]
Starting from \(s_0=s\), multiply by \(\gamma^t\), take the expected value, and then add for \(t=0,\ldots,n-1\). The value terms are canceled out by the telescopic sum.
\[
\mathbb E_s^\pi\left[\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\right]
\le\hat v(s)-\gamma^n\mathbb E_s^\pi[\hat v(s_n)].
\]
Since \(\hat v\) is bounded in finite state space, the absolute value of the last term is \(\gamma^n\|\hat v\|_\infty\to0\). Since the compensated partial sum is governed by \(R_{\max}/(1-\gamma)\), the limit can pass into the expectation. Therefore, it is \(v^\pi(s)\le\hat v(s)\).
Since all HR policies are below this upper limit and \(d\) achieves the upper limit, it is \(v^*=\hat v=v^d\). This argument does not require \(\pi\) to be Markov or normal. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
text:
9.7 Problem 7. Stochastic Optimum Policy
Prove the necessary and sufficient condition for a normal Markov policy to be optimal in all states. What does this condition mean when there are no ties?






TipHint





Sufficiency is fixed-point uniqueness, and necessity is the weighted sum of non-negative optimality differences. If there are no ties, a probability of 1 must be assigned to the unique optimal action of each state.









NoteSOLUTION





Let \(A^*(s)=\arg\max_aq^*(s,a)\). The necessary and sufficient condition for a normal Markov policy \(\pi\) to be optimal in all states is
\[
\operatorname{supp}\pi(\cdot\mid s)\subseteq A^*(s)\qquad\forall s
\]
is.
Sufficientity: Since \(q^*(s,a)=v^*(s)\) in all actions with positive probability when the condition is satisfied
\[
(\mathcal T^\pi v^*)(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)q^*(s,a)=v^*(s).
\]
It is \(v^\pi=v^*\) due to fixed point uniqueness.
Necessity: If \(v^\pi=v^*\), then the policy evaluation formula is \(\mathcal T^\pi v^*=v^*\). Therefore
\[
0=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)[v^*(s)-q^*(s,a)].
\]
All numbers inside the square brackets are non-negative. Therefore, if \(\pi(a\mid s)>0\), it must be \(q^*(s,a)=v^*(s)\). This is the desired condition.
If there are no ties, each \(A^*(s)\) has only one element, so that action must be assigned a probability of 1. The optimal policy is deterministic and simultaneously an element of the probabilistic policy class. If there are ties, the optimal actions can be freely mixed. This condition applies not only to a specific initial distribution but to optimality in all states. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.8 Problem 8. Constant Movement and Finite Horizon
text:
9.8 Problem 8. Constant Movement and Finite Horizon
Prove that if the terminal reward of the finite horizon is replaced with \(g+c\), all \(V_t\) increase by exactly \(c\) and the optimal action set remains unchanged. Explain why the equation and coefficients differ from those of the discounted infinite horizon \(\mathcal T(v+c\mathbf1)\).






TipHint





Inductively starting from the terminal and going backward. The finite horizon of this document is not discounted. Since the infinite horizon operator multiplies the next time step value by \(\gamma\), the constant movement also becomes \(\gamma c\).









NoteSOLUTION





Let \(g+c\) be the value obtained by changing the terminal reward to \(g+c\) and the action value be \(\widetilde V_t\) and \(\widetilde Q_t\), respectively. At the terminal, it is \(\widetilde V_N(s)=g(s)+c=V_N(s)+c\).
Assuming \(\widetilde V_{t+1}=V_{t+1}+c\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde Q_t(s,a)
&=r_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'}p_t(s'\mid s,a)[V_{t+1}(s')+c]\\
&=Q_t(s,a)+c.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since the same constant is added to all actions
\[
\widetilde V_t(s)=V_t(s)+c,\qquad
\arg\max_a\widetilde Q_t(s,a)=\arg\max_aQ_t(s,a).
\]
holds for all \(t\) via reverse induction. Since the terminal reward is received only once per path, \(c\) does not accumulate over the remaining period.
On the other hand, the one-step operator of the discount infinite horizon multiplies the next state value by \(\gamma\), so
\[
\mathcal T(v+c\mathbf1)(s)
=\max_a\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v(s')+\gamma c\right]
=\mathcal T v(s)+\gamma c.
\]
The difference lies in the presence or absence of discounting and the object being compared. The first expression is the endpoint reward change for the problem without discounting, while the second expression is the shift of a constant of a value candidate for a one-step update. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.9 Problem 9. MC inconvenience and truncation error
text:
9.9 Problem 9. MC inconvenience and truncation error
Prove that the sample mean of a full return is biased. Calculate the upper bound of the truncation bias at steps \(T\) from \(|r_t|\le R_{\max}\), and explain whether this bias disappears if only the sample size is increased.






TipHint





Unbiasedness is the linearity of the expected value. The truncation error is limited by the remaining discount series \(\sum_{t=T}^\infty\gamma^tR_{\max}\). The fixed \(T\) bias does not disappear solely by increasing the sample size. Distinguish between full returns and truncation returns.









NoteSOLUTION





Let us assume that the complete returns ZZZPH0013664ZZZ and \(G^{(i)}\) obtained from the same starting state \(s\) all satisfy \(\mathbb E[G^{(i)}]=v^\pi(s)\). The expected value of the sample mean is
\[
\mathbb E\left[\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mG^{(i)}\right]
=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb E[G^{(i)}]=v^\pi(s).
\]
Therefore, it is inconvenient. Independence is not required for this equation, but to write the variance of the sample mean as \(\operatorname{Var}(G)/m\), conditions such as independence and identical distribution are required.
When cut to \(G_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tr_t\)
\[
|G-G_T|\le\sum_{t=T}^{\infty}\gamma^t|r_t|
\le\frac{\gamma^TR_{\max}}{1-\gamma}.
\]
Therefore, for the truncated sample mean \(\hat v_{m,T}\)
\[
\left|\mathbb E[\hat v_{m,T}]-v^\pi(s)\right|
=|\mathbb E[G_T]-\mathbb E[G]|
\le\frac{\gamma^TR_{\max}}{1-\gamma}.
\]
\(m\) is not present in this bias equation. Increasing the sample size can reduce the random error of the sample mean, but the truncation bias at a fixed \(T\) generally remains. For example, if the reward at each time step is 1, the truncation bias is exactly \(-\gamma^T/(1-\gamma)\) and is independent of \(m\). To reduce the upper bound of the truncation bias, \(T\) must be increased. \(\square\)

title: Markov Decision Process
section: 9.10 Problem 10. Distinguishing between Evaluation and Optimality with a Two-State Example
text:
9.10 Problem 10. Distinguishing between Evaluation and Optimality with a Two-State Example
Let \(\gamma=0.9\) in the preceding two-state model. Find the value of the normal policy that selects \(a_{11}\) with probability \(q\) and \(a_{12}\) with probability \(1-q\) from \(s_1\). Then, verify that the candidate \(v=(1,-10)\) satisfies the Bellman optimality equation, and explain why the policy that selects \(a_{12}\) is optimal even when compared to all other policies.






TipHint





\(v^\pi(s_2)=-10\) and \(R^\pi(s_1)=10-5q\), \(P^\pi(s_1,s_1)=q/2\) so
\[
v^\pi(s_1)=\frac{1-0.5q}{1-0.45q}.
\]
In candidate \(v=(1,-10)\), the action values for \(s_1\) are \(a_{11}\) for \(0.95\) and \(a_{12}\) for \(1\). Since the update value for \(s_2\) is \(-10\), the candidate is a fixed point. Applying the Bellman Optimality Theorem, \(v=v^*\), the argmax policy is optimal. We do not write that we have proven the optimality of the entire HR policy merely by comparing the values of two normal policies.









NoteSOLUTION





Let Let \(a_{11}\) be the probability that the policy chooses \(s_1\) from \(q\in[0,1]\). Since \(s_2\) continues to receive the reward \(-1\),
\[
v^\pi(s_2)=-1+0.9v^\pi(s_2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v^\pi(s_2)=-10.
\]
If we set it to \(x=v^\pi(s_1)\), the average reward is \(10-5q\), and the probability of returning to \(s_1\) is \(q/2\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
x&=10-5q+0.9\left[\frac q2x+\left(1-\frac q2\right)(-10)\right]\\
&=1-0.5q+0.45qx.
\end{aligned}
\]
\(1-0.45q\ge0.55>0\) Therefore
\[
v^\pi(s_1)=\frac{1-0.5q}{1-0.45q},\qquad v^\pi(s_2)=-10.
\]
In particular, if \(q=1\), then \(v^\pi(s_1)=10/11\), and if \(q=0\), then \(1\). Now, moving beyond comparisons between normal policies, we verify overall optimality. For candidate \(v=(1,-10)\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_v(s_1,a_{11})&=5+0.9\left[\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(-10)\right]=0.95,\\
q_v(s_1,a_{12})&=10+0.9(-10)=1,\\
q_v(s_2,a_{21})&=-1+0.9(-10)=-10.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, \(\mathcal T v=(1,-10)=v\). Since the unique fixed point of the Bellman operator is the optimal value for all HR policies, it is \(v=v^*\). For \(s_1\), \(a_{12}\) is the unique maximum action, and for \(s_2\), only \(a_{21}\) is possible. For this greedy policy \(d\), it is \(\mathcal T^dv=v\), so due to the uniqueness of policy evaluation, it is \(v^d=v=v^*\). Therefore, \(d\) is optimal even when compared to history-dependent and abnormal policies. \(\square\)

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 3.1 What kind of problem is reinforcement learning?
text:
3.1 What kind of problem is reinforcement learning?
A question to consider first. In the MDPs discussed so far, \(p\) and \(r\) were given. What does the agent exchange with the environment, and what does it gain from that exchange?
Answer. Reinforcement learning is the problem of goal-oriented agents interacting with an uncertain environment. The agent sends out an action (decision), and the environment returns the next state and a reward (feedback). Through this interaction, the agent learns about the environment while simultaneously learning a better policy. In other words
\[
\text{interaction}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{adaptation}.
\]






TipSignificance






“Goal-oriented” means that there is an objective function (expected cumulative reward). This is the root of optimal control → Section 4.1
“Adaptation through interaction” is rooted in trial-and-error learning → Section 4.2
Most model-free methods do not explicitly estimate the environment’s model \(p\) in interactions. They directly update values or policies → Section 8.1




↓ Scroll Down: Section 3.1.1

3.1.1 If intelligent systems are viewed as Data → Information → Decision Making, what role does RL play?
Answer. Taking autonomous vehicles as an example, intelligence can be divided into two stages.
\[
\underbrace{\text{Data}\to\text{Information}}_{\text{센서 데이터에서 주변 차량·보행자 정보 추출}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\text{Information}\to\text{Decision}}_{\text{교통 상황에 맞는 주행 판단}}
\]
Usually, the two parts are designed separately, but RL can be an algorithm that learns end-to-end from data to decision-making. Such a system must adapt to uncertainties such as other vehicles and people, weather, road construction, and passengers.
↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 4.1 What does optimal control solve, and where does DP get stuck?
text:
4.1 What does optimal control solve, and where does DP get stuck?
First question to consider. When applying VI·PI earlier, (i) what did you absolutely have to know, and (ii) what was the amount of computation proportional to?
Answer. Optimal control is the problem of designing a controller that maximizes the performance of a dynamic system over an entire time interval (finite or infinite). The key point is that the objective is the performance of the entire interval, not the performance at a single point in time. Although Bellman’s dynamic programming in the 1950s laid the foundation for this problem, DP has two limitations.

Model Knowledge: You must fully understand \(p\) (and \(r\)) to apply the Bellman operator → Section 4.1.2
Scalability: State space grows exponentially with respect to dimension (curse of dimension) → Section 4.1.1

RL is an attempt to solve these two problems of (stochastic) optimal control. It can be used without a model and finds a tractable approximate solution instead of the exact optimal solution.






TipSignificance: The goal determines the year





In the path problem from a starting point to a destination, if the goal is time reduction, one path becomes optimal, and if the goal is fuel minimization, the other path becomes optimal. In optimal control, “optimal” is meaningful only with respect to the objective function. This is the same reason why the reward design determines the outcome policy in RL.



↓ Down: Section 4.1.1 · Section 4.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.1.1 If you write the Curse of Dimensions as a number
First question to consider. If the state consists of \(d\) components and each component is discretized into \(k\) steps, what is \(|S|\)? VI What is the cost of one step?
Answer. \[
|S|=k^d,\qquad
\text{VI 1회 비용}=O\big(|S|^2|A|\big)=O\big(k^{2d}|A|\big),\qquad
\text{결정적 stationary 정책 수}=|A|^{|S|}=|A|^{k^d}.
\]






NoteBasis






VI 1 time: Calculate \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v(s')\) for all \((s,a)\). Since \((s,a)\) is the sum of \(|S||A|\), each \(|S|\) term, \(|S|^2|A|\).
Number of Policies: Since one action is chosen independently for each state, \(|A|^{|S|}\). As MDP theory has shown that deterministic stationary policies are sufficient, the search space is finite, but its size is an exponent of \(|S|\).
Example: If \(d=10\) and \(k=10\), then \(|S|=10^{10}\). Just storing \(v\) requires \(10^{10}\) elements.










TipSignificance





As long as \(v\) or \(Q\) are treated exactly as a tabular, this cost cannot be avoided. Therefore, RL abandons exact solutions from the outset and reduces the representation using functional approximations (linear features, neural networks). The price for this is the difficulty of “limited representation” → Section 7.1.2



↑ Go Up: Section 4.1


4.1.2 Where is model dependency hidden in VI·PI?
Answer. There are three places.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{VI}:\quad& v_{k+1}=Tv_k &&\leftarrow\ T\text{ 안의 }\textstyle\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v(s')\\
\text{PI 평가}:\quad& v^{\pi}=T^{\pi}v^{\pi}\ \Leftrightarrow\ (I-\gamma P^\pi)v^\pi=R^\pi &&\leftarrow\ P^\pi\\
\text{PI 향상}:\quad& \pi'(s)\in\arg\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\textstyle\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)v^\pi(s')\Big] &&\leftarrow\ p
\end{aligned}
\]






TipSignificance






The enhancement step of PI becomes \(\pi'(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^\pi(s,a)\) when \(Q^\pi\) is used, and the model disappears. What remains is “how to calculate the expected value \(\sum_{s'}p(\cdot)\) without the model”.
The answer to this question is the next topic, stochastic approximation. We replace the expectation with the sample and gradually reduce the step size so that the noise in the sample disappears over time.




↑ Go Up: Section 4.1

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 4.2 What does trial and error learning mean?
text:
4.2 What does trial and error learning mean?
Answer. It has roots in psychology.

Thorndike (1911), Law of Effect: Among various responses to the same situation, responses accompanied by satisfaction have a stronger connection to the situation and appear more frequently when the situation arises again, while responses accompanied by discomfort have a weaker connection and appear less frequently.
Klopf (1972): Connected this idea to trial-and-error learning and related it to vast experimental data in animal learning psychology.
Sutton & Barto (1970–80s): Temporal-Difference (TD) learning is the algorithm developed from this.







TipSignificance: If you interpret the law of effect as a probabilistic policy





The statement “responses accompanied by satisfaction appear more readily” can be interpreted as an update that increases the probability of actions with higher rewards in a stochastic policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\). This aligns with the intuition of policy gradient. On the other hand, if interpreted as storing and updating the “strength of the connection between situation and response” numerically, it aligns with the intuition of the value-based method that updates \(Q(s,a)\) → Section 8.1



↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 4.3 What becomes of two roots when combined
text:
4.3 What becomes of two roots when combined
Answer. If written in one line
\[
\text{RL}=\text{시행착오 학습으로 최적 제어(MDP) 문제를 푸는 방법}.
\]
The representative algorithm family is as follows.








Series
Representative
Year




value-based
Q-learning (Watkins)
1989


policy-based
policy gradient (Williams; Marbach & Tsitsiklis)
1987; 1998

actor-critic (Witten, Barto, Sutton, Degris, White, etc.)
—









TipSignificance






Until around 2010, applications were limited to games like Tetris and chess, and some robotics, mostly remaining at the toy level. The main reason was the limitations of expression.
Since the 2010s, with the advancement of deep learning and computational resources, deep RL, which expresses values and policies using neural networks, has expanded to practical problems.




↓ Down: Section 8.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 5.1 What is the difference between RL and supervised learning?
text:
5.1 What is the difference between RL and supervised learning?
Answer.

No supervisor and only reward signals → Section 5.1.1
Feedback is not immediate and is delayed → Section 5.1.2
Time is important. It is a sequential decision and the data is not iid → Section 5.1.2
Agent’s behavior affects data to be received later → Section 5.1.3
There is a trade-off between exploration and exploitation → Section 5.1.4







TipSignificance





4 is the most fundamental. In supervised learning, the data distribution is fixed regardless of the learner. In RL, if the learner changes the policy, the data distribution changes. 5 is a direct consequence of 4. Since the learner must decide for themselves which data to look at, they must choose between an action that looks good now and an action that provides more information.



↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

5.1.1 ✍ Why Rewards Cannot Serve as Correct Answer Labels
Guide Question:

What do we need to know to provide the “correct action” as the label for supervised learning in the state \(s\)? If we write it as \(Q^*\)?
What is the difference between \(r(s,a)\) and \(Q^*(s,a)\)? Does \(\arg\max_ar(s,a)=\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a)\) always hold?
If \(\gamma=0\), then it is \(Q^*=r\). In that case, is RL supervised learning?







NoteSolution





1. The correct action is \(\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a)\). In other words, to be the label, you must know the long-term gain \(Q^*(s,a)\).
2. \[
Q^*(s,a)-r(s,a)=\gamma\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s').
\] This difference depends on \(a\) (since the action changes the distribution of the next state). Therefore, the argmax of immediate reward and the argmax of long-term gain are generally different. A counterexample is found in Section 6.1.1’s example. Reward is not the correct label because it measures only immediate gain.
3. No. If it is \(\gamma=0\), the lag problem disappears, but only the reward for a single selected action is observed. Since the reward for unselected actions is not visible, “which action was the correct answer” is still not given (bandit feedback). In supervised learning, the correct answer is given for every input, but here, only the score for the chosen action is given. Therefore, even if it is \(\gamma=0\), the search problem (Section 5.1.4) remains.









TipSignificance





There are two reasons why rewards cannot serve as supervised learning labels: (i) temporal: rewards do not reflect long-term gains (when \(\gamma>0\)). (ii) counterfactual: the consequences of uneven behavior are not observed (even when \(\gamma=0\)). RL algorithms treat (i) as the Bellman equation and (ii) as search.



↑ Go Up: Section 5.1


5.1.2 Why is feedback delayed, and why is the data not iid?
First question to consider. When following a stationary policy \(\pi\), write the state distribution at time \(t\) in terms of the initial distribution and transition.
Answer. \(P^\pi(s,s'):=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\,p(s'\mid s,a)\), if we let the state distribution be the row vector \(\mu_t\), \[
\mu_{t+1}=\mu_tP^\pi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu_t=\mu_0(P^\pi)^t,\qquad
(s_t,a_t)\sim\mu_t(s)\,\pi(a\mid s).
\]

Not iid: \(s_{t+1}\) is not independent because it depends on \(s_t\), and it is not identically distributed because \(\mu_t\) varies according to \(t\).
Feedback is delayed: Action \(a_t\) changes the distribution of \(s_{t+1}\), and this propagates to \(\mu_{t+2},\mu_{t+3},\dots\). The result of \(a_t\) appears not just in \(r_t\), but across the entire subsequent reward system. The current choice changes the very paths that can be taken later.







TipSignificance






The convergence logic of supervised learning (iid sample mean) cannot be used as is. This is why a “conditional” mean \(0\) condition (conditional on past history \(\mathcal{F}_k\)) is applied to the noise in subsequent convergence analysis.
Reducing inter-sample correlations with experience replay in deep RL also targets the same problem.




↑ Go Up: Section 5.1


5.1.3 What exactly does it mean that behavior changes the data distribution?
Answer. In the equation Section 5.1.2, the distribution of data \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\) is a function of the policy \(\pi\) through \(\mu_0(P^\pi)^t\)Z and \(\pi\). If the policy changes to \(\pi_k\to\pi_{k+1}\) during training, the distribution of the next collected data also changes.






TipSignificance






Supervised learning: Fixed data distribution → Model training. It is one-way.
RL: Policy → Data Distribution → Policy Update → Data Distribution … There is a feedback loop.

In an unfamiliar environment, whether to choose the path that seems best based on the information (or belief) currently available, or to choose an action that provides more information because one knows less, depends on the situation. There is generally no known method to optimally balance these two → Section 5.1.4



↑ Go Up: Section 5.1


5.1.4 Why does the search-utilization trade-off occur, and what goes wrong without search
First question to consider. If we always choose the greedy action \(\arg\max_a\hat Q(s,a)\) for the current estimate \(\hat Q\), what happens to the estimate of the action that was once underestimated?
Answer. It is not updated. This is because new data does not arrive due to unevenness. Therefore, if the initial estimate is unfortunately wrong, it can remain in the suboptimal state forever.






NoteExample: Case where greedy fails with a probability of 0.3 or higher





Two actions, one state (bandit that is \(\gamma=0\)).

Action A: The reward is always \(0.5\).
Action B: The rewards are \(0.7\) with probabilities \(1\) and \(0.3\) with probabilities \(0\). Since the expected value is \(0.7\), B is optimal.

Try each action once, use the sample mean as the estimate, and then choose greedy.

If B’s first reward is \(0\) (probability \(0.3\)), then \(\hat Q(B)=0<0.5=\hat Q(A)\). After that, always choose A, A’s estimate remains \(0.5\), and B is not tried again. It stays on A forever.
Even if B’s first reward is \(1\), the same thing happens if B’s sample mean unfortunately drops below \(0.5\) afterwards.

Therefore, the probability of failure is at least \(0.3\). It does not decrease no matter how long data is collected.









TipSignificance






The cause of the trade-off is that the environment model (\(p\), \(r\)) is unknown. If the model were known, there would be no reason to search. Therefore, this is not a problem unique to RL, but a problem in all sequential decision-making problems where the model is unknown.
Choosing an action that provides more information, even if it means sacrificing a small immediate gain (greedy), can be advantageous in the long run. The simplest implementation is \(\varepsilon\)-greedy (\(1-\varepsilon\) probability greedy, \(\varepsilon\) probability random).
The Q-learning convergence theorem assumes that “all \((s,a)\) are visited infinitely often” to exclude the failure shown in this example.




↑ Go Up: Section 5.1

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 6.1 What are the components and policies of an RL problem?
text:
6.1 What are the components and policies of an RL problem?
Answer.

State \(s_t\in S\): State of the environment (system).
Action \(a_t\in A\): Determined by the agent and affects the state.
Reward \(r(s_t,a_t)\): Evaluates the benefits of the state and action.
Policy \(\pi\): A transition from state to action. It is the subject of optimization. \[
\text{결정적: }\ \pi(s_t)=a_t,\qquad
\text{확률적: }\ \pi(a\mid s)=\Pr(a_t=a\mid s_t=s).
\]

The goal of sequential decision-making is to select actions over time to maximize the expected cumulative reward.






TipSignificance: Why use probabilistic policies





Since the optimal policy of an MDP exists among deterministic and stationary policies, a stochastic policy is not necessary in terms of optimality alone. However, stochastic policies are useful in RL algorithms.

Search can be put into the policy itself(\(\varepsilon\)-greedy, Boltzmann) → Section 5.1.4
Since \(\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\) is differentiable with respect to \(\theta\), we can use the policy gradient. The argmax of the deterministic policy is not differentiable → Section 8.1




↓ Down: Section 6.1.1 · Section 6.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.1.1 ✍ Why Behavior Has Long-Term Effects, and How Immediate Rewards Are Sacrificed
Guide Question:

What does \(a_t\) change other than \(r_t\)? How does that lead to \(r_{t+1},r_{t+2},\dots\)?
If we write “sacrificing immediate rewards” as an equation, what are the short-sighted choice \(\arg\max_ar(s,a)\) and the optimal choice, respectively?
Compare the two choices in the MDP below.

Settings: \(S=\{0,1\}\), \(A=\{\text{stay},\text{move}\}\), \(\gamma=0.9\), Transition is deterministic.



\((s,a)\)
\(r\)
Next status




\((0,\text{stay})\)
1
0


\((0,\text{move})\)
0
1


\((1,\text{stay})\)
2
1


\((1,\text{move})\)
0
0









NoteSolution





1. \(a_t\) changes the distribution of \(s_{t+1}\) through \(p(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)\). Since subsequent rewards depend on subsequent states, the effect of \(a_t\) propagates to all future rewards via \(\mu_{t+1},\mu_{t+2},\dots\), as shown in the equation Section 5.1.2.
2. \[
\text{근시안: }\ \arg\max_a\,r(s,a),\qquad
\text{최적: }\ \arg\max_a\Big[\underbrace{r(s,a)}_{\text{즉각}}+\underbrace{\gamma\textstyle\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v^*(s')}_{\text{장기}}\Big]=\arg\max_aQ^*(s,a).
\] Even if the immediate term is small, the action is optimal if the long-term term is sufficiently large. The Bellman equation accurately provides this comparison.
3. Repeating stay in state 1 is \(2/(1-0.9)=20\). Since move is \(0.9\,v(0)\le0.9\times20\), stay is better. \(v^*(1)=20\).
In state 0: \[
Q^*(0,\text{stay})=\frac{1}{1-0.9}=10,\qquad
Q^*(0,\text{move})=0+0.9\times20=18.
\] The short-sighted choice is stay(\(r=1>0\)) and the value is \(10\). The optimal choice is move. We give up the immediate reward \(1\) and receive \(0\), but move to state 1, which has a higher reward, so the value becomes \(18\). \(v^*=(18,20)\).









TipSignificance





This example is also a counterexample to Section 5.1.1. In state 0, it is \(\arg\max_ar(0,a)=\text{stay}\) and \(\arg\max_aQ^*(0,a)=\text{move}\). If the reward is used as a label, incorrect behavior is learned.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1


6.1.2 Why are MDP problems difficult to solve?
\[
\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_{t=0}^\infty\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\Big].
\]
First question to consider. Look at the decision variable, the calculation of the objective function, and the size of the search space, respectively.
Answer. It is triple-layered difficult.

The decision variable is a function. The optimization target is not a number but a policy, that is, a \(S\to A\) (or \(S\to\Delta(A)\)) event. Even when narrowed down to deterministic stationary policies, there are \(|A|^{|S|}\) candidates → Section 4.1.1
A model is required even to calculate a single objective function. The value of a single policy, \(\mathbb{E}^\pi[\cdot]\), is the expected value of the trajectory distribution over an infinite number of time points, and that distribution is defined as \(p\) and \(\pi\). To calculate this, \((I-\gamma P^\pi)v^\pi=R^\pi\) must be solved, and \(p\) is input into it → Section 4.1.2
Scale. Even when solved exactly, the cost is a polynomial with respect to \(|S|\), and \(|S|\) itself is exponential with respect to the state dimension.







TipSignificance





MDP theory solved the difficulty of 1 using the Bellman equation and contraction mapping. Instead of directly exploring the policy space, it found fixed points in the value space. What remains are 2 (model) and 3 (scale), which are exactly the two limits of DP. RL treats 2 as samples and 3 as approximations.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
section: 7.1 What is an RL problem, and how is it approached?
text:
7.1 What is an RL problem, and how is it approached?
Answer.

Objective: Solve the MDP problem Section 6.1.2 when model \((p,r)\) is unknown.
Approach: Trial and error. The agent accumulates experience (data) through actions and gradually updates values or policies using that data. The basic unit of data is the transition sample \((s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})\).

↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 · Section 7.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

7.1.1 What is assumed not to be known
Answer. In most cases, it is assumed that only \(p\) is unknown. Since the reward function is designed by the user, it is often known.
However, mathematically, it is possible to handle cases where even \(r\) is unknown. It can be viewed as a black box (e.g., expert scoring) where inputting \((s_t,a_t)\) yields only the signal \(r_t\), and it can be assumed that the signal is contaminated with noise. \[
r_t=r(s_t,a_t)+\eta_t,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\eta_t\mid s_t,a_t]=0.
\]






NoteReasoning: Why noisy compensation does not change the problem





The objective function is the expected value. \[
\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_t\gamma^t r_t\Big]=\sum_t\gamma^t\,\mathbb{E}^\pi\big[\mathbb{E}[r(s_t,a_t)+\eta_t\mid s_t,a_t]\big]=\mathbb{E}^\pi\Big[\sum_t\gamma^tr(s_t,a_t)\Big].
\] Noise with a conditional mean of \(0\) disappears due to the tower property (assuming the reward is bounded and \(\gamma<1\) allows for an exchange between the sum and the expectation). Therefore, the optimal policy is the same. Noise only slows down learning and does not change the goal.



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1


7.1.2 Why RL is useful and why it is difficult
Answer.







Useful reason
Difficult reason




Flexibility: Can be used without model information
Limited Knowledge: No model information


Adaptability: Since it does not rely on a fixed model, it can continue to update even if the environment changes
Exploration vs. Exploitation: It is unclear what to try → Section 5.1.4


Extensibility: Can be used for large-scale problems because it abandons exact solutions from the start and obtains tractable approximate solutions
Bound Representation: It is unclear in what functional form the values and policies of complex problems should be approximated









TipSignificance: Each row of the table is a two-sided representation of the same property.






The fact that “there is no model” becomes flexibility on the first line and limited knowledge on the right. It is a double-edged sword.
Line 2: Since it does not rely on a fixed model, it can adapt, but that is precisely why you have to decide for yourself what to try.
Line 3: Since we chose an approximation, it can be used for large-scale problems, but if the form of the approximation is chosen incorrectly, it cannot even come close to the optimal.




↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
section: 3.1 Can the fixed-point problem be solved model-free?
text:
3.1 Can the fixed-point problem be solved model-free?
First question to consider. Where exactly was the transition probability \(p\) used at each step of VI and PI? If you do not know \(p\)Z and can only obtain the transition sample \((s,a,r,s')\), what can be used to replace it?
Answer. VI and PI are both methods for solving the fixed-point problem. And the model is placed in the expected value position, \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)(\cdot)\), inside the Bellman operator. The expected value can be approximated by samples. However, a single sample can differ significantly from the expected value. Therefore, stochastic approximation (SA) is designed so that this error (noise) is averaged out and disappears through iteration.
\[
\textbf{Key question: } \text{How can we solve fixed point problems in a model-free manner?}
\]






TipSignificance





SA is the theoretical framework for value-based RL algorithms (TD, Q-learning). Subsequently, Q-learning is derived as “applying Robbins–Monroe SA to the Bellman equation for \(Q^*\)” → Section 5.1.2



↓ Scroll Down: Section 3.1.1

3.1.1 What kind of fixed-point problem was VI·PI?
Answer.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{정책 평가:}\quad & v=T^\pi v
&&\Longleftrightarrow\quad v(s)=r(s,\pi(s))+\gamma\textstyle\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,\pi(s))\,v(s'),\\
\text{최적성 방정식:}\quad & v=Tv
&&\Longleftrightarrow\quad v(s)=\max_a\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\textstyle\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)\,v(s')\Big].
\end{aligned}
\]
\(T^\pi\) is an affine operator, and \(T\) is a non-linear operator because of \(\max\). Both are contractions of \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) to \(\gamma\). Therefore, by the Banach fixed point theorem, \(v_{k+1}=Tv_k\) (or \(T^\pi v_k\)) converges to the unique fixed point. However, \(p\) is required for each application of the operator.






TipSignificance





If PI’s policy improvement phase uses \(Q^\pi\), it becomes \(\pi'(s)\in\arg\max_aQ^\pi(s,a)\), causing the model to disappear. The remaining problem is the evaluation phase and VI fixed point calculation. SA targets precisely this area.



↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
text:
4.1 Deterministic repetitions and relaxation repetitions
Questions to consider first. Do \(x_{k+1}=Hx_k\) and \(x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_kHx_k\) have the same fixed point? If \(H\) is a contraction of \(\beta\), is the mapping of the second iteration also a contraction?
Answer. The two deterministic iterations for the general fixed-point problem \(Hx=x\) are as follows.
\[
x_{k+1}=Hx_k,\qquad
x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_kHx_k,\quad \alpha_k\in(0,1].
\]
The second equation is a weighted average with weights of \(1-\alpha_k\) for the previous estimate and \(Hx_k\) for the new information \(\alpha_k\). The fixed points of the two iterations are the same, and if \(H\) is a reduction, both converge to \(x^*\).






NoteBasis





Let’s set the constant \(\alpha\) to \(H_\alpha:=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha H\).

The fixed point is the same: \(H_\alpha x=x \iff \alpha(Hx-x)=0 \iff Hx=x\).
Reduction Factor: If \(H\) is \(\|\cdot\|\)-reduction for \(\beta\) \[
\|H_\alpha x-H_\alpha y\|\le(1-\alpha)\|x-y\|+\alpha\beta\|x-y\|=\big(1-\alpha(1-\beta)\big)\|x-y\|.
\] Since \(1-\alpha(1-\beta)<1\), \(H_\alpha\) is also a reduction. As the coefficients approach 1 more than \(\beta\), convergence slows down in deterministic cases.










TipSignificance





In critical cases, there seems to be no reason to use relaxation iterations. However, the situation changes if you use a noisy value instead of \(Hx_k\). In that case, \(\alpha_k\) becomes the handle that determines how much to trust the noise. This is the core of SA → Section 4.2



↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
section: 4.2 When \(H\) is unknown: Repeat with noisy observations
text:
4.2 When \(H\) is unknown: Repeat with noisy observations
First question to consider. When \(Hx_k\) cannot be calculated exactly, what must be assumed to be accessible in order to continue the iteration?
Answer. Consider the case where the structure of \(H\) is completely unknown or it is difficult to calculate \(Hx_k\) accurately. Instead, assume that access to the following random variables is available.
\[
s_k=Hx_k+w_k,\qquad w_k:\text{ random noise}.
\]
\(Hx_k\) and \(w_k\) are not observed individually, and only their sum \(s_k\) is observed. If \(s_k\) is substituted for \(Hx_k\) in the relaxation iteration, it becomes a stochastic approximation algorithm.
\[
x_{k+1}:=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_k\underbrace{(Hx_k+w_k)}_{s_k}.
\]

\(s_k\) can often be obtained from sample data (simulations or experiments).
\(s_k\) may be very different from \(Hx_k\).
However, if appropriate conditions are applied to the noise \(w_k\), the difference does not significantly affect the calculation of \(x^*\) in the long run.

↓ Down: Section 4.2.1 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

4.2.1 Reasons why noise can disappear over time
Answer. If the update equation is written by separating it into the movement direction and noise, it is as follows.
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k\underbrace{(Hx_k-x_k)}_{\text{평균적 방향}}+\alpha_k\underbrace{w_k}_{\text{잡음}}.
\]
When accumulated up to the step \(k\), the contribution of noise is in the form \(\sum_{j<k}\alpha_jw_j\). If the conditional mean of the noise is 0, this sum is a martingale. Therefore, they cancel each other out, and if the step size decreases sufficiently quickly, the tail goes to 0. On the other hand, the contribution in the average direction \(Hx_k-x_k\) continues to accumulate in proportion to \(\sum\alpha_k\). Eventually, the noise is averaged out and disappears, and the trajectory follows a deterministic iteration.






TipSignificance






This intuition directly translates into two types of assumptions. The noise side is a conditional mean of 0 and bounded variance → Section 7.1. The step size side is that the average direction accumulates endlessly (\(\sum\alpha=\infty\)), and the noise is tamed (\(\sum\alpha^2<\infty\)) → Section 6.2
When viewed as a small \(\alpha_k\), the locus follows the ODE \(\dot x=Hx-x\) (ODE method). If \(H\) is a contraction, the equilibrium point \(x^*\) of this ODE is globally asymptotically stable.




↑ Go Up: Section 4.2

title: Stochastic Approximation
text:
5.1 Viewing the Bellman equation as \(x=\mathbb{E}[f(x,\xi)]\)
First question to consider. When the expected value is unknown, what is the simplest way to approximate it using \(N\) samples? What is the problem with using that method in every iteration?
Answer. View the Bellman equation in the following abstract form.
\[
x=\mathbb{E}[f(x,\xi)],\qquad \xi:\text{ 확률 변수}.
\]
Given sample \(\{\hat\xi_1,\dots,\hat\xi_N\}\), the process can be repeated by replacing the expected value with the sample mean.
\[
x_{k+1}:=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_k\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nf(x_k,\hat\xi_i).
\]
However, since \(N\) must be evaluated in every iteration, computational efficiency is poor if \(N\) is large. Therefore, only one sample is used per iteration.
\[
\boxed{\,x_{k+1}:=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_kf(x_k,\hat\xi_k)\,}\qquad\text{(Robbins–Monro 알고리즘)}
\]






TipSignificance: Relationship with SGD





Robbins–Monro is originally an algorithm \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG(x_k,\hat\xi_k)\) that finds the roots of \(g(x):=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)]=0\). To transform this into a fixed-point form, one can set it to \(Hx:=x-g(x)\). In particular, if it is \(G=\nabla_xF\), it becomes SGD that minimizes \(\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\). Therefore, the step size condition of SGD and the step size condition of SA share the same root.



↓ Down: Section 5.1.1 · Section 5.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

5.1.1 ✍ Why is single-sample update SA, and why is the noise mean 0?
Guide Question:

To fit the Robbins–Monro expression into the form \(x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)x_k+\alpha_k(Hx_k+w_k)\), what should \(Hx_k\) and \(w_k\) be defined as, respectively?
If \(\hat\xi_k\) is drawn from the same distribution as \(\xi\) independently of the past, what is the conditional mean of \(w_k\) when \(x_k\) is given?







NoteSolution





1. \[
Hx_k:=\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)],\qquad
w_k:=f(x_k,\hat\xi_k)-\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)].
\] Then \(Hx_k+w_k=f(x_k,\hat\xi_k)\), so Robbins–Monro is a special case of SA. Here, the expected value is taken only for \(\xi\), while fixing \(x_k\).
2. \(x_k\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_k\) and since \(\hat\xi_k\perp\mathcal F_k\) \[
\mathbb{E}[w_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\mathbb{E}\big[f(x_k,\hat\xi_k)\mid\mathcal F_k\big]-\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)]=\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)]-\mathbb{E}[f(x_k,\xi)]=0.
\]









TipSignificance





Among the noise conditions of SA, “conditional mean 0(Section 7.1)” is not an artificial assumption. It holds automatically if the expected value is substituted with a sample. It is sufficient that the sample is drawn without bias.



↑ Go Up: Section 5.1


5.1.2 ✍ Which Bellman equation fits this form
Guide Question:

In Policy Evaluation \(v=T^\pi v\), if the coordinates corresponding to state \(s\)Z are written in the form \(\mathbb{E}[f(v,\xi)]\), what are \(\xi\) and \(f\)?
What is the order of \(\max\) and the expected value in the optimality equation \(v=Tv\)? Can an unbiased estimate of \((Tv)(s)\) be made with a single sample?
What is the order in the Bellman equation for \(Q^*\)?







NoteSolution





If you set it to 1. \(\xi=s'\sim p(\cdot\mid s,\pi(s))\), \(f(v,s')=r(s,\pi(s))+\gamma v(s')\) \[
v(s)=\mathbb{E}_{s'}\big[r(s,\pi(s))+\gamma v(s')\big].
\] Applying Robbins–Monro results in \(v_{k+1}(s)=(1-\alpha_k)v_k(s)+\alpha_k\big(r+\gamma v_k(s')\big)\). This is TD(0).
2. \((Tv)(s)=\max_a\mathbb{E}_{s'}[\cdots]\), i.e., \(\max\), is outside the expected value. A single sample gives only \(s'\) for a single action. If we take \(\max\) for the single-sample estimate of each action, it becomes \(\mathbb{E}[\max_a\hat q_a]\ge\max_a\mathbb{E}[\hat q_a]\) due to the Jensen inequality, which is biased upward. Therefore, it does not fit this form.
3. \[
Q^*(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{s'\sim p(\cdot\mid s,a)}\Big[r(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')\Big].
\] This time, \(\max\) is inside the expected value. Therefore, if we set \(x=Q\), \(\xi=s'\), and \(f(Q,s')=r(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\), it is exactly in the form \(x=\mathbb{E}[f(x,\xi)]\). If we apply Robbins–Monro, \[
Q_{k+1}(s,a)=(1-\alpha_k)Q_k(s,a)+\alpha_k\Big(r(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}Q_k(s',a')\Big).
\] This is Q-learning.









TipSignificance





There are two reasons why the value-based method learns \(Q\) instead of \(v\): (i) The policy can be extracted without a model. (ii) The optimality equation takes the form where \(\max\) is contained within the expectation, allowing Robbins–Monro to be applied directly.



↑ Go Up: Section 5.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
section: 6.1 Algorithms and step directions by coordinate
text:
6.1 Algorithms and step directions by coordinate
Answer. If different step sizes are allowed for each coordinate, a typical SA is as follows.
\[
x_{k+1}(i)=(1-\alpha_k(i))\,x_k(i)+\alpha_k(i)\big[(Hx_k)(i)+w_k(i)\big].
\]
Assumption: For each \(i\), there are infinitely many \(\alpha_k(i)>0\)Z and \(k\). In other words, all coordinates are updated infinitely often.
Rearranging gives \(x_{k+1}(i)=x_k(i)+\alpha_k(i)\big[(Hx_k)(i)-x_k(i)+w_k(i)\big]\). Therefore, the step direction is \((Hx_k)(i)-x_k(i)+w_k(i)\), and the remaining problem is how to choose \(\alpha_k(i)\).






TipSignificance: Asynchronous update





In Q-learning, the coordinates \(i\) represent the pair \((s,a)\). In a single transition, only the visited coordinate \((s_k,a_k)\) is updated, while the remaining coordinate is \(\alpha_k(i)=0\). Therefore, the assumption that “it is updated infinitely often” becomes the search condition that all \((s,a)\) are visited infinitely often. Since whether a coordinate is visited depends on the trajectory, the step size is also a random variable. This is the reason why “with a probability of 1” is attached to the subsequent condition.



↓ Down: Section 6.1.1 · Section 6.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.1.1 ✍ Constant step size: Variance remains
Let the coordinates \(i\) be fixed, and let the variance of \(w_k(i)\)Z be \(\sigma^2\), and let \(w_k\) be independent of \(x_k\).
Guide Question:

When \(\alpha_k(i)\equiv\alpha\), what is the lower bound of \(\operatorname{Var}(x_{k+1}(i))\)?
In the simplest case, \(Hx\equiv c\) (constant, reduction factor 0), where do the mean and variance of the error \(e_k:=x_k-c\) go?







NoteSolution





1. \(x_{k+1}(i)=\underbrace{(1-\alpha)x_k(i)+\alpha(Hx_k)(i)}_{A_k}+\alpha w_k(i)\), and since \(A_k\) is a function of \(x_k\), it is independent of \(w_k\). \[
\operatorname{Var}(x_{k+1}(i))=\operatorname{Var}(A_k)+\alpha^2\sigma^2\ \ge\ \alpha^2\sigma^2.
\] At every step, new noise adds variance by \(\alpha^2\sigma^2\), so the variance cannot go to 0.
2. \(e_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)e_k+\alpha w_k\) is.

Average: \(\mathbb{E}e_k=(1-\alpha)^ke_0\to0\).
Variance: \(V_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)^2V_k+\alpha^2\sigma^2\), so the normal value is as follows. \[
V_\infty=\frac{\alpha^2\sigma^2}{1-(1-\alpha)^2}=\frac{\alpha\,\sigma^2}{2-\alpha}>0.
\]

The average goes to \(x^*\), but \(x_k\) continues to move randomly within a radius \(O(\sqrt\alpha\,\sigma)\)Z around \(x^*\).









TipSignificance





With a constant step size, it reaches the vicinity of \(x^*\) at best and does not converge. For convergence to occur, it must be \(\alpha_k\to0\)** so that the influence of noise eventually diminishes. Conversely, as \(\alpha\) becomes smaller, the size of the vicinity \(\sqrt{\alpha/(2-\alpha)}\,\sigma\) decreases, but the average error decreases slowly to \((1-\alpha)^k\). This is the bias-variance trade-off of a constant step size. In non-stationary environments, a constant step size may actually be advantageous.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1


6.1.2 If you shrink too fast: cannot escape
First question to consider. If \(\sum_k\alpha_k(i)=A<\infty\) and the step direction is bounded at \(B\), how far can \(x_k(i)\) go from \(x_0(i)\)?
Answer. If you accumulate the update formula
\[
|x_k(i)-x_0(i)|\le\sum_{\tau=0}^{k-1}\alpha_\tau(i)\,\big|(Hx_\tau)(i)-x_\tau(i)+w_\tau(i)\big|\le A\,B.
\]
That is, \(x_k\) cannot go beyond the fixed vicinity of radius \(AB\) centered on \(x_0\). If \(x^*\) is outside of it, it cannot be reached.






TipSignificance





Reduce the step size, but the cumulative movable amount \(\sum\alpha_k\) must be infinite. This ensures that no matter how far the initial point is, it can sufficiently traverse the domain of \(H\) and reach \(x^*\). Combined with Section 6.1.1, this becomes “Do not make it too big, nor too small too quickly.”



↑ Go Up: Section 6.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
text:
6.2 Step size condition
Answer. Assume that the following holds with a probability of 1.
\[
\text{(S1)}\ \ \sum_{k=0}^\infty\alpha_k(i)=+\infty\quad\forall i,
\qquad
\text{(S2)}\ \ \sum_{k=0}^\infty\alpha_k(i)^2<+\infty\quad\forall i.
\]

(S1) prevents it from shrinking too quickly → prevents the inescapable problem (Section 6.1.2).
(S2) eventually causes it to decrease sufficiently quickly → prevents the residual variance problem (Section 6.1.1).

A representative example is \(\alpha_k=1/(k+1)\).
↓ Down: Section 6.2.1 · Section 6.2.2 · Section 6.2.3 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

6.2.1 The sum of ✍ \(1/(k+1)\) diverges, and the sum of squares converges.
If you set it to \(n=k+1\), it is the same as looking at \(\sum_{n\ge1}1/n\) and \(\sum_{n\ge1}1/n^2\).
Guide Question:

If the terms of \(\sum 1/n\) are grouped into intervals \((2^{m-1},2^m]\), what is the sum of each group greater than or equal to?
Can \(1/n^2\) be pressed from above as a telescopic series term in \(n\ge2\)?
When \(\alpha_k=1/(k+1)^p\), what is the range of \(p\) that simultaneously satisfies (S1) and (S2)?







NoteSolution





1. The interval \((2^{m-1},2^m]\) contains \(2^{m-1}\) terms, and each term is \(\ge1/2^m\). Therefore, the sum of the group is \(\ge1/2\). \[
\sum_{n=1}^{2^M}\frac1n\ \ge\ 1+\frac M2\ \xrightarrow{M\to\infty}\ \infty.
\] When compared using integrals, it is \(\sum_{n=1}^N1/n\ge\int_1^{N+1}dx/x=\ln(N+1)\). It diverges, but at a rate of \(\ln N\), it diverges very slowly.
2. Since \(n^2>n(n-1)\), it is \(\dfrac1{n^2}<\dfrac1{n-1}-\dfrac1n\). When combined, the middle terms cancel out. \[
\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1{n^2}<1+\Big(1-\frac1N\Big)<2.
\] The partial sum of the positive term series converges because it is monotonically increasing and bounded. The limit value \(\pi^2/6\) (Basel problem) is not required for the SA condition, and only the fact that it is finite is required.
3. By integral comparison, it is \(\sum n^{-p}<\infty\iff p>1\).

To satisfy (S1), \(p\le1\).
To satisfy (S2), \(2p>1\).

Therefore, it is \(p\in(1/2,\,1]\). \(1/(k+1)\) is the right end of this interval, that is, the fastest decreasing case among the allowed ones.









TipSignificance





The key point of the grouping argument in problem 1 is that when the size of the term decreases by a factor of \(1/2\), the number of terms increases by exactly double. Therefore, each group contributes a fixed amount. When squared, the size of the term decreases by a factor of \(1/4\) and the number doubles, so the sum of the groups decreases in a geometric sequence. This is why \(p=1\) is the boundary.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2


6.2.2 If ✍ \(\alpha_k=1/(k+1)\), then SA is the sample mean.
Let’s consider the simplest case, \(f(x,\xi)=\xi\), that is, \(x=\mathbb{E}[\xi]\).
Guide Question:

If you solve \(x_{k+1}=\frac{k}{k+1}x_k+\frac1{k+1}\hat\xi_k\), what is \(x_k\)? Where does \(x_0\) go?
If \(\hat\xi_j\) is iid and the variance is \(\sigma^2\), what is \(\operatorname{Var}(x_k)\)? If we write this as \(\alpha\)?







NoteSolution





1. Multiplying both sides by \(k+1\) gives \((k+1)x_{k+1}=kx_k+\hat\xi_k\). Therefore, \(kx_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\hat\xi_j\), and (in \(k=0\), the coefficient of \(x_0\) becomes 0) \[
x_k=\frac1k\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\hat\xi_j\qquad(k\ge1).
\] Since \(\alpha_0=1\) is in the first update, the initial value is immediately erased. \(x_k\) is the sample mean.
2. \(\operatorname{Var}(x_k)=\sigma^2/k=\sigma^2\alpha_{k-1}\to0\). By the law of strong large numbers \(x_k\to\mathbb{E}\xi\) (probability 1).









TipSignificance





SA is a generalization of the method for iteratively (online) calculating the sample mean. \(1/(k+1)\) is the choice that gives equal weight to all samples. Decreasing more slowly (\(p<1\)) gives greater weight to recent samples. This results in slightly larger variance in exchange for quickly forgetting the initial values and initial estimation errors. In the general case where \(H\) depends on \(x\), \(Hx_k\) itself is inaccurate in the initial iterations, so \(p<1\) is often actually better.



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2


6.2.3 If you write the roles of the two conditions accurately
First question to consider. In the case of the scalar \(Hx\equiv c\), how is the error \(e_k=x_k-c\) divided into the initial value term and the noise term?
Answer. If you solve \(e_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)e_k+\alpha_kw_k\)
\[
e_k=\underbrace{e_0\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_j)}_{\text{초기값의 흔적}}
+\underbrace{\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\alpha_jw_j\prod_{l=j+1}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_l)}_{\text{누적 잡음}}.
\]

(S1) forgets initial value: \(\prod(1-\alpha_j)\to0\iff\sum\alpha_j=\infty\).
(S2) tames the cumulative noise to probability 1: the cumulative sum of the noise \(M_k=\sum_{j<k}\alpha_jw_j\) converges to probability 1.







NoteBasis





Let’s call it (S1) \(\alpha_j\in[0,1)\).

Since \(1-\alpha\le e^{-\alpha}\), it is \(\prod_{j<k}(1-\alpha_j)\le\exp\big(-\sum_{j<k}\alpha_j\big)\). Therefore, if it is \(\sum\alpha=\infty\), the product goes to 0.
Conversely, from \(\alpha\le1/2\), it becomes \(\ln(1-\alpha)\ge-\alpha-\alpha^2\). Therefore, if it is \(\sum\alpha<\infty\), the product has a positive lower bound.

If (S2) \(\mathbb{E}[w_j\mid\mathcal F_j]=0\) and \(\mathbb{E}[w_j^2\mid\mathcal F_j]\le\sigma^2\), then \(M_k\) is a martingale. Since the increments at different times are orthogonal, \[
\mathbb{E}[M_k^2]=\sum_{j<k}\alpha_j^2\,\mathbb{E}[w_j^2]\le\sigma^2\sum_j\alpha_j^2<\infty.
\] , that is, \(M_k\) is a \(L^2\)-bounded martingale, and by the martingale convergence theorem, it converges to a probability of 1. Therefore, it is tail \(\sum_{j\ge J}\alpha_jw_j\to0\). The amount of noise at late time points shaking the trajectory eventually becomes zero.
Mean squared error also becomes 0 through the same decomposition. The second moment of the noise term is \(\sigma^2\sum_j\alpha_j^2\prod_{l>j}(1-\alpha_l)^2\). Let’s split this sum in two at time point \(J\). The part after \(J\) can be reduced to \(\sigma^2\sum_{j\ge J}\alpha_j^2\) (S2). The part before \(J\) is multiplied by \(\prod_{l\ge J}(1-\alpha_l)^2\to0\) and cancels out (S1).









TipSignificance





Strictly speaking, if we only want mean square convergence, \(\alpha_k\to0\) and (S1) are sufficient. Where (S2) is essentially used is probability 1 convergence. The accumulated noise must converge to a single martingale for each locus to eventually follow a deterministic iteration. Therefore, the convergence theorem is described as “with probability 1” → Section 8.1



↑ Go Up: Section 6.2

title: Stochastic Approximation
section: 7.1 What conditions are required for noise?
text:
7.1 What conditions are required for noise?
Answer. For each \(i\) and \(k\), assume the following.
\[
\text{(N1)}\ \ \mathbb{E}[w_k(i)\mid\mathcal F_k]=0,
\qquad
\text{(N2)}\ \ \mathbb{E}[w_k(i)^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le C_0+C_1\|x_k\|^2.
\]

(N1) is the condition that the conditional mean is 0. Noise does not continuously push in a specific direction.
(N2) is the condition that the conditional variance is bounded. However, it is not a constant, but is allowed to increase proportionally to \(\|x_k\|^2\).







TipSignificance






The reason for using conditional instead of unconditional \(\mathbb{E}[w_k]=0\) is that the RL data is not iid. Samples on the trajectory depend on the past. However, it is sufficient if the new sample is unbiased given the past.
The reason (N2) allows \(\|x_k\|^2\) is that, as seen in Section 7.1.2, the sample noise of the Bellman operator is proportional to the magnitude of the current estimate.




↓ Down: Section 7.1.1 · Section 7.1.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

7.1.1 What goes into history \(\mathcal F_k\)
Answer.
\[
\mathcal F_k:=\{x_0,\dots,x_k,\ w_0,\dots,w_{k-1},\ \alpha_0,\dots,\alpha_k\}.
\]

\(x_k\) enters: The current estimate is already known.
Only up to \(w_{k-1}\): This noise \(w_k\) is unknown yet.
step size goes up to \(\alpha_k\): step size can be a random variable that depends on the trajectory, such as the number of visits, but is determined before seeing \(w_k\).







NoteNotation caution





Some literature uses \(\gamma_k\) for the step size, so \(\mathcal F_k\)Z and \(\gamma_0,\dots,\gamma_k\) appear. This is the step size, not the discount rate.









TipSignificance





Since \(\alpha_k\) enters \(\mathcal F_k\), it becomes \(\mathbb{E}[\alpha_kw_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\alpha_k\mathbb{E}[w_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\). Thanks to this property, the accumulated noise \(\sum\alpha_jw_j\) of Section 6.2.3 becomes a martingale. If the step size is determined based on this noise, this property is broken.



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1


7.1.2 ✍ Do the noises in Robbins–Monroe and Q-learning satisfy the conditions?
Guide Question:

In Robbins–Monro, if \(|f(x,\xi)|\le a+b\|x\|\) (\(a,b\) constant), can \(C_0,C_1\) of (N2) be captured?
Check (N1) and (N2) for Q-learning \(f(Q,s')=r(s,a)+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\). Let the reward be \(|r|\le R_{\max}\) and be bounded.







NoteSolution





1. (N1) was shown in Section 5.1.1. Since variance can be compressed by the second moment, \[
\mathbb{E}[w_k^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\operatorname{Var}\big(f(x_k,\xi)\big)\le\mathbb{E}\big[f(x_k,\xi)^2\big]\le(a+b\|x_k\|)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\|x_k\|^2.
\] Therefore, you can set it to \(C_0=2a^2\) and \(C_1=2b^2\).
2.

(N1): \(s'\) originates from \(p(\cdot\mid s_k,a_k)\) when the entire past is given (Markov property). Therefore, even if the trajectory is not iid, it is \(\mathbb{E}[w_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\).
(N2): \(|f(Q,s')|\le R_{\max}+\gamma\|Q\|_\infty\le R_{\max}+\gamma\|Q\|_2\). If you input \(a=R_{\max}\) and \(b=\gamma\) into the result of 1, it is \(C_0=2R_{\max}^2\) and \(C_1=2\gamma^2\).










TipSignificance





The noise in Q-learning comes from ZZZPH0015186ZZZ \(\max_{a'}Q(s',a')\), and its magnitude is proportional to the magnitude of the current \(Q\). This case cannot be handled with a constant variance bound. Therefore, (N2) is of the form \(C_0+C_1\|x_k\|^2\).



↑ Go Up: Section 7.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
text:
8.1 Convergence under contraction
Answer.






ImportantSummary 1 (Abbreviation)



If the step size conditions (S1)–(S2) and noise conditions (N1)–(N2) hold, and \(H\) is a reduction mapping for the (weighted) maximum norm, then \(x_k\) converges to the fixed point \(x^*\) of \(H\) with probability 1.


The proof is in Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis, Neuro-Dynamic Programming (1996), Section 4.3.6. Only the result is written here.






TipSignificance






Bellman Operator. The Bellman operators for \(T\), \(T^\pi\), and \(Q\) are all \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) to \(\gamma\)-reductions. Therefore, the convergence of tabular TD(0) and Q-learning is derived directly from this theorem. → Section 8.2.2
The assumptions are a direct transfer of the intuition of Section 6.1.1–Section 6.2.3. The noise must have a conditional mean of 0 and a variance that is appropriately bounded, and the step size must tame the noise by endlessly stacking the average direction.
However, in actual applications, especially when using functional approximations, this assumption often does not hold. It is sufficient to understand it as a criterion for distinguishing between regions with and without theoretical guarantees.




↑ Go Up: Section 3.1

title: Stochastic Approximation
text:
8.2 Convergence under monotony
Answer. Even if \(H\) is not a contraction, convergence can be shown under the following conditions.






ImportantTheorem 2 (Monotonicity)



Let’s assume that \(H\) satisfies the following.

Monotonic: \(x\le x'\Rightarrow Hx\le Hx'\) (Element-wise inequality).
Unique Fixed Point: \(Hx^*=x^*\) and \(x^*\) exist uniquely.
Inequality for constant shift: For any \(\eta>0\) \[
Hx-\eta\mathbf 1\ \le\ H(x-\eta\mathbf 1)\ \le\ H(x+\eta\mathbf 1)\ \le\ Hx+\eta\mathbf 1.
\]

If (S1)–(S2), (N1)–(N2) holds and the sequence \(x_k\) generated by SA is bounded with probability 1, then \(x_k\) converges to \(x^*\) with probability 1.








TipSignificance





requires monotonality and boundedness instead of abbreviation. The cost is that the boundedness of \(x_k\) must be demonstrated separately. While boundedness follows with abbreviation, it is assumed here.



↓ Down: Section 8.2.1 · Section 8.2.2 ↑ Up: Section 3.1

8.2.1 ✍ What does assumption (3) mean?
Guide Question:

Where does the middle inequality \(H(x-\eta\mathbf 1)\le H(x+\eta\mathbf 1)\) of assumption (3) come from? Actually, the new content is the two outer inequalities, but how would you put it?
Show that combining assumptions (1) and (3) gives \(\|Hx-Hy\|_\infty\le\|x-y\|_\infty\)







NoteSolution





1. The middle inequality is derived directly from monotonicity (1). The two outer inequalities are as follows. \[
H(x+\eta\mathbf 1)\le Hx+\eta\mathbf 1,\qquad H(x-\eta\mathbf 1)\ge Hx-\eta\mathbf 1.
\] If all components of the input are raised (or lowered) by a constant \(\eta\), the output increases (or decreases) by at most \(\eta\) for each component. In other words, there is no amplification in the \(\mathbf 1\) direction.
2. If set to \(\eta:=\|x-y\|_\infty\), it becomes \(y-\eta\mathbf 1\le x\le y+\eta\mathbf 1\). By monotonicity and (3) \[
Hy-\eta\mathbf 1\le H(y-\eta\mathbf 1)\le Hx\le H(y+\eta\mathbf 1)\le Hy+\eta\mathbf 1.
\] Therefore, it is \(\|Hx-Hy\|_\infty\le\eta=\|x-y\|_\infty\).









TipSignificance





When combining monotonality and (3), \(H\) is a non-expansive mapping from \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\). It is non-expansive but may not be contracted. This implies that the contraction coefficient is allowed up to 1. In this case, the uniqueness of the fixed point (Assumption 2) and the boundedness of the trajectory do not arise automatically, so they are assumed separately.



↑ Go Up: Section 8.2


8.2.2 ✍ Does the Bellman operator satisfy the assumptions of the two theorems?
Guide Question:

Is \(T\) a forma? What if you write \(T(v+\eta\mathbf 1)\) as \(Tv\)?
Which theorem can be applied when \(\gamma<1\) and when \(\gamma=1\), respectively?







NoteSolution





1.

Modification: If \(v\le v'\), then for each \(a\)Z, it is \(r+\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,v\le r+\gamma\sum_{s'}p\,v'\). Since \(\max\) is forged, it is \(Tv\le Tv'\).
Constant Shift: Since \(\sum_{s'}p(s'\mid s,a)=1\), it is \(T(v+\eta\mathbf 1)=Tv+\gamma\eta\mathbf 1\). Therefore \[
Tv-\eta\mathbf 1\le Tv-\gamma\eta\mathbf 1=T(v-\eta\mathbf 1)\le T(v+\eta\mathbf 1)=Tv+\gamma\eta\mathbf 1\le Tv+\eta\mathbf 1.
\] If \(\gamma\le1\), then assumption (3) holds. The Bellman operator for \(T^\pi\) and \(Q\) is verified in the same way.

2.

If \(\gamma<1\), then \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) is a contraction of \(\gamma\), so write Theorem 1.
If \(\gamma=1\) (e.g., a stochastic shortest path problem with a termination state), \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\)-reduction is not guaranteed. In this case, monotonicity and (3) still hold. Therefore, if we separately show that the fixed point is unique and the iteration is bounded, we can write Theorem 2.










TipSignificance





The two theorems rely on different properties of the Bellman operator. Theorem 1 relies on discounting (contraction), and Theorem 2 relies on preservation of the order of expectation and \(\max\) (monotonicity). Theorem 2 is used to extend the convergence of Q-learning to problems without discounting.



↑ Go Up: Section 8.2
